Title: Opening address at the official opening of the new academic year at the University of National and World Economy, Sofia, September 17, 2012.
text: Opening address by Mr. Ivan Iskrov, Governor of the Bulgarian National Bank at the official opening of the new academic year at the University of National and World Economy, Sofia, 17 September 2012 Dear Mr. Rector, Ladies and gentlemen professors, Dear students, Dear colleagues, It is a great honour and a pleasure for me to participate in the opening of the new academic year at the University of National and World Economy (UNWE). I would like to thank the Rector, Prof. Statev, for the invitation and the opportunity to congratulate the academic staff and fresher students of one of the oldest higher economic schools not only in Bulgaria but in this part of Europe as well. With its over 90 years of history UNWE has been for a long time the leading higher education institution in Bulgaria and a benchmark of high quality education in economics, management and administration, law and politics. Those of us, who are, in one way or another, related to UNWE, have all the grounds to be proud both of the past and the present of our University. I, as an UNWE graduate of 20 years or so ago, find a striking change in the ambience and the full modernization of the university campus and facilities. I and the people of my generation can only nobly envy present day UNWE students for the fantastic conditions for study and vast access to information, which regretfully we did not have at our time. For all these things we should deservedly praise the whole team that has managed the university in the recent years. Nevertheless, this is only the outer and most visible side of all the positive processes underway in UNWE. The most valuable asset of the university are the people in it, its students and professors. It is no chance phenomenon that the university preserved its high academic reputation even after the changes in Bulgaria in the late 1980-ies. As prescribed by the tradition of its more than 90-year-long history, UNWE has generated and continues to produce many of the management personnel in the economy, and many of the people on the most responsible government positions, including tens of ministers and politicians have graduated UNWE. There is no Bulgarian government, I know of, in the recent 20 years that could not boast of at least a few key ministers  UNWE graduates. Therefore, my first message to todays young people is to be proud of the UNWE history and to find inspiration and motivation in the achievements of the Universitys past graduates. Having in mind the example of the people before you, remember that your fate is in your own hands and that anything can be attained if a person sets to himself clear goals and then invests consistent efforts to achieve them. Each success begins with dreams, and development stops when a man gives up hoping and fighting. Dreams and plans, however, are always personal and each of you should find the best path for himself and travel it, and what is important travel it with his own efforts. Therefore, you should think out of the box, put everything to the test of doubt (even what you are taught by your professors!), but first and foremost  you should be critical to yourselves and always seek first your own fault in case of eventual failure. Difficulties, criticism and hurdles both in the learning process and in your professional career should not discourage you, because they are just natural challenges on your way. Great successes are attained by solving great problems, and not by bypassing difficulties. The strategy of seeking easy solutions is very likely to eventually prove a losing one. I can confirm this from my own experience as the father of a young man of your generation, the Internet generation, which from a very early age gets used to working in a copy-paste style, often without making much own effort or a deeper and more critical analysis. Google is a good thing indeed, but do not rely on it alone. Read in depth and try to analyse! Relying on your own minds and your own work is a prerequisite not only for the individual but also for the collective success of all of us. This was the thinking of the initiator, the founder and first Rector of this University, Prof. Stefan Bobchev, whose monument stands in front of the university building. Analysing the status of the Bulgarian economy in the early 20th century and realising the need for its speedy development, Prof. Bobchev wrote: We are our salvation, it comes from the united efforts of the people... and no one can help us if we ourselves do not get to work together and help one another. Arent these words valid for todays Bulgaria as well? Many people in our country still believe that somebody else will do our job for us, that we should always pay heed to and take in good faith the advice of various experts or institutions from abroad. But is it really true that foreign authorities in all cases have more knowledge, more successful experience or better intentions when it comes to the fate of Bulgaria and the Bulgarian people, and the Bulgarian economy in particular? Do our national interests always coincide with the interests of other countries, even if these countries are, for instance, among the biggest countries in the European Union or the world? On the contrary, we should always look for the Bulgarian perspective and try to draw lessons from our own experience and stand up for the national interests. We must be constructive but not naive in our relations with the rest of the world. This is a good opportunity for me to specifically address again the young people here. Please remember and keep the Bulgarian traditions, build your confidence on the achievements of Bulgaria and keep your patriotism, on whichever area your efforts will be focused in future or in whichever part of the world you will be. These are no abstract topics or declarations. I would say that actually this is the approach that the institution headed by me is trying to follow. The BNB is an active participant in many bodies, working groups, and various initiatives within the EU, the ESCB, the ESRB and the European supervisory authorities. Though this side of the activities of our central bank usually is not in the limelight, it involves much of our efforts and is essential for maintaining the financial stability and ensuring the right conditions for Bulgarias economic development. I can give tens of examples, covering a long period of our history, of ideas and proposals which came from outside of Bulgaria and did not consider the economic and financial interests of Bulgaria. Such examples are also connected with many of todays hot topics relating to the global financial crisis and the attempts to resolve this crisis in the euro area. For instance, some of the planned reforms at euro area or EU level are not constructive or appropriate for us. A textbook example in this respect are the attempts of some big member-states to enforce coordination of the tax policies in the EU. This may directly damage the competitiveness of the Bulgarian economy and our freedom to pursue an adequate economic policy. We have always defended the position that Bulgaria must uphold its sovereign tax policy. The latter also includes the low tax rates which are an important economic advantage of Bulgaria and a factor for the attractiveness of our country as an investment destination and a place for doing business. Another example is related to the recently launched idea of the so-called banking union in the EU. The BNB supports in principle the idea of increased integration and governance within the euro area, including a fiscal union, banking union, political union, as due to the significant imbalances accumulated in the euro area this may be the only way for its stabilization. However, we are against Bulgarias accession to the euro areas banking union at this stage. Where limitations of the national competences and transferring of rights are contemplated, responsibilities should also be discussed. But it is clear from the proposals made by the European Commission a few days ago that any accession by Bulgaria to the thus contemplated banking union will mainly boil down to an unilateral transfer of considerable national sovereignty to Frankfurt and Brussels, against which the country will receive nothing back. Besides, unified supervision goes hand in hand with establishing a common deposit guarantee scheme and a common bank restructuring framework. An element that is presently missing in the proposal, and we still do not know what that will look like. The only reason I give these two examples is not to provide some exhaustive analysis on the subject, but to bring your attention, the attention of young Bulgarian university students, to something of great importance: always look through the prism of the interests of our nation. I will share with you that unfortunately we often face the disappointment to work with our compatriots abroad who have forgotten their Bulgarian origins. Some of them wouldnt even think twice to do harm to Bulgaria if that would benefit their own selfish interest or if in that way they would earn the approval of their superiors. No one, however, could succeed as a result of cutting their Bulgarian roots. Never forget that you are Bulgarians and always protect the interests of our motherland! Because, no doubt, numerous possibilities are open to you. I did not know back then when I was a student at UNWE that I would one day become Governor of the Central Bank of Bulgaria. You too should not be surprised today that you are the future economists, financiers, industrialists  the leaders of tomorrows Bulgaria. And enjoying the full rights of citizens of the EU, many of you will achieve successful realization abroad as well, including at senior positions at European or other international institutions. Wherever you may find yourselves to be and at all times, do not forget that your motherland is Bulgaria. Here is where your roots are! This in no way runs counter to the common European values. And finally, I wish all UNWE students today, and especially the freshmen, to learn a lot and useful things during the new academic year, and dont forget to pass your exams too. May this year be both successful and enjoyable, and a year to remember all your life! Good luck! PAGE 1

Title: Speech delivered before the Association of Banks in Bulgaria on the occasion of the Bankers Day, Sofia, December 6, 2012.
text: Speech of Mr. Ivan Iskrov, Governor of the Bulgarian National Bank, delivered before the Association of Banks in Bulgaria on the occasion of the Bankers Day, Sofia, 6 December 2012 Dear Mr. Hampartzoumian, Dear members of the ABB Executive Board, Ladies and Gentlemen, Today, in keeping with the tradition, we are here to celebrate together on 6th December the Bankers Day - Saint Nicholas Day. This year is quite special, as exactly 20 years ago the professional bankers association was restored, as well as the tradition to celebrate this day as our professional holiday. We are here together, my colleagues of the BNB Governing Council and I, to express the esteem of our institution to the efforts put forth by each of you in the past year. Together with the usual congratulations and wishes on such a holiday, let our todays meeting be an occasion for a professional discussion of certain topical issues and of the challenges facing us. We will remember 2012 as a demanding year, during which a number of external factors and the difficulties relating to the economic juncture at home influenced the decisions in the individual credit institutions. The challenging economic environment bore upon the asset quality and the profitability of the banking system. Bulgaria did manage during this year as well to preserve a positive real growth in the economy, but the growth rate does not allow for abrupt improvement of the existing borrowers economic profile and does not stimulate greater demand for new bank loans. In 2013 we expect the process of recovery of the EU economies, including Bulgaria, to continue at a slow pace. International financial markets will remain vulnerable. This will continue to create uncertainty and anxiety as regards the banks abilities to generate the interest income that is of paramount importance for them. In spite of the difficulties today our banks have deserved congratulations and praise for their achievements in 2012. Through you, the representatives of Bulgarian credit institutions managements, I would like to thank all colleagues across the whole banking community all those more than 33 thousand people working in the banking sector. In the fourth year of the economic crisis the banking system in Bulgaria preserved its significant buffers protecting it from capital and liquidity pressures. The capital adequacy of the sector remains very high according to European and international standards, and as of September the overall capital adequacy ratio was 16.59%, while the adequacy of Tier 1 capital was 15.12%. The ratio of liquid assets to total liabilities was 26.38% as of end-October. The share of non-performing loans more than 90 days past due is growing but at a slower rate. At the end of September the gross share of non-performing more than 90 days loans was 17.25%, while their net share was 11.6%. For the purposes of asset quality risk assessment, this net share is indicative, as it nets out the already made impairments, i.e. it takes into consideration the risk that has been already provisioned, as reported in the income statements. Non-performing loans have an adequate degree of coverage by provisions and existing buffers in the system (including the loan impairments under the International Financial Reporting Standards, specific provisions for credit risk and the capital adequacy surplus). Only the savings of households have increased on an annual basis until October by 12.7%. In parallel, the sound structural trend of replacing foreign attracted funds with domestic ones continued throughout the year. All in all, we expect the banking system to end 2012 with a positive financial result of at least BGN 600 million. As the case is, quite logically in 2012, as in prior years, Bulgaria remained one of the few EU Member States where no credit institution needed to be rescued with state budget or central bank funds. This confirmed a conclusion made in the recent years: opposite to other places in Europe and worldwide, where sometimes banks were among the factors for the financial crisis or turned into a source of systemic risks, the banks in Bulgaria were and remain an important pillar of overall financial stability in the country. We are glad to note the understanding existing in our business community and in the society of the banking sectors contribution to maintaining Bulgarias macroeconomic stability. The responsible behavior of the media in the country has played an important role to this effect, as they have demonstrated a notable professional maturity and a high level of respect to the public interest. In times of frenzy and panic in Western Europe our media reacted fittingly with dignity. I would like to note that the BNB is carefully monitoring the public information and media space. We are a conservative institution, we rarely come into the spotlight of the media, but we follow very carefully the debates in them and the suggestions they are trying to make. I am saying this to let people know that the central bank has sensitive perception of public attitudes, particularly in the areas relating to banks; therefore we cant help congratulating the media in Bulgaria for their professionalism. This holiday, dear colleagues, is also the traditional time to strike a balance of some important events and processes during the year. One of the things 2012 will be remembered for are the active discussions among institutions on various banking system-related issues. These discussions continued along different channels and featured a different degree of constructive dialogue. The start of the year surprised us with the unexpected idea of the need to regulate the size and setting of interest rates on loans. The representatives of the banking community put quite a lot of energy in explaining the threats that could have been caused by a hasty administrative intervention in the free contracting between banks and their clients. Thanks to the timely initiative of the Head of the Prime Ministers Office and the personal participation of the Prime Minister himself, there have been a series of productive discussions, together with the Association of Banks in Bulgaria (ABB). These talks reached an understanding of the risks arising from a possible arbitrary implementation of mechanical restrictions in the lending process. The Prime Ministers idea and his insistence, during the meetings, on more intensive communications so as to assure maximum transparency in the dealings with clients and the protection of their rights very much helped for the good dialogue later in the year between the state regulator, i.e. the Consumer Protection Commission (CPC), and the banks. Having reviewed the general conditions of consumer and mortgage loans to physical persons, the banks confirmed their preparedness to assist the CPC in removing any possible omissions or faults where such have been established. This served as a good example of constructive behaviour and positive dialogue between institutions. At the same time, considering the great importance of public communications for financial stability, I take this opportunity to draw your attention to one specific threat that the coming year 2013 might bring. Only in a months time we will begin another year  an election year and we at the central bank cannot ignore the risk of possible attempts of politicising banking sector-related topics. It is very likely that some local candidates for political glory, just in order to get in the medias pre-election spotlight, may be tempted to try to sell fear by attacking individual banks or the system as a whole. We already see how the various insufficiently recognised experts, greedy for public attention, are trying to get into the public space; these are people who traditionally want to be noticed a few months before and after the elections. From our long experience we know very well that such behaviour has never brought any political benefits to anyone. Nevertheless there will always be those seeking popularity at the expense of banks, so we all have to be watchful! Sadly, among the problems that could not be resolved even this year are the so called backdated insolvencies. Years back the BNB and the ABB did warn the institutions which had the power to remove the possibility of manipulating the initial date of insolvency and nullifying the items of collateral pledged after that date. The relevant legislative proposals are already drafted and we are hoping that these are going to be adopted during the mandate of this parliament. The BNB and the ABB remained correct partners of the state institutions after the request of the Ombudsman of the Republic of Bulgaria to challenge before the Constitutional Court the procedural rights of credit institutions in establishing their receivables. With respect for the autonomy and competence of the Constitutional Court, the representatives of the banking sector have not been tempted to use the public space and media in order to defend their position or try to influence the ruling of the Court. Regrettably this, however, was not the Ombudsmans behaviour. Eventually, with a unanimous ruling of all its members, the Constitutional Court rejected the Ombudsmans request. In this way the Court averted a threat of possibly prolonging the procedures and increasing the costs to banks and their clients while managing the so called bad loans  only a bunch of lawyers would have profited from this but it could have tremendously hindered and discouraged banks in granting new loans to the Bulgarian economy. This year has been very calm in terms of consolidations and change of ownership in the banks in Bulgaria. The BNB carried out strict supervision of credit institutions. Here I would like to thank for the understanding and assistance shown by the managements of those banks which this year had to fulfill recommendations or instructions of the central bank. I would like to specially mention and single out the correct relations with the banks with Greek ownership in Bulgaria and with their parent banks in Greece when they had to fulfil certain recommendations of a preventive nature made by the BNB so as to protect our banking system from potential external risks. Also, despite the intense competition between credit institutions in this country, we are impressed by their collegial behaviour to one another. The dynamic changes in the market shares of individual banks over the year resulted only from using their own competitive advantages and not from exploiting, for example through non-market methods, the temporary difficulties of a competitor. Speaking about the competitive pressures which make banks continue to strive for higher efficiency, I remind you about the possibilities which the Cash Services Company (CSC) offers to you. Now there are 27 credit institutions that have agreements with the CSC, but even these do not fully take advantage of the potential to reach lower costs of processing and servicing cash operations over the entire currency cycle. For instance, the history of BORICA Bankservice illustrates the banking industrys positive experience of building common solutions which save costs and make the system more efficient in the spheres where economies of scale are possible. An issue that still needs to be addressed in the banking sector concerns the future bank ownership transformations in the country. As you are aware, a consolidation of two of the largest banks here could be expected to take place next year. From the BNB standpoint, such processes are only natural; however they need to be evaluated through the prism of how much these would contribute to the stability of the sector and to Bulgarias economy in general. Therefore, in our view, the banking sector in Bulgaria should comprise only well-capitalized and liquid credit institutions with clear long-term business strategies for their operations in the country, and with management bodies well experienced and of immaculate reputation. This is the vision which for many years has been governing our supervisory policy and practice with regard to licenses, authorisations and shareholders structure of the banks in Bulgaria. As for us, dear Colleagues, I can assure you that we, at the BNB, will go on performing our tasks in compliance with our statutory functions. Our intention is to continue as a predictable and open to dialogue institution. This will continue to be our guiding goal not only domestically, but internationally as well, where the BNB will keep on consistently asserting the national economic interests. In regard to this, I would like to finally touch on an issue of immediate relevance to the banks in Bulgaria  the so-called banking union in the euro area, in particular the idea of a single supervisory mechanism advanced in 2012. We fully support further integration and improvement of governance in the euro area. Our view is that a banking union is among the prerequisites underpinning the reform of the institutional architecture of the euro area, necessary to attain a full-fledged economic and monetary union there and adjust for the accumulated imbalances. At the same time, the BNB has a number of objections with regard to the shortcomings in the Commissions proposals. Our reserves coincide with the concerns that have already been voiced by representatives of the executive and the National Assembly in Bulgaria, as well as by the majority of EU Member States, including the non-euro area Member States, as well as Germany for instance. A well-known fact is that our country would assume significant risks if it joined the single supervisory mechanism in the euro area at this stage. If we take such a step, the banks in the country, unlike the banks within the euro area, would still have access neither to a liquidity support from the ECB nor to capital support from the European Stabilisation Mechanism in case of need. The non-euro area Member States, Bulgaria included would not be able to participate in the final decision-making in exercising the single supervision. According to the proposed legislative texts, there would be a factual division and two supervisory categories among the Member States, with the countries outside the euro area not enjoying the equal treatment. Joining the single supervisory mechanism at the current stage would imply that Bulgaria would entrust the protection of our financial stability to an institution dominated by representatives of countries, which experienced supervisory failures during the crisis, and an institution that itself has not had any supervisory experience so far. The ECB is among the most reputable international institutions and stands out with its indisputable professional authority and successful experience in conducting monetary policy, including in the course of the crisis. The ECB, however, is yet to accumulate supervisory expertise. A country of proven efficient and strict banking supervision, such as Bulgaria, conceding the responsibility of supervision over its banking system to an authority, which is yet in the formation, would be as good as if the government entrusted its only nuclear submarine to be steered by a professor of nuclear physics who never served in the navy! Please, allow me to finish with this my statement and to convey, on behalf of the BNB Governing Council and personally on my behalf, our most-sincere wishes for professional and personal well-being in the new 2013 year! May you brim over with health and positive energy! Happy Bankers Day, dear Colleagues! PAGE 1

Title: Speech at the roundtable discussion organized by the Bank of the Year Association, Sofia, July 2, 2013.
text: Speech by Mr. Ivan Iskrov, Governor of the Bulgarian National Bank at the roundtable discussion organised by the Bank of the Year Association, Sofia, 2 July 2013 Ladies and gentlemen, Dear colleagues and friends, It is a great pleasure for me to take part in this roundtable discussion organised for a third year in a row by the Bank of the Year Association in relation to presenting the annual banking awards and the big award Bank of the Year 2012. I would like to thank the Chairman of the Associations Board of Directors, Mr. Panayotov, for the invitation. The announced subject of the discussions  Bank efficiency in an economy facing continuing crisis: Sources of banking profit in the conditions of a deteriorating business environment  is particularly topical these days, and is of key importance both for our banking sector colleagues, and for the BNB. As part of this discussion, I will dwell on the issues of efficiency from a banking supervision point of view, and will reflect on the income-earning opportunities for the banks in Bulgaria and on some future risks. Banks are enterprises assigned a specific economic function and having an important public role related to the public interest. At the same time, banks are capitalist enterprises that operate with the aim to make profit. If shareholders do not make any profit, they would not, first of all, have the incentive to invest in such an industry as banking. Discussing the subject of consumer protection, that is so topical these days, we should not forget this  banks should indeed be fair in their relations with customers, but they should not be considered as some kind of public organizations providing free public services. At the same time, banks profitability and efficiency are of primary importance both for their shareholders and for their depositors. More efficient banks earn higher profit, and the profit is an additional source of capitalization for a bank, thus strengthening the buffers supporting its stability. This aspect should also be taken into consideration when discussing banks income from interest and fee charges. Specifics of the business model of the banks in Bulgaria It is a known fact that banks in Bulgaria do the traditional type of commercial banking  extending loans on the basis of deposits collected from the public. The so called investment banking is not a typical business for the banks in this country. This is seen from the structure of their assets. As of end-May, loans and receivables amounted to 75% of the banking system assets. This ratio was similar at the end of 2008 (80%). Financial instruments hold an 11% share in the banking system assets at the end of May, compared to 8% as of end-2008. That is, from the assets structure perspective, the crisis has practically not affected the business model of the banks in Bulgaria  they engage primarily in lending (Chart 1). The liabilities structure is relatively simple, as is typical for commercial banks engaging in traditional forms of financial intermediation. At the end of this May, 82% of the banking system liabilities (excluding capital) consisted of funds attracted from households and companies. The remaining liabilities comprised funds attracted from banks (14%), subordinated liabilities (3%) and other liabilities (Chart 2). The business model of the domestic banks determines the structure of the sources of income, hence the possibilities for optimization and generation of profit. For the period from the beginning of the year to the end of May, net interest income had a 68% share in the net income of the banking system, while the respective share of net income from charges and fees was 22%. Not much different was also the structure of income in 2008: 75% share of the net interest income and 21% share of the net income from charges and fees. Banks in Bulgaria generate income predominantly from their core activity (lending). The crisis has not changed this. Its only logical that in the future lending will continue to be the main source of income for the banks in Bulgaria. Costs and profitability during the crisis The crisis has visibly and directly impacted banks costs: in terms of both size and structure. While in 2008 non-interest costs (overhead costs  administrative and for amortisation, plus the costs for provisioning and impairment) amounted to BGN 2.2 billion in total for the banking system, in 2012 this sum has grown to BGN 3.2 billion. Furthermore, the share of provisioning and impairment costs within the non-interest costs has increased from 15% in 2008 to 38% in 2012. The growth of the provisioning and impairment costs is due to the deteriorated quality of loan portfolios during the crisis. At the same time, however, the banks costs for their liabilities have not decreased: the banking system paid as interest expenses BGN 2.1 billion in 2008 and almost the same amount, BGN 2.2 billion, in 2012. In parallel, the subdued demand for loans during the crisis limited the banks opportunities to earn interest income. All these factors brought about a decline in key profitability indicators of the banking system during the crisis (Chart 3): 2008 (%) 2012 (%) Decline (p. p.) ROA 2.12 0.71 1.41 ROE 20.26 5.71 14.55 Net Interest Margin 4.91 3.61 1.30 The conclusion is that banks and their shareholders were forced to pay their price for the crisis. It seems this fact is not in the focus of public attention, but it should be underscored that both banks and their customers shouldered part of the crisis burden. The banking sector in Bulgaria is among the most efficient in Europe Regardless of the severe drop in the banking sector profitability, the return on assets and the return on equity of the Bulgarian banking sector rank second highest in the EU (Charts 4 and 5). The efficiency in Bulgaria is also demonstrated by the fact that we have the second lowest cost/income ratio (of overhead - administrative and amortization - costs to income, Chart 6). In Bulgaria the share of net interest income in the total revenue is among the highest in the EU (Chart 7). This illustrates both the efficiency of banks core activities, and the sustainability of their traditional business model. The efficiency of the banking sector in Bulgaria is combined with prudent management of credit risk. An international comparison would clearly show that our banking sector has one of the highest rates of provisioning of non-performing loans across the EU (with all the reservations about such comparisons due to differences in the definitions and supervisory practices, Chart 8). The excellent international performance of our banking sector in terms of efficiency is owing to both the prudent management of the banks themselves, and the conservative and counter-cyclical banking supervision. On the one hand, banks in Bulgaria rely primarily on the humdrum traditional banking business related to lending to the real sector, rather than aiming at one-off effects from high-risk financial investments. On the other hand, the supervisory policies pursued by the BNB provided incentives for our banks to accumulate reserves before the crisis and also to maintain them throughout the whole crisis. Thus, the banks could meet their provisioning and impairment costs during the crisis without any pressure on their shareholders equity and without any threat to their financial stability, which would have made their funding more difficult or would have increased the costs of attracted resources. Opportunities for generating income and some risks With a view to the traditional business model of the banks in Bulgaria, their income generating opportunities will continue to be related mostly with lending. However, the prospects for income from core activities (lending) will remain constrained until we see signs of a sustained economic recovery. The demand for loans is conditioned by the propensity of companies and households for investment and consumption. This propensity, in turn, depends both on the available resources and disposable income, and on the expected economic prospects and the willingness to take risks. Credit growth will remain of key importance to banks not just as a source of new income, but also to allow them to keep the existing capital buffers. It is a well-known fact that the banking sector in Bulgaria has weathered the crisis with impressively high capital adequacy ratios (at the end of the first quarter of 2013 the Tier 1 capital adequacy ratio reached 15.37%, and the overall capital adequacy ratio  16.78%). But because of the general adverse economic situation, the banks in Bulgaria are still faced with the double challenge  on the one hand, the available reserves are under pressure due to the impaired exposures on the banks balance sheets; on the other hand, the weak demand for new loans is hindering the generation of profit that would be the source of additional capital buffers. The business strategies of the banks in Bulgaria should remain focused on lending. The banks should actively look for new lending opportunities (perhaps, even using a certain share from the available capital buffers) by entering new credit segments more innovatively or reaching customers who have until now remained outside the business of the respective bank. Of course, the banks behaviour should be governed (like it has been so far) by the principle of prudent risk management. Many banks will continue to rely on corporate lending. Traditionally, corporate customers hold the bigger part of the banks loans. For example, at banking system level, the banks exposures to corporates are more than twice as many as retail exposures (BGN 38 billion against BGN 18 billion at end-May 2013). Also, the companies are an attractive segment for the banks because normally they are the first to respond to the positive signals for economic recovery and they are themselves the driver of economic growth. And yet, retail lending has its own potential too. Here the banks should take great care as to the individual customers sensitivity. On the one hand, in their role as borrowers, the individuals are more informed and have better consumer awareness, expecting (justifiably) ever better-quality bank services. On the other hand, in their role as depositors and payment services recipients, the individual customers are under a price pressure. While interest rates on deposits are falling, occasionally the various charges to customers are rising, and also the controversial tax on term deposits was introduced at the start of this year. The banks in Bulgaria, which largely rely on the savings of their individual customers, should be well aware that these same customers are now receiving very low real income on their deposits: considering altogether the inflation rate, charges (including on payment operations) and the new tax. Implications of the international environment We cannot quite exclude the possibility of certain external (for Bulgaria) factors bringing new risks, even with regard to the abilities of the banks in Bulgaria to generate income. For example, the large central banks in the world are signalling the ending of monetary policy aimed at the so called quantitative easing and accommodation. The banks in this country should be prepared for these changes because they would trigger a new interest rate cycle: raising interest rates on the international money and capital markets. The higher interest rates abroad would pass through to the interest rates domestically, to an extent that depends on the sovereign and risk premiums here. The new interest rate cycle, which maybe the sovereign debt markets are already indicating (Chart 9), would affect the abilities of the banks in Bulgaria to generate income though a few channels. On the one hand, the costs of liabilities may start rising. This would probably be a slow process because of the available banks high liquidity and the populations propensity to save. But the higher costs of liabilities would imply new risks for banks. If the more expensive attracted resources would have to be covered by higher interest rates on loans, this would additionally impede lending. Besides, with the rising cost of the attracted resources, the banks must keep a very close eye on the interest rate risk, and particularly on the risk they have taken when offering fixed-rate loans. On the other hand, with a future increase in the euro-area interest rates, the banks investments in low-risk government securities (including issues of the euro-area core countries) would cause repricing losses. The external environment will be influencing the operations of the banking sector in Bulgaria through the governance reforms and the changes in the economic policies at the EU level. As regards the widely debated banking union topic, here I would like to mention the new bank recovery and resolution framework that is being discussed nowadays. Bulgaria has a clear and constructive position on the banking union, including a unanimous statement of the 41st National Assembly of the Republic of Bulgaria. Bulgaria has always demonstrated its support for the banking union in the euro area, as long as its creation does not bring any negative effects for the non-euro area countries, including Bulgaria. From this perspective, the Bulgarian National Bank is content with the compromising decisions on the bank resolution framework that were made at the ECOFIN meeting in Brussels last week. Practically, that meeting adopted the position which several non-euro area countries (Bulgaria among them) had advocated, i.e. that the national bank resolution authorities should have enough flexibility in using various internal sources of bank recapitalisation. In this way they could use shareholders funds and funds accumulated in advance from banks own contributions to a national bank resolution fund and to the bank deposit insurance fund, instead of hair-cutting the deposits of large taxpayers (of course, the amount of insured deposits of up to EUR 100 000 remains). And the new Directive on bank resolution will take effect in 2018, not in 2015 as initially planned. Banks should work in a calm and predictable environment which enables them to carry out their core business. Please let me finish my statement by wishing all of us to have such a favourable environment: both domestically and internationally!

Title: Speech delivered before the Association of Banks in Bulgaria on the occasion of the Bankers Day, Sofia, December 5, 2013.
text: Speech of Mr. Ivan Iskrov, Governor of the Bulgarian National Bank, delivered before the Association of Banks in Bulgaria on the occasion of the Bankers Day, Sofia, 5 December 2013 Ladies and Gentlemen, This year, we keep the tradition to celebrate together our professional holiday. On the eve of Saint Nicholas Day  Bankers Day  we are here with my colleagues from the BNB Governing Council, to emphasize our esteem for the representatives of banks managements and our appreciation of the efforts put forth by the banking community as a whole to operate in an environment not particularly facilitating business. As is our tradition at such meetings, the festive evening provides an opportunity to remember things that have happened this year and to discuss the big topics and the new challenges the next 2014 year is expected to bring. The context of the overall economic and market situation determines the tally of results for the ending 2013. As I have often commented, in a market economy the banking system guarantees the overall financial stability, being a key factor of economic growth. At the same time, however, commercial banks are most of all intermediaries for the other sectors, hence, their activities and results depend on the condition and dynamics of processes in the real economy. Regretfully, this is another year in which the very difficult recovery of economic growth in this country interfered with the improvement of the quality of banks assets, curtailed banks profitability and restrained their opportunities for income from their core activity  lending to businesses and households. Moreover, the very length of the crisis puts severe pressure on banks existing capital reserves and requires ongoing streamlining of their business strategies. This unfavourable environment further stresses the importance of the results achieved by the banks in Bulgaria. I would gladly use the opportunity provided by the Bankers Day to express deserved congratulations to all professionals in the banking sector  from the top management to the rank-and-file members of our community engaged in routine operating activities. Dear colleagues, with your work you continue to contribute to the exceptionally sound results of our banking sector, which outline it against the international background as an example of successful adjustment in times of the greatest global crisis in decades. Indeed, in 2013 the banking system continued to demonstrate very high capital adequacy and liquidity indicators. As of September, the overall capital adequacy ratio was 16.89%, and Tier 1 capital adequacy - 15.61%. In October the liquid assets to total assets ratio was 25.25%. As a result of the banks active efforts, in 2013 we already report systemwide stabilization of the share of non-performing exposures more than 90 days past due. As of end-October, their book value was 10.66% of the book value of the systems loan portfolio, compared to 10.62% as of end-2012 (respectively, the gross share of these loans was 17.20%, against16.62% as of end-2012). This share reflects the impairments made that were deducted in the income statement, i.e. it reports the already provisioned risk. Apart from the impairments under the International Financial Reporting Standards, the coverage of non-performing loans has been additionally strengthened by the specific provisions for credit risk and the capital surplus. Another source of capitalization and a stability maintaining reserve is the profit which the banking system continues to generate in spite of the adverse conditions. The sector is expected to close 2013 with a positive financial result, comparable to the results in previous years (in the range of BGN 500-550 million). Banks stability attracts depositors who entrust their savings with them. Household deposits alone have increased by BGN 3.1 billion (9.3%) year-on-year as of end-October. Thus depositors have practically confirmed their high confidence in the banks. The stabilizing role of the banking sector in the Bulgarian economy is appreciated and understood by the general public and generally by the business community, by the economic policy makers, and last but not least, by the media, which upheld their high professionalism and responsible behaviour with regard to the banking system. At the same time, 2013 will be remembered with the intense ingress in the public communications of attempts at politicizing bank-related matters. Exactly a year ago, in my address to you, I warned that in an elections year it was normal to expect that the banking area would attract political interest and would become a focal point of critiques. On the one hand, competent professional discussions can be really helpful and result in finding optimal solutions of actual problems (e.g. in the relations between banks and borrowers). On the other hand, this is a time when new candidates for public attention try to bring the spotlights on themselves, and when tireless old-time politicians make themselves noticed, seeking new popularity at the expense of banks. A time when individual under-appreciated experts, always hungry for media attention, come thick and fast with their usual opinions, no matter that the strictly expert issues under discussion are usually beyond their competence. Against this background, dear colleagues, I would like to underscore the responsible conduct of the management teams of our banks. With a concrete and purely professional approach, including through your measured media appearances, many of you, for yet another year, not just provided an example of dialogue and hearing the other side, but demonstrated leadership insight and intellectual capacity during discussions on matters related to the operation of banks. Along with all this, in the year the banking sector performed its functions, even taking active part in finding new solutions for improvement of its infrastructure and expanding the scope of banking transactions. In this relation, for example, banks put much effort in support of the project, jointly implemented by the BNB and the Ministry of Finance, for linking the BNB Government Securities Registration and Settlement System as an auxiliary TARGET2-BNB system. I would like to particularly thank the colleagues from banks that participated in a series of integrated tests in relation to the settlement in euro of the funds leg of government securities transactions. After the successful completion of the tests in October, since the end of November participants in the government securities market have been able to settle in euro through their accounts with the central bank the funds leg of the primary and secondary market transactions in government securities denominated and payable in euro. Also, practically several days ago, Clearstream Banking S.A., Luxembourg joined as a direct participant in the Government Securities Registration and Settlement System at the BNB. Thus, a direct link was established between the BNB Government Securities Depository and the Luxembourg-based International Central Depository, part of Clearstream International, S.A. In addition to stimulating attracting foreign investors in Bulgarian debt securities, the new opportunities will ease the access of Bulgarian banks to credit lines from international financial institutions, as our banks are already able to effect cross-border transfers of lev-denominated government securities to central depositories of other EU member states. As regards the BNB, in addition to our internal tasks, this year we participated in a broad range of discussions and projects of the EU, ESCB, ESRB and the European supervision authorities. Although this effort usually remains unnoticed by the general public, these activities absorb a significant part of our expert resources and are of paramount importance for the operation of the banking system and for maintaining stability in Bulgaria. As a fully fledged and well prepared participant in the operation of the numerous European institutions, committees and working groups, BNB has held clear and consistent positions in support of our national interests in the discussion and negotiation of the reforms in the governance and economic policies in the EU. For example, on the issue of the so-called banking union, BNB, together with the other Bulgarian institution, has always expressed its full support to intensifying integration and improving governance in the euro area. However, the creation of a banking union should not bring negative effects for non-euro area EU member states, Bulgaria included. We have no intentions to join the Single Supervisory Mechanism of the euro area (the first element of the banking union), the legislative package of which was ultimately adopted in October, and with regard to which the ECB is to play the leading role from 4 November 2014. The reasons for this are well known  our country would take great risks if it joined the Single Supervisory Mechanism before it joining the euro area. If we join, on the one hand we would transfer significant national supervisory powers and would leave the protection of our financial stability with an institution with great authority and rich experience in other areas (such as monetary policy), but which would still have to build up supervisory expertise. On the other hand, even under this scenario, in case of need banks in Bulgaria, opposite to euro area banks, will have access neither to liquidity support from the ECB, nor to capital support from the European Stability Mechanism. Besides, non-euro area member states may not participate in making final decisions in the process of exercising single supervision. In parallel to establishing the Single Supervisory Mechanism for the euro area member states, intensive work was underway in 2013 on EU level on the Directive on recovery and resolution of credit institutions. BNB actively participated in formulating and maintaining Bulgarias position on the framework for resolution of banks in the EU. We were aiming at a maximum degree of exclusion of deposits from the scope of instruments which may be used for recapitalization from internal sources (the so-called bail-in). Our country insisted on attaining a balance between setting up the general framework and providing for the national authorities flexibility in implementing this instrument. More specifically, the non-euro area member states were to keep such degree of flexibility, as well as the possibility to have a sufficiently long period for smooth adjustment to the new resolution rules. In terms of the package of measures and rules, it was imperative to achieve a balance between the host and home member state in case of cross-border banking crises. The intense debate on the Directive continues with the BNB being actively involved from the Bulgarian side, with so far satisfactory compromises reached in June at the ECOFIN Council meeting in Brussels. At that meeting, several non-euro area countries (Bulgaria among them) had their requests endorsed for national resolution authorities to have sufficient flexibility in using various internal sources of bank recapitalisation. Besides, the ECOFIN Council approved the option for the bail-in tool to be introduced by 2018 - instead of 2015, which was the position upheld by many member states and by some of the institutions involved in the consultation process. Looking at the environment in which banks will operate in 2014, I would note in the first place the anticipated continuing low economic growth within the EU, Bulgaria including. Such environment will continue to weigh down on credit demand and, despite the limited possibilities for new placements, banks will continue to cover the existing costs on assets, including in relation to managing impaired assets. Banks should also cover the cost of attracted funds. Paradoxically as it may seem at first glance, the higher investor confidence and the substantial inflow of savings to the system to some extent poses a challenge to banks which in the situation of crisis have little possibilities to perform their main function of financial intermediaries. Along with the slow economic recovery, it is highly probable that we would also witness continuing uncertainty and considerable fluctuations on the international financial markets. This year, we already witnessed episodes of volatility and periods of tangible changes in the prices of benchmark financial assets. Such instances included the sharp plunge in the price of gold in mid April (more than 14% between 12 and 15 of April) and the quick movement in the yield curves in the USA and Germany (a rise of the yields on the 10-year government bonds of these countries by more than 100 and 50 basis points from the beginning of May and to this day). In 2014, the fluctuations on the financial markets might become even greater mainly as a result of expectations for change in the monetary policy of the worlds major central banks. A new upward interest rate cycle could eventually lead to ending the period of historically low interest rates, in the euro area for instance. Thus, banks would have even more challenges to face in relation to their returns and risks. As on previous occasions, now again I would put a special emphasis on the interest rate risk and notably the risk in lending at fixed interest rates. Banks ought to consider carefully the assumption of these risks and manage them with precision within the context of a scenario of rising prices of attracted funds. Yet, perhaps the most serious challenges to face in the coming year are to be sought outside the purely economic and financial aspects of the environment in which banks will operate. Only a few weeks are left until a kind of supervisory revolution occurs in Bulgaria. I will dwell on this issue in more detail. It would not be too much to say that 2014 will be the year of the largest one-off change in our regulatory framework over the last already more than 15 years. From 1 of January, the Bulgarian legislation will have to incorporate the Capital Requirements Directive and the Capital Requirements Regulation adopted in June this year by the European Parliament and by the Council. The Directive and the Regulation introduce at the EU level the provisions of the new Basel Capital Accord,known as Basel III. The Regulation is a first step towards introducing the so-called Single rulebook leading to a maximum harmonisation of the treatment of institutions across the EU. A precedent vis-a-vis the current bank regulation practice is the fact that a directly applicable EU act (the Regulation) incorporates the requirements for banks in our country concerning capital, liquidity, risk management and internal corporate governance. That calls for serious amendments to the Law on Credit Institutions and the regulatory framework. While Basel III aims at enhancing the capital quality and its relatedness to inherent risks, as well as strengthening the conservative character of supervisory standards at the global and European level, in countries like Bulgaria (where traditionally a more conservative local treatment of banks is practiced) introducing the new provisions would actually lead to some liberalisation of capital adequacy requirements. The statutory minimum capital adequacy will be reduced from the current 12% down to 8%. At the same time, however, that will be compensated by introducing a number of capital buffer regimes  the so-called capital conservation buffer of 2.5% and a systemic risk buffer of up to 3% of risk-weighted assets. After these buffers are added in full to the new 6% minimum ratio of primary capital, Tier 1 total capital adequacy would reach 11.5%. Combined with the existing subordinated debt, recognised as Tier 2 capital, the total capital adequacy ratio at the banking system level would exceed the current 12% regulatory minimum. In addition, the new regime would allow setting up the so-called countercyclical buffer at between 0% and 2.5% depending on the macroeconomic situation in the country. At the current stage in Bulgaria we do not foresee that additional buffer. Another fundamental change as a result of the need to introduce the Capital Requirements Directive and Regulation would be repealing a number of Ordinances among which Ordinance No 9 regulating specific provisions for credit risk. These provisions were a specific feature of the supervisory regime in Bulgaria which helped the banking sector accumulate and preserve capital buffers and retain acceptable profitability during both the pre-crisis period and in the current crisis. In place of the specific provisions allocated so far, from 1 of January 2014 the banks will be expected to implement additional accounting provisions under the International Financial Reporting Standards intended to reduce the book value of 90 days past-due loans. These actions would have a different impact across the individual credit institutions. A note should also be made here that the BNB banking supervision will continue to be able to impose individual Pillar 2 capital requirements for each bank, part of these requirements possibly being at the expense of the currently available specific provisions for credit risk. I hope that these fundamental changes in the capital regime, along with the other requirements stemming from the new regulatory framework in EU, would be introduced in time by the Bulgarian legislator. The above described significant amendments to the Law on Credit Institutions are already being discussed in the National Assembly. It would also be necessary to continue the existing active dialogue and the constructive joint work between banks representatives and the BNB banking supervision. This would allow for the smooth transition and initial functioning of the new supervisory regime, at minimal costs for banks while keeping the stability and the high capital and liquidity indicators in the sector. And last but not least, dear colleagues, on the eve of the Bankers Day we should not bypass the topic of relations with the customers. In my review of the developments over the past year, I already stressed how especially sensitive these issues are within the context of the current socio-political and economic situation. You can make further efforts to enhance transparency and predictability in the price formation of banking products and services. Indeed, there is still a lot to be done for strengthening borrowers trust, including by demonstrating more dialogue on part of banks in negotiating or changing price terms on loans. Apart from this, many banks can further streamline their business practices in relation to customer servicing. I continue to assert, based on our analyses, that the bulk of signals and complaints could be resolved on site - at the branches and offices of individual banks. An effectively organized decision-making process on customer complaints could even save the trouble of escalating the issues to the credit institutions head offices. I would also repeat something Ive shared with you before: a happy customer is the cheapest advertisement of a bank. The opposite is also true: a disappointed customer (no matter justifiably or not) is of detriment to the most valuable asset of any bank, to its reputation. Allow me with this issue to finish my statement and on behalf of the BNB Governing Council and personally on my behalf to convey our most cordial and best wishes for professional and personal well-being in the year 2014! Happy Bankers Day, dear Colleagues! __________ A few years ago I explained why I avoid the expression consumer of financial services. It brings associations of consumerism, without any effort and one-off, whereby the intent of the counterparty is considered mala fide. While customer to me holds a message for mutuality, discreteness and a long-term relationship. PAGE 1

Title: Welcome address on the Occasion of the 135th Anniversary of the Bulgarian National Bank, Sofia, Ivan Vazov National Theatre, June 6, 2014, 7 p.m.
text: Welcome address by Mr. Ivan Iskrov, BNB Governor, on the Occasion of the 135th Anniversary of the Bulgarian National Bank, Sofia, Ivan Vazov National Theatre, 6 June 2014, 7 p.m. Mr. President of the Republic of Bulgaria, Mr. Speaker of the National Assembly, Mr. Prime Minister, Your Grace, Members of Parliament and Ministers, Your Excellencies, Distinguished Guests, Ladies and Gentlemen, Allow me to welcome you at the gala concert for the 135th anniversary of the Bulgarian National Bank. It is an honour and a privilege to stand here exactly on 6 June  the day on which in 1879 the BNB effected the first financial transaction that set the beginning of the central banks operations. The bank was established a few months earlier  on 25 January of the same year. Thus, the BNB is one of the first state institutions of newly liberated and resurging Bulgaria. Elated by the newly acquired freedom and led by their love for their motherland, many Bulgarians who studied in and graduated the most prestigious European universities came back home. These young patriots promptly took to building the new Bulgarian institutional architecture. An important part of it was the Bulgarian National Bank, established with the active effort of already renowned public figures of authority. The names of Georgi Zhelyazkovich who graduated finance in Paris, of Mikhail Tenev  a graduate of the Geneva University, of the great politician and statesman Ivan Geshov, as well as many other distinguished visionaries after them built their efforts and dreams, their devotion and insight into the foundations of our central bank. Exactly on this awe-inspiring strong alloy of youth and wisdom, of academic knowledge and practical experience, the institutional platform of the Bulgarian National Bank was built. You surely realize how highly bound we feel, as the modern successors of these praiseworthy forerunners, to continue with honour and diligence in their steps and to build further on the good heritage they left us. As exactly the continuous aspiration for developing a modern and efficient financial system is the reason why we presently have a developed and competitive banking sector and a payment system offering state-of-the-art products and services in support of the national economy and of the public. Our banking system  one of the best regulated and most transparent industries in Bulgaria  is presently well-capitalized, highly liquid, and smoothly operating, ready to support the domestic economys growth. And as each significant institutional success is backed both by national consensus and public support, and by the wisdom gained through the effort and pain of previous generations, please allow me to quote Sir Isaac Newtons remarkable aphorism of 1676: If I have seen further it is by standing on the shoulders of giants. Ladies and gentlemen, today is the day to remember all these honourable predecessors of ours, who have left us their example of diligence and patriotism; an example of creativity and perseverance, combined with the conviction that Bulgaria is part of Europe. This aspiration towards Europe came to fruition with Bulgarias full EU accession into the European Union on 1 January 2007 when Bulgaria took its well-deserved place in the European family. Since that date, the Bulgarian National Bank has been a member of the European System of Central Banks and has gradually earned significant experience as a bank of a full-fledged EU member state, but also an undisputable repute of an esteemed institution. During these first seven years of EU membership, the BNB has proven itself as a serious partner with a responsible and predictable behaviour. This is a valuable capital to be used in the next stage of our European integration  the full-fledged membership in the euro area. As is widely known, this is our commitment taken by signing the Treaty of Accession to the European Union. At the same time, this is our strategic goal which is fully aligned to our historically European orientation and which will reaffirm unequivocally our geopolitical affiliation to the core of the European continent. Our membership in the euro area however should not be taken as yet the next slogan used in political squabbling. Quite on the contrary, the driving force behind this process should be our clear conviction that we ourselves need a reformed and competitive economy involving efforts at enhancing human capital quality over the longer-term horizon and that these efforts are also supported by a clear social and political consensus - because strategic goals could only be attained on the back of a national consensus. Only if these conditions, which we set to ourselves, are fulfilled, will Bulgaria become a predictable, contributing and esteemed euro area member. Dear Guests, Allow me on a day like this, when we are taking stock of where we are and where we want to be, to express my sincere appreciation first to my colleagues from the Bulgarian National Bank, to those unknown to the media or the public hard-working employees, experts and managers whose dedicated and qualified daily efforts measure up to the high societal expectations. Thank you, dear colleagues! I would like to express my personal appreciation for the considerable presence and respect shown by our partners from international financial institutions and central banks with whom the Bulgarian National Bank has great and fruitful cooperation, which I sincerely believe will further evolve in the future. Ive left the most important for the end: I thank all Bulgarian citizens for their trust in the Bulgarian National Bank! Of all the assets that we have, trust is the most precious: many times exceeding the worth of the substantial international reserves at the Central Bank! Dear Ladies and Gentlemen, Its been equally a huge responsibility and a great honour for me, over more than 10 years now, to be in charge of this institution  the Bulgarian National Bank! Thank you for your attention! PAGE \* MERGEFORMAT1

Title: Interview with the BNB Governor, in The day begins with  Georgy Lyubenov on BNT, September 21, 2014.
Subtitle: Broadcaster: Mr Iskrov, in the beginning please let me thank you for agreeing to talk on this so electrifying subject  KTB - and for giving an interview only for the Bulgarian National Television. Thank you!
text: Interview with the BNB Governor, Mr Ivan Iskrov, in The day begins with Georgy Lyubenov on BNT, 21 September 2014 Broadcaster: Mr Iskrov, in the beginning please let me thank you for agreeing to talk on this so electrifying subject  KTB - and for giving an interview only for the Bulgarian National Television. Thank you! Ivan Iskrov: I thank you too for your visit to this extremely reputable institution as the Central Bank cannot go around visiting all morning TV programmes and answering any single person or any statement. We have chosen you because you are the Bulgarian National Television. Otherwise we treat all media equally, and it is not accidental that we prefer working through our website. Broadcaster: However, allow me, Mr Iskrov, to start this interview with this favourite question to all bankers  Is it true that Money loves silence? Ivan Iskrov: Well, it is true and it also very well fits with the thesis expressed by a chairwoman of a bank in 1998. If you remember, she has said what the easiest way to kill a bank and a fly is  well, with a newspaper. So, the more the noise around banks, whether in the US, Europe, Japan or any other country, including Bulgaria, the more it influences the behaviour of their clients, which in all cases is not in the interest of countries economic growth. Broadcaster: Let me take you three months back when you placed KTB under special supervision. Practically you closed the bank. Why did this happen? Ivan Iskrov: Thank you, because in the daily debates we seem to forget how things started. Actually, you remember rightly that on 20 June, nearly three months ago, after massive deposit withdrawals, for reasons beyond the Central Banks control, I reiterate  for reasons beyond the BNBs control, Corporate Commercial Bank became illiquid and at midday, it was Friday 20 June, the banks management submitted a request for the bank to be placed under special supervision so as to ensure its protection. The same thing happened to their subsidiary bank Credit Agricole Bulgaria, now renamed Victoria Commercial Bank, whose management later on that day, sometime around the end of the working time, also submitted a letter, stating that as a result of the panic surrounding the parent bank they had received an enormous number of payment orders which they were unable to proceed, and therefore they requested that bank to be placed under special supervision. Of course, the Central Bank, all of us working here, including myself, very well know how a large systemically important bank could affect the entire economy. Thats why from day one we initiated consultations with the Government and the major parties represented in the 42nd National Assembly so as to find an acceptable solution for the bank to reopen as quickly as possible and thus ensure the normal operation of tens of businesses, hospitals, municipalities, citizens, and other depositors and clients of the bank. So, from the very beginning the Central Bank is fully aware of the role of the banking sector and, particularly, of the two affected banks. Broadcaster: Mr Iskrov, did you believe that then those three months would be enough to resolve the crisis? Why didnt you then carry out the supervisory procedures in the maximum period of time, as you did this week? Ivan Iskrov: Well, it is not necessary. When adopting the Law on Credit Institutions, the legislator obviously knew that it was a very complex process. It cannot be resolved in three days, as a former officer of the Central Bank claimed some time ago. Some specific legal procedures have to be followed, so the legislator has prescribed a six-month period. We have always been hoping and working to speed things up. It is another matter altogether that many processes were delayed for reasons beyond our control. For example, you know that with the support of the parties represented in the 42nd National Assembly we and the Government developed a few optional solutions to somehow reopen KTB. At first we discussed the idea of nationalising the bank so that it could quickly open to the public again, but as the auditors 10-day review showed very high uncertainties about KTBs assets, later we proposed a solution that is well-known in western practices  separating the bank into a good bank and a bad bank. And thus all depositors and clients, I stress - without exception, could have access to their accounts from 21 July, only a month after the bank was placed under special supervision. Anyway, again for reasons beyond our control (the politicians may not like my saying this, but I will keep repeating it again and again from now on), we did not receive political support for this to happen. And you know that after the meeting at the Presidents Office on 14 July, the President himself announced that no consensus could be reached and the BNB would continue to act strictly in accordance with the existing law. Broadcaster: Now that you mentioned the politicians, you know that the politicians have a rock-solid alibi when they say  the BNBs banking supervision is the one that must take care of the good or bad state of a private bank. Ivan Iskrov: It is true and it is not true. They are absolutely right to say that the banking supervision and the Central Bank are independent institutions and are responsible for the oversight of payment systems, the banking system, and a series of other operations. In this case, however, it is not a matter of banking supervision; it is a matter of restructuring a troubled commercial bank and its smaller subsidiary bank. Just as this happened in the entire Western Europe without exception, and by the way, as it happened in the United States too. Theres no way that politicians can evade their responsibility because this indeed is not responsibility of the Central Bank. On my full responsibility, as Governor of the Central Bank (I guess, your records are kept for at least a hundred years ahead) I declare that Corporate Commercial Bank cannot reopen only with the efforts of the Bulgarian National Bank, and not because the Bulgarian National Bank does not want that. This has not been possible anywhere in the world. I remind you, for example, of the difficulties of several banks in the US. Then the Congress, despite the almighty US Federal Reserve, was forced to adopt special decisions, to approve special programmes, together with President Bushs Administration. Remember that almost the entire banking sector of Ireland got into difficulties and was restructured into good and bad banks. Again, the Central Bank played the technical role but it was Parliament and the government who adopted the relevant legal amendments. Please note that this has happened in a number of advanced countries. 2/3 of the banks in the United Kingdom are still nationalised - again with a decision of Parliament and the government, not of the Bank of England. The same thing happened to many powerful names in the banking history of Europe. Think back of Fortis Bank in Benelux! Or the largest bank in France and Belgium  Dexia! These were also separated into good and bad banks. This was done by legislative initiative; otherwise it could not be done. In the largest European country, the largest mortgage creditor Hypo Real Estate. Try to remember that its largest bank Bayerische Landesbank sold its bank in Bulgaria - MKB Unionbank - for that same reason, because it was rescued by the German government and had to pay money back? Broadcaster: Please let me ask you one personal question... Ivan Iskrov: Therefore, let me point out  this is not a supervisory issue any more. Broadcaster: We may go back to the banking supervision later. Especially considering the news from the Prosecutors Office and the refusal to release Mr Gounev, but well come back to this in a moment. If you allow me one more personal question  Do you, Mr Iskrov, yourself have deposits with KTB? Ivan Iskrov: These are personal matters, but as I am Governor of the Central Bank, I have never tried to evade the question about where the Governor keeps his money in principle. Over the years I have always said and I repeat now: the Governor of the Central Bank has always kept his money on bank deposits as the most secure instrument, and always with Bulgarian banks. And in this particular case, as I read some speculations in the social media I want to repeat, by the way Ive already announced it publicly, that I have never had any relations with Corporate Commercial Bank or Victoria Commercial Bank, nor have I had any deposits there. Broadcaster: Of course, this is a personal matter but I ask you because many personal matters have actually become public  politicians, members of Parliament. Ivan Iskrov: You do make a distinction between personal matters and allegations of personal matters, dont you? Broadcaster: Of course I do but... Ivan Iskrov: If you ask me, Mr Benovskas just said on Nova TV that I have travelled on Mr Vassilevs private planes. Now I use this opportunity, through you, to make all your viewers hear this: Ivan Iskrov has never travelled on private planes. The only three non-regular flights I have been on in my entire public life have been on the governments plane, as a member of state delegations. Broadcaster: Of course they say many things and whatnot, even about the amount of your monthly salary, but the question is different  Will you sue these who say it? Ivan Iskrov: Yes. These are myths too. The entire Governing Council is not paid such an amount per month. This is being done on purpose to increase... Broadcaster: You talk about the amount of 80 000 a month? Ivan Iskrov: ... Again to increase the negative attitude towards the Central Bank and to avoid discussing the real problems of society. Broadcaster: Well than let me ask you just that  These politicians who now claim that you are dependent, that you are paid, do you really intend to sue them, as you epistolarily threatened to do so this week? Also, an accusation came from Belgrade, the new epithet you were given the other day  Mr Tsvetan Vassilev called you a puppet... Ivan Iskrov: Look, I do not wish to comment on accused persons. In this case it would be better if Mr Vassilev could say what he has done with the depositors money and how he would possibly pay it back. So do not make me comment on such ... I have never been anybodys puppet. All my actions are public and obey the law. Let them mention specific facts, specific actions which even vaguely imply puppetry, and then I will comment on them. As for the other slanderers, in principle I am a very tolerant man. But when they go to extremes, just as the former Minister of Culture and member of Parliament candidate, Mr Rashidov, has gone to extremes, yes, I have already taken the relevant steps. It is quite another matter that my solicitor cannot find him to serve him with some documents. Perhaps I will have to send him to one of the rallies Mr Rashidov goes to. It is because I feel offended not only for myself but I feel offended for our nation when a former minister of culture, not of whatever, not of energy, not of agriculture, it is a minister of culture that sinks so low broadcasting slanders. Broadcaster: Since you started talking about Mr Rashidov... Ivan Iskrov: No, no. I do not want to talk about anybody, you just mentioned that I had filed a lawsuit and thats why .... Otherwise, since I was a child I have observed a principle. My mother and father, who passed away a long time ago, may they rest in peace, have brought me up to never comment on, let alone insult people. You may have noticed that too. I have held this position for years now, and very rarely, only in exceptional circumstances, I have had to... Broadcaster: Do you really believe, Mr Iskrov, that politicians are to blame for what is happening now? Ivan Iskrov: I dont want to say who is to blame and who is not. I know what Ivan Iskrov has been doing and what the Governing Council of the Central Bank has been doing, what solutions we have put forward. And I know who which decisions supported or did not support. Or else, I do not wish to point the finger or express any thanks. What I want to say is that without a political decision on the KTB issue the bank cannot and will not reopen. The only option, ever more theoretical in our view, is for the current shareholders to come and empty a big bag full of money, nearly 6.5 billion, and remit that money to the Central Banks accounts, and also to replenish the capital after the final assessment, and we can reopen the bank.
