Title: Interview, 24 chasa daily
Subtitle:
DIMITAR RADEV: THE BANKING SYSTEM IS NO LONGER AN
OBSTACLE BUT A DRIVER FOR BULGARIAS ENTRY INTO THE EURO AREA
text: Interview with the BNB Governor Dimitar Radev, on pages 19 and 26 of 24 chasa daily, 17 May 2017 DIMITAR RADEV: THE BANKING SYSTEM IS NO LONGER AN OBSTACLE BUT A DRIVER FOR BULGARIAS ENTRY INTO THE EURO AREA Since I took office as Governor there have been no attempts at political intervention, says the Governor of the central bank More highlights: We are going to print euro banknotes  this is prestige and economic benefits for us Now we have a full range of bank resolution tools The prospect is that interest rate levels will be rising, and this will be felt on the Bulgarian market too The participation of strategic investors in the banking consolidation is important. KBCs deal for UBB is a positive fact We are going to print euro banknotes, Mr Radev. This is indicative of what? Most of all this is recognition of our efforts in the joint venture company with the French partners. In a wider context, it is a matter of prestige and economic benefits for our country. The company now operates in 24-hour regime, and the number of produced banknotes grew from 60 million to 1 billion. All this means new jobs and more tax for the state budget. The year 2017 began with political unrest, and the economies, not only ours, are not exactly booming. How is the financial system feeling in this situation? There are fewer and fewer political unknowns in our country and in Europe after the latest elections. This, and the measures we have taken, positively affect our banking system. Lending in Bulgaria is rebounding, the banking sectors financial results are good and the level of bad loans is falling. Of course, there are challenges too. On the one hand, we have narrower interest rate margins which restrict banks incomes. On the other hand, there is a prospect, in the foreseeable future, that interest rate levels will be rising, which requires good management of credit expansion and credit risk. Our banking sector is getting prepared to meet these challenges adequately. You have said that an irrational fiscal policy could wreck the currency board. Have you any concerns now? The three-year state budget programme, announced by the Ministry of Finance a couple of days ago, contains a clear commitment to continuing the fiscal consolidation. So I have no concerns in this respect. Keeping the currency board arrangements stability is the foundation of our mandate as a central bank. We do ensure adequate coverage of the CBA with foreign currency reserves and we will continue to do so in the future. Until recently there was noisy political talk about the euro area. And silence by the BNB. Is this guilty silence; are there any hindrances in our banking system? I have repeatedly stated that the ongoing integration into the European financial infrastructure is the BNBs main priority. This strategic objective was clearly defined by the new government as well. However, the central bank is not a political institution and it must not be expected to be an active participant in all the political talk on this topic. Our task it to assist this process with expertise and we are doing it to the best of our ability, keeping the major political factors properly informed. For example, early this year we presented to the Coordination Council, set up on governmental level, a detailed costs and benefits analysis of Bulgarias entry into the euro area. In this sense, our banking system is not an obstacle but rather a driver of the integration process. Then tell us what the BNB did to make us a part of the European financial infrastructure? And what it did not do? First and foremost, the BNB maintains the stability of the Bulgarian lev and our monetary regime; without this stability all other actions for joining the euro area would be futile. Next, we are building and keeping our financial infrastructure in compliance with the requirements of the euro area. For example, our payment systems fully meet these requirements; and as regards the financial stability statistics, we are well ahead of many Member States. Despite the progress we have made in some other spheres, there is more to be done, for example, in banking supervision and regarding the framework for the bank recovery and resolution. Is the BNB autonomous? The ECB has several times expressed concerns about unacceptable political interventions. Are there such interventions now? The BNBs independence is guaranteed by law and by the Treaty on the Functioning of the EU. At least since I took office as Governor, there have been no attempts at political intervention. What will change if we go into the waiting room to the euro area? Will the banks be more secure, more controlled? The Bulgarian Levs participation in the ERM II mechanism is one of the requirements for Bulgaria to join the euro area. This participation, when it happens, will have no direct nominal effect on our monetary regime and banking sector, but it will give us a clear perspective on our membership in the euro area. Normally, a countrys participation in the ERM II takes at least 2  2.5 years before it joins the euro area and adopts the euro. Not long ago you expressed your concerns that savings were increasing worldwide but there were no projects of good quality that could make money generate more money. And the solution is? I was talking about the gap between savings and investments in the EU. The solution to this problem requires measures on supranational and on national level. For this purpose the banking and financial integration should speed up, and the process of real conversion in the EU too, and the quality of investment projects must improve. On national level more efforts are needed with regard to the banking sector, fiscal consolidation, and structural reforms. Bulgaria is a good example of what can be done in the banking and fiscal sphere. You initiated massive changes in banking supervision. How do you plan to continue these changes? Indeed, banking supervision is in far better shape after the changes weve made. However, a lot more is to be done. Weve made a comprehensive review of the internal prudential regulations so as to bring them in compliance with the international standards. The first set of new regulations has already been adopted by the Governing Council. The process is going to be completed by the end of this year. We also started a project of building a new information system for banking supervision needs. Banking consolidation is going smoothly. Why then do you always imply changes in the tools for resolution of banks? In the last two years we managed to set up a solid institutional framework for recovery and resolution of banks, a framework which was not in place during the turmoil in 2014. As a result, now we have a full set of legalised resolution tools which can be used whenever necessary, including sale of business, bridge institution, asset separation and sharing of losses, as well as government financial stability instruments, including state capital support and temporary public ownership. We developed a funding mechanism for resolution measures through the Bank Resolution Fund where nearly BGN 300 million is already accumulated. Now we are seeking to improve the capacity in this area to ensure its proper functioning. Will s deal for UBB be the biggest on the banking market? When will there be a decision for Victoria Commercial Bank? For us, it is the participation of strategic investors in the banking consolidation process that is very important, not the scale of a deal. In this context, the purchase of UBB by a strategic investor, such as , is a very positive fact. As regards Victoria Commercial Bank, we are following the legal rules and procedures. Now there is no news. Have you received applications for new banks or for new branches? Formally, so far we have received no such applications. Nevertheless, over 270 EEA credit institutions have informed us about their potential intentions to provide banking services in Bulgaria under whats called the single European passport principle. The list is on our website. The banking and financial industry is steadily moving to Internet banking. Does this require changes in control to ensure security? Yes, definitely. The new EU payment services directive sets specific requirements for the so called payment service providers  these are banks, payment institutions and electronic money institutions. By the beginning of 2018 the Member States must implement these requirements in regard to the security of electronic payments and internet payments. In Bulgaria this will be done by means of a completely new Law on Payment Services and Payment Systems, whose preliminary draft is already prepared. Let us finish with an interest rate projection  will there be good news for savers, not only for borrowers as its been for some time now? The Federal Reserves latest decisions and the debates within the European System of Central Banks indicate that interest rates tend to rise globally, and this will also affect the Bulgarian market. Central banks actions aim to make this process gradual and well-managed. PAGE \* MERGEFORMAT2

Title: Interview for "BANKER" newspaper
Subtitle: - ,        ,           ,                (ERM II). ,  ,            ,     ?     ,           ?
text: Interview with Mr. Dimitar Radev, Governor of BNB, on 7th street in "BANKER" newspaper, December 22, 2017. Mr. Radev, at the end of the year and representatives of the European Commission, and people from the Bulgarian government again began to broadcast optimistic signals that there are no grounds for Bulgaria not to be adopted in the two-year mechanism for the introduction of the euro (ERM II). Howdo you think there are real opportunities for this to happen in the near future  let's say, within a year? The BNB's policy on this issue is clear and we are working very seriously to ensure that all the conditions that are set within our mandate are met. We are also conducting intensive technical consultations. Let's summarize again  if Bulgaria enters the euro adoption mechanism in question, what specific benefits will this bring to Bulgaria's economy and finances? And are there any risks  of any nature , from the country's entry into ERRM II, for which we must prepare? One of the immediate results will be the increase in the country's credit rating, with all the resulting positive effects on the economy. This was clearly highlighted only days ago by the leading credit agencies . and we will keep the fixed rate of bgn to the euro until our accession to the euro area. Does entering this mechanism guarantee us entry into the euro area in two, three or five years, or can we get stuck in it for a decade that and for more? So far, there has been only one such case  Denmark, and I do not expect there to be another exception. The optimal deadline for the adoption of the euro after the accession ofTHE BGN to THE ERM II is two to three years. There is a lot of talk in the European Union and european regulators about the need to reduce problem loans. The European Banking Authority has even developed a specific document giving guidance in this area. What additional supervisory regulations and recommendations should banks expect in the next oneor two years and how do you think they will affect our market? This discussion should be conducted in the right context for Bulgaria. It mainly includes three things: current trends in the level of NPLs; impairment coverage (e.g. line  this is the financial term for the provisions set aside under the loans) and capital surplus and an appropriate environment for reducing non-performing loans. Since 2015, there has been a clear downward trend in NPLs in Bulgaria. At the end of 2014, their level was around 17 per cent, at the end of 2017 it is now around 11 per cent. Another important factor, which is not usually the subject of public discussion, is the level of coverage of non-performing loans in bulgaria with provisions. It amounts to 52% and is about 7 percentage points higher than the EU average. The third important element is: what we are doing from now on to consolidate the downward trend in NPLs to their eu average levels. The focus is on creating the right environment for banks to make these loans cut. To this end, we will soon issuea prudential guide for non-performing loans, which we have sent to banks and their auditors to hear their comment. At the end of November 2017, the National Assembly adopted amendments to the Law on Credit Institutions, which transfer much of the decision-making powers for granting approvals and licenses fromthe sub-manager responsible for banking supervision management to the collective body  the Management Board of the BNB. authorisations and licences? This consolidates the central bank's overall governance model. You probably know that this model already applies to our bank recovery and resolution function. is widespread in the EU. For this reason, the changes have also received support from the ECB. They definitely affect internal procedures, but we organize the work so that we don'thave to change the deadlines already set. Does this act of the National Assembly not reduce the personal responsibility of the sub-manager by turning it into a collective, transferring it to the Management Board? This act continues the line we adopted as early as 2015 offully committing the responsibility of the Management Board in the decision-making process without reducing the personal responsibility of the individual sub-governors for the preparation of these decisions. And MPs rejected some of the requests for changes to the law, which were intended to allow the Banking Supervision to carry out more comprehensive and stricter controls on domestic loans and related party loans. Indeed, the proposed definition was limited in the part on economic connectivity. The aim of the proposal was to avoid cases that we had after the asset quality review last year . Recently, the BNB Board decided to increase the capital buffers for systemic risk of its designated as systemically important bulgarianbanks. How should we interpret this measure? We have introduced capital buffers in the context of the Basel III global regulatory framework. BNB had to determine the capital buffer for other systemically important institutions, the firststep being to determine which of the banks are systemically important for Bulgaria and then to determine the specific buffer levels. With our latest decision, we identified 11 banks in bulgaria as systemically important. The relevant buffer rates reflect not the risk, but the contribution of individual banks to maintaining the stability of the banking system  which in turn implies capital commitments. In order to gradually spread the burden over time, the BNB has set a phased peak buffer level in2020, starting in 2017. Can we expect the countercyclical buffer to be triggered next year and at what levels of cretaceousgrowth will it emerge from its current zero level? This buffer has already been introduced for banks in Bulgaria  since the beginning of 2016. BNB quarterly sets its level, with a current level equal to zero. The purpose of the countercyclical buffer is to respond adequately to the accumulation of systemic risk. Its level is determined on the basis of a model of how the bank credit-to-GDP ratio deviates from the long-term historical value. If that ratio exceeds the long-term value in our mo del in the future, this will give us a reason to set a level, other than zero. PAGE \* MERGEFORMAT3

Title: Publication in the Financial Times based on an interview
Subtitle: Bulgarias central bank governor aims to prevent return of crisis
text: Publication in the Financial Times based on an interview of the BNB Governor Dimitar Radev of 11 January 2018 Bulgarias central bank governor aims to prevent return of crisis Dimitar Radev is dealing with the legacy of a bank collapse halfway through his term In countries where opaque networks of influence connect politics, business and the state administration, the central bank often strives to protect the integrity of the financial system. Dimitar Radev, governor of the Bulgarian National Bank, says his institutions independence is more than a slogan. I dont just support the principle, I think were a good example, he tells the Financial Times. Mr Radev, 61, took up his post in July 2015, one year after the collapse of Corporate Commercial Bank, then the nations fourth-largest lender, plunged Bulgaria into its worst financial turmoil since a currency and banking crisis in 1996-97. In Corpbanks collapse, unsound lending practices and poor prudential regulation came to light (as they had in 1996-97), and in July 2017 prosecutors indicted two former deputy central bank governors for failing to carry out their professional duties with regard to supervision. (Sixteen others were also indicted.) When I took this position, we reviewed very carefully the events in 2014 and the role of the central bank, says Mr Radev. There were two main conclusions. First, our banking supervision practices were not strong enough to prevent events like Corporate Commercial Bank. Second, we totally lacked the proper institutional framework to resolve crises like this. So banking supervision has been a major priority... The Corporate Commercial Bank collapse was an important lesson not only for the central bank, but for the political class and the nations institutions.The International Monetary Fund, where Mr Radev worked in the fiscal affairs department before his appointment, recognises the progress achieved under the new governor. In a review of the Bulgarian economy published on December 14, the IMF praised a reform that placed decision-making authority in the central bank at the level of its governing council. The BNB needs to quickly put in place procedures for a smooth transition to the new governance model, and ensure that the new collective process does not hamper decision-making. We appreciate that this is a major task, the IMF said. There is no question, Bulgaria should do much more to strengthen basic institutions Dimitar Radev Now the central bank is building up a dedicated resolution fund which Mr Radev says should account, by 2024, for 2 per cent of the banking systems covered deposits. At the systemic level, the Bulgarian banking system is very solid. Capital adequacy and liquidity ratios are higher than the EU average. Profitability is high by historical standards and close to the pre-crisis level [before 2009] for the second year in a row, Mr Radev says. According to private sector bankers, one lingering concern is the uncertainty surrounding First Investment Bank, now Bulgarias fourth-largest lender. After an asset quality review in 2016, the central bank asked First Investment Bank to undertake measures such as a recapitalisation, offloading riskier assets and strengthening governance. Unlike United Bulgarian Bank, whose acquisition by KBC of Belgium was completed in June, First Investment Bank has not yet found a buyer. We can expect some news in this direction, probably, says Mr Radev. Mr Radev is also hard at work preparing Bulgaria for possible entry into the eurozone. We do a lot of stuff that is under the radar but very important. We stepped up our analytical work, including with regard to the benefits and costs of integration into the EU financial infrastructure. We keep our payments system fully in line with the eurozones requirements. We maintain the highest quality of statistics.Some policymakers at the European Central Bank and in eurozone capitals think it would be premature to admit Bulgaria as the currency unions 20th member, citing the nations low income levels and the deficiencies of its judicial system. But Mr Radev observes that Bulgaria broadly meets the so-called Maastricht criteria on public debt, budget deficits, low inflation and long-term interest rates. The question is whether this, in itself, is sufficient to justify Bulgaria joining the club. There are two schools of thought. One, that if a country meets the criteria, it should not be blocked, Mr Radev says. The other is that the broader state of public institutions should be taken into account. Its not a black and white issue. There is no question, Bulgaria should do much more to strengthen basic institutions, not least the judiciary. But other institutions are solid... It remains to be seen how things will evolve. Probably, there will be an appropriate combination of these two approaches.In Bulgarias favour is its use since 1997 of a currency board, tying the lev to the D-Mark and then to the euro. The currency board arrangements have never been compromised, in good or bad times, even during the global financial crisis, Mr Radev notes. Would Mr Radev serve a second six-year term as governor? I focus on what needs to be done... Well see. I went to the IMF for one year and ended up staying 15 years. All original text can be read HYPERLINK "

Title: Publication in the Quarterly Bulletin of the Association of Banks in Bulgaria
Subtitle: PROSPECTS AND EXPECTATIONS FOR THE BANKING SECTOR IN 2018
text: Publication of Mr. Dimitar Radev, BNB Governor, in the Quarterly Bulletin of the Association of Banks in Bulgaria, issue 52, January 2018 PROSPECTS AND EXPECTATIONS FOR THE BANKING SECTOR IN 2018 The past 2017 confirmed the positive trends in Bulgarias banking system. The profit in the sector approached historically high levels since before the global crisis. The capital adequacy and liquidity indicators remained high, exceeding the EU averages. Banks lending increased and non-performing loans continued to decline. The assessment of the sectors position is also complemented by the generally good implementation of the measures undertaken by individual credit institutions after the asset quality review and stress test in 2016. The 2018 prospects for banks remain positive against the background of favourable developments in the macroeconomic environment. In the latest forecast of the Bulgarian National Bank we are expecting the real GDP growth to exceed 4% in 2018, due primarily to private consumption growth. The average annual rate of unemployment is projected to remain below 6%. The expected boost of economic activity and improved economic profile of borrowers combined with continuing low interest rates will help further strengthen bank lending to non-financial corporations and households. At the same time, banks should use the more favourable environment to address challenges inherited from the years of economic crisis or accompanying the restored credit activity. From the perspective of the Bulgarian National Bank as a regulator and supervisor of the banking sector, the focus of commercial banks management should be on the following three areas: First, the low interest rates on the banks asset operations, and limited options for optimization of costs on the liability side of banks balance sheets, will continue to put pressure on profitability. Increasing the volume of lending remains a principal means of increasing revenues, as long as the net interest income remains the key element in the structure of net operating income (according to the latest data its share is 71% at system level). Second, gross non-performing loans in Bulgaria are adequately covered by impairments and capital surplus; however their share remains above the EU average. Banks efforts to reduce non-performing loans in their balance sheets, including by selling portfolios with such loans, are therefore appropriate. According to monetary statistics data, in 2017 loans worth BGN 360 million were sold in the banking system. The reduction in non-performing loans continues. According to the most recent supervisory data for November 2017 the share of gross non-performing loans has reached 11% and the share of net non-performing loans  5.8%. We expect these positive trends to continue in 2018. Third, the growth in lending requires high attention on credit risk. The times of credit expansion are also times of accumulating a potential for future realisation of credit risk and emergence of new assets of problematic quality. The issue is particularly relevant given the perspective of entering a new rising interest rate cycle in the medium-term. Achieving individual objectives, related to credit growth or market share indicators, should not compromise the adequate evaluation and management of credit risk. The stable condition and potential of the Bulgarian banking sector implies higher investors interest. We may well see during the year more transactions involving transformation of bank ownership in our country, including through mergers or acquisitions. That could bring about further consolidation in the sector based on market mechanisms  a process to which the Bulgarian National Bank has declared support on numerous occasions. Above all, acquisitions or increase of qualified holdings require good preparation and responsibility of investors, shareholders and managers of credit institutions. Next in terms of commitment in the procedures come the relevant public institutions and authorities, among which is the Bulgarian National Bank. The specific and important role of banking supervision in such decisions stems from the need to provide respective prudential assessments. The Bulgarian National Bank will continue to be governed in the process by the respective legal provisions and the strict implementation of the Law on Credit Institutions and the applicable Guidelines of the European supervisory authorities, in particular.

Title: Interview published in Views. The EUROFI Magazine disseminated during The Eurofi High Level Seminar 2018 held in Sofia
Subtitle:
EVOLUTION OF MONETARY POLICIES AND
INTEGRATION OF THE EU BANKING MARKETS
text: Interview with the BNB Governor Mr. Dimitar Radev published in Views. The EUROFI Magazine disseminated during The Eurofi High Level Seminar 2018 held in Sofia, 25 - 27 April 2018 EVOLUTION OF MONETARY POLICIES AND INTEGRATION OF THE EU BANKING MARKETS How are monetary policies and tools likely to evolve within the EU in the foreseeable future? The monetary policy normalization is not generally questioned. Indeed, the ECB unconventional measures allowed the euro area banking sector to sail safe, avoiding a liquidity drain. However, keeping such measures for very long might have unfavourable consequences. Banks may become accustomed to accommodative financing conditions and easy access to liquidity, postponing necessary restructuring or strengthening of their balance sheets. Therefore, the remaining issue is not the direction in which monetary policies would evolve, but rather the pace of normalization. Broadly speaking, future steps will depend on two major factors: economic developments and inflation dynamics. On the one hand, we are already witnessing a broad-based economic expansion and a decline in unemployment in the EU, which may require phasing-out the unconventional monetary policy measures sooner than later. On the other hand, economic expansion has not yet translated into higher underlying inflation that may justify continuation of monetary stimulus. Under the circumstances, the process of monetary policy normalization should be gradual, dependent on both broader economic developments and inflation dynamics, and carefully communicated. As for the policy tools, further recalibration of the asset purchase program may be expected until the ECB sees a sustained adjustment in the path of inflation consistent with its inflation target. As currently communicated, the reinvestment of the principal payments from maturing securities purchased under the program would continue after the end of net purchases for an extended period of time. The sentiment of market participants is that the ECB would change the forward guidance on the interest rates later this year before increasing them around the middle of 2019. It is reasonable to expect that the evolution of monetary policy conditions in the non-euro area EU member states, such as Bulgaria, will generally follow the developments in the euro area. Otherwise, a widening of the interest rate differential vis-a-vis the euro area may give rise to volatility in capital flows and exchange rates within the EU. Depending on the specific economic and inflation developments the pace of monetary policy normalization may differ, but not significantly, across those countries. In Bulgaria, more specifically, the monetary stance under the currency board arrangements will remain strongly influenced by the ECB monetary policy. How to rebuild enough monetary policy firepower within the EU in order to deal with a potential future crisis? Our recent experience suggests that we need flexible and complementary policy measures to effectively deal with a crisis. The ECB response to the global crisis was well managed and precisely scaled. The risks of a liquidity collapse and complete disintegration of financial markets were avoided. However, in the midst of the crisis the monetary policy measures were supported by fiscal measures, as well as by urgent decisions to shape and implement structural reforms in different sectors of the economy. The lesson we learned was that it was erroneous to place all expectations for economic recovery and sustainability in the monetary policy basket. Monetary policy can be effective in dealing with a crisis only if supported by other economic policy instruments. Looking forward, the standard monetary policy measures can mitigate cyclical fluctuations in the economy in the short run. However, their longer-term effectiveness in alleviating the impact of a crisis or stimulating economic growth would depend on the overall resilience and flexibility of the economy. The latter are conditional on policies that are outside the mandate and tools of central banks, and involves a wide set of fiscal and structural policy measures. As of today, the low inflation rate remains a challenge to the monetary policy suggesting continuation of the ECB low interest rates policy while the acceleration of economic growth, driven by domestic demand, might signal an accumulation of overheating pressures in some euro area countries, and perhaps requiring non-monetary policy interventions. In a more strategic context, having the worst of the global crisis behind us, now is the time to rebuild buffers, to restructure and strengthen institutions, and to streamline regulations. To this end, the staged broad-based reforms in banking sector regulation, fiscal policy, labour and product markets should be completed as perceived. Specific priorities are well known and include further deepening of the EMU by: completing the Banking Union; building a Capital Markets Union; continuing with fiscal consolidation and filling up fiscal buffers; and further developing a sound crisis-prevention framework. How to address the obstacles that hinder further integration of the EU banking markets? And is there a need to restore trust between the national supervisors? The Bulgarian Presidency of the Council of the EU places strong emphasis on the completion of the Banking Union and the continuing work on the development of the Capital Markets Union. These are landmark institutional changes in the EMU providing an essential response to fragmentation in the EU single market in financial services. Financial integration is not an end in itself but a means for an efficient and sustainable monetary union. The remaining fragmentation in the EU banking sector, more specifically, remains a challenge for the increasingly integrated EU economy. Moreover, if banks assets are weakly diversified across member states they are prone to country-specific shocks, and if losses are incurred they will mostly be borne by creditors, investors or ultimately national budgets. In this context, the key priority is to complete the Banking Union. EU financial integration also requires, and will be facilitated by, convergence in the regulatory standards and practices of supervision. Since 2011 the European Banking Authority has contributed substantially to the creation of the European Single Rulebook in banking. More recently, the Single Supervisory Mechanism and the Single Resolution Mechanism have centralised decision-making in the respective areas, also providing the framework for intensive and efficient cooperation between national authorities in both the euro area and non-euro area member states. The multitude of currently working supervisory and resolution colleges in the EU give plenty of examples for very good cooperation. In this context, the slowing down of financial integration in the aftermath of the global crisis does not necessarily reflect a lack of trust between national authorities. Still, there is a need to further enhance cooperation, nationally and across borders. The recent crisis gave us important insights into details of supervisory and economic policies and practices that had been hard to see in normal times. Equipped with new knowledge and experience now, we should be capable of better responding to a crisis in the future. PAGE \* MERGEFORMAT 1

Title: Statement during the meeting of the Board of the European Banking Federation, held in Sofia
text: Statement by Mr Dimitar Radev, Governor of the BNB, during the meeting of the Board of the European Banking Federation, held in Sofia on 18 May 2018 Dear colleagues, Thank you for inviting me to attend your Board meeting and say a few introductory words. The European Banking Federation is among the most representative and influential industry associations in Europe. It unites more than 30 national banking associations, including the Association of Banks in Bulgaria, which celebrated its 25th anniversary last year, and with which we maintain an excellent relationship. I will shortly touch upon two issues: the overall environment for banks in Europe, and the latest developments in the Bulgarian banking sector. When referring to the overall environment I mean a couple of things. First, I would refer to the broader economic environment in Europe, which is positive. We are witnessing a broad-based economic expansion (although with some moderation recently) and banks play a fundamental role in financing this expansion. Still, economic environment is currently somewhat transitional  the stabilization and restored lending growth are behind us, while ahead of us central banks monetary policy normalization is anticipated with the associated forthcoming cycle of increasing interest rates. These processes require banks renewed attention, among other things, to the proper management of various types of risk. Another important dimension is the regulatory and institutional environment in the EU in the area of financial services, where work is still underway. Some of the banking industrys current concerns are understandable  the ongoing work and the lack of clarity on important issues are not exactly the predictable and supportive environment banks need. To address the remaining issues, the Bulgarian Presidency of the Council of the EU puts strong emphasis on the finalisation of key steps in banking regulation reforms. The priorities of our Presidency include completing the Banking Union, reaching the maximum possible balanced compromise on the risk reduction package, and building the Capital Markets Union. Your agenda today is focused on important details regarding the current steps in these areas, including the risk reduction package, the implementation of the new global prudential standards, and the European Supervisory Authorities Review. I do believe, your deliberations will provide an important further input on behalf of the industry to the ongoing discussions. To sum up on this issue, banks play a critical role in financing current economic expansion, but to continue to do this properly they need stability and predictability with respect to both their own balance sheets and operations, which is largely in their own hands, and the institutional and regulatory environment in which they function, which is a key responsibility of policymakers and regulators. Let me now turn to the latest developments in the banking sector in Bulgaria. The banking sector in Bulgaria is operating in a generally favourable environment. The economy is doing well with one of the highest GDP growth rates in the EU for the last couple of years. The budget is balanced and the debt-to-GDP ratio is the third lowest in the EU. There is increased focus on the structural reform agenda, as its implementation was lagging behind. Within this broader context, the banking sector performance remains strong with a positive effect on economic expansion. Capital adequacy and liquidity stay above the EU averages, and loans to the non-government sector continue growing. In addition, the banking sector is making good progress on a number of specific issues. Let me mention a few of them. Non-performing loans (NPLs), a legacy issue from previous years, are going down. At the end of March the share of gross NPLs and advances in the banking system was 9.3%, down from 17% at the end of 2014. The share of net NPLs and advances, representing the potential credit risk in the bank balance sheets (calculated after deducting the impairments already incurred), was 4.6% at the end of the first quarter. At a system level, net NPLs and advances are also fully covered by the capital excess over the 8% regulatory minimum and the mandatory capital buffers. Our sector has smoothly introduced IFRS 9. The effects, however, continue to be a matter of BNBs attention. Last year we were monitoring banks preparedness and action plans for the forthcoming IFRS 9 requirements. Now we are at the stage of reviewing and evaluating banks disclosure practices in connection with the implementation of this new standard. We have transposed the Payment Services Directive (PSD 2) into Bulgarian law since March. Furthermore, both regulations and supervisory practices related to payment services are being overhauled as the BNB is adopting a number of guidelines of the European Banking Authority. I may go on with the Bulgarian banking highlights, but I will stop here. Fundamentally, the processes in our banking sector are part of the pan-European context and our banks face similar challenges, including with regard to the regulatory environment, challenges that will be discussed in detail during todays Board meeting. Let me finally wish you a very successful working event. Thank you for your attention! ____________ The statement was published in the ABB Quarterly Bulletin, issue 53, May 2018 and can be seen HYPERLINK " " here.

Title: Foreword to the 2018 OMFIF Global Public Investor
Subtitle: THE IMPORTANT JOURNEY TO EURO ACCESSION
text: Foreword of BNB Governor Dimitar Radev to the 2018 OMFIF Global Public Investor, published on 23 May 2018 THE IMPORTANT JOURNEY TO EURO ACCESSION Bulgaria must translate strong economic recovery into durable convergence The joint themes of reform and transition run through this years OMFIF Global Public Investor. The international economy, after almost a decade of recovery from the 2008-09 crisis, may be approaching a turning point, while the world as a whole has to weather the changes wrought by the shifts in US foreign policy and the rise of China. As a future member of the European single currency, Bulgaria is keenly interested in euro area reforms. Within this broader context, the completion of the banking union, for instance, is among the priorities of the Bulgarian presidency of the Council of the European Union in the first half of 2018. At the same time, we are well aware that if we want Bulgaria to be a full-fledged participant in the reform process at the European level, we need to further deepen our own reform agenda. We need to translate our strong economic recovery into durable real convergence. Indeed, Bulgarias macroeconomic performance is solid. Monetary stability has been in place for over two decades. The exchange rate is fixed to the euro and the currency board is uncompromised in both good and bad times, even during the 2008 financial crisis. Bulgaria keeps a broadly balanced budget and is reputed to have the third-lowest debt-to-GDP ratio in the EU. The banking sector is robust, with capital adequacy and liquidity exceeding the EU averages. It is logical to expect that a country with such a record should not be blocked, but rather welcomed to start its journey towards joining the euro area through the participation of the lev, the national currency, in the exchange rate mechanism II. The actual timing of euro adoption will depend less on the nominal Maastricht convergence criteria, which Bulgaria has been meeting broadly for many years, and more on the real convergence of the economy. There are structural and institutional policies that need to be implemented and consistently pursued, in order to speed up real convergence. Thus the process of euro area accession, starting with the participation of the national currency in the ERM II, will be a catalyst for further improvements, adjustments and reforms. All of this will ultimately be beneficial for the economy, irrespective of whether we are in or still out. The journey is at least as important as reaching the final destination. The same holds true for many Global Public Investors that OMFIF highlights in this 2018 edition, which I am sure will fulfil its purpose of spreading better public investment practices worldwide. Dimitar Radev is Governor of the Bulgarian National Bank. ____________ You may download the whole report HYPERLINK " . PAGE \* MERGEFORMAT 1

Title: Publication to the Euromoney Yearbook: Global Banking & Policy Review 2018
text: Publication by BNB Governor Dimitar Radev to the Euromoney Yearbook: Global Banking & Policy Review 2018, 19 October 2018 In recent years the euro area had to deal with the dual pressure of effects from the global financial crisis and its own structural challenges. In response to that, the euro area needed to design and implement a multitude of institutional reforms. Although Bulgaria is not a member of the euro area yet, its reforms do matter for us because of both their global impact and our commitment to join the European Monetary Union. Adopting the euro is an obligation under the EU Accession Treaty and a long-standing objective for Bulgaria. Further to the formal part of it, Bulgarian membership of the euro area may benefit both sides. On the one hand, Bulgaria may contribute to the strength and stability of the euro area. The country has displayed an impressive track record of practically meeting the nominal Maastricht convergence criteria for many years. For example, Bulgarias prudent public financial management produced broadly balanced budgets for most of the past two decades. As of today, Bulgarias debt-to-GDP ratio is the third-lowest in the EU. Therefore, adding one more voice of common sense in dealing with the public financial management issues in the euro area would be a good thing for everybody. On the other hand, the very process of acceding to the euro area invigorates the policymaking and mobilises the institutions in Bulgaria. The related reform efforts are geared towards speeding up the real euro area convergence of our national economy. Given the upsides of Bulgaria becoming part of the euro area, is the process taking too long? The answer lies beyond the assessment of how the various convergence criteria are being met. Today, Bulgarias overall preparedness is analysed from the perspective of the euro areas own lessons from the recent financial crisis. The Banking Union is a new key segment of the euro areas architecture, non-existent only a few years ago. Also, areas such as institutional quality and governance have been acknowledged as important factors in the macroeconomic performance. Nowadays, an applicant aspiring to join the euro area and its Single Supervisory Mechanism ought to prove, among other things, the strength of its financial system as well as the quality and efficiency of its institutions. That is the rationale behind the recently announced new approach to be applied in the case of Bulgaria with respect to the process of the Bulgarian levs participation in the Exchange Rate Mechanism II (ERM II). In line with these new developments, the Bulgarian authorities undertook various commitments to implement measures and policies which should ensure a smooth transition to joining simultaneously the ERM II and the Banking Union. Bulgarias new road to full-fledged euro area membership will lead us through so far uncharted territory, including the use of the mechanism of close cooperation. There may be risks of both external and domestic origin, affecting the progress towards the euro adoption in Bulgaria. These are concerns which are well-acknowledged and rather explicable. Richer in experience and institutionally evolved, the euro area of today is different from a decade ago. That is why, any future euro area enlargement will be different from the past. ____________ You may download the whole report HYPERLINK " . PAGE \* MERGEFORMAT 1

Title: Interview published in "24 Hours"
text: Interview with the Manager of the BNB Mr. Dimitar Radev, published in "24 Hours", p. 14 and 15, 20 October 2018. ENTERING THE BANKING UNION AND THE EXCHANGE RATE MECHANISM WILL NOT CHANGE THE EXISTING MONETARY REGIME Highlights : There will be a change only after our adoption in the euro area, but it will not lead to the release of reserves. Credit growth is good for the economy, but it increases the credit risk that will occur when the economic situation changes. It is indicative that the level of non-performing loans of 17% at the end of 2014 is already below 9% with a trend of continuing reduction. The ECB has two recommendations for the independence of the BNB. We are looking for a solution to the first one that fits the constitution, as far asparliament and the president are talking. We have prepared a proposal for legislative changes to impose, where appropriate, measures on banks' credit activities. There is no danger of high inflation under the monetary regime. However, let's not forget that the main factor for it in bulgaria is international prices. "The exact timing of the adoption of the euro will depend not so much on the Maastricht criteria for nominal convergence, which we have largely met for many years, but on the real convergence of the economy." These are your words before we have a yes from Brussels and Frankfurt, Mr Radev. Is the second condition already in place? It takes time for that. Our economy is growing at a higher rate than the economies of developed countries, but we are moving from a low level andwe still have a path to go. "The lesson we learned was that it is wrong to put all our expectations of economic recovery and sustainability in the monetary policy basket." At supranational level, there is a good understanding, at least within the EU, that needs to be supported by real action. However, the answer would be different at country level. There are still examples of irrational fiscal and structural measures in some countries. I asked if it was scientific, because authoritative institutions of the imf and SB rank imply that a new crisis is coming. "It's not raining yet, but it's already growling," Christine Lagarde said these days. Do you see any dangerous symptoms? There are signs of a slowdown in global economic growth. Normal cyclicality of the global economy is further burdened with uncertainty related tointernational trade, emerging markets and Brexit. "Bad loans are piling up in good times," you said at the start ofthis year. Credit activity in the country has increased at an increasing rate over the past three years. This is good for the economy, but it also increases the credit risk that will manifest itself in changing the economic situation. Or if I have to continue the words of Christine Lagarde, it is good to take care of the roof beforeit is even raining. Will our banks "get away" with just warnings? Will bnb's credit risk management and capital buffer decisions prove sufficient? We have actually taken two groups of action. First, we decided to activate the countercyclical capital buffer next year. In fact, we have prepared a proposal for legislative changes to impose, where appropriate, measures on banks' credit activities. What is the purpose of the two measures? What will it show you that they are already working? In short, these are preventive measures aimed at both preventing potential excessive indebtedness of borrowers and increasing banks' resilience to losses in future materialisation of credit risk. We are prepared to impose additional measures if these prove insufficient to achieve the objective set. Credit growth has surpassed that of income and GDP. How do you determine the levels that are dangerous and when does the BNB intervene as it has done? This is based on a methodology that we have published. When will the direction of the trend turn and at what rate? Will it happen before banks "get used to stimulating financing and easy access to liquidity, delaying restructuring or strengthening their balance sheets," I quote you? In general, banks are adapting well to changing conditions. We have, including ongoing, examples of continued restructuring and strengthening of their balance sheets. It is indicative that the level of non-performing loansof 17% at the end of 2014 is now below 9% with a continuing decrease. Will they be able to recalibrate people and companies that have taken out long-term debt? Your advice to them? All participants in the credit process  banks, companies and households  are responsible for the decisions they make. The central bank is implementing so-called macro-prudential measures to limit overall creditrisk. Is there a danger that the BNB will lose control of inflation. There are such implicit concerns both outside and in our country. And it is now important not only for the economy, but also for our entry into the euro area? There is no such danger under the money regime. However, it should not be taken into account that the main factor for inflation in our country is international prices, above all energy prices atthe moment. How do you solve this seemingly paragraph 22 - in order to grow the economy, you need a fresh financial resource, it carries risks, and sometimes it accumulates the potential for crises? The shortest answer is - through good business projects. How are the negotiations going, BNB- ECB? How will the supervision of the banks working in our country be shared and where will it be recorded, in law? This is not about negotiations, it is about working together expert teams working on several main topics: the regulatory framework, banking supervision, the bank resolution regime. There has also been good progress on these topics. For example, the draft legislative changes related to the exercise of supervisory activities have been finalised at expert level and we expect to receive a formal opinion from the ECB soon. Some say the ECB will "report" the five biggest ban ki and enter the rest when it decides. Others argue that the ECB can "enter" when and wherever it decides, i.e. in all banks. The organization and conduct of supervisory activities in Bulgaria under the terms of the Banking Union will not differprinces from the way in which this activity is organized and carried out in the euro area countries. Our entry into the banking union goes through stress tests and asset valuation. They will also be an assessment of your team that has already conducted them. Do you expect manydifferent oesults now and in what direction? We are currently discussing the scope, administrative procedure and other details of this assessment to be carried out by the ECB next year. I don't expect systemic problems if that's what you're asking me about, but the indie results will be different compared to the 2016 review, which took place on a data-based basis towards the end of2015, while the new review will be conducted on a data basis towards the end of 2018. that we have launched and are working with the ECB on this project. On the occasion of our membership of the banking union, there were quite divergent claims about the so-called "no-go zones". mechanism for close cooperation. And criticism of why we accepted it. What kindof negatives does he bring us? We as a central bank strongly support the idea of the banking union, but we have had occasions to express certain reservations regarding the near-cooperation mechanism that regulates the order of accession to the EU of non-euro area countries. They are mainly related to possible imbalances inthe decision-making process and access to liquidity and capital support. This discussion is now behind us. We are now actively working with our partners, so that this prozzes run smoothly. Have you already consulted frankfurt plans on how to release the reserves that now guarantee the currency board? If you think this could be a topic of broader debate, share them? This is not at all a topic of debate in our joint work on this project. Joining the Banking Union and the exchange rate mechanism will practically nothing change the existing monetary regime and the management of foreign exchange reserves. A change in the monetary regimewill not be made until after our adoption in the euro area, but it will not lead to the release of the reserves. Your forecast of the time horizon in which we entered both the banking union and the waiting room as we requested? What could disrupt the implementation of the roadmap? This will take at least a few years. At this stage, we have an indicative deadline of about one year to take the first step - joining the Banking Union and the exchange rate mechanism. I would like to stress that for us the main priority is the quality of the p rozz, not so specific deadlines. We are also aware that there are political and technical risks to the implementation of the project. Externally, the political risks are related to the lack in some countries of broad public support and enthusiasm for the enlargement of the euro area, but internally with the possibility of using the topic not to consolidate efforts, political speculation and opposition. Such a process of joining the euro area is being implemented for the first time. This also raises many additional technical issues, but they are resolved. What awaits us once the eurozone door opens - a "paradise" full of cheap resources, for example, or "hell" with hard-to-control inflation? Is the BNB resource to cope with both challenges? We are looking forward to new higher and more complex responsibilities for realising the opportunities for economic and social prosperity that membership of the euro area would provide. This exceeds the mandate of the BNB and requires a nationwide effort. At the ECB's insistence, the independence of the BNB, and the governor in particular, will be guaranteed by law. Insistence comes after signals from here of pressure, or simply advice, say from the executive, or just a routine rule for the euro area that applies to everyone? Theindependentness of the BNB and the governor in particular is currently guaranteed by both the EU treaty and the Bulgarian legislation, and there are no changes here. which it does not currently exist. And secondly, to extend explicitly the scope of the existing ban on BNB funding the government and other public institutions, as well as to request and follow instructions from them, so that this ban applies to other governments and public institutions throughout the EU, including the EC. Lawyers are seeking a decision on the first recommendation that complies with the constitution, as far as parliament and thepresident have decided, and the second recommendation is indisputable and legislative changes on it have already been prepared. Title: Interview published in the Banker newspaper
Subtitle: ERM
text: Interview with the Manager of the BNB Mr. Dimitar Radev, published in banker newspaper, issue 48/2018, p. 6 and 7, 30 November 2018 BULGARIA MUST ENTER BOTH THE BANKING UNION AND ERM II Highlights: Bulgaria's entry into the Banking Union and exchange rate mechanism first, and in the longer term to the euro area will not lead to an increase in price indices. BNB will apply mandatory requirements to banks related to their relations with theborrowers. An imminent reversal of the interest rate cycle, possibly coupled with delayed economic activity, will lead to more credit risk accumulating and realising in bank balance sheets. However, the share of non-performing loans and advances in our banking system exceeds the EUand euro area average. Mr. Radev, the government engages Bulgaria with a serious effort to enter the Banking Union and theSingle Supervisory Mechanism as conditions for the admission of our country to ERM II. How will the supervisory commitments between the ECB and BNB be allocated upon Bulgaria's entry into the Banking Union? This is a simultaneous act of the country's accession to the Banking Union and the inclusion of the Bulgarian lev in the ERM II exchange rate mechanism. The Single Supervisory Mechanism (SSM) is one element of theso-called banking union. Our accession to the Banking Union should be realised by establishing the so-called closecooperation with the ECB. This is the mechanism for membership of the Banking Union for a non-euro area country. In the case of membership of the Single Supervisory Mechanism of the Banking Union, through close cooperation, the BNB will implement the ECB's supervisory decisions, and the BNBwill issue the relevant acts. The supervisory commitments of the ECB and the BNB will be distributed in the same way that they are distributed between the ECB and the supervisory authorities of the euro area countries, namely the ECB will directly supervise the so-called significant banki  usually the three largest banks, which can be expanded and the BNB will directly supervise the other banks. Like euro area countries, the ECB will also exercise common control over supervisory practices. Will there be any impacton the management of the currency reserve and the issue policy of the BNB the possible entry of Bulgaria into the Banking Union? Not. text: Interview with the Manager of the BNB Mr. Dimitar Radev from the show "The day begins with Georgi Lyubenov" on BNT, December 9, 2018. In an interview with the Bulgarian National Television for the show "The day begins with Georgi Lyubenov" the Governor of the BNB Mr. Dimitar Radev commented on the upcoming assessment of the quality of the assets and stress tests of the banks in Bulgaria, which will be carried out by the European Central Bank (ECB) with the assistance of the Bulgarian National Bank with a view to the process of joining the ERM II exchange rate mechanism and the banking union through close cooperation with the ECB. issues related to the development of bank lending, consolidation in the sector, interest, economic growth, investment and savings. Early next year, an in-depth assessment of the banks in bulgaria will be carried out. The banking sector has been in improving conditioning for the last three years, 2018 is no exception, said the Governor of the BNB. What we arecurrently doing, in coordination with our partners, including the ECB, ensures a smooth running of the process. cooperation between the ECB and the BNB, which will be no different from the developmentof these activities in the euro area. With regard to the monetary regime, there will be no grounds for excessive inflation. This does not mean that prices will remain constant as long as we are in the process of real convergence, which means approaching the average levels in Europe of both income and prices, according to Dimitar Radev. Title: Interview published in the magazine "Manager"
text: Interview of the Manager of the BNB Mr. Dimitar Radev, published in the magazine "Manager", issue 1/2014 1, 2019. IT DEPENDS MOST ON THE ECONOMY WHEN WE ADOPT THE EURO Mr. Radev, how will the combination of raising interest rates and slowing economic growth affect the banking system? Are there a possibility of unpleasant surprises for banks in 2019 and how do you see the economic development in the country? Our banking system has welcomed 2019 in very good conditioning, with high capital adequacy and liquidity. Profitability is at a historically high level. Overall, the positive development of the banking system is expected to continue. In addition, over the last few yearswe have been paying attention to the fact that banks are accumulating more and more credit risk. This risk can materialise in both a general rate hike and a slowdown in economic activity. BNB has already taken concrete action in this area. For example, we have decided to activate this year's countercyclical capital buffer. In addition, we proposed legal changes for the introduction of an additional toolbox of measures regarding the creditactivity of banks, for example restrictions on the ratio between credit and collateral or between credit and income ofthe borrower. This type of measure aims to better protect both borrowers and their lenders in the face of banks. In the context of the macroeconomic environment, recent indications are growing that the international situation is about to go through a less good period than in recent years. At what stage are we in the consolidation of the banking system and how many and what banks will operate in our country when we enter the euro area? The acceleration of the consolidation process in the banking sector in Bulgaria is a fact. We are witnessing major transactions in the acquisition and merger of banks. They change the distribution of ownership structure in the sector and market shares. Today's market conditions require increasing efficiency on the part of market participants, which stimulates consolidation processes. These processes will determine the optimal number of credit institutions in Bulgaria. BNB has traditionally supported the consolidation of thesec fertilizer  on a market basis and without artificial stimulation by regulatory or administrative means. To what extent are we ready to enter the ERM II exchange rate mechanism? How will this process change the banking system? Bulgaria is currently following the steps described in the action plan related to the intention of joiningERM II and the Banking Union. Froman operational point of view, the ERM II stage should have a neutral effect  at least in so far as it will not lead to a change in monetary regime and monetary policy in Bulgaria. It is extremely important for us to reach the agreement agreed last summer with our European partners both accession of Bulgaria to the Banking Union and the inclusion of BGN in the ERM II exchange rate mechanism. At the same time, I stress that the focus on Bulgaria's accession to the Banking Union and the inclusion of the Bulgarian lev in the ERM II exchange rate mechanism cannot be focused only on the activities of the BNB and the asset quality review and stress tests carried out by the European Central Bank. In today's situation, as required by what we have accepted as a commitment to comply, as a candidate to join ERM II and the Single Supervisory Mechanism, we need to demonstrate, in additionto the stability of our entire financial system, which also includes the non-banking financial sector, the quality and effectiveness of public institutions. After membership of ERM II, we should also apply for our admission to the euroarea a. Is a realistic accelerated scenario in which in just a few years the euro will replace the BGN? You know that the adoption of the euro is both our obligation under the Treaty of Accession to the European Union and a long-standing strategic objectiveof Bulgaria. The adoption of the euro in Bulgaria will happen when Bulgaria is ready and evaluated as ready. The date is not important, but the preparation process itself - for us the main priority is the quality of the process, not the search for specific deadlines. Structural and institutional policies need to be implemented in our country to create the conditions for accelerated and sustainable growth that brings our economy closer to euro area levels. For years, we have been largely meeting the Maastricht criteria for non-industrial convergence. The so-called real convergence, which is linked to the economy moving closer to the European average, remains a challenge for us. Our economy is growing at a higher rate than the euro area average, but we are going from a low level. The real convergence of the Bulgarian economy will depend most heavily on the exact moment of adoption of the euro. Convergence towards prices in the euro area to what inflation do you expect it to lead to and what are the tools to manage it? The level of prices in Bulgaria in the medium term will continue to be determined mainly by international prices and by the dynamics in the labour market and not by the process of adopting the euro. and at prices. The market will continue to be the main price regulator in the process of joining the euro area. In this process, no price rise is expected under the monetary regime. We have a firm commitment to which we adhere strictly and it is to maintain the stability of the fixed exchange rate regime. The only way out of this regime is the adoption of the euro. How will businesses feel the pros of replacing the eurowith the euro? For an economy in which the monetary regime has been based on a fixed rate of national currency to the euro for two decades, the expected effects of adoptingthe ED currency should not be exaggerated. The individual economic agents and sectors in Bulgaria have been working in practice for a long time in a Euroized environment. It is important to continue to develop good business projects. One day after our entry into the Banking Union, how will the work of the BNB change? So far, what challenges does the central bank face? One of the important areas we are working on is synchronising our supervisory practices with the European Central Bank. In this respect, there are no particular challenges for us, this is a working process. as is now the the the place in the euro area countries. On the other hand, as I have repeatedly stressed, joining the Banking Union and ERM II will not change the work of the Bulgarian National Bank related to ourmain m andat and the management of our monetary regime. Title: Welcome speech at the opening of the 99th academic year of the University of National and World Economy
text: Welcome speech by the BNB Governor Mr. Dimitar Radev at the opening of the 99th academic year of the University of National and World Economy, 30 September 2019 In his welcome speech during the 99th academic year opening ceremony at the University of National and World Economy (UNWE), the BNB Governor Mr. Dimitar Radev spoke about the history of the BNB and the UNWE and the cooperation between the two institutions, the economic and financial challenges in our country, the ECBs non-conventional monetary policy, the BNB actions and the progress in implementing the strategic goal of joining the euro area. The global and European economy are slowing down amid a growing uncertainty associated with the world trade and the international political framework. External demand risks for a small and open economy like Bulgaria are coupled with the effects of the very low and negative interest rate levels in the euro area. The BNB analyses indicate that we are currently in an upturn of cyclic risks accumulation. This has motivated us to adopt some decisions, such as we have been among the first central banks to activate, increase in our case, the anticyclical capital buffer for banks, said the BNB Governor Radev. In 2018, we initiated legislative amendments, already approved by the National Assembly, expanding the so-called macroprudential powers of the BNB. Therefore, now we command a wide range of tools for implementing measures concerning banks credit activities, complementing the BNB traditionally applied measures with regard to bank capital. Our approach aims to ensure that credit activity stays at sound levels with respect to both the economy and banks, by keeping cyclic risks accumulation under control, the central banks Governor pointed out. These actions of the BNB are taking place within the wider context of our countrys joining the euro area. That is a strategic choice which should not be influenced by challenges related to the economic or political developments. Bulgaria has already made considerable progress. Our monetary regime allows the lev to join instantly and smoothly the Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM II). Our payment systems are set to euro area standards. The regulatory framework and the technical infrastructure for joining the Single Supervision Mechanism and the Single Resolution Mechanism are virtually in place. Even the fact that euro notes are already in print in Bulgaria demonstrates our technical capacity. Given the sound and disciplined fiscal stance of our country, Bulgaria has no concerns as regards the condition of its public finances, Mr. Radev was definite. The longer-term goal  joining the euro area  requires much effort to achieve the so-called real convergence, including in bringing the incomes in Bulgaria close to the EU average income. Mr. Radev highlighted that the initiative to join the Banking Union, the ERM II and the euro area started on the basis of a political act. The political factor will be present at each stage of the process. Our country is at a very good starting position, but at the same time the process of joining is taking place in a complicated environment of external risks and uncertainty, the BNB Governor summed up. In the Golden book of the UNWE, the BNB Governor wrote the following message: I believe that education is at the heart of every mans success. In a world of ever-increasing demands for knowledge and skills, this will be even more valid tomorrow than it is today. In recognition of the work and efforts of generations at the UNWE over the years, I am confident that the institution UNWE will continue to serve as an example of high-quality education in an increasingly competitive environment. text: Interview of the Manager of the BNB Mr. Dimitar Radev, published in "24 Hours" newspaper, p. 1. 14 - 15, 6 December 2019 THERE IS NO REASON TO EXPECT A GLOBAL CRISIS ON THE SCALE OF THAT FROM A DOZEN YEARS AGO Highlights : BNB's approach to banks is conservative to maintain higher capital. The ECB's monetary policy stimulus is a logical response to global and regional economic processes. What is being discussed today are the specific instruments and parameters of this policy. In order for this discussion to be constructive, it must be put in the context of two interconnected processes. clear definition and implementation of the necessary supportive steps in the field of fiscal and structural policies. The policy of low interest rates has both advantages and disadvantages. Especially for our country, it is an important factor in increased activity credit to support economic growth. But increased lending also creates an environment for the manifestation of cyclical risks d0 something that the BNB has expressed a position for many times. the stronger the potential to realise different risksd0 both in the economy and in banks. This requires preventivemeasures. "In good times, bad loans are piling up," you said at the beginning of the m.d., and you were right. Low interest rates and income growth are fueling appetite for loans and "accumulating systemic risk." You have activated the countercyclical buffer, will this prove to be enough, but as a measure, or will others be imposed? Activating and raising the level of the countercyclical capital buffer is an example of a preventive measure. However, this is part of a broader systemic approach of the BNB, which consists in the implementation of a policy that is adopted to be called macroprudential. Its main instruments traditionally applied by the BNB are the capital buffers of banks. In this respect, the approach of the BNB is conservative. In addition, the BNB has a practice of applying to banks additional individual caps. requirements. Last but not least, we have new legal options to require banks to impose restrictions on borrowers. Will the ecb's new lending rules, also approved by the BNB, change the lending mechanism? How? There are two groups of lending rules that have become part of our legal framework in recent years. Firstly, these are the guidelines of the European Banking Authority, which are valid for all EU countries and which the BNB has agreed to apply in Bulgaria. Secondly, the macroprudential powers of the BNB were strong, including by the possibility of imposing limits on the loan-to-collateral ratio or between credit and income of the borrower. existing capital andbanks is even better protection for both borrowers and banks. Was now the time to ask for membership in ERM-2? The situation is difficult and complex, full of unknowns. We think more about what will happen if we are cut off, but are there risks if they say yes. The participation of BGN in ERM-2 is not associated with risks. The aim of this mechanism is to stabilise the exchange rate of a national currency against the euro before the adoption ofthe country concerned in the euroarea. What will be the advantages, benefits of Bulgaria's membership in ERM-2? The direct effects of this first step towards the euro area will be the continued increase in the country's credit rating and the improvement of the external perception of the investment environment in Bulgaria. How will our partnership continue whenwe enter the Banking Union? Our partnership with the ECB is very active at this stage, but it willbe further strengthened after it is adopted in the Banking Union. the banks in Bulgaria and experts of the BNB will participate in the work of the Joint Supervisory Teams d0 both for the purposes of ongoing monitoring and risk assessment under remote supervision, as well as in inspections of banks operating in Bulgaria. BNB will retain re-supervisionof the other banks, but we will continuously exchange supervisory information with the ECB. The banking union is still like an unfinished house without all the rules. What pluses of our entry prevailed over the negative effects that we even tied thereception in the "waiting room" before the euro to it? The Banking Union will bring additional guarantees for the stability of our banking sector. It will also improve funding and lending conditions. The fact is that this is still an incomplete project, mainly in the deposit guarantee part. A better option forthe country is to be an active participant in the process of completing the Banking Union than a bystander.
