Title: Summary of a speech during the forum "Annual meeting of business with the government"
text: Summary of a speech by the Governor of the BNB Mr. Dimitar Radev during the forum "Annual meeting of business with the government", Sofia, 28 January 2020. In a speech during the XIV Annual Meeting of Business with the Government, the Governor of the BulgarianPeople's Republic of Bulgaria, Dimitar Radev, carried out a detailed review of the latest amendments to the Bulgarian legislation related to the accession to the ERM II exchange rate mechanism and commented on the strategic context of this process aimed at deepening bulgaria's European and non-integration. Compliance of the legislation is one of the most important factors in the process of joining ERM II and this explains the need for the latest changes in theBNB Act, Mr Radev said. The timeline of the events leading up to this initiative begins with the receipt at the end of 2019 of information from the lawyers of the European Central Bank and the European Commission that there is inconsistency between Bulgaria's legislative framework and theEuropean legal framework on exchange rates under the ERM II exchange rate mechanism. as in the current text of Art. 29 of the BNB Act. Mr. Radev said that this case has been known to us for years. Our position was to make sufficient progress before we took the necessary measures. "Now is the time for the veryfirst discrepancy in question to be remedied," the BNB governor added. The solution proposed by the central bank was to preserve the existing Art. 29, supplementing it with a new paragraph. This paragraph makes it possible to approve exchange rates after Bulgaria becomes a member of the exchange rate mechanismunder the European legal framework. The proposed change was agreed with the European Central Bank. The logistics of the legislative process are consistent with the fact thatthe BNB does not have the right to legis as an initiative. The Governor of the BNB stressed that this purely technical and procedural issue means that we are indeed in the final rights to join the currencymechanics. "Bulgaria is indeed now close to participating in euro area institutions. At the same time, this does not mean in any way a change in the currency board regime, a change in the level of the currency board, a change in our position", Mr. Radev stressed. partners abroad. Mr Radev strongly refuted the speculation that the proposed compliance of the Bulgarian legislation with the European legal framework opens the risk of a change in the existing fixed rate of BGN to the euro. The European Council resolution establishing an exchange rate mechanism in the third stage of Economic and Monetary Union Amsterdam, 16 June 1997 (97/C 236/03) restson the construction of floating exchange rates typical of most p liners at the time. be changed now in the case of Bulgaria. "Even if there is such a request, it cannot be realized because the differences within the exchange rate mechanism are taken by consensus, and this consensus includes two votes from Bulgaria  the Minister of Finance and the Governor of the Central Bank", explained Mr Radev. Within the exchange ratemechanism, the participants in the exchange rate process are euro area finance ministers, the European Central Bank and the ministers and governors of the central banks of countries that are members of the exchange rate mechanism but are not members of the euro area (now only Denmark has such status , but if we have the process successfully completed, Bulgaria will be the second country with such status). Concluding on the subject of the changes in the BNB Act, the Governor called for this legal and procedural issue not to be overexposedin a way that would undermine the country's position "at a very important stage of the accession process to the European Exchange Rate Mechanism and the Banking Union". Mr Radev summed up that Bulgaria is indeed close to a strategic breakthrough on the path of European integration. Before we are even a member of the euro area, our country can become a member of euro area institutions. These are the exchange rate mechanism and the two segments of the Banking Union - the Single Supervisory Mechanism and the Single Resolution Mechanism. These institutions belong to the "core" of the European Union and we are very close to this strategic breakthrough "regardless of our geographical situation", in the words of Mr Radev. "What's more," said the BNB governor, "as this process begins, things become very largely irreversible." What has been done in recent years allows us to be at a stage, until recently unachievable for Bulgaria. In response to a question about the European Central Bank's monetary policy launch review, the BNB Governor commented that the review is expected to be completed by the end of this year and will address many aspects beyond the sphere of interest rates. The review will also cover strategic issues related to the objectives and manner of monetary policy in the euro area. In parallel, Mr. Ra dev noted, the European Central Bank will continue to monitor and analyse the situation on a regular basis. The President of the European Central Bank has confirmed that they will act according to current developments and data in the euro area, and this does not preclude the movement of interest rates deeper into the negative territory. that while the strategic review is ongoing, monetary policy in the euro area "will not be on autopilot," Mr Radev said. According tothe BNB's head of government, at this stage it is difficult to expect sharp movements in interest rates in one direction or another. Transferred to Bulgaria, this topic is related to the issue of the credit activity of the banks and the general economic growth. The effects here are "rather positive", according to Mr. Radev, who added that these low interest rates also create serious credit risks and risks in terms of the profitability of the banks. BNB monitors credit processes and central bank decisions will be based on data analysis. Low interest rates in our country not only do not hinder creditactivation, but we are seeing exactly the opposite question  it is actively credited and this supports economic growth. "What we are trying to do and what we want commercial banks to do is manage this process so that the risks that are incorporated into the N ego are addressed in the best possible way," the BNB governor summed up. Title: Interview for Nova TV
text: Interview of Mr. Dimitar Radev, Governor of BNB, for Nova TV, 30 March 2020 The Governor of the Bulgarian National Bank Dimitar Radev in an interview with Nova TV stressed the stability of the banking sector in Bulgaria and predicted that borrowers will be able to rely on rescheduling payments. "We are definitely witnessingan unprecedented health crisis that is growing economically. In this situation, of course, words matter greatly, but actions are more important. Especially if we are talking about maintaining and using critical infrastructure, such as the banking sector", said Mr Radev. "The banking sector in bulgaria is currently in very good conditioning as a result of what has been done in recent years. Therefore, it can be said that he is ready for the current crisis, especially if we speak in a horizon of 3 to 6 months", said the Governor of the Bulgarian National Bank DimitarRadev and summarized that the banking sector is entering this crisis as part of the solution and not as part of the problem. "Our banking sector has in recent years underwent large-scale inspections, which also included an assessment of the quality of their assets and stress tests. Among the objectives of these stress tests was also to assess the sustainability of the banking sector in the face of an acute economic crisis", explained Dimitar Radev. The negative economic forecasts we used were hypothetical, but now they are happening. "What we do at the Bulgarian National Bank is to develop different scenarios for possible development and to assess, as far as possible, their effect on the banking system and the economy. We are developing these scenarios on the basis of new information, but it is too early to speculate on numbers at thisstage. "Commercial banks behave extremely adequately inthis area. They started working individually with their customers even before the state of emergency was declared. What will happen and it will be within the next week is to create an additional framework for such measures by commercial banks. At the heart of these measures is the introduction of a targeted and temporary moratorium postponing or suspending payments on bank loans", announced Mr Radev. "What the BNB cares a lot about, as we are an active participant in the process in our capacity as head of the Board of Supervisors ofthe European Banking Authority, is that there needs to be a pan-European approach on this issue", added the BNB Manager. "People with mortgage loans need to talk to the banks and this is precisely the purpose of the regulatory measures proposed by the BNB. To give additional flexibility, additional opportunities for commercial banks so that with this individual approach to their customers they do not fall into a more severe situation in terms of capital adequacy or credit risk management," the Central Bank governor said. For people with deposits, the BNB manager explained that they do not have much maneuverability, but their deposits are safe. The BNB Governor stressed that further strengthening of the capital and liquidity of commercial banks is being worked on. The package of measures already announced by the BNB amounts to over EUR 9 billion and BGN 300 million and these measures have for the most part already been implemented. "We treat all banksin Bulgaria in the same way," the BNB governor said. Asked how much calmer we would be if we were in the euro zone, the BNB governor explained: "We don't have a lender of last resort, like the ECB. This certainly puts us in a more personal position than the countries that are in the euro area and limits the measures we can take. We are likely to feel this stronger as the crisisunfolds, but also then when the consequences of the crisis have to be addressed. We made a mistake in the last global financial crisis, then we have taken a position to wait on this topic. We should not repeat this error once again, since the price for both people and business, this time it will be significantly higher,the Governor of the Central Bank said. The crisis that is currently starting is taking us away from the euro in the sense that the deadlines for implementing the first step, joining the banking union and the exchange rate mechanism are no longer realistic. But that doesn't mean that work on this issue must stop. "If we continue the way we have worked so far, if politicians, because this is a political decision, and institutions, including the BNB, continue to act, regardless of the very difficult and complex environment in which we are in, a postponement for 2021 will not be fatal." Dimitar Radev was adamant. "Another new waiting cycle, like the previous one of 10 years, this time there will be a high cost  economic recovery, stabilization, low incomes. I don't think it's a price we'll be able to pay both politically, economically and financially," the governor said.

Title: Interview for This Morning, BTW
text: Interview of the Governor of the Bulgarian National Bank Mr. Dimitar Radev, for This Morning, BTW, 30 April 2020 The depth and duration of the crisis related to the situation around COVID-19 are two great unknowns to date. Dimitar Radev also commented on the swap line between bnb and the ECB. Outside the technical frameworks, the agreement is an expression of confidence in Bulgaria and the BNB. It shows Bulgaria as a country with a goodfinancial reputation that markets and investors can trust. When asked if euro liquidity is needed for Bulgarian banks now, the governor wasquoted as saying: "Not at the moment. We publish these data every week  the gross foreign exchange international reserve of the Bulgarian National Bank is at a historically high level. The level of reserves of the banks in the balance sheet of the Issue management is also high. that we do not intend to withdraw swap amounts. Asked if the swap line was part of our path to the euro area, the BNB governor said: "Legally not, meaningfully yes." Asked if we were ready to enter the currency mechanism in July, Mr Radev said: "We are ready to go in, categorically". In response to the question of whether the coronavirus crisis will have an impact, Mr Radev said that in addition to a political process, there can always be developments in the political sphere that are difficult to predict. Both Bulgarian and European institutions are now committed to the coronavirus. an administrative and bureaucratic process that engages not only the Bulgarian government and the BNB, but also the ECB, the European Commission, 19 euro area member states, plus Denmark. But I really expect development within the next three months, said Mr. D. Imiter Radev. There will be no devaluation of the BGN before our entry into the so-called waiting room of the euro area, the Governor of the BNB was adamant. We have historically the highest level of the gross international currency reserve of the BNB and the currency market is calm. As regards the state of the banks, the BNB governor stressed that banks are much better prepared now than in the 2008crisis. Dimitar Radev also commented on the bnb's package of measures for over 9 billion euro. and 300 million euro. Lv. We have adopted three groups of measures in relation to the crisis. The second group is to strengthen the capital and liquidity position of banks so that they are even better prepared for the crisis and ableto and alleviate the conditions and consequences of the crisis for their customers. Measures include full capitalisation of profits in the banking sector, reduction of foreign exposures and cancellation of envisaged increases in the countercyclical capital buffer. All these merks have already been fully implemented and without exceptions, including by the branches of banks and their subsidiaries. Asked what interest is in rescheduling loans from commercial banks, Mr. Dimitar Radev noted that the deferral is already significant as a br o.N. BNB has created a regulatory framework, the so-called moratorium, for commercial banks to be able to defer payments of loans to their clients. (a) deferral of loans of which more than 25 000 have been approved. The governor indicated that he expects the government to emerge as an issuer in international markets, but also drew attention to the regular issue of government securities inside the country. "We still have the luxury of saying no. You know that in the case of the issue, which is administered by the BNB, the Ministry of Finance refused because of the price to realize the issue. So we are in a good position.

Title: Interview for "24 Hours"
text: Interview of the Governor of the Bulgarian National Bank Mr. Dimitar Radev for "24 Hours", p. 1, 14 and 15, 8 May 2020 BUSINESS AND PEOPLE DO NOT NEED ADVICE, BUT SUPPORT d0 BANKS HAVE A RELIABLE PARTNER A sharp decline and a long exit from the crisis are predicted by many analysts and experts. Are there any new or corrections in the announced forecast of the BNB and what it brings - rather optimism or more pessimism, Mr. Radev? It all comes down to how quickly and how successfully it will restart the economy. For all the conditionality of this assessment, every additional month in which the global and regional economy remains stranded worsens the annual GDP estimate by about 2%. We are currently witnessing an unprecedented decline in economic activity. Optimism or pessimism depends on how quickly this decline will be overcome. You have already announced an ambitious package of measures totalling db9.3 billion. Lv. To support the real economy. Will they all be used and what effect do you expect from them to say that they have been successful? We were one of the first central banks to implement such measures. They were clearly formulated and easily measurable and included the capitalisation of all profits in the banking sector, a significant reduction in foreign exposures of commercial banks and the cancellation of the envisaged increases in the countercyclical capital buffer. They were fully implemented, as can be seen in the balance sheet of BNB and commercial banks. these measures have not only strengthened the capital and liquidity position of banks, but also their ability to respond adequately in the severely disadvantaged economic environment, including its impact on their citizens and companies. You often say that our banking system is in good shape, which has been proven by two consecutive stress tests and valuations of their assets in recent years. Wouldn't it take some of that conditioning away from them if this started happening, is there a"cure"? Asset quality assessments and both stress tests not only showed that our banking system was in good shape, but helped to further improve this conditioning. Negative scenarios in which the tests took place prepared banks for work in a drastically deterioration economic environmentas we are currently witnessing. Drilled board, insurance for future risks, strengthening the bgn before ERM-2 or something else is the swap line you negotiated with the European Central Bank (ECB)? The swap line is a good signal and is thus relied on by markets and investors. This is a currency agreement under which the BNB can at any time receive euro from the ECB against bgn under the fixed rate. central bank and its currency. Apart from the unambiguously positive signal to the international financial community, this swap line is an additional guarantee for the country's economy and monetary regime. Experience shows - extra security isnever superfluous, especially in the face of a crisis. Are our banks prepared for an option where the panic of the epidemic lasted longer and for objective or subjective reasons provoked a greater desire of people to collect their deposits in asafer place, at home. These traditions are not what they used to be, at least if we've been talking about the last more than 20 years. For this period, the trends are exactly the opposite, as can clearly be seen from the development and growth of the deposit base, and are a testament to the confidence in the banking sector. We, together with commercial banks, do everything necessary to maintain this confidence in the current crisis, including through our systematic approach and well-formulated and implemented measures. Let's look beyond the crisis - will our financial system have the resources to help not only people who are struggling to pay their loans, but those who want to revive their business, start a new one, for example? A significant part of the current measures are focused precisely in this direction, including those we have discussed to strengthen the capital and liquidity position of the banks. We are ready to escalate the measures if the situation develops. However, the EC has announced that it will accept temporary lending relief so as not to slow down. Do you know what they will be? We are talking about a package of measures that give banks greater flexibility to support people and businesses during the crisis Key measures of this year, including the establishment of a moratorium on loan repayments and the refrain from distributing dividends to shareholders were initiated by BNB in March and have already been implemented in terms ofdividends and are in the process of being implemented in moratorium. The EC's actions are important to us as they support these measures in terms of EU accounting and prudential rules. Please lift the veil slightly behind 'additional measures for the smooth functioning of the p-regime and related infrastructure, including for theavailable-monetary circulation, payment systems and activities of the BNB as a fiscal agent of the government'. to function, personal consumption d0 too? Categorically yes, but this does not exhaust these measures. With them, we have created spare capacity so that the cash regime, payment system, cash servicing of the budget and debt administrationwork without any shocks in the context of the crisis. Shifting the deadlines for our admission to the euro area waiting room is understandable and natural. Does the waitcreate risks - for example, higher inflation, or does it just deprive us of additional resources to manage the crisis? There are only adaptations to certain technical deadlines, but not to the deadlines for making a decision, which is expected by the end of July. The risk to macroeconomic indicators is if no positive solution is reached. The direct effect, as the world's credit agencies have publicly announced, will be a reduction in the country's credit rating and hence a deterioration in the financing conditions of the state and of business d0 something extremely undesirable, especially in the context of a crisis. Finish, please, with advice - to businesses and to people to help them not carry their panic and dissatisfaction from a healthcrisis to the financial system. Business and people do not need advice, but adequate support. I can only assure them that in this difficult period they can find in the face of banks a truly reliable partner.

Title: Interview for Capital newspaper
text: Interview with the Manager of the BNB Mr. Dimitar Radev for Capital newspaper, p. 1. 24, 2014 in New Year's Day. 25, August 7, 2020 BNB GOVERNOR DIMITAR RADEV: THE FACT THAT THERE ARE CHALLENGES FACING THE EURO AREA IS NOT A REASON TO STAND ON THE PERIPHERY OF THE EU The adoption of BGN in ERM II and the conclusion by the BNB of close cooperation with the ECB are definitely key events for the institution you have managed for five years. But how do they affect people and businesses - will anything change from July 2020? These are events of long-term importance, as they start the process of integrating the country into the core of the European Union. This process will have a growing influence on people and businesses by accelerating the modernization and prose of the country. It is probably difficult to realize this in the context of a health, economic and political crisis, but Iam convinced that it will happen. Over the past two years, many reforms have been made - changes in legislation and bank supervision practices. How would you describe the work of entering the exchange rate mechanismand the banking union from within and what were the biggest difficulties? In fact, we have come a long way since 2015 from a situation where no one wants to talk to us on the topic of exchange rate mechanism and banking union, to a situation where we are a full member. The working process was well structured and just as well implemented. It included a clear policy framework, The main difficulties were related to the fact that such a process of joining the banking union of a non-euro area country , while including its shaft in the exchange rate mechanism, was carried out for the first time. technical and procedural nature, which had to be decided on the go. Literally until the final days before the decision to accept Bulgaria, there was one obstacle left - the raising of capital by FIB. Its implementation left certain doubts in society. The accessionprocess was successfully completed without any open themes for the competent institutions, Bulgarian and European, which monitored it very closely, including with regard to the implementation of fib's capital plan. sufficient other examples. Do you expect the ECB to wish to include FIB in the list of system banks to supervise directly and how many institutions do you expect to be supervised by joint supervisory teams with the ECB? The list of systemic banks to be overseen directly by the ECB is set at expertlevel. In recent years, there have been a lot of voices against the adoption of the euro. How will you respond to the arguments put forward by critics of the single currency? In making such an important decision, what matters is institutionalised knowledge and institutionalised expertise. I do not think there is an institution on the political, economic and financial spectrum in our country that is opposed to the adoption of the euro. there is no reason to stand on the periphery of the EU. Bulgaria will be in a much stronger position if it is part of the solution to these challenges, not a side observer or a victim. Is there a clear estimate of the pros and cons and an analysis to show which of them prevail in terms of Bulgaria's accession to the euro area? This is a question of more than twenty years of limitation and the answer has always been in favour of the country joining the euro area. The BNB has prepared a similar analysis of the benefits, costs and challenges associated with the adoption of the euro and in the start of the process of joining the exchange rate mechanism, and it gives reason to draw the same conclusion. financial stability is significantly higher on the periphery than it would be at the core of the European Union, especially in times of crisis. The experience of the newly adopted countries of Central and Eastern Europe shows that the accession process and the accession itself to the euro area are a catalyst for accelerating what we call real convergence, which means convergence in the structure of the economy, as well as in the level of income and living standards. which, in good preparation, are easily overcome. It is often pointed out that Bulgaria loses sovereignty and that even representatives of the BNB have stated that the banking union is not advantageous for non-euro area countries - how will you comment? By definition, small economies are very difficult to conduct sovereign monetary policy, regardless of monetary policy. In this sense, shared monetary sovereignty within the euro area is a better alternative in terms of monetary policy formulation and implementation. I myself have repeatedly and publicly expressed reservations about separating the process of accession to the Banking Union from the euro area accession process. In general, the possibility for countries to choose or be directed when and to which segment of the EU to join and who does not work against the objectives of European integration. Brexit is an extreme result of such an approach. It also leads to a number of operational problems. Decision-making asymmetry is one of them. institutionalized by letter of intent to the European institutions, it was this approach for Bulgaria to start with the simultaneous accession of the country to the banking union and the bgn to the exchange rate mechanism. the group decided to apply this approach in the same way to all other countries that will join the euro area in the future. The entry into ERM II took place against the backdrop of protests in Bulgaria. Can the complicated political situation delay the country's entry into the euro area and, for you, when is the realistic deadline to do so? Political instability will in any case not help the process. If it is overcome relatively quickly, we do not significantly deteriorate our good starting position, including with regard to maastricht criteria, and the institutions act decisively,it is highly realistic to join by 2024. process may take 10 years or more. The data showed a sharp contraction in profit in the second quarter and even losses for individual banks, despite the moratorium. With the expiry of the six-month deferral of loaninstallments, can we expect a sharp deterioration in loan portfolios and on what scale? Such a development is no surprise. It is an expression of an adequate response by banks to the emerging credit risk associated with the global pandemic by increasing impairment rates and, accordingly, shrinking profits. This is a guarantee against the inevitable deterioration of credit portfolios. The extent of this deterioration will depend on how quickly economic activity willrecover. easing debt servicing for borrowers with temporary difficulties caused by the pandemic and without changing banks' requirements to assess their solvency. Preferential prudential treatment will lapse after the end of the m oratorium, and exposures will be serviced under new repayment plans that reflect the economic expectations and capacity of borrowers to service their loans. What are your priorities for the last year of your term asbnb's government? Do you have ambitions for another term? My priorities are basically three. The first is permanent and includes strict adherence to the mandate of the BNB with a focus on price stability and stability of the BGN. The second is a seamless transition to the new banking sector supervisory regime from 1 October this year and ensuring from the outset a full and full membership of the banking union. I made commitments for one term. The most important of these was: stabilising the banking sector and joining the European Exchange Rate Mechanism. What I can safely say is that at the moment our banking sector is oneof the safest in Europe, regardless of the crisis situation, and the lev is already a full participant in the European Exchange Rate Mechanism. is whether I am prepared to make new commitments after the end of my current mandate.

Title: Interview for a magazine of the Bulgarian Chamber of Commerce
text: Interview of the Governor of the BNB Mr. Dimitar Radev, conducted on 18 August 2020, for a magazine of the Bulgarian Chamber of Commerce, Noblesse oblige, Issue 6/2020 1. Mr. Radev, on July 14th this year, exactly 5 years have come since Parliament elected you as governor of the Bulgarian National Bank. In 2015, bnb and our banking sector were at the center of the political discussion, which was not healthy for the sector and for the economy ingeneral. not political criteria. During this period, our banking sects have gone through unprecedented checks in scale and depth. Their aim, among other things, was to improve its sustainability, including in the worsteconomicdevelopments. Banking supervision by one of the most vulnerable has become one of the strongest units of the system. The excellent state of banking supervision is one of the leading factors for establishing close cooperation between the BNB and the ECB. I must alsopoint to the huge, quality progress of integrating the country into European financial infrastructure, which in 2015 seemed very difficult to achieve and for which the BNB makes an important contribution. These are institutional, not personalachievements, i.e. all those who work in the BNB contribute to them. In the coming months, we will work very hard, within our mandate, to mitigate and overcome the consequences of the crisis, and also to fully and fully participatein the institutions of the euro area of which we have recently become members. 2. A historic step for which the Bulgarian Chamber of Commerce has always encouraged the competent institutions is the acceptance of our country in the ERM II exchange rate mechanism and the banking union. We highly appreciate the support for our efforts, provided to us over the years by employers' organizations and trade unions in Bulgaria. This support was a key element in shaping the shi rock public support of the goal of deepening thecountry's European integration. Our accession to ERM II and the Banking Union is a realisation of this goal. Before adopting the euro, individual countries had different periods of participation in ERM II. The record holder is Lithuania  10 and a half years, except, of course, Denmark, which has participated in ERM II since 1999 but which does not plan to join the euro area. Our expectation, as well as that of our European partners, is that the stay in the exchange rate mechanism will not take place over time. The purpose of this stay is to demonstrate a formal fulfilment of one of the Maastrichtcriteria (for the stability of the exchange rate)  something that the currency board provides to us seamlessly. After fulfilling this and the other Maastricht criteria, as well as with an appropriate degree of institutional and real convergence achieved, Bulgaria will be ready to adopt the euro in 2023-2024. 3. And after the waiting room, when the adoption of the euro happened, how would the life of the Bulgarian pre-match and citizen change? Will the euro raise prices? The short answer is no. This is a speculative statement that is not supported by facts from the history of the introduction of the euro in other countries. All historical statistics in such cases are categorical  an increase is reported in very few goods and services. And even with such individual raises, it is not clear whether they are caused by the currency change. In the long term, both prices and incomes in Bulgaria are expected to move upwards. This will be a normal consequence of the real convergence of our economy towards the euro area. The currency we use is not in itself a factor in price rises or decreases. 4.Will bank fees and commissions be reduced after our accession to the Euro area? The prices of banking products and services are mainly a function of the level of development and competition in the sector. They do not directly follow from the currency we use. At the same time, however, accession to the euro area would represent a key stage for accelerating and deepening in general the integration of the Bulgarian financial sector into the euro area. This, on equal terms, will mean that our banks will operate in a more complex and competitive environment  from which it makes sense for bank customers to be profitable. 5.Will there be easier access for Bulgarian business to credit resources from European banks? The majority of the banking sector in Bulgaria is made up of banks that are part of European banking groups. These banks can borrow resources fromtheir "mothers" in the euro area, which can be used to lend to Bulgarian businesses and businesses. Single Market rules also allow direct access to lending to Bulgarian companies by banks operating in other EU Member States (whether in the euro area or not). In order for this to happen in practice, however, it is necessary at least that the bank knows the company concerned well. The borrower must present, and the creditor bank to assess, financial and business indicators, potential risks, credit history, legal arrangements for the establishment and realization of collateral. 6.Before the COVID-19 crisis, you were adamant that our banking system was stable. Are you still of this opinion? What were the effects of the pandemic on the banking theme in Europe and Bulgaria? Our banking system welcomed the situation with COVID-19 in very good conditioning, consisting in high capital adequacy, a strong liquidity position and a falling share of non-performing loans. Initial negative expectations in banks related to the ability to generate losses due to the sharply deteriorating profile of their customers have been mitigated by the moratorium on deferralof liabilities to banks. In light of the new challenges, the BNB adopted as early as March this year a comprehensive package of measures aimed at further strengthening the capital and liquidity of banks. 7.What measures did the BNB take to support the Bulgarian economy to deal withthe crisis? Bnb's measures focused on the legal spheres of our competences and responsibilities. With regard to the banking system, in March the BNB adopted measures with a quantitative effect of EUR 9.3 billion. bgn, to capitalize the entire profit in the sector,to reduce the envisaged increases in the countercyclical capital buffer and to reduce the foreign exposures of the banks. In April, a draft order for deferral and settlement of due liabilities to banks and theirsubsidiaries  financial institutions in connection with the state of emergency introduced by the National Assembly on 13 March 2020 was approved by the Management Board of the BNB. This represents the so-called "no-fly zone". moratorium within the meaning of the EBA guidelines. As of the end of June, a total of 118,584 requests for liabilities with a gross carrying amount of BGN 9 772 million had been submitted to the banks. Lv. 8.Has the total amount of loans and deposits in the banking system changed during the pandemic period? In the second quarter, in particular, household resources grew by 937 million euro. bgn, and by the companies  by BGN 440 million. Lv. This is generally the result of a combination of three factors  confidence in the banking system, insufficient investment alternatives and motivation to save due to the economic uncertainty associated with the situation around the pandemic. During the same period, we introduced new credit reporting, in line with the application of European regulations. 9.What are your expectations for the recovery and development of the Bulgarian economy? The state and development of the Bulgarian economy corresponds to the profile of economic dynamicsin E wroc, in particular the euro area. Since the beginning of this year, we have seen extraordinary negative effects on the economy due to the unusual pandemic risk and the unprecedented restrictive measures imposed. The impact was the hardest hit in the second quarter. Progressive measures tolimit the spread of the virus have been relaxed and various compensatory and stimulating economic measures have been put in place. The NSI recently published an express estimate of GDP in Bulgaria, according to which in the second quarter our economy contracted by 9.8 percent on a chain basis compared to the previous quarter. We are currently in aparticular situation of uncertainty associated with both pandemic and political situations. Due to the volatility of the macroeconomic picture and the importance of the currently released data, the BNB plans to republish a forecast by the beginning of October. This publication will nextto the established timetable, according to which the BNB publishes macroeconomic forecasts twice a year  in issue two and number four of the economic review edition.

Title: Interview for Global Finance Magazine
Subtitle: Early on in the pandemic, the Bulgarian National Bank implemented a significant package of measures to get banks lending and to enhance liquidity in the financial system. How well are those measures working in terms of encouraging banks to lend to businesses, particularly microenterprises and small businesses, and in helping minimise the economic impact of the pandemic?
text: Interview of the BNB Governor Mr. Dimitar Radev for Global Finance Magazine, conducted on 21 September 2020, issue October 2020 Early on in the pandemic, the Bulgarian National Bank implemented a significant package of measures to get banks lending and to enhance liquidity in the financial system. How well are those measures working in terms of encouraging banks to lend to businesses, particularly microenterprises and small businesses, and in helping minimise the economic impact of the pandemic? We realized we needed to act swiftly and decisively at the very onset of the pandemic to further strengthen the capital position and liquidity of the banking system. To this end, we implemented a package of measures for over 8 percent of GDP, including capitalization of the 2019 profit; increase in liquidity by reducing riskier foreign exposures of commercial banks; and cancellation of the increase of the countercyclical capital buffer planned for 2020 and 2021. These, in combination with fiscal measures, helped absorb the pandemic shock and alleviate the financial conditions for businesses and households. One of the main instruments we use is a moratorium scheme for bank loan payments until 31 March 2021. The incoming data confirm that our banking system continued to perform smoothly its intermediation functions in support of the economy. During the second quarter, which bore the brunt of the shock in the aftermath of the pandemic outbreak, company and household deposits increased by 1.6 percent and the stock of bank loans to households and small and medium enterprises increased, respectively, by 0.8 percent and 2.2 percent. However, we are fully aware that pandemic-related developments are far from over and stay ready to deploy additional measures as needed. How long are the measures that the BNB introduced to deal with the pandemic likely to remain in place? The shortest answer, I guess, is as long as needed. Of course, we monitor carefully the economic situation and trends in the banking system and in all areas relevant to our tasks and responsibilities as a central bank. The good news is that we know much more today, compared to just months ago, about the economic and financial costs of the pandemic. Nevertheless, uncertainty remains notably high. Until a more stable outlook for the course of the pandemic emerges, we need to stay vigilant and ready to act. How much do you expect the Bulgarian economy to shrink by in 2020 as a result of the pandemic, and what are your predictions for growth next year? One thing I can be fairly confident in is that the decline in Bulgarias GDP this year will be less severe that initially expected. It is reasonable to assume that our economic trajectory will closely follow, but stay relatively better than, the profile of the euro area. We are finalizing now the work on our updated macroeconomic projections, and will publish them in October. Even though our forecasts are usually rather cautious, I might say I would not be surprised to see Bulgaria among the EUs most resilient economic performers in 2020. Although flash GDP contracted by more than 9% in the second quarter of this year, according to ING Bank, the contraction was not as big as some expected and ING predicts that the country is likely to post one of the smallest contractions in GDP in the EU. To what extent is this attributable to the measures that the central bank has taken? It sounds strange to consider in somewhat positive terms an economic contraction of that size. But, yes, as I said I share the prediction that the contraction of the GDP in Bulgaria will remain below the EU average. Such outcome reflects the existence and application of various government and central bank measures aimed to alleviate the negative impact from the pandemic. Without them, the picture would have been different. However, a precise analysis of the contribution of the separate policy measures to our GDP dynamics would require longer and more detailed data series. We are still very early in the process, but there will be plenty of such research to publicly communicate in due time. How confident were you going into the pandemic that the Bulgarian banking sector was strong and well capitalised? The banks in Bulgaria entered the new coronavirus period very well prepared and resilient by any common metrics. At the end of 2019 the banking system had an over 19 percent CET1 capital ratio and a 270 percent liquidity coverage ratio. The sectors traditionally maintained high capital adequacy and liquidity have been bolstered further in recent years as a result of the asset quality reviews and stress tests done by the BNB and the ECB. The BNB measures noted above aimed to ensure even more safeguards in the face of the unprecedented nature of risks around the pandemic. How has the pandemic impacted your and commercial bank's efforts to integrate or align themselves more closely with the EU financial infrastructure as part of your path towards adopting the euro in early 2023? Contrary to some concerns earlier this year, the pandemic situation did not impede our progress towards deeper European integration. It is a rather remarkable achievement that in this period, despite enormous economic, financial, even political complications following the spread of the pandemic, we managed to complete successfully the all-important projects of entering ERM II and the Banking Union. Thus we remained on track towards the next stage, adopting the euro. Our understanding is that an optimal strategy for the country is to aim to stay in ERM II as short as possible. From todays perspective this suggests 2024 as Bulgarias year of accession to the euro area. Understandably, however, any such timeline is subject to a substantial degree of complexity and uncertainty involving so many developments in the economy, finances, and the political landscape  both in the euro area and domestically. Therefore, our focus as a central bank is on the quality of the process, meaning that we need to do the right things, rather than on a specific deadline. Link to the interview: HYPERLINK " "

Title: Webinar with the American Chamber of Commerce in Bulgaria
text: The BNB Governor Mr. Dimitar Radev in a webinar with the American Chamber of Commerce in Bulgaria, 21 October 2020 On 21 October 2020 the American Chamber of Commerce in Bulgaria (AmCham) welcomed Mr. Dimitar Radev, Governor of the Bulgarian National Bank, to a webinar for its members. The topic of the webinar was on the ERM II accession and its impact on the Bulgarian economy and business. The event, moderated by Bojidar Neytchev, AmCham Bulgaria Board Member and South East Europe Deals Leader, PwC, was attended by more than 70 members of AmCham. In his introductory remarks Mr. Dimitar Radev said that the participation of the Bulgarian lev in ERM II is a critical milestone on Bulgarias path towards joining the euro area. Participation in ERM II is a convergence criterion for entry into the euro area and it has two main purposes. First, to ensure that exchange rate fluctuations between the euro and the national currencies do not disturb economic stability within the Single Market. Second, to help the respective non-euro area country to prepare for participation in the euro area. By design ERM II is not a complicated mechanism. It is based on an agreement between the finance ministers of the euro area Member States, the European Central Bank, and the finance ministers and central bank governors of the non-euro area countries. First, they agree on a central rate between the euro and the respective national currency. Then the national currency is allowed to fluctuate by up to 15% above or below this central rate. The currency is supported, if needed, by interventions coordinated by the ECB and the national central bank in order to keep the fluctuations within this band. However, a country can adopt a narrower fluctuation band, including a zero band. For example, Denmark (whose Danish krone has been part of ERM II since 1999 but Denmark is not in the euro area) maintains a fluctuation band of /- 2.25%. Mr. Dimitar Radev explained that ERM II is monitored and administered by the General Council of the ECB, which includes the governors of the central banks of the EU Member States, including the Governor of the Bulgarian National Bank. On 10 July the ERM II parties agreed to keep the current euro-lev exchange rate, namely 1.95583, as the central rate between the euro and the lev. Furthermore, based on a unilateral commitment by the Bulgarian authorities, the ERM II parties agreed that Bulgaria would continue its currency board arrangements, including a zero fluctuation band, during the ERM II period. This ended the speculations that the ERM exchange rate could somehow differ from the fixed exchange rate that has been in place in Bulgaria for over 23 years. Therefore, the participation of the lev in ERM II does not require any changes to the regime of the fixed exchange rate under the currency board arrangements. So, we are not concerned whatsoever, presently and also in the horizon of the ERM II period, about the stability of our exchange rate arrangements, recapped the BNB Governor. Mr. Dimitar Radev supported this with the example of an indicator - the so-called coverage ratio of the currency board. It shows how much of our high-quality foreign exchange reserves stand behind the monetary liabilities of the BNB. The coverage ratio is calculated by dividing the total assets of the BNBs Issue Department by the sum of the banknotes and coins in circulation, the liabilities to banks, to the government, and to budget institutions. The last weeks balance sheet indicated that the coverage ratio was 160%, said Mr. Radev. The ERM II positive implications on the broader economy can be illustrated with three recent events. First, the establishment of the swap line between the ECB and the Bulgarian National Bank. The ECBs website shows that swap lines with such favourable conditions have been extended only to the three ERM II countries  Bulgaria, Croatia, and Denmark. This represents a very strong signal to the markets. Second, Bulgaria issued a BGN 5 billion debt on the international capital market. The investors huge interest was unprecedented, not only for Bulgaria but also for the current market conditions. Our participation in ERM II played an important role for this outcome. Third, the very recent upgrade of our credit rating by Moodys in an environment in which the opposite is more common  for example, a few days ago Moodys downgraded the UK. To sum up: the ERM II developments have led to better financing conditions for Bulgaria, something very important during the difficult times we are in. The BNB Governor also addressed the question of the ERM II timeframe. This varies from country to country. For example, Denmark has been in ERM II for more than 20 years, but it is the only country in the EU, after the UK is already out, with an opt-out clause regarding euro adoption. From the remaining countries, the Lithuanian litas stayed the longest in ERM II  more than 10 years. Bulgarias aim is to stay in ERM II for as short a time as possible. Realistically, it means that in 2024 we could join the euro area. The most important question, Mr. Radev shared, is what needs to be done while we are in ERM II. We need to be fully compliant with the convergence criteria (so-called Maastricht criteria). They require control of inflation, public debt, public deficit, exchange rate stability, and domestic interest rates. It means that we need to maintain inflation no more than 1.5 percentage points higher than the average of the three EU Member States with the lowest inflation, to keep the budget deficit less than 3% and the gross government debt less than 60% of GDP, to keep the exchange rate stable within the ERM II framework and the nominal long-term interest rates no more than 2 percentage points higher than in the three lowest inflation Member States. Mr. Dimitar Radev said that as of today we broadly meet the convergence criteria and we have good chances to keep it that way if we maintain the sound fiscal and monetary stance regardless of the current crisis. In addition to the Maastricht criteria, the entire process includes fulfilment of commitments both prior to joining the ERM II and thereafter until euro adoption. Before ERM II, Bulgaria took commitments in six policy areas. Two of them were within the mandate of the BNB - these were Banking Union and Macroprudential supervision. Four areas were under the mandate of the government  Non-banking supervision, Insolvency framework, Anti-money laundering framework, and State-owned enterprises. The post-ERM II commitments include further measures in these four areas under the governments mandate. The BNB Governor added that an action plan for implementing these measures has already been adopted. He highlighted that the fact that we no longer have commitments to implement measures regarding the banking sector is another recognition for the significant progress in this area. The introductory remarks of the BNB Governor were followed by a Q&A session. Bojidar Neytchev started this part of the AmCham webinar by asking if the ERM II period would be till 2024. Governor Radev answered that this would be realistic if we maintain our stable fiscal and monetary stance. At the same time, it is a bit ambitious having in mind that we need to comply with the Maastricht criteria, to fulfil the post-ERM II commitments, and to address the complex logistical and administrative issues. Stanislava Taneva, AmCham Bulgaria First Vice President, and Country Chair of Citibank in Bulgaria, asked a couple of questions on the payment infrastructure until our entry into the euro area. Mr. Dimitar Radev told how RINGS and BISERA will cease functioning when we join the euro. The RINGS payments will migrate to the TARGET platform for euro payments. And the bank clients payments through BISERA will migrate to SEPA euro payments. The national payments traffic will be entirely transformed. Presently, together with BORICA we are implementing a project for instant leva payments to up to 100,000 leva. These payments will comply with the pan-European SEPA credit transfer framework. From November 2022 there will be a new consolidated TARGET platform unifying TARGET2, TARGET2-Securities, and TIPS. Accordingly, the BNB, 18 commercial banks, BORICA, and the central depositories are preparing for this new consolidated platform. Another question of AmCham VP Stanislava Taneva was related to the COVID-19 pandemic and the response measures. She asked for details especially with regard to the increased liquidity on the local market and about possible expected new measures. The BNB Governor noted the well-recognized fact that the BNB reacted swiftly and decisively to the crisis. The central bank introduced a sizeable package of measures accounting to over 8% of GDP. These measures, which were announced publicly, included the full capitalization of the 2019 profit of the commercial banks, increase in liquidity, reducing the riskier foreign exposures of the banks, and the cancellation of the increase of the counter-cyclical capital buffer planned for this and next year. The BNB then, Mr. Radev added, approved the private moratorium of bank loan repayments proposed by the banking industry. The ECB swap line can be added to this list, too. This swap line is yet another safeguard for the financial and monetary stability. Our banks were already strong even before the crisis; even so these measures helped further. All this allowed the banks to mitigate the impact of the COVID-19 crisis for their clients. With regard to the liquidity before and after the COVID-19 crisis broke out, the Governor recalled that as part of the preparation for ERM II, measures were adopted that further strengthened the sector. Lending remains stable so far, but it is also a process reflecting both supply and demand. In times like the present, banks actively seek good bankable projects. However, banks should remain cautious in identifying and pricing the risks they take when they lend. Regardless of the incentives to increase lending, banks should not do it at any cost or at any risk. Mr. Dimitar Radev went on saying that the BNB does not plan to further extend the moratorium of bank loan repayments. The central bank stays ready to apply, if needed, additional measures  most of them related to the capital requirements, and it is monitoring the situation carefully. Teodora Petkova, CEO of UniCredit Bulbank asked about our countrys entry into the Banking Union and the effects on the banks, emphasizing that Bulgaria is in the Banking Union but not in the euro area yet. In his response the BNB Governor told about the simultaneous entry into the Banking Union along with the inclusion of the lev in ERM II. As a matter of fact, the BNB is the first Bulgarian institution that is already a member of institutions of the euro area, such as is the Banking Union. The advantages of joining the Banking Union before joining the euro area are several. One of them is that we no longer need to implement any post-commitments in this area. Another advantage is that the banks will reduce their costs after our inclusion in the two segments of the Banking Union  the Single Supervisory Mechanism and the Single Resolution Mechanism. The new supervisory fees on banks will be insignificant. At the same time the resolution fees within the Single Resolution Mechanism will be zero for the next few years. Mr. Dimitar Radev explained that this is due to the high level of funds already accumulated in the national Bank Resolution Fund, adding that no dramatic changes are expected for the banks with regard to how the supervisory process is conducted, while the BNB is gaining more capacity, expertise, and access to information. Martin Pytlik, Executive Director, Raiffeisen Bank Bulgaria, asked about the cooperation between the ECB and BNB with regard to the direct supervision of five Bulgarian banks, and whether supervision rulings adopted towards these banks can be expected to be automatically adopted to the banks that are not under the ECBs direct supervision? As Mr. Radev stated, the cooperation between the Bulgarian National Bank and the ECB was and remains excellent. An integrated model will be applied to supervision, rather than two separate models. In summary, the final sanctions will be determined in Frankfurt but Sofia will be very closely involved in the decision-making process. Besides, during the period of participation in ERM II the administrative acts with regard to banks in Bulgaria will be issued by the BNB. As the banking sector is very well regulated, the strict application of the regulations cannot be expected to lead to different decisions regardless of the particular processes. The participation in the Banking Union marks a qualitative new stage in our European integration. Therefore, other things equal, we may expect intensifying competition, efficiency pressure, and perhaps  consolidation, Mr. Radev also said. Answering an additional question by Teodora Petkova, CEO of UniCredit Bulbank, about any possible adverse scenarios in the short-term horizon, the Governor noted that the BNB was traditionally more conservative in its projections about the countrys macroeconomic developments and their implications for the banks. The stress tests conducted by the central bank in the last couple of years were based on highly negative scenarios. However, now that the negative scenarios are materializing, the banking sector is ready. The current macroeconomic forecast of the BNB remains a bit more conservative than those of some other institutions. However, the uncertainty increases, and it is getting more difficult to assess the parameters of the possible scenarios. Nevertheless, we expect the banking sector will remain resilient to any adverse developments in the environment, Mr. Radev explained. Bozhidar Neichev asked for a comparison between the banking sector in Bulgaria and in other EU Member States. According to the Governor, the fact that Bulgaria joined the Banking Union in 2020 is a proof of the strength of the Bulgarian banking sector. Our indicators, including capital adequacy, liquidity ratio, and profitability, are better than the EU average. The only exception is the level of the non-performing loans that, following a steady decline in recent years, has reached around 6% while the EU average is 3%. Valentin Galabov, Chairman of the Executive Board of TBI Bank, asked which were the areas for implementing test environments, (the so-called sandboxes) where more Fintech-prone banks can experiment. As Mr. Radev explained, sandboxes represent a secure regulatory environment where companies will test their products while regulators will be monitoring them. This very concept aims to allow banks to experiment in the Fintech areas. The BNB Governor reminded that earlier this year the Minister of Finance had announced the intention to promote the setting-up of a regulatory sandbox in Bulgaria. The Bulgarian National Bank has been involved in these talks though things are at an early stage, added Mr. Radev. Georgi Drenski, Senior Associate, Boyanov & CO., asked if the banking sector consolidation evidenced in recent years would continue. Mr. Radev answered that the short answer was yes. First, because of the pressure on the profitability of the banks and second, because of our participation in the Banking Union, which creates the appropriate environment for such developments. Jock Nunan, Partner in PwC, asked if according to the BNB there was a scenario for Bulgaria under which the exchange rate would not be fixed. The BNB Governor denied any possibility of such a scenario noting, for example, that the coverage ratio of the currency board remains well above the minimum level for the smooth operation of our exchange rate regime. Neither is there any pressure from the fiscal policy now despite the current accommodation of the fiscal space. Our track record also proves the resilience of our fixed exchange rate regime. It has been tested in both good and bad times, such as the Global Financial Crisis of 2008-2009. The monetary regime in Bulgaria is rock solid and it will also remain like this during the ERM II, the Governor concluded. Maria Janeva, CEO, AGRI Bulgaria, asked the Governor to comment on the political situation in Bulgaria and to what extent it could have any adverse effect in the longer term. As Mr. Radev said, political tensions are not generally benefiting the economy. At the same time, however, the political cycles do not necessarily translate into economic ones. Therefore, banking stability is not expected to be affected by the political environment. The political class should focus on the management of the fundamental transition processes underway  from the stage of protection against the pandemic, through economic recovery, to the next phase of transformation in the economy. Boyan Petkov, Head of Capital Markets Division, Raiffeisen Bank Bulgaria, asked if the BNB planned any educational or communication campaign on the changeover to the euro. In Mr. Radevs words, such a campaign should be led by politicians while the role of professional institutions, including the Bulgarian National Bank, is to actively participate. For that purpose, within our mandate we are providing adequate resources and capacity. For example, almost every day there are media publications based on information and data provided by the Bulgarian National Bank, said Mr. Radev in conclusion.
