Title: Interview for the Banker newspaper
text: Interview with Mr. Dimitar Radev, Governor of the BNB, for the Banker newspaper, pp. 6-7, 4 December 2020 Mr. Radev, on a few previous occasions you have shared your expectations that our country will be ready for the adoption of the euro in three or four years. What leads you to make such projections? A few things. Firstly, the experience from the first, and in many respects more difficult step on the road to the euro area, namely joining the European Exchange Rate Mechanism and the Banking Union. Formally, we started the process in July 2018 and finalised it in July 2020. Secondly, the fulfilment of the Maastricht criteria, which is the main formal requirement for the adoption of the euro after a countrys currency is already included in the European Exchange Rate Mechanism, as is our case. Bulgaria currently fulfils all these criteria, including for budget balance (taking into account the exception for COVID-19 expenditure), debt, currency stability, inflation, and interest rates. Also, we have significant reserves as regards the fiscal and monetary stability. Therefore, the task is to prevent a substantial deterioration compared to the situation at present, and this is a fully feasible task in the specified time horizon. And thirdly, the fact that we are already a full participant in a key institution of the euro area, such as the Banking Union, and operating in a close cooperation regime between the Bulgarian National Bank and the European Central Bank. This has a strong consolidating effect on the overall process of joining the euro area. What could be the potential obstacles in the process and where might they come from? We must not forget that, in the end, this is a political process that must be finalised with a political act. Consequently, political upheavals, internal or external, can affect the time frame. But in terms of technical capacity and capabilities, finalisation of the process by 2024 is totally achievable. However, the slow catching up with the average income levels should leave us in the waiting room for longer... It is logical to expect that the formal start of the process of joining the euro area, by including the lev in the Exchange Rate Mechanism and the countrys entry in the Banking Union, along with fulfilling the nominal convergence criteria, such as those of Maastricht, will accelerate the process of real convergence, including in terms of incomes. We should not overlook the fact that in the recent years, incomes in the country have been growing at a faster pace than the European average. Understandably, however, this cannot change peoples attitudes to this issue, as we are starting from a very low level. Following some government decisions this summer, businesses have been compelled to catch up with public sector wages. Is it right for this to happen, since businesses have suffered the most from anti-pandemic measures? The wage ratio between the public and private sectors is a complex issue. I do not think there are unequivocal answers to this question. I will give you an example with the BNB. We are concerned about the increased percentage of job applicants who have won the competitions but refuse to sign a contract due to the level of pay, and the salaries at the BNB are at a relatively good level. These are highly qualified specialists from the IT sector, lawyers, auditors, as well as colleagues from the banking system. The reason why they opt for the private sector is the pay gap. Therefore, at least when we talk about people with good education and high qualifications, I do not think that the private sector is placed in a situation to catch up with salaries in the public sector. In general, however, your question is relevant, but it must be discussed in a strategic context, and not from the point of view of the emergency situation in which we find ourselves. The legal amendments related to the supervision and resolution of credit institutions are already a fact. How will the approach and work of the BNB change after the close cooperation with the ECB? As of 1 October 2020, Bulgaria is effectively a member of the Banking Union which includes our simultaneous participation in the Single Supervisory Mechanism and the Single Resolution Mechanism. This became a fact after years of reforms and reorganisation in the relevant areas in the Bulgarian National Bank, as well as comprehensive regulatory changes. Thanks to the good preparation and successful fulfilment of all requirements of the European Central Bank, the transition to the period of participation in the Banking Union went smoothly and, I would say, practically unnoticed by the banks and their customers. Today, the BNB's activities related to banking supervision and the resolution of credit institutions are already in full sync with our ECB counterparts. Despite the known division of our functions in relation to the banks under the ECB direct supervision and the other banks, essentially we have a unified model of operation, fully compliant with the requirements and practices in the euro area. For months now there has been a steady growth of deposits of individuals and businesses, however at interest rates close to zero and even negative. When do you expect the precautionary saving to end and what will be the interest rate dynamics? The desire to save, triggered by the uncertainty in this crisis and the anxious expectations for the future, is indeed a factor for the continued growth of deposits in our banking system. At this stage the low interest rates and returns on deposits remain secondary as an incentive for saving in banks. It is precisely these attitudes that are likely to continue as long as the measures imposed to curb the spread of the pandemic are in place and until citizens and businesses begin to regain optimism about the development of the economy and their own financial situation. As for interest rates, they are expected to remain low over the foreseeable horizon. Interest rates in Bulgaria follow the monetary conditions in the euro area, respectively they are a function of the strongly stimulating monetary policy pursued there. On the other hand, there seems to be no serious appetite for lending. Is the market going to pick up soon? Over the last few months of the crisis, one of the greatest achievements of our banking sector, and from the point of view of the Bulgarian National Bank as a supervisory and regulatory authority, is the continuing lending activity. Creating conditions for banks to keep their capacity for continuity of the lending process was one of the purposes of the measures which we adopted back in March this year when the state of emergency was declared in Bulgaria. But lending is a two-way process driven by both supply and demand. With regard to demand, the factors in this crisis are similar to those in the dynamics of deposits  potential borrowers attitudes and expectations for the future influence their willingness to take debt. With an overall economic normalisation, we would naturally expect an increase in lending. On the whole, the crisis has drastically shrunk the profits of the banking sector and has increased provision costs. Do you have concerns about the banks financial results and does the BNB need to introduce additional measures aimed at keeping the resilience of banks? The banks in Bulgaria entered the period of the crisis being in a very good starting position, with high levels of capital adequacy, liquidity, profitability, and an overall decrease in non-performing loans over the last few years. But the current environment in which the banks are operating does affect their results. Since the beginning of the pandemics spread and the ensuing negative developments in the economy, the Bulgarian National Bank took wide-ranging measures to facilitate the banks customers in servicing their debts, and to strengthen the entire sector. That required additional reinforcement of the banks capital and liquidity positions. Thanks to all the measures taken so far and the effective and prudent behaviour that the banks themselves are trying to follow, todays reports indicate a preserved stability of the system. Of course, the adverse implications of the crisis are continuing, and the whole environment remains uneasy. We are carefully checking and analysing the current data and we are ready, as we have been until now, to activate additional measures, if needed. These measures could be in the area of our macroprudential powers, with our traditional focus on the banks capital. Do you expect a growth in non-performing loans after March 2021? All other things equal, a slowdown in economic recovery would imply a worsened financial profile of borrowers. As much as this may cause problems with the servicing of bank loans, these dynamics would shift towards banks balance sheets in the form of deteriorating quality of their assets. Unfortunately, to date and based on the available data and the current trends, we dont see many reasons to expect a rapid recovery or an accelerated growth in the economy next year. All this suggests a reversal of the trend of decreasing non-performing loans that we have seen in recent years. The deterioration in loan portfolios will not be an isolated Bulgarian phenomenon. Leading representatives of EU regulatory and supervisory authorities have lately been warning about similar negative trends in the banking systems in the entire European Union. As you see, we are monitoring a complex and extensive process within which the expiry of the bank loan repayments moratorium  which you probably had in mind when you mentioned March 2021  could indeed be followed by a one-off effect of new non-performing loans appearing. According to the latest data, the banks have rescheduled loans worth BGN 9 billion. What is the effect of the so-called loan repayment moratorium on the banks impairment costs? Days ago, the BNB published the latest data, according to which as of 31 October the banks have approved about 88 500 customer requests for deferral and settlement of payable debts worth BGN 8.5 billion in total. As the moratorium has been designed to create a regulatory possibility for a pause in the application of the current prudential framework, whereby the deferral of loans would not require their re-classification, then we should not look for a direct effect on the dynamics of impairment costs. I would rather draw your attention to another interesting aspect. The BNBs regularly published data show that, as compared to the August peak of the total number and amount of outstanding requests approved under the moratorium, recently we have seen a slight decrease. This can be explained by the expiry of the grace period of already approved requests and even cases of customers ceasing taking advantage of relief measures applied . So, behind these numbers a complex picture stands, including the individual stories of thousands of people, households and companies. Some of them, despite the difficulties after the initial shock, seem to have stabilised their position, even thanks to the temporary relief measures granted under the moratorium. Do you think that the sector would have incurred losses by now, if the moratorium had not been introduced? We can seek the answer to this question in the essential logic of the moratoria implemented in accordance with the EU-wide framework discussed and approved by the European Banking Authority. The present-day crisis  in its economic aspects  is historically unprecedented as it is a result not of financial or market circumstances, but of the actions of the public authorities which have imposed restrictions on businesses and entire sectors in order to prevent the spread of the pandemic. And these regulatory and administratively imposed limitations, logically, would be followed by actions, again of the public authorities, in the form of a set of measures to support or ease consumers and companies. One of these public responses to the crisis were the moratoria. Viewed from this perspective, the moratoria were to a very large extent inevitable due to the nature of this crisis. Undoubtedly, without the moratorium, the banks would have had a growth in non-performing exposures, and subsequently more provision costs than they have now. The moratorium does not eliminate the need of adequate assessment, classification and provisioning of banks exposures. Sooner or later when the moratorium is over, new non-performing loans would appear. However, the moratorium aims not to reduce banks costs but to support and provide flexibility to their customers. Keeping the customers financial position during these difficult times would allow them, in time, to again have full relationships with banks, including in taking and servicing loans. And these are strategic benefits from the moratorium that the very banks could experience.

Title: Participation in The Year1 on Darik Radio
text: Participation of Mr. Dimitar Radev, BNB Governor, in The Year1 on Darik Radio on 19 December 2020 Unprecedented is the word for 2020, Mr. Radev stated in an interview for The Year on Darik Radio. The two main challenges to the central bank and the banking sector this year were COVID-19 and the accession to Exchange Rate Mechanism ERM II and the Banking Union. The coronavirus crisis was a surprise, while we had been well prepared for ERM II and the Banking Union. Coping with the crisis in the year past proved the existing capabilities of the financial sector in Bulgaria, whereas ERM II and the Banking Union outline its longer-term prospects. As a comment on the consequences of the COVID-19 crisis, Mr. Radev recapped the measures introduced by the BNB in March, aimed at creating an additional capacity in the banking system and easing the conditions for banks customers. The moratorium on bank loan repayments, approved by the BNB, can be viewed as an extension of the central banks measures. As of today, the goals we set ourselves with these measures seem to have been achieved, the Governor noted. The main indicators of the banking system are not worse today than in the period before the onset of the coronavirus crisis. The banking sector remains viable and will stay so in 2021, Mr. Radev said. The BNB Governor also commented on what actions can be taken by governments and central banks for the post-crisis recovery of the economy. The loan repayment moratorium is not a tool to be used in the long-term, however the BNB will remain focused on the instruments in its macro-prudential mandate, which will be applied as long as needed. Mr. Radev shared some details of the chronology of events that ended with the accession to the Exchange Rate Mechanism and the Banking Union. Asked what the consequences of the ERM II and Banking Union membership would be, the Governor pointed out the expected acceleration of real convergence and the convergence of our economys structure to that of the euro area. This also presupposes convergence of incomes in Bulgaria to the European averages. To implement these positive processes, two conditions have to be met  preserving the long-sustained financial stability and achieving an economic growth rate higher than the average in Europe. Such a growth rate should be as a minimum similar to the one registered in the period before the pandemic, and even better if much higher. The Governor was very clear that a referendum on euro adoption would not be a working option as it would mean abandoning Bulgarias EU accession treaty. The entire political class is behind the goal of our countrys accession to the euro area and such a topic is not discussed among the serious political factors. Bulgaria will adopt the single currency when it is ready and has fulfilled all conditions, Mr. Dimitar Radev underlined, adding that in principle he avoids specifying dates for the introduction of the euro. The normal process of preparing a country for the euro, once its currency is part of the exchange rate mechanism, takes two years; however there are a number of technical, organisational and administrative processes to go through. From todays position, it is quite possible to consider 1 January 2024 as a good indicative date for the adoption of the euro in Bulgaria, Mr. Radev pointed out. The Governor also outlined the important tasks related to joining the euro area in the next three years. In the first place, the country must satisfy the Maastricht criteria, Currently, Bulgaria as a whole fulfils these requirements. In terms of public finances, despite the higher government spending associated with the pandemic, we are meeting the Maastricht limits on state budget and debt. By participating in ERM II, we are already fulfilling the criterion of exchange rate stability as well. We fulfil the long-term interest rates criterion. There is a discussion on inflation, but we are in a very good starting position on this criterion too, as long as we keep the good policies, Mr. Radev said. Commenting on interest rate levels during the ERM II period and after joining the euro area, the Governor identified the European Central Bank's policy as the main factor influencing all economies in the European Union, whether in the euro area or not. Within the short-term horizon, it can be predicted with a high degree of certainty that interest rates, and the price of loans respectively, will remain at current levels, said Mr. Radev. The BNB Governor ended the interview with an expectation of optimism for 2021. The word this year will be associated with is promising, Mr. Radev shared.

Title: Participation in the show "Nova Sunday" on Nova TV
text: Participation of Mr. Dimitar Radev, Governor of bnb, in the show "Nova Sunday" on Nova TV, December 20, 2020. The accession of the BGN to the European Exchange Rate Mechanism and the country to the Banking Union is a remarkable achievement, in a very difficult and dark year. This act, among other things, shows that the country has the capacity to solve complex strategist tasks even underdifficult conditions. Such a development is an expression of confidence in what Bulgaria is doing and also, in contrast to what has been happening in recent times  including Brexit  shows that the European project has a future. very important and difficult step. And that is why I say that in a really complex year this is a remarkable achievement, added the manager of the BNB. According to him, what the government and the Ministry of Finance did under vladislav Goranov at the time played a crucial role. This was a common effort that was met with understanding by our partners, he said. the governor stressed. Asked what accession to the Banking Union gives us, the BNB governor said that this issue should be viewed strategically, not only in terms of the crisis we are in. The Banking Union is the first euro area institution to which Bulgaria becomes a full member with all the rights and responsibilities that result, including with regard to taking the most important decisions related to the supervision and resolution of European banks. which we did not have before accession. Making informed decisions regarding the banking sector is something that is as important as any other sector,Dimitar Radev said. Asked about the main challenges in the coming year 2020, the Governor of the Central Bank pointed to two themes: the pandemic and the accession of the BGN to the European Exchange Rate Mechanism. The challenges of joining the European Exchange Rate Mechanism were related to the scale, the complexity of this task, but this was an exercise that was well planned and well executed. Until the pandemic came unexpectedly and decisive measures had to be taken without sufficient time to prepare. The results show that in both cases the Central Bank and the banking sector as a whole have acted adequately. These results can be seen, including in the moratorium, which has been extended and gives financial relief to households and businesses during a very difficult period. But also in credit activity, which not only did not stagnate this year, but also increased compared tolast year, the BNB manager stressed. Both loans for households are increasing. The most serious growth is in mortgage loans, Mr. Radev said. What we did was mainly in order to achieve these two things  firstly, to create capacity in the banking sector to allow it to meet potential losses related to the crisis; and secondly to create conditions so that banks do not have difficulties in their main function, namely the provision of loans, the Governor is adamant. The additional measures, which were adopted as early as March, have increased their reserves and capacity to absorb losses, including the moratorium. If we are talking about borrowers, we must clearly say that those who are bad faith cannot benefit from the moratorium. he pointed out. More than 14,000 people have been companies and about 95,000 Households have benefited from a moratorium on loans during the first wave of the pandemic. The total amount of deferred loans is over BGN 9 billion. The relief that reschedules payments does not absoil intereston them, reminded the Governor of the Bulgarian National Bank and stressed that there should be no such expectation of remission or any other form of cancellation of these obligations by the Central Bank and commercial banks. to give a breath of air and opportunity to businesses and households  and this opportunity through the deferral of loan payments is serious, seeing what numbers are at issue, precisely to overcome this most severe period of the crisis. in which we are actively involved. But the second peak of the pandemic, the indicators in the economy, the indicators in the banking sector showed that we can afford a second such extension of the moratorium, the banker explained. In the result of all the measures taken, the banking sector is not ina worse position than the start of the pandemic and this is also a remarkable achievement for all those working in the banking sector. the Governor of the Central Bank. What they are doing outside the moratorium and they havenot stopped doing so is to negotiate with their customers schemes that will help them pay off their debts, including under relaxed conditions. even outside the moratorium. But it is not a case of forgiveness. We must not forget that banks are commercial entities, how all market participants, the central banker pointed out. What the BNB has as a tool is to continue the measures we introduced in March. They are mainly related to the management of banks' capital, tothe creation of an additional cap, to additional reserves that will help banks respond to adverse developments. One much discussed topic lately is that of the dividends that banks pay. We have made clear our position that we will continue with the dividend restrictions next year, the Governor of the Central Bank noted. Recently there have been discussions, decisions of the European Central Bank  there is a loophole where banks can pay such dividends, but we have made it very clear that we will continue our policy from this year  we will recommend that banks do not distribute dividends in the coming year. the manager of the BNB is adamant. So this is a very important measure. We have decided in the Governing Council on 17 December to continue to maintain the so-called countercyclical capital buffer level, we have kept it at a very low level. Mr Radev stressed. In his view, it is difficult to predict exactly how the crisis will develop in the coming year  there are signs in both direction and in the other direction. will recover to the level it was before the crisis. There are, of course, scenarios that we are obliged to take into account, although they are, in my view, less likely that the crisis will deepen, to last. We hope that the development will be better, but all we do is prepare the banks for possible bad scenarios. Regarding the forecast for the recovery of the economy from the crisis in mid-2022, Mr Radev indicated that this is a realistic forecast, given what would be realistic deadlines for the implementation of the measures now beingtaken globally. No one predicted in March or April that there would be a second peak of these scales, that there will be a re-closure of economies. Now it's something that happens everywhere and will have its economic impact. There is usually one lag in time, these effects are reflected in the economy a little later. It is realistic enough from the position of the moment to say that the economy will start to recover next year. Asked about the measures and the state's handling of the crown crisis, the governor commented that at the beginning Bulgaria reacted quickly and adequately. After that, the measures that were taken were not much different from what was happening in Europe and not only, Dimitar Radev said. It would be very good to go beyond the political context, because if this becomes a political discussion, the results can be even more severe. And we see this not only in our country, but even in the US. The pandemic should not be the subject of a political discussion. The best approach would be to have consolidation on this subject by all decision-makers, he said. Regarding comments that only the measures taken by the BNB are those that guarantee security for citizens andbusinesses, the manager said: "I do not think such comments are correct and I say this completely objectively based on the information available to me. jobs retention schemes, all schemes which also pass through the banking sector one way or another to provide loans under relaxed conditions have a positive effect. Government spending has also increased a lot. This is a huge theme of what would be the most appropriate financial measures. In general, the financial measures are basically two one is to increase fiscal expenditure so as to make up for the losses of businesses and households due to the constraints imposed on them, and the second  what is called monetary stimulus policy. For the first, governments are responsible for the second central banks. mr. Radev, it is everywhere. If you open the messages from the meetings of the ECB and the other banking authorities, you will see that one of the main themes there is that governments need to do more, they need to spend more to overcome the consequences of the crisis. There are suggestions, of course, and with regard to the measures that central banks apply. the case is that we as a central bank emphasize what is called macroprudential approach  to define systemic risks for the banking sector and to take measures so that they do not materialize, explained Mr. Dimitar Radev. When asked if the current crisis gives new chances, the BNB governor pointed out that this crisis is special. What the crisis has shown specifically for the banking sector is that Bulgaria has a strong central bank and a healthy and disciplined banking sector, the BNB's governor is adamant. Not only does this apply to the banking sector, of course, but specifically for the banking sector, the current situation opens up new opportunities, Mr Dimitar Radev summed up. PAGE \* MERGEFORMAT2

Title: Participation in the virtual edition of the annual Euromoney Forum on Central and Eastern Europe
text: Participation of Mr. Dimitar Radev, Governor of the BNB, in the virtual edition of the annual Euromoney Forum on Central and Eastern Europe, 14 January 2021. On January 14, 2021, the Governor of the Bulgarian National Bank, DimitarRadev, participated in a discussion in the framework of hyperlink annual forum on Central and Eastern Europe. and different approaches to joining the euro area with a focus on participation in the exchange rate mechanism (ERM II) and preparing for the adoption of the single currency. Mr. Dimitar Radev presented bulgaria's background and strategic motivation for the inclusion of the Bulgarian lev in ERM II as a key step on the way to the euro. that the adoption of the euro in Bulgaria will represent a smooth process, said Mr Radev. According to the Governor of the BNB, the adoption of the euro will accelerate the real convergence of the Bulgarian economy and will make a key contribution to growth and well-being in the country. Even the very process of preparing for the euro disciplines and stimulates the good policies needed to achieve a high degree of convergence of the country's economy to the euro area even before joining to it. At the other end, Mr Radev stressed, the euro does not in itself guarantee sustainable convergence. Bulgaria should therefore continue with prudent macroeconomic policies to be implemented by targeted and effective institutions. During the discussion, Mr. Dimitar Radev also touched on issues related to Bulgaria's membership in the Banking Union, carried out simultaneously with the inclusion in ERM II. The Governor told of the successful establishment of the close cooperation of the Bulgarian National Bank with the European Central Bank. Bulgaria participated in the Banking Union fully with the euro area countries . the first months of participation in the Banking Union have brought us concrete benefits, for example related to supervisory capacity and expanding access to information.

Title: Interview for The Banker Magazine, part of Financial Times Ltd.
Subtitle: DIMITAR RADEV, Q&A
text: Interview of the BNB Governor Mr. Dimitar Radev for The Banker Magazine, part of Financial Times Ltd., conducted on 30 March 2021, issue May 2021 DIMITAR RADEV, Q&A The governor of the Bulgarian National Bank, talks to Kit Gillet about getting the country through the Covid- 19 pandemic and plans to adopt the euro in early 2024. Dimitar Radev has served as governor of Bulgarian National Bank (BNB) since 2015, overseeing it through key moments in Bulgarias recent past. In 2020, in the face of the pandemic, the central bank adopted a package of measures that exceed 8% of gross domestic product (GDP), aimed at strengthening the resilience of banks in terms of both capital and liquidity. Q: How tough was 2020 for you and the banking sector? A: The last year was exceptional for everyone. Facing utterly unknown risks, as policy-makers and regulators we needed to come up with solutions with significant effects for businesses, households and the economy at large. We felt the full brunt of our enormous responsibility to society. It was the overall sequence of unusual circumstances as the pandemic evolved, rather than a single point in time. Critical as they have been, our anti-crisis measures fell back on the BNBs rich experience as macro-prudential authority for the banking sector. Their positive effects on the economy were complemented by the prudent behaviour of the banks themselves, as well as the governments fiscal and other support measures. Q: How did the banking sector perform in 2020? Were there any major or unexpected challenges? A: Our banks entered the pandemic with solid capital and liquidity positions. The BNB measures to boost the resilience of the sector were pre-emptive, aiming to further enhance banks loss-absorbing capacity in case the new risks would turn out to materialise. On the back of notably higher impairment costs, the 2020 profit generated by the sector was about half that of the previous year. Our banks have succeeded in maintaining comfortable levels of capital and liquidity, continuing to provide lending to the economy. Banks and supervisors alike are gaining knowledge and experience in coping with the unprecedented challenges stemming from the pandemic. As long as the coronavirus stays with us, along with the restrictive measures affecting the economy, we need to keep monitoring the timely recognition of credit risks by the banks. Their prudent provisioning remains our supervisory priority. One challenge to watch out for in the coming months is the dynamics of banks asset quality following the expiration of the temporary moratorium on bank loans repayments. Q: Bulgaria joined the Exchange Rate Mechanism II (ERM II) in 2020 and is targeting euro adoption in January 2024. Do you think this is a realistic target? A: It is ambitious, but achievable. There is an immense amount of work to be done in preparation for the euro, but I believe the Bulgarian institutions are strongly motivated and well-equipped to complete all steps and requirements. The euro adoption has long been a strategic goal for Bulgaria. The closer we get to accomplishing it, the stronger we are going to feel the upsides of being members of the European monetary union. Even well before the actual changeover to the euro, the very process of moving forward has so far benefited Bulgaria though consolidating our reform efforts, strengthening our policies and enhancing our institutional capacity. This was already demonstrated by the process of joining the ERM II and the EU Banking Union, completed last year, which involved prior requirements to fulfil policy commitments in several key areas. Q: How has the banking sector developed during your time in office? Are there lingering issues related to the bank runs of 2014, which occurred shortly before you took office? A: The case of bank runs back in 2014 was an isolated one with no ensuing effects. But the memories of those events, and the policy lessons we tried so hard to learn as a result, have certainly been the driver for deep transformations in recent years. Both the banking sector and supervision in Bulgaria have come a long way and look markedly different today than several years ago. The sector has undergone consolidation of ownership, and has strengthened through the asset quality reviews and stress tests in 2016 and 2019  the latter in the run up to joining the Banking Union. The banking supervision function of the BNB has been completely overhauled in many aspects, ranging from supervisory procedures to decision-making and governance. Q: When it comes to economic growth for Bulgaria, what challenges still need to be overcome? A: Our economy performed robustly in recent years, real GDP growing between 3% and 4% annually. The monetary policy regime of the currency board has underpinned the financial and macroeconomic stability in Bulgaria for nearly a quarter of a century. Competitiveness of the economy has kept improving, as reflected in the continuous rise in our exports. At the same time, there are notable structural challenges to the growth potential of the Bulgarian economy. Institutional deficiencies, adverse demographic trends including ageing, a shrinking labour force, and emerging skills shortages, are among areas of top concern. The baseline scenario remains that this year should see the turning point in setting up a stable trajectory of economic recovery in Europe, including the Bulgarian economy. One year since the outbreak of the pandemic, however, macroeconomic projections are still veiled by high levels of uncertainty. PAGE \* MERGEFORMAT 2

Title: Interview for Bloomberg Businessweek BG
Subtitle: JOINING THE EUROZONE IS AN EXAMPLE OF POLITICAL CONSISTENCY
text: Interview of the BNB Governor Mr. Dimitar Radev for Bloomberg Businessweek BG, issue May 2021 JOINING THE EUROZONE IS AN EXAMPLE OF POLITICAL CONSISTENCY In an interview for Bloomberg Businessweek BG with Ivaylo Lakov, the governor of the Bulgarian National Bank (BNB) Dimitar Radev shared how the central bank was one of the first to initiate and then follow through on an anti-crisis package of over BGN 9 billion. Mr. Radev, what risks do you currently see for the financial system from potential political instability or a political crisis? Every political crisis has its price. From the standpoint of the central bank, the worst-case scenario is if this price is paid at the expense of delaying economic recovery and undermining financial stability. Therefore, we at the BNB strive in this difficult environment, and within our mandate, to guarantee the stability of the monetary regime and thus the price stability in the country, as well as the unobstructed access to credit for businesses and households. Where is the political consensus at when it comes to Bulgaria joining the Eurozone? Despite the dynamic political processes, joining the Eurozone is shaping up to be an example of political consistency in Bulgaria. Moreover, it is a suitable national goal whose achievement can consolidate the heavily fragmented political arena and accelerate reforms aimed at modernising the country. How do you explain the campaign for stoking peoples fears that prices will rise due to the introduction of the Euro, that we would be using Bulgarian funds to pay the obligations of rich Western countries, etc.? Those opposing the Euro have never reached critical mass within Bulgarian public opinion due to the obvious advantages of European integration. Its facilitation via the introduction of the Euro is not going to decrease, but boost these advantages. Still, the introduction of the new currency will be preceded by the relevant communication campaign. This will help to raise awareness about the actual circumstances and effects accompanying this process. As a result, all hypothetical scenarios and fears should be allayed by objective arguments. Why is Eurozone membership a defining Bulgarian national interest? The road to the Eurozone and the membership itself will improve not only the structure of our economy and income levels, but also the quality of institutions, including political ones. Membership will raise the status of our country as a full participant in the strategic discussions on the continent. Bulgaria will become a member with the potential to make an actual contribution both to the responsibilities and to the solutions in the heart of Europe  including those most relevant to ourselves. This is the intersection between our national interest and Eurozone membership. How has Bulgaria benefited from joining the Banking Union and the European Exchange Rate Mechanism? The immediate effects were obvious, including improvement of the financing conditions, within an incredibly complicated and difficult environment. It is indicative that in the context of joining, Bulgaria issued debt at a historically low price. In addition to recognition of the stability of our monetary regime, bringing the Bulgarian lev into the European Exchange Rate Mechanism is a decisive step towards fulfilling one of the most important criteria for joining the Eurozone  that of exchange rate stability. On the other hand, our joining the Banking Union as a full member means achieving full harmonisation with the rules and practices applied in the banking sector within the EU, direct access to expertise and information resources, as well as direct participation in the decision-making processes in the sector at the Eurozone level. How would this improve control and discipline in the bank sector? By joining the Banking Union, we are building on what we have already achieved in banking supervision during recent years. This means that control and discipline in the sector meet even the highest European standards. We must not forget that without the huge advances made in the field during the past years, our membership in the Banking union would not be possible. What do we need to do by 2024 as preparation for the Eurozone, which ECB requirements have we yet to fulfil? We need to continue to comply with the nominal Maastricht criteria. In addition to the prudent macroeconomic policies, including in the field of public finances, introducing the Euro would require a mobilisation of resources and precision in order to solve complicated technical and organisation tasks. The BNB has already created an internal organisation for tackling the issues within our areas of competence, including areas such as banknotes and coins, credit institutions, payments systems and payment services providers, statistics, accounting, and information systems. We are also maintaining the relevant working communication with the ECB. We have the great advantage of already being part of one Eurozone institution  the Banking Union, including the Single Supervisory Mechanism and the Single Resolution Mechanism. To put things differently, we can say that the country has already achieved real progress in its preparation for joining over nearly three years time  that is, the two years from the process of applying to the actual joining of the Banking Union, to which we can add the past around eight months of full membership. What is your bottom line when it comes to tackling the crisis of the past year? We were one of the first central banks to initiate as early as March 2020 and subsequently implement an anti-crisis package of over BGN 9 billion. Our measures managed to achieve three goals: strengthening of the stability in the banking sector by reinforcing its capital and liquidity position; maintaining credit activity during the pandemic; and temporarily easing the debt payments of businesses and households via a private moratorium offered by the sector and approved by the BNB. What situation is the banking sector in now, how are banks weathering the crisis? As a result of the measures taken, the main sustainability indicators in the banking sector are better than at the start of the pandemic and they remain higher than average for the European Union. According to the latest data, the total capital adequacy of the sector amounts to 22.7%, and its liquidity sustainability is measured through a 294% coverage of the net liquidity outflows by a liquidity buffer  substantially more than regulatory requirements. Profit in the sector during the past year decreased approximately twofold as compared to the pre-crisis period, as a result of larger impairment costs, but there is a recovery trend at the start of this year. How did the moratorium on loans imposed due to the pandemic affect the banks? The moratorium provided temporary relief to the companies and households affected by the crisis. Its expiry will inevitably lead to some losses in the sector, however, the sector is fully prepared to absorb them. Understandably, we carefully analyse the effect of the moratorium on the quality of assets and on the credit risk in the sector, and we are prepared to initiate additional measures if necessary. Are banks prepared for a longer crisis? The short answer is yes. We expect economic recovery to start this year, and for the Bulgarian economy to have reached pre-crisis levels by mid-2022. Meanwhile, we are obligated to also prepare for more pessimistic scenarios. Like we have declared many times, we are ready to move forward with effective anti-crisis measures so long as necessary. What does the growth in bank deposits mean during the crisis (and before it)? It shows continuing trust in the bank sector during a period of low or even negative interest rates. At the same time, this growth signifies ongoing uncertainty in the economic environment and limited investment opportunities, and this is not a good sign for economic activity  neither for businesses, nor for households. What has been happening with loans during the past year? Loans to businesses and households have continued to increase rather than stagnate as per preliminary expectations. Herein lies one of the big goals achieved by the measures we took at the start of the pandemic. According to the latest data from monetary statistics, in March of this year as compared to March 2020, company loans have increased by 2.7%, and household loans  by 7.1%. This development shows that the banking sector has been fulfilling and continues to fulfil its main function  the provision of loans. What scenario are you working on now, when will the Bulgarian economy begin to recover? Due to the dynamic environment and the high level of uncertainty, we have started publishing our macroeconomic forecasts on a quarterly basis. We published the latest one only recently. It reflects our view that we will see a return to growth of real GDP in 2021, which will be mostly owing to the forecast transition to positive contribution by the net exports and gross fixed capital formation. The main risk facing the economy is still the dynamic of the Covid-19 spread and the potential need for new restrictions. The Bulgarian economy could also experience negative effects from the political situation in the country this year  a risk that has not been calculated in our latest estimates. Why are central banks eager to create digital currencies  Euro, dollar, Yuan  what would this change? This is another interesting topic we are following very closely, but without planning any practical steps outside the Eurosystem. A digital currency issued by a central bank should further facilitate payments using a new digital form of money. In addition to being convenient and widely accepted for payments, the digital currency should also bear security and protect personal data in transactions, similar to the anonymity of physical banknotes and coins. Similar issues were reviewed in detail by the ECB after the broad public consultation on the digital Euro, the results of which were published last month. PAGE \* MERGEFORMAT 3

Title: The BNB Governor for the STANDARD newspaper
Subtitle: DIMITAR RADEV: OUR BANKING MARKET IS BECOMING MORE AND MORE ATTRACTIVE. THE BNB HAS ACTIVATED AND COMPLETED AN ANTI-CRISIS PACKAGE OF MEASURES WORTH OVER BGN 9 BILLION
text: The BNB Governor Mr. Dimitar Radev for the STANDARD newspaper, 3 December 2021 DIMITAR RADEV: OUR BANKING MARKET IS BECOMING MORE AND MORE ATTRACTIVE. THE BNB HAS ACTIVATED AND COMPLETED AN ANTI-CRISIS PACKAGE OF MEASURES WORTH OVER BGN 9 BILLION We are hoping that the year 2022 will bring a gradually improving, although still uneasy, business environment This year has passed under the sign of the difficult recovery of the economy, with continuing uncertainty and the risks associated with the spread of the Covid-19. In this environment the banks in Bulgaria continued to operate fully and effectively as evidenced by the growing deposits and loans and by the objective indicators of the banking sector. As of today we can restate that the banking system is highly liquid, well-capitalised, profitable and enjoying the trust of depositors and customers. Todays good results, however, could not have been achieved without the exceptional efforts of the banks themselves and our efforts as supervisors and regulators. When, nearly two years ago, we were faced with the unusual challenges caused by the pandemic, fast and ambitious actions had to be taken. The BNB was one of the first central banks that, back in March 2020, activated and later fully completed a sizable anti-crisis package of measures for the banking sector, worth over BGN 9 billion. At that time our measures had three objectives: first, to further strengthen the resilience of the banking sector by reinforcing its capital and liquidity position; second, to support banks lending during the pandemic; and third, to temporarily relieve the debt payments of businesses and households by means of a private moratorium prepared by the industry and later approved by the BNB. The above-listed objectives have been accomplished. In particular, the expiry of the term of the moratorium a few months ago ran smoothly. In spite of the worsened credit risk, the generally positive economic dynamics benefited borrowers, and disruptions in the quality of the banking systems aggregate loan portfolio were avoided. Globally, both banks and their regulators and supervisors have gained new knowledge and experience in handling the unprecedented challenges of the pandemic. One of the clear conclusions at this stage is related to the need of constant alertness and a conservative credit risk management approach. While the corona virus is circulating in society and the economy, our priority will be to ensure that banks timely recognise, adequately assess and provide for credit risk. At the same time, the BNB will urge the banking system to be prepared for accumulation and realization of potential risks, using the capital buffers as macroprudential tools to keep the capital reserves in the system. Looking ahead, one of the strategic aspects of the anticipated evolution of the Bulgarian banking sector will be its consolidation. The processes of consolidating the ownership of the banks in Bulgaria have speeded up over recent years and were pushed further following the asset quality reviews and stress tests conducted in 2016 and 2019. Today, now as part of the Banking Union, the prospects of the Bulgarian banking market, in terms of investment, are becoming more and more attractive, as is demonstrated by the latest consolidation developments. The banking sector in Bulgaria has successfully overcome one more year of severe challenges. We are hoping that the year 2022 will bring a gradually improving, although still uneasy, economic environment where banks will remain resilient and will continue to operate in top gear, with prudent risk management and to the benefit of depositors and all customers.
