Title: Interview for the 24 HOURS newspaper
Subtitle:
DIMITAR RADEV, BNB GOVERNOR: BULGARIA IS IN A GOOD 
POSITION TO ADOPT THE EURO. THE BNB IS READY TO DO 
THE ENORMOUS TECHNICAL WORK FOR THIS
text: Interview with Mr. Dimitar Radev, BNB Governor, for the 24 HOURS newspaper, pgs. 1, 15, 16, 6 December 2021 DIMITAR RADEV, BNB GOVERNOR: BULGARIA IS IN A GOOD POSITION TO ADOPT THE EURO. THE BNB IS READY TO DO THE ENORMOUS TECHNICAL WORK FOR THIS We are seeing off a very difficult year, Mr. Radev. A pandemic, a recession, and in Bulgaria, to top it all, elections after elections, of course with the concomitant populism and political talk. However, the banking system remained stable. What is the secret for this? Banks were well-prepared when they entered the crisis brought about by the pandemic. Moreover, in the last nearly two years they further strengthened their capital and liquidity positions. According to the latest data, the total capital adequacy of the banking sector reaches 22.4%, and the liquidity coverage ratio is 313.5%. The BNBs conservative supervisory polity underlies all these results as this policy focuses on the prevention and the maintenance of the banking systems stability in view of existing or potentially accumulated risks. And yet, dont you see any hidden dangers? For example, you alerted to a possible growth of bad loans and you announced an increase in the countercyclical capital buffer rate from next year. Is this a sign of coming problems or is it just preventing them from appearing? There are risks and these are not hidden. The likelihood of increasing bad loans is one of those risks. That is exactly why we are taking preventive measures which should be viewed in the context of the overall objective of the BNBs macroprudential policy. And this objective is that the banking system is able to keep its capital position and, if necessary, to accumulate more reserves. These reserves must prepare banks to assume losses in case of realisation of accumulated credit risk in banks balance sheets, if this happens due to the manifestation of various risks in the economic environment, cyclical or long-term ones. Brussels thinks that we are inflating a real-estate bubble, we are denying it. Who is right? Are any temporary restrictions needed in mortgage lending or we are very far from such a measure that the BNB has already taken before and knows how to do it? As there is no technical definition, lets use the word bubble in the general meaning in which it is used in connection with past crises in the real estate market. In this context, now we cannot speak of a real-estate bubble, but there are distinct trends that, if not countered, might lead to such a bubble. We have identified the relevant risks and we are applying measures, at this stage targeted at lenders only, and these measures are designed to prevent the materialisation of these risks. For example, at its last session the Governing Council of the BNB confirmed the systemic risk buffer at 3% for all banks, applicable to all exposures in Bulgaria. Before that we increased the countercyclical capital buffer rate up to 1%, effective as of 1 October next year. In the middle of this month we are going to announce a new decision based on the quarterly review of the countercyclical capital buffer rate. Have central banks caused the unprecedented inflation by printing money and by their overall monetary policy? Let me just say that the BNB is not to blame as its hands are tied by the currency board arrangement. The current inflation is a result of numerous and concurrent factors. You know that there are different viewpoints. Economies are passing through untypical challenges and are changing. The pandemic has further reinforced expectations of supportive monetary and fiscal policies, but price increases are a deeper process, reflecting movements in commodities, energy, labour, possible difficulties and changes in international or inter-company production and supply chains. What is your forecast, how long will the inflation storm last? Although we are talking about imported inflation, how can it be curbed so that it does not prevent our entry into the euro area? And can it be curbed? This is the big question about inflation and its forecasting - to what extent it is the result of transitory or longer-term structural factors, such as those related to labour costs. Depending on the evolution of these determinants, the analysis will show what direction and speed consumer price movements will take. The situation in the country is largely determined by the external environment and factors due to the high share in consumption of imported goods and services. There are specifics, but in general Bulgaria should not be expected to start implementing policies that would bring a sharper inflation differential vis-a-vis the euro area or the EU. We will pay particular attention to this issue in our next macroeconomic forecast, which we will publish in January. When will the time of low interest rates end, which keeps getting postponed? Are banks turning into vaults that simply store people's money, now also for a fee and with negative interest rates or ones close to zero? Does this phenomenon require a change in the supervisory policy of central banks? Banks' interest rate and fee policies reflect market conditions and banks' competitive position. They also derive from efficiency and cost optimisation. The interest rates and fees of individual banks are not subject to direct administrative control or supervisory policy. What can be said as a framework for analysis is that the reversal of the interest rate cycle will follow a combination of changes in economic and financial conditions, as well as the adjustment of relevant monetary policies. As more and more banks refuse to open new savings deposits and redirect people to other investment products, again carried out by them or their funds, what is the supervisory response to these new functions? Are new risks not emerging with this entry into the investment sphere? Banking supervision aims to maintain the stability of the banking system and protect depositors, not investors in various financial products. When banks' customers decide to switch funds to relatively more lucrative but riskier exposures, they should consider the boundary beyond which they have moved from being depositors to being investors. Why has the Magnitsky Act caused such an uproar in our country that there was even a parliamentary committee on the subject? And why has the BNB received accusations of causing a "civil death"? What did the BNB actually do and why, let us clarify this remaining pending question. The actions of both the BNB and of the banks in Bulgaria after the announcement of the Magnitsky list were aimed, no more and no less, at applying the existing legal framework in Bulgaria. In some cases the banks had imposed restrictions on the transactions of persons on the list on other grounds, even before the Magnitsky sanctions were announced. The case turned out to be equivocal. On the one hand, banks could suffer real reputational or financial damage, as financial institutions that maintain dollar accounts and make payments in dollars are by definition subject to this sanctions regime, and on the other hand, it was clear that Magnitsky has no direct legal effect in Bulgaria. That is why the BNB has been calling from the outset for a stable legislative solution on how such sanctions by third countries can be applied in our country. As the parliamentary cycle returns to normal, work in this direction could also be stimulated. An important nuance, however, should also be to achieve compliance with EU-wide law and applicability at the EU level. Once every two years, or even every year, bank purchases and mergers take place in our country. Are we heading towards the market predicted by experts, where there are 2-3 giants and a few small boutique vaults? And more importantly, are we not creating banking monopolies that have no interest in competing with each other, to the detriment of their customers? Just a few weeks ago, the largest acquisition deal in terms of size and price in our banking market was announced. This is a good sign both for the state of the sector and for its development prospects. From a legal and procedural point of view, any such consolidation transaction necessarily goes through an assessment of the competitive environment and effects. But customer protection rests above all on sound market logic and arguments relating to the improvement of the credit institutions themselves. Consolidation in the sector is a natural process, driven by cost optimisation considerations and increasing the overall efficiency of banks. Customers should therefore benefit if, as a result of mergers and ownership consolidations, more stable and more competitive institutions continue to operate in the market. 2024 is approaching, which is also the deadline for Bulgaria to adopt the euro. Do the pandemic and the crisis threaten our road map? We must not forget that, despite all the political turbulence, we are still in a very good starting position for the euro, including in terms of the fiscal criteria, and we can still control the process to a large extent. It would be a historic mistake if we hesitate and lose this control or if we allow a breach in the management of public finances. What we need now is decisive action on the political front, like the one Croatia has already taken. For its part, the BNB is fully prepared to carry out the huge amount of technical work involved in adopting the euro. Its been several months now since your term of office ended and Parliament has still not got round to electing a new team. Let me ask you first of all, if you are invited, will you stand for a second term? If you are not going to, what important advice will you give to your successor? When the selection process gets under way, I will make my position public. What do you wish bankers for their traditional holiday? I warmly congratulate them on the excellent results achieved during the difficult and complex year 2021 and wish them good health and new successes. And their customers? Health with the assurance that all Bulgarian banks are good for their money. PAGE \* MERGEFORMAT 4

Title: Interview for "24 Hours"
text: Interview of Mr. Dimitar Radev, Governor of the BNB, for the "24 Hours" newspaper, pp. 15 and 19, 3 March 2022 THE BNB AND THE BANKING SECTOR ARE READY TO RESPOND ADEQUATELY TO THE WAR IN UKRAINE In Bulgaria, unlike other European countries, there are no Russian banks. That's why our banks are insulated from direct risks Mr. Radev, how do the events of the last week affect the banking system of Bulgaria? Are the BNB and the banking sector ready to react adequately? The war in Ukraine is a huge challenge, including for the banking sector. The short answer to your question is  yes, the BNB and the banking sector are ready to respond adequately to this challenge. In recent years, we have built a serious capacity for the sector to work in crisis situations. We proved it during the covid crisis, when we activated and implemented an anti-crisis package for over EUR 9 billion. leva. Yes, but the causes of the crisis are now different. That's right. Therefore, we adapt our measures to the specific situation. These measures, which have already been activated, affect key areas such as cybersecurity, business continuity, payment systems, money circulation, reserve management, logistics preparation. We are guided by two principles. Firstly, that we need to act quickly and decisively, and secondly, that the measures must be proportionate to the evolution of the situation. That is why we are following the course of events very closely and are ready to escalate measures if necessary. Will these measures affect the banks' customers  people and businesses? No, these measures are specifically aimed at the BNB and the banking sector. The effect on people and businesses of these measures will be in the smooth functioning of the banking sector. We work so that, like the covid crisis, the banking sector is part of the solution, and not part of the problems that people and businesses face. At the end of last week, you participated in an informal meeting of the Council of Finance Ministers and Governors of Central Banks in the EU, ECOFIN, together with Deputy Prime Minister and Minister Asen Vassilev. How do you assess the reaction of the European institutions? I have participated in similar forums many times. This is the first time I have witnessed such determination and consolidation of the position of the European institutions and member states. How does Bulgaria stand in this process? I can, of course, speak only about the BNB and the banking sector. We work closely with the ECB. The banking sector is the only sector in the country that is de facto part of the euro area through our full participation in the European Banking Union. We are already in the second year of our full participation in this union. The situation at the moment emphasizes even more strongly the advantages for the country of this participation. We have access to critical information, we are involved in making the most important decisions for European banks and in the implementation of relevant prevention and response mechanisms, such as the Single Supervisory Mechanism and the Single Resolution Mechanism. This significantly increases the safety and resilience of our banking sector. The European Union has already adopted decisions on restrictive measures against Russia's financial system. What follows from these decisions? The European Union has banned all transactions related to the management of reserves as well as assets of the Central Bank of Russia and imposed restrictions on the supply of euro banknotes to Russia. In addition, seven Russian banks have been excluded from the international financial messaging system SWIFT as of March 12 this year, which is the financial "nervous system" of the modern world, which supports international financial flows and connects more than 11,000 institutions in more than 200 countries. We apply these measures insofar as they affect the BNB and our banking system. You are also aware of the developments of the last few days with Sberbank. What is known so far? The situation with Sberbank is very dynamic, it changes literally in hours. Sberbank in Austria was declared in liquidation. Its branches in Slovenia and Croatia have been restructured, branches in Serbia and Bosnia and Herzegovina have been sold to local banks, steps have been taken in the Czech Republic to revoke the license of the Sberbank branch, and Hungary has already revoked the license of the branch in this country. We, of course, are very well aware of these events. Is there a risk of such developments in Bulgaria? Not. The events with Sberbank in recent days confirm the correctness of the strategic choices made by the BNB. Banks in Bulgaria have an insignificant share (less than 0.5%) of credit exposures, attracted funds and financial transactions to and from Russia. In Bulgaria, unlike other European countries, we do not have Russian banks. That is why our banking sector is isolated from direct risks arising from the war in Ukraine. Nevertheless, we are in constant communication with banks that monitor certain transactions of their customers with caution. And what will be the economic consequences for Bulgaria of the deepening crisis? We expect the economic consequences to manifest themselves mainly in two directions  a slowdown in economic growth and an increase in inflation. The nominal levels of deterioration of the economic environment will depend on the specific development of the processes. Our analysis and expectations will be reflected in the next macroeconomic forecast, which we will publish in April. You pointed out the advantages of the country's participation in the Banking Union. In this context, how do you assess the country's chances of the country's accession to the euro area on January 1, 2024? There are voices to postpone this process, including due to the war in Ukraine. Contrary. With new developments, this process must continue more decisively than before. Let's not forget that the same voices for postponement were heard regarding the country's accession to the European Banking Union and the lev to the European Exchange Rate Mechanism, which happened in the midst of the covid crisis. We have every chance to join the euro area on January 1, 2024. All that is needed is real, not declarative, political will, because in the end it is a political decision. And here we are talking not only about specific benefits, but about the strategic affiliation and direction of the country's development. Finally, I cannot help but ask you about the upcoming election of the Governor of the BNB and your intentions? As of today, I have no comment on this topic.

Title: Speech by the BNB Governor Mr. Dimitar Radev at the conference "Bulgaria in the Eurozone - Advantages and Opportunities", Sofia, 9 December 2022
text: Statement by the BNB Governor Mr. Dimitar Radev at the conference Bulgaria in the Euro Area  Advantages and Opportunities, Sofia, 9 December 2022 Ladies and Gentlemen, First, I would like to thank the organisers for the invitation and, of course, for the very initiative to organise this event. Along with other things, this is indicative of a growing interest in the subject of Bulgarias accession to the euro area and the adoption of the euro. I will try to address the question of why we are doing this, why we want to join the euro area and introduce the euro. On the surface, the euro introduction may be viewed as a technical process. Such a view has its rationale, with at least two points. First, the Bulgarian lev has been pegged to the euro since the very launch of the European single currency; and, second, the euro is Bulgarias reserve currency that ensures the coverage and warrants the stability of the Bulgarian lev. In this sense, it is indeed a technical process of converting Bulgarias reserve currency into a local national currency. In practice, however, the introduction of the euro is much more than just a technical process. It has important implications for the development and modernisation of the country. I will refer to three of the implications that supports such a conclusion: 1. Normalising and building on our monetary regime; 2. Speeding up the process of real convergence; 3. Enhancing the quality and efficiency of institutions. Normalising and building on our monetary regime We have operated a currency board for the past quarter century. This regime was put in place in response to the severe financial crisis into which Bulgaria fell in the mid-1990s. At that time, we were looking for an anchor that would achieve and later sustain financial stability in the country. The currency board was exactly that anchor for establishing and, subsequently, sustaining financial stability in Bulgaria. Based on the achieved results, we can say that it has accomplished its purpose in the best possible way. It is no accident that, in retrospect, the currency board is considered to have been the most successful reform carried out in our monetary (and, to some extent, economic) history. At the same time, the currency board has imposed very stringent and serious restrictions. It has deprived us of the possibility of pursuing monetary, and consequently, fully-fledged macroeconomic policy. Key functions of a normal central bank, as the BNB is, have been strongly constrained, practically prohibited, such as the lender of last resort function. The initial expectations at the time were that the currency board would be in place for a relatively short period and would be a natural transition to the introduction of the euro. It is no accident that the currency board was regarded at first as the Bulgarian version of the ERM II. Apparently, the expectations of the time frame have not come to pass, but the position remains unchanged that the introduction of the euro is the only good, wise, and to a large extent possible exit from the currency board. Now we are just on the verge of such an exit. Among other things, this will lead to normalisation and building on our monetary regime. Why normalisation? Because in this way the implementation of monetary policy and, consequently, of fully-fledged macroeconomic policy will be resumed, as well as the performance of all key functions typical of a normal central bank. Why building on? Because this will be done by joining one of the largest and most modern monetary unions, and by introducing one of the two largest and most significant currencies in the world, which will also become Bulgarias local national currency as a result of this transition. Speeding up the process of real convergence The speeded-up real conversion process has no good alternative. The question is whether this speed-up can happen before or after accession to the euro area. I will point out that, apart from modernising the economy and bringing it closer to the structure of the euro area economy, this process also means pushing incomes up to the average European levels. Obviously, in the case of a non-euro area country like Bulgaria, this process is running very slowly and we continue to be the country with the lowest incomes among the EU member states. Remaining in this state poses yet higher risks. The most serious risk of all is the opposition to the objectives of financial stability and the objectives of increasing the peoples incomes and improving their well-being. The latest developments, including in the budget debates going on now, show that there are growing sentiments along these lines, in support of disproportionately increasing public spending and, in turn, deficits and debt. Experience, including our own experience, teaches us that this path is going nowhere. Over time, the outcome will be loss of financial stability - the most important and probably the only macroeconomic advantage that we have earned internationally - and real deterioration in the peoples welfare. My firm conviction is that accession to the euro area will resolve this potential conflict, by speeding up the process of real conversion. Only in this way, the higher incomes in Bulgaria will not be at the expense of financial stability. This process certainly depends on the pursuing of good policies. In the Bulgarian environment, pursuing such policies will be much more likely if the country is a part of the euro area than if it is on the periphery of the EU. On the one hand, the very act of accession requires the compliance with and fulfilment of a series of criteria, including curbed inflation and a disciplined budget, and this can be achieved by implementing good policies. On the other hand, accession to the euro area would accelerate the process of structural reforms in Bulgaria, a process that is in serious delay, it would also improve the conditions for financing the economy and would promote investment  the latter provides motivation for good, and not for risky policies. The combination of all these factors creates an environment promoting sustained outpacing economic growth, and this is exactly the leading factor for speeded-up convergence and higher incomes. Enhancing the quality and efficiency of institutions Accession to the euro area has the potential to become a catalyst for strengthening the quality and efficiency of institutions. We already have a specific example: the BNB and our banking system. The general context of the large-scale reforms that we undertook at the central bank and in the banking sector after the 2014 turmoil was indeed the full integration into the European financial infrastructure and institutions. In addition, we have already gained two-year practical experience from our full membership in the European banking union, including in the Single Supervisory Mechanism and the Single Resolution Mechanism. Now we see the concrete results. The banking sector in Bulgaria is enjoying ratios of capital adequacy, liquidity and profitability above the average for the EU. This, inter alia, is a result of the preparation for accession and of the BNBs full-fledged participation in euro area institutions over the last two years. This institutional example could also be reproduced in other sectors when Bulgaria joins the euro area. If the banking sector can achieve results above the average of the EU member countries, then any other sector can do it. With this let me come back to the initial question: Why are we doing this? Of course, there is more than one answer. Based on what I have just said, let me offer the following one: We are doing this in order to normalise and build on our monetary regime; to speed up the real convergence of the economy, including to ensure higher incomes not because of growing deficits and debts, but because of sustained outpacing economic growth; and to enhance the quality and efficiency of Bulgarias institutions. Thank you.

Title: Presentation by Mr. Kalin Hristov, Deputy Governor of the Bulgarian National Bank, presented at the General Assembly of the European Banknote Conference, Sofia, 8 June 2023
text: Interview of Mr. Dimitar Radev, Governor of the BNB, for BTA, 24 July 2023 SIMULTANEOUS TIGHTENING OF MONETARY AND FISCAL POLICY IS NEEDED TO COUNTERACT INFLATION On the BG euro coins - the Madara Horseman, St. Ivan Rilski, Paisii Hilendarski and the inscription "stotinka" Mr. Radev, congratulations on your election for a second term at the helm of the BNB. What do you think are the key challenges facing the institution? Thank you! The immediate challenges relate to the uncertain and evolving macroeconomic environment. Also on the agenda are the tasks of building the necessary institutional and technical framework for the successful introduction of the euro in Bulgaria. What do you think are the macroeconomic risks facing the country and how do you see their resolution? There are two topics and they are interrelated: inflation and economic growth. Their development depends to a certain extent on external factors, but internal factors are also increasingly important, and in particular the development of monetary and fiscal conditions in the country. The BNB pursues a systematic and consistent policy of tightening monetary conditions. The last step in this regard, effective from July 1 this year, is the increase of 12 percent of the mandatory minimum reserves that banks must keep with the BNB. In practice, this means the withdrawal of several billion levs from commercial banks. The aim is to reduce the credit expansion of banks, primarily in the segment of housing loans. This will push down demand and consumption, and therefore inflation. Decisions to tighten monetary conditions are difficult decisions for any central bank. They need to be calibrated in such a way as to help curb inflation without stagnating the economy. And this is what we are doing and will be doing in the horizon of this year and to a large extent next year. How would you comment on the fiscal conditions you mentioned, especially in the context of the adoption of the 2023 budget? The intention to keep the budget deficit within 3 percent of GDP is a step in the right direction. At the same time, taking into account the trajectory of the economic cycle and the change in the structure of budget spending, a 3 percent deficit means a limited but ongoing fiscal expansion. Fiscal expansion is not a factor in curbing inflation, quite the opposite. In this regard, it is extremely important to work towards synchronization of fiscal and monetary conditions. From the point of view of the objective of controlling inflation, the direction of this synchronization in the short term should be towards tightening both monetary and fiscal conditions. In the long run, which is better to control inflation - keeping the currency board or joining the eurozone? Participation in an economic and monetary union with historically lower inflation, such as the euro area, is a factor, other things being equal, for better control of inflationary processes, both in the short and long term. This is shown by all data since the creation of the euro area until today. Does the date of January 1, 2025 remain realistic for Bulgaria's accession to the euro area? Yes, if we do the right things and fulfill the necessary conditions with a focus on inflation. The only formal condition for the BNB is to maintain currency stability. This condition is fulfilled through the participation of the lev in the European Exchange Rate Mechanism. There is no scenario in which this condition can be violated. The other main task for the BNB is technical preparation. Based on the progress achieved so far, I can say that the BNB and the banking sector will be ready for the introduction of the euro well before the deadline. If the current political structure turns out to be sufficiently stable, I expect the government to fulfill the rest, more in number, conditions within its competence. Which symbols and graphic symbols do you consider appropriate to be depicted on Bulgarian euro coins? How far has the process of minting test euro coins reached? After the signing in December last year of a memorandum on this issue with the European Commission and the Eurogroup, we now have the full documentation for the minting of Bulgarian euro coins. At its last meeting, the Governing Council of the BNB united around the idea to reproduce the design of the current circulation coins, which will ensure continuity in the currency used and will facilitate the recognition of the new currency by Bulgarian citizens, namely: the Madara Horseman  on the small coins, St. Nicholas the Great. Ivan Rilski  on the 1 euro coin, and Paisii Hilendarski  on the 2 euro coin. On the national side of the Bulgarian euro coins it is envisaged that the word "Bulgaria" will be written in Cyrillic, as well as the word "euro" (for the coins of 1 and 2 euros) and "stotinka", respectively "stotinki" (for the coins of 1, 2, 5, 10, 20 and 50 euro cents). On the edge of the largest 2 euro coin it is planned to be inscribed with the text in Cyrillic "GOD, SAVE BULGARIA", which is in accordance with the Bulgarian historical traditions in coinage. The development of the art projects that will be submitted to the Coordination Council for Bulgaria's preparation for membership in the euro area is forthcoming. After their final approval, the projects will be presented to the Council of the European Union, the European Commission and the euro area member states. Croatia joined the eurozone at the beginning of this year. What experience do your colleagues from Zagreb, and the euro area as a whole, pass on in relation to the transition from a national currency to the euro? There have been no unexpected developments since Croatia's accession to the euro area. The country's credit rating, which was worse than Bulgaria's before joining the euro area, is now better, which has significantly improved the conditions for its financing. Inflation is decreasing, not increasing. There is a boom in tourism and investment. The contact with our Croatian colleagues is very good. We helped them in the beginning, when we were leaders in the process, now we rely on their support, as well as on the support of the other central banks of the euro area. How do you assess the credit market in Bulgaria and do you think that additional measures are needed to influence its sustainable growth? Has the BNB used all its tools in this direction? The pace of credit expansion is decreasing. We influence the process through three sets of measures. Firstly, using the available monetary policy instruments  for example, the already mentioned decision to increase the minimum reserve requirements. Secondly, using supervisory and macroprudential policy instruments  for example, the increase in the countercyclical capital buffer. And thirdly, accelerating the transmission of the ECB's monetary policy, which pursues the same objective. We are closely monitoring the process and are ready to activate additional measures if necessary. When can we expect an increase in interest rates on deposits? The increase in interest rates in Bulgaria is slower due to the high liquidity of our banking system. The upward trend will emerge more clearly towards the end of this year and next year. And this applies to both interest rates on deposits and interest rates on loans. Is a new stress test envisaged for the banking system? This process has not stopped. Under the Credit Institutions Act, the BNB conducts annual stress tests of banks. Based on the results, we determine the capital and other mandatory requirements for banks. The fact that this process no longer arouses broad public interest, like the stress tests of 2016 and 2019, is actually good news. During the COVID-19 pandemic, the IMF decided to allocate 650 billion. among the countries participating in the Fund. Bulgaria received nearly 859 million special drawing rights with the equivalent of about 2 billion euros. Lv. What were these funds used for? This decision was taken by the IMF Board of Governors, of which I am a member. With the funds received, we increased the foreign exchange reserves. This, among other things, is an example of the benefits of our integration into the European and global financial infrastructure. Similarly, our future participation in the ECB's capital as a member of the euro area will provide us with access to the Eurosystem's monetary income.

Title: Speech by Ms. Nina Stoyanova, Deputy Governor of the Bulgarian National Bank, Head of the Banking Department, at the Bulgarian School of Politics "Dimitry Panitza", Borovets, July 2, 2023
text: Interview with Mr. Dimitar Radev, BNB Governor, for BTA, 24 July 2023 WE SHOULD TIGHTEN BOTH MONETARY AND FISCAL POLICIES TO KEEP INFLATION IN CHECK The Bulgarian euro coins will feature the Madara Horseman, St. Ivan Rilski, Paisy Hilendarski, and the inscription stotinka(s) Mr. Radev, congratulations on your re-appointment as BNB Governor for a second term of office. What are, in your opinion, the key challenges facing the institution? Thank you! The immediate challenges are arising from the uncertain and changing macroeconomic environment. The agenda also includes the tasks of creating the necessary institutional and technical framework for the successful introduction of the euro in Bulgaria. What are, in your opinion, the macroeconomic risks for Bulgaria and how do you see their resolution? These are two subjects and they are interrelated: inflation and economic growth. How they would evolve depends to some extent on external factors, but internal factors, particularly the development of the monetary and fiscal conditions in Bulgaria, are of growing importance. The BNB has been pursuing a systematic and consistent policy of tightening monetary conditions. The last step in this direction, which came into effect as of 1 July this year, was the increase to 12 percent of the minimum required reserves that banks must hold at the BNB. Practically, this means pulling several billions of levs out of commercial banks. The purpose is to reduce banks credit expansion, primarily in the housing loan segment. This will push demand and consumption down, and subsequently inflation. The decisions to tighten monetary conditions are tough decisions for any central bank. They must be calibrated in a way that helps curbing inflation, without stifling the economy. And this is what we are doing and what we will be doing this year and largely next year. How would you comment on the fiscal conditions that you mentioned, especially in the context of the adoption of the 2023 budget? The intent to keep budget deficit down to 3 percent of GDP is a step in the right direction. At the same time, considering the trajectory of the economic cycle and the changes in the structure of budgetary expenditures, a 3 percent deficit means a limited but continuing fiscal expansion. Fiscal expansion is not a factor that contains inflation, quite the opposite. Therefore, it is of utmost importance for us to seek to synchronise the fiscal and monetary conditions. With the objective of controlling inflation in view, this synchronisation in the short run should go towards tightening both monetary and fiscal conditions. In the long run, which is better for controlling inflation  to keep the currency board in place or to join the euro area? Participation in an economic and monetary union with historically lower inflation, as the euro area, is a factor, other things being equal, for better control of inflationary processes, both in the short and in the long run. This has been shown by all the data since the formation of the euro area. Is the date of 1 January 2025 still a realistic target date for Bulgarias entry in the euro area? Yes, if we do the right things and meet the required conditions, focusing on inflation. The only formal condition that the BNB must fulfil is to maintain monetary stability. This condition is fulfilled through the participation of the lev in the European Exchange Rate Mechanism. There is no scenario in which this condition may be breached. The other major task of the BNB is the technical preparations. Considering the progress made so far, I can say that the BNB and the banking sector will be ready for the euro changeover well before the deadline. If the current political construction proves to be sufficiently stable, I expect that the Government will manage to comply with the remaining, actually the majority of, conditions within its competence. Which symbols and graphic elements do you think would be appropriate to feature on the Bulgarian euro coins? How far has the process of minting trial euro coins gone? Having signed a memorandum on this issue with the EC and the Eurogroup last December, now we have the complete documentation to mint the Bulgarian euro coins. At its last session, the BNB Governing Council have united around the idea that the design of the currently circulating coins should be reproduced, which will ensure continuity of the used currency and will facilitate the recognition of the new currency by the Bulgarian citizens, specifically the image of the Madara Horseman on the low-value coins, St. Ivan Rilski on the 1 coin, and Paisy Hilendarski on the 2 coin. The national side of the Bulgarian euro coins will feature the inscriptions Bulgaria in Cyrillic and euro (for the coins of 1 and 2), together with stotinka or stotinkas respectively (for the coins of 1, 2, 5, 10, 20 and 50 euro cents). An inscription on the edge of the highest-value coin of 2 will read GOD SAVE BULGARIA in Cyrillic, which is in line with the Bulgarian historical coinage traditions. The artistic designs are going to be created and submitted to the Coordinating Council for Bulgaria's preparations for euro area membership. Once they are finally approved, the designs will be presented to the Council of the European Union, the European Commission, and the euro area Member States. Croatia joined the euro area at the beginning of this year. What experience are your colleagues from Zagreb and from all euro area countries sharing from the changeover to the euro? There have been no unexpected developments since Croatia joined the euro area. The country's credit rating, which was worse than that of Bulgaria before Croatia joined the euro area, is now better, thereby significantly improving its financing conditions. Inflation is falling, not rising. There is a boom in tourism and investment. The contacts with our Croatian colleagues are very good. We were helping them in the beginning when we were in the lead of this process, and now we are counting on their support and on the support of the other euro area central banks. How do you assess the credit market in Bulgaria and do you think that additional measures are needed to influence its sustainable growth? Has the BNB used all its tools in this direction? The pace of credit expansion is slowing down. We have been influencing the process, using three sets of measures. Firstly, we are using the available monetary policy tools, such as the already mentioned decision to increase the minimum required reserves. Secondly, we are using supervisory and macroprudential policy tools, such as raising the countercyclical capital buffer. And thirdly, the transmission of the ECB monetary policy is accelerating, as it is pursuing the same objective. We are monitoring the process closely and stand ready to initiate additional measures if necessary. When could we expect an increase in deposit interest rates? Interest rates in Bulgaria have been rising more slowly due to the high liquidity of our banking system. The upward trend will become clearer towards the end of this year and during next year. And this applies to interest rates on both deposits and loans. Do you plan any new stress tests for the banking system? This process has never been halted. Under the Law on Credit Institutions, the BNB conducts stress tests of banks every year. Based on the test results, we set the capital and other mandatory requirements for banks. This process is no longer an issue of wide public interest as were the stress tests in 2016 and 2019, and this is actually good news. During the COVID-19 pandemic, the IMF decided to distribute USD 650 billion among the countries participating in the Fund. Bulgaria received nearly USD 859 million special drawing rights equivalent to about BGN 2 billion. How were these funds used? This decision was taken by the IMF Board of Governors, in which I participate. We used the received funds to increase the foreign exchange reserves. This, inter alia, is an example of the benefits from our integration into the European and global financial infrastructure. Similarly, our future participation in the ECBs capital as a member of the euro area will enable us to have access to the monetary income of the Eurosystem.

Title: Opening speech by Mr. Iliya Lingorski, Member of the BNB Board, at the opening of the IX Annual International Scientific Conference "INFLATION 2022  CIRCUMSTANCES, CHALLENGES, IMPACT", Sofia, 18-20 September 2023
text: Interview with Mr. Dimitar Radev, Governor of the BNB, for the More of the Day programme on BNT, 27 July 2023 INTEREST RATES ON LOANS AND DEPOSITS IN OUR COUNTRY WILL INCREASE MORE AND MORE NOTICEABLY About the euro area, about the election of Deputy Governors, about inflation and interest on loans, as well as why one of the Bulgarian euro coins will feature the inscription GOD SAVE BULGARIA We are in the office of the Governor of the Bulgarian National Bank, Mr. Dimitar Radev. Hello, Mr. Radev! Hello, welcome to the Bulgarian National Bank! Thank you very much. You are entering a second term of office with a very ambitious task  to have Bulgaria enter the euro area from 1 January 2025. What are the major obstacles on this path? I wouldn't talk about big obstacles, but about challenges. Obviously, from a criteria and process perspective, inflation is one of those challenges. From another point of view, it is very important that there is broad political support for the process. Something that hasn't been so certain in the last two years. So there are factors going both ways. But I think in the end what we have to do will be done. We will talk in detail about the euro area and I would like you to tell us about your specific steps. Still, the condition for a 3% deficit was the reason why two days ago the Finance Minister even got offended by the MPs that they were excessively inflating the expenses, while not taking care of the revenues in the budget. Is this the biggest challenge facing a country's finances  not being able to manage revenues and expenses well, and is this the challenge facing Bulgaria now? This is a macroeconomic challenge that should not be underestimated. It is also very important, from the point of view of what we started the conversation with  the inflation criteria in relation to the euro area. We are clearly at a stage in the economic cycle where a more disciplined fiscal policy should be in place. A 3% deficit is a good target initially, but it still means fiscal expansion. So the question is macroeconomic. It is important even outside the context of the euro area. The change in the cost structure that is being made also has a big impact: investment is reduced, wage costs are increased, that is, when we have such a cost structure, it is definitely a factor for increasing inflation, not decreasing it. There are many aspects to this question. But what Bulgaria needs is a disciplined fiscal policy. So what do you say to the MPs: Be careful, stick to that three percent deficit. Right? Absolutely. I think that the three percent limit is beyond doubt. The question is how it will be achieved. Do you have any doubts that this may be an obstacle to not being fulfilled this year and next year as well? I do not see many serious obstacles to the fiscal policy, strategically, since we have a long period of disciplined fiscal policy. The traditions, the attitudes are where they should be. The point is not to change th trajectory that we have followed for decades and I think that is the most important issue at the moment  the step they are taking to keep the budget deficit within 3% is very good from that point of view. In the July economic forecast, you predict a growth of 1% of GDP for 2023. However, the forecast of the BNB differs from that of the Minister of Finance, who announced 1.8% growth. Are you being overly cautious or is the Government overestimating its capabilities? We are traditionally conservative in all our macroeconomic assessments. What lies behind these estimates are the assumptions as to what exactly will happen, how all the other macroeconomic factors will develop. But I don't see any dramatic difference between what we envision and what the Ministry of Finance envisions. Both institutions expect economic growth and this is good news. Your choice of Deputy Governors of the BNB has led some political commentators to say that this is how you have secured political comfort. You were proposed by GERB, MPs from We Continue the Change and DPS are the ones you chose and proposed as Deputy Governors. Have you sought political balance and how will you ensure that you do not succumb to political pressure with this choice? That's a good question. In fact, my criteria for choosing Deputy Governors were three: the first one, certainly, is professional experience and expertise, the second  personal qualities, and third, of course, is that they generate broad support. I had occasion to say in Parliament during the hearings that there is a built-in conflict in the process itself. The conflict is between the independence  the political independence of the Central Bank and the political choice of its management. Therefore, the big challenge is to find exactly the intersection between this professional, expert approach and the political approach. And I think that in the case of the election of the two new Deputy Governors, this intersection was reached in an optimal way. And in terms of political pressure? There is a lot of evidence, including during the last mandate, that the Bulgarian National Bank does not give in to such pressure. In truth, I have never witnessed such pressure. Of course, in various ways there are attempts to influence some decisions in comments. But I don't think we've ever made a decision that was influenced by political pressure. Politicians don't call you directly, overestimating their capabilities and the influence they can have? No. If it comes to decisions in the banking sector, definitely not. Right-wing politicians call on you to privatise the Bulgarian Development Bank. Even during the hearing in the group of We Continue the Change - Democratic Bulgaria that you had, they urged you to think about this issue. What do you think? The position of the Bulgarian National Bank is very clear in these cases. The initiative must come from the owner. In this case, the owner is the state, the Council of Ministers, represented by one of the economic ministries. So if there is something they have to offer, it will come to us and we will respond. A very important detail is omitted here  that from 2020, when we became a member of the Banking Union, these permissions are practically given by the European Central Bank. We participate in making these decisions, but we have one voice. So let's see what the offer is. We can give technical advice on one thing or another. But we haven't seen a concrete proposal yet. I am asking you about this because some politicians say that the Bulgarian Development Bank is the money box of the oligarchy, which gave out large loans uncontrollably. And in this way, we may even witness a repeat of the KTB case. What is the guarantee that this will not happen? I will start from the fact that a recurrence of the KTB case is impossible. Everything we have done in recent years precludes such a scenario. Regarding development banks in general, I was for 6 years on the board of the oldest development bank in Europe. I dealt with this problem in my previous professional life. And actually there is a very interesting trend. If you look globally, the problems with the national development banks grow the more you move east and south, while we are somewhere on the border. On the surface, the problems with these banks look different, but the genesis of the problem with these banks is always the same  political interference. We have a state-owned bank  the actual owner, shareholder of this bank is the Government; politicians are the ones who manage the bank. Once we have politicians running the bank, inevitably the questions come up cyclically as to whether this bank should act, whether it is acting in accordance with the statute or in violation of it. What I can say definitely is that when it comes to the Bulgarian Development Bank  inside the country I have not been asked this question, but always those who look from the outside say: why are you pushing the conditions so much for this bank? Because the development banks, the state development banks, are seen as the most trouble-free institutions from a banking point of view, because the state is behind them and whatever happens, the state will provide assistance. And actually the answer is yes  because of these very political speculations, in some cases they are true, in others they are not. So with these types of banks, these questions will exist. So I'm waiting to see what the offer will be. But the bank is actually the bank with the highest capital adequacy in the country and with very high liquidity. So, whatever happens, even the worst case scenario with all these loans being speculated, if they develop in a way they shouldn't develop, the bank will not pose a problem for the financial stability of the country and right here is the responsibility of the Bulgarian National Bank. What is sometimes not understood is that the BNB does not manage the business of individual banks. It does not say who should be given credit and who should not. The business of the bank is the responsibility of those who run it, the shareholders and the management. The responsibility of the BNB is that if there is a problem in this bank, it does not become a problem for financial stability, it does not become a problem for taxpayers. That's why I say that a scenario similar to the one with KTB is out of the question. What about the commercial banks? What is their situation and is there a risk for the banking market in our country? Our banks are in very good condition. This is evident from all public data, from independent publications. The OECD report came out recently. In fact, it clearly states that the indicators of our commercial banks are above the EU average. So I sometimes ask: Can you imagine all economic sectors having such indicators? Our banks are in very good condition. Of course, we constantly assess risks, set requirements, mandatory requirements for banks. You know that very recently, effective as of 1 July of this year, we introduced new requirements for the banks  we will withdraw a significant resource of several billion from these banks by increasing the requirements for their minimum reserves at the central bank. But here the goal is broader. On the one hand, to impact inflation because by withdrawing such a resource from the economy it affects consumption, thereby pushing inflation down. But the other goal is related to possible credit risks. In case of a change in the situation, as I told you at the beginning, we always work according to the most conservative and worst possible scenario, we have to do it to make sure that it does not cause a serious problem. Is this the biggest risk we could be exposed to  too many loans to be extended and then, for various reasons, these loans cannot be repaid? This is a risk that the banking sector takes into account. I would not say that in our banking system it is of dramatic proportions because the process is well regulated. But we are keeping a close watch on how things are going on. This is not the only tool that we are using  the minimum required reserves. We were the first or one of the first central banks to re-activate the so called countercyclical capital buffer. In terms of macroprudential policy, it aims for the same thing  to create conditions so that if certain risks manifested in the economy, this would not cause any serious problems in the banking sector. You mentioned inflation. Inflation is slowing down. This is shown by all types of statistics. It, however, is the main topic in the mass media. There is incessant talk about fighting inflation. The Government, in the programme that it has just adopted, has written down a separate item on the anti-inflationary measures that it will undertake. Politicians are levelling all kinds of accusations at one another about who is to blame for rises in inflation. In your opinion, what is the main reason behind inflation in Bulgaria? It is not only in the media and in the political circles, macroeconomic inflation continues to be No. 1 topic. The reasons are well-known. If we look at inflation inside Bulgaria, many of the factors behind it are external. I do not need to repeat again what has happened in recent times. All these unexpected shocks, the war in Ukraine is undoubtedly a factor in that direction. But what we should focus on are the internal conditions conducive to inflation. There was a line of explanation that inflation comes entirely from outside the country, which was true at some stage. But internal conditions are growing in importance. What we are doing, and I stressed that repeatedly, is that we need to do tightening in two major spheres  monetary conditions and fiscal conditions. What central banks, the European Central Bank, are doing by increasing interest rates is aimed at that. What we have been doing, with the limited tools that we have available under the currency board arrangement, follows the same direction. When we take such decisions, whereby pulling billions out of the economy, these decisions seek to achieve that objective  to contain inflation. We have been talking a lot about this issue; it took us six months to make this decision. Why?! Because this tightening of the monetary conditions has an impact on the entire economy. Our objective is not to stifle banks or to get the economy stagnant, it is to keep inflation in check, but in a very balanced way. Therefore, the second important factor is the fiscal policy  to fully synchronise monetary and fiscal conditions in this country. This is not what we see now. There is a clear trend of tightening monetary conditions. As regards fiscal conditions, there are political signs that we are going to achieve a 3% deficit, but in practice we still have continuing fiscal expansion, and it is not working to contain inflation. Quite the opposite. In this sense, are politicians in debt to the people? They are, by definition, in debt, even with regard to this topic. The BNBs primary objective is to maintain price stability, you mentioned the war. Is this not especially difficult in the conditions of war, of political uncertainty, after many successive elections in the country? It is difficult indeed, but there is an interesting fact related to the war. Actually Bulgaria is one of the very few European countries where no Russian banks have operated or are operating. Our banking sector has virtually no exposures to Russia or to the Russian banking sector. Therefore, the implications of the war, resulting from the sanctions imposed on the Russian banking sector have not affected our banks in any way. And yet, of course, the general deterioration of the economic conditions due to the war has indirect effects on our banking sector as well. It is the first time, from a historical perspective, that we have such an accumulation of unfavourable developments, starting with the Covid-19 pandemic, the war. This has been the real test of our banking sector. In 2016 we conducted extensive tests of our banking sector, another test was carried out by the European Central Bank in 2019 and then we worked under the worst possible scenarios. We never believed that these scenarios would ever come to happen. In reality they did happen. But these tests under the most conservative, the worst expectations, have helped the banking sector to cope with the crises well. And not only cope well, but also to support the economy and households. You probably remember the anti-crisis programme that we activated in March 2020, literally, when they were explaining what Covid was and whether something would happen or would not happen. So, then we activated this programme, we fully completed it and this helped us initiate a private moratorium on loan payments which benefited tens of thousands businesses and households. Is this good management  to foresee crises, to foresee events that have not yet happened but are likely to happen? Is this how the BNB is working? I think so. This is exactly how the BNB is working. I have been asked, even during the hearings  are you not going to conduct tests again; actually we have not stopped doing tests. We carry out tests every year and this is why I pointed out that the lack of public interest on this issue is, in fact, good news  it means that we are on the right track. These tests are carried out continuously. We participate, but now in a European context, in the preparation of macroeconomic scenarios. Before we only used to apply them, now we are actively involved in the process. So, yes, this is, in my opinion, good management and I strongly hope that this will continue. Will loans become more expensive? And will interest rates be rising? Today the ECB will probably raise the interest rate by 25 points. The short answer is yes. But here this is happening more slowly. Why is it happening more slowly  because our banking system has very high liquidity? What we are doing, including the measures that I mentioned, is to speed up the transmission of the European Central Banks policy into Bulgaria. This trend of increasing interest rates will be noticeable towards the end of this year and next year. But the short answer is yes  interest rates will be rising, both on loans and on deposits. Politicians are asking you, I will ask you too  Arent you late with the information campaign about the euro area? A huge topic, I do not want to revisit what we had to do over the last two years. As a matter of fact the campaign had to begin on 1 October 2021. We need to act, to be active, and the Bulgarian National Bank is ready to do it. A minute detail is that now there is a set of data prepared, quite a vast one, which contains not only sections on the various topics, but also video clips, including draft contracts with the media. The owner of this dataset is the Government, represented by the Ministry of Finance. They are the ones to say yes for the information campaign to begin. I expect that we will hear this yes very soon. Yet, of course, we, as a central bank, have been working hard on this issue. Now there is general agreement in the Governing Council that we should do more on this issue and this will be seen in the coming weeks. The critics of the euro adoption see loss of national identity. How would you counter their criticism? I would say that it is not true. It is not true along a few lines  first, what we have as a monetary regime now is actually a very restrictive, very costly monetary regime, giving us very limited tools to use. This has been mentioned several times in relation to what we have been doing. We cannot virtually set base interest rates for policy purposes, we cannot use open market operations, what the European Central Bank does. I have made a comparison and I do not know how correct it is, that at the moment we are like a sculptor who has been given only the hammer, but not the chisel. Achieving the same result with the hammer is considerably more difficult, more expensive and wastes a lot of material. When we join the euro area, we will have the chisel too. If one looks at this issue, even purely symbolically, we are now talking about the design of the coins. There is agreement in the Governing Council, we are moving the issue forward and all the Bulgarian symbols will be there. Instead of being used by several million people in Bulgaria, these coins will be used by over 300 million in the euro area and probably just as many outside the euro area. GOD SAVE BULGARIA  why did you choose this inscription to feature on the 2 euro coin? Because this is the tradition. When we resumed minting coins, this inscription was included in the design of the coins until 1942-43. This is in line with the best coin minting traditions that we have. You are speaking of traditions, then what do you think about the modern way of life  how is an institution like the BNB run in the world of cryptocurrencies and artificial intelligence? Cryptocurrencies, for now, are outside the scope of action of central banks. As a symbol of the world, I mean. The symbol that I acknowledge is the digital euro. A big topic. We are an active participant in the discussions about the digital euro. You know that recently the European Commission has adopted the framework for these projects. There is enthusiasm, there is somewhat moderate scepticism about when precisely this will happen. But the enthusiasts are speaking about a digital revolution in the sphere of money, and I am inclined to believe them. The question is whether Bulgaria will be part of this revolution or will stand by and wait to see what and how will happen and how things will come to us. And the last question, Mr. Radev  which is the painting in your office that you look at more closely? I see several paintings here. On the whole, all three  these are more than 100 years old, at least two of them. The other one is by Dechko Uzunov. So I have not replaced them, I have kept them and I enjoy looking at them. Thank you for this interview for More of the Day. Thank you.

Title: Blitz interview of Mr. Dimitar Radev, Governor of the Bulgarian National Bank, for BTA, Marrakech, October 13, 2023
text: Blitz interview with Mr. Dimitar Radev, Governor of the BNB, for BTA, Marrakech, 13 October 2023 FISCAL STABILITY AND THE FIGHT AGAINST INFLATION ARE NOT IN CONFLICT, ACCORDING TO DIMITAR RADEV The BNB Governor to BTA: The draft law on the euro is at the final stage of preparation Is Bulgaria going to participate in the quota increase at the International Monetary Fund (IMF)? At this stage, Bulgaria actively participates in the debate on the 16th Review of the IMF quotas. Member countries are expected to reach a consensus on this issue by the end of this year. In your opinion, what should be the objective of the (Bulgarian) 2023 Budget - fiscal stability or anti-inflationary measures? The two objectives are not conflicting but complementary. They must be achieved both in the context of 2023 and in the preparation and implementation of the 2024 Budget. Of course, the formal answer to this question will be given by the Ministry of Finance and the Government. After the support of the European Central Bank (ECB) for the Bulgarian National Bank (BNB), which legal acts regarding the BNB still need to be adopted and/or agreed? The most important act, from the central banks perspective, is the Law on the BNB; its draft has already received the ECBs support. I expect that it will be approved before the end of this year. Next is the draft law on the introduction of the euro, which is the result of an interdepartmental effort and is at the final stage of preparation. The IMF suggested that a part of the larger profits of the European banks, coming from the increased interest rates on loans, should go into buffers and reserves. Does the BNB plan any measures in this regard? The BNB was one of the first central banks to introduce similar measures. I will mention, for example, our decisions to increase banks' minimum reserve requirements and the level of the countercyclical capital buffer. We are ready to impose additional measures, if necessary. How do you assess the current level of lending in our country? Are additional measures needed to cool it down? The specified measures and the policy to accelerate the transmission of the ECB's policy aim, inter alia, to control credit expansion and the related risks. Our purpose is to implement these measures in a way that will not stagnate the economy.

Title: Interview of Mr. Dimitar Radev, Governor of the Bulgarian National Bank, for the show "More from the Day" on BNT, July 27, 2023
text: Speech by Mr. Petar Chobanov, BNB Deputy Governor in charge of the Banking Department, at the opening of the DIGI PAY 2023 Conference, Inter Expo Centre, 5 October 2023 DEVELOPMENTS IN THE PAYMENTS SECTOR AND ITS INTEGRATION WITH THE EURO AREA I would like to thank the organisers for the invitation. It is an honour and pleasure for me to take part in today's conference, and I believe that it will contribute both generally to the functioning of the business and to the better awareness of end users. The topics included in today's program are extremely important and relevant to the field of payments. I would like to begin with the dynamic development of the payment market in our country over the last few years. In general, the financial sector in our country and in Europe is undoubtedly one of the areas in which innovations advance most rapidly and have a great impact on a wide range of products and services. The digitalisation of processes and products leads to the emergence of increasingly diverse payment instruments and technologies, which in turn are used by all market participants. The development of payment services in Bulgaria is characterised by a positive evolution. The official data in the BNBs payment statistics, maintained according to the ECB's methodology, highlights a steady trend of rising basic indicators regarding payment services in our country, especially the services provided electronically. In 2022, the number of cashless customer payments made in the country increased by about with respect to the previous year. The number of payments with cards issued in Bulgaria grew nearly 1/3 compared to 2021. The growth in e-money payments is driving attention, where the number of payments in 2022 increased by over 40% compared to the previous year. The increase in the value of card payments initiated at virtual POS terminals is also remarkable  the growth in 2022 is over 50% compared to 2021. Electronically-initiated credit transfers (i.e. through electronic and mobile banking channels) grew substantially as well  in 2022, the increase was over 30% compared to the previous year in terms of the value of initiated transfers. These data clearly show the robust development of the Bulgarian financial sector and the change in consumers attitude towards the intensive use of digital payment channels. Next, I would like to point out that the development of payment services in Europe is effectively regulated and greatly facilitated by the policies of the European and national regulators. The second Payment Services Directive (PSD2), which has been in effect since 2018, created an extremely favourable environment for this development. Among many other aspects, PSD2 introduced for the first time "open banking" regulation, which laid the foundation for the development of new business models, services and solutions. These include account information services (AIS) and payment initiation services (PIS) which have enabled the creation of innovative products, such as account data aggregation and centralised initiation of payments from accounts with many different payment service providers. The Bulgarian National Bank is a leading partner in the regulatory discussions on the implementation of new requirements and in handling the obstacles to open banking. As a result of the discussions among the national competent authorities, the European Banking Authority (EBA) issues opinions promoting the harmonised treatment at European level of the emerging challenges facing open banking. At the same time, the BNB has active communications with the open banking service providers licensed in Bulgaria and with the banking community, which foster the more efficient functioning of these new services. In this way, the BNB provides partnership cooperation with the business in order to ensure a level playing field for market players in the spirit of support, mediation and coordination. In this regard, we can state that PSD2 has been fully integrated in both the supervisory and in the business practices in Bulgaria. On the basis of PSD2, a new European legislation in the field of payments has been put forward  the proposals for a new Payment Services Directive 3 (PSD3) and a Payment Services Regulation (PSR). The PSD3 proposal is largely based on the relevant provisions of PSD2 and the Electronic Money Directive (EMD) in terms of authorisation and supervision requirements. In this way, PSD3 will build on and refine the provisions regarding the licensing and supervision of payment institutions. An important aspect of the PSD3 proposal is also the envisaged amendment to the Directive on settlement finality in payment and securities settlement systems, aimed to ensure direct access of non-bank payment service providers to all payment systems in the EU. The PSR proposal regulates basic rights and obligations in the provision of payment services in the EU, including rules for the execution of payment operations, the liability for unauthorised payment transactions and incorrectly executed payment transactions, open banking, transparency requirements, and payment security requirements. Some key changes that PSR proposes are the introduction of a dedicated interface for accessing payment accounts via open banking, as well as the possibility for users to manage the permissions they have given for access to their financial data through the so-called "dashboard". It is also envisaged an obligation for payment service providers to additionally check whether a credit transfer recipient matches the account number as specified by the ordering party, which will further enhance the security of digital payments. The PSD2 Directive is a multi-layered and complex European legislation incorporating the "maximum harmonisation" principle. It is not by chance that the revision of this directive led to proposals for the separation of certain aspects in different legal acts, with the aim of their further development and refinement. The proposals for upgrading regulations, among which the proposal for a Regulation on a framework for Financial Data Access (FIDA) stands out, is in itself an evidence of greater market maturity, as this regulatory framework actually aims to upgrade the existing regulation of open banking. This complementary legislation will affect the effective management of data throughout the entire financial system by integrating information about all financial products so that they can be used by third parties for the convenience of consumers and to optimally meet their needs. Regarding the plans for the implementation at national level of the upcoming new legislation in the field of payment and financial services, I can note that at the moment the licensing of payment institutions and electronic money institutions, as well as the registration of account information service providers, are regulated in the Law on Payment Services and Payment Systems (LPSPS) and the related secondary legislation. After the successful finalisation of the new European legal framework  PSD3, PSR and FIDA, this will entail changes in the LPSPS, the Law on the BNB and the relevant Ordinances, with a view to full transposition and compliance with the requirements of the proposals. The LPSPS already contains the national provisions that have introduced the requirements of the PSD2 Directive into the legislation. In this regard, after the entry into force of the PSR Regulation, the relevant provisions in the national legal framework will be amended insofar as the provisions of the Regulation will be directly applicable. I would also like to mention the preparations for the euro area accession in terms of the payments sector. In the field of harmonisation of the payment systems in relation to the introduction of the euro in our country, which fall within the competences of the BNB, we are actively working on several projects developing in parallel. In the first place, this is the migration to the new consolidated platform for TARGET services of the Eurosystem, which we already implemented in March this year with our partners from the banking community in Bulgaria, BORICA AD and Central Depository AD. The TARGET platform is a kind of backbone of the financial market infrastructure of the euro area and provides access to several services simultaneously. The first one is the real-time cash settlement service in euro. The second service is the euro-denominated securities settlement platform TARGET2-Securities (T2S), which offers pan-European settlement  of cash and securities, in central bank money. The third service in TARGET is TIPS, which provides access to instant payments in euro. The changes introduced through this new consolidated platform enabled the use of ISO 20022 SWIFT messages, a harmonised access interface and common components with regard to all TARGET services. Second is the project for the migration of budget payments to the standards of the Single Euro Payments Area (SEPA), which is currently being finalised and will lead to overall optimisation and acceleration of the budget banking process. Thus, the migration of customer credit transfers in BGN to the standards of the Single Euro Payments Area can be considered completed, as a result of which customer credit transfers can now be executed in less than an hour. The next project to mention is the instant credit transfers, which are executed within 10 seconds, and such transfers are already being offered in BGN and their reachability is up to over 90% of customer accounts in the country. The project to connect the BISERA7-EUR payment system operated by BORICA AD to the Eurosystem's service for the settlement of instant transfers in euro TIPS is also progressing rapidly, which will allow the banks in the country to offer instant transfers in euro as well. The Bulgarian National Bank and BORICA AD are also working to ensure full reachability for the execution of customer SEPA credit transfers in euro in the Single Euro Payments Area. Thus, in the near future, it is expected to ensure full reachability when executing credit transfers in euro to more than 4,800 payment service providers in all countries of the SEPA area while applying a prepaid model with continuous settlement, which will reduce the time to perform credit transfers in euro. In September this year, the projects to onboard the Depository of Government Securities at the BNB and Central Depository AD to the securities settlement platform TARGET2-Securities were successfully completed and on 11 September 2023 the depositories migrated to the live T2S environment. This platform is one of the main pan-European market infrastructures developed and maintained by the Eurosystem. Currently, 24 depositories from European countries use T2S, and participation in the platform already contributes to better accessibility of Bulgarian securities for EU investors. From a technical point of view, we are already witnessing the favourable and catalysing effect of the mentioned projects, which have been completed or are in the process of completion, on optimising the payment process and improving the banking conditions in our country. As a result of the efforts already mentioned, we hope by the end of next year to finalise all projects related to the adoption of the euro in the Republic of Bulgaria and on 1 January 2025 to congratulate ourselves on being part of the big euro area family. Without a doubt, today's development of the payment market in our country and in Europe is driven and inspired by new technologies and supported by European regulations, which create a favourable environment for competition and innovation for the benefit of consumers. The measures related to the introduction of the euro support the rapid and effective integration of the financial market infrastructures in our country with those in the euro area. The development of competition, but also partnership, between the FinTech sector and banks leads to the emergence of many new, convenient and secure financial and payment products. Thank you for your attention and I wish fruitful work to all participants in today's conference. PAGE \* MERGEFORMAT 4

Title: Speech by Mr. Andrey Gyurov, Deputy Governor of the Bulgarian National Bank, Head of Issue Department, at the Sixth Banking and Finance Forum: "The Future of Money", organized by Manager Magazine, Sofia, October 17, 2023
text: QD I O' *anKS in *ulgaria D MEMBER OF THE EUROPEAN BANKING FEDERATION #76 QUARTERLY BULLETIN October 2023 Development and innovation in the payments and securities settlement sector Petar Chobanov Member of the Executive Board of the ABB Deputy Governor in charge of the Banking Department, Bulgarian National Bank In recent years, Bulgaria has seen quite a positive progress both in the field of payments and in the settlement of securities. This progress is systematic and purposeful, being generated on the one hand by technological innovations in the field of payments and the changing needs of consumers, and on the other hand by the evolution of regulatory requirements and standards.
