Title: Interview on pages 15 and 16 of the 24 CHASA Daily, 1 July 2017
Subtitle:
THE CURRENCY BOARD ELIMINATES THE POSSIBILITY 
OF PEOPLES SAVINGS FALLING IN VALUE
text: Interview by the BNB Deputy Governor in charge of the Issue Department, Mr. Kalin Hristov, on pages 15 and 16 of the 24 CHASA Daily, 1 July 2017 THE CURRENCY BOARD ELIMINATES THE POSSIBILITY OF PEOPLEd5S SAVINGS FALLING IN VALUE The only way out of it without disruption to the Bulgarian economy is the entry into the euro area, says the BNB Deputy Governor Price stability is the main objective not only of the BNB but of all central banks in the world The Bulgarian levd5s potential participation in the Exchange Rate Mechanism II will in no way change the mechanism of the currency board 20 years of a currency board arrangement. 20 years of a straitjacket for a series of governments. 20 years of a central bank without full autonomy. Do you agree with such a reading of this anniversary Mr. Hristov? None of the interpretations implied in your question is true. The currency board arrangement (CBA) is a monetary policy regime based on a pegged exchange rate, whose main objective is the same as the main objective of any central bank in the world d0 to achieve and maintain price stability (i.e. low and stable inflation). The currency board arrangement has successfully achieved this objective for the Bulgarian economy over the last twenty years. Each country chooses its monetary policy regime. Generally speaking, the options are two d0 either a regime based on a fixed exchange rate (please note that in practice all euro area countries have a fixed exchange rate), or following an inflation targeting strategy with a relatively free movement of the exchange rate. Bulgariad5s choice was predetermined by the complete failure of the floating exchange rate-based monetary policy pursued until mid-1997. Following a monetary policy based on a floating exchange rate resulted in the profound economic and financial crisis with hyperinflation. Then there were two basic factors for this: the absence of a clearly defined rule of the monetary policy pursued by the central bank, and the lacking independence of the BNB. The result was uncontrolled and unsecured commercial banks refinancing and state budget deficit financing directly from the central bank. The end result of this policy was the collapse of the economy and hyperinflation in the country. This is how salaries, wages, pensions and the peopled5s savings fell in value, while the heavily indebted companies were practically rewarded by depreciation of their debts. The introduction of a currency board arrangement on 1 July 1997 established a clear and transparent monetary policy rule in this country and it virtually gave the BNB independence as the central bank was explicitly banned from financing the government directly or indirectly and from providing unsecured refinancing to commercial banks. Why do politicians, bankers and financiers answer every question about the CBA with some trickery, such as d4The CBA is stable.d5, d4It must not be removed.d5, d4We will not allow it.d5? What hides behind this very rare consensus? Isnd5t it some kind of omerta among our elite? This is a completely rational attitude. And we are talking about a very broad consensus which goes beyond what you call d4the elited5. Behind the unconditional support for the CBA by the citizens, entrepreneurs and the political class stands the clear understanding that this regime operates successfully in Bulgaria and achieves the main purpose for which it was put in place d0 to keep low and stable inflation and to eliminate the possibility of peopled5s savings falling in value. Few voices are also heard: from d4The printing of money is actually not so bad.d5 to more courageous ones such as d4The CBA is already impeding the economy.d5 Where is the truth, somewhere in the middle? Ex prime ministers, I mean Ivan Kostov, recommend dismantling certain elements of the CBA, which have become obstructive. Your question illustrates the misunderstanding by a small part of our society, including some looking for an audience d4expertsd5, about the role of the monetary policy in an economy d0 i.e. what it can and what it cannot achieve. As I already mentioned, the key role of a monetary policy (with a floating or a fixed exchange rate) is to maintain low and stable inflation. The accomplishment of this purpose creates conditions and environment for financial stability and economic growth. Therefore, price stability is the main objective of the BNB and of all central banks in the developed world, including the European Central Bank. What sometimes is not understood is that monetary policy cannot influence the long-term rates of economic growth and employment. These are determined by structural factors, not by the monetary policy. This fact has been proved theoretically and empirically. It is not by chance that central banks do not have a mandate to directly generate economic growth. One deficiency of monetary policy regimes based on a fixed exchange rate, which the traditional theory points out, is the impossibility of lowering interest rates in the short run in case of cyclic negative development of the economy, so as to achieve a short-term stabilising effect on consumption and investments, and consequently on employment. Experience however shows that monetary policy can have such a stabilising effect, and only partially, only in a large economy that issues a global currency (e.g. US dollar, euro, pound sterling, Japanese yen, yuan) and its population and businesses receive loans in that currency, which is the national currency in that country. In small economies there is no such effect. Furthermore, there is a destabilising effect in small economies because the households and businesses there frequently have debts in a foreign currency and the decreasing interest rates in the national currency would lead to devaluation of the exchange rate and hence to a strong increase in debt. This effect caused a lot of pain in many countries of Central and Eastern Europe during the global financial crisis in 2008 d0 2009. It is thanks to the currency board in place that the Bulgarian economy could avert this effect. A number of studies in the wake of the global financial crisis rather suggest a negative effect on the long-term rates of economic growth from a pursued anti-cyclical monetary policy. This effect takes place as follows: in the cases where we have a floating exchange rate-based monetary policy and the central bank applies the rule of lowering interest rates with slowing economic growth and decreasing inflation, then in times of economic boom households and businesses accumulate higher and higher levels of debt, hoping that in times of crisis the central bank would lower interest rates. In the long run this would lead to so-called d4moral hazardd5 and excessive debts of households and companies. Thus in times of crisis central banks reduce interest rates to lower and lower levels; but this would not promote the economy, it would rather pose risks to financial stability. The recent recession was an extreme example of such risks. In order to ease adjustment to the depth of that recession, central banks had to introduce not just low but negative interest rates. In practice, this is a tax on savers. Therefore, such a monetary policy mechanism could create wrong incentives and would allow ineffective companies to continue to exist despite their excessive debts. Bailing out ineffective and heavily indebted companies, so-called d4zombie companiesd5, is in contradiction to the natural economic laws and is detrimental in the longer run. This effect of the monetary policy would lead to ineffective distribution of capital in the economy and would negatively affect the long-term investment growth rates, and subsequently the economic growth rates. Does all this mean that Bulgaria will never abandon the currency board arrangement? Bulgariad5s only and natural mechanism for exiting the CBA without disruptions to the Bulgarian economy and without risks to the savings of the Bulgarian citizens would be to join the euro area with its current exchange rate of 1.95583 BGN for 1 EUR. That was the exit strategy of Estonia and Lithuania as they too operated currency board arrangements. Do you know more about the irresistible offer that we are expecting from Brussels? Could you prognosticate when this long-awaited event would take place? Yes, I know. There is no such offer. On 31 May the European Commission (EC) published the d4Reflection Paper on the Deepening of the Economic and Monetary Uniond5. As we can expect, this type of paper does not contain any conceptions and approaches typically used in Hollywood movies which show the mafiad5s activities, i.e. there is no d4offer you cand5t refused5. Of course this EC paper in no way reveals or aims to create any d4short cutsd5 for the non-euro area countries to the single currency. This paper is designed to describe possible steps and solutions for the so needed stabilisation of the euro area within the current Treaty on European Union. It is another matter that the cited document gives no answer to the main structural problem of the euro area d0 the absence of a single fiscal policy and the possibility of fiscal transfers that could be used as a stabilising tool in times of economic crisis. And it is well-known that in history there has never been a monetary union that existed for a long period of time without a single fiscal policy and a fiscal transfer mechanism. The explanation why at this stage such a mechanism cannot be built in the euro area is simple. The euro area economies largely differ structurally and this creates different levels of competitiveness and resilience to economic crises. In such environment the setting up of a fiscal transfer mechanism would mean only one thing d0 constant one-way transfers of incomes from certain countries to other countries. From a political perspective, in the current environment itd5s very difficult to implement such a mechanism in the euro area. In this context, given this problem, it is quite clear why non-euro area countries cannot be allowed to take d4short cutsd5. This could be even less expected for economies which have not yet achieved a sufficient level of sustainable real convergence. How will the CBA be affected when we enter the d4waiting roomd5 of the euro area? By d4waiting roomd5 I suppose you mean so-called Exchange Rate Mechanism II (ERM II). First, a few things must be made clear: it is not a country but its currency that joins the ERM II. Second, it is a mechanism of fixed exchange rates which could, theoretically but not mandatorily, fluctuate within a margin of b1 15 percent. Third, this mechanism is run by the ECB. Fourth, there are no explicitly defined criteria to assess whether a countryd5s currency is ready to join ERM II. Fifth, it is an official criterion for euro area membership that a member stated5s national currency must have participated in this mechanism for at least two years without devaluing its exchange rate against the euro. As regards the Bulgarian levd5s potential participation in ERM II, our strategy was defined back in 2007 when the first negotiations for the levd5s joining this mechanism took place. The lev would join the euro area at the existing exchange rate of 1.95583 BGN for 1 EUR, with the BNBd5s unilateral commitment to keeping a zero deviation of the exchange rate. That approach was used for Estonia and Lithuania which had run currency boards too. It is important to note that the Bulgarian levd5s potential participation in ERM II will in no way change the mechanism and operation of the CBA. In practice it would bring our country in compliance with one of the convergence criteria for joining the euro area. After our country joins the euro area will we be able to pursue an independent monetary policy that would allow lower levels of interest rates and would let the Bulgarian government get rid of the straitjacket? When Bulgaria becomes a euro area member, the BNB will not be able to follow its independent monetary policy. The BNB is going to take part in the formulation and implementation of the common monetary policy in the euro area. The BNB Governor will be a member of the Governing Council of the ECB and will be entitled to vote, and in accordance with the rules he will be there in his personal capacity and not as a representative of the BNB or of Bulgaria. He is going to vote on decisions regarding the ECBd5s monetary policy considering the economic conditions in the entire euro area, and not just data or issues regarding only Bulgaria. In certain cases, the policy followed by the ECB may even temporarily diverge from the cycle and situation in a given euro area economy. This means that as the Bulgarian economy is relatively small and would have a very small weight in the overall euro area data, the adoption of the single currency would not allow us to have interest rates set by the central bank, which would reflect only the condition of the Bulgarian economy. For this reason it is exceptionally important for our countryd5s euro area membership that we in advance achieve convergence and synchronisation of the Bulgarian economyd5s business cycle with the cycle of the large economies in the euro area. In the euro area there is a common monetary policy for all member states, which is transmitted into the individual economies, with interest rate conditions differing across countries. The rates on loans to households, companies and the government vary across the countries and are a function of the risk which is specific of the particular euro area economy. The wide differentiation of interest rates across the euro area member states has been increasing further since the 2009 crisis. As regards the restriction on central bank lending to the government, it is retained even after a country joins the euro area. Besides, in the fiscal policy area it should be well understood that the Stability and Growth Pact rules are even stricter for the governments of the euro area member states than for the other EU countries. In other words, instilling expectations of considerable relaxing of the macroeconomic policy after our country joins the euro area is dangerous and counterproductive. This only signals our euro area partners that we do not understand how the single currency works. Our countryd5s participation in the euro area would also bring benefits for the Bulgarian economy as our national currency would be the second most important global currency with all the resultant advantages in terms of easier access to liquidity. With our entry into the euro area we would also introduce much more rigorous EU regulations on the banks in Bulgaria, and this would reduce the danger of banking crises happening. The banking sector regulations are the same in all EU member states whether they are members of the euro area or not. In terms of the regulatory framework, the approach adopted by the EU after 2008 was so-called d4maximum harmonisationd5, i.e. a unified regulatory framework with minimum national discretion for non-compliance with this framework. The so-called banking union includes all euro area member states and consists of three pillars: (1) the single supervisory mechanism is run by the ECB which directly supervises the systemically important banks in the euro area (each bank with total assets in excess of db30 billion, or 20% of the countryd5s GDP; in the countries where there are no such banks, the three largest banks); (2) the single resolution mechanism is an independent institution and is responsible for restructuring credit institutions; and (3) the European deposit insurance scheme, whose project was designed by the EC a long time ago but the member states still cannot reach agreement on its adoption. The common EU regulations on the banking sector generally aim to build up a framework to be applied by the national supervisory authorities or the ECB so as to minimise the chances of banking crises occurring. However, the common regulations and their application do not at all aim to remove all possibility of failing banks. This is absolutely impossible and cannot be an objective of banking supervision. I will only give an example that over the last month the ECB announced three large euro area banks, under its direct supervision (one in Spain and two in Italy), which are d4likely to faild5. Respectively, the Spanish bank was restructured and the two Italian banks were wound up. 1

Title: Publication in Views. The EUROFI Magazine disseminated during The Eurofi High Level Seminar 2018 held in Sofia, 25 - 27 April 2018
Subtitle:
WHY THE BANKING UNION IS NOT A
REASONABLE OPTION FOR NON-EURO AREA COUNTRIES?
text: Publication by BNB Deputy Governor in charge of the Issue Department Mr. Kalin Hristov published in Views. The EUROFI Magazine disseminated during The Eurofi High Level Seminar 2018 held in Sofia, 25 - 27 April 2018 WHY THE BANKING UNION IS NOT A REASONABLE OPTION FOR NON-EURO AREA COUNTRIES? The creation of the Banking Union was a response to the banking and sovereign crisis in the euro area. While impossible to prevent occurrences of future banking crises, a well-designed Banking Union should minimise their likelihood or their systemic impact for the EU banking systems. The Banking Union was launched in the euro area but, being based on EU law and needing to respect the integrity of the Single Market, was left open for participation of the non-euro area Member States. The latter, however, have so far shown no interest. A summary of reasons explains why. A primary objective of the Banking Union was to intensify integration of banking supervision and thus reduce market fragmentation. Another key motivation was to ensure more efficient supervision at the national level, unimpeded by non-prudential considerations stemming from industry pressure on domestic supervisors. However, these expected merits of the Banking Union invoke different perspectives from the non-euro Member States. First, a degree of market fragmentation/differentiation may be healthy. Such differentiation, among other things, reflects risks associated with a particular national economy or banking system. Country-specific risks always remain. They need to be differentiated, not blurred, to let market forces play their disciplining role. Second, the argument against regulatory capture can also extend to a unified supervision. Whereas a banking entity of only domestic significance may hardly influence a supranational supervisory authority, this may not be the case with big cross-border banks. In addition, there are clear disincentives embodied in the close cooperation, the mechanism devised for Member States whose currency is not the euro to join the Single Supervisory Mechanism. A country with close cooperation will face hugely asymmetric treatment: It will remain excluded from the ultimate decision-making on supervisory issues in the ECB Governing Council. The supervisory decisions of the ECB, which are not legally binding outside the euro area, will have to be replicated by acts of the domestic supervisor. The latter will be held responsible and liable in case of disputes. It will remain without access to ECB liquidity assistance. It will have no access to the ESM as a potential source of funds for direct or indirect bank recapitalisations. The asymmetries and inequalities between euro area and non-euro area Member States are further exacerbated in the Single Resolution Mechanism, which is automatically joined if a country joins the Single Supervisory Mechanism with close cooperation. The above provides reasons why it is risky to join the Banking Union with close cooperation before becoming a member of the euro area.

Title: Summary of the statement at the First Annual Fintech Summit, Sofia, 30 May 2018
text: Summary of the statement made by Mr Kalin Hristov, BNB Deputy Governor in charge of the Issue Department, at the First Annual Fintech Summit, Sofia, 30 May 2018 Today it is fashionable to talk about the so called fintech despite the absence of a generally accepted definition and a common understanding of what this term stands for. The interest in this topic, especially from financiers, is probably incited by the following. On the one hand, information technologies have widely and a long time ago entered other business spheres and industries, but their application is relatively less advanced in finance. On the other hand, financial transactions and institutions operate on the basis of information flows and data sets, which makes the intersection point of finance, information and technology mandatory. Hence, there are expectations that information technologies and the new solutions based on them have a big and unrealised potential in the area of finance and could bring added value and profit. New technologies will not change the nature and essence of finance. For example, banks will continue to perform the function of financial intermediation between savings and investments. They take deposits from the public and transform this resource into loans and investments for users who do not have the required funds. In the course of that process banks take certain risks. The application of new technologies affects some of these risks which are fundamental to financial (banking) intermediation. I will mention two areas where fintech is likely to relate to increased risks, instead of (only) the optimisation or the better management of risks. First, providing payment services is a typical and traditionally profitable banking business. The de facto monopoly of banks, ensuing from the fact that payment services are based upon accounts held with banks, causes other organisations interest in accessing bank accounts. The new Payment Services Directive (PSD2) now establishes such access of non-banks to information on accounts and to banks payment infrastructure. Apart from the competitive pressure issue, banks have to focus their attention on new risks related to the described process, such as security and personal data protection. Also, if external access to accounts becomes standardised and automated, we could possibly come to situations where clients will be offered deposit (interest rate) arbitration easily. From banks perspective, this would involve more volatility and insecurity on the liabilities side of their balance sheets. Second, there are great expectations regarding assessment of credit risk with the aid of new technologies, using artificial intelligence based applications, in particular. By definition, artificial intelligence operates based on past observations and already realised experience. This means that irrespective of the process of learning from own experience, there is no way to foresee future situations of realized credit risk, generated by circumstances that have not happened before. In other words, credit ratings and decisions based on artificial intelligence could be highly procyclical  where the recent environment has been favourable, ratings will be favourable, and vice versa. This would underrate credit risk and lead to adverse consequences in case of structural changes or reversal of the cycle. The above examples should be used as an argument against new technologies in finance. There are areas, where fintech may boost the efficiency of financial institutions. For example nowadays banks are forced to shoulder an increasing regulatory burden, part of which is related to increased reporting and data provision requirements. In this area the new technologies can bring about optimizations. Technologies can also make a positive contribution in the changing environment of supply and distribution of products and services. For example, online banking will reduce more significantly the physical presence of banks and their branches, with the further development and spreading of the forms of electronic identification, and through them the channels for remote access to end customers, including for direct extension of loans. And at the end a few words on the so-called cryptocurrencies, which are sometimes intuitively related with the subject of fintech. First and foremost, there is no such thing as cryptocurrencies. What is in the focus of attention should rather be defined cryptoassets. There are three generally accepted characteristics of money, which every currency should possess. Cryptoassets do not meet any of the respective definitions: Money serves as a medium of exchange, whereas cryptoassets are accepted as a medium of exchange by a very limited circle of users. Money serves as a store of value, whereas the extreme volatility in the price of cryptoassets makes them a very unattractive medium for storing value. Money serves as a unit of account. Yet who would keep their business accounts in cryptoassets that are not accepted as universal legal tender with their price being highly volatile? Besides, unlike other assets, cryptoassets have no intrinsic value. They are not backed by expectations of generating future income based on a business or a business model that is able to generate a steady cash flow. Therefore, cryptoassets are attractive mainly to two groups of users: speculators who buy this asset led only by the expectation of increase in its price, and those relying with the help of cryptoassets to remain anonymous in carrying out transactions allowing them to evade legal restrictions.

Title: Speech before the Sixth Annual Conference "Banks and Business", Sofia, 20 November 2018.
text: Speech by Mr. Kalin Hristov, Deputy Governor of the BNB, managing director "Issue", before the Sixth Annual Conference "Banks and Business", Sofia, 20 November 2018. Dear ladies and gentlemen, Thanks for inviting me to open today's conference. The conference programme sets out various and very broad themes that would be difficult to cover in a speechprofessionally enough and in the necessary analytical depth. To this end, I will focus on the macroeconomic environment (external and internal) and the specific effects for banks in bulgaria. In so far as one of the announced topics of theconference today directly affects the mandate of the BNB, I will also share thoughts about the ongoing development of the process arising from the announced intention to join the Bulgarian lev to the ERM II exchange rate mechanism. With regard to the macroeconomic environment, I will start by finding thated 2014 has an economic recovery in almost all euro area countries except those that, for deep structural reasons, have growth rates close to zero. Growth in euro area countries has been driven by an unprecedented scale and duration of ecb monetary policy stimulus, including the maintenance of very low, even negative, interest rates and asset purchases. The ECB's policy favoured a rise in financial asset prices, a low cost of banks' loans, cheaper servicing of loans already granted to households and businesses, and stronger demand for new loans. favourable to banks. The big question is how much of the growth is driven by structural improvements in the economy and not cyclical due to stimulus monetary policy. There are arguments that growth is mostly cyclical in nature. For example, growth has also been seen in euro area countries in recent years with deep and unresolved structural problems. Even one Italy was growing, albeit at a rate lower than the euro area average, which reinforced the differentiation of the Italian economy characteristic of it from the very beginning of its membership of the euro area. Another important aspect of the observed recovery ineuro area strategists is that it not only did not lead to a decrease in indebtedness, but on the contrary continued to increase both private and sovereign debt (with few exceptions in some countries). Since the beginning of 2018, economic growth in euro zone countries has slowed. The German economy, the largest in the euro area, shrank in the third quarter. This should also add to the effect of us-China trade disputes and their indirect impact on international trade, as well as political instability in some euro area countries and Brexit uncertainty. What does growth in the economy, which is mostly cyclical and unstable, mean for banks? It means that the existing credit risk on their balance sheets is not decreasing, and the likelihood of its realisation is growing. In addition, historically low interest rates maintained for a long time suggest a more significant increase in interest rate risk. This interest rate risk could subsequently be transformed into credit risk, given the relatively high indebtedness of companies and households. Currently, in euro area countries, we are seeing a slowdown in GDP growth, combined with rising prices and still low interest rates. There is a certain adverse scenario forthe continuation of current trends in growth, prices and interest rates in which to go through a period of "stagflation"  a phenomenon known from other historical episodes and other economies. The ECB's stimulus policy has given euro area economies a period of opportunity to implement the necessary structural policies, which does not appear to have been used by governments. Bulgaria is always directly affected by the economic cycle in the euro area. Moreover, the ECB's monetary policy is moving rapidly in ourcountry through the mechanisms of the currency board, the integration of the banking sector and the high trade link. The external effects also affect the behavior of banks in Bulgaria. For example, the dynamics of interest rates in Bulgaria follow that of the euro area. Accordingly, the cost of servicing loans in Bulgaria has been falling steadily over the last few years. However, this hasalso led to higher levels of indebtedness. As a result, today in bulgaria's banks, the price of both the loan granted and the borrowed average is much lower than in2008, when the economic cycle reversed. september2018. Over the same period, the annual weighted interest rate on loan balances for non-financial corporations fell from 9% to 3.8%. interest on new household deposits fell from 5% to 0.2%, and interest on new deposits of non-financial corporations fell from 4.9% to 0.3% from December 2008 to September 2018. At the same time, the volume of loans and deposits has increased significantly over the same period. Loans to households have increased since 18091. Lv. 21417 million euro. Deposits of households increased from BGN 21956 million to BGN 49817 million and deposits of non-financial enterprises increased from BGN 13420 million to BGN 23853 million. These figures highlight three trends - a significant increase in savings in the case of massive reductions in deposit rates; an increase in credit and indebtedness; and a significant reduction in borrowing rates. So logically we come to two big questions. First, what will be the rate and degree of "normalisation" of interest rates? The parameters of "normalization" of interest rates are difficult to predict. and then in each of the last two years it has increased by about 100 basis points. If there is a similar trajectory of "normalisation" in the euro area, for Bulgaria these amendments will be the minimum. The cost of the loanmay also include an additional country-specific premium. As regards the issue of transferring increased interest rates to borrowers, it can generally be expected that such a transfer (especially to households) will bepartially limited but  both by the sensitivity of the response and by the economic capacity of borrowers, as well as by factors of a political and economic nature. Banks' inability to pass on the increase in liabilities interest to assets on balance sheets would further reduce the alreadynarrowed net interest margin. and regulatory ceilings for the amount of bank fees and commissions. Another restrictive factor in increasing banks' revenue from fees and commissions is increased competition in the field of payment services following the introduction of the new European Payment Services Dir (the so-called PSD2). In other words, the new interest rate cycle will bring a transformation of interest rate risk into credit, a deterioration in the quality of loans, a need for more providence and hence a lower rate of profit for banks. Due to the potential risks described in general, we have decided in the BNB to activate the countercyclical capital buffer from 1 October 2019. The decision to activate this buffer was based on internal analysis, taking into account the dynamics of a group of indicators. This analysis goes beyond the use of the credit/GDP indicator recommended by European regulations, in particular its deviation from debt, calculated by applying the Hodrick-Prescott filter. If we were to follow the recommendations of the European Systemic Risk Board literally, we would have been in danger of delaying the identification of a build-up of cyclical systemic risk during a period of excessivegrowth. Ladies and gentlemen, I will also address in particular the topic of steps and actions related to the announced intention to join our national currency with ERM II. As is well known, the participation of the national currency in ERM II is one of the five Maastricht criteria on which a country's readiness to join the euro area is assessed. Bulgaria is currently not fulfilling this Maastricht criterion. The exception of formal requirements for joining ERM II makes the process subjective and political. Accordingly, the fulfilment of this criterion for membership of the euro areais not fully under the control of the applicant country. The only document relating to ERM II principles is a two-page Decision of the European Council taken in1997 in Amsterdam. The application and decision-making process itself is well defined. The relevant procedure is very clear. In this procedure, the request is sent bythe finance minister and the central bank governor from the respective country on Friday, after closing the financial markets, and the decision is taken on Saturday and announced on Sun 2 before the markets open. This three-day procedure has not so far been formally launched and completed by the Bulgarian side. What was done was our unilateral commitment to certain commitments to be fulfilled in advance  in order to obtain a potentially positive assessment, with which we are expected to have the basis for a request for accession of the BGN to ERM II. Here it will be useful to make the following clarifications. The absence of formal criteria for joining ERM II, as well as the historical p-ratic of all previousaccessions of national currencies to ERM II, do not preclude member states from adding new conditions or creating new criteria. Such new conditions or criteria may, for example, take into account the evolution of the institutions in the euro area. However, in order for these new conditions and criteria to be mandatory for new applicants, a change in European legislation is needed. There is no such change, although the Single Supervisory Mechanisation (SSM) and the Single Resolution Mechanism (SRM) have been established in the euro area, i.e. erm II has been in force the same written rules that have been in place for more than 20 years. Therefore, the combination of new requirements and unchanged rules means the following. The only way to applythe rules is if the candidate country itself requests them unilaterally in the form of conditions that it sets itself. There is no doubt that for Bulgaria the participation of bgn in ERM II will not constitute any effort, nor will it require any change in our monetary regime. It is important to highlight another feature in our case. In other words, according to the objective thus stated, we cannot have accession to the SSM before joining ERM II, or vice versa, i.e. the two must be implemented at the same time. Joining the euro area is a further stage. According to the objectives announced in the summer, we must join the SSM through close cooperation with the SRM before joining the euro area. Participation in the SSM and SRM prior to euro area membership bears anassimilation of the resulting risks, which are well known. Bulgaria has already agreed to bear these risks. The process of establishing close cooperation with the ECB on the basis of Art. 7 of Council Regulation (EU) No 1024/2013 of 15 October2013 This process covers three blocks. First, it is a legislative basis  changes to the Bulgarian legislation are needed to transfer supervisory powers from the BNB to the ECB and, moreover, to provide legal certainty to the ECB when implementing its decisions in Bulgaria. Thirdly comes the overall assessment of some banks in Bulgaria, an ECB-led process that includes an asset quality review and a stress test of banks. On 12 November 2018, the ECB published information on the assessmentof banks. In particular, the asset quality review is expected to be carried out on the basis of bank balance sheet data by the end of 2018 and usinga new ECB methodology published in June 2018. Finally, I will briefly address the expected effects on the credit process related to the overall assessment of banks. The first expected effect is the slowdown in lending during the review period. Such are the historical dataseen in the euro area in 2014 in the assessment of banks prior to the launch of the SSM, as well as in bulgaria in the asset review in 2016. and the removal of loan portfolios from balance sheets. All this generally reduces the volume of existing credit. The second expected effect is related to the asymmability of the impact on the credit market. Title: Address at the opening of the The Next Big Thing Conference, organized by Bloomberg TV Bulgaria, Sofia, 17 October 2019
text: Address by Kalin Hristov, BNB Deputy Governor in charge of the Issue Department, at the opening of the The Next Big Thing Conference, organized by Bloomberg TV Bulgaria, Sofia, 17 October 2019 In his address at the opening of the fourth annual conference The Next Big Thing, organized by Bloomberg TV Bulgaria, the BNB Deputy Governor in charge of the Issue Department, Mr Kalin Hristov talked about the global economic trends, institutional and structural challenges facing the eurozone, the negative interest rates and the impact of the above processes on Bulgaria. The global economic structure, as we know it today, is the function of two significant events in the recent fifty years, said Mr Kalin Hristov. First, the liberalization and trade integration of China into the global economy. In addition, global processes have been strongly impacted by the dynamics of the political and economic integration in Europe, particularly after the changes in Central and Eastern Europe at the end of 1980s. China demonstrates the need of progress along the whole technological chain without skipping stages in this progress. Starting from the lower technological levels, with the gradual accumulation of knowledge and building upon the educational system, a capacity for production using cutting-edge technologies is achieved, according to the BNB Deputy Governor. In Mr. Christovs words, besides its positive economic effects, the economic freedom of Central and Eastern Europe and its integration into the EU common market has a negative side owing to the significant outflow of qualified labour from our region. This reduces the labour force and subdues our growth potential. As regards the integration process in Western Europe, Mr Hristov noted that its acceleration in the last decade of the 20th century occurred when the German politicians agreed to relinquish their national currency and to welcome the creation of the euro as a guarantee of the irrevocability of the German unification. The creation of the euro is more of a political project than an example of a well-designed common currency, Mr Hristov added, underlying the absence of the key economic foundations required for a successful monetary union  fiscal capacity for direct transfers between individual Member States and a common, well-developed and regulated financial market. The global financial crisis demonstrated the deficits of the existing eurozone structure. For the euro to be preserved in the medium and long term, pressure for further integration was made evident, Mr Hristov reminded, also underscoring that no will for implementation of radical institutional changes and structural policies in the eurozone has been evidenced. Against this background, the European Central Bank was forced to pursue extremely accommodative monetary policy along two channels  through the interest rate policy, which reached its extreme form with the negative interest rates, and via the policy of quantitative easing, which has in practice led to financing directly the eurozone governments by purchasing their debt. Are we sure we know which problem such a policy solves, and are we not today actually laying down further problems for the future?, Mr Hristov asked. The BNB Deputy Governor in charge of the Issue Department also discussed in detail the subject of negative interest rates and their potential effects on the economy. The positive interest rate is a reward for refraining from consuming something today, i.e. a reward for deferred consumption. Thus, the positive interest rate creates prerequisites for accumulation of funds for investment. By contrast, the negative interest rate changes the economic culture, particularly that of the younger generations, by depriving them of the incentive to save but rather encouraging them to assume excessive debt. Mr. Kalin Hristov dwelled on the importance of the demographic structure of the population. Negative interest rates result in different incentives and predetermine different behaviour depending on the stage in the life cycle of a given group. Aging households perceive negative interest rates as a threat to the possibility to preserve their current level of consumption after retiring. Hence, negative interest rates force these households to accumulate more savings, which may earn a very low and even a negative return, only to be able to have after a time funds at their disposal for keeping a certain level of consumption. This is all seen from the data. At first sight, it looks illogical why savings still grow even given the so low interest rates. This phenomenon, however, is brought forth mostly by people in active age that are prevailing due to the aging of the population, rather than being explained with the younger peoples behaviour. Businesses also respond to the negative interest rates. When interest rates are declining, companies are expected to borrow more and to invest more. However, when these interest rates become negative, the business starts treating them as a signal of future uncertainty. Furthermore, if the businesses judge rationally, they also take into consideration the aging population and understand it will not be able to keep up the current level of consumption in the future. This lowers the potential of return on investment. Highly negative interest rates have a deterrent effect on investment, as can be seen from the data Mr Kalin Hristov said. Analyzing the consequences for banks, another adverse effect from the very low interest rates is that risk is no longer differentiated within the cost of lending. It seems today anyone can obtain a loan, and when the interest rate approximates zero any investment project looks good. This is a potential for future problems in loan servicing, Mr Hristov said, adding that the higher interest rates eliminate the unprofitable ventures, while an environment of very low interest rates allows for supporting the existence of highly indebted low-productivity companies  the so-called zombie companies. In Bulgaria also interest rates are already very low. In Mr Hristovs words, any entrepreneur can ask himself the question  do I deserve so low interest rates and does the cost of my loan sufficiently evaluate the risk entailed in my business model? More generally  from the point of view of political economy  an important aspect of negative interest rates is related to their feature as a tax on savings. However, this tax is imposed by the institution of central banks, which are not elected directly by the people. Mr. Hristov stated this violates a basic principle of democracy  there should be no taxation without respective political representation. Due to the fixing of the Bulgarian lev to the Deutsche mark, and later to the euro, today the effects of from the eurozones monetary policy quickly spill over to Bulgaria. This can be seen in the very low interest rates on deposits and loans. The mechanism of our currency board grants us a great advantage - we cannot purchase government debt, which is among the main factors for the fiscal discipline of governments, Mr Hristov underscored in conclusion.

Title: Statement at the Banks and Businesses Seventh Annual Conference, Sofia, 14 November 2019
Subtitle:
THE ECONOMY AND THE BANKS:
THIS TIME IT IS DIFFERENT, IT IS STRUCTURAL
text: Statement by Mr. Kalin Hristov, BNB Deputy Governor in charge of the Issue Department, at the Banks and Businesses Seventh Annual Conference, Sofia, 14 November 2019 THE ECONOMY AND THE BANKS: THIS TIME IT IS DIFFERENT, IT IS STRUCTURAL Dear Ladies and Gentlemen, I thank you for the invitation to once again open this traditional conference organised by Economedia AD. In previous years, the topic of the Banks and Businesses conference series was usually associated with the understanding that banks, through the lending process, are a source of impetus for developing businesses, hence the economy as a whole. Today, we have a new, uncharted environment, where the economy of the euro area is facing a situation that requires the European Central Banks (ECBs) continuous accommodative policy based on non-conventional measures. This environment is carried over to the Bulgarian economy by way of our trade integration with the euro area and the transmission of the ECBs monetary policy through the currency board mechanism. The behaviour of banks themselves is mostly conditioned by this unusual economic and monetary environment. Therefore, this time the title of my statement is with a focus on how the condition of the economy impacts banks. Sources of shocks to the Bulgarian economy With the topic thus introduced, let us start by recalling the historical background. The economic growth in Bulgaria after 1997  the year we introduced the currency board is conditioned by two groups of factors: those stemming from the external environment and those relating to our domestic policies. Over this past period, the external environment experienced several severe crises, at the same time as Bulgaria had only one episode of recession (around 2009) which, too, was triggered by the external shock of the global financial crisis. We can draw the conclusion that we seem to have learnt lessons from the economic and financial crises between 1990 and 1997, and have since pursued effective macroeconomic policies so as to prevent a domestically generated crisis from causing economic downturn. Following this logic, the Bulgarian economy is likely to sharply slow down its growth or fall into recession if we were to be affected by strongly negative external factors. Given our export structure and our high level of integration with the economy of the European Union (EU), we would be most vulnerable to shocks coming from the EU and notably the euro area. And the euro area itself could slow down its economic growth or fall into recession both under the impact of internal factors and as a result of the continuous global standoff between the USA and China, or the aggravating of the EU economic and trade relations with the USA. Much has been said about the anticipated effects from Brexit; however it would not cause any dramatic economic, trade or financial shocks neither to Great Britain, nor to the EU, in whatever form it is to be effected. One reason for this is the long period of time the process has taken so far, which in fact has allowed the most vulnerable sectors to prepare. Another reason that major shocks are unlikely to occur, is if indeed both Great Britain and the EU prove to each other through their actions that they are supporters of the free trade principles (as they claim to be). Adhering to these principles, both parties should soon after Brexit (if failing to do so before Brexit) establish a mutually satisfactory regime of cooperation in terms of their trade relations. Factors in the euro area Today, a widely shared expectation is that the euro area is heading towards an economic slowdown even if there were no major shock or deep recession to occur. All official forecasts of institutions such as the ECB, the European Commission and the International Monetary Fund point to a slowdown of the economic growth in the euro area for next year. The underlying factors are well known and are more structural rather than cyclical: adverse demographic developments coupled with slow technological development, leading to increasingly low productivity and loss in competitiveness, high levels of private and public debt, and changing principles and structure of global trade. This occurs in an ultra-accommodative monetary environment with low and negative interest rates and monetary policy of direct asset purchases conducted over an infinite horizon by the ECB. Given these starting conditions and if the development of the economy were to take a negative turn from the baseline scenario, the monetary policy would have exhausted its potential even for a short-term cyclical stimulus. A recent academic research by Brunnermeier and Koby from Princeton University has demonstrated that the efficiency limit of monetary policy is characterised by the so-called reversal interest rate. If it falls below that interest rate level, the over-accommodative monetary policy would lead to reducing rather than increasing bank lending and to depressing the overall economy. The negative interest rates and their potential negative side effects are a broad subject, which I recently discussed during the conference held by Bloomberg TV Bulgaria. The negative interest rates, especially if maintained over a sustained period of time, have rather negative effects on the demand by households and firms alike, as well as on the overall economic growth. They create an environment conducive to over-indebtedness, financial asset price bubbles and accumulation of related risks. Real estate prices would also rise, at a pace and to levels rendering entire social groups in isolation and precluding the possibility for younger generations to enter the real estate market (except at the cost of high indebtedness early in life). The effects in Bulgaria We have a currency board in Bulgaria which by design quickly and fully transfers the monetary conditions from the euro area. The low public debt, which historically leads to a low risk premium, and the households high propensity to save are further factors for the direct transmission of the monetary conditions from the euro area. This is why, today in Bulgaria we can see interest rates on retail deposits verging on zero and some deposits of firms already having negative interest rates. It is hard to imagine such interest rates as encouraging the households and firms to save less and to consume and invest more. If the deposits do not earn interest, this actually creates an incentive for households to save more today in order to make sure they keep a certain level of consumption in the future. Also, if they become negative, the interest rates on the deposits of households become a type of tax, and just as any other tax, they restrict consumption. Negative interest rates are an extra cost to firms reducing the return on their capital and stifling their propensity to invest. Overall, continuously sustained low or negative interest rates are perceived as a signal of uncertainty and a coming slowdown of the economy, which is why economic agents slow down consumption and revise their investment plans downwards. This picture is not optimistic, yet it does not even reflect effects of potential strongly adverse shocks. This is only under the baseline scenario, which does not foresee deterioration of the external environment, as well as under the assumption that the ECB current policy will continue as it is. Under the baseline scenario, expectations are for likely positive, yet low rates of economic growth. Under this baseline scenario of economic development in our country, there will be a slowdown of employment growth (without necessarily increasing unemployment, but largely due to the mechanic effect of the declining population), further increases in wages, an overall rise in savings with banks (despite the low interest rates) and an excess liquidity of banks. While the excess liquidity of banks would be perceived as a positive indicator in normal times, in the current situation it is a significant factor for banks to take additional credit risk. Having to deal with negative returns on the low-risk liquid assets, where they can invest their excess liquidity, the banks are forced to seek new borrowers by decreasing the interest rates on loans, aiming to achieve some positive return. The low interest rates on loans, however, make it already increasingly difficult to diversify between the quality of individual projects as well as uncertain as to whether these cover the cost of risk. As a result of all this, the private sector indebtedness will increase more significantly with respect to households. Banks will be less credit risk averse also because of the pressure from the margin squeeze. The competition among banks and the competitive pressure on banks by non-bank payment service providers, which are flexible and high tech, will limit the income from banks payment transactions. The banks revenues will be restricted also because of the new European regulations related to further liberalisation of products and services are traditionally dominated by banks, as well as placing limits on some fees charged by the banks. However, from the point of view of their liabilities, the cost reduction possibilities are limited. A key limiting factor, for example, is the zero bound for interest rates on retail deposits. A negative interest rate on retail deposits, which are such an important funding source for the banks in Bulgaria, will entail a risk of eroding these deposits. We may note additional areas of pressure for banks higher costs, e.g. in relation to cyber security and for supervisory compliance. As a result of the above factors, the interest rate margin and profitability of banks will be under constant pressure. In this context, the BNBs policy will remain aimed at maintaining high capital requirements for banks, including through continuing enforcement of all capital buffers and additional calibration of the countercyclical buffer levels, so as to cover the risks accumulating on the banks balance sheets. Conclusions We are dealing here not with temporary or cyclical developments and effects, but rather with long-term trends. The state of the euro area economy and the expected slowdown in the economic growth there require an ultra-accommodative monetary policy. This condition of the euro area and this monetary policy of the ECB will spill over to our country through the trade integration of the Bulgarian economy with the euro area economy and through the currency board mechanism. Within the context of todays conference topic, this deteriorating state of the euro area economy and the resulting monetary policy brings up the question about the effects on banks. My expectation is for retaining and further easing of the monetary conditions, which would lead to activating the so-called reversal interest rate. Households and businesses will continue to accrue savings. Banks will assume more credit risk in search of profitability and with very limited possibilities to fully capture the risk in the cost of credit. The interest margin will continue to shrink in combination with an ever stronger competition in the payment services area, the imposing of administrative ceilings on certain bank fees and the growing regulatory and cybersecurity costs. From the BNB perspective as a regulator, that would require higher levels of the countercyclical buffer, despite the fact that the trends described are rather long-term. Thank you for your attention! ____________ As Mario Draghi has recently remarked in his farewell speech upon ending his term of office as President of the ECB: Today, we are in a situation where low interest rates are not delivering the same degree of stimulus as in the past, because the rate of return on investment in the economy has fallen. Monetary policy can still achieve its objective, but it can do so faster and with fewer side effects if fiscal policies are aligned with it. (Mario Draghis remarks can be read HYPERLINK " " here). Markus K. Brunnermeier, Yann Koby, The Reversal Interest Rate, NBER Working Paper 25406, December 2018. But if the funding received by central banks goes to continue the ongoing lack of structural policies, the long-term problems remain unresolved. What are the risks to business? When financed at very low interest rates, people think that this low price adequately reflects the risk of their business model. The interest rate must be positive and not close to zero in order to sift through the effective of inefficient investment projects. When banks lend at 1%, each project seems to be able to generate a positive cash flow. This distorts the distribution of capital and keeps zombie companies that are not effective but persist only because the funding rate is low. Such companies use workers who might otherwise work elsewhere more efficiently. This is one explanation for the ever-falling labour productivity in the Western world. What would you advise people in the business? The workforce will shrink, meaning more things will have to be done with capital rather than labour. In a way, the presence of low interest rates is positive because it makes it easier to invest in capital. But low interest rates are incentivising people to over-in debt. perhaps in search of alternatives for investment they will be attracted to bubble sectors because they currently see the positive profit ability.

text: Interview of Mr. Kalin Hristov, Deputy Governor of the BNB, managing department "Issue", for the electronic edition Money.bg, 20 August 2020. BA?Y????? ?OP? E ?APA?????A ?A ?O???P?A?E ?A ???C?PA??? ?YPC ?A ?E?A What is your general view of macroeconomic situation inthe euro area by the end of this and in the next 2-3 years? In the euro area, growth began to slow even before the COVID-19 pandemic. The economic recovery there, which we have seen in recent years, has been driven mainly by the ECB'sultra-stimulus monetary policy. This policy is expressed by negative interest rates and massive purchases of euro area government securities. Such monetary policy can only affect economic growth in the short term and then the effects subside. The growing problems in global trade, mainly related to trade disputes between the US and China, have further diminished the effects of the ECB's actions. Remember that at the last meeting of the Governing Council of the ECB, led by Mario Drag, decisions were adopted to reduce the interest rate on the deposit facility and restart the ECB's asset purchase programme. And all this was before the COVID-19 shock. The pandemic and the restrictive measures imposed have already created a strained economic dynamic in the euro area. Many economies there, including those with very high public debt, have not solved their deep structural problems. With much monetary policy depleted and very limited fiscal maneuvering opportunities, the euro area as a whole has welcomed COVID-19 in a worse state than it was at the start of the global financial crisis a decade ago. The ECB's natural response was to provide more liquidity to credit institutions and start even more asset purchases. The effects (or perhaps implicit objectives) of this policy are generally two d0 ensuring that over-indebted governments have access to finance at thelowest possible cost and maintaining the prices of financial assets in the euro area in order to support banking systems there. Given the great uncertainty at this stage, it is risky to forecast economic development over the next few years. We probably won't see a V-shaped recovery. A number of factorsremain not specified, including the development of the viral pandemic, the development and accessibility of an effective vaccine and treatment, the new restrictive measures that the authorities would impose in the event of an accelerated development of the pandemic, possibly given the high economic and social cost of such measures, the relevant behaviour of the different sectors of the economy, including those more sensitive to the current shock (e.g. transport, tourism and retail). The situation around COVID-19 further hampers trade and hinders the resolution of structural economic problems. What will be the macroeconomic and financial consequences (including for Bulgaria) offurther expanding the ECB's balance sheet by taking on new volumes of bonds that commercial banks are betting against refinancing under the various ECB programmes? The macroeconomic and financial picture in Bulgaria follows the euro area symmetrically. The restrictive measuresflowing from COVID-19 were imposed in Bulgaria at almost the same time as in other European countries. in2009, Bulgaria's GDP shrank by 3.4%, increased by 6.1% in 2008. In view of Bulgaria's low public debt and therefore the lack of need to support the prices ofBulgarian government securities, the intensification of monetary policy in the euro area has no great direct effect for us. It was also interesting that the announcement of the ECB's swap line with BNB initially led to the expansion of the spread of Bulgarian debt on international markets, I.e. investors interpreted this information as a signal of increased potential risk related to Bulgaria. This was natural as the swap lines between central banks are an anti-crisis instrument. This reaction was subsequently fully corrected after it became clear that the swap line in question was entirely re-reactive and did not need to be activated. The ECB's provision of liquidity to banks in the euro area will also not lead to visible effects in our country. The Bulgarian banking system was super-liquid even before COVID-19. Liquidity of banks in Bulgaria is then expected to increase further in the context of the crisis due to an increase in savings due to the uncertainty and depositionof consumption and investment. What do these general developments mean for economic activity in the euro area and Bulgaria? The ECB's latest forecast is from June 2020, in which they dramatically revised expectations of economic growth in the euro area in a negative direction. To reflect the high uncertainty in the current environment, the ECB has published a forecast with a key, optimistic and negative scenario for growth and inflation. The baseline scenario foresees for 2020. economic growth of -8.7 percent (at a forecast of 0.8 percent in March this year) for the euro area and inflation of 0.3 percent (at a forecast of 1.1 percent in March). Bnb's current forecast is also from June 2020 and is based on data and information until 17 June, with data and developments after that date not reflected in the forecast (including current political volatility). This forecast is completely confed in the ECB's baseline scenario, and in terms of expectations for the development of the external environment, it is entirely based on this scenario. We forecast that real GDP for the Bulgarian economy willdecrease by 8.5% in 2020, with uncertainty over the forecast being unusually high due to both the unprecedented nature of the economic shock, measures to limit the spread of COVID-19 and uncertainty about the future development of the epidemiological situation. The decline in real GDP will be mainly determined by a decrease in private consumption (contribution from -3.4 BC) and investments in fixed capital (contribution from -3.2 BC) and to a lesser extent by the negative contribution of net exports (contribution from -2.6BC). which will reflect the material decline of energy products in line with the fall in the price of oil on an annual basis. Unlike the ECB for years, our approach toillustrating the uncertainty of p cornosis is graphical using a fan-like graph (there is a similar approach by the Bank of England). Due to the unprecedented nature of the economic shock caused by the measures against COVID-19 and the uncertainty about the future development of the epidemiological situation, the uncertainty interval in the current forecast is unusually wide, even in the short term. As a result, according to the constructed probability distribution around the central forecast for gdp change in 2020, there is a 60% probability that the real GDP in the current year will be in the range of -4.1% to -13.1% Details of the forecast are presented in the second issue of the Economic Review of the BNB, which under the bank's rules is published in August. What are the prospectsfor raising the ECB's interest rates? In my view, in the short and medium term, such a outlook tends to zero. There are deep structural reasons for the central bank's low interest rates associatedwith long-term trends of producer decline and unfavorable demography, a phenomenon that economic science calls "secular stagnation." Other factors are likely to dominate in the longer term. The reduction of europe's workforce and the drive to move production from Asia back to Europe will lead to an increase in inflation and interest rates. Is it possible that market interestrates in the European financial markets will rise even without (or before) the ECB raises its set interest rates? Theoretically, yes, if risk premiums for financial assets are raised. Under what circumstances, however, could this happen? Interest rates on euro area government securities may rise if purchases by the ECB reach any limit and other investors start to demand yields corresponding to their perceptions of the risk of investment in such securities. Other debt instruments, market interest rates on which they may rise, are corporate debt securities. even bankruptcies, of issuers. In the event of a persistently deteriorating economic situation, the latter would be a logical stage. On the other hand, we cannot expect the ECB to endlessly buy up financial assets or accept them as collateral, since the ECB's mandate still excludes a target for returning to a planned economy in which virtually all financial assets are in the central bank's balan. Since the accession of the Bulgarian lev to the ERM II exchange rate mechanism in Bulgarian society, there are concerns about possible changes in the fixed exchange rate of the bgn to the euro within the /-15 percent range announced by the ECB. Under what conditionscan this happen? The central exchange rate of the Bulgarian lev to the euro remains equal to the existing one, i.e. BGN 1.95583 for 1 euro. The currency board mode remains unchanged. The Bulgarian National Bank has made a unilateral commitment to zero deviation from theu-exchange rate, as it has been for the entire period since the introduction of the exchange rate board. Has the currency swap contract between bnb and the ECB already been concluded? If so, what are the commitments of both parties to the treaty? How can the BNB use the money from this currency swap in the conditions of a currency board? However, it has only a signal character, underlining the ECB's confidence in the currency board in Bulgaria, and the Bulgarian National Bank has no intention of activating it. This is explained by the fact that the mechanism of the foreign exchange board excludes the need for additional instruments to support its functioning. The foreign exchange board has an adequate level of coverage through international foreign exchange reserves. Moreover, the BNB currently has historically one of the highest amounts of international foreign exchange reserves for Bulgaria. What EU safeguards or funds will we gain access to after joining ERM II and the Banking Union? As for joining ERM II, the responsibility for maintaining the fixed rate with zero deviation remains with the Bulgarian National Bank. The currency board operates without the need for external safeguards. Joining the Banking Union now also does not lead to access to new supporting mechanisms. as well as an additional guarantee from the Bulgarian government of EUR 32.5 million. euro. The funds in the existing Bulgarian Bank Resolution Fund, where until now we have accumulated contributions from the banks amounting to BGN 701 million, will be used as a source for payment of the initial installment and future contributions to the SRF. Joining ERM II and the Banking Union does not bring new, unaffordable to Bulgaria untilnow, European Protection Mechanisms or Funds. After joining ERM II and the Banking Union, what new costs is Bulgaria and our banking system engaged in? The ECB collects fees for its supervisory activities. Therefore, the banks in Bulgaria will have an additional amount related tothese charges. This cost is yet to be calculated. With regard to the restructuring activities, the banks in Bulgaria have so far deposited amounts in the Bulgarian Bank Resolution Fund. With the accession to the Banking Union, the contributions of the banksin F onanda for restructuring will undergo some reduction, which is yet to be calculated, as the target level of the Bulgarian fund has so far been higher than the level of the European Restructuring Fund. In addition, the European Press Council collects fees for its activities. This will lead to a new cost for the banks in bulgaria, as we have never charged fees in our capacity asa resolution authority. So the net financial effect of the costs to the banking system and banks in Bulgaria resulting from accession to the Banking Union has yet to be calculated. During participation in ERM II, will the BNB be able to maintain a regime of minimum reserve requirements other than that of the ECB? As long as Bulgaria is not a member of the euro area, the minimum reserve requirements of the banks in Bulgaria will continue to be determined by the Bulgarian National Bank. Does membership of the Banking Union guarantee that we are protected from bank failures? The role and purpose of banking supervision is not to eliminate bank failures, but to minimise their likelihood, as well as possible risks to the banking system and the economy as a whole in the event of the insolvency of an individual bank. The very history of the Single Supervisory Mechanism is indicative. Since its completion at the end of 2014, there have been 5 systemically important banks in the euro area that have been under the direct supervision of the ECB and which the ECB itself has declared "failing or likely to become failing". There is a hypothesis that by entering the Banking Union banking groups from EU countries will transform their banks in Bulgaria from subsidiaries into branches. In general, large cross-border banks and banking groups have an incentive to optimise their capital structure,supervisory costs and costs associated with the implementation of regulations (so-called compliance costs). Searching for these optimisations is the main reason for transforming subsidiaries of banks into branches. Such a legal possibility exists now, but joining the Single Supervisory Mechanism facilitates such processes, at least because working with one supervisory authority means fewer procedures for the bank concerned. The effects of transformations of subsidiaries into branches are related to the danger of transforming a significant part of our banking system into a capital-free mode of operation. Branches do not have a requirement to maintain capital. Against the background of the lack of capital and capital buffers in branches, it should bestressed that in any event deposit insurance remains a national liability, as the third pillar of the Banking Union (single European deposit guarantee scheme) is not built. fiscal transfers between countries. And how difficult it is for the leaders of European countries to agree on this subject, we have seen recently in the disputes around the negotiation of the so-called EU reconstruction fund. What will happen to the regulatory buffers currently set by the BNB and measures in terms of dividends and liquidity? With regard to banks identified as significant, the ecb's powers will be conferred. For these banks, the ECB could send a request to the BNB to issue an act to change or lift the ban on dividend distribution and reduction of foreign exposures. GNI B is not allowed to apply discretion to these ECB instructions.
