text: Speech by Mr. Kalin Hristov, Deputy Governor of the BNB, managing director "Issue", before the 8th Annual Conference "Banks and Business", Sofia, 2 December 2020. ECONOMY AND BANKS  (THIS TIME IT'S DIFFERENT, STRUCTURALLY)N Dear ladies and gentlemen, Ithank the organizers for the opportunity to present again the views of the Bulgarian National Bank on the development of the economy in the current year and next, as well as on the role of the banking sector in this process. This year is unusual. In my speech, I will first present our expectations for this year in the context of the conversation wehad at about the same time a year ago at the same conference. banking sector and the banking sector's relations with the economy. Ochaquania a year ago A year ago, we discussed the relationship between the economy and the banks again. This slowdown was driven by several factors, including the US-China global trade dispute affecting the whole world amid a contraction in global trade, which has also affected economicgrowth in Europe and especially in the euro area. the highly open nature of its economy. An additional factor in slowing growth was brexit uncertainty. However, the big factor was the practical exhaustion of the effects of highly stimulating monetary policy in the euro area, together with the possibility for governments through fiscal policy to provide additional economic stimulus (which in technical language we call a lack of fiscal space). the over-indebtedness of many governments there, the growing indebtedness of the corporate sector, falling productivity in virtually all countries and an ageing population as an additional factor limiting potential growth. At the time, wewere expecting a euro zone rate of around 1% - 1.2%, which means growth slowing but still positive. This slowdown was naturally expected to be carried over to the Bulgarian economy with lag, which is traditional for the relationship between the Bulgarian economy and the euro zone. At the time Bulgaria still had a growth rate higher than in the euro area, which was also delayed as a result of the euro area's slowdown. Bulgaria's economy was in good shape in terms of we had relative growth and employment due to both a shrinking workforce, a growing economy and high demand in the labour market, which in turn also generated wage and consumption growth. and households, with faster growth in the household segment. Then, a year ago, we expected the challenges to bemore associated with a potentially moderate slowdown in the economy in 2020, putting pressure on the profitability of the banking system, given that interest rates on deposits and loans had already fallen a lot. that we will face such an economic shock as the new coronavirus. The unique crisis and the policies of the euro area In practice, the pandemic created a type of economic crisis unknown to us. Until now, the modern world does not have a well-described economic crisis caused by a pandemic. The closest analogy that can be made is with the Spanish flu from1919 to 1920. In addition, the world emerged from the First World War and the destructive effects of it coincided with the flu. These are fundamentally different starting conditions from today. In addition, knowledge in both medicine and economic theory and in the management of economies was much less than what we currently have. It is therefore very difficult to draw an analogy and draw conclusions about how the current economic crisis would proceed globally. The current crisis is unique in that the economic downturn is caused by decisions by governments. The authorities decide to limit economic activity in order to prevent the spread of the pandemic and to control the morbidity of the population. We have a slowing economic growth initiated by government policy. This is unusual. households or companies, the government impose restrictions on economic activity, they naturally develop an expectation that this other type of policy will still have to compensate for the decline of economies and create compensation mechanisms. As I have already commented, at the previous stage of the development of the European economy, and in particular the euro area, monetary policy was virtually depleted. Interest rates in the euro area were negative, and further reductions would have been associated with negative effects for the financial sector, households and businesses. Therefore, the two main types of economic policies remained fiscal. However, it was also severely limited in the euro area, given the over-indebtedness of many PRassets. has in practice become part of the fiscal one. The central bank de facto supports government policies so that they, in their high indebtedness, generate fiscal stimulus in the economy. The main channels for such fiscal stimulusare known  providing direct aid to households and companies and government guarantees on debt in order to reduce credit risk for creditors. bulgaria in the pandemic and our first measures Bulgaria was in a much better economic state, given our monetary policy regime, the currency board, and our historically conservative and very responsible fiscal policy over the years. which is not possible under our regime, but through market financing, insteadof quite good conditions thanks to the global over-liquidity. In practice, the compensatory economic mechanism in Bulgaria is the same as in the euro area  through fiscal policy with a significant increase in the budget deficit due to the simultaneous slowdown in budgetary revenues and an increase in government expenditure. I will also address the topic of the state of the banking systemand our supervisory and supervisory policy. Bulgaria's banking system has also met the current crisis with very good baselines. It had a very high level of liquidity and capital adequacy. At the same time, non-performing loans decreased, due to two factors. Firstly, the cyclical factor of high economic growth over the last 3 years. The relatively high growth rate of around 10% of loans to households and businesses had led us to raise the countercyclical buffer 3 times  once effectively to 0.5% and with two further increases of 0.5% thatwere due in 2020 and January 2021. these low interest rates probably did not take into account all the embedded credit risk. The Governing Council of the BNB also held a meeting on 12 March and, taking into account the significant change in the economic and financial cycle and anticipating a sharp decline in economic activity, adopted measures aimed at further strengthening the capital position of the banks. This profit, which the sector had to recapitalise, was at a record high due to economic growth and therefore credit growth last year. some of which were not of the highest credit quality. Given that the economic crises have led to a decrease in the credit quality of counterparties, we have introduced a measure to reduce the concentration of liquidity and increase its credit quality. 1 April 2020 and from 1 January 2021, they no longer had an economiccm. These decisions the Bulgarian National Bank took long before other central banks took measures. I recall, for example, that on 12 March 2020 the European Central Bank also held a meeting but did not take any measures in relation to the pandemic. Theeuro area economy development report, which they published on 12 March, still contained an expectation of 1% growth in the euro area in 2020. The moratorium on payments on bank loans In April, across the European Union, governments curbed economic activity. Accordingly, these actions would have led to difficulties in servicing bank loans to companies and households. This, in turn, has raised the question of what can be done to introduce facilities for the servicing of these loans. As the issue has been raised by all sides, a regulatory framework has been adopted within the European Union to introduce rules on moratoriums on bank loan payments. This measure, which is not typical central banking or supervisory, was the result of discussions in the European Banking Authority. There was the idea of creating rules for a temporary moratorium - that is, during the period during which economic agents were restricted from operating due to factors beyond their control, they would not be obliged to repay debts tobanks. The Bulgarian National Bank agreed to attach the guidelines approved by the European Banking Authority. In accordance with the conditions in these guidelines, the Association of Banks in Bulgaria has drafted rules for a moratorium, which we have approved. The first term of the moratorium was from April to the end of June. at the end of September, taking into account the development of the pandemic and the economy within the European Union, the European Banking Authority decided that there was no need for further extension of the deadlines. By the end of June, 98% of applications were submitted by businesses and 89% of approvals on these applications were issued. and then over the next three months  the effect is exhausted. This has its logic relating to the fact that those who have received a direct economic hit from the restrictive measures have immediately requested to avail themselves of the possibilities of the moratorium. The practical effect of the moratorium is then starting to be reduced to the retention of non-performing loans. As a result of this effect of the moratorium, which allows thereclassification of loans as non-performing loans, as of September, we still see the preservation of non-performing exposures at their level since the beginning of the year. In the banking system, we are also seeing an increase in capital adequacy as a result of our measure ofnon-distribution of sorrow in the sector. "quick fix". Without going into detailed technical explanations, this is, in short, a reduction in certain risk weights for certain exposures of banks, which automatically increases their capital adequacy. We are also witnessing the preservation of high liquidity in our banking system, regardless of the moratorium. The explanation for this is contained in the very high level of savings generated by home loans  rational behaviour given the uncertainty they face for their employment and futureincome. we predicted it. Corporate credit, for example, slows faster than consumer and mortgage, but overall positive credit growth remains. The conclusion is that we have a banking system that retains a very high level of capital adequacyand liquidity, allowing it to continue to provide loans in the existing demand from companies and households. Expectations for next year Under the current conditions, what do we expect for 2021? The most important question is what the profile of the recovery of the Bulgarian and global economy would be . Until September this year, the prevailing understanding was that a recovery process would begin in2021. Today we are at a stage where virtually all European countries have a second wave and restrictions on economic activity. In this situation, it is difficult to predict that 2021 will be a year of rapid recovery . or what the population's propensity to undergo vaccination would be. Therefore, it is difficult for vaccines to give us the basis to predict a trajectory of rapid recovery. We should not forget the deepstructural problems mentioned in European economies and the high indebtedness of governments, which is only increasing this year. As a result of the pandemic, we will also have sectors in the economy that will be structurally and long-term affected. These are the sectors related to travel or the provision of services to people in close spaces and requiring close contact. In these sectors, the recovery is likely to be slower and incomplete, given the change in consumer attitudes. Bulgaria still remains in low indebtedness, despite the high budget deficit, which this year will be able to be financed relativelycheaply. In the banking sector, it makes sense to expect an increase in NPLs. In view of the high level of capitalisation and liquidity, the banking system will be able to absorb this pressure and retain the ability to credit the sectors in which demand will be. In the last days after the introduction of the new restrictive measures in Bulgaria, questions are again raised about compensatory economic policies. The reinstatement of the moratorium on bank loan payments is being commented on. Such a step will not, in principle, have major effects, as the moratoriums are only effective as temporary measures. The long-term postponement of credit servicing cannot be a supervisory policy tool, as we may already have permanently affected sectors of ic onomics. Such sectors will have a long-term solvency problem and are not about liquidity problems, to be decided by deferring credit payments. Therefore, even if, at European level, the Guidelines on moratoriums of the European Banking Authority are renewed, they are unlikely to be in the direction of very long extension periods. With regard to the policy of the Bulgarian National Bank, our analysis shows that the measures of March 2020 were verytimely and resulted in high capitulation and liquidity in the banking system. In addition to these, new regulations are expected, one in the area of minimum requirements for own funds and eligible liabilities. significant pressure on the banking system. text: Interview of Mr. Kalin Hristov, Deputy Governor of the BNB, managing director "Issue", for the edition "BGlobal", issue 1/2014 4, 2020. Mr Hristov, how do you assess the macroeconomic outlook for the EU, the euro area and Bulgaria? Since last year, the economies of the euro area and those of EU countries, but outside the euro area, have different dynamics. Since the second half of 2019, the euro area has slowed and it is no coincidence that last September the European Central Bank(ECB) introduced additional stimulus. the reaction of the economies to the first wave of the pandemic confirms the historically existing link that countries with long-term structural problems and lack of fiscal space (due to high public debt and budget deficit) have less opportunity to react and suffer a higher economic cost. At European level, the data show a deep decline in GDP in the second quarter and expectations for a recovery in the third. The decline in Central and Eastern Europe, including Bulgaria, is smaller than in the main euro area countries. It is clear from high-frequency indicators that there is a sharp recovery in indicators in early July, but they do not reachpre-crisis levels and start to show a slowdown again after August. In addition, a sharp increase in the autumn infected in most countries in the euro area and the measures taken to contain the infection will lead to a suppression of economic growth this year, as well as the trajectory of recovery in the coming years. For individual countries and certain sectors of the economy, this crisis will have a long-term effect on the potential for their recovery to pre-crisis levels. Given the significant depletion of the ability of monetary policy in the euro area to have incentive action, in the current economic environment fiscal policy is the main tool for responding. The ECB's policy of massive liquidity provision to commercial banks andpurchases of GS in their new Pandemic Emergency Purchase Programme supports access to finance for high-indebted governments and maintains the prices of financial assets. The main question is how and when this policy will be terminated. The profile of the current crisis does not suggest that the governments of most euro area countries will be able to shrink their deficits in the near future. effectiveness and reduce incentives to address structural problems. What about a specific growth forecast in Bulgaria? Prudent fiscal policy, which hasbeen in place since the introduction of the currency board, has allowed the government to face the great economic shock caused by the Covid-19 pandemic with good fiscal indicators. Bulgaria's real GDP will decrease by 5.5% in 2020, which will be mainly determined by a decrease in private consumption (contribution by -1.9 percentage points), a decrease in fixed capital investment (-1.8 BC) and to a lesser extent by the negative contribution of net exports (-1.2 BC). bulgaria in the third quarter of 2020 is characterised by significant uncertainty, including in the short term, due to the rapid spread of the pandemic both in bulgaria and in the world. The European Central Bank has talked about the introduction of a digital euro  what isthe goal? Digital currencies issued by central banks (the so-called The first is the classic with the level at which central banks can cut interest rates(so-called " Effective lower bound). Where interest rates are negative  currently the interest rate on the ECB's deposit facility, which has a major impact on financial markets and the economy, is minus 0.5%, it appears that the preference is to store savings in the form of banknotes where the interest rate is zero. negative interest rates will also be imposed on them. This means de facto impoverishment of people, whether they keep their money in a bank or have it in some form? Interestrates are, in practice, a tax on savings, which should not be imposed by central banks, because in democratic countries taxes can only be introduced by a parliament drawn up as a result of elections. In other words, the first goal of the digital euro is to cut interest rates toact on banknotes if people keep their savings in such a form. The second goal is that, especially in the ECB and in continental Europe, concern about the so-called "european economy" is gaining strength. big tech  the big tech companies that are not european, such as Google, Amazon, Facebook and China's Alibaba and Tencent. These companies intend to introduce their own currencies (stable coins) and if people have private digital money with which to easily transaction with each other, they would use much less of the euro. the less effective the monetary policy of the central bank issuer and the less its influence in thefinancial economy. So the worry of big tech's issuance is also causing central banks to make digital money for people to use instead of the money created by tech companies. The aim is to reduce the roleof these companies in global monetary competition. The fees and commissions charged by banks are a major source of profit formation at current interest rates  how will the possible introduction of a digital euro affect? Banks are already suffering fromthe fintech sector and the solutions they offer and plan to offer the tech giants. To be precise, the data show that the fees and commissions of the banks in Bulgaria contribute about 23% of the net operating income. Interest income is stilla bigger contributor, but indeed its share is declining. The answer to this question depends on the technical design of digital currencies. Depends on how they're introduced. Studies so far have identified two models. The first provides for everyone to receive an account with the central bank from which they can pay electronically anywhere. Such a decision would have a huge transformational effect  all of them would move their money from commercial banks to the central bank for the security they would receive. What could motivate the commercial bank to leave money behind is a difference in the interest paid. Commercial banks will be forced to pay a premium. to attract savers. However, their deposit costs will increase and ultimately this will havea negligible negative effect for commercial banks. That is, in this option will create something like BNB at the time of communism  monobank? Yes, even if we don't call it that directly, it would mean a monobank. It is no coincidence that almost no one intends to go in this direction. A more favorable and market-oriented model is a hybrid model, as is the project of the Bank of China. In this version, commercial banks are allowed to distribution of digital money issued by the central bank. The second scenario for the emergence of digital currencies, for which a technological solution has not yet been proposed, is that digital money is not in an account with the central bank, and banknotes can be "tokenized" and people can transfer tokens via mobile devices. which is impossible for banknotes today. If this happens, how quickly will the effects be carried? The FAitself, which has so far not allowed Facebook to start implementing its "Libra" currency project, indirectly shows what the expected effects are. Facebook and its apps (Messanger) have 2.7 billion in assets. This shows the capacity of private currencies issued by big tech companies to compete with official currencies. In September, the European Commission proposed regulation related to the issuance of stable coins. which will promote them on a huge scale. Let's go back to Bulgaria  by the end of the year the deadlines of the various moratoriums on servicing loans introduced because of the blocking of business life by anti-kovide measures are expected to expire. What are the prospects for the regulatory treatment of loans after the moratoriums? It is known that until now citizens and companies have requested a moratorium on their loans worth about BGN 10 billion  about BGN 8 billion and about 2 billion per individuals. What will be the quality of the loans will then be seen in time. For now, the banking system has high capital adequacy, a surplus of capital andcould take pressure, if some of these loans become non-performing. The real effect of the co-operation on the banking system will occur in the spring of next year. At the end of the summer there was an increase in capital adequacy in the banking system as a result ofsome regulatory changes... Two measures affected capital adequacy. The first is the so-called " quick fix, which came into force at the end of June and reduced risk weights for certain exposures. The second measure was the actual increase in the capital of the banks under the radi ban imposed by the BNB for the payment of dividends. This measure ensured that an additionalBGN 1.3 billion should be retained in bulgaria's banking system. In these new conditions, how wide is the field of action for Bulgarian banks when it comes to the providence of bad loans and possibly the need for new capital? The true manifestation of the problem will be seen early next year. There is a very strong factor that gives banks a big buffer  our requirement even before the crisis to hold morecapital. A "quick fix" has created additional space for them to come under pressure from an increase in bad loans. Meanwhile, they have begun to increase their provisions. What stages can you highlight in the integration of the Bulgarian banking system intothe European Banking Union? Our participation in the Single Supervisory Mechanism has many dimensions. The first is that so-called significant banks pass under the direct supervision of the ECB. The remaining, less significant banks remain under the supervision of the BNB, but the ECB has theright to adjust the supervisory actions in respect of those banks. It is important to clarify that the supervision of banks, even significant ones, will take place under our legal framework and our regulations. All the measures that we have taken so far continue to operate unless significant banks feel that they need to change. If there are such changes, the BNB will have to decide whether to change similar measures for less significant banks. In what directions do you expect the relationship between banking groups and their subsidiaries in Bulgaria to develop? Cross-border banks have natural incentives to want to optimise their capital and costs. Now that the supervisory authority is one, such incentives will increase. Time will tell what behaviour of cross-border banks and banking groups we will see. Will the BNB lose the ability to impose bans on dividend distribution and can the ECB ask the BNB not to impose such measures? The measures currently in force in Bulgaria are in force for all banks, but from here on on, this type of measures for significant banks are no longer the power of the BNB. And can the ECB at some point ask for their cancellation? All decisions of the BNB adopted before 1 October are in force until they are revised by a new act. Joining the Banking Union and ERM-2 did not lead to the automatic increase in the credit rating, how do we understand this? This is no surprise, as experts know that there has never been a mechanical link between participation in the exchange rate mechanism and the increase in the credit rating. Too many factors influence a country's credit rating. The European Central Bank is reviewing its monetary policy strategy. What are the main conclusions reached at this time? The ECB announced a review last December, suspended it because of the crown crisis and has now resumed it. The ECB's monetary policy objective is defined as achieving price stability with inflation on an annual basis close but below 2 percent. It is obvious that in the last 6 years this goal has not been achieved. A similar review has already been carried out by the US Federal Reserve. A weakness of both the ECB and the Fed is that they do not analyse the extent to which the failure to meet the inflation target is due to factors beyond their control. It is possible that lower inflation is due to deep structural factors, respectively  to expect this inflation to continue for a long time. Such factors arean ageing population, a decrease in labour productivity, china's changing role in the global economy. On the other hand, failure to achieve the target serves as an argument for continued monetary stimulus on the part of central banks. But if there are structural factors thatprejudge low inflation, then these persistent stimulus poses risks. The Fed's decision, for example, has caused a lot of controversy. which creates very great uncertainty in what period of inflation will be targeted. Therefore, the leading thing in the discussions is that such an approach is too vague and risky and probably will not work. We are yet to see what the ECB will share in its review. There is an incentive to choose something close to the Fed, but given the criticism of this approach, I expect it will rather refrain from it. PAGE \* MERGEFORMAT 5

Title: Interview for capital newspaper, 19 March 2021.
text: Interview of Mr. Kalin Hristov, Deputy Governor of the BNB, Managing Management "Issue", for capital newspaper, 19 March 2021 CENTRAL BANKS ARE ALREADY HOSTAGE TO GOVERNMENTS In its December forecast, the BNB bet on 3.7% GDP growth for 2021. Last week, the NSI published preliminary data on GDP in 2020, confirming our latest forecasts. We are currently working on our new quarterly macroeconomic forecast, which will be published in April. If we view vaccination as a major impetus for normalisation and acceleration of economic activity, there is no reason to believe that it will have a rapid economic effect. The vaccination process in bulgaria, as we see, is slow mainly due to the shortage of vaccines observed globally (but especially in the EU ). before the coronavirus. The rise in government bond yields in developed markets has raised concerns about inflation. Do you expect central banks to tolerate higher levels in the coming years? Causation is reversed  inflation expectations drive bond yields. The changes in yields reflect the usual role for financial markets to react ahead of time. Another isthat inflation expectations are justified in the large-scale fiscal stimulus of governments financed by central bank purchases of government securities. expectations of an increase in inflation would be normal. There are also deeper structural factors for such expectations. For example, the current trend of deglobalisation, including the rupture of cross-border supply chains, will increase production costs. This will inevitably be carried over to the final prices of many goods. Also at a global level, the population is ageing, which meansshrinking the workforce. This will also increase the cost of labour and hence the outputs and services. This process is already clearly visible in Central and Eastern Europe, including Bulgaria. This process is accelerated by higher mortality rates and higher birth rates in Bulgaria over the past year. higher rates than labour productivity, which will also have a pro-inflation effect. Other factors for expected inflation come from the energy sector. The political pressure to transition to the so-called "no-fly zone" has been mounting. a green economy may prove pro-inflation to the extent that the exploitation of renewable energy sources can come at a morecostly time compared to traditional energy production. Global central banks play a key role in managing inflation expectations. There are currently signals that the Fed isinclined to tolerate a rise in government bond yields and higher rates of consumer price growth. purchases of their bonds. However, if market participants adjust their inflation expectations substantially, due to some of the factors I have listed, including if they expect an economic revival after the pandemic, the ECB's continued massive purchases of bonds will start to hamper inflation expectations. Is monetary policy in danger of becoming a long-term hostage to soaring government debt because of measures to tackle the pandemic? Tolering slightly higher inflation may also be aimed at solving the problem of government debt. Any inflation eases the servicing of nominally fixed liabilities. we've had for a few decades is already turning around. What long-term effects will it have? Central banks with a monopoly on monetary supply have historically been constrained in creating money from a rule relating to the exchangeability of their money against a certain amount of gold. This rule, known as the "gold standard," was often repealed during wars when central banks financed government spending through a cash issue. The collapse of the Bretton-Wood currency system in 1971 marked the end of suchexplelicable rules restricting central bank monetary supply. Today, many imagine that this independence is a historical given, but this is not the case. The phenomenon is cyclical. For example, the shock of the global financial crisis of 2008, which now, during the coronal pandemic, has intensified, leading to a new need to finance hugegovernment spending. The logical outcome of a comeback and a significant acceleration of inflation, which we have already talked about, will be an occasion for restoring the independence of central banks. Bulgaria seems to be doing well against this backdrop with low debt and record low GS yields. But do you expect budget deficits to be easily reducedas the pandemic subsides? Bulgaria really stands well fiscally due to its unique macro-construction of the currency board, which sets monetary and price stability and prevents the possibility of fiscal dominance over monetary policy. The currency board is aninstitution for a strong budget constraint and helps to conduct prudent fiscal policy - only temporary budget deficits in a downward economic cycle with a subsequent aspiration for balancing. And the level of yield of Bulgarian government securities is the result, above all, of THE ECB's policy, the effects of which are carried over quickly and strongly in our country through the mechanism of the currency board. Therefore, the yield levels are not indicative, but the spreads of our sovereign debt relative to the price of germany's debt, which is fiscally the most stable country in the euro area. Reducing budget deficits after the pandemic will depend on what the long-term effects of it will remain. Certain policies of increased welfare payments have also been adopted, which will be more difficult to stop. But if the reduction of budget deficits in Bulgaria will not be easily achievable, it will be almost impossible in some countries in the euro area, such as Italy and Greece. Howmany major shocks can we expect when countries (and Bulgaria in particular) start withdrawing fiscal measures to support the economy and households? The various aid and relief was a consequence of the state's own restrictions on business to limit the spread ofcoronavirus. In practice, however, the picture willbe more complex in so far as, for example, there will be sectors that will be affected and depressed long-term. Last year, banks reported significant growth in provisions, with no rise in bad loans yet seen because of the moratorium. Do you think the risk is adequately covered, or will the performance of the banking sector come under even more impairment pressure this year? In principle, the economic downturn leads to a deterioration in the quality of bank assets. In 2020, this usual relationship was violated by the moratorium. Banks, understanding well that the moratorium delays over time but does noteliminate a realized level of credit risk, have been actively - I would say ahead of time - over the past year. At this stage, before the expiry of the moratorium, it cannot be said to what extent the provisions are sufficient. However, given the BNB's policy of requiring high levels ofcapit al in banks, especially through capital buffers, the residual credit risk in the system is most likely adequately covered. However, if we go back to the theme of inflation, a possible rise in yields on sovereign debt and market interest rates could lead to a scenario where banks will suffer an interest rate risk . After the previous crisis, clearing the balance sheets from bad loans was getting quite smooth. Now with changed regulations and a more active secondary market, how long do you expect it to take? The crisis of 2008-20 09 is not a good benchmark foranalysing the current situation, as it has had a completely different nature of its genesis. For example, it is not yet known which sectors and to what extent they will now find themselves permanently affected and will have difficulties after the pandemic. This makes it difficult to forecast the secondary market for assets expected to be transferred from such sectors. However, one thing is a definite fact if we compare with the previous crisis  today banks have a much higher capacity for managing NPLs. The current situation of negative interest rates, abundant liquidity, economic shock and continued growth in lending risks underestimating the risk in the banking system. What levers does the BNB have to prevent or mitigate this? The ECB's policy of negative interest rates and massive asset purchases on the balance sheet of the Eurosystem logically leads financialmarket participants to liquidate low-risk positions and take positions in riskier investments. The shock of the pandemic has led to a further strengthening of the stimulus policy of the central bank of the euro area. The scale of its effects is already so great that the prices of financial assetsare largely detached from the assessment of their risk. The instruments of the BNB for maintaining financial stability have been well known and implemented in Bulgaria for years. Since Bulgaria's accession to the Single Supervisory Mechanism, the macro-supervisory toolbox remains within our national powers. very high levels of banks' capital buffers. Over the past year, we have also implemented additional measures, including requiring banks to further strengthen their capital position by holding back accumulated profits rather than allocating them through dividends to shareholders. How much in this environment of tightening regulations does competition from fintech companies affect banks' performance? Yes, since 2008, at global level, banks have gone through a cycle of strong tightening of regulations. This not only limitedthe flexibility of banks, but they began to generate significant (so-called compliance costs) to comply with ever-increasing and complex regulatory and regulatory requirements. At the same time, regulations have been liberalised, allowing banks to enter traditional banking areas such as payments. A number of non-banks focused on offering high-tech financial products and services, having started with payments, are already expanding their activities in areas, until recently typical mainly for banks, such as lending. Rising regulatory costs and competition from non-bank financial institutions are putting a powerful combined pressure on banks' financial performance. Ideas about a European bad bank or a network of national bad banks are circulating in the EU. The European Commission has such a proposal. In the course of its discussion, the view prevails that such an idea is largely contrary to the direction of development of the last decade of European legislation relating to bankrestructuring and. A guiding principle of EU-level regulation built in response to the previous global financial crisis is for troubled banks to apply different resolution instruments withoutrecourse to public support. For example, there is an instrument called asset separation, in the application of which assets can be transferred from resolution banks to asset management companies. It is thereforeunclear what the creation of special "bad banks" would bring  apart from the risk of undermining the EU-built bank resolution regime by returning to using public resources to support troubled banks. Could the current crisisspeed up the completion of the Banking Union with a single deposit guarantee scheme, or, on the contrary, with the risks rising, will the votes against intensify? Deposit guarantee is essentially a fiscal issue. There is simply no national fund anywhere,with the order covering 100% of covered deposits, and therefore governments always stand as a potential fiscal guarantor. However, we see how the current crisis is worsening the unsustainable fiscal positions of many European countries. For these reasons, it is unlikely that they will agree on a pan-European deposit guarantee scheme. Another reason not to be optimistic in this direction is that merging fiscal commitments between Member States  which single deposit guarantee implies  would require a change in the EU legal framework. The latter requires strong political will for even stronger centralisation in the EU and the transfer of national resources  something which, especially today against the background of the ongoing pandemic crisis, seems increasingly difficult to defend at national democratic level. What are your impressionsof the first half year of "close cooperation" with the ECB? First impressions are distorted by the fact that 2020 was dominated by the shock of the coronavirus. Today, our focus remains on our macro-prudential measures related to further strengthening the capital and liquidity position of the banks. These measures, including the approval of the moratorium proposed to the BNB by the Association of Banks in Bulgaria, fall within the perimeter of supervisory sovereignty, which remained preserved after the entry into the Single Nadzo Ren Mechanism. In fact, over the past year, the supervisory priorities of the BNB have coincided with those of the ECB itself. For example, in relation to the new risks, the ECB recommended that the large banks in the euro area refrain from distributing dividends, since the BNB has alreadyintroduced a measure in a similar direction. In the context of the pandemic situation, the BNB limited on-the-spot supervisory inspections, which also delayed the manifestation of specific new effects of joint supervision in close cooperation with the ECB. Of course, I must stress that in recent monthsthe volume of coordination and integration work in the BNB has increased due to our participation in the activities of the Single Supervisory Mechanism related to banks and banking groups throughout the euro area. Do you share the view not to stay in ERM II for long, what are the risks and benefits and arethe deadlines realistic? The participation of the Bulgarian lev in the ERM II exchange rate mechanism is based on the mechanism of our exchange rate board. Therefore, practically participation in ERM II can continue indefinitely and without creating risks for the Bulgarian economy. Under the EU accession treaty, Bulgaria has an obligation to introduce the euro. However, any sovereign state has been left with the right to decide when it would bethe best time for it to abandon its national currency. they had. The same countries today remain with the most unsustainable fiscal indicators and are the most vulnerable. Therefore, the deadline for Bulgaria's accession to the euro area should be a consequence of the assessment of our preparedness (structural and not only nominal according to maastricht criteria) but also from our expectations for the future evolution of the euro area itself. However, you yourself have argued that the Banking Union is not a reasonable option for non-euro area countries as they are asymmetrically treated. Isn't it better then to shorten this period to the maximum? From the management of the bank we have really pointed out this asymability. I fully agree with you that the right approach requires risk balance analysis and assessment of benefits and negatives. Such an analysis is especially necessary when it comes to solutions with long-term effects for the country and processes that are irreversible or at a huge cost for reversibility in the future. An indicative example is the globally discussed balance of risks associated with and use of vaccines against coronavirus. These analyses represent a reasonable approach before decision-making, which must be based on technical and scientific arguments and not ideologically. In the above-mentioned horizon, this risk assessment must be carried out.

Title: Interview for the CAPITAL newspaper, 29 November 2021
Subtitle:
KALIN HRISTOV: IN THE NEXT THREE YEARS IT IS
MORE AND MORE LIKELY THAT INFLATION WOULD REMAIN HIGH
text: Interview with Mr. Kalin Hristov, BNB Deputy Governor in charge of the Issue Department, for the CAPITAL newspaper, 29 November 2021 KALIN HRISTOV: IN THE NEXT THREE YEARS IT IS MORE AND MORE LIKELY THAT INFLATION WOULD REMAIN HIGH The BNB Deputy Governor for the CAPITAL newspaper on the price pressures, the interest rate levels, and the recovery of the economy Kalin Hristov is a Deputy Governor of the BNB. From 2009, for two consecutive terms of office, he was in charge of the Issue Department. His second term of office expired in October 2021 and Mr. Hristov will continue to hold this position until Parliament elects a new Deputy Governor. He spent his entire career at the BNB where, until 2009, he was Advisor to the Governor of the Central Bank. In 2013 he was Minister of Finance in the caretaker government of Mr. Marin Raikov. Mr. Hristov will be a keynote speaker at the Banks and the Business Conference organised by the CAPITAL newspaper on 2 December 2021. The big question that is of interest to all now is whether the current high levels of inflation will be temporary or will persist. The BNBs projection is that inflation will fall next year, but what are these expectations based on, and do you see any risks that it might stay higher than expected? In the long term, any high inflation is always temporary. Within the next 3 years it is more and more likely that inflation would remain at the current high levels. According to an estimate of the BNB, imported goods and services account for about 42% of the consumption in Bulgaria, which means that the inflation in the country is highly influenced by what is happening on international markets. For this very reason, the profile of inflation in the BNBs projection is also largely determined by the market expectations of the dynamics of commodity prices, such as petrol, food, and metals. Technically, the expectations in the BNBs projection as to how commodity prices would change are based on assumptions defined by the European Central Bank (ECB). This year, the assumptions that we have been receiving from the ECB understate the global inflation developments in the short term and suggest stabilisation of, or even decrease in, international prices in the medium term. Such dynamics of commodity prices contributes to the ECBs ideological position that the acceleration of inflation is temporary and monetary policy stimuli need not be withdrawn. We, however, think that these assumptions do not sufficiently reflect the price effects of the structural turmoil caused by the pandemic, combined with the continuing strongly stimulating monetary and fiscal policies in spite of the faster than predicted rebound in global economic activity, the labour shortage, the restructuring of global supply chains, as well as the indirect effects on inflation of the increased energy prices. For this reason, the BNBs macroeconomic projection of September 2021 paid closer attention to rising inflation risks compared to the baseline scenario, illustrated by the strong asymmetry in the fan chart for inflation. The differences between our views and the ECBs assumptions on the trajectory of main commodity prices in the medium term are subject to discussions within the Bank about the approach used to make the projection of inflation in Bulgaria, and it will be modified as soon as in our Decembers projection. In addition to the external factors, we anticipate that the internal factors related with the strong consumption, the increase in the labour costs and other production costs, especially following the energy price rise, would continue to have an inflationary impact in the medium term. How would, in your opinion, inflation and inflationary expectations affect the behaviour of businesses and individuals and their willingness to invest, consume or make savings respectively? Do you expect any significant changes in interest rates and in the volumes of deposits and loans? Higher inflation limits the consumption of households. The current price rise reflects to a large degree the higher prices of goods and services which are characterised by low price elasticity and cannot be substituted in the short term (e.g. transport fuels, electricity, heat, essential foodstuffs). Therefore, we expect that higher inflation would limit the real disposable income of households, which would induce a slower growth in the real private consumption in the country. This effect would be partially compensated by the available mechanisms for indexation of certain social payments (such as pensions), and also by the demands of the employed for indexation of wages. Under the conditions of growing shortage of labour and negative demographic trends, employees bargaining power would probably be increasing which would strengthen the link between inflation and wage growth. Companies capacities to index wages, by sectors, vary according to the degree in which final demand is restored after the negative shock of the initial spread of the pandemic in 2020, and according to the possibilities of streamlining production costs considering the substantial rise in the international prices of main commodities. Companies increasing production costs (the costs of labour and raw materials) may restrict their investment capacities. We may expect that next year deposit interest rates would again stay close to 0%. In a context of rising inflation, real deposit interest rates are becoming increasingly negative, which encourages economic agents to seek alternative forms of saving. Interest rates on new time deposits have followed a steady downward trend, with negative interest rates already observed for corporations, and close to 0% for households, over the past year and a half. These trends reflect the ECB's maintenance of negative interest rates for a prolonged period of time and its highly stimulating monetary policy, which due to the currency board regime has an impact on interest rates in Bulgaria. Another important factor is the high liquidity in the banking system and the growing inflow of attracted funds. Deposit interest rates can be expected to remain close to 0% in the coming year as well. At the same time, since 2021 banks have started to introduce a custodial fee for funds above a certain amount, with some of them lowering the threshold above which the fee applies. However, the alternatives for investing spare funds, especially by households, are relatively limited, which is why deposits continue to grow at a high pace and we do not expect this pace to slow down significantly. A potential limiting factor on deposit growth is precisely the custodial fee introduced this year for funds above a certain amount and the likely increase in the number of banks that charge such a fee, as well as lowering the threshold above which the fee is applicable. Among the few possible alternatives is investing in residential properties, as the last year has seen an increase in demand on the property market and a growing volume of transactions, which has also led to an increase in the rate of growth of house prices while supply is lagging. Factors further supporting demand for housing include rising labour income, improving household sentiment, and historically low interest rates on housing loans, which are also currently negative in real terms. On the supply side, banks have significant liquidity resources, and over the past two quarters they have also reported a loosening of housing lending standards following their significant tightening in 2020. Trends in lending are upward, with stronger growth in credit to households and especially in credit for house purchases. Growth in corporate loans is significantly lower, due to more constrained demand and the banks more conservative policies, as well as banks write-offs and sales of loans. The NSI has reported a GDP growth for the third quarter of 2021 which is weaker than expected and also compared to other EU countries. What are the reasons for this slowdown in the recovery, which does not seem to correspond to other economic indicators? According to the current seasonally adjusted data, the recovery of economic activity to the pre-COVID-19 pandemic levels is slower in Bulgaria compared to the average level in other EU Member States. In the third quarter of 2021, the recovery of economic activity in Bulgaria reached 96.7% of the level in the fourth quarter of 2019, compared to an average recovery of 99.8% for the EU Member States and 99.5% for the euro area Member States. The question of why the recovery observed in Bulgaria is weaker has two dimensions. The first dimension is purely technical and relates to the accuracy of the currently available statistics. The current NSI data for the third quarter of 2021 are still very preliminary, and the picture may possibly change in the future with the publication of the final data. The NSI publishes the flash estimates only on the basis of seasonally adjusted data, whose time series back to 2000 were substantially revised on 18 October this year. With the new data from the beginning of the year, there is a significant difference between annual growth according to seasonally adjusted and unadjusted GDP data, with the unadjusted data, which are the primary source of information, signalling a faster recovery in GDP and correlating more closely with the higher frequency conjunctural indicators. This largely explains why current seasonally adjusted GDP data do not correspond well to other economic and conjunctural indicators available for Bulgaria. This issue is discussed in detail in the forthcoming issue of the BNB Economic Review. The second dimension is related to country-specific factors that limit the economic recovery. Here we can distinguish factors such as the political cycle in the country, which limits the amount of public and private investment, as well as the higher share in the economy of the tourism sector compared to the average for EU Member States. The recovery of activity in the tourism sector is lagging behind other sectors, and this was further affected by the deterioration of the epidemiological situation in the country in the third quarter of 2021.

Title: Speech before the conference "Banks and Business", Sofia, 2 December 2021.
text: Speech by Mr. Kalin Hristov, Deputy Governor of the BNB, managing director "Issue", before the conference "Banks and Business", Sofia, 2 December 2021. ECONOMY AND BANKS Dear ladies and gentlemen, I thank the organizers for the opportunity to present again the views of the Bulgarian National Bank on the development of the economy and the role of the banking sector in the current and next year. I will start by recalling the baseline conditions in 2019 before the discovery of the new coronavirus and its spread. The growth of the global economy, and especially the euro area economy, was slowing. This was happening against the backdrop of trade disputes between the US and China and Brexit, but the big factor in the economic slowdown was the practical exhaustion of the effectsof highly stimulating monetary policy in the euro area, together with the lack of opportunity for governments through fiscal policy to provide additional economic stimulus. This has also been combined with the over-resupply of the problems in euro areacountries d0 the over-indebtedness of many governments there, the growing indebtedness of the corporate sector, falling productivity in virtually all countries and an ageing population as an additional factor limiting potential growth. Bulgaria's economy was in a good cyclical state in terms of having relatively high growth and employment. The shrinking workforce, a growing economy and strong demand in the labour market in turn have led to wage and consumptiongrowth. In early 2020, the pandemic triggered an unknown type of economic crisis. the slowdown in economic growth has proved to have been initiated by the policyof the right, which is very unusual historically. When the government imposes restrictions on the economic activity of individual private agents, households or companies, the latter naturally develop an expectation that the government, again through another type oflytic, must propose compensation measures. It happened just like that d0 the reaction of economic policy (fiscal, monetary and supervisory) took the form of different compensation mechanisms. In the US, instead of a subsidy policy, they provided direct aid to the population. Fiscal incentives around the world also included temporary reductions in indirect taxes, government guarantees and rescheduling of obligations to the state. Monetary policy, given negative interest rates in the euro area, uses the balance sheet of central banks as a key tool. They were directly buying up government debt, which financed the fiscal stimulus. This was done in countries with ultra-high levels of sovereign debt. The stimulus policy also included providing unlimited liquidity to commercial banks at a subsidised price and a significant decrease in the quality of benefits. Supervisory and regulatory policy in the banking sector included a temporary reduction in the risk weights of certain exposures in order to save capital, with the expected accumulation of new credit risk and a deterioration in the quality of creditportfolios. Fiscal and monetary policy stimulus has traditionally been made in economic civing phases when we have a decline in demand in theeconomy . impact on demand. This led to a postponement of consumption and investment, as well as a build-up of savings in economies (savings that were later at the heart of the rapid recovery in consumption). The aim of the incentives was not to have an immediate effect on demand, but to maintain confidence in the economy and financial markets and to give governments access to finance. The closure of economies was conceived as a one-off and temporary measure until better information and understanding of the nature of the virus is obtained and until a vaccine is created that protects against infection. However, we see the dynamics in the development of perceptions of the role of vaccines. , but to ensure less consequences of infection and reduce pressure on the health system and mortality. Along with this evolution in understanding the purpose of the vaccine, combined with the accessibility of vaccines globally, as well as the propensity of the population to get vaccinated, there has been a cyclicality and seasonality in the spread of the virus, as well as government measures to limit its spread. In Bulgaria, the BNB and the government have also taken concrete measures in response to the situation caused by the new coronavirus. Bnb's measures included the following: Prohibition of distribution ofunallocated profits from previous years in order to strengthen the capital base; Restrictions on the level of concentration and quality of assets in which banks can invest their liquid assets; Cancellation of the envisaged increases in the countercyclicalca pital buffer; A private moratorium proposed by the Association of Banks in Bulgaria on payments on bank loans has been approved by the BNB Management Board. With regard to the banking system, a significant proportion of banks' credit exposures have been placed under a moratorium. The ratio of approved volumes to total credit exposure amounts to 6.6% for households and 16.7% for businesses. This has helped keep the level of non-performing loans unchanged. combined with reduced demand for credit, resulted in a 52 per cent reduction in the bank system's profit level in 2020. Fiscal measures of the Bulgarian government included the following: Subsidisation of employment (e.g.under the so-called Programme 60/40); Payments to pensioners (initially declared as one-offs, subsequently becoming permanent); Health care costs, including frontline medical staff; Guarantee of loans by the Bulgarian Development Bank; Tax breaks (reduction of the VAT rate for certain goods and services, extension of the deadlines for the addition ofcorporation tax and increase the amount of tax relief for persons). What kind of economic recovery have we seen in this environment? The economic recovery, which started to take place after the second quarter of 2020, did not have the profile that most governments and central banks expected. There was a rapid recovery in demand (mainly consumer demand and global trade) and almost no recovery in private investment. On the other hand, supply has not recovered so quickly, which has led to an adjustment of the economy through price increases. There are many explanations for the slow recovery in supply: The clich8ed destruction of supply and supply chains has ledto a slower, more expensive supply of intermediates and final consumer goods; Not only did trade disputes between China and America not ease, but the pandemic exacerbated them. The European Union is also discussing a more isolationist policy, evoicunder the concept of "strategic sovereignty"; The contraction of the workforce, which even before the pandemic was a long-term trend in advanced economies, China and Bulgaria, was strengthened by the pandemic with the decrease in labour marketparticipation a. An obstacle to the recovery is also the increase in energy prices, which is realized due to a number of factors, including the steps towards the so-called "green deal". In these circumstances, central banks have continued their stimulus fiscal and monetary policies from2020 and into 2021. The Bulgarian economy has a similar dynamics of recovery, which is characterized by the following elements: Main contribution of private consumption; Reimbursement of exports of goods, not services; Negative contribution of investment, including government investment, as a result of the political cycle; Wage growth (faster in the public sector given the political cycle); Slower recovery in employment and labour market participation; It is noted that in relative terms the amount of Bulgarian fiscal stimulus in response to the situation with the coronavirus is lower than other countries. According to bnb estimates, this stimulus in Bulgariais based on 3.2% of GDP in 2020 and 4.3% of GDP in 2021. In this environment, the important events and facts regarding the banking systemwere as follows: At the end of 2020, the moratorium was extended, but the effect of this proved negligible; The high level of saving has led to a further reduction in interest rates onborrowed funds in the banking system, with banks with market share introducing negative interest rates on deposits above a certain threshold. High liquidity has led to a roll-out of credit standards in the mortgage-backed consumer and homeloans segment and an increase in supply. In practice, all credit institutions compete in this segment; Rising incomes, as well as negative interest rates, have been an additional factor in increased demand for housing; Corporate credit was recovering very poorly due to low corporate investment, driven by ongoing uncertainty; The performance of the banks wasdetermined by a decrease not at the level of impairments and a recovery of profits in the banking system due to the lower costs of impairments and contributions to the Bank Resolution Fund and the Bank Deposit Guarantee Fund. BNB's policy included maintaining measures in terms of profit distribution and liquidity management. Accelerating borrowing at historically lowlevels of borrowing rates, rising inflation leading to very negative real borrowing rates, and accelerating the pace of house price growth have led to a change in the cyclical risk assessment and an increase by the BNB of the acticyclic capital buffer by 0.5 percentage points from October 2022. What to expect in 2022? Under the current conditions, the difficulty of defining a forecast for 2022 is understandable. A key question is what would be the profile of recovery of the global and Bulgarian economy. At the same time, this slowdown has been coupled with a significant acceleration in therate of inflation. Initially, central banks viewed this inflation as temporary. The latest developments are increasinglyrevealing many factors that will lead to inflationary pressures. Therefore, central bank monetary policy cannot remain in its current highly stimulating position (low interest rates and significant asset purchases). All leading central banks are heading towards ending securities purchases and starting a cycle of interest rate rises. which continues to maintain the thesis of the temporary nature of inflation. Title: Interview with Ms. Nina Stoyanova, Deputy Governor of the Bulgarian National Bank, Head of Banking Department, for bTV, 22 February 2022
text: Statement by Mr. Kalin Hristov, Deputy Governor of the BNB, Head of the Issue Department, at a round table on "Inflation and Economic Growth. Introduction of the Single European Currency in the Republic of Bulgaria  Benefits, Challenges and Risks", organized by the Budget and Finance Committee in the National Assembly, Sofia, 31 May 2022. FACTORS DETERMINING INFLATION IN BULGARIA Dear Mr. President, Dear Ladies and Gentlemen Members of Parliament, Dear colleagues, I am grateful for the opportunity to present the view of the Bulgarian National Bank (BNB) regarding the factors determining the dynamics of inflation in the country and the possible policies for its suppression in the short term and reduction in the medium term. In order to determine appropriate measures to limit inflation, it is necessary to understand its nature  which processes determine it and how they develop over time.  Global Inflationary Processes The current inflation is of the most painful and persistent type  it is the result of a combination of hard-to-resolve and deepening constraints on the supply of raw materials, goods and labor, persistent changes in global supply chains and unsustainable high demand caused by errors in the conduct of monetary and fiscal policy in major developed economies, including the United States and the euro area. The main part of the processes that determine inflation today began even before the spread of COVID-19. Four years ago, the main topic of discussion among fiscal and monetary policymakers was the state of the so-called secular stagnation, in which the economies of the United States and the euro area have fallen, and the retention of inflation in the major developed economies, including in the United States and Europe, at persistently low levels. This understanding was one of the reasons for the prolonged period of highly expansionary fiscal and monetary policy by governments and major central banks, including the Federal Reserve and the ECB, which was a major driver of the rise in financial asset and real estate prices. As a result of the continued failure to meet the inflation target, the Federal Reserve and the ECB launched a process of reviewing their monetary policy execution strategies at the beginning of 2019 and 2020 respectively. At the same time, the process of lasting change in the foreign trade policy of the United States, and hence in that of Europe, which began in early 2018, took place, which grew into the so-called trade war between the United States and China. This trade war triggered changes in global supply chains, leading to a sustained increase in companies' production costs. The spread of COVID-19 in early 2020 and the measures taken to contain it caused a very large shock both on the demand side (due to inability to consume and high uncertainty) and on the supply side (due to production closures and further disruptions in global supply chains). Central banks and governments have responded to these developments by undertaking ultra-stimulus monetary and fiscal policy measures, including massive purchases of government securities, the provision of long-term liquidity to commercial banks at negative interest rates, subsidised employment measures and direct transfers to households. These measures, combined with the gradual adaptation of economic agents to the restrictive measures, have led to a rapid recovery in the labour market and aggregate demand, while supply remains constrained due to ongoing bottlenecks in global supply chains. At the same time, monetary and fiscal policy remained ultra-stimulating even after the lifting of anti-epidemic measures, which led to unsustainably high demand for consumer goods and services, and financial assets. Since the beginning of 2021, a rapid and substantial increase in global inflation has begun, amid continued growth in consumer demand and rising prices of energy and non-energy raw materials. In addition, in August 2020 and July 2021, respectively, the Federal Reserve and the ECB completed the review of their monetary policy strategies, and defined new inflation targets that were essentially pro-inflationary in nature. In autumn 2021, continued high demand and a corresponding increase in energy prices contributed to a further acceleration of inflation, especially in Europe and in particular in the euro area. During this period, the Federal Reserve began to gradually withdraw its monetary policy stimulus, while the ECB continued to maintain its view that inflation is temporary and to impose the expectation that inflation will start to decline in early 2022 without the need for an increase in interest rates. Russia's invasion of Ukraine at the end of February 2022 and the strict containment measures taken in China due to the spread of the Omicron variant of the SARS-CoV-2 virus have created additional significant inflationary pressures globally, following the limited supply of energy and food raw materials amid still strong demand. In March and May 2022, the United States Federal Reserve raised the federal funds rate corridor by 25 and 50 basis points, respectively, to 0.75-1.00% and announced that it would undertake further monetary policy tightening at the next meetings. The ECB did not change key interest rates in the euro area and continued to carry out significant net asset purchases, albeit at a gradual pace compared to the end of 2021, signalling their cessation in the third quarter of 2022. As a result of these processes, inflation in the United States and the euro area reached very high levels. As of May 2022, annual inflation in the euro area, as measured by the HICP, was at an all-time high of 8.1% (the highest inflation recorded in Estonia (20.1%), Lithuania (18.5%) and Latvia (16.4%)).  Inflation in Bulgaria Bulgaria is a small and open economy. Accordingly, international prices of raw materials and commodities, as well as the ECB's monetary policy measures, have a significant impact on inflationary processes in the country. In the context of labor shortages, internal factors affecting inflation are also significantly amplified. After almost four years of deflation between mid-2013 and the end of 2016, followed by four years of moderate price growth (an average of 1.9% for the period 2017-2020), inflation in Bulgaria began to accelerate significantly from the beginning of 2021, and this process continues to this day. At the beginning of 2021, the acceleration in inflation was mainly imported in nature and was mainly driven by the rise in energy prices, which were recovering from the declines recorded in 2020 related to the negative effects of the COVID-19 pandemic. Within 2021, the strong recovery in global economic activity, the emergence of difficulties in global supply chains and the global shortage of certain production components further increased the upward pressure on import prices and inflation in Bulgaria. In the second half of 2021, international oil, gas and electricity prices rose significantly above their pre-pandemic levels, putting additional pressure on firms' production costs. While at the end of 2021 inflation was mainly concentrated in food and energy groups, price increases have spread to the HICP basket since the beginning of 2022, with the share of groups with a price growth rate above 5% rising from 37% in December 2021 to 70% in April 2022. Annual inflation, as measured by the HICP, amounted to 12.1% in April 2022 (compared to 1.9% in April 2021 and 0.0% in December 2020). The price increase was broad by component and reflected an increase in the prices of goods and services along the entire supply chain - from the prices of imported goods in the country, through producer prices in the domestic industry, and wholesale and retail prices. The most significant impact on these developments was the increase in energy prices (oil and natural gas) and food on international markets, the upward dynamics of which have strengthened significantly since the end of February 2022 as a result of the global supply shock caused by the war in Ukraine. Core inflation also accelerated, driven by spillovers from rising commodity prices, but also by strong household spending and increased unit labour costs. Graphic: Inflation on an annual basis and the contribution of the main groups of goods and services to it (%, etc.) Source: NSI, BNB calculations Firms' production costs continued to be under pressure from rising labor costs due to labor shortages, which stimulated firms to compete with each other on the basis of the wages offered. Labor shortages peaked before the pandemic, when 32% of companies in Bulgaria cited labor shortages as a limiting factor in their production activities. Although in 2020 the pandemic temporarily reduced firms' difficulties with staffing shortages on both the supply and demand sides, the available data suggest that shortages are rapidly returning to their pre-pandemic levels (26% of firms as of April 2022 indicated difficulties due to such shortages). Graphic: Companies citing labor shortages as a factor limiting their activities (% of all firms) Source: NSI, BNB calculations Even in 2020, when economic activity in the country decreased significantly due to the negative effects of the COVID-19 pandemic, the compensation per employee in total for the economy increased by 7.2%. The average growth of compensation per employee in total for the economy over the past 5 years (2017-2021) amounts to 8.8%, while that of real productivity per employee is 1.9% and inflation is 2.1%. This leads to an increase in unit labour costs for firms, with the ratio of compensation costs to gross value added for the economy as a whole rising from 49.4% in 2017 to 52.3% in 2021, thus approaching the average for EU countries. Graphic: Share of employee compensation in value added, % Source: Eurostat, BNB calculations Wage growth, combined with low nominal and negative real interest rates, is also a major factor for the rise in private consumption, which has been the main driver of economic activity in Bulgaria in recent years. For the period 2017-2021, the cumulative growth of real GDP amounted to 6.4%, with the contribution of private consumption being 11.2 percentage points. (cumulative growth of 18%). In 2021, the share of private consumption in total GDP amounted to 59.4% (an average share of 59.5% for the period 2017-2021). Under the influence of strong domestic demand, for the period 2017-2021, net exports had a negative contribution to real GDP growth. The cumulative growth of imports of goods for the last five years amounted to 18.1%, and according to BNB calculations, about 7.6 percentage points of this growth are imports for consumption. The growth in imports of goods and services was only partially offset by an increase in exports (cumulative growth of 2.2%). At the same time, investments in fixed capital decreased for the period 2017-2021 by 1.3%, as their contribution to the cumulative growth of economic activity amounted to -0.2 percentage points. In 2021, the share of investments in total GDP decreased to 16.6% (compared to 18.3% in 2017). Given the large-scale and significant increase in consumer prices, producer prices and the problems with labor shortages in Bulgaria and the rise in unit labor prices, there are significant risks of forming a spiral between inflation and wages, which will make controlling inflation much more difficult and slow, even in a scenario in which the prices of basic raw materials on international markets stop rising. Negative demographic trends and labor shortages will continue to put pressure on firms' production costs in the coming years. Long-term demographic projections suggest that the working-age population (15-64 years) will shrink by 9.1% by 2030 compared to 2021. At the same time, structural changes stemming from the war in Ukraine, the transition to carbon neutrality in the countries of the European Union and the stated intentions of these countries to reduce their dependence on energy imports from Russia are a prerequisite for the prices of basic raw materials to remain high in the medium term.  Economic policy conclusions Given the above factors and the structural features of the Bulgarian economy, inflation in the country can only be curbed through a combination of monetary policy tightening by the ECB, fiscal consolidation in Bulgaria and measures to overcome supply-side constraints, especially labour supply constraints. In view of the large share of private consumption in the structure of GDP, fiscal measures to support households should be limited to measures to support the lowest income households. Otherwise, fiscal policy measures to support all households will act pro-inflationary and may create risks for the formation of an inflationary spiral and undermining the sustainability of public finances. ____________
