Subtitle: Rumyana Dencheva, the 24 Hours: Would you like us first to clarify what KTB is, Mr Kostov? A systemically important bank under conservatorship or an investment scheme using depositors money to finance the projects of its majority owner? I ask you because both theses are circulating in the public space.
text: Interview with Mr Dimitar Kostov, BNB Deputy Governor, on pg. 13 of the 24 Hours, 19 September 2014 BNB: Decision on KTB is due by 20 November. And when it becomes clear that the bank is able to meet its obligations to clients Dimitar Kostov, BNB Deputy Governor: Those who want KTB to reopen immediately, are they really sure that we will not see a repeat of 19 June*. For its recovery we should find a way to balance the interests of depositors, shareholders and taxpayers. Rumyana Dencheva, the 24 Hours: Would you like us first to clarify what KTB is, Mr Kostov? d4A systemically important bank under conservatorshipd5 or d4an investment scheme using depositorsd5 money to finance the projects of its majority ownerd5? I ask you because both theses are circulating in the public space. Dimitar Kostov: I prefer simpler definitions. To my mind, this is a big bank in terms of the Bulgarian market, which was placed under conservatorship because the people who manage it could not cope with the depositorsd5 sudden mass desire to withdraw their money, and waved the white flag. It is true that during the first half of June this bank had liquid funds in the order of BGN 1.5 billion, and as of 17-18 June the funds were already around BGN 1 billion. Simultaneously the bank did not then have available government securities against which the BNB could provide it with temporary funding. I also have no information about them requesting state aid from the budget, although I too reminded them about this procedure. If we assume that KTB is a systemically important bank, can its instability affect the banking system? From now on the definitions d4a systemically important bankd5 or d4an investment schemed5, etc. are a question of collecting enough data and additional analyses. There are no direct implications for the system because the bank has no significant obligations to other banks, nor can it disrupt the operation of the payment systems in this country. The indirect effects could be identified after analysing a lot more factors and circumstances, including how events are covered by the mass media. Even during the week of 23 - 27 June we saw an attempt to provoke panic through means of mass communication. As for d4investment schemesd5, before passing judgement, I would prefer to wait for more data to be gathered, relying on the auditors and the law-enforcement authorities alike. d4The BNB cannot alone recover KTB because all proposed plans are based on state aidd5 is the signal that you have been sending out persistently. Will you explain what kind of state involvement you have in mind? The BNB being unable to recover KTB is not just a signal; it is a reminder that without the involvement of the state it is not going to happen. This bank needs most of all liquidity support. Only after the final asset assessment is available we will be able to evaluate the capital needs. In all cases d4KTB recoveryd5 means giving money d0 something the BNB may not do within its powers which are very clearly defined in the law. The legal provisions must be observed. But it does make a difference how much the money is and who gives it. Apparently d4recoveryd5 means, inter alia, achieving a balance of various interests. Depositors have their interests which differ across secured, guaranteed and unprotected deposits. Borrowers too have their own interests, which may differ depending on the type of loan they have obtained and on how their business is performing. Shareholders are strongly interested in both to preserve the value of their investment and to limit their liability. Taxpayers are undoubtedly concerned about what the money collected from them is spent on and if they would have to pay higher taxes. Letd5s not forget that a person, even though he or she does not at all use banking services, in practice pays the Treasury 35 stotinki out of each lev spent. It turns out that no one is unbiased, whatever the decision is. I could cite many more objective reasons for d4biasd5 towards one or another of the possible decisions. A socially acceptable balance of all these interests cannot be achieved without the involvement of all institutions of parliamentary democracy, i.e. not only Parliament and the government, but also the so called social partners and formal and informal non-governmental organisations. When you placed KTB under conservatorship, you promised that the conservators would say how much and what support would be needed for the bank to reopen. How much is it today, where will the financial resource come from, and is it available at all? No such promise has ever been made. At the time when the bank got into critical liquidity difficulties, suspicions of the loan portfolio quality began to spread around in spite of the data in the bankd5s reports. For that reason the conservators were instructed to organise an asset quality review as quickly as possible. Unfortunately, poor management of the bankd5s processes was found out. What do you mean by poor management? When a multimillion-lev loan has been granted, the bank should at least demand a quarterly financial statement and regular updating of the business plans and it should analyse this data. When a loan agreement requires some kind of collateral, the credit file must contain a document attesting that the collateral has been provided, and subsequently it must be revalued regularly. This is the reason why the auditors are not in a position to give an opinion about loans worth BGN 3.5 billion in a short period of time. russian Does the fact that they are not in a position to express an opinion imply that these loans are d4badd5? Missing data in itself is not a reason to claim that these loans are definitely bad, but is a sufficient reason for doubts, therefore the evaluation of assets is continuing. Besides, the questions d4how muchd5 and d4whatd5 is needed for the bankd5s d4recoveryd5 cannot be answered before having answers to the questions d4whend5 and d4howd5, especially when we are talking of liquidity support. Those who demand that the bank be d4openedd5 almost at once do not say why we may not expect a repeat of the 19 June events when nearly BGN 900 million was withdrawn in one day. Then our proposals to the Government and the political parties represented in Parliament were to see what answers could be given to the questions d4whend5 and d4howd5. However, both auditors and conservators are pretty slow? This is sending bad signals to everybody. The people having deposits and accounts are wondering d4Well, they have been unable to come up with a decision on a single bank for such a long time; and if something similar happened to the rest of the banks, what would we do then?d5 There is absolutely no delay in the asset assessment being conducted by the conservators and auditors. There too external appraisers are reviewing the quality of assets and, although the review is based on a limited sample, they have been working for 9 months now. Any attempt to do all the required work for a shorter period would be voluntarism, which we cannot afford. Is the BNB providing liquidity support to another bank outside KTB? Is there a resource left available out of the BGN 3.3 billion approved by the EC? In what form could it be used for KTB too? I ask because there are suspicions of d4double standardsd5. The BNB has not provided liquidity support. What the EC approved was a liquidity support scheme of the Government for Bulgarian banks d0 state aid. The BNBd5s assistance consisted of verifying that the bank and the restructuring plan proposed by it complied with the prudential requirements. That liquidity support scheme was notified to and approved by the EC on 29 June for the purpose of safeguarding the other banks against potential attacks similar to the one that occurred over the preceding couple of days. Therefore, this scheme may not be used in the case of KTB. If a state aid scheme is to be designed for this specific case, then a separate application for approval must be submitted to the EC, well-substantiated as compliant with the competition rules and conditions. Some have accused the BNB and banking supervision of not having done their job. How do you feel about these accusations? I accept them in their constructive part. This is why we have asked assistance through the European Banking Authority for a professional review of, and advice on, the applied banking supervision rules and procedures and for overall management of supervisory processes. We have approached the IMF and the World Bank asking them too to conduct such a review. We are also considering the possibility of organising a comprehensive external review of all banksd5 assets d0 just like the one running at the large banks in the European Union, and recently such reviews were carried out in individual member states. There are other accusations that BNB officials are heavily dependent on third persons. Mr Iskrov is going to sue Mr Vezdy Rashidov for such words. Do you or any of the others at the BNB feel offended? I understand Mr Rashidovd5s concerns about the savings resulting from his work and talent, but I absolutely cannot and do not want to understand the slanders. ____________ * On 19 June 2014, BGN 900 million was withdrawn from KTB in one day. And in order to curb the panic, the BNB placed the bank under conservatorship for a period of three months, reserving its right to extend that period later. --------------- ------------------------------------------------------------ --------------- ------------------------------------------------------------ 1

Title: Speech at the opening of the Banks and Business Conference
text: Speech delivered by the BNB Deputy Governor in charge of the Banking Supervision Department at the opening of the d4Banks and Businessd5 Conference organised by the Capital newspaper, Sofia, 24 November 2016 Ladies and Gentlemen, The asset quality review (AQR) and the stress test of the banks in Bulgaria is an event of importance for maintaining public confidence in the banking system and the development of banking supervision. Within 12 months a very complex process was organised, coordinated, controlled and completed. The task that the Parliament assigned to us covered all the 22 banks supervised by the BNB and operating in this country, except for branches. Apart from the consultant hired by the BNB, eight more consulting companies provided 22 teams. Altogether 900 people, all outside experts for the banks, were involved in this process. Around one third of them come from abroad because we required that all key processes and controls be run by people with practical experience in such an exercise. Forty people on average were involved per bank. By comparison, in the ECB-led asset quality review conducted in 2014, which covered the 128 largest euro area banks, the average number of people involved was 46. The technology is labour intensive and requires certain resources whatever the size of the bank under review. The review was carried out, following the ECBd5s methodology of 2014, with minimal adaptation so as to better match the real level of complexity of financial intermediation in our country and to better encompass the risks that we are facing. That adaptation did not change the conservative approach of the methodology and was communicated early enough not only to those involved in the process, but also to all who would be interested. In addition to the ECBd5s AQR standard methodology, the BNB requested the external consultants to examine the exposures in terms of connected persons and large exposures. The stress test was executed, following the EBA good practices that were applied to the EU banks stress test this year. We used macroeconomic scenarios founded on the data available at March this year, and the adverse scenarios were in conformity with the requirements for conservative simulation of plausible but very unlikely hypothetical trends. The development of the economy since then and the updated statistical information have shown that, in practice, the stress test has been executed with a higher level of conservatism than the initial assessments. The main finding from the asset quality review and the stress test is that the banks in Bulgaria have solid capital buffers; they follow sound asset valuation practices and are able to withstand unexpected adverse developments in the external environment, which, though quite unlikely, would have a significant impact on the banks. In brief, the conclusion is that the banks in this country are stable enough to keep our money. Two banks were identified to have depleted capital buffers, but these banks continued to meet the minimum requirements. We demanded that they provide plans for replenishing their capital buffers, with both reducing the risk of assets and expanding the scope of shareholders support. These capital plans are well under way. The results of the asset quality review and the stress test represent an external, standardised and conservative financial health check carried out at once in all banks. It is a good opportunity for us to make more precise and develop further the supervisory strategies for each bank, and for the banks to improve their risk assessment and management mechanisms, and, last but not least, it will help market participants to broaden the basis of their assessments. At the same time we should not forget that this is a financial health check at a certain point in time, and if we ignore the dynamics and trends, we could underrate the risks and challenges that we are up against. The risks to economic growth, the still weak investment activity and high levels of uncertainty inevitably affect financial intermediation. If we look at the last 18 months (from March 2015 to March 2016), we will see that savings were on the increase. The deposits of non-financial corporations and households with banks grew by BGN 6.6 billion, or by a little over 10 percent. On the other side of the balance sheet we see a reduction in loan portfolios, just a little though. For a year and a half they shrank by around BGN 600 million, or by around 1.2 percent. Of course, this does not mean that banks are staying idle. Statistics indicate that every month the banks grant nearly BGN 1.5 billion worth of new loans, and in some months it is even close to BGN 2.0 billion. This process takes a lot of work, but obviously what has been achieved cannot compensate for the repayments. As a result, the banking system is building high liquidity, which at the end-September 2016 reached over 37 percent, although in the meantime a part of the last 18 monthsd5 excess liquidity was aimed at decreasing the funds attracted by credit institutions. These trends suggest that there is insufficient creditworthy demand for loans. The situation is getting even worse by the high levels of loans where the borrowers are having varying degrees of difficulty repaying their debts to banks. In reality, the portion of loans that is certainly deemed to be a reliable source of incomes, i.e. performing loans, was 80 percent of the total portfolio both at March 2015 and at September 2016. This means that 6-7 percent of the assets that are supposed to be high-return assets are actually underperforming. In the above situation banks must make serious efforts to achieve results that would meet both the cost of capital and the future needs of capital support. For now the results are good. Last year the banking system generated return on equity of 9.3 percent, and this year it reaches around 13 percent. However, there are some temporary favourable effects due to the low interest rate levels on deposits as a result of the low and negative interest rates in the European financial markets. The current year result is also influenced by the one-off effect from the positive revaluations of VISA shares, approximately BGN 186 million. In the light of the main conclusion from the asset quality review and the stress test, namely that the capital position of banks at system level is stable, and in view of the existing circumstances often comes the question as to couldnd5t the banks move to financing riskier venture and be d4more opend5 towards businesses, thus giving each other mutual support. The short answer is d4nod5, and the incomplete list of arguments is the following: 1. The macroeconomic environment will continue to be characterised by a high level of insecurity and low investment activity. That would limit the creditworthy demand for borrowing and respectively the possibilities for risk diversification. 2. The rise in interest rates on the international markets is inevitable and would most likely start happening already next year. That would increase the price of borrowing with the related effects on both banks and borrowers. 3. The regulatory environment will continue to be restrictive, i.e. requiring a higher level of coverage for assumed risks. The requirements for additional capital buffers for the banks of national systemic importance, which are the ten largest ones, will be announced next month. The minimum requirements for own funds and eligible liabilities are due to be set next year. 4. Since the beginning of 2018 the risk weights of Bulgarian euro-denominated government securities will start to gradually increase for banks using the standardised approach for credit risk, and for those using the standardised approach for market risk there will be a gradual increase of the capital requirements for the open positions in EUR/BGN. 5. Next year, banks will have to prepare for the adoption of the new IAS 9 for assessment of financial assets, which is more conservative than the current IAS 39. Assessments will have to be based on expected losses over the life cycle of a financial asset rather than on realised losses. All these expected trends and requirements will involve a substantial part of the own funds which may at present seem relatively free to engage in riskier venture. To sum up, I would say that if we put together the outcomes of the asset quality review and the stress test, and the facts of the current trends plus the regulatory requirements, we can conclude that bank mediation will continue to be a tough business. Of course, banks will continue to be dynamic and innovative. They will certainly develop and offer new products and services keeping up with and setting out market dynamics, and with the aim to support enterprises, including their restructuring and dynamisation. I would also briefly highlight the process of reforming and further developing banking supervision. On 4 November, a report on the performance of the tasks set out in the Plan on banking supervision reform and development was published. Although the asset quality review and the stress test have taken much of the time and efforts, a great deal of the envisaged measures have already been or are well into the process of being implemented. The actions towards enhanced governance model and internal organisation of banking supervision are a fact. Changes in coordination and consultation of processes with the BNB Governing Council have been regulated. The envisaged structural changes, the most important ones involving separating off-site supervision from on-site inspections, have been realised. The regulatory framework review has provided the base for follow-up actions in the development process. Priorities setting would also be facilitated by the financial system assessment that is being conducted by the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank. Based on the established and generally recognised methodology, the assessment will build on and detail the evaluations and recommendations contained in the report issued by these institutions last year for supervisory activities compliance with the so-called Basel principles for effective banking supervision. Along these lines, supervisory process development will target to incorporate to a maximum extent possible the established good practices. At the same time, we will participate in the processes of developing the supervisory practices in the European Union, particularly in the euro area. It is a fact that the vast majority of the Bulgarian banks falls into groups whose consolidated supervision is carried out by the ECB, and the Bulgarian banking supervision is a part of this process. We also aim to ensure uniform supervisory activities in terms of quality and level with regard to the rest of the banking system. The process of developing the supervisory activities can also be followed on the BNB websited5s growing section, which publishes the European Commissiond5s regulations and delegated acts, and the European Banking Authorityd5s guidelines of relevance for the supervisory process. In the context of the relations between the banks and businesses, I should point out that at the individual bank level the supervisory activities will stick to fulfilling its main objective, namely ensure compliance with the prudential requirements in the regulatory framework towards secure and sound governance of banks and of the risks they are or may be exposed to, and maintaining risk-adequate own funds. Furthermore, it is important to note that we aim this to be done uniformly and with equal measure of rigour across banks. In conclusion, if I may once again say that the banking business is not just mediation between savings and investments. In order to be able to lend, banks must ensure two other things at least, which are: safety of savings and the possibility of reliable and effective payments. Regulations and supervision, including the stress tests and asset quality reviews, are not a substitute for the market: they ultimately aim to ensure aligning the current business dynamics and innovation with these basic conditions so that banking mediation is stable and successful. I wish you fruitful discussions and I thank you for your attention.

Title: Interview in charge of the Banking Supervision Department
Subtitle: SUPERVISION KNOWS WHAT IS HAPPENING IN BANKS
text: Interview with the BNB Deputy Governor in charge of the Banking Supervision Department Dimitar Kostov on pages 46  49 of Capital weekly, 23 June 2017 SUPERVISION KNOWS WHAT IS HAPPENING IN BANKS What is the present condition of the banking sector almost a year after the asset quality review and the stress tests in 2016? BNB very regularly provides information about the banking system, which allows for following both the dynamics of bank intermediation and the main quality characteristics. The total volume of banks core activities  lending and attracting deposits  has increased by 5.7% since 2016, and by 6.9% in the first quarter of this year. The transaction business measured by the volume of payments also registered a 7.1% growth for the previous year. Compared to the GDP nominal growth of 4.6% and 6.5% respectively, these numbers indicate the banking system is performing its functions and role in the countrys economy. The capital adequacy indicators and the liquid asset ratio indicate the system has available good buffers for risk management purposes. What have you at the BNB learned from the review and were there any surprises for you, not found previously by supervision inspections? The asset quality review gave a lot both to the BNB and to the banks. First, this was an external expert view applying a unified standard  the ECBs methodology  with independent quality control ensured. The result is an enormous volume of information that is as useful to the supervision as to the management of each individual bank. It cannot be said any surprises were found. The existence of nonperforming loans and impairment was a known fact. The same applies to large loans and loans to related parties. What is important is that the magnitude of these problems was not such as to require government programmes, as has been the case in the recent years in a number of European countries. At the same time it should be noted these are not challenges unique for Bulgaria, but rather issues topical for the European Union as a whole. An important part of the guidelines adopted by the European Banking Authority (EBA) are aimed at establishing best practice standards of management and supervision of such issues. The BNB implements these guidelines which facilitates the development of risk management and supervision in banking intermediation. A suitable example are the guidelines on credit risk management and accounting of expected loan losses, that was adopted last month. After the review BNB made recommendations to two banks  FIB and Investbank, which included capital increases. To what an extent were the recommendations implemented and is the BNB satisfied with the measures pursued by the two banks? The exact wording of the recommendations was "recovery of the capital buffers". This is a much more complex task than simply increasing the capital, as it requires also mitigation of the risk in the existing portfolios and improving the credit risk management practices and procedures. The banks are going in the right direction and at a good rate, and they will naturally remain under enhanced supervisory monitoring until they reach sustainably good results. Is any interest expressed before the Banking Supervision by potential candidates to purchase FIB or any other bank? FIB has announced what measures they are pursuing. Supervision is only monitoring if they really implement them. They can have any indicative offers in September at the earliest. Generally, work is done methodically. When you took the position as Governor in charge of Banking Supervision, the launch of a supervision reform was announced. The task at hand was strengthening banking supervision. Is the reform complete and is supervision strengthened? How is it operating presently? What was mentioned actually was reform and development. The initial step  reform was pursued to create better organization, confidence and mutual control between supervisory processes. Their division into on-site supervisory inspections and off-site supervision was part of the reform. The other part  development is an ongoing process. It continues even now. At the time, it was announced that the reform and development plan will be implemented for a period of around a year and a half. It was announced in the context of the other task  conducting a review and assessment of the stability of the countrys financial system by the IMF and the World Bank (FSAP). The publication of the supplements to the main report made public on 22 May is pending within two weeks. As part of the ideas of these two parts of the overall report, we are pursuing specific activities. In the area of the regulatory framework we are taking into consideration the processes going on within the EU. EBA also has powers to assist further standardization and unification of regulations and supervisory practices. We have taken all this into account. Thus, in practice the process of development of supervision is continuing. This also corresponds to the fact banking intermediation is continuously developing. What is different now in the work of the supervision vis-a-vis the banks? What supervision inspections are conducted? A key aspect is that now on-site supervision inspection are conducted with the participation of more staff. In the recent month, there were additional appointments. On the other hand, there is strengthened ex-post control through the newly established off-site supervision directorate. Thus banks continue to be subject of oversight even after the findings made by the on-site inspections. There are changes in the regime of dialogue with banks. We have discussed with each bank their asset review results and what should be done. In March and April the Banking Supervision Department collected information from the banks how they have organized their preparations for the implementation of the new financial reporting standard 9 and at what stage they were. The goal is for the preparation process to flow in a more organized manner, as the implementation of the new standard is a challenge. Previously there was no such communication. The EBA guidelines and standards are also useful in facilitating the processes. In April EBA issued guidelines on communication with external auditors of banks with the purpose to achieve better synchronization between supervisory and accounting estimates. What is different three years after KTB? It was said then that the supervision was not fully aware what exactly was happening in the bank, because it submitted incomplete information. Are there such possibilities or situations, in which supervision is not fully aware what exactly is happening in a bank? There is practically no such possibility. Representatives of the audit profession also realized they have their respective liabilities. This mutual control is definitely something different. Is there any pressure exerted on the supervision in its work during supervision inspections in banks? No, there is no such pressure, but there is an issue with the expectation that supervision is doing its work, if it does not permit any bank failures, which is imposed upon supervision as a function even by the media, and this is the general perception of the public. Supervision has rather to identify bad practices which have to be penalized and corrected ... Would the close cooperation with the Single Supervisory Mechanism (SSM) help prevent practices of lending to related parties, etc. as those in KTB and FIB? This would not help in any way. Close cooperation does not mean on-site inspections by ECB, but rather off-site supervision. ECB does not conduct any on-site supervision inspections at banks. I am satisfied with our cooperation with EBA. There is very close cooperation within the ECB supervisory colleges and it covers large part of banks along the lines of banking groups. Will not SSM instil respect in banks  not allowing them bad practices or having a respect instilling effect on the domestic environment? The asset review itself has a much more respect-instilling effect. At that time all the banks felt themselves in the crosshairs and that had an impact on them. Can the situation with KTB be repeated and how would supervision react, how would the state react? Are you prepared now for a crisis with a bank? This is the subject of the so-called protection network, which is also included in the financial stability assessment made by the IMF. The financial system protection network covers deposit insurance, bank resolution  resolution plans, resolution activities, possible state assistance, if there is readiness to respond or not. We created a separate resolution directorate by a separate law of 170 pages. These are significant differences compared to the situation in 2014. At that time there were no written resolution rules  when and how it happens, through what means. EBA also issues standard guidelines further developing the resolution regime. Does the IMF assessment contain a recommendation regarding providing support in case of a liquidity crisis with banks? What is being done in this regard? This is one of the many potential elements of a protection network. It marks an idea existing as early as 1997, when the currency board was established  why should and how could such a mechanism operate. Since 1997, any time the issue of the need of a fiscal reserve was posed, this was one of the arguments  to act as a supplementing extension of the highly restricted abilities of the creditor of last resort under the currency board. Extending these abilities is a matter of economic policy. The Ministry of Finance should have the leading role, as this should be incorporated in the overall fiscal policy, and it should be clear there is a political decision to act in this way, because it is a matter of using public funds. To date, there is only a proposal by the IMF and the World Bank. The IMF also drew attention to the issue of lending to related parties. Does the supervision have the capacity to trace the chain of relatedness in lending, i.e. to whom the bank lends? It is a matter of large exposures. Businesses do not work with centralized structures, but rather with multiple satellite structures. On the one hand, relatedness is along the line of ownership  a common owner of borrower entities, which means a potential common risk. On the other hand, there is economic relatedness. In the recent couple of years, the focus on clearly regulating economic relatedness increased. EBA issues guidelines in this relation with the purpose of clearer rules for establishing such economic relatedness, because as it turns out formal relatedness along the line of ownership is not sufficient. Two companies can be absolutely independent in terms of ownership and be economically related which causes common risk. The IMF technical contain the idea to publicly announce the criteria and ways for determining relatedness. Is there anything that interferes with detecting relatedness in lending by the supervision? What can be done in this relation to increase supervisions capacity? The diversity of economic relations and structures is also great. Not always the banks themselves manage to find the relatedness. What I have in mind is fully purposeful lending to related persons, as was the case with KTB, and now this problem is mentioned for FIB, too. It is not clear what the analogy in this question is based on. In the final run, an exacting team was operating in FIB, who found no such analogies. In the case of KTB it became clear that supervision had no clear picture what was happening there. At that time, inspections were rare, this is true. On-site inspections were conducted by smaller teams. Are there presently any risks of repetition of such cases? No. That is why the asset review by external evaluators was useful. How would you answer to the critiques in the February report of the European Commission on the operation of the banking supervision in relation to the stress tests and asset assessment? The European Commission notes issues relating to the transparency and design of the review. At the same time, the Commission itself uses the results of the conducted review in its analyses and assessments. I believe the answer to the questions posed by the Commission is contained in the IMFs assessment of the asset quality review. According to it, it was made with a minimum deviation from the adopted methodology, with the required control of the quality of the review, with sufficiently clear independence of those conducting it. IMF confirmed the appropriateness of the small deviations from the ECB methodology owing to the fact the banking system here is not of the scale and complexity of the banks reviewed by the ECB. Two thirds of the types of operations included in the asset review there are not effected by banks in Bulgaria. EC has a recommendation to improve the method of evaluation of security... EC made recommendations to this effect as work with nonperforming loans, and it is a recommendation for the whole European Union. EU member states have assigned to the EC to develop rules for standardization, and the process is at the working group stage. But to point it out as our issue only is not quite correct. One of the many problems is the lack of an evaluators infrastructure with a reference data base, on the basis of which assessments are to be made. This was one of the subjects central to the asset assessment  exactly the securities were reviewed, informing banks of the ECBs requirements in this relation. For a security to be accepted as marked-to-market, there should be transactions effected with it. It can be done better, improvement is needed. But this is not something to be done by the state, but by the businesses themselves. Another key problem noted by the IMF, and by the EC, is the high level of nonperforming loans. For Bulgaria this level is 12.6%, while the average for the EU is around 5%. Yes, it is higher. But there was a big play with the measure of this indicator and how it is calculated. As an absolute value the volume is clear, and so is the definition. The detail is in the calculation method. What puzzled me is that at the time of announcement of the EC report there was a group of countries, which usually have no problem, but at the time of announcement the level of their nonperforming loans was around 10%. This is also a high level. When it is noted that the nonperforming loans are a problem, regretfully it is never clarified how big the problem is. They were a problem, indeed, and a disastrous one for Ireland, Greece, and Cyprus. For Bulgaria the levels are relatively high, but it is a fact this results in no bail-out agreements for the state. This is a problem which the banking system should be encouraged to work on. Banks themselves understand they should cope with it. In this sense, the level of nonperforming loans is a common problem for the whole EU. It is our desire, and we have the agreement of the IMF and the World Bank, to encourage banks to work on this problem. This will probably happen with the calibration of the regulations. EBA is also preparing standards in this relation, which we will take into consideration. Nonperforming loans are not by any means a disastrous problem for Bulgaria. Are there any banks which do not report correctly all their nonperforming loans and sweep under the carpet? They report everything correctly, and the asset review proved this. Will banks have any problems with the new accounting standard 9? Will they report more losses and a need of more provisions? At this stage there is not sufficient information to make a quantitative assessment. In its research the IMF uses as reference information an EBA study conducted last year for the enormous banks. It came to the conclusion of an average value of 10% of additional impairments, and in individual cases of a maximum value of existing impairment growth by 33%. In our case the existing levels of impairment are a priori by 2025 percent higher. BNB is monitoring, encouraging and assisting banks in their preparations for the implementation of the new accounting standard of assessment of financial assets. The existence of commercial bank Victoria after KTB was declared in bankruptcy dragged on. What is the BNBs view on its prospects? This question should rather be toward KTBs trustees in bankruptcy. BNB is following the process with enhanced supervisory attention. A long-term vision for the banks future is needed. The trustees in bankruptcy cannot provide a long-term vision. I can only add that a license is not a security, but rather a commitment and the capabilities for its implementation should be demonstrated and proved. PAGE \* MERGEFORMAT1

Title: Interview heading Banking Supervision Department
Subtitle: THE BANKS ASSETS REVIEW IS NOT A PANACEA AGAINST FAILURES
text: Interview with Mr. Dimitar Kostov, BNB Deputy Governor heading Banking Supervision Department, on p. 7-8 in the Banker Weekly, 14 July 2017 THE BANKS ASSETS REVIEW IS NOT A PANACEA AGAINST FAILURES Mr. Kostov, after the banks asset quality review was completed our society trusts that, in the next few years, cases such as those with KTB cannot be repeated. Could we say that these asset quality reviews are a panacea against bank failures and, if they truly have this effect, why not adopt legal rules to conduct them on a regular basis at least every three years? Definitely, it cannot be argued that the asset quality review is a panacea against bank failures. It is a complex and costly exercise, whereas the dynamics of the processes in a small and open market economy such as Bulgaria is so high that over the time needed to organise, conduct and analyse the outcome of the asset review multiple adverse trends might develop. Global experience over the recent seven-to-eight years has shown that this instrument is successfully used in identifying the consequences of the economic and financial crisis and in transferring supervisory powers, as was done during the introduction of the Single Supervisory Mechanism. Applying this instrument in our country was certainly of benefit to the supervision, the banks and the society at large; however the efforts and the resources involved should not be underestimated. Following the asset quality review, the BNB announced supervisory recommendations for a number of banks to take measures towards increasing their capital base. Could you specify how much of these recommendations relate to first Tier capital and how much to capital buffers? How do the individual banks follow these recommendations? The exact wording of the recommendations is capital buffer replenishment. Meaning that banks cover the minimum capital requirements and the case at hand concerns a task of a larger scale than merely increasing their capital. The requirement thus set involves: the need to mitigate the risk in the existing loan portfolio, including by providing additional collateral and reducing the non-performing loans through restructuring; it is also about selling or initiating insolvency proceedings for debtors, disposal of tangible assets acquired through sale of collateral, and optimisation of earnings, among others. Resolving these tasks would allow the relevant banks to formulate a stable long-term strategy for their market presence, the realisation of which would require that a capital support be sought. It is a proper direction and we can see that the banks, to which these recommendations were addressed, have taken organised actions using this approach exactly. From the moment you took over the mandate of a Deputy Governor in charge of Banking Supervision Department you started a large-scale reform in this sector of the BNB. What are the milestones of this reform? Which of the envisaged tasks have you succeeded to complete and what remains to be done? In early October 2016, an 18-month horizon plan to reform and enhance the banking activities was announced. All major tasks have been completed. Approval of supervision manuals is done by the Governing Council and every quarter the Council is updated on the macroprudential assessment of the banking systems condition and the supervisory process. A Consultative Council has been set up in Banking Supervision Department to assist the Deputy Governor in making decisions for consistency and coordination of actions. Off-site supervision is separated from on-site supervision with a gain in the number of staff. This way, the resources are expanded; the focus of supervisory activities is improved, and complementarity and reciprocal control within the single supervisory process is ensured. These reforms create the necessary institutional arrangement to enable the supervision development process, which must in effect be continuous. Now that the IMF and the World Bank have completed their assessment of the condition of the financial system in our country, we have a broad range of ideas and proposals for streamlining the supervisory activities which will be incorporated into a medium-term plan for further development. An immediate task is achieving better synchronisation between the applied supervisory assessment systems and the existing guidelines of the European Banking Authority concerning the process of supervisory review and assessment. The external findings show that the methodologies and methods applied in our country are overall good; however they should continuously be improved and developed to keep up with the ongoing banking business developments. A special attention was given on numerous occasions to the need for more in-depth assessment of the banks risk concentration to connected parties lending. Has banking supervision changed its practices for assessing these risks and in what direction? Basically, its about concentration risk, the risk of large exposures and the risk of insider loans. These risks are also subject to regulatory restrictions; however in most cases both the banks and the supervision need additional analysis and assessment of the potential dimensions of these risks, their interrelatedness, the risks of contagion, the management mechanisms, capital adequacy with regard to covering the adverse effects should such risks materialise, and a host of other related issues. If we take for illustration the risk of large exposures, given the existing 25% regulatory restriction and the capital-to-liquidity ratio of 1 to 10, a bank can meet the restrictions even if only working with 35-40 big customers. If these customers have the highest rating, then probably the risks would be under control. If not, such a business model cannot be sustainable although it meets this particular restriction. Actually, there is no legal framework in place which could spare the need for banks and supervisors to analyse and assess risks or to run adequate risk management systems. The FSAP review report of the IMF and the World Bank highlights the need for a special supervisory attention to resolving the nonperforming loans issue. The report notes that after adopting the risk assessment and provisioning rules under IFRS 9, which is due to become effective from the beginning of 2018, their volume would significantly increase. What supervisory measures does the BNB envisage in this direction and is there any need for changes in the legislation towards reducing the risks for banks related to such bad debts? The nonperforming loans issue obviously deserves analysis and assessment and is in the focus of attention EU-wide. For the Bulgarian banking system this is not a matter for concern. The relatively high levels of nonperforming loans are accompanied by higher levels of impairment (editors notes  green provisions) and high levels of available resources which cover potential risks in the unimpaired (editors notes  non-provisioned) part. Regardless of this, it is appropriate that banks be supported and encouraged to cope with the existing nonperforming loans and limit the conditions for accumulating new ones in the future. The development of processes is subject of monitoring by banking supervision both in terms of the results from the banks efforts and in relation to the regulatory and legislation initiatives within the European Union. Preparations to adopt IFRS 9 are also subject to monitoring. At present, the banks in general have not reached preparedness for definitive quantitative assessments with regard to the effects of applying this international accounting standard. We expect to receive more specific information about the possible impacts in September. The available data however do not give rise to concerns of significant impairments. Currently, the observation of the preparation process shows that banks will continue to comply with the supervisory criteria for determining the category of nonperforming loans. From 2018, the Bulgarian financial and in particular banking sector will once again be subject to the rule for foreign exchange risk, which is related to the balance between euro denominated assets and liabilities. Title: Welcome to the participants in the conference "Digital Banking  the Future Today", organized by Bankera, Sofia, November 9, 2016.
text: Welcome of the Deputy Governor of the BNB and Head of Management "Bank" Mrs. Nina Stoyanova to the participants in the conference "Digital Banking  the Future Today", organized by Bankera, Sofia, November 9, 2016. Dear colleagues and guests, I would like to welcome you to the conference of the "Banker" section on "Digital Banking  the Future Today". The development of financial services and payments in both the European Union and Bulgaria has been largely influenced by the influx of technology, alternative and remote payment and service channels and related innovations. The regulatory framework in Bulgaria takes into account all European trends and requirements aimed at achieving an integrated European market,harmonising the order and conditions for the provision of payment services, promoting innovative payment methods, achieving a high level of payment security and better consumer protection. One of the steps in this direction is related to the so-called " SEPA Regulation - Regulation(EC) No 260/2012 laying down technical and business requirements for credit transfers and direct debits in euro and the recent deadline (31 October 2016) for Bulgaria and the other non-euro area Member States, after which credit transfers and direct debits in euro covered by reg lamenta should be executed in accordance with its requirements, these include the use of the XML standard, the requirement to designate bic by payment service users, to ensure interoperability of small payment systems with others in the EU, is waived. In this regard, changes have been made to Regulation No 13 on the application of an international bank account number and BAE codes enabling non-bank payment service providers to designate payment accounts with an international bank account number (IBAN). This will allow them to access and use the existing payment infrastructure more effectively and to expand services, which they offer. The main task of the BNB,and in particular for the management of Banking this year and next year, is the transposition of the Second Payment Services Directive into the Law on Payment Services and Payment Systems (PSPS). countries outside Europe and when paying in currencies of countries outside those of the European Union. An important new element is the provisions on the security of payments made through remote access and on the internet, as well as the reporting of incidents by payment service providers. This year, changes have been made to the PSPP and its implementing regulations relating to the introduction of the provisions of Directive 2014/92/EU on the comparability of payment account fees, the transfer of payment accounts and access to payment accountswith basic features. facilitate cross-border access to basic banking services, as well as improve transparency of payment service charges and consumer awareness. BNB is also working on the creation of a register of bank accounts and safe deposit boxes, which we expect to start work from January 1, 2017,within the deadline set by the legislator. These are only some of the current payment themes where significant progress has been made, but there are still many challenges to be addressed related to the growing demands of payment service users stimulated by the development of information and communication technologies. which will allow credit transfers to be made and received in euro in seconds, at any time, and will bring many advantages to payment service users and providers. Last but not least, I would like to emphasise that payment innovation and technology are also a challenge for supervisors and regulators, who should ensure the efficiency and security of the payment process and payment infrastructure, while adhering to precise supervisory requirements and standards, good market practices and national market specificities. I wish interesting and fruitful work to the participants in the conference.

Title: Address at a ceremony on the occasion of 65th anniversary of the establishment of the Finance and Credit Department of the Academy of Economics Dimitar Tsenov and receiving on behalf of the BNB the honorary medal for merits for the development of the finance and credit system in Bulgaria, Svishtov
text: Address by Ms. Nina Stoyanova, BNB Deputy Governor in charge of Banking Department, at a ceremony on the occasion of 65th anniversary of the establishment of the Finance and Credit Department of the Academy of Economics Dimitar Tsenov and receiving on behalf of the BNB the honorary medal for merits for the development of the finance and credit system in Bulgaria, Svishtov, 7 April 2017 Dear Prof. Marchevski, Dear Prof. Zahariev, Dear lecturers and guests, Dear students, It is an honour for me to celebrate with you the 65th anniversary of the establishment of the first finance department in Bulgaria and to receive on behalf of the Bulgarian National Bank the honorary medal for merits for the development of the finance and credit system in Bulgaria. Going back in history is a good opportunity to recall that the persons history remembers are those who managed to decipher in the present day the needs of the future. A convincing example of this is the story of the donor Dimitar Tsenov who, as back as 1912, foresaw the need of establishment in Bulgaria of a higher trade school modeled after German examples and with his donation in his testament he preordained studying banking and finance sciences in it. This is exactly the core around which later evolved the Finance and Credit department of the Svishtov Academy of Economics Dimitar Tsenov, whose anniversary we are celebrating today. Over the years, it gave Bulgaria quite a few prominent figures of science, governance, banking finance  professionals who left a trail in the development of economy and society. And now we see the dream of the donor Dimitar Tsenov through the Higher Trade School to contribute .even more to the welfare, and the economic and national success of our nation and our country - come true. We extend our great appreciation to the professors of the Svishtov finance school lead by Prof. Minko Russenov. Thanks to them, now the Svishtov Academy has its leading position among the economic universities in Bulgaria, and its Finance and Credit diploma has its heft. As we at the BNB have the opportunity to see, its graduates have skills and competences meeting the real requirements of practice, and are known for their high professional, linguistic, computer knowledge and team work skills. I will support this with facts. Sixteen of the BNB directorates employ graduates of programmes offered by the Svishtov Academy of Economics. They found their fulfillment in governance areas such as reserve management and risk analysis, issue and cash operations, payment systems and payment supervision, banking supervision and financial stability, fiscal agency and depositary of the state, statistics, international relations, accounting, human resource management, etc. Among the 38 BNB employees who have graduated the Svishtov Academy of Economics Dimitar Tsenov, those with a diploma in Finance and Accounting and Control have the greatest share - 34% and 26%, respectively. Among the other specialties, more prominent are Banking and Finance Management, International Economic Relations, Economic and Business Informatics, Insurance and Social Security, Public Administration, etc. Presently, the oldest diploma of the Svishtov Academy at the BNB is of 1978, and the most recent  of January 2015. Two students of the Finance and Credit department won BNB scholarships and worked on assessment of the impact of the regulatory frameworks according the Basel Standards, and on subjects related to the instruments of foreign reserve management in central banks. I believe in the future we will meet more Svishtov graduates as participants in our programmes and as BNB employees. I would like to conclude saying that now, when education started being identified as a priority in the social and political life in Bulgaria, it is even more important to underscore that it should prepare students that meet the practical needs and the challenges of the new realities and technologies. I am convinced that building on its traditions, the Finance and Credit department of the Svishtov Academy of Economics will uphold its high professional level. And we at the BNB are open for cooperation and for employing capable financiers. PAGE \* MERGEFORMAT1

Title: Address at the opening of the 19th Finance Tech Forum The Modern Financial Institution  Digitalization and Effectiveness in Action, Sofia
text: Address by Mrs. Nina Stoyanova, Deputy Governor in charge of the BNB Banking Department at the opening of the 19th Finance Tech Forum The Modern Financial Institution  Digitalization and Effectiveness in Action, Sofia, 27 April 2017 Dear colleagues and guests, I would like to bid you welcome at the 19th issue of the Finance Tech Forum organized by ICT Media and ISACA-Sofia Chapter. The introduction and use of technology in all spheres of life is more and more perceptible and it is, in turn, a condition for achieving sustainable development and increasing competitiveness in the financial sector. The new projects we implement at the BNB, as well as our work as a supervisory and regulatory institution, including in the payments and payment infrastructure area, target further modernization of the sector based on digitalization and innovations. Since the beginning of 2017, a centralized information system Register of Bank Accounts and Safe Deposit Boxes at the BNB has started operation.. There have been already thousands of inquiries made monthly by both the institutions authorized by the law, and by the banks. By the end of the year, it is expected that the access to information in the Register by all authorized institutions will be carried through primarily electronically. Also, in relation to an agreement reached between the Ministry of Finance, BNB, and market participants, the BNB in its capacity of a fiscal agent of the government completed its work on a project for the technical implementation of a direct link between the Government Securities Depository and the E-BOND system of the BLOOMBERG PROFESSIONAL platform. At the same time, amendments to the regulatory framework governing the government securities market were adopted and the Minister of Finance and the Governor of the BNB approved. Rules on Trading, Closing and Monitoring of Government Securities Transactions of BLOOMBERG E-BOND Trading System, which will allow government securities to be traded in this system starting by the middle of this year. In parallel, the BNB is soon starting work on a project for establishing a direct link between the Government Securities Depository and the system of the Bulgarian Stock Exchange AD. With the implementation of the two projects, it is expected that government securities will begin to be traded on a regulated market as well. This will further develop the government securities market and promote its further integration into the Single EU financial market will be encouraged. In the past year, our work was also committed to the transposition into national legislation of the Directive on the comparability of fees related to payment accounts, payment account switching and access to payment accounts with basic features. The new regulations are already being applied and all banks in the country that work with consumers offer their customers the new product  a payment account with basic features. More work is needed, however, for the promotion of this type of account and its features. This year we have been e working on the transposition into Bulgarian legislation of the Second Payment Services Directive. The directive introduces two new types of payment services that are fully effected in a remote, internet environment  payment initiation services and account information services, and regulates the activities of the providers of such services. The directive also envisages changes in the information requirements and the rights and obligations of payment service users and providers, including a detailed regulation of the internal procedure for handling of complaints and a maximum period for responding to a customer. The reach of the payment transactions falling within the scope of the directive is expanded, now including transactions in which only one of the providers is located on the territory of the EU and which are effected in all currencies, and not only transactions fully effected within the EU and denominated in euro or in the currencies of the member states, as was the case so far. Another important new element, ensuring protection of payment service users, are the requirements for enhancing payment security by implementing strong customer authentication for payments effected via remote and online access, and the requirement for payment service providers to report security-related incidents to the supervisory authorities. The presentation that the BNB colleagues will be deliver later today will reflect exactly on these and other important changes in the directive. The directive will be transposed into a new Law on Payment Services and Payment Systems, a draft of which is being consulted with the relevant institutions and payment service providers, and is expected to be sent by mid-year to the Ministry of Finance for submission to the Council of Ministers and adoption by the National Assembly within the deadline for implementation of the directive by the EU member states  13 January 2018. The above-mentioned new projects are aimed at providing a more favourable environment for market participants and a better guaranty of payment service users rights, while recognizing the changes related to technology development. I wish an interesting and useful work to all forum participants. PAGE \* MERGEFORMAT2

Title: Speech at the opening of the Innovations Financial Forum, Sofia
text: Speech by Ms. Nina Stoyanova, BNB Deputy Governor in charge of Banking Department, at the opening of the Innovations Financial Forum, Sofia, 13 June 2017 Dear colleagues and guests, I would like to welcome you at the Innovations Financial Forum organised for the fourth year in a row by the 'Bank of the Year' Association. Over the recent years, we have seen an increasing trend in the volume of electronic trading, electronic payments and the emergence of innovative payment services. The need for both private companies and public bodies to provide electronic services is becoming more and more perceptible. The digitalisation of services and the innovations in the payments area have led to a number of changes and thus to the revision of the Payment Services Directive and the adoption of an entirely new Second Directive on the payment services in the internal market, which we have been working on since the end of 2016 towards transposing. The directive lays down a number of requirements for payment service providers (banks, payment systems and electronic money companies) with regard to payments carried out electronically and via internet. The new payment services directive introduces two new types of payment services that are carried out completely electronically  payment initiation services and account information services  and regulates the activities of the providers of such services. The directive also envisages changes in the information requirements and the rights and obligations of payment service users and providers. The scope of payment transactions falling within the application field of the directive is expanded, already including transactions in which only one of the providers is located on the territory of the EU and which are effected in all currencies, and not only transactions fully effected within the EU and denominated in euro or in the currencies of the member states, as was the case so far. An important area of the directive, ensuring protection of users of payment services effected online or by other remote means, is introducing in-depth authentication of the payers identity by the payment service provider. This involves, in case of a payment, at least two identification elements categorised as knowledge (something only the user knows), possession (something only the user possesses) and characteristic feature (something integral to the user) that are independent so that the breach of one of the elements does not compromise the reliability of the others, and the procedure is designed in such a way as to protect the confidentiality of the authentication data. The practice so far has shown that of the three elements those most commonly applied by payment system providers are passwords (something only the user knows) and one-off dynamic codes for authentication of a payment generated by token devices or received by message through a personal mobile phone or e-mail (something only the user possesses). As to the third element regarding a customers characteristic feature, i.e. something integral to the user, this could be identification through biometric data such as a fingerprint or an iris scan, to name a few. Also, payment service providers will have to put measures in place to mitigate and control operational risks and the risks related to the payment services they provide, guidelines on that being currently drafted by the European Banking Authority. In the event of a significant operational or security incident, payment service providers will be obliged to report to the competent supervision authority. The directive will be adopted by a new Law on Payment Services and Payment Systems, which is expected to be sent by the middle of this year to the Ministry of Finance for submission to the Council of Ministers and approval by the National Assembly within the deadline for implementation of the directive by the EU member states  13 January 2018. The new law will also incorporate the texts of the other directives governing the payment infrastructure and services: the Settlement Finality Directive, the Second Electronic Money Directive, and the Directive on the compatibility of payment account fees, payment account switching and access to basic payment accounts. What's more, the implementation of the Regulation establishing technical and business requirements for credit transfers and direct debits in euro and the Regulation on interchange fees for card-based payment transactions, which are already in force in our country, have created further conditions for integration of the European payments market. The provisions of the Second Payment Services Directive and the new implementing law aim to ensure a more favourable and secure environment for market participants and to better guarantee users rights while taking account of the changes related to technological developments. I wish the forums participants interesting and fruitful work. PAGE \* MERGEFORMAT1

Title: Interview on the Bloomberg TV Bulgarias show In Progress hosted by Delyan Petrishki
Subtitle: How fast is the digitalisation of the financial sphere in Bulgaria developing and are we lagging behind in this new evolution from the other European countries?
text: Interview with Mrs. Nina Stoyanova, BNB Deputy Governor heading Banking Department and Fiscal Services Department, on the Bloomberg TV Bulgarias show In Progress hosted by Delyan Petrishki, 6 October 2017 How fast is the digitalisation of the financial sphere in Bulgaria developing and are we lagging behind in this new evolution from the other European countries? Technologies are entering fast the financial sphere of Bulgaria. In the last three years, it could be said that non-cash payments have been increasing at a very high pace. Thus, for instance, the number and value of card payments over the last three years have grown by 40%, which is even ahead of the EU average rates. The number and value of payments made through the Internet and through virtual POS terminals have increased by 20%, and the physical POS terminals  by 15%. That is, the process is going on at breakneck speed so we could catch up with the average levels in Western Europe? The process is moving on a very fast development track, which is, of course, highly favourable. And some additional information: more than half of the credit transfers in 2016 were initiated electronically. The data that I am quoting are from the ECB statistics by country, which is published on their website and which is contributed by the member-states. They show that Bulgarias financial infrastructure has been developing very well, that it is prepared and meets all EU requirements, also with regard to up taking the relevant innovations which are entering the field very fast. And as a response comes the new legislation. The second version of the Law on Payment Services is as a response to the new directive regulating these activities. How would the landscape change with the entry into force of this new law? Thirteenth of January 2018 is the optimal deadline for introducing it, and what are we fighting for? 13 January 2018 is the deadline for implementing the new Payment Services Directive in the legislations of the member-states. Earlier implementation is also possible, and 1 January 2018 could be a good starting date. That would depend on the pace of the legislative process at Parliament. Hopefully, the time would allow for it to be approved at first and second reading by the end of the year and enter into force in due time. What is going to change is that users will have access to more payment services at higher security requirements level and at better awareness and protection of customer rights. The last one has always been at the centre of the European legislation and each next directive takes it a step further. What safeguards would be put in place? The authentication of payment services users will be three-factor authentication... This three-factor authentication is as a response to the increased volume of online payments and via other remote modes of access that weve been discussing, which is taking place both in Europe and in our country. It will be applied to this type of payments. The procedure is referred to as strong customer authentication. It requires that at least two out of three independent of each other elements be applied, where a problem with each of the three elements does not affect the others. These elements are: knowledge, possession and inherence, knowledge being passwords and possession  dynamic codes generated through tokens and sms messages, among others. Inherence is biometrical data such as fingerprints and iris scans, to name a few. Currently, the most widely used of these are the first two attributes  knowledge and possession. A part of the Bulgarian banks are even introducing or have already introduced these requirements. In general, the deadline will be 18 months from adoption of the relevant European Commissions regulatory technical standards, which are soon expected to be ready and which will describe the process in detail. And if the three elements are introduced, this implies that when a user instructs and uses a payment service, that user will have to apply all three of them? Two of the three elements are required; the third one is optional. Of course, these technical requirements are turned towards the future and towards adopting the relevant novelties in the field. They aim to reduce the number of frauds in online payments. Within the field of the new law on payment services and payment systems, who else will fall under its scope? It is expected that there will be two new types of payment services and a larger variety of payment services on the market. The new types of services are: payment initiation services and account information services. The interesting point about these services is that they are executed only online. The first service of payment initiation will allow customers who do not possess bank cards to shop online and make payments. How does that happen: a connection occurs between the online trader platform and the respective account servicing bank platform. This way, the customer initiates remotely a credit transfer for the respective purchase. With regard to the other service  account information services  customers will be able to see summarised information on their own accounts in one place, and without having to access online each individual payment service providers platform. What is important about the two types of services is that their providers will actually serve only as intermediaries between the online trading platform and the account servicing payment service provider without having control over the customers funds at any given point of time. The law and the directive provide for relevant secure standards for communication, exchange and protection of information. What challenges is this law on payment services and payment systems going to pose to online payments? New services, new more stringent requirements are being introduced. We hope all this would make the market even more competitive, even more advantageous to users, with a wider choice and higher security of their payments. An important novelty that I would like to mention, and which has lately been so widely commented upon, is the planned creation by the Bulgarian National Bank of a website for comparison of fees on payment services. The deadline for this is the end of next year at the latest and it takes into consideration the issue of regulatory technical standards, which are going to be adopted by the European Commission in a couple of months and which are going to introduce a standardised payment services terminology on European Union level and a standard fee information document on payment services. You understand that this also aims to better inform users and to help them choose a payment service provider according to the types of payment services which they use most frequently and the fees which they find most acceptable. This new legislation is in response to the entering new agents of, until recently, traditional banking services, which means competition. And competition means better conditions for the users of these payment services. But where will be the balance between creating a favourable competitive environment between the non-banks and the banks which offer such payments, and the new regulatory requirements, so as not to kill competition in embryo? I would like to go back a bit, if you allow me. Even the first Payment Services Directive around 10 years ago opened this market of bank-provided payment services to other participants too, and these were payment institutions and electronic money institutions which today are successfully operating in Bulgaria as well. Now this market opens up even more with the new services and their providers. This, of course, is useful, competitive and beneficial. Where is the balance? In my opinion, the legislation should not go behind technologies; it must be adopted in time. In this case, the requirements that I mentioned, the ones for strong customer authentication, for facilitating e-commerce, stem from life, from economic development, from the advancement of technologies, and this is well-timed legislation. I do not think it would hinder providers. Quite the opposite, the higher security requirements for payments are very important to providers and customers alike. True, but banks will have to open up. The information for these new customers, will it be a problem for them? They are not used to providing it. This is the trend. This is the requirement incorporated in both the directive and the law, for the entire EU market  its competitiveness must increase by allowing the entry of new players which are non-bank financial institutions. May we talk now about the practice? How will this new landscape actually ease e-commerce? Could you give an example? First, e-commerce will be eased by the service that will allow the people who do not have cards to make payments. But, of course, only if there are providers who would offer that service and who would be licensed by the BNB. It is also certain that the trend of increasing payments via virtual POS terminals will continue. And the issue with the providers outside the European Union, because this is another key point covered by this directive and the related legislation that we are planning to put in place? This directive, and the preceding one, and all other directives, adhere to the single passport principle. A provider of banking or payment services who is authorised in one EU Member State has the right, under a relatively simple procedure (by notifications between the competent authorities), to do business, remotely or on-site, via a branch, anywhere else in the Union. This is a key feature of the European market, of the free movement of goods and services and of the free competition on the whole market. We expect there will be such providers  they could come from the European Union; such providers could be authorised here in Bulgaria. And I expect that after 1 January such applications will be submitted and considered. In conclusion, this law puts an end to a dilemma  who must be regulated and who stood above the regulations; we are talking about banks, about non-bank financial technology companies, at least in the payment services area, and the new possibilities provided, there after all will be a level playing field from a regulatory perspective. It is so, regulations are important to ensure a level playing field, they are important for competition, for the marketdiscipline, and for the protection of consumers. I believe this law comes exactly on time; it meets some new developments that are happening or have already happened related to the technologies on the payment services market, and I do expect positive effects both in Bulgaria and in the European Union, just as it was intended. So that in a year or two, for example, the numbers we started our conversation with, which you cited, about the trends at which e-commerceand E-money payments are growing, can reach the volume levels typical of the advanced European economies. Title: Welcome at the opening of the conference "Banks and Business", organized by Capital newspaper, Sofia, 21 November 2017.
text: Welcome of the Deputy Governor of BNB and Head of Management "Bank" Mrs. Nina Stoyanova at the opening of the conference "Banks and Business", organized by Capital newspaper, Sofia, 21 November 2017. Dear colleagues and guests, I would like towelcome you with the opening of the Fifth Annual Conference, organized by Capital newspaper, on "Banks and Business".
