First of all, I will address the forthcoming adoption of the new Payment Services and Payment Systems Act, which is being considered at first reading by the relevantcommissions in the National Assembly. experience gained in payment supervision. The novelties in the bill are mainly in the following areas: Introduction of new types of payment services  payment initiation services and account information services, fully implementedon the Internet environment; New requirements for the security of payments, in particular when carried out on the internet or by other remote means, by applying a standard of strong authentication of the payer; Extendingthe scope of payment transactions falling within the scope of the law to transactions where only one payment service provider is within the European Union for that part of the transaction to be carried out in the EU, as well as operating transactions carried out in all currencies and not only in the currencies of EU Member States; Increase consumer protection and awareness by setting up a website to compare fees for the most representative payment account services; further developing texts relating to a payment account with basic features; introducing a maximum time limit for responding to complaints from payment service providers; reducing from 300 to 100 the maximum amount responsible unauthorised payment transactions arising from the use of a lost, stolen or misappropriated payment instrument, etc. An upcoming innovation in the field of small payments, which we will be talking about next year, isa project for the so-called "small payments". instant payments. They represent the next step in the development of the EU payment services market, taking into account the change in consumer behaviour and the application of innovative technologies. It is envisaged that the process from initiating payment by the originator to receiving the funds in the payee's account will take place within a maximum of 20 seconds. The service will be available 24 hours a day, 7 days a week and 365 days per year. BNB, as the operator of the TARGET2-BNB system component, points out that many of the country's banks are willing to use this service when it is launched in November 2018 or at a later stage. Next, in order to meet the increased European transparency and liquidity requirements for trading in financial instruments and to enable banks to freely choose the trading venue for government securities, as of June 2017, the possibility of secondary trading in GS was also created on the E-BOND platform of the BLOOMBERG system, and since the beginning of November 2017 For this purpose, a link was established between the Depository of GS with the BNB and the two systems mentioned in order to register with the BNB in a timely manner the concluded transactions on both platforms. The launch of trading in government securities in organised trading venues is expected to lead to further positive economic effects, such as facilitating access for a wider range of investors, including foreign investors, to local debt instruments, in the context of further integration into the European Union's single financial market. Access to the register has been granted electronically to the banks and to the majority of the authorities and institutions authorized by law. Data on more than 16 million bank accounts have been submitted in the Register of Bank Accounts and Safe Deposit boxes, and since the beginning of the year more than 400 thousand reports have been carried out, over 90% of which have been carried out by electronic means. the other way around. In 2018, updates are to be developed in the information system of the register for the submission of data on the presence of preservation in bank accounts, as well as to expand the information on the accounts of the budgetary organizations. By the end of 2018, functionality for submitting and receiving data from the users of the Central Credit Register for personswho are co-debtors, guarantors and avalists on loans provided will be developed, and we expect this to contribute to a more effective and thorough assessment and analysis of the creditworthiness of the clients of banks and financial institutions. Title: Address at the opening of the 20th Finance Tech Forum Digitalisation  Catalyst for Modernisation of the Financial Sector, Sofia
text: Address by Ms Nina Stoyanova, BNB Deputy Governor in charge of the Banking Department, at the opening of the 20th Finance Tech Forum Digitalisation  Catalyst for Modernisation of the Financial Sector, Sofia, 12 April 2018 Dear colleagues and guests, I would like to welcome you at the 20th jubilee edition of the Finance Tech Forum. The advance in information technologies isconducive to more effective, competitive and innovative financial services, which are spreading widely and rapidly among clients. In Bulgaria the volume of cashless payments has been also growing steadily. More specifically, over the three-year period from 2014 to 2016: the number of card payments increased by 44%, and the value of card payments increased by 38%; the number and value of card payments initiated through a virtual POS terminals grew by over 20%; in 2016, more than 50% of credit transfers were initiated electronically by users, which represents two thirds of the total value of all credit transfers. According to the BNBs preliminary data for 2017, the increasing trend in the above-mentioned indicators has been maintained. . The new Law on Payment Services and Payment Systems, which transposes in the Bulgarian law the requirements of the second Directive on payment services (PSD2), came into effect on 6 March 2018. It contains substantive changes regarding electronic payment services. It is well-known that this law introduces two new types of payment services executed via internet only  payment initiation services and account information services. Main focus in the Law is placed on the security of cashless payments, especially those initiated via internet or via other remote mode of access, and on the relevant measures that payment services providers must undertake in this direction. In this regard, the European Commission adopted a delegated regulation on regulatory technical standards for strong customer authentication and common and secure open standards of communication. Payment services providers are required to bring their business in compliance with the Regulation by 14 September 2019 at the latest. For the first time in 2018 payment services providers will have to assess operational risks and security risks, and to monitor and report to the BNB major operational or security incidents. Also, the BNB will be provided with data on fraud relating to different means of payment in a way defined in the European Banking Authoritys draft guidelines which will take effect in early 2019. Another important change that would affect the payment services market is the European Commissions proposed amendment, published at the end of March 2018, to Regulation (EC) No. 924/2009 on cross-border payments in the Community. Payment services providers in non-euro area EU Member States are expected to equalise their fees for cross-border payments in euro and for domestic payments in the national currency of the respective country. Until now such a requirement existed in the Regulation only with regard to equal fees for domestic and cross-border payments in euro. This amendment is planned to come into effect as of 1 January 2019 and to cause relevant changes in the payment service providers tariffs in Bulgaria. The proposed amendment aims at further deepening of the Single Market in the European Union and creating greater equality between payment service users in accessing less expensive cross-border payments. The amendments to the legal framework are designed to ensure a secure environment that is consistent with the dynamic development of technologies. We expect that the introduction of the new regulations would, in turn, have a beneficial effect on the market, ensuring a wider choice of payment services, more secure payments, and more market players with competitive prices for users. I wish productive work to the participants in this Forum. PAGE \* MERGEFORMAT 1

In addition, there will be an opportunity for competition between network service providers that will connect banks to the consolidated platform. Title: Welcome at the opening of the conference "Future of Money", Sofia, 22 May 2019.
text: Welcome of the Deputy Governor of the BNB and Head of Management "Bank" Mrs. Nina Stoyanova at the opening of the conference "Future of Money", Sofia, 22 May 2019. Dear colleagues, Dear guests, I would like to welcome you with the opening of the Future of Money conference. Money can be seen as value when we talk about the cost of credit and deposit interest, as a means of payment, when we talk about cash payments or by a lackof available means, or as an occasion for innovation when we talk about recent developments in payment processes and infrastructure. Title: Questions for an interview in the Standard newspaper, 4 December 2020
text: Questions to Ms. Nina Stoyanova, BNB Deputy Governor, Banking Department, for an interview in the Standard newspaper, p. 11, 4 December 2020 How has the COVID-19 crisis changed our banking system and, in particular, payments? The crisis created by the COVID-19 pandemic has speeded up the trends of digitalising banking services. Payment services are among the most widely used financial services by the people and there this trend is especially visible. Our data indicate an increasing use of electronic payments, particularly card payments. This trend is seen in both payments on physical POS terminals and internet payments. This process has also been influenced by the increased limit on contactless payments without having to enter a PIN code; this spring the limit was raised up to the maximum permitted by law, which is BGN 100 per payment transaction. Whether these changes in peoples behaviours and habits will remain post-pandemic and will endure after the crisis is over is yet to be seen. Digitalisation is priority No. 1 in the financial sector. The Retail Payments Strategy for the EU and the Digital Finance Strategy for the EU aim to ensure transition to instant payments executed in a matter of seconds, 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. When will this type of payments, called in the Strategy the new normal, become a fact in Bulgaria? Instant payments where the funds are made available for use by the payee within a few seconds, are a central theme in the above strategies. The European Commissions ambition is the development of a high-tech, safe and cheap way of making payments based on them, both at national level and at cross-border within the EU. Along with the development of mobile technology, instant payments can be an alternative to card payments both in online shopping and at physical stores. The national payment system operator BORICA AD is at an advanced stage of developing a project for instant payments in BGN, and it is planned to be launched in 2021. The payments will be based on the modern requirements of the SEPA Instant Credit Transfer (SCT Inst) scheme used also for instant payments in euro. Digital banking is the future. What other changes could we expect? Some modern services with a good potential for development in the coming years are based on the concept of the so-called open finance. The first steps in this direction in Europe were made specifically in the area of payments with the second Payment Services Directive in 2015; this directive introduced two new types of payment services executed entirely online through open banking  payment initiation services and account information services. The consumers who wish to use the new services can give access to the data from their payment accounts to a special category of regulated entities which will provide them with a series of services  from consolidating data on a consumers accounts with one or more banks, through financial analyses and recommendations, to ordering payments, without the consumer having to use a bank card. Access is granted through secure data sharing protocols and with the consumers explicit consent, which guarantees the security of data. These services are already offered in our country too, but they are not sufficiently widespread yet, both in Bulgaria and in the European Union. Shopping with a phone in hand. Are the Bulgarians ready for this and what should they change in their financial culture to move with the times? On the domestic market, now there are a number of solutions allowing consumers to use their mobile phones for contactless payments, offered both by local banks and non-bank payment service providers and by foreign entities. The convenience of this method of payment is undeniable, and we should note that it greatly enhances the security of the payment process as it uses biometric data. Especially important during the pandemic is the fact that there is no need of physical contact with the POS terminal because these payments are made without needing to enter a PIN code, and the user is identified using his/her fingerprint or password directly in the phone. The mobile phone is also increasingly used for authorisation of internet payments, by generating one-time passwords via a mobile application, called software token, installed on the phone. In this way the mobile phone becomes a kind of portal to our payment account. In spite of all technological safeguards implemented by the payment service providers and the device manufacturers, consumers must beware of who uses their mobile phones because thus they provide access to their finances. What is the future of cash payments? Both Bulgarian and European legislation guarantees that banknotes and coins are legal tender and despite all modern methods of payment, access to cash must be guaranteed. This is one of the topics addressed in the recently announced EU Retail Payments Strategy. Moreover, according to an ECB study on payment attitudes of consumers in the euro area, published on 2 December 2020, in 2019 cash payment is the most widely used method  73% of adult consumers payments are in banknotes and coins. Of the non-cash payment instruments, the largest is the share of card payments  24% of all payments. The share of other non-cash payment instruments (credit transfers, direct debits, etc.) is relatively low  each with a share of less than 1% of total payments. At the same time, digitalisation is covering new territories, with the European Central Bank launching a public consultation earlier this year to explore the possibility of issuing a digital euro. How is the security of electronic payments guaranteed? The security of electronic payments has been the focus of sectoral legislation for many years now and we should emphasize the obligation for strong customer authentication established as a standard by the Second Payment Services Directive across Europe. In practice, this requirement means that when making an electronic payment, the payment service provider must make sure that it is initiated by the customer. For this purpose, at least two independent elements from different categories must be used, for which there is detailed legal regulation. The admissible categories of elements are three: knowledge, possession and inherence. Knowledge is something that only the customer knows  such as a username and static password or a PIN code. Possession is something that only the customer possesses  for example, a SIM card on a mobile phone, a payment card equipped with a chip, an electronic signature. The inherence is something that characterizes the user  for example, fingerprint, iris scanning, facial recognition and more. In the case of remote payments, for example on the Internet, there is an additional requirement to perform the so-called dynamic linking, namely linking the code for each transaction with a specific amount and a specific payee, which is practically done by specifying this data in the payment service providers messages containing one-time code. In 2021, an analysis of the implementation of existing legislation to reduce fraud will be carried out at European level and, if necessary, new measures will be envisaged, especially to counter the most modern types of fraud such as phishing. With it, thinking that he\she is visiting a legitimate site, the client reveals to hackers sensitive data such as passwords and one-time codes, which are subsequently used for unauthorized access to his\hers payment account. Efforts to ensure the security of electronic payments are thus required from customers themselves. They should be extremely cautious when making payments online and should always compare whether the amount and the payee indicated in the message from their payment service provider correspond to the payment they are making. The personalised security credentials of cards and other payment instruments that allow remote access to the account must be carefully protected by customers. For example, receiving emails about a blocked account with a prompt to enter passwords and one-time codes is a sure sign of fraud. Further strengthening the control over payment service providers is envisaged. In what direction? The area is sufficiently regulated and the review of the second Payment Services Directive, which is planned for 2021, will focus on even higher requirements for security in the payment process, on measures to prevent new types of fraud, removal of obstacles before the wider spread of immediate payments, etc. Other issues will also be discussed, such as the possibility of adopting an individually determined maximum limit for contactless payments, the introduction of requirement for matching between the name of the payee specified in the payment order and the name of the account holder, wider use of electronic identification and other technical solutions in accordance with market developments and practices. What will you wish your colleagues for Banker's Day, December 6? Above all, I wish them health, keeping our strength and optimism and hoping for a better year, despite the difficulties!

Title: Statement at the opening of the Fintech Summit Conference, organized by Capital newspaper, 30 March 2021
text: Statement by Ms Nina Stoyanova, BNB Deputy Governor in charge of the Banking Department, at the opening of the Fintech Summit Conference, organized by Capital newspaper, 30 March 2021 I would like to welcome you to the annual Fintech Summit organised by Capital Weekly. Until a few years ago the term fintech was mainly associated with small innovative companies that by using digital technologies were trying to redefine the provision of financial services and find their own place on the market. Today and even more after the watershed year of 2020, we can assert that technologies and innovations have become an intrinsic feature of the financial sector and a trigger for its rapid developing. Recent trends show expanding cooperation and technical exchange between banks and fintech companies, which is to the benefit of clients, and results in better, faster and more secure services. The coronavirus crisis and expected recovery act as an impetus for further modernisation and digitalisation in response to consumers demand and changes in society. In this context, the ambitions for accelerated reforms were also confirmed by the European Commission in the EU Digital Finance Strategy and the EU Retail Payments Strategy published in September 2020. Almost half a year after their launch, we can already note the first concrete steps in the implementation of the goals set in these strategies. First and foremost, I would like to focus on instant payments introduced in response to the dynamic development of communications, digital services and e-commerce. Instant payments outline the forthcoming changes in payment infrastructure both in the EU and in the country. Their advantage is the possibility for synchronisation between dispatching of goods and receipt of payment. Transferred funds are immediately available, which enhances the security and trust in business relations and in the payment process. In the EU Retail Payments Strategy, instant payments are called the new normal. The Commission aims at full uptake of instant payments in the EU by the end of 2021. In Bulgaria the project of instant payments in the national currency (BGN) is already at an advanced stage. It has been developed by the BISERA6 retail payment system operator- BORICA AD with the assistance of the BNB as the operator of the national RTGS system RINGS. Recently, the necessary amendments have been made to the legal framework and the payment systems. Technical and functional changes were implemented in the BNB-operated RINGS system that ensure a possibility for making instant payments. The license of BORICA AD as the operator of the BISERA6 payment system was updated, thus allowing the system to process instant payments of up to BGN 100 000. The operator BORICA AD developed the necessary infrastructure that made possible the launch of testing and implementation of the new functionality with market participants. Instant payments are based on the SEPA Instant Credit Transfer scheme. It will be possible for instant payments to be made 24 hours a day within 10 seconds from debiting the payers account to crediting the payees account and receipt of confirmation by the payer. Instant payments will be settled applying the widely used in Europe pre-funding model. It requires a special account with the central bank, intended only for settlement of instant payments. All banks are expected to be able to receive instant payments by April 2023. Meanwhile, as a next stage of the same project, the preparation for processing of customer batch credit transfers in the national currency is underway. These payments are based on the requirements of the SEPA Credit Transfer scheme. Customer transfers will be send by the originator bank in batches for processing by BISERA6 and the pre-funding model will be used for their settlement. This will speed up customer payments that will be credited to the payee account within less than an hour. Banks in Bulgaria are expected to migrate from credit transfers with predefined moment of settlement (three times a day), to processing of batch payments by the end of 2021. Preparation of the payment service providers and payment infrastructure for processing instant payments and customer batch payments in the national currency based on SEPA credit transfer schemes would allow, upon the adoption of the euro as a legal tender in the country, for smooth transition of the services without major modifications of the payment systems and banks internal systems. Further modernisation and enhanced security of the payment process remains a constant priority across the EU and on national level. One of the main targets continues to be provision of high level of security of remotely initiated electronic payment transactions by ensuring the completion of migration to strong customer authentication for card internet payments. Efforts continue for exploiting the full potential of open banking and eliminating any obstacles in the interfaces of payment service providers. In the same vein is the Opinion of the European Banking Authority on supervisory actions to ensure the removal of obstacles to accessing accounts under PSD2, published in February 2021. In order to address the new developments in financial technology the European Commission has already launched a public consultation aiming at update and amendments of the Settlement Finality Directive. In addition, review of other basic legal acts related to payments as the Payment Services Directive and the Electronic Money Directive is expected to start by the end of 2021. text: Speech by Mrs. Nina Stoyanova, Deputy Governor of the BNB, Head of Bank Management, at the Forum of Bulgaria ON AIR TV  "Future-Money", 6 June 2021. The mobile phone becomes a kind of portal to our payment account, and technology allows it to be used as a tool for initiating electronic payment transactions. This is also possible thanks to the ability to digitise payment cards, use of digital wallets as well as mobile banking applications. In addition to convenience, this also brings a significant increase in the security of the payment process, allowing the generation of one-off passwords and the use of biometric data for customer identification. Another important feature is the ability to transfer between accounts with payment service providers with a mobile number. instead of a phone account number based on technology that requires linking the phone number to the IBAN account number. Another important trend at the moment is the development of instant payments implemented within seconds. In a recently published EU strategy on retail payments, instant payments are called the "new rate". They allow payment to be executed within seconds, 24 hours a day, 365 days a year. with the development of mobile technologies, instant payments can be an alternative to card payments in both online shopping and physical store payments. In April this year, the pilot project "BLINK" of "Bonika" JSC for immediate payments in BGN based on the requirements of sepa instant credit transfer scheme was launched. There has also been increased interest in cryptocurrencies recently (also known as virtual currencies or cryptocurrencies). It should be noted that cryptocurrencies are not currencies in the traditional sense, as long as they are not legal tender. insufficient protection for the user. In this regard, Europeanregulators have repeatedly published clarifications and warnings to consumers, regulatory changes are also being prepared. At European level and in Bulgaria, an obligation was introduced for persons providing exchange services between virtual and traditional currencies, as well as the storage and transfer of virtual currencies, to apply the statutory anti-money laundering measures. In Bulgaria they are subject to registration with the NRA. to activates aimed at defining certain types of cryptoactives and laying down the rules for issuing and marketing them, as well as licensing and supervision of persons providing exchange and trading services for such assets. In conclusion, we can summarise that the payment services sector is one of the sectors most affected by digital transformation. This is a very dynamic area where regulators are not onlyobservers, but actively support and guide the market in order to stimulate competition and protect the interests of consumers and businesses.

Title: Statement at the opening of the Financial Forum Innovations, organized by Association Bank of the year, 9 June 2021
text: Statement by Ms Nina Stoyanova, BNB Deputy Governor in charge of the Banking Department, at the opening of the Financial Forum Innovations, organized by Association Bank of the year, 9 June 2021 Market developments today are driven by the new technologies. They provide a basis for increasingly diverse and innovative payment products. Digitalization of processes and services has led to development in the financial sector in Europe further stimulated by the policies of the European and national regulators. Payment services are getting more convenient, secure and accessible. Today, when consumers make on-line purchases, they expect the payments to be executed swiftly and smoothly, requiring no additional time or effort. The global pandemic increased the interest of different businesses to the payment sector. We witness a quick acceleration of digitalization in most of the spheres of life, such as work, shopping and administrative services. This has also generated a demand for alternative methods of payment. According to the latest public data, three out of four users worldwide have changed their method of payment owing to the Covid-19 crisis. Half of the consumers would opt to shop online, where possible. During the pandemic large part of consumers have tried for the first time a new shopping or payment method. Currently, we observe an enhanced activity of the innovative payment market players. These are FinTech companies that have proven themselves in other sectors but also the so-called challenger banks. Using digital technologies, they try to redefine the provision of financial services to improve customer experience and to find their place on this highly competitive market. These new players position themselves mostly in market niches with a potential for further development. Such niches are, for example, the digital wallets, person-to-person (P2P) and business-to-business (B2B) payments, as well as value added services offered on the basis of existing traditional payment services. With the Second Payment Services Directive (PSD 2), two new types of electronic payment services were regulated in the European Union - payment initiation services and account information services. These new services are already offered in Bulgaria and provide technological basis for the implementation of the so-called open banking. It enables FinTech companies to enter the payment market more easily by introducing new business models, services and solutions. Examples for such services are aggregation of payment account data from different payment service providers, carrying out financial analysis, initiating payments from accounts held with other payment service providers, etc. Security of electronic payments remains in the focus of the European and Bulgarian regulators. Increased use of electronic payments and the recent boom in e-commerce pose new challenges with respect to protecting security of payments and electronic identity of customers. The most significant progress here was made in 2019 when the Europe-wide obligation for strong customer authentication was introduced. For this purpose, at least two independent elements of different categories must be used (knowledge, possession and inherence) when processing electronically initiated payments. In case of remote payments, such as Internet payments, an additional requirement has been introduced for the so-called dynamic linking. It requires linking each transaction to a specific amount and a particular payee by sending one-time code messages by the payment service providers. The forthcoming review of the PSD 2 will provide a comprehensive assessment of the strong customer authentication impact on the level of payment fraud. New requirements are considered in order to reduce social engineering and phishing types of fraud, including a requirement to match the payees name in the payment order with that of the account holder. Special emphasis will be placed on the prevention of instant payment fraud. Electronic identification and certificate-based solutions are explored as means of strong customer authentication. Recently, a special focus has been placed on re-defining and strengthening the oversight of the wider payment ecosystem. Specific steps in this aspect have been taken by the ECB with the draft of a single Eurosystem oversight framework for electronic payment instruments, schemes and arrangements (PISA framework), published last year. PISA framework aims to cover not only the traditional payment schemes and instruments (e.g. payment cards), but also innovative instruments, such as digital payment tokens backed by assets (e.g. stablecoins). Last September the European Commission published a Proposal for a Regulation on Markets in Crypto-assets (MiCA), which is currently under discussion. The goal of this Regulation is to ensure a more rigorous regulatory treatment of issuance and transactions with some types of crypto-assets and the crypto-asset service providers will be subject to authorisation and control. The long-term trends in Europe are related to achieving a greater integration and autonomy of the European payment system. In its centre are positioned the instant payments and application of common technical and business standards across Europe. Bulgaria is an active participant in these processes. EU initiatives for development of retail payments are in the process of implementation on our domestic payments market. A still open question is whether the changes in the peoples payment habits will stay as a permanent feature and will set a direction for the forthcoming technical developments in the payments sector. In this very dynamic area the EU regulators will continue playing an active role. I wish interesting and productive work to all the participants in todays financial forum. PAGE \* MERGEFORMAT 1

Title: Interview for Telegraph daily, 25.06.2021
Subtitle:
THE MONEY TRANSFER WITHIN AN HOUR  A REALITY BY THE YEAR END
INSTANT PAYMENTS MAY BE CHEAPER THAN THE STANDARD SERVICE MOBILE PHONE BECOMES A KIND OF PORTAL TO OUR PAYMENT ACCOUNT
text: Interview of Mrs. Nina Stoyanova, BNB Deputy Governor in charge of the Banking Department, for Telegraph daily, 25.06.2021, page 13 THE MONEY TRANSFER WITHIN AN HOUR  A REALITY BY THE YEAR END INSTANT PAYMENTS MAY BE CHEAPER THAN THE STANDARD SERVICE MOBILE PHONE BECOMES A KIND OF PORTAL TO OUR PAYMENT ACCOUNT Mrs. Stoyanova, how much have card payments increased in the context of the pandemic? The Covid-19 pandemic with all its undeniable negative effects acted as a catalyst for the ongoing processes of digitalization in the area of payment services. According to a Study of the European Central Bank (ECB) on the Payment Attitudes of Consumers in the Euro Area, published in December 2020, nearly 50% of consumers would prefer to pay with a card or another cashless payment instrument. As per data of the ECB payment statistics, in recent years the payment card has been established as the most commonly used payment instrument in Europe, with already more than half of the cashless payments in the EU being initiated by a card. In addition, the results of an ECB public consultation on a digital euro, published in April 2021, indicate that when it comes to payments European citizens value most features like privacy, security and wide cross-border reach. Another important conclusion from the consultation is that payment cards, digital wallets and smartphones may be adapted to provide features closer to cash payments. How are payment services developing in Bulgaria? The use of payment services in Bulgaria develops dynamically, as the number of card payments initiated via virtual POS terminals has increased by almost 90% in the recent five years. Cards continue to be a widely used payment instrument in the pandemic conditions, while preserving the upward trend in the volume of payments. The card payments at physical POS terminals evidence higher growth than card payments via Internet. This is favourably influenced by the last years increase of the limit for contactless payments not requiring PIN entry from BGN 50 to BGN 100 per transaction. The final 2020 statistical data on payments in the European Union, including in Bulgaria, presented by type of payment services, are to be published by the ECB in July this year. In the same vein, in spite of the initial negative impact of the pandemic, felt in the second quarter of 2020, a growth of cashless payments compared to past periods was evidenced later in the year  as accounted in the large value payment systems RINGS and TARGET2. This trend continues also currently, with an increase in the value of payments processed in RINGS in the period January  April 2021 by 27% compared to the same period of 2020 and by almost 30% compared to the same period of 2019. Growth is registered by both customer and interbank payments. BORICAs project for instant payments in BGN will facilitate customers, but will this service be more costly and how much more? Is there a new deadline for its implementation? Instant payments are positioned centrally when it comes to the future development of payment services in Europe. Work is being done in this aspect also in Bulgaria, as in April BORICA AD launched its BLINK pilot project for instant payments in BGN, which has been developed in accordance with the pan-European SEPA Instant Credit Transfer scheme. Instant payments will be executed 24 hours per day, 365 days in the year, and the recipient will have the funds at its disposal in less than ten seconds from the initiation of the transfer. Full coverage of the domestic market is expected to be reached in the next two years. In this regard, the BISERA6 payment system, operated by BORICA AD, has already been configured to process instant payments, and the fees for the payment service providers will be lower than the fees charged for sending and receiving standard customer credit transfers in Bulgaria. Of course, eventually the end fees to be paid by customers for instant payments will depend on the pricing policies and business models put in place by the payment service providers. When can we expect iris recognition digital services to enter the market, and would you explain how these services will be executed? The security of electronic payments has been in the focus of the EU and Bulgarian legislation for quite a while. In this regard, already in 2019 the obligation for strong customer authentication was introduced across Europe. For this purpose, when processing an electronically initiated payment, the payment service provider has to make sure that the payment has been ordered by that particular customer. During the authentication process, at least two independent elements of three different categories (knowledge, possession and inherence) must be used. The latter category includes elements characterising the user, and here biometric data recognition is essential, namely a fingerprint scanning, iris scanning, face or voice recognition, etc. In this sense, biometric authentication is something that many payment service providers in Bulgaria have already introduced using mobile phone banking applications. Thus, the mobile phone becomes a kind of portal to our payment account. Apart from convenience, this also significantly enhances the security of the payment process by allowing the use of biometric data for customer identification. Which identification technologies are most widespread? Currently, the most widely employed technologies are facial recognition and fingerprint identification due to the fact that they work well with the most common smartphone models on the market. According to experts in the field, the technology of iris scanning via smartphone is not yet sufficiently sophisticated and can be "cheated". In this sense, the risk to the security of users when using digital services with iris recognition via phone currently seems greater, hence the delay in establishing this method as a means of customer identification. Are there any requirements regarding digital payments that our country needs to fulfil with respect to entering the euro area? For large-value payments, participation in the euro area gross settlement system TARGET2 is a key requirement. The Bulgarian National Bank provided the banks in the country with access to this system as already in 2010 and through them customers can make payments in euro in real time. As of November 2022, a new TARGET services platform is planned to be implemented bringing together TARGET2, the TARGET2-Securities settlement system and the TARGET Instant Payments Settlement Service (TIPS). The Bulgarian National Bank, the banking community and ancillary system operators are actively working on the project to join the new consolidated TARGET Services platform so as to complete the activities in time, according to the ECB's schedule. What's next? Upon adopting the euro, all customer payments within the country currently executed in BGN, including budget payments, will have to migrate to payments in euro. They must be carried out in line with the technical and business requirements, in compliance with the European Payments Council's (EPC) pan-European SEPA payment schemes. Also, work has already begun to introduce the processing of batch customer transfers in BGN. This will allow reducing the time necessary to complete a client transfer and make the funds available on the payee's account to less than an hour. Batch customer transfers processing is expected to start by the end of this year. PAGE \* MERGEFORMAT 2

Title: Interview for the Business.BG programme on BNT, 28 November 2021
Subtitle: Guest in our studio is Mrs. Nina Stoyanova, BNB Deputy Governor and Head of the Banking Department. What trends have emerged in the area of payments in relation to the Covid-19 pandemic? How are we paying more?
text: Interview of Mrs. Nina Stoyanova, BNB Deputy Governor in charge of the Banking Department, for the Business.BG programme on BNT, 28 November 2021 Guest in our studio is Mrs. Nina Stoyanova, BNB Deputy Governor and Head of the Banking Department. What trends have emerged in the area of payments in relation to the Covid-19 pandemic? How are we paying more? The Covid-19 pandemic led to a shift in consumer behaviour in all areas of life, including the payments sector. There has been an increasing use of digital channels for making payments, as well as an intensification of the process of migration from cash to cashless electronic payments, which has started already before the pandemic. The data also show this. In Europe, for example, half of the cashless payments are now made using bank cards. The trends in Bulgaria are similar. For the first six months of 2021, the number of card payments and e-money payments in the country increased by around 30% compared to the same period last year. The figures for the value of payments made through the payment system RINGS are also consistent with this development showing a 30% increase in payments processed in the first six months of 2021 compared to the first half of 2020. For the viewers, let's say what the system itself is, just to be clear. It is a real-time gross settlement payment system in BGN (RINGS) operated by the Bulgarian National Bank, through which practically all payments in the country are processed. And you say we have 30% growth there. Is that a sufficient signal to say that business is recovering? Yes, this can be interpreted as a signal for economic recovery, but it can also be taken as evidence in the field of data and statistics that the electronic payment channels provided by the banks and other payment service providers in the country are being increasingly used. And during Covid what does the data show, surely there was some kind of freeze, decline in the early months? I do not exactly have that data to compare at the moment. Nevertheless, the fact is that this year the data show a significant acceleration in payments in our country, after the initial decline caused by the pandemic. What do you foresee for next year, will this upward trend continue? Yes, most likely it will persist in the coming year and will revolve around innovations in the field of payment services, which can be clustered around a few key segments. These are open banking, instant payments and mobile technology. For example, the mobile phone is increasingly becoming a kind of virtual bank counter, a portal for initiating various payment transactions, which is being used more and more frequently. Will there come a time when we will not use cards like Mastercard and Visa? It is too early to say that this moment has come, but the combination of the technologies I mention  mobile applications, instant payments, the QR codes scanning capability  it is a whole new payment strategy and infrastructure around which processes will certainly be driven in Europe in the next few years, and is also a trend worldwide. This will inevitably lead to a technological competition between already established payment models, including the widespread cards, and new payment models that will provide additional speed and security of the payment process. What about instant payments? How will they be different and how will customers assess them? Instant payments are payment transactions that are executed 365 days a year, 24 hours a day, and by changing the payment and settlement technology, they allow the payment to take place in about 10 seconds. From the moment the payment is ordered, to the time the beneficiary receives the money, 10 seconds or even less pass. When can we see this in mass use in Bulgaria? It is good to divide this topic into two areas. Firstly, I should mention that since 2010 the BNB has been the operator of the TARGET2-BNB component, which enables Bulgarian banks to conduct payments in euro. In 2018, an additional functionality called TIPS was added to this component  for instant payments in euro, to which we are connected and Bulgarian banks are able to participate in it. In Europe, however, the so-called "SEPA instant payments indicator", which measures instant payments to normal credit transfers in the euro area, shows that they are around 10%, which is recognized by European regulators as low, and various measures, including administrative ones, are being adopted to speed up this process. (For example, it is a mandatory requirement that all payment service providers that have joined the SEPA Instant Credit Transfer Scheme and are reachable in TARGET2 should also join TIPS by the end of 2021.) In the field of instant payments in Bulgaria, there are projects that are developed by BORICA AD, as a payment system operator, with the participation of the banking community and with the support of the BNB as the operator of the payment system RINGS. There are actually two projects. One is for the introduction of instant payments in BGN, the technical platform for which is already in place and two banks are currently participating in it. The number of participating banks is expected to increase next year. The other project is for the so-called "batch" credit transfers, which is expected to be launched in early 2022 and will involve all banks. In practice, all customer credit transfers in BGN in the country are thus envisaged to switch to this new technology, with expected time for the money to reach the beneficiary's account within one hour. In this way, a significant speeding up and optimisation of payment processes in the country is expected in the coming year. This is related with the implementation of quite complex infrastructure projects involving the entire banking community, BORICA AD and the BNB, which has implemented the necessary functional changes to the settlement mechanism in RINGS. This will have a significant impact and the public will feel it. Open banking is not so well known in our country. How is it different? The Second Payment Services Directive introduced for the first time in the EU specific regulation of the so-called "open banking". It introduces two new types of payment services  payment initiation and account information provision. Is this introduced by the bank? To make this clear to the people. I will explain the process. The advantages are that it increases competition in the payment market and introduces two new types of market players who are operators of these particular services - namely providers specialising in the provision of these two new types of services. They enable the customer to have access through a single entry point to all banking information or information held at payment service providers on the customers accounts, greater convenience and speed in checking balances, reporting on transactions made or ordering new payments from the accounts. To make it quite clear  supposing I were a customer and there is an open banking platform that I can access, what should I do? A customer can enter and initiate a payment via any one of the customers accounts, in any bank, the customer can get information on the movement on their accounts. The added value is that open banking also allows for building up additional services on top of the payment services, such as financial analysis, creditworthiness assessment, provision of additional accounting and financial services, investment services, etc. A whole galaxy of new services that will evolve around these platforms and will improve the customer services. If I understand correctly, this will shorten the process  what is it, for example, for which I will not need to go to the bank? Generally, this is related rather to payment transactions, but it can be expanded to include other services as well. Even now we have to go to the bank for just about nothing, and this is also a big change because 5 or 10 years ago we used to visit the bank quite often, and now we simply use online banking Let me ask you about cryptocurrencies  eventually, are they going to be legalised and regulated? First of all, it should be noted that cryptocurrencies are not currencies in the traditional sense of the word as they are not legal tender, and they are perceived rather as speculative assets. Even today cryptocurrencies are subject to regulations, e.g. with regard to one of their biggest disadvantages from a regulatory perspective  the need of combating money laundering. Currently, both in Europe and in Bulgaria, the persons who provide services of converting virtual into traditional currencies and back, and of keeping and transferring virtual currencies, are required to apply the legal anti-money laundering measures. Moreover, a new EU regulation is expected next year, which will broaden the requirements for the information accompanying the transfer of crypto-assets, such as the names of the ordering party and the recipient, addresses, etc. In this way, it is expected the regulations in this area to be strengthened, by limiting the anonymity in the transactions in a cryptocurrency that now is posing a risk. In 2022, an extensive EU regulation is going to be finalised, and it will regulate both the issuers of crypto-assets and the trading platforms for them. An authorisation regime is planned for issuers of crypto-assets as well as for crypto-asset service providers (such as trading platform operators) which now are subject only to registration. At present, there is not much prospect for cryptocurrencies to become an official means of payment ever, and yet these are assets that can be converted into traditional money. Therefore, regulations need to be expanded with regard to cryptocurrencies insofar respective markets are still evolving and the risk of money laundering needs to be eliminated completely. ____________ Real-time Interbank Gross-settlement System The national component system TARGET2-BNB in Bulgaria of the euro area payment system TARGET2 (Trans-European Automated Real-time Gross settlement Express Transfer system) A new processing model where groups of individual payments will be sent in a common (batch) file from the originator's bank to the BISERA6 payment system The broad term crypto-assets, which includes cryptocurrencies, has become widespread in Europe PAGE \* MERGEFORMAT 3

Title: Interview for 24 Hours newspaper, 28 December 2021
text: Interview of Ms. Nina Stoyanova, BNB Deputy Governor in charge of Banking Department, for 24 Hours newspaper, 28 December 2021, pages 1; 3; and 10 THE PHONE BECOMES A BANK CARD FROM NEXT YEAR, BATCH PAYMENTS IN BGN WILL BE MADE WITHIN AN HOUR This will be the time from the initiation of the transfer to the receipt of the money in the recipient's account, says the BNB Deputy Governor. Euro payments to be introduced via new platform. Increasing the limit for card payments without requesting a PIN above 100 BGN is impossible for now, changes in the law are needed Ms. Stoyanova, why is mobile banking becoming more and more popular, what are its advantages? Mobile technologies can be defined as one of the innovation hubs. Phones, through mobile banking applications and the installation of digital wallets, are becoming payment initiation tools and kind of virtual bank counters offering access to a variety of online services. Mobile banking is also distinguished by enhanced security for payment service users through the use of two-factor authentication elements. The growth in payments initiated via mobile is expected to reach 23% over a 5-year period, from 2019 to 2024, according to a global study by PricewaterhouseCoopers. One of the new features, for example, support transfers via phones between accounts with payment service providers by specifying a mobile phone number instead of an account number, based on technology that allows linking the telephone number to the IBAN of the account. In Europe, the service is expected to be developed on the basis of the SEPA Proxy Lookup scheme of the European Payments Council. In our country, a similar service for paying by specifying a mobile number instead of an account number is already offered by some payment service providers, but only for transfers between accounts with the respective provider. The feature to pay from a phone number to a phone number when transferring between accounts with different payment service providers is due to be implemented in Bulgaria, with BORICA AD currently working on such a project. How is the safety of online banking ensured? In Europe, the security of payments has been a constant focus of regulators in recent years. As of September 2019, it has become mandatory in the EU to implement strong customer authentication. This means that when an electronic payment is initiated, at least two independent elements from different categories must be used in the process - knowledge (e.g. password), possession (e.g. smartphone or token) and inherence (e.g. fingerprint). In the case of remote payments, for example on the internet, an additional requirement is introduced to perform so-called dynamic linking  linking the code for each transaction to a specific amount and a particular recipient. Systems for monitoring and analysis of the risk with transactions (Transaction risk analysis, TRA) are also increasingly used. All these requirements are met by payment service providers in the country, which is also monitored by the BNB. Recently, biometric authentication has also shown great potential by providing verification of elements characterising the user  fingerprint, iris scan, facial recognition, etc. Many payment service providers in Bulgaria have already introduced similar customer authentication methods using mobile banking applications. Apart from customer convenience and speed of payments, this also leads to a significant enhancement of the payment process security. Do financial institutions align the limit for contactless payments with the usual amounts of transfers via virtual POS terminals? Do you expect a new change, for example, that PIN will not be required also for transactions over BGN 100? In relation to the pandemic, in the spring of 2020 the limit for contactless payments without PIN in Bulgaria was raised to the maximum allowable amount of BGN 100 per transaction. When paying a larger amount at a physical POS terminal, the transaction can be initiated contactlessly, but will only be executed after the relevant PIN of the payment card has been correctly entered. The exemption from PIN entry for contactless payments is statutorily limited to BGN 100 per transaction and further change of this amount would not be possible without relevant changes in the applicable European and national legislation. In particular, compliance with this limit is necessary with respect to the current payment security requirements in Europe set out in the Regulatory Technical Standards on strong customer authentication. In addition to enabling payments 24 hours a day, 365 days per year, are instant payments within seconds already a fact in our country? In our country, instant payments in local currency are introduced by BORICA as the operator of the payment system for retail payments BISERA6 in cooperation with the banking community and with the support of BNB as regulator and the operator of the payment system for real-time gross settlement in levs RINGS. The preparation of the process required payment system operators and participating payment service providers to make technological changes to their systems and corresponding investments to ensure the processing of instant payments in BGN according to the requirements for their execution. As a result of the substantial efforts made, technical capability to make instant payments in BGN has now been provided and two banks participate in a real environment on a platform maintained by BORICA AD. The number of banks participating in the instant payments platform is expected to increase next year and all banks in Bulgaria to be able to receive instant payments by April 2023. All this corresponds with the ongoing developments in the payment services sector in Europe, where the move towards instant payments is one of the priorities in the EU Retail Payments Strategy published by the European Commission a year ago. When Bulgaria adopts the euro, how are we going to technically move from payments in BGN to payments in EUR? The preparation of this process has practically begun in February 2010 when the BNB joined the Eurosystems real-time gross settlement system (TARGET2), as a central bank operating the TARGET2-BNB component, which enables the Bulgarian banks to exchange payments in euro, both in our country and in Europe, with the banks participating in TARGET2. Moreover, also since February 2010, the BISERA7-EUR system of BORICA AD has been operational, which is a payment system processing client transfers in euro, based on the rules, practices and standards of the Single Euro Payments Area (SEPA). On the basis of the ensured interoperability and communication connections with other European systems for euro payments, BISERA7-EUR enables the exchange of SEPA credit transfers between the Bulgarian banking community and those of other EU Member States. Once the euro is introduced as the national currency, the payments in BGN will begin to be conducted as payments in EUR via TARGET2-BNB. The client payments in BGN that are currently executed via the payment system for small value payments BISERA6, operated by BORICA, will have to be migrated to SEPA euro payments. This process has already started with the planned introduction of the so-called batch payments in BGN based on the SEPA standards for credit transfers. How will cryptocurrencies trading be regulated? It is important to clarify that these are not typical currencies, they are rather assets. Is the registration at the National Revenue Agency (NRA) sufficient, as part of their legalisation? When is the authorisation of cryptocurrencies trading platform operators likely to be introduced? Indeed, cryptocurrencies are not currencies in the traditional sense of the word as they are not legal tender, and they are perceived rather as speculative assets. For this type of instruments, in the EU regulatory sphere it is widely used the broader term crypto-assets, which includes also the cryptocurrencies. Since 2019, in line with the European requirements, the entities in our country who provide services of converting crypto into traditional currencies, and of keeping and transferring cryptocurrencies, have been required to apply the legal anti-money laundering measures. Such service providers operating in Bulgaria are subject to registration by the NRA. With respect to the necessity of strengthening the regulations in this area, in the middle of this year the draft of a new EU regulation was put forward which will increase the requirements on the information accompanying the transfer of crypto-assets (e.g. names and addresses of the ordering party and the recipient) and thus will limit the anonymity in the cryptocurrency transactions. This draft regulation is part of the new package of AML/CFT measures adopted by the European Commission in July 2021. Another very detailed EU regulation, called Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation (MiCA), is being discussed. It is aimed at regulating the activities of both crypto-asset issuers and crypto-asset trading platforms, and is expected to be finalised in 2022. The purpose of the regulation is to support innovation in the financial sphere but in a way that would maintain financial stability and ensure investors protection. The MiCA regulation stipulates specific requirements with regard to the crypto-asset issuers operating in the EU, and it puts in place an authorisation regime for the issuers of certain types of crypto-assets and for crypto-asset service providers, such as trading platform operators. How will the protection of consumers be ensured in such transactions? The users of crypto-assets are attracted by features like speed and low cost of transactions, global reach, and profit possibilities. At the same time, these instruments involve a lot of risks, such as exchange rate volatility and insufficient protection of consumers against fraud. In this respect, the European and national regulators have repeatedly published clarifications and warnings for consumers. The implementation of the MiCA regulation is supposed to considerably improve the protection of consumers. Apart from the requirements that crypto-asset issuers and traders must be authorised and their activities regulated by a public body, there are also other requirements that will ensure a more adequate protection of crypto-asset users. For example, some of these requirements guarantee the provision by the crypto-asset issuer of complete and understandable information on the features and risks inherent in the respective product. The regulation also includes requirements for crypto-asset issuers and service providers with regard to the safekeeping of clients funds. What other innovations and changes are coming in the area of payment services? A very important project that is well underway is the so-called batch credit transfers. It is being implemented by BORICA AD with the participation of the banking community and the cooperation of BNB. This project is practically introducing the SEPA credit transfer requirements for the payments in BGN. It is envisaged that client credit transfers are going to be sent in a common (batch) file from the originator's bank to the BISERA6 payment system, and the time from the initiation of a transfer to the receipt of the money on the beneficiarys account will be up to one hour. This service will be available 24 hours a day, all year round. The banks in the country are expected to begin to carry out this type of transfers in the beginning of next year. At a later stage, the payments currently executed to and from the budget are also expected to be migrated to payments based on the SEPA credit transfer scheme. All this altogether is a good preparation in the area of payment services for the forthcoming adoption of the euro in Bulgaria. In November 2022, the BNB and the banks participating in the national component system TARGET2-BNB are going to join the Eurosystems new consolidation platform for TARGET services. The development of this new consolidation platform was driven by technology innovations in the area of payments, the evolution of the regulatory requirements and the changing needs of consumers. Thus, the existing payment infrastructure in Europe, which we are part of, will be modernised and the overall efficiency and security of payments will increase. PAGE \* MERGEFORMAT 2

Title: Interview of Mrs. Nina Stoyanova, Deputy Governor of the Bulgarian National Bank, Head of the Banking Department, for the Banker newspaper, p. Jan. 4-5, Jan. 14, 2022
text: Interview of Mrs. Nina Stoyanova, BNB Deputy Governor in charge of Banking Department, for the Banker newspaper, pp. 4-5, 14 January 2022 Mrs. Stoyanova, the pandemic has triggered a boom in the use of digital channels and payment technologies. How do you assess these trends, will the digital transformation continue with the same momentum and what challenges arise from it? The Covid-19 pandemic did serve as a catalyst for existing processes of change in consumer behaviour. The migration from cash to electronic payments, which had already started before, accelerated. According to an October 2021 report by the international consulting company McKinsey, cash payments worldwide declined by 16% in 2020. The development in the use of payment services in Bulgaria is also dynamic. For example, the number of card payments initiated through virtual POS terminals has doubled in the last five years. For the first six months of 2021, in the country was registered an increase of more than 22% in the total number of cashless payments compared to the same period in 2020. Over the same period, electronically initiated credit transfers increased by almost 28%. All this signals a clear and sustained change in payment habits in our country. The current policies of European and national regulators support digital transformation to achieve more accessible and secure payment solutions. Payment services in our country have been developing dynamically, following the trends in Europe. Among the significant technological innovations, it can be distinguished the development of mobile banking, digital wallets and digitised payment cards, the use of portable smart devices to initiate contactless payments, such as smart watches, etc. The increased use of digital payment channels also poses new challenges. Ensuring the security of payments and customer data is a constant focus for regulators and market participants, with measures being implemented in line with technological developments. Could you highlight the most important regulatory requirements of recent years that payment service providers have to comply with? The application of the strong customer authentication requirements is one of the fundamental changes introduced on the basis of the Second Payment Services Directive. This aspect was developed in detail through the regulatory technical standards for strong customer authentication, which entered into force in 2019. Their requirements started to apply immediately to credit transfers made via internet and mobile banking platforms. However, for online card payments, due to the significant technical changes required with respect to both payment service providers and merchants, an additional transition period was granted, harmonised at European level, until 31 December 2020. Thus, in 2021, payment service providers completed the migration of their systems and products and already apply all the requirements for strong customer authentication. Recently, efforts have also been invested in improving the legal framework in view of the emergence of new technologies and business models in the payments market and the risks involved. In September 2020, the European Commission published a foundational document called EU Digital Finance Strategy, part of which is a proposal for a Regulation on digital operational resilience for the financial sector. This regulation complements and harmonises existing requirements in the area of payment security. It aims to strengthen cyber security and the operational resilience of the financial sector as a whole, including payment service providers. Among the important requirements to be introduced are those regarding the management of IT risks and risks stemming from IT technology and service providers. Work at European level to refine the regulation is ongoing and it is expected to be finalised this year. What can we expect in 2022 on the regulatory front and also in terms of innovation in payment services? The review of the Second Payment Services Directive is due to start in the second half of 2022. An analysis of the results of its implementation in a number of directions is expected. Firstly, an impact assessment will be carried out on strong customer authentication and updating, where necessary, of the technical solutions applied. The focus will be on strengthening payer protection and preventing new types of fraud, especially in the context of instant payments and threats such as phishing and social engineering. It is expected a review and revision of services falling outside the scope of the Directive, etc. The reporting framework for payment statistics under Regulation (EU) No 1409/2013 of the European Central Bank is also being developed further and supplemented. In line with the adopted amendments to the regulation, from 2022 reporting will cover a broader and more versatile set of indicators, published at a higher frequency  quarterly and semi-annually. This will allow the public to receive more timely and detailed information on the development of payments in Bulgaria and the EU. In the current year, a significant change in the technology and speed of execution of low value payments up to BGN 100,000 is forthcoming. In the final phase of implementation are the projects of BORICA AD, as the operator of the BISERA6 payment system for customer payments, for the execution of instant credit transfers and credit transfers in line with the applicable SEPA standards. Banking community and the BNB, as regulator and operator of the RINGS large value payments system, are actively involved in these projects. One of the projects is for the implementation of instant payments in BGN, with execution of transactions within 10 seconds. It should be noted here that the BGN instant payments platform has already been launched in a live environment, with two banks currently participating, and the number of participating banks is expected to increase in 2022. The other project is for the introduction of credit transfers in BGN based on the SEPA standard (the so-called batch credit transfers). The execution of such transfers in real terms is envisaged to start by the end of January this year, with all banks in Bulgaria participating in the project. The time from the initiation of the transfer to the receipt of the funds in the beneficiary account is expected to be within one hour. In your statements, you often highlight open banking with the corresponding benefits it brings. However, in terms of customer data security, how does the BNB monitor the implementation of the Second Payment Services Directive and have you encountered any malpractices in the exchange of data between banks and the so-called third parties? Indeed, the so-called open banking is a much-discussed topic lately, given its great importance for the development of the payments market in Europe and in our country. The term open banking in the European context covers the two new payment services  payment initiation service and account information service. At the heart of these new processes is a consistently pursued policy aimed at fair competition, equal treatment of payment service providers and application of high customer data security standards. The providers of the new services are innovative high-tech companies. In parallel, however, they are regulated institutions and have to go through a licensing or registration procedure, depending on the type of services offered. They should be proven to meet a number of conditions, in accordance with the legal framework, including having the qualifications, reliability and suitability of the persons managing and representing the respective company, implementation of effective security rules and mechanisms against identified risks, fraud or illegal use of sensitive and personal data, etc. The technical basis for the development of these new processes was laid with the adoption of Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2018/389, which introduced the regulatory technical standards for strong customer authentication and common and secure open standards of communication. In order to meet the regulatory requirements regarding open banking, banks in Bulgaria, like most banks in Europe, have predominantly opted for the development of dedicated interfaces known as Application Programming Interfaces (API). These special interfaces ensure the providers of the new services have access to banking systems, providing a high degree of security, speed and the ability to handle a significant number of simultaneous requests. However, there are quite a few challenges with respect to their development and implementation, given the complexity of the processes. Insofar as the legal regulation in Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2018/389 is more general, its practical application raises a host of questions that require further interpretation at European level. It should be noted that in some European countries, such as Sweden, the Netherlands, Germany, the United Kingdom, etc., the practical provision of payment initiation and account information services had already developed before the adoption of the Second Payment Services Directive. In other EU countries, however, the processes have been developing more as a consequence of the European legal framework. In accordance with that framework, the BNB issued the first licences for the provision of the new services in the second half of 2019. Again in 2019, the first exemptions were granted to account servicing payment service providers from the obligation to implement fallback mechanism in addition to the developed application programming interfaces. This process continued and ended in 2020, when a consultation procedure between the national competent authorities and the European Banking Authority (EBA) was already required for each specific exemption. For the purpose of ensuring consistent supervisory practices and addressing emerging technological issues, in June 2020 the EBA published its Opinion on obstacles under Article 32(3) of the regulatory technical standards on strong customer authentication and common and secure communication (EBA/OP/2020/10). The EBA has also published clarifications on a number of questions related to the application of the uniform supervisory framework in the field of open banking. The regulatory discussions led by the EBA, in which the BNB is an active participant, have a catalytic role in interpreting and treating emerging obstacles and issues in a consistent manner at European level. This process continued during the past 2021 so as to ensure the use of a unified approach in responding the questions raised by the Member States and market participants. In its Opinion on supervisory actions to ensure the removal of obstacles to account access (EBA/OP/2021/02) of February 2021, the EBA specified that, although many account servicing payment service providers had removed some of the obstacles to account access, other obstacles remained. The European Banking Authority expects national competent authorities to take the necessary actions to ensure that the identified obstacles are removed within reasonable time. Such actions were also taken by the BNB which, in order to ensure the removal of the obstacles for open banking in Bulgaria, had active communication on specific issues both with the account servicing payment service providers and the providers of the new types of payment services throughout the year. The consolidation and further standardisation of the legal framework for dedicated interfaces is included in the work on the forthcoming review of the Second Payment Services Directive. In 2021, there was a lot of discussion on the regulation of the crypto-assets activities. When could we expect Bulgaria to adopt specific legislation in this area, and has the BNB any obligation currently, and a mechanism, to detect suspicious activities related to cryptocurrencies? The topic of cryptocurrencies is indeed a very relevant one, considering their proliferation and the increasing public interest in them. The European regulators consider this type of instruments within the broader term crypto-assets, and a number of warnings have been issued and published, describing the risks of this type of investments. Currently cryptocurrencies are subject to regulation in Europe primarily with regard to the prevention of money laundering and terrorist financing. From 2019 onward, in line with the European requirements, the entities in our country which provide services of converting crypto into traditional currencies, and of keeping and transferring cryptocurrencies, are required to apply the legal anti-money laundering and counter financing of terrorism (AML/CFT) measures. Such service providers operating in Bulgaria are subject to registration by the National Revenue Agency (NRA). Leading role in the activities for the application of the AML/CFT measures is assigned to the State Agency for National Security. In 2022 two new EU regulations regarding crypto-assets are going to be finalised. One of them will complement Regulation (EU) 2015/847 on information accompanying transfers of funds, with the obligation to collect such information also on certain crypto-assets. This is expected to limit the anonymity in the cryptocurrency transactions. The other EU regulation, called Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation (MiCA), will be more extensive and aims to regulate comprehensively the issuance and offering of crypto-assets as well as the related activities and services. This regulation stipulates authorisation and control of both crypto-asset issuers and crypto-asset service providers, such as crypto-asset trading platform operators. It is not clear yet which institution will be the competent authority in Bulgaria for this new regulation, but it is expected the institution to be granted serious legal powers with regard to the crypto-assets issued and offered in our country.
