Title: Speech by Ms. Nina Stoyanova, Deputy Governor of the Bulgarian National Bank, Head of the Banking Department, at the opening of the event of the Banker newspaper "Digitalization and Cybersecurity 2022", June 3, 2022
text: Interview with Mrs. Nina Stoyanova, BNB Deputy Governor in charge of Banking Department, for bTV, 22 February 2022 Payments in Bulgaria are already effected within an hour, what are the next innovations that the businesses and users will face? Indeed, a significant change is underway in the payment infrastructure in Bulgaria that allows for considerable reduction of the time for execution of customer payments, and the results of this will be felt in 2022. These infrastructure projects have had their effect in reducing payment completion time for customer credit transfers. Since the end of January this year, customer transfers have been executed using a new technology that allows the time for receiving the transfer to be reduced to less than an hour. In practice, this is done by changing the settlement mechanism. Whereas previously it was three times a day, in the morning, at midday and in the afternoon (at 10:00, 13:30 and 16:00 respectively), and the final time of receipt of the transfer depended on this, now in practice settlement takes place throughout the day and transfers are received with effect close to instant, in less than an hour. This is a project that significantly improves the financial infrastructure and its efficiency. There is another following step, one additional project, which is for instant payments in BGN. It has also been prepared, the infrastructure for it is set up. Already 3 banks and 1 non-bank institution (non-bank payment service provider) are participating in it. More banks are expected to join this year and this will allow, in practice, transfers between their customers to take place really instantly - in about 10 seconds, 365 days a year, 24 hours a day. The lead institution for these projects has been BORICA, the operator of the client payments system. The whole banking community is involved in them as well as the Bulgarian National Bank, as the operator of the RINGS payment system and the regulator, and I really hope that this year the effects will be felt. What is the total amount of money that has been paid out via Internet in 2021, given the pandemic that has made us shop more from home? According to the latest public data available to us, which are prepared according to the methodology of the European Central Bank's (ECB) payment statistics, for the first six months of 2021 about BGN 270 billion were paid through electronically initiated cashless transactions (editors comment: payments ordered via the Internet, through electronic or mobile banking). If we look at it in dynamics  the first half of 2021 to the first half of 2020, we have a 22% growth in electronic cashless payments. Another interesting fact is that when we compare this data with the European Union (EU) statistics, the growth rate of cashless payments in Bulgaria has outpaced the EU average in recent years. This in itself testifies to the dynamics of these processes and to the qualitative development in cashless payments and payment infrastructure in our country, which makes it more attractive to the customers. How prepared are the payment systems in Bulgaria if, say, we adopt the euro tomorrow? Since 2010, the BNB has been operating a component system in the European real-time gross settlement system in euro TARGET2. This system is, in principle, a euro area one, but it is also open for participation of non-euro area banks, and we have made use of this opportunity. This allows the Bulgarian banking community to make transfers in euro within the country and within the European Union via TARGET2 even now. This infrastructure is complemented by the BISERA7-EUR payment system for customer payments in euro, operated by BORICA, which, through the reachability and connectivity that has been established with other similar systems in Europe, enables customer-level transfers to reach other European banks and for such transfers to be received by Bulgarian customers. What the public sees in the new projects is speed, but behind that speed there is a certain technology. The change in the technology for executing transfers that I mentioned was in practice the result of the completed migration of customer credit transfers in BGN to the SEPA standard, which is a prerequisite for the future processing of these payments as payments in euro. From a technical point of view, customer credit transfers in BGN already meet the technical and business requirements of the SEPA transfer standards. In the case of eventual introduction of the euro, we will be able to change the payment currency and, with some technical adjustments, the transition will be easy. There is one last part left in this infrastructure and it is related to public sector payments, to budget transfers, which are also to be migrated to SEPA standards. This is also included as an activity in the plan for the introduction of the euro in Bulgaria. This activity is to be carried out jointly by the Ministry of Finance, the banks in the country, BORICA and with our participation. It is not necessarily and invariably linked only to the euro area accession. These projects would have been done either way, because they are a next step in the development of the payment infrastructure. We can say that if the introduction of the euro were to happen, in a short period of time, the payment system could be transformed and will start settling all payments in euro. Only the project of migration of the budget credit transfers remains to be implemented. What needs to be changed in the legislation in the area of activity of the Banking Department regarding payments so that we meet the euro area requirements? The plan for the introduction of the euro provides for drafting of the so-called 'euro law', which should regulate at a general level all matters relating to the currency conversion, the dual display of prices, the dual circulation period of the two currencies and all other such issues that concern the entire society and can be resolved in a regulatory manner that is universal for all and does not require individual changes. Perhaps what is most important in terms of payments is that the real-time gross settlement system RINGS will cease to function, as it is designed to operate in the national currency only. All payments will be switched to TARGET2 for processing and settlement, which will also require legislative amendments. Do you think that the adoption of the euro and the related technical transformations could have an impact on the price level in Bulgaria? The experience of other countries that have joined the euro area in the last ten years shows that there is no such effect. All these measures and mechanisms that are envisaged in the plan for the introduction of the euro in our country, following the experience of other countries, ensure this. One such measure is, for example, the double display of prices, which will be over a long period of time. The communication campaign, the oversight that will be carried out by the consumer protection authorities, also comes into this context. So there is no room for concern that the euro itself will cause any inflation or price change. Could you tell us what exactly open banking, which is gaining popularity, means and how it will help to facilitate the activities of businesses and consumers? Open banking means two new types of payment services: account information and payment initiation services. These are executed entirely electronically. What is actually different from the so far existing services is that they can be executed from a single entry point, from a single platform, through which the customer or legal entity is able to see all their accounts and all the movements on them as well as to order payments. In addition to the convenience of seeing the information in one place, this makes it possible to build up additional services based on the analysis of the information thus collected, for example investment services, services related to accounting activities, financial analysis and so on. With open banking, companies can, for example, provide access to their accounts of their accounting offices, who can see bank statements and transactions, and the accounting office can order transfers from a single point, regardless of which bank and which account is concerned, depending on how it manages cash flows. Will the information from open banking help build a consumer's credit file to facilitate borrowing? Yes, because it will show balances, movements, payments and when this is added to other financial information it can give a good analytical result. Also, it is important to say that apart from this upgrade in terms of additional services, open banking will enable the development of the payment infrastructure. For example, if open banking services are combined with instant payments, which are gaining momentum, with the scanning of QR codes as a means of initiating payments, we get a new ecosystem, and this has a future in Europe and in our country. In Bulgaria, these services have already got some development. At the end of 2019, their first two providers were licensed. In 2019, the interfaces of the banks were built, respectively the exemption from the fallback mechanism where applicable, so that the providers of these new services can access the bank data through these interfaces. This was an important technological change that required conducting a separate procedure for each bank. In 2021 and 2022, this process is being finalised, in line with the requirements and opinions of the European Banking Authority on removing obstacles and problems with the interfaces. In 2022, we expect these mechanisms, with our active assistance, to be fully functional and deliver their full potential to the public. Is there interest? Yes, there is interest. These services have a great future and the "third party" providers of the new services have their customers. The operation of the services depends on the technical infrastructure to function completely unobstructed and this will be the case within a few months. Will the NRA be able to access this data from open banking, bypassing bank secrecy? Access to these accounts, through these new providers, through open banking, can only be based on a contract between the customer and the provider that operates such a platform. The NRA has other ways of accessing information described in their legal framework. The BNB has had a register of bank accounts and safe deposit boxes in operation for 5-6 years, but without data on the balances in these, and public investigative bodies, including the NRA, have access to this register. However, in order to obtain information on account transactions and balances, disclosure of bank secrecy is necessary. What is the mood of central banks in Europe about cryptocurrencies and cryptoassets  rather to regulate them or to ban them? Both opinions exist. This year, a new European regulation with the acronym MiCA is expected to come into force, which will regulate cryptoasset markets, including cryptocurrencies. This is perhaps the most far-reaching regulation that has ever been made regarding cryptocurrencies. This regulation will govern cryptocurrencies, their issuers, trading platforms. It divides cryptocurrencies, or cryptoassets, into different categories, depending on their functionalities, and they can be separated into two broad groups  those cryptoassets that have a peg of their value to the value of other currencies or assets  the so-called stablecoins, and the other category are assets that do not have such a peg. A classic example is Bitcoin. The regulation requires more information for investors. This is the so-called 'white paper' in which information will have to be provided on the type of asset, its features, the risks it entails, so that investors can be fully informed before making such a purchase. Projects to regulate the trading of cryptoassets are also being discussed in the US and the UK, again with a focus on investor protection and awareness. In your opinion, is it possible that holders of cryptoasset wallets are obliged to declare them in some way? The MiCA regulation does not reflect on the tax side of the matter, but there is such a side and like any asset, they should be subject to tax regulation. I think they are subject even now, even as we get into the subject gradually with the other part of the countries that are banning, there are countries, such as Russia and India, that are trying to restrict the cryptocurrency trade precisely through high tax rates. There are also other countries that ban them completely. One such very interesting example is China, which used to be at the forefront, or even first in the world, in mining ('digging') cryptocurrencies, but has banned them completely, both from being mined and from being traded. This means we are moving towards regulation? Yes, definitely. We cannot solve the problems related to such infrastructures simply by banning them. The way out is regulation. In this line of thought, will a digital euro be a euro based on blockchain technology or something else, let us say a few words on this topic, for example some basic differences (from cryptoassets). No institution stands behind cryptoassets, no central bank, no country or some other regulator. Their supporters could even perceive this as a plus. Another difference is that cryptoassets may be accepted as a medium of exchange but they are not universal legal tender. The European Central Bank prepared and published a report on the topic of digital euro in 2020, followed by a public consultation on this issue. At the end of last year it was announced that an investigation phase starts which would take two years. This investigation phase will answer all questions, primarily at the technical level, such as how a digital euro could be designed, what could be the ways for distribution to the accounts of various persons, where these accounts will be held, what would be the impact on financial markets and intermediaries, what the risks will be, etc. Thereafter, a final decision will have to be made. Actually, central bank digital currencies emerge as a result of several factors. First, we are witnessing how digitalization is affecting more and more all spheres of life, especially the payment sphere. This is becoming increasingly evident year after year. Second, the global trend is the decreasing use of cash as a means of payment and digital channels are preferred more and more, and the public demand for such new digital means creates the need for new developments. Last but not least, a role to play has also the entry of new technological companies, including cryptocurrencies, which are trying to offer an alternative to traditional types of payment and investment. Will the digital euro look like a stablecoin? I would not say so. What should be noted about the digital euro, and about central bank digital currencies in general, is that they are a digital alternative to cash and they would complement cash, without replacing it. They provide additional means and ways of making payments and storing value, but they are a digital analogue of paper money. Therefore, we cannot say that this is a stablecoin because the currencies of central banks are backed by their own foreign exchange reserves, their reputation, the country as institutions and credibility, while cryptocurrencies are backed by none of that. What is more likely to happen  we will see a digital lev or Bulgaria will directly move to a digital euro? Bulgaria, as a member of the European Union, adheres to and uses the mechanisms offered by the ECB. As yet, the ECB has not made a decision on the launch of a digital currency, but if such a decision is made and we have joined the euro area - yes. Last week the International Monetary Fund issued a report on central bank digital currencies and it states that nearly 100 countries are at various stages (investigation, experimental, tests, or even full scale launch) of exploring possibilities of issuing their own digital currency. The report was presented by Ms. Kristalina Georgieva (editors comment: IMF Managing Director) in a speech entitled The Future of Money. For example, China has undertaken a pilot for a digital yuan, and the digital yuan has been issued in 10 bigger cities and regions. What are the other challenges facing the Banking Department headed by you in the medium term, apart from the projects we talked about? This year, in November, the BNB is going to join the ECBs new consolidated platform for TARGET Services. It will include three services. The first one is the real-time settlement service in euro - TARGET2, in which we are already participating but we will migrate to the next level. The second service is the securities settlement platform in euro TARGET2-Securities which used to be a separate system, and now it is being integrated with the new TARGET Services platform. We are working to join this platform, together with the Central Depository and a team of the ECB. As a result, Bulgarian government bonds will be available for transfer via TARGET2-Securities platform, completing both legs of the operation  the cash one, related to the transfer of money, and the transfer of securities. Thus Bulgarian government bonds will be more easily accessible to investors across the European Union. And the third service in this new consolidation platform is TIPS. These are instant euro transfers, and we are supposed to join this service as well when we join the euro area in the future. Another big project that I want to mention is named AnaCredit. It is in the area of statistics and in fact will allow reporting entities to report all the information on loans and credit risk through a single-entry point, here at the BNB, through a single platform. The platform may be used not only for statistical purposes, but also for the needs of the banking supervision, loan restructuring, and economic analyses. Thus, reporting entities will report via one system and according to common standards for Bulgaria and the EU, which will reduce their workload and will improve the quality and consistency of the collected information. At the same time, the continuous development of the legal framework and the technical requirements which our country must meet as a member of the EU, and the BNB as a participant in the European System of Central Banks, as well as the challenges related to our future accession to the euro area, require very high professionalism and responsibility, on which I would like to congratulate our employees. Title: Interview of Mr. Dimitar Radev, Governor of the Bulgarian National Bank, for 24 Chasa newspaper, pp. 15 and 19, March 3, 2022
text: Speech by Ms Nina Stoyanova, BNB Deputy Governor in charge of the Banking Department, at the opening of the Digitalisation and cybersecurity 2022 event organised by the Banker newspaper, 3 June 2022 Nowadays digitalisation is increasingly entering all spheres of life, such as banking services, e-commerce, public services, electronic government, and many others. More specifically, digitalisation started a long time ago in the area of payment and financial services, and the Covid-19 pandemic served as an additional catalyst for the processes of transforming business models and services. On the other hand, the increased use of digital channels for receiving services and the development of electronic trade pose new challenges associated with the protection of clients data and the security of services. The link between digitalisation and cybersecurity is a very topical issue, especially today in the context of the recent events in Europe. The advancement of innovative payment products and services is now a sustained trend at European and national level. Many Fintech companies came up and they began to offer new products and services alongside the already well-established market players. At the same time, the entry of more innovative products and participants in the payment market, in the face of intense competition, leads to increased risks and vulnerabilities. In Europe and in our country the mobile phone is more and more used as a portal to various payment services, including the digitalisation of payment cards and the use of digital wallets, mobile POS terminals, mobile banking applications, and other additional functionalities based on the existing payment schemes. In the light of all these developments, the security of electronic payments and data protection continue to be the focus of the European and Bulgarian legislation. This was one of the primary legislative objectives in recent years, and the Second Payment Services Directive (PSD2) introduced specific provisions in this vein. Thus, back in 2019 across Europe was introduced the requirement for strong customer authentication (SCA) based on the use of at least two independent elements from different categories, i.e. knowledge, possession and inherence. The last category covers elements that characterise the user, e.g. biometric data: fingerprint, facial recognition, etc. Biometric authentication has already been introduced in our country with the help of mobile banking applications. In general, in 2021 payment service providers in Bulgaria completed the migration of their systems and products and are already applying all the requirements for strong customer authentication. As a result of the efforts made by the competent authorities and payment service providers, there has been a lasting reduction in electronic payment fraud spread out before the introduction of strong customer authentication. The improvement of the legal framework at European level in this area continues. A review of the Second Payment Services Directive is due to start this year, and a comprehensive assessment of the impact of strong customer authentication on the level of payment fraud is expected. The possibilities for using electronic authentication and solutions based on trust services when logging into a client's account and initiating payment transactions are also explored. Particular attention will be paid to strengthening protection against new types of fraud, which are observed following the introduction of strong customer authentication, especially in the context of instant payments and phishing and social engineering threats. In September 2020, the European Commission published an EU Digital Finance Package, part of which is a draft Regulation on Digital Operational Resilience (DORA). This regulation complements and harmonises the existing requirements in the field of payment security. It aims to strengthen the cybersecurity and operational resilience of the financial sector as a whole, including payment service providers. Among the important requirements to be introduced are those related to IT risk management, optimisation of the legal framework for notifying regulators in the event of incidents, requirements for testing the digital operational resilience of financial entities and managing risks related to third party providers of IT technologies and services. The regulation will also encourage financial entities to exchange information on cyber threats on a voluntary basis in order to improve and strengthen their cyber resilience. The regulation is expected to be finalised in the course of this year. With regard to the security of financial market infrastructures, the European Framework for Threat Intelligence-based Ethical Red Teaming (TIBER-EU) published by the European Central Bank is also of great importance. TIBER-EU tests mimic the tactics, techniques and procedures of real-life cyber-attackers based on a special threat intelligence. They are appropriately designed to simulate an attack on the critical functions of an infrastructure and its basic elements, i.e. people, processes and technologies. The test is intended to reveal the strengths and weaknesses of the tested entity, which allows it to achieve a higher level of cyber-maturity. In December 2020, the European Commission published a proposal for a directive on measures for a high common level of cybersecurity across the Union to replace the existing directive concerning measures for a high common level of security of network and information systems across the Union (NIS Directive). Among the main goals are increase in the level of cyber resilience in all relevant EU sectors and reduction of disparities in different parts of the EU internal market. The level of awareness and collective capacity to prepare for and respond to threats are expected to improve by ensuring effective cooperation within the Union. According to the proposed directive, Member States are required to adopt national cybersecurity strategies in order to set strategic objectives, appropriate policies and regulatory measures with a view to achieving and maintaining a high level of cybersecurity. In conclusion, I would like to point out that the trends in Europe are towards the development of a harmonised and integrated financial and payment infrastructure based on common standards and security instruments. Work at European level to refine the proposed new legal framework continues, and its various elements (regulations and directives) are expected to be finalised in a timely manner, given the importance of the proposed changes for the smooth and secure functioning of the markets. I wish interesting and fruitful work to all the participants in today's conference. PAGE \* MERGEFORMAT 2

Title: Speech by Ms. Nina Stoyanova, Deputy Governor of the Bulgarian National Bank, Head of Banking Department, at the opening of the Innovation Financial Forum, organized by the Bank of the Year Association, June 9, 2022
text: Statement by Ms Nina Stoyanova, BNB Deputy Governor in charge of the Banking Department, at the opening of the Financial Forum Innovations, organised by Association Bank of the year, 9 June 2022 First, I would like to thank the organisers for the invitation to me to open todays Innovations Forum, organised by the Association Bank of the Year. Today, more than ever, the digital development of the financial sector is on the agenda of the businesses, regulators and the state as a whole. Each stakeholder has a role to play in the process of creating a modern digital environment  banks and financial institutions that offer new products, users of payment and financial services that are increasingly active, informed and seeking innovations, as well as regulators who need to create a secure, predictable and modern legal and supervisory framework in line with the dynamics of the processes. A favourable environment for the development of payment services is provided by the Second Payment Services Directive (PSD2), which is due to be reviewed this year. Today I would like to focus on several topical subjects, including the development of open banking, insofar as it is part of the subjects of today's forum, as well as on issues related to the development of the payment infrastructure and regulatory framework in the short and medium term. It is well-known that Delegated Regulation (EU) 2018/389 introduced regulatory technical standards for strong customer authentication and common and secure open standards of communication. The regulation created the technical framework for the implementation of services related to the so-called open banking performed entirely in an electronic environment  payment initiation and providing account information through third party providers. In accordance with the terms and conditions provided in the European legal framework, authorisation procedures have been carried out of third party providers, application programming interfaces (APIs), chosen by the majority of payment service providers as a secure channel for access to their systems, have been developed, as well as the subsequent exemption from the obligation to create a fallback mechanism to the developed application programming interfaces, where the requirements for this are met. The Bulgarian National Bank (BNB) actively participates in regulatory discussions, as a result of which the European Banking Authority (EBA) issues opinions and maintains a section with questions and answers, supporting the harmonised treatment of emerging obstacles and issues at European level. At the same time, the BNB maintains ongoing communication with both authorised third party providers in Bulgaria and the banking community, which contributes to the horizontal treatment and effective removal of any emerging obstacles, in accordance with the EBA's positions and national specificities. It is no coincidence that now is the time to assess the impact of the application of the existing regulatory framework and the need for changes and improvements. The consolidation and further standardisation of the regulation of the APIs is scheduled in the work on the forthcoming revision of the Second Payment Services Directive. In this regard, on 10 May this year the European Commission (EC) launched a public consultation on the revision of PSD2 and collecting information on a possible new legal framework for open finance to build upon the existing open banking regulation. The purpose of such new framework is to allow, with the customers consent, for their data that are outside the scope of PSD2 to be shared and reused by financial service providers to create new and improved services, and for more effective implementation of data protection measures. The EC consultation is available in all languages of the European Union (EU) and lasts 12 weeks  until 2 August 2022. As regards the development of the financial market infrastructure in Bulgaria, we have accomplished a lot so far, but we still have a way to go. Since 2010, the BNB has been operating a component system in the Eurosystems real-time gross settlement system in euro (TARGET2). This allows the Bulgarian banking community to make EUR-denominated transfers via TARGET2 within Bulgaria and across borders. This infrastructure is also complemented by the payment system for servicing client payments BISERA7-EUR, operated by BORICA AD, which system, through its connections to other systems in Europe, enables the exchange of client transfers in euro with the other European payment service providers. As a participant in TARGET2, in November this year the BNB is going to join the new consolidated platform for TARGET Services of the European Central Bank (ECB). It will provide access to several services at once. The first one is the service for real-time settlement in euro, i.e. the TARGET2 system, in which we already participate. The second service is the platform for settlement of euro-denominated securities TARGET2-Securities (T2S), which was functioning separately until now. Now we are working on connecting the government securities depository at the BNB and the Central Depository AD to T2S. The T2S platform offers settlement across Europe, of cash and of securities, in central bank money. In this way the Bulgarian securities will be more accessible for the investors from the European Union. The third service in the new consolidated platform is TIPS. It provides access to instant payments in euro, which we should also adopt when we become a part of the euro area. Furthermore, in the beginning of this year the project for migration of client credit transfers in BGN to the standards of the Single Euro Payments Area (SEPA) was implemented. Thus, the client credit transfers in BGN practically meet the technical and business requirements of the standards for SEPA transfers, which is a prerequisite for a smooth future migration of these payments to the euro. The realisation of this project and the use of new payment settlement mechanisms currently allow for these credit transfers to be executed within less than an hour from the time they are ordered to the time the recipients account is credited. Another important project that was technically prepared last year was about the execution of instant payments in BGN where transactions are processed within 10 seconds, 365 days a year, 24 hours a day. Four banks and a non-bank payment service provider have already joined the platform for instant payments in BGN. Among the participants are some of the biggest banks in the country, and consequently more than a half of the accounts in Bulgaria are now reachable for instant payments in BGN. Another big bank and a non-bank payment service provider are expected to join the platform by the end of this month. The deadline for migration to the new platform is April 2023. The progress is commensurate with the European Unions average reachability of instant payments in euro. The realisation of the project on instant payments in BGN will facilitate the future migration to instant payments in euro in the TIPS platform of the euro area, which will be a part of the Eurosystems new consolidated platform for TARGET Services. More work remains to be done regarding the public sector payments in Bulgaria, which are also to be migrated to SEPA standards. This is also set as an activity in the plan for the introduction of the euro in Bulgaria. This activity is to be carried out jointly with the Ministry of Finance, the banks in the country, BORICA AD and the BNB. In this regard, an interagency working group has already started work with the participation of the relevant institutions and representatives of the payment industry in the country. The work on this project will use the good practices and the progress made on already successfully completed sectoral projects implemented jointly by the BNB and the National Revenue Agency, the Road Infrastructure Agency and the National Customs Agency, with the participation of BORICA AD. These projects have led to optimisation of the payment processes, refinement towards minimising the detailed information in payment instructions, required for payments of this type, and modernisation of the services offered in connection with the processing of a significant part of budget revenues. With regard to the new European regulations, Regulation (EU) 2022/858 of the European Parliament and of the Council on a pilot regime for market infrastructures based on distributed ledger technology (DLT) was published at the end of May this year. The Regulation sets out requirements for market infrastructures based on DLT and regulates cooperation between operators of such infrastructures, national competent authorities and the European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA). It will apply from 23 March 2023, with the exception of a few provisions that will come into force already this month. In 2022, two new European regulations are expected to be finalised. The first one is the Regulation on Markets in Crypto-Assets (MiCA), which is a comprehensive legal framework that seeks thorough regulation of the issuance and trade of crypto-assets, as well as related activities and services. Another important project is the Regulation on the Digital Operational Resilience (DORA). It aims to develop and harmonise the existing requirements in the field of security of participants and infrastructures in the financial sector, with the main emphasis on strengthening cybersecurity and operational resilience of the financial sector as a whole, including payment service providers. The development of payment services in Bulgaria has a clear positive dynamics. It testifies to the good cooperation and efforts of all participants within their functions and competencies  the BNB as a regulator and operator of the real-time gross settlement system (RINGS), BORICA AD as an operator of payment systems and schemes, as well as the entire banking sector and non-bank payment service providers. At the end of the first quarter of 2022, the number and value of cashless payments increased by about 20% on an annual basis, and the number of card payments initiated on virtual POS terminals  by about 50%. These data clearly show the volume of work done by the financial sector, the growing prevalence of electronic payment services in the country and the clear change in consumer attitudes towards digitalisation, related to convenience and security. I wish all participants in this forum interesting and fruitful work. PAGE \* MERGEFORMAT 3

Title: Opening address by Mr. Kalin Hristov, Deputy Governor of the Bulgarian National Bank, at the conference "Monetary Unions in History", organized jointly by the Bulgarian National Bank and the European Association for Banking and Financial History (eabh), Sofia, July 1, 2022
text: Interview with Ms Nina Stoyanova, BNB Deputy Governor in charge of the Banking Department, for the bTVs program This Sunday and businessnovinite.bg, 26 June 2022 Host: The Deputy Governor of the Bulgarian National Bank in charge of the Banking Department, Nina Stoyanova, is answering important questions, asked by This Sunday and businessnovinite.bg, as to whether banks and cryptocurrencies can coexist in the future, when the end of cash will be, what the bank of the future looks like, how secure electronic payments are, and whether Bulgaria is ready for the euro area. Host: Do banks and cryptocurrencies have a common future and what is it like? What will be the impact of crypto-assets regulation on investors and users? Nina Stoyanova: If we try to compare banks, cryptocurrencies and crypto trading platforms, we will find that, in terms of the degree of regulation, they stand at the two extremes. Banks and the financial sector as a whole are one of the most heavily regulated spheres in Europe and in the world. Crypto trading platforms, on the other hand, are mostly unregulated. In this regard, it is important to say that an extensive regulation is going to be adopted in Europe by the end of this year  the Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation, which is over 120 pages long. This regulation will exhaustively govern the business of crypto trading platforms, the issuance of cryptocurrencies, the keeping of crypto-asset accounts and, most of all, it will provide a very standardised format of information for users, for future investors in crypto-assets, about the risks involved in an asset, its features, and all the information that users must have to make such an investment. Host: How will crypto-assets regulation affect investors and users? Nina Stoyanova: As I already said, the obligations for providing information to consumers and investors, because they may not be only natural persons, are especially important. It is essential to ensure the provision of standardised information and that the information should contain all the required features of the instruments. As regards the regulation of crypto-assets, work is being done not only in Europe but also in countries with large markets, such as the US and the UK, and there this focus on information is also relevant. So, once crypto-assets are properly regulated, which will happen in the very near future, then they might have a place in the regulated financial sector, with their proper legal framework. It is also important to strengthen the regulation on countering money laundering and addressing the anonymity issues in such transactions. Host: In this case, is cash coming to an end? Nina Stoyanova: This question has been asked repeatedly over the last years, and the reason for asking is the expanding digitalisation, the increase in electronic payments through digital channels. It is a fact indeed; it is evident both in Bulgaria and in Europe that more and more payments are made by card and electronically. On the other hand, however, the money in circulation is growing both in Europe and in Bulgaria. In one of its last years studies the European Central Bank calls this a paradox: how come electronic payments are increasing on one hand and, on the other hand, the cash in circulation is increasing too. However, reports indicate that only about 20% of cash is actually used for payments in Europe, and about 15 years ago this percentage was over 30. The explanation behind all this is in the functions that cash has. Firstly, cash is something that we possess, we can hold it in our hand, and keep it in our wallet. It is physically with us, unlike the funds on accounts which are held with banks or other financial institutions. Also, cash is a universal means of payment. It can be used by everybody with no need of any technical devices. Cash also continues to have a social function for these groups in society which are still unbanked, they have no bank accounts despite the efforts in this regard. Cash is the instrument these people use to make their payment transactions. Last but not least, in times of crisis, as was the pandemic or the current war in Ukraine, cash is a means of making savings and this gives the people greater peace of mind that they have funds in case of crisis. Therefore, the short answer is that cash remains an important instrument, at least in the medium term, and maybe even further on. Host: And what are the risks, after all? Nina Stoyanova: Digitalisation, like any technical tool that we use, has advantages which are numerous, but it also has risks. Every use of technical means involves risks too. People see digitalisation, the increasing use of electronic channels, as an advantage. When they discover the advantage of paying online by card, of shopping online, of not having to go to a bank and submit a payment order, as they used to do 10 years ago  this changes consumer attitudes. The security of electronic payment channels has always been in the focus of the regulators in Europe and in our country. The existing types of fraud in connection with the payment process itself have been largely overcome  via the introduction of the so-called strong customer authentication, which translated means that when we access our accounts online, as well as through a mobile application, we enter a username, password and receive a dynamic code used to confirm the execution of transaction. This has produced a very good effect in Europe and in our country. Host: What will the bank of the future look like? Nina Stoyanova: The bank of the future will certainly be more and more digital. In this regard, the review of the Second Payment Services Directive, which is due this year, also envisages the adoption of several technical measures to address the new types of fraud that are emerging, such as phishing and social engineering. In these scams, the customer usually perceives that the bank is sending a message to him, while in fact he is a victim of a scam in which he discloses his personalised security credentials. In this regard, measures are possible in two directions  one is certainly by increasing financial literacy, because we couldnt possibly use digital channels without the necessary knowledge and caution. On the other hand are the technical means, such as linking the IBAN number of the recipient's account with the name of the recipient, so that we can be sure that the transfer goes exactly to the person for whom it is intended. This is one of the measures that may be adopted after the revision of the Directive. Even now, there are banks in our and European markets that are entirely digital. There are banks that operate without physical offices and these banks certainly have a place in the future development of the market, but at the moment they are targeting a more limited segment of customers and services. The universal bank still provides many services in the market that require a physical presence, but there is one element of change in this service that is more related to the provision of consulting services in offices or assisting clients to perform various operations. Electronic channels predominate when it comes to payments. If we have to talk about the bank of the future and the services of the future, I would like to mention three things that, in the medium term, over the next few years, may change the landscape of the financial infrastructure and payments. Host: Instant payments in BGN  what does this mean? Nina Stoyanova: First of all, I should point out the instant payments. They are being established and the policy of the European Central Bank is to introduce them more and more intensively, even with certain administrative measures. There is also such a project in Bulgaria and it is developing very well. In second place is the combination of instant payments using mobile phones, with a QR code as a means of initiating payment. The combination of these technologies may in the coming years prevail over the spread of card payments in Europe, i.e. instant payments may replace card payments in the medium term in European countries. The third point I would like to address is the so-called open banking. Open banking is associated with relatively new services in both the European and our market. They are already available and this allows us from one entry point, through a specialised provider, to access all our accounts with all banks or non-bank payment service providers, where these are held. Through this single point, maintained by a specialised provider, we can, if desired, order payments through any of these accounts. This is also something that we will talk about and that will increasingly shape the landscape of the payment infrastructure in the medium term in European countries. Host: Will there be new financial institutions to join the instant payments project? Nina Stoyanova: I would like to start with the following: since the beginning of this year, clients credit transfers in the country are performed with an effect close to the instant one. Currently, the execution of a credit transfer in the country takes less than an hour from the order of the transfer to the receipt of the funds by their recipient on his account. With regard to instant payments, in practice this period for the execution of the transfer is up to 10 seconds, which is why they are called instant. The other specificity is that they are available around the clock, not only during the working hours of the banks. Instant payments are an important project for the European infrastructure. In our country we already have five participating banks and two non-bank payment service providers in this instant payments platform, which was developed last year. New banks are expected to join this year and the process is scheduled to be completed by the spring next year. However, I would like to note that a large part of the significant for our country banks are already participating or are about to join and this allows instant payments to be made between their customers even now. Just a few words from a technical point of view: the implementation of these projects in practice introduces the requirements of the SEPA credit transfer standards on the Bulgarian market. SEPA stands for Single Euro Payments Area. This allows us, among all other advantages  such as speed and security of payments  in the future introduction of the euro in the country to realign the payment infrastructure more easily to the requirements of the euro area. These projects in Bulgaria are conducted entirely on a market basis with the participation of the banking community, the BNB and BORICA as a payment system operator. Indeed, the involvement of the whole community is very important and essential for their success. Host: This year the euro celebrates 20 years. We expect it to appear in digital form as well, but what does this mean in practice for us consumers? Nina Stoyanova: Thank you very much for that question. It is quite appropriate to note for your viewers the fact that this year the euro celebrates its 20th anniversary. This means that in 2002, 20 years ago, the euro was introduced in its definitive form as euro banknotes and coins in the countries, which formed the euro area at that time. Today, the euro is used as a means of payment by more than 340 million European citizens. There are 19 euro area Member States, with a tendency to become 20 when Croatia joins the euro area in January next year. Twenty countries out of 27 Member States are to use the euro as a means of payment. The digital euro is a project of great importance. In 2020 the European Central Bank published a report on the digital euro. It was subject to public consultation and a technical study is currently underway on the possible risks and technical and regulatory aspects of the future introduction and issuance of digital euro. It should be noted here that there are many central banks around the world working on digital currency projects, both in larger and smaller countries. So, the central bank digital currency has its place in the future. As for the digital euro and other digital currencies, I should point out that they are not replacing cash, but will coexist with it as another channel for payments and savings. What is interesting about central bank digital currencies, and which is also a subject of research in the case of the euro, is that, as the digital currency is issued by the central bank, this would mean in practice that individuals and companies would be able to have accounts directly with the central bank, something that has not been possible so far. Here, however, a very careful assessment has to be made, so that central banks do not take over the financial intermediation function that commercial banks have, because that is not the purpose. It is considered, therefore, that there should be a certain limit to the funds individuals and entities will be able to hold as digital euros with the central bank, and that the rest of their funds, as before, should be with the commercial banks, because deposits are one of the sources of credit. There are a lot of questions to be answered and the final decision is expected to be taken in the autumn of next year, when this study phase ends. If the euro is introduced as a Bulgarian currency, this will also affect Bulgarian citizens. Host: How much money has been paid online and via POS terminals since the beginning of the year? Nina Stoyanova: Every year we observe an increase in these values, and we can say in general that electronic payments in Bulgaria, even as an average, exceed the average for the European Union in terms of growth in recent years. If the EU average growth rate is around 8%, in Bulgaria we observe an average growth of around 10%. Broken down by individual payment channels, the year-on-year data at the end of the first quarter of this year, compared to the first quarter of last year, show growth rates of 20% for total cashless payments, 50% for payments initiated via a virtual POS terminal (most often made in online shops), and even e-money payments evidence an increase  by nearly 50% year-on-year. Host: Let's move on to the euro and where Bulgaria stands from this point of view. What do the EC and the ECB require from Bulgaria in the area of legislation in order to meet the conditions for euro area accession? Nina Stoyanova: Every two years the European Commission (EC) and the European Central Bank (ECB) publish the so-called convergence reports. These reports examine the economic convergence and the fulfilment of certain legal requirements with regard to the EU Member States that are not yet members of the euro area but have such an obligation to become members. In this regard, the regular reports of the EC and the ECB were published at the beginning of June this year. There are some nonconformities in both the economic and legal part. In the economic part, they must be seen in the light of the consequences of the war in Ukraine and the measures being taken in this regard. However, what is important to note is that Bulgaria has consistently over the years met the economic convergence criteria and this has been taken into account in these regular reports. This compliance gave Bulgaria the opportunity two years ago to join the ERM II with the fixed exchange rate of the BGN to the euro. Then, in October 2020, Bulgaria also joined the Single Supervisory Mechanism and the Single Resolution Mechanism. Also, if this date remains according to the plan for the introduction of the euro in Bulgaria  from January 2024, then in the spring of the following year a new convergence report should be requested to be issued by the EC and the ECB, specifically for Bulgaria, which should again measure the economic and legal compliance as of an actual date at that future time. I believe that if we have a common effort, a common understanding, the introduction of the euro is an achievable goal. I think it is particularly important in this regard to work on a communication campaign, something that is also part of the euro area accession plan, as it is very important to communicate properly to the public what is coming, what the measures that will be taken will be. For example, the dual display of prices for a certain period of time, the dual circulation of currencies, the measures with respect to merchants  so that people can be reassured that something positive is coming. Title: Speech by Ms. Nina Stoyanova, Deputy Governor of the Bulgarian National Bank, Head of the Banking Department, at the opening of the DIGI PAY 2022 conference, Inter Expo Center, 5 October 2022
text: Speech by Ms. Nina Stoyanova, BNB Deputy Governor in charge of the Banking Department, at the opening of the DIGI PAY 2022 Conference, Inter Expo Centre, 5 October 2022 EVOLUTION OF THE MARKET AND THE REGULATIONS IN THE PAYMENTS SECTOR I would like to thank the organisers for the invitation to take part in this event. It is a pleasure for me to open todays conference, which will address important topics related to the development of payment instruments, fraud prevention, and open banking. There is no doubt whatsoever that the current development of the payment market is driven and inspired by the new technologies. We see the positive tendency for payment services to become more and more convenient and accessible, and consumers attitudes are changing in search of fast, secure and convenient digital channels for payments. According to a report of the World Bank, issued in June 2022, in the advanced economies the share of the adults who initiate or receive electronic payments is now nearly 95%, whereas in the developing countries that share increased from 35% in 2014 to 57% in 2021. In recent years, the development of the payment services in Europe was also significantly fostered by the policies pursued by the EU and national regulators. A favourable environment for the development of payment services was created by the Second Payment Services Directive (PSD2), the review of which was launched this year. Along with other important aspects, through this directive the open banking was regulated for the first time, which laid the foundations for the introduction of new business models, services and solutions. Examples for such services are aggregating data on accounts with different payment service providers and initiating payments from accounts led by other payment service providers. The Bulgarian National Bank is an active participant in the regulatory discussions, as a result of which the European Banking Authority (EBA) issues opinions promoting the harmonised treatment of obstacles and issues in open banking across the EU. At the same time, the BNB is actively communicating with the open banking service providers authorised in Bulgaria as well as the banking community, which supports a positive progress in removing identified obstacles with respect to the implemented dedicated interfaces, in compliance with the EBA opinions, the EU-wide practice and the national specificities. The BNB continues to closely monitor the progress in these processes and to seek solutions to issues, together with market participants. Now, after more than four and a half years of the Second Payment Services Directive being in effect, the time has come to assess the impact of its application in the EU countries and the need for amendments and refinement. The consolidation and further standardisation of the regulation of dedicated interfaces is included in the already initiated review of PSD2. In this regard, in August this year ended the public consultation of the European Commission on the review of PSD2 and the gathering of information about a possible new open finance framework, which will build on the existing open banking regulation. The purpose of such a new framework would be to enable, with the customers consent, financial service providers to share and reuse customers data, which fall outside the scope of PSD2, to develop new and enhanced services. The review of PSD2 is expected to include also an assessment of the impact of strong customer authentication on the level of payment frauds. Electronic identification and trust services-based solutions are being explored as means for strong customer authentication. Another innovation that opens the way for new developments, including in the area of payments, are the central bank digital currencies and, more specifically, the digital euro. The digital euro is envisaged to be an electronic form of money issued by the Eurosystem, which will be available to all citizens and companies. The European Central Bank (ECB) is going through an investigation phase regarding the technical and regulatory aspects and the potential risks of a possible future introduction of a digital euro. During this phase, the Eurosystem is actively collaborating with a wide range of stakeholders, at an institutional level as well as with market participants. As stated by Mr. Fabio Panetta, a member of the ECBs Executive Board, a few days ago at the Committee on Economic and Monetary Affairs of the European Parliament (ECON), The combined efforts of the public and private sectors were key to building the European payment system we have today, which is one of the most efficient in the world., and therefore We now need to draw on this cooperation once again in order to build the digital euro ecosystem. The digital euro is expected to give people more choice on how to pay, contribute to the development of new and even more efficient pan-European retail payment solutions and foster financial inclusion. In order to guarantee the function of financial intermediation that commercial banks have, the possibility of a certain limit of the funds that individuals will be able to keep in the form of a digital euro account with the central bank is being considered. The European Central Bank is also actively working on choosing a technical design for the digital euro that will allow its efficient and secure use both online and offline. The final decision on the fate of the digital euro is expected to be made after October 2023, when the investigation phase of the project ends. In Bulgaria, work continues on the development of the payment infrastructure, which aims to both introduce modern technological solutions and guarantee the security of the payment process, as well as preparation for the introduction of the euro. In November of this year, migration to the new consolidated platform for TARGET services of the Eurosystem is expected. It will give access to several services at the same time. The first is the real-time euro settlement service  this is actually the TARGET2 system that we already participate in. The second service is the TARGET2-Securities (T2S) euro securities settlement platform, which is currently separate. A project to connect the Depository of Government Securities at the BNB and Central Depository AD to T2S is in the process of implementation. The T2S platform offers pan-European settlement  of cash and securities, in central bank money. In this way, Bulgarian securities will have a better accessibility for investors from the European Union. The third service in the new consolidated platform is TIPS. It provides access to instant payments in euro, which we should also join when we become part of the euro area. The changes will allow the use of ISO 20022 SWIFT messages, a harmonised access interface and common components across all TARGET services. In addition, early this year, the project for migration of customer credit transfers in BGN to the standards of the Single Euro Payments Area (SEPA) was implemented. Among other technological advantages, this project allowed the execution time of standard customer credit transfers to be reduced to under one hour. In the final phase is the work related to the introduction of the necessary changes regarding payments in the public sector, which are also about to migrate to SEPA standards. This project covers a wide range of tasks related, for example, to defining the structure of budget payments in ISO 20022 format, settlement of budget transfers in the new platform of the BISERA6 payment system for payments in BGN based on SEPA schemes, changes in the Electronic Budget Payments System (SEBRA) and the information exchange in it, etc. The development of payment services in Bulgaria maintains its positive dynamics. According to data from the BNB's payment statistics, which are kept according to the methodology of the ECB's statistics, for the first half of 2022 nearly 370 million non-cash customer payments were initiated in our country, which represents an increase of about 22% compared to the first half of last year. The growth in card payments is even more tangible, with the total number of payments with cards issued in Bulgaria increasing by nearly 32% in the first half of this year compared to the same period in 2021. The number of card payments initiated through virtual POS terminals is growing even more  the increase in the first half of this year is almost 37% compared to the first six months of 2021. Electronic money continues to become more and more popular in our country and the data shows an increase by over 60% in the number of initiated electronic money payments for the first half of 2022 compared to the same period last year. These data clearly show the good development of the financial sector in the country and the change in consumer habits towards increased use of the digital channels. I wish interesting and fruitful work to all participants in today's conference. PAGE \* MERGEFORMAT 3

Title: Publication by Ms. Nina Stoyanova, Deputy Governor of the BNB, Head of the Banking Department, in the quarterly bulletin of the Association of Banks in Bulgaria, issue 72, October 2022
text: QD I O' *anKS in *ulgaria MEMBER OF THE EUROPEAN BANKING FEDERATION #72 QUARTERLY BULLETIN October 2022 Forthcoming developments related to payment and settlement systems Nina Stoyanova Deputy Governor of the BNB, in charge of the Banking Department The payment and settlement systems in Bulgaria continue their development, which aims to both introduce modern technological solutions and guarantee the security of the payment process, as well as preparation for the introduction of the euro in Bulgaria. The Bulgarian National Bank (BNB), the banks and payment systems - participants in the Bulgarian national component system (TARGET2-BNB) of the system for large value payments in euro TARGET2, are actively working to join the new consolidated TARGET Services platform. It will combine on a technical and functional level the TARGET2 payment system, the securities settlement platform TARGET2-Securities (T2S) and the service for instant transfers in euro TIPS, and as of November 2023 also a single Eurosystem Collateral Management System (ECMS). The launch of the consolidated platform in live environment is scheduled for 20 March 2023. The implementation of the new platform is determined by technological innovations in the field of payments, regulatory requirements and the changing needs of the participants. The changes will allow the use of ISO 20022 messages, a harmonized access interface and common components in relation to all TARGET services and will lead to the modernization of the systems and the improvement of their overall efficiency and security. In addition, at the beginning of this year, the project for migration of customer credit transfers in BGN to the standards of the Single Euro Payments Area (SEPA) was implemented. In this way, the processing of these payments went from being settled at a specific time three times a day to being settled throughout the day, within an hour. Thus, in practice, clients transfers in BGN already fulfil the technical and business requirements of the SEPA transfer standards, which also apply to payments in the euro area. Another important project, which started last year and is already in live phase, is for the execution of instant payments in BGN, where transactions are carried out within 10 seconds, 365 days a year, 24 hours a day. Nearly 2/3 of the customer accounts in Bulgaria are now reachable for instant payments. The deadline for migration to the new platform for instant payments in BGN is April 2023. The successful implementation of these projects and the broad participation of the banking community in them are prerequisites for a smooth future migration of all customer payments to payments in euro, in accordance with the standards applicable in the euro area. i oss x i of barns in bulgaria The Bulgarian National Bank, as the regulator and operator of the component system TARGET2-BNB, provides the necessary assistance to BORICA AD in the process of preparing the payment systems operated by the company for the introduction of the euro and ensuring full reachability for banks when executing SEPA customer payments in euro through the BISERA7-EUR system. In October 2022, a working meeting of the subgroup Payment systems and payment service providers1 was held, at which the BNB and BORICA AD clarified issues related to the development of payment systems in the country, in the context of the future introduction of the euro. In order to prepare and organise the migration of payments in the public sector in the country to the SEPA standards, an interdepartmental working group was created, which holds regular meetings. The project covers a wide range of tasks related to defining the structure of budget payments in ISO 20022 format, settlement of budget transfers in the new platform of BISERA6 for payments in BGN, based on the SEPA credit transfer scheme (SCT) of the European Payments Council, optimization of processes of centralization of budget funds, changes in the SEBRA system and the information exchange in it, and others. Changes in payment orders and the way of processing transfers from/to the budget are will affect the banking community, the budget administrators and municipalities. It is envisaged to increase the maximum limit for transfers processed through BISERA6 from BGN 100 000 to BGN 500 000, and at a later stage to completely remove it, in accordance with the SEPA requirements, where payment systems do not have a limit on the value of processed transfer orders. Upon dropping this transaction limit, the large value payment systems in BGN (RINGS) and EUR (TARGET2-BNB) will in practice continue to process mainly interbank credit transfers and settlement requests submitted by the participating payment systems and securities settlement systems. With regard to the securities settlement systems in the country, changes are being prepared in accordance with the measures and activities foreseen in the National Euro Changeover Plan of the Republic of Bulgaria 22, and more specifically, joining of the Depository for Government Securities in the BNB (BNBGSSS) and the Central Depository AD (CD AD) to TARGET2-Securities. In September 2022, an explanatory seminar was held with the banks participating in the BNBGSSS with regard to the activities in the T2S accession project. TARGET2-Securities offers pan-European settlement - of cash and securities, in central bank money. In this way Bulgarian securities will have a better accessibility for investors from the European Union (EU). The T2S platform provides harmonized and standardized settlement services, based on the Delivery vs Payment (DvP) principle, on a real-time gross basis. Currently, 20 European Central Securities Depositories (CSDs) use T2S. In line with the ECB schedule, it is planned that BNBGSSS will join T2S during the next migration window - in September 2023, together with Central Depository AD and 3 other CSDs from the EU. After November 2023 only securities settled in T2S will be able to be used as collateral in the Eurosystems main refinancing operations if they meet the relevant criteria. Link between T2S and ECMS is foreseen, and the #72 October 2022 2 oss x i of barns in bulgaria funds for these operations will be settled on the accounts in the new TARGET Services platform. In accordance with the requirements of the ECB for joining T2S, BNBGSSS and CD AD completed the preparation of the self-assessments of their systems and business processes. In the current fourth quarter of 2022 the signing of Framework Agreements for participation in T2S (T2S Framework Agreement) is also planned. In accordance with the Eurosystems schedule for testing and inclusion of new CSDs in T2S, tests with depositories should begin in December 2022, and tests with the participation of banks - in the second quarter of 2023. Initially, BNBGSSS participants will be included in T2S as indirect participants (Indirectly connected parties) and will continue to send government securities settlement instructions to the BNBGSSS operated system, which, after validation and matching, will be sent to T2S. In this way, the communication between the BNBGSSS and its participants will remain unchanged and this will not require changes in the internal government securities systems operated by the participants. Communication with T2S via messages in XML format (ISO 20022), according to the requirements of the platform, will be a commitment of BNBGSSS. For the settlement of securities transactions in T2S, BNBGSSS will open securities accounts in T2S for its participants. BNBGSSS participants should ensure liquidity in special payment accounts in T2S (Dedicated Cash Accounts) opened at the BNB or at another central bank in the TARGET Services platform. T2S will be accessed through the Eurosystem Single Market Infrastructure Gateway (ESMIG), which will be used for the consolidated platform for TARGET services. In conclusion, it should be noted that the changes in our country fully correspond to the trends in Europe towards the development of a harmonized and integrated financial and payment infrastructure based on common standards and instruments. The intensely ongoing processes, coordinated with all market participants, are a prerequisite for implementing the necessary changes in the payment systems and moving to the settlement of all payments in euro upon the countrys accession to the euro area. 1.
