I hope that this will not happen to the maximum extent in Bulgaria, and I think that the foreign banks, operating here, will pay serious attention to the Bulgarian economy and invest more funds in it. This is a real problem, because in a great number of countries foreign banks do have a considerable share. In Bulgaria this share may soon reach up to 80%, which implies that the whole financial system is dependent on the decisions of the head offices outside Bulgaria. I think that this is a serious problem and I hope it will not be faced by our country. We can not disregard the good experience and the new services offered by them. However, I think that so far the foreign banks have to a large degree fallen in line or operated in tune with the behaviour of Bulgarian banks. Similarly, they are cautious in lending, as they are unwilling to take a high risk, and I would like to see this behaviour changed. We are looking forward to a great event in the beginning of next year. To my mind, this is an event, which will bring about a world-wide change  and this is the introduction of the Euro. I think we are ready to face this great challenge and that it will not cause any disturbances among the public, and of course, within the banking system. In any case, for the time being I have no information whatsoever about any existing problems with regard to the provision of banknotes or information on these banknotes. Anyway, some tension during the first months of introducing the Euro would seem quite normal to expect in Europe and world-wide, but lets hope it does not last too long. The level of deposit guarantee was increased, which to a large extent backs up the mass of deposits within the banking system. I believe that this will strengthen the public confidence and will boost up deposit growth. This, on the one hand, will have a positive effect, and on the other  will create a problem: you will be at a loss as to how to handle the funds thus collected, given the sufficient resources that you already have. This has its good and its bad side. Nevertheless, I believe that the economy has taken a good direction and there are already large companies, both local and foreign, which can use funding from the banking system. I do not know why we still rely on the stability pact, which, to my mind, is just an idea  we have only been listening about projects for over two years now. I, personally, have not seen any such project implemented. We discussed the reduction in the minimum reserve requirement. The development of the banking system does not need any abrupt changes as this would only bring about, time and again, pressure on the foreign exchange market in a direction of foreign currency demand. However, we have not given up completely the idea, or the discussions of any such ideas. I think it would be good to discuss the possibility of differentiation, reduction of the minimum required reserve against the long-term deposits, held by banks. I will reiterate that in the next year I hope there will be no disruptions. I think that we have sufficient reserves to meet both economy development and the enhancement of its efficiency, so there is no need to revise any exchange rates or abandon the Currency Board Arrangement. Our way of walking out of the currency board will be the accession to the Euro. When I say the Euro, I certainly do not mean euroisation. With our accession to the EU, and our participation in the European System of Central Banks we will in effect walk out of the currency board. That is the most favourable exit for Bulgaria. I would like to wish you much health and success. PAGE PAGE 3

Title: Presentation at the Seminar on Currency Boards  Experience and Prospects organised by Bank of Estonia, Tallinn
Subtitle: EXIT STRATEGIES FROM CURRENCY BOARD ARRANGEMENTS
text: Presentation by Mr. Roumen Avramov, Member of the Managing Board of the BNB, at the Seminar on Currency Boards  Experience and Prospects organised by Bank of Estonia, Tallinn, 5-6 May 2000 EXIT STRATEGIES FROM CURRENCY BOARD ARRANGEMENTS 1. The Changing Perspective on Exit Strategies  From Return to Normality to Transitional Step 1.1. With their revival, in the early 90s, CBA have been widely considered as a deviation from normality. This judgement was based on several, basically correct but somewhat fragmentary historical parallels and assumptions: That a CBA is a punishment for an irresponsible monetary policy in the past. That it is a sort of gold-standard enclave in the modern monetary system. That a CBA has colonial roots and hence it can be considered as an atavism in the realm of the diversity of modern monetary nationalism. Any one of those points of view confirmed the perception of CBA as an aberration, a temporary arrangement, and a monetary constitution that should be removed sooner or later. Hence the textbook exit problem. 1.2. A perceptible change of the perspective on CBA has been observed during the last years. It was supported by different, sometimes unrelated developments. The success stories of countries that introduced CBA  Honk-Kong, Argentina, Estonia, Bulgaria. Although the reasons for success are different, the underlying common factor is the stabilising effect of CBA. The fact that CBA faced successfully the Asian and the Russian financial crises. The global trend towards a simplification of the world monetary system with the emergence of more clearly delineated currency areas. The institutionalisation of the Euro has been a major step in this direction. The spreading understanding that discretionary monetary policy is not the best and sustainable option for small open economies. The growing debate on the Pros and Cons of an early unilateral introduction of the Euro and/or on the dollarization in Latin America. 1.3. A more balanced, and certainly a more positive, image of CBA emerged from those developments. Backward looking  CBA proved to be an extremely effective instrument in dealing with economies having a poor track record in monetary policy management. Forward looking  CBA are increasingly considered as a natural transitional stage towards a monetary union. They even present many advantages compared to the conventional scheme for a classical central bank. In this perspective a CBA is not longer seen as an aberration, but rather as a logical step inherent to a global trend. 2. The Risks 2.1. CBA could be defined as a long-term investment (a specific social contract) in a stable monetary constitution. It entails costs in terms of lost monetary sovereignty and hence, in lost instruments of adjustment. In order to yield a positive return, this investment is expected to increase  not to decrease  the monetary stability at maturity. The stability culture developed during CBA should be preserved. An exit from CBA is a risky operation in two main respects. A non-managed scenario could undermine (even annihilate) the stabilisation acquis accumulated during the CBA period. As a rule-operated system, CBA is highly sensitive to any perspective of changes in the accepted conventions. Uncertainties surrounding the exit perspective may have a strong destabilising effect. The main risk stems from the possibility to re-introduce a floating exchange rate. Even if the rate towards non-reserve currencies is not fixed under CBA, the economy has lost its reflexes to adjust trough parity changes and to behave in a floating rate context. A return to this regime could easily produce an overshooting. Even worse  a publicly pre-announced perspective of re-introduction of floating could be considered as an official invitation for a speculative attack against the national currency. It will inevitably generate growing expectations and pressures for devaluation. According to common sense rules, among a set of possible strategies to attain a specific goal optimal is the simplest one with the lowest transitional costs. If the desirable outcome of an exit strategy is the highest standards of monetary stability, they should be attained with minimum deviations and risky, superfluous movements. In an EU framework the question is why make an apprentissage of something which will not be utilised  why re-test a monetary system (full-fledged Central bank) if this system will be abandoned with the adoption of the Euro. 3. Possible Options  The General Framework 3.1. Theoretically, the options for an exit from a CBA are two: first, return to a central bank regime with autonomous monetary policy; second, join a monetary union. The first possibility presents CBA as a transitional arrangement the main goals of which have been exhausted with the achievement of macroeconomic and monetary stability. This exit corresponds to a narrow understanding of CBA as a strictly stabilisation device. It supposes that the immediate causes of financial instability have been removed and that the country is able to operate a monetary system with the full set of adjustment instruments. The second option puts CBA in the context of its intrinsic development logic. CBA is considered as a stage in the evolution of the monetary system towards a monetary union. The option of a unilateral adoption of the Euro before accession to the EU is not discussed as it represents a truncated monetary union (a surrogate implantation of the Euro) that eliminates the institutional benefits of an authentic monetary union. 4. Possible Options  The EU Context 4.1. As an acceding country to the EU, Bulgaria faces the imperative perspective to join the Euro area i.e. to complete a monetary union. This understanding has been explicitly incorporated in the Bulgarian National Bank Law with the choice of the DEM as a reserve currency in 1997 and by the eventual adoption of the Euro as a reserve currency since January 1 of 1999. Any institutional framework that departs from this path is counter-productive and/or backward oriented. Thus the CBA should be primarily assessed from the point of view of its compliance to the basic requirements of a future monetary union: An institutional modelling of the national central bank that matches the existing institutional framework in the new currency area. A transfer of monetary sovereignty. A closer coordination of the macroeconomic policy with that in the core countries. A reshaping of the monetary and financial instruments in line with those in the new currency area. 4.2. It has been widely acknowledged that in the context of EU/EMU accession CBA rises many conceptual, economic and legal problems. The issue has been addressed in various circumstances in 1999. As since the Helsinki Summit there are four CBA economies among the 12 acceding countries (the Latvian case could be treated as CBA-like economy) the point becomes increasingly relevant. The position of the Governing Council of the ECB, expressed on April 13 by ECB Vice-President Christian Noyer marks a substantial advance in the debate. It takes into account the peculiarity of CBA, accepts the need for a flexible approach and for the first time officializes the possibility to introduce less orthodox arrangements. This position answers many of the concerns formulated by the Central banks of CBA countries in previous occasions. Obviously, much remains to be done in order to concretise and to develop this conceptual scheme. Numerous details should be discussed before reaching a clear-cut agreement on every specific case. Thus, it is worth to try summarising pending issues. At this relatively early stage of the path to EMU it is important to follow two principles: Not to discard any option a priori if it meets the basic principles of the Treaty. To refrain to oppose legalistic logic to economic logic. Every solution that corresponds to economic rationality should be explored in view of a possible, legally acceptable arrangement. 4.3. It is essential to assess strictly the assets and the liabilities of CBA in their particular quality of transitional arrangements towards the EMU acquis. Three are the main assets: High standards of independence of the central bank, compatible with Treaty requirements. Prohibition of monetary financing of government deficits and privileged access of public authorities to financial institutions. Strictly fixed exchange rate to the Euro. While those issues are of fundamental importance, an ambiguous area remains. It concerns the modality and the timing of the interface between CBA and the Euro zone. The focal controversy arises from what might be called the CBA-compatibility problem with two main aspects. The most visible issue is the ERM-II problem  how to reconcile the more flexible parameters of this exchange rate mechanism with the realm of fixed rates, proper to the acceding countries before (under CBA regimes) and after EU accession (with the adoption of the Euro). ERM-II makes CBA incompatible with EU membership by simply re-introducing the float. A broader (more substantial) issue is the compatibility of CBA with the Statute of the ESCB concerning the set of eligible instruments and the scope of allowed monetary policy. A careful reading of the texts related to the ESCB and ERM-II in the light of the special case of CBA-countries is extremely insightful, both as a starting point and as a source of questions. 4.4. ESCB-related problems Art.14 of the Protocol (N.3) on the Statute of the ESCB and of the ECB indicates that Member states shall ensure, at the latest at the date of the establishment of the ESCB, that their national legislation, including the statutes of their NCB, is compatible with the Treaty and the Statute. As the ESCB was established in June 1998, the corollary is that EU membership of the acceding countries is incompatible with a statute of their NCB that departs from the Statute. Every NCB becomes a member of the ESCB from the moment of accession to EU, although the member states with derogation participate in the ESCB on a restricted basis. An exception from this principle, however, exists. In the Convergence Report of March 1998 the Swedish case is treated in a special manner. It is recognised that the legal integration of the Sveriges Riksbank in the ESCB is not anticipated in the draft legislation by the date of the establishment of the ESCB. This was required in order the legislation to become effective as from the date of the adoption of the single currency. Alternatively, the mainstream case of Greece addresses both the periods in which the NCB is not an integral part of ESCB as well as the situation in which the country has adopted the Euro. The common logic behind those two cases is the principle of a double-step procedure  preparation of the legal integration of the NCB into the ESCB; activation of the amendments in the moment of accession to the Euro area. The two stages are clearly outlined. A membership in the ESCB supposes the availability of monetary functions and operations of the NCB. This means, in particular, the performance of open market and credit operations, which contradicts the basic principles of CBA. At the same time, countries with derogation shall retain their powers in the field of monetary policy according to national law. (Art. 43.2) There are two possible readings of this text. First, it is tacitly assumed that the Central bank is a classical one and that it performs monetary functions, with the transitional provision (Art.43) that the instruments (very traditional ones) are not subordinated to the ECB. Second, following the 1998 Convergence Report, national monetary policy instruments are to be compared with those contained in the Treaty and Statute and incompatibilities need to be removed: strictu sensu incompatibility means the presence of unacceptable instruments but not necessarily the absence of acceptable ones (the CBA case). A more far-reaching stipulation indicates that credit operations will be based on adequate collateral. This means that the national financial system should be mature enough to provide instruments of the standards and quality required by the ECB. Two CBA-related conclusions could be drawn from this re-reading. The independence acquis concerning NCB should be in place by the date of the accession to the EU. The NCB preparation for its legal integration in the ESCB (EMU acquis) is desirable and feasible before the EU accession. The activation of the corresponding legislation, however, is possible only with the accession to the Euro area. This could be interpreted as an implicit possibility to maintain a CBA until the adoption of the Euro. The crucial economic pre-conditions for the activation of the EMU-related acquis and the adoption of the Euro are macroeconomic stability and the smooth functioning of financial markets and the overall financial infrastructure in acceding countries. Those requirements can be met before/at/after the EU accession. 4.5. ERM-II related problems ERM-II exists on two levels  conceptual and functional. The first one formulates the basic principles as they were adopted in Amsterdam (16 June 1997) by the Resolution of the European Council on the Establishment of an Exchange Rate Mechanism in the Third Stage of EMU. The operative level exists as a concrete agreement (1 September 1998) between the ECB and the NCB of the Member States outside the Euro area (namely Denmark and Greece). Although many of Amsterdam Resolution texts are directly inserted in the agreement it is clear that the clauses of ERM-II are negotiable within the scope of the basic principles. The raison detre of ERM-II is to discipline the use of the monetary policy instruments left at the discretion of NCB in the countries with derogation. This is achieved by subordinating them to one goal  the convergence towards the macroeconomic policy in the Euro area. It is easy to demonstrate that this logic matches completely the logic of CBA. Let us recall that the ERM-II principles formulated in Amsterdam are the following: Lasting convergence of economic fundamentals as a prerequisite for sustainable exchange rate stability. To this end, in the third stage all Member states must pursue disciplined and responsible monetary policies directed towards price stability. Sound fiscal and structural policies are, at least, equally essential for sustainable exchange rate stability. Stable economic environment in order to eliminate exchange rate misalignments or excessive nominal fluctuations. Help to ensure that participating Member states outside the Euro area orient their policies to stability, foster convergence and thereby help them in efforts to adopt the Euro. It will provide those Member states with a reference for their conduct of sound economic policies in general and monetary policy in particular. At the same time the mechanism will also protect them and the Member states adopting the Euro from unwarranted pressures in the foreign exchange markets. The above principles represent an almost textbook description of the aims of a CBA. On economic terms both mechanisms pursue the same goal from different starting points. An Euro-based CBA reaches them top down as it has introduced tight monetary frames that go even beyond the EMU framework. ERM-II reaches the same goals from below, trough a more gradual fix of the macroeconomic policy by the exchange rate anchor to the Euro. From the perspective of a CBA-acceding country some details in ERM-II are of crucial importance. The Amsterdam decision indicates that the participation in ERM-II is voluntary and/or can be deferred as a Member state may decide to participate at a later date. Although the historical context of this decision is clear, and that it is qualified with the statement that member states with derogation can be expected to join the mechanism, it introduces an important reference for acceding countries. The principle of automatic interventions at the edge of the fluctuation bands does not contradict directly CBA fundamentals as it materialises in very short-term credit facilities between NCB and the ECB. What does not fit in a CBA framework is the possibility to agree coordinated intramarginal interventions that supposes the flexible use of interest rates. Formally agreed fluctuation bands narrower than the standard one and backed up in principle by automatic interventions and financing may be set at the request of the Member states concerned. Developed to its logical extreme this principle leads to the elegant Estonian proposal to agree 0% fluctuation bands. Although this solution is very appealing, it is very difficult to conceive an operational framework for it in the case of a binding obligation for the ECB. In fact, such an agreement would force the ECB to intervene continuously in order to support the de facto fixed exchange rate to the Euro. In any case, the option to agree narrower bands stresses the similitude between ERM-II and a CBA. The Treaty foresees a two-year report by the Commission and the ECB on the observation of the convergence criteria in the countries with derogation. This term could be shortened at the request of the concerned Member State. Thus the lifting of the derogation could occur earlier and the period under ERM-II could be shortened. It is often argued that ERM-II constitutes a market test for the equilibrium exchange rate and the sustainability of the monetary policy in an EU framework. In fact this is not exactly the case. The central rate is a parity agreed between the governments of the Member States, the ECB and the NCB - although the rate could reflect the prevailing market level before ERM-II membership, a wide non-market discretionary margin remains in the determination of the central rate. Furthermore, the exchange mechanism is clearly not a test under a floating regime as it allows automatic interventions (at the edge or intra-marginal) and the foreseen fluctuation bands are relatively narrow. Rather the contrary, ERM-II is a test of the exchange rate stability in circumstances, which are very close to the tough restrictions of a fixed exchange rate. If there is something that a successful CBA demonstrates it is precisely the capacity of the economy to behave under such a regime. Finally, the historical context for the setting out of ERM-II should be carefully assessed. The mechanism was conceived in 1996  1997 as an answer to a well-defined specific problem  the fact that some Member States may not participate in the Euro area due to non-fulfilment of the convergence criteria. ERM-II regulates the relationships between ins and pre-in members with the aim to build a monetary stability framework between the Euro and the non-Euro area currencies in the EU. Clearly, the focus has been on an internal EU issue and on the possible difficulty for some countries to meet the macroeconomic pre-conditions for the participation in the Euro area. Two conclusions can be formulated from this brief discussion. ERM-II terms are negotiable and thus subject to specific agreements in the frame of some general principles. In extremis those principles allow the non-activation of ERM-II (voluntarity principle) or the arrangement of an ERM-II compatible design with a fixed exchange rate. Nothing precludes the possibility to attain the inherent goals of ERM-II, to meet the convergence criteria and to achieve the needed financial stability for the accession to the Euro area under a mechanism different from ERM-II and/or before accession to the EU. 5. Summary  Entry Strategies The relevant problem for acceding CBA-countries is not the exit but the entry strategy into the Euro area. The following brief summary is formulated without ruling out any option on the basis of a priori assumptions. Accordingly, it is understood that each case should be treated individually. 5.1. The path already advanced publicly by the ECB, at least for the non-CBA acceding countries, is the three-stage continuum including pre-accession to the EU, EMU membership with a derogation and full EMU membership. In broad terms it replicates the scheme followed by Greece in 1998  2000. Under this option nothing prevents to keep the CBA till EU accession. It is clear from the above discussion, however, that this scheme does not deal in a satisfactory way with the problems related to the transitional period between the accession to the EU and the adoption of the single currency. That option is less acceptable to CBA countries. 5.2. A hybrid strategy could be explored. This approach seems much more plausible after the recently expressed positions of the Governing Council of ECB. It consists in the search for an arrangement that can retain the basic features of a CBA (fixed exchange rate; freezing of the monetary policy instruments; elimination of monetary financing of government deficits) beyond the accession to the EU, until the adoption of the Euro. The legal preparation for the integration of the NCB into the ESCB should be achieved during this transitional period in order to be activated at the moment of the accession in the Euro area. The required but unfinished structural reforms should be completed in the meantime - the assumption is that CBA economies will mature during this interim period. The details of such an arrangement could be discussed during the accession negotiations. It is clear that they should incorporate the individual peculiarities of the different economies. 5.3. Finally, a theoretical possibility that could be explored in terms of its compatibility with the Treaty is the simultaneous (concurrent) accession in the EU and the Euro area. This option simply eliminates the ERM-II problem. Obviously, there are no precedents and the proposal may seem even provocative. Its feasibility is subject to numerous pre-conditions. A successful functioning of the CBA till the accession to EU. Fulfilment of the convergence criteria. The fixed exchange rate to the Euro under the CBA regime should be considered as a fulfilment of the exchange rate criterion. Legal integration of the NCB in the ESCB should be prepared in advance. As some of the principles in the Statute of the ESCB contradict the fundamentals of a CBA the prepared legislation could be treated as dormant and activated in the moment of accession. An important portion of the EMU-related legislation could enter into force before accession. Overall and sustainable macroeconomic stability should be attained. The financial markets and the available instruments should meet the ECB/EU standards. The basic structural reforms should have been completed. The outlined hypothesis rests on the understanding that many of the goals of the preparation stage for EMU can be attained ex ante. It is clear that the failure to meet any one of the pre-conditions makes this exit strategy unfeasible. In a broader sense, however, the possible viability of this approach transcends the CBA case by touching the accession strategy under different monetary regimes. Such an option could meet the growing aspiration of acceding countries for shortening the accession period to the Euro area. PAGE PAGE 1

Title: Speech published at the Banker Newspaper
Subtitle:
THE CURRENCY BOARD ARRANGEMENT REMAINS
EVEN AFTER BULGARIA'S ACCESSION TO THE EU
text: Interview given by Mr. Bojidar Kabakchiev, Deputy Governor of the Bulgarian National Bank, published at the Banker Newspaper, issue 21/29 May - 4 June 2000 THE CURRENCY BOARD ARRANGEMENT REMAINS EVEN AFTER BULGARIA'S ACCESSION TO THE EU Mr. Kabakchiev, at what stage is the agreement between Bulgaria and the European Union on the chapters that the BNB is negotiating? Now our countrys position on individual topics, including Chapter 11 on the Economic and Monetary Union, is being prepared. The BNB actively participates in the working group preparing Bulgarias position on this topic. In early April a delegation of the BNB visited the European Central Bank. The major issue that we discussed at the meetings was the scheme for our countrys accession to the European Monetary Union. We shared our view that Bulgaria must retain the CBA for the period between its accession to the EU and its joining to the European Monetary Union. To join that union, under the current scheme, the EU member countries must keep the so-called Exchange Rate Mechanism 2 (ERM2) for a certain period of time. We believe that the currency board arrangement can fully replace this mechanism and it even has some advantages over it. What is this exchange rate mechanism (ERM2)? It obliges the applying country to keep a floating rate of its currency, which within two years should not fluctuate by over 15% against the Euro. At present Greece is maintaining such an exchange rate mechanism. This mechanism also operates in Denmark, but there the band is smaller /- 2%. This scheme, however, has been developed for countries without a CBA. Bulgaria, Estonia, Lithuania and Latvia are the first countries with CBAs to be negotiating for accession to the European Union. Our official position was shared with the European Central Bank during our meeting on 10 April 2000. Up to that moment the ECB had no explicit opinion on that matter. At the official press conference, held on 13 April, representatives of the ECB formulated a position that conforms completely to our own. At the same press conference they stated also that the ECB was against any unilateral adoption of the Euro by any country which is not a member of the European Monetary Union. The BNB agrees that the rapid unilateral adoption of the Euro is undesirable and inappropriate. What are the disadvantages of adopting the Euro as an official currency in Bulgaria? The BNB is going to lose the revenues from the seignorage. But this is not the most important thing. I emphasise that the introduction of the Euro must be coordinated with the European Central Bank. Is this obligatory? No, it isnt obligatory, but its advisable. The opposite would be, as Mr. Roumen Avramov (member of the BNBs Managing Board) said, an uncivilised barbarous act. What is the position of Estonia, for example, on retaining the CBA till the county joins the European Monetary Union? On 4 and 5 May in Tallinn there was a meeting of representatives of the countries with CBAs which are applying for membership in the European Union. It was also attended by representatives of the ECB and other countries with CBAs, such as Argentina and Hong Kong. The schemes of joining the EU and the European Monetary Union were discussed. It seems that Estonia is inclined to accept the option which the BNB and the Bulgarian Government support. What is your explanation of the heated discussions on abandoning the currency board arrangement, which are periodically held in the press? It is interesting that they discuss a problem which does not exist. So far I have not heard any serious arguments for abandoning the currency board arrangement. I have met businessmen saying that the CBA hinders them very much. However no one of them could answer me what exactly bothers them. Do you have an answer to this question  who is hindered by the currency board arrangement and in what way? No. I only see advantages. Does our accession to the European Monetary Union imply an abandonment of the currency board arrangement? After our accession to the European Monetary Union, the currency board arrangement will be removed. Nevertheless we must be aware that we may only be approved in at least seven years time. There is, however, another more curious question: what is the currency board arrangement in our country? This is the core policy which European central banks pursue, clothed in a law. European central banks do not finance their governments. The refinancing of banks is allowed, but it is only provided against extremely high guarantees. Once the BNB has joined the family of European central banks, it will become a normal central bank with the normal set of instruments typical of such an institution in an EMU member country. Interviewer: Peter Illiev. PAGE PAGE 2

Title: Interview published at the Banker weekly
Subtitle: WE CAN ALREADY DO WITHOUT LOANS FROM THE IMF
text: Interview given by Mr. Svetoslav Gavriiski, Governor of the Bulgarian National Bank, published at the Banker weekly, issue 17/28 April - 4 May 2001 WE CAN ALREADY DO WITHOUT LOANS FROM THE IMF Mr. Gavriiski, what will be the face of the banking sector in the next couple of years? Its larger part has passed into the hands of foreign capitals. Do small banks have the chance to survive the pressure of competition? The banks in Bulgaria are not so many in number and, in my view, each one of them can find its place under the sun. There is a huge need of financing for small and medium-sized enterprises, and this niche could be occupied by the credit institutions with smaller assets and capitals. However, if anybody believes that they could survive by granting one or two loans only, they are totally wrong. The growing competition of the large credit institutions would of course imply that the smaller ones would begin to consolidate. But as yet there are no indications of similar processes starting in the banking sphere. There is some talk in the financial circles that NEFTINVESTBANK and EUROBANK are about to merge? I hear them talking of a purchase, not a merger. You mean that NEFTINVESTBANK is buying EUROBANK? This is what they say. What is your personal assessment of the offer, which HEBROSBANK made for the purchase of BIOCHIM? I am not a member of the Board of Directors of the Bank Consolidation Company, but I think that the offer must be considered very carefully. Now the privatisation of BIOCHIM is not a pressing matter, and the bank should be sold only if the BCC would receive an extremely good offer. After all, we are talking about one of the biggest banks in Bulgaria. I personally would prefer it to be bought by a large strategic investor. Do you think that if another tender should be held for BIOCHIM, strategic investors might turn up? If you can recall, with the current tender a few large West European credit institutions showed an interest in the bank, among them were Austria Bank, BNP-Pariba, Banco Nazionale del Lavoro, but eventually no one of these submitted an offer? There are reasons for this. The period when the offers had to be submitted coincided with deals of the same large banks in the Czech Republic, Poland and Slovakia. Representatives of some of these banks even said that they would withdraw from the tender for BIOCHIM because they were unable to carry out any serious due diligence having focused their efforts in other East European countries. Besides, there was some negative perception of the financial condition of BIOCHIM, which was not true. Only now it has become clear that this is a stable bank with large capital and high earnings, a bank with large potential. Therefore, I believe that HEBROSBANKs current offer for BIOCHIM must be examined very carefully. Mr. Gavriiski, with the approach of the elections, the comments on the condition of the economy and the banking sector will become more and more aggressive. What is your assessment of the banking system position at the moment and, more generally, of the economy? There is hardly anyone in Bulgaria who still doubts the stability of the banking sector, and in my opinion, this year it will continue to increase the lending. As regards the economy as a whole, almost all discussions at the meetings of the EU at Malmo and the EBRD in London cited Bulgaria as an example of a country with a stable economy, which at the same time is among the countries with the highest GDP growth. To my mind, these are the realities, irrespective of the commentaries that may be made during the pre-election debates. I think that in Bulgaria the economy is no longer influenced by political forecasts, by predictions of collapses, nor by negative expectations of what might happen after the elections. I think that the people here are able to make a real evaluation of what they have been through over the past four years. The final evaluation will show that the economic policy chosen and pursued over recent years was right, and the people will not be misled by empty promises or some catastrophic projections. All can see that the currency board is working well; the fixed exchange rate has no negative impact on the economy. What should be done from now on is to encourage investments, develop the businesses, and create new jobs. Even so, dont you have any concerns that after the elections the distribution of forces in the new parliament might change, and we may see a turnabout in the current economic policy? In my opinion, such a turnabout cannot happen. The policy being pursued by Bulgaria now is followed by almost all states seeking an EU membership. There arent any serious alternatives to it, and the people in power, whoever they are, will have to keep this in mind, if they still aim to get Bulgaria into the Union. The only possibility left to the politicians is to make more effective the measures leading to stabilisation and to reduction in the foreign debt and the inflation. Any sharp change in the current economic priorities would bring a collapse, not an improvement in the business climate in this country. However, some political power might decide that it is able to maintain financial stabilisation not with the currency board in place, but with a floating exchange rate? The abandonment of the currency board is no longer discussed and should not be discussed further. After the consultations that we had with the European Central Bank, it announced its position that the fixed exchange rate is not a constraint on the development of the economy. On the contrary, it is a factor of stability and each change in the current conditions, even a discussion on this matter, may cause disruptions in the forex market and raise the inflation. What do you think, is it absolutely necessary for Bulgaria to have a new agreement with the IMF? The international financial institutions do not think that Bulgaria in all cases needs an agreement with the Fund. Nobody of course is denying that our country has to continue its co-operation with the IMF, and mostly with the World Bank, especially regarding the loans that we need to finance the ongoing structural reforms. But these are loans for specific projects, this is not financing for the balance of payments of this country. At present Bulgaria does not need the loans we used to receive from the IMF in order to cope with the service of our foreign debt obligations. The Fund itself is ready to sign an agreement with Bulgaria if we think that we would need its financial aid. In my view, it will be most appropriate for us to sign an agreement, which would allow us to take loans from the IMF only if they were extremely necessary. But if Bulgaria has no agreement with the IMF, wouldnt that deter foreign investors? I repeat again that absolutely nobody puts the question or discusses whether Bulgaria will have or not an agreement with the Fund. Such a problem exists no more. All investment banks offer us to issue euro bonds for our country. So, these banks believe that our country is able, on its own, to service both its current and new foreign obligations. You should agree that there hardly would be any investor to offer us the issuance of euro bonds if he would suspect that we may need IMF loans to pay them. Will Bulgaria, then, issue any euro bonds by the end of this year? Now Bulgaria does not need any new external loans. We expect to receive one more tranche from the IMF, and no more. When preparing the balance of payments and the budget for this year, we decided that our country does not need any additional financing. We have not planned to issue any euro bonds by the end of the year either. This will probably happen next year, but all countries with stable economies get financed through euro bonds. There is no country that can exist without using loans from international financial markets. Interviewer: Peter Illiev PAGE PAGE 1

Title: Statement at a Press Conference held at the Central bank
text: Statement of the BNBs Governor, Mr. Svetoslav Gavriiski at a Press Conference held at the Central bank, 11 May 2000 First of all I would like to welcome you! I see that the room is full of people, and this shows that the topic of todays meeting rouses much interest. As was announced, today we will present the official position of the BNBs Managing Board on major issues of the central banks policy on which uncommitted opinions and frivolous interpretations have been expressed lately. I am talking about the currency board arrangement, its current condition, the presence or absence of some scenarios for abandoning it, rumours of changes in the legislation, of negotiations about its removal given the future accession of Bulgaria to the EU and the EMU, etc. Please let me remind you that in the past year the CBA in Bulgaria has been functioning under not too good an external environment. I mean the external events which adversely affected our economy: world-wide financial crises, the war near our western border last year, increased petrol prices in international markets, and the devaluation of the Euro in the last few months. With all these unfavourable factors, the CBA proved its right of existence by protecting our country from collapses and sharp negative implications. Moreover, our improved credit rating suggests that Bulgaria achieved financial stability, and the current developments give us reasons to believe that this stability will persist in the years to come. Ungrounded critical comments and impersonally stated views on the strengths and weaknesses of the CBA would hardly provoke any discussion. And yet, if now anyone raises the question of the exit from this system, would he be so kind as to explain on whose behalf he is speaking, and the most important thing, what arguments he has to support his view. I have not heard of any political party, governmental or public institution in Bulgaria to have set such a requirement. Neither the BNB nor the Government have discussed the exit from the CBA. Furthermore, if we look at the official programmes and current statements of the parliamentary-presented political powers, we will definitely see that they all do not oppose to this system; on the contrary, they openly insist on preserving it. I will present to you some statistics in support of my thesis. The CBA has existed in Bulgaria for three years, and during that period we have witnessed a continuous increase in our foreign currency reserves. It has been so this year as well. Early in the year the reserve was DEM 6,272 million, and at present it is DEM 6,165 million. Practically, there is no change regardless of the fact that since the beginning of the year 2000 DEM 800 million has been paid on foreign debts of Bulgaria. In this sense, the CBA has asserted itself both as a system and as a fixed exchange rate level, since this level does not impede the operation of the economy. This is, briefly, the domestic picture. There were rumours in the media which linked the existence of the currency board arrangement with Bulgarias negotiations for accession to the EU and EMU, i.e. that the EU had laid down the condition of our abandoning the CBA and that the BNB were preparing options for this. I would like to stress right away that the existence of the CBA in Bulgaria has no connection whatsoever with our accession to the European Union. Things stand as follows. The EU and the EMU has not so far accepted any country with a currency board arrangement. Such a system has not existed in any of the member states at the time they applied for membership in the EU and the EMU. Three countries of the new twelve candidates have a CBA. These are Bulgaria, Lithuania and Estonia. Therefore, a new point comes up in the negotiations and a need for new mechanisms to be developed. The institutions of both the applying countries and our EC partners understand the need to consider this situation and take a decision on how to proceed further. This was the topic of the unofficial talks which some people interpreted as negotiations and freely completed with scenarios devised by themselves. We welcome the position of the ECB Board of 13 April 2000 in principle admits the possibility of the CBA being preserved in some countries after they have joined the EU and till their accession to the EMU. I am going to give you a few more clarifications in this respect. The EU Exchange Rate Mechanism requires that a country keep a stable exchange rate for at least two years before its accession to EMU, with a maximally acceptable fluctuation band of /- 15%. During that period the country must come to meet the other criteria of the Maastricht Treaty. Only after these conditions have been complied with, the Euro may be adopted as an official legal tender. If we should follow the logic of this procedure, we should introduce a floating exchange rate for a short time, and then fix it back. Apparently the specified procedure has been designed for countries in different conditions, and we believe that its mechanical application in our case will be of no benefit either to us or to the EU. In our discussions with the ECB we advanced the view that we could go through the pre-in phase retaining the fixed exchange rate, and the CBA system respectively. I have already mentioned the ECB position of 13 April 2000 which shows that the arguments of the central banks of Bulgaria, Lithuania and Estonia have been taken into account. Therefore I wish to strongly emphasize that with the ECB and the EU we have not been discussing Bulgarias exit from the CBA, but what will be the procedure for the countries having CBAs in place at the time of the negotiations for accession. Our talks in Frankfurt have not finished yet. We keep on our contacts with the ECB about the accession problems. The BNB has set up a working group, headed by the Deputy Governor, Mr. Bojidar Kabakchiev, and the Board member, Mr. Roumen Avramov, to consider this issue. PAGE PAGE 2

Title: Answers to the questions of Universal News, New York correspondent
Subtitle: Universal News: Mr. Governor, what do you think about such a vision: Bulgaria - the success story of the Balkans. Financial and economic stability.
text: Answers given by BNB Governor Mr. Svetoslav Gavriiski to the qestions of Universal News, New York correspondent Ms. Blanca Santos, November 2000 Universal News: Mr. Governor, what do you think about such a vision: Bulgaria - the success story of the Balkans. Financial and economic stability. Bulgarias economic development in the 1990s should be looked at in the light of the global and regional trends formed in that period. First of all I would like to say that the transition from centrally planned to market-oriented economy is an unprecedented process. This transformation process has no analogue in the world economic history and poses enormous challenges to the economic theory and policy. Another distinctive feature of Bulgarias transition is the fact that during this transformation, besides the internal challenges, our country was faced with numerous external challenges. In the 1990s we witnessed a series of financial crises (the ERM crisis 1992-93, the Mexican crisis 1994-95, the Asian crisis 1997-98, the Russian crisis 1998), and these directly and indirectly affected the Bulgarian economy. It was not only the financial crises which had an impact - the political situation on the Balkans in that period was extremely unstable. The four wars in the former Yugoslavia had a strong negative effect on the investment climate in the region. They considerably restricted the possibilities of Balkan countries to compete for foreign investments with other economies under transformation (primarily the Central European countries). In the 1990s the other Balkan countries also developed in the environment described above, except Greece and Turkey which were not faced with the challenges of the transition from centrally planned to market economy. A comparison of the basic macroeconomic indicators of the countries in the region enables us to say that Bulgaria is an example of a successful transition to market economy (Table 1). Our country achieved financial stability overcoming the macroeconomic misbalances typical of transforming economies. UN: Stability factors. Currency board arrangement, inflation, interest rates, government balance, banking system The transition to market economy entails profound institutional and structural changes in the economy. The achieved economic stability in the country is a result of the consistent policy of reforms which began after the severe economic crisis at the end of 1996 and early 1997. Bulgarias transition to market economy started in the same year when this process began in other Central and East European countries. In the period 1991-1996 the process of economic changes was not consistent, and it often deviated from the principles generally accepted and applied in other countries. Because of this inconsistency and the delay of reforms the country ended in a severe financial and economic crisis at the end of 1996 and early 1997. Confronted with this unprecedented financial and economic crisis Bulgaria undertook full-scope and consistent institutional and structural changes in the economy, including the introduction of a currency board arrangement (CBA). The CBA should not be looked at separately from its accompanying measures, which ensure its successful functioning. The balanced state budget, the stabilisation of the banking system and the CBA operation rapidly brought down the inflation and interest rates. In this respect Bulgaria is a good example of fast financial stabilisation based on a CBA. The initial effects of the financial stabilisation were followed by restored lending to the private sector and households, higher incomes and consumption and, consequently, higher economic growth. UN: Privatisation of state-owned banks; condition of the banking sector; BNBs role as a regulator of this sector The stabilisation of the banking sector after the deep banking crisis in 1996 was an obligatory condition for the successful operation of the CBA. It is generally accepted that a successful stabilisation program, based on a pegged exchange rate, is impossible without a stable banking system. The policy of administered lending to insolvent state companies was brought to an end and insolvent banks were closed (this process was carried out in 1996, i.e. before the introduction of the CBA) which allowed commercial banks to get rid of the non-performing loans in their portfolios and to put their activities on sound principles. This policy substantially improved the portfolios of banks, and the portion of non-performing loans in mid-2000 was 5.6% (Table 2). This was the first step of restructuring the banking system. The second important step was the integration of the domestic banking system into the European financial system. This step aimed at importing managerial skills and know-how and improving the competitiveness of domestic banks in the period of financial services globalisation. The integration of Bulgarias domestic banking system into the European system was conducted by privatising state banks, and this process may be considered nearly finished with the privatisation of the biggest state bank (Bulbank) in mid-2000. UN: Biggest challenges to ensure stability and economic growth; harmonisation with the EU standards; depreciation of the Euro and stability of the CBA The major challenge is the high level of unemployment in the country caused by the deep and rapid microeconomic changes in the time after the introduction of the CBA. In spite of the GDP growth seen in three consecutive years, the unemployment rises since companies have been seeking to improve their competitiveness by increasing the labour production. After achieving macroeconomic stability by means of the changes conducted in mid-1997 and by putting the fiscal, monetary policies and the banking system on sound principles, thus ensuring sustained development, the main challenge for the economy in the long run would be the real convergence to the incomes level in the European Union. Though the country largely reached the nominal convergence in terms of the basic macroeconomic indicators (inflation rate, budget deficit, interest rates, government debt), as regards the real convergence our country is behind the other countries negotiating for EU membership. The real convergence is a long process that can be supported by the central bank ensuring stability of prices and of the financial system. Our experience from the ten-year transition shows that the currency board arrangement monetary system guarantees price and financial stability in the best possible way. As for whether the depreciation of the Euro (our reserve currency) would threaten the stability of the CBA, the answer could be sought in the monetary policy of the ECB. If the concern is that the depreciation of the reserve currency would import inflation - and to a larger or lesser extent we have the same effect in the Euro area - than we should ask ourselves what would be the reaction of the ECB to the price rise in the Euro area. This is the major question, because with the introduction of the CBA we agreed to import the ECB monetary policy, firmly believing that in the medium term the ECB would achieve its main objective of price stability and this would also ensure price stability in Bulgaria. In other words, we consider the depreciation of the Euro as a short-term and reversible tendency which does not threaten the price stability in the country. PAGE PAGE 2

Title: Interview to Welt News Agency, Frankfurt
Subtitle: Q: Dear Governor, may I kindly ask you to make a brief overview of the situation in Bulgaria of today in comparison with that of three years ago?
text: Interview given by BNB Governor Mr. Svetoslav Gavriiski to Welt News Agency, Frankfurt, September 2000 Q: Dear Governor, may I kindly ask you to make a brief overview of the situation in Bulgaria of today in comparison with that of three years ago? A: The situation now is very different if we compare it with that of three years ago. I mean, the end of 1996 and the beginning of 1997. At that time people received pensions amounting to 5 dollars and salaries 10 or 15 dollars. It was a very big crisis which led to the political changes. Firm will and decisiive steps of the new government changed the situation. We signed an agreement with the IMF in the first quarter of 1997 and decided to implement the Currency Board, which in Bulgarian reality works as a strong financial system. Q: Did you personally develop the idea to establish the Currency Board? A: As a minister of finance in the caretaker government I started negotiations with the IMF about the Currency Board implementation. My personal opinion was that CB was the last possibility for Bulgaria to stabilise the financial situation and the economy. Now we can see that was a right decision. We reached financial stabilisation quickly. In February 1997 inflation was over 200%, in April it was already negative. We succeeded in six months to stabilise the situation. Since then the stabilisation is a real fact and we managed in making this process sustainable. Now we expect to see a growth in GDP. We expected growth of about 4% in 1999 but you know regional events hit the Bulgarian economy, especially in terms of export and transportation. Nevertheless we expect a 2.5% growth of the GDP for 1999. Let me stress on another important feature of the CB System. We succeeded to increase foreign exchange reserves. In comparison with beginning of 1997, reserves increased 8 times: we started with 400 million dollars and now we have 3.2 billion dollars. Q: Why did you decide to peg the Lev to the Deutsche Mark instead of the US dollar? A: We discussed which currency to peg the Lev to and maybe the political decision prevailed because we wanted to start negotiations with the European Union. So we pegged the Lev to a European currency instead of the dollar. We included in our 1997 Law on the National Bank that we peg our currency to the Deutsche Mark and immediately after the Euro implementation we would be pegged to the Euro. Now our currency is pegged to the Euro. The rate is 1.96. Q: How do you see the implementation of the Euro, with your experience with the success of the monetary policy here. How do you see the success of the Euro in Europe and how will that ultimately affect you? A: I think that the Euro has a good future and its depreciation in the first year of implementation is temporary. I believe that after the initial difficulties the situation will be different and the exchange rate of the Euro will be higher than it is now. Concerning Bulgaria, I can say the implementation of the Euro is successful because we increased our export to the European Union - now it is almost 55%. Probably you know that some years ago our export was 80% orientated to the former socialist countries. Today Bulgarian export to Russia and the other countries of the former Eastern Block is comparatively low. To Russia it is about 6% and that fact was favourable, giving us possibilities to avoid the negative consiquences of the Russian financial crises. Having in mind these structural changes in our export you could understand why the implementation of the Euro is important for us. We have a stable currency, our payments are in a stable currency. We do not have problems with the balance of payments. And I do believe that the implementation of the Euro is a successful initiative. We think that when we finish the negotiations on accession to the European Union we will be able to implement the Euro. We have already had discussions with the European Central Bank about our financial system and its coordination with ECB. Probably it is possible to keep the Currency Board System during the long period of negotiations and after that to implement the Euro. For us this is the last stage of negotiations for accession to the European Union. Q: Given your experience and the role that the Central Bank plays now in the stability of the Bulgarian economy, what do you think are the main priorities and the main steps that still need to be taken to solidify the integration into the European Union? A: The government started the negotiations with the European Union. The role of the central banks is not very big. The main issue which the central banks will negotiate concerns the free movement of capital and this is a very significant issue to discuss. Another issue of importance is our legislation - independence of the Central Bank is something which the European Central Bank sticks to. We have a new Law on the Central Bank and according to that law we are fully independent. We are responsible only to the Parliament. Parliament appoints governor and deputy governors. We do not depend on the Government neather we lend funds to the Goverment. These in brief are the main issues. And the main target of the Central Bank is to maintain the stability of prices and to keep the rate of inflation low. I think that together with the Government we manage to maintain the prices stable. In 1998 inflation was 1% and in 1999 we expect 6.2%. The reason of this higher figure is the price of oil which doubled last year. Almost all prices in Bulgaria depend on the import of oil, prime and row materials. This is the main reason why inflation was higher in 1999. We expect the prices to stay stable this year. Our understanding and my perception is that the Currency Board works well, without problems. There is a theoretical position that a fixed exchange rate is an obstacle for development but I think we have sufficient reserves in improving the efficiency of our economy: high internal expenditures make the prices of our goods high. So, we have to reduce the cost of the production. Our economy is not efficient enough and we have to invest a lot of money for reconstruction of the industry. In this link we rely very much on privatization because this is the way to finance the economy. I can say that we have good achievements in finalising the process of restructuring and privatisation in 1999. Our oil refinery Neftochim, which is the biggest refinery on the Balkan Peninsula, has been privatized last year. Well, there are some big deals which are still at the level of negotiation: Bulgarian Telecommunication company for instance. Another field in which we pay special attention is our foreign economic policy, on regional and continental level. Although it is not easy to differ the questions and the projects by this scheme having in mind the process of globalization as well as the fact that Bulgaria and Romania negotiate with the EU. I think that start of the negotiations could be stimulating factor for our relations with the neighbouring countries. We rely very much on the improvment of the situation on the Danube because the destroyed bridges create big obstacles for us, especially for our transport. We also think that we will be able to reach an agreement with Romania about the construction of a new bridge over the Danube. Improvement of the conditions for our export is a strategic goal. Not only because we have a negative current account balance for 1999. Yes, it is important to increase the support for the export in order to improve the trade balance but it is more important to organize transport routes which will serve for decades. Despite this negative trade balance, I can say that we do not have problems with the balance of payments because we have direct foreign investment flow and revenues from tourism and other services. I would like to mention our good relations with foreign financial institutions. Our three-year agreement with the IMF, as well as the agreements with the World Bank and the European Union provide sufficient financing for Bulgaria. Q: Regarding this financing, you have set down the basis now for economic reconstruction which is in its final phases. You have a solid base, an extremely successful Currency Board but regarding the relationship with the European Union and foreign institutions, how important are your close ties with Germany and German financial institutions for your future and current policies? A: I think that our relations with Germany are very important. Germany is the biggest foreign investor in Bulgaria and our currency is pegged to the Deutsche Mark. Especially in the banking system, I expect to see German banks in Bulgaria. It is important for the banking system good foreign banks to operate here because, frankly speaking, the experience of our bankers needs to be improved. It is necessary to create real competition in the banking sector. And I rely very much on the participation of foreign banks to help in this direction. Unfortunately so far German participation is not remarkable. I would like to see more German banks, why not Deutsche Bank, to participate in the tender of Bulbank. Q: But you said that there has been a lack of German banks and financial institutions participation in Bulgaria. Do you think that perhaps the image of the country or the region for that matter is tarnished by the Kosovo crisis? Do you think that maybe those variables have influenced or overshadowed the opportunities that exist in Bulgaria? A: Yes that is true. And I think that is understandable. It is very difficult to think that foreign companies will invest in a region where there is a war and other related problems. But after the end of Kosovo war the situation is different. And the relations between Bulgaria, Romania, Macedonia and Albania could not keep the old cliches. We try to improve these relations and I think that the need for reconstruction of the region is crucial for all of us. New projects and well grounded ideas could attract foreign investors. There are already indications from some German and other foreign banks. Q: You mentioned that the financial sector has solidified and it is now stable here in Bulgaria. Eventually it needs more investment - how would you actively propose to reach potential German investors and institutions, to differentiate perhaps Bulgaria from the rest of the region and show the things that you have mentioned such as the stability of the system, the stability of the currency and some of the opportunities that you just mentioned? A: Having in mind the financial stability and sound situation as a whole I can say that now Bulgaria is the most stable country in the region. We hope the financial stabilisation and the good prospects for development could attract foreign investors. They could prefer to stay in this country because the situation is stable, the environment is good, and the legislation is very close to the European. These key factors could attract foreign capital. I understand that it is necessary for the investors to see their interest. I do not expect them to stay here only for the sake of Bulgaria. And I could assure them: there are good business possibilities here. Believe me, the situation will be different very soon. Q: How do you think the increase of the involvement of foreign banks and foreign institutions will affect the competition, which you said is good. A: I understand our bankers very well. They had a very bad experience with a huge amount of bad loans some years ago and they are reluctant to extend new credit. Credit activities are relatively low. It is necessary for them to see good examples, to see how the good banks work. That is why we pay attention on the bank privatization. New owners will bring know how, new atmosphere, new investments. And our bankers will be stimulated to increase their lending activity. Participation of foreign banks could only improve the competition and subsequently the lending conditions. Interviewer Karen Herzog. PAGE PAGE 3

Title: Interview published at the Banker weekly
Subtitle: THE SSB SHARES ARE AN EXPENSIVE MEDICINE FOR THE STOCK EXCHANGE
text: Interview given by Mr. Svetoslav Gavriiski, Governor of the Bulgarian National Bank, published at the Banker weekly, issue 4/26 January  1 February 2002 THE SSB SHARES ARE AN EXPENSIVE MEDICINE FOR THE STOCK EXCHANGE After the events in Argentina, many questions came up about the future existence of the currency board arrangement in our country. Is there any danger of our ever having the fate of the Latin Americans? In spite of all debates, we came to the conclusion that the currency board arrangement in Bulgaria should not be abolished. It is quite clear to everybody that there is no exchange rate  fixed or floating  that can play the role of a medicine for the economy. At the same time, the five-year successful functioning of the currency board in this country showed that with a reasonable fiscal and structural policy the economy can develop. If the present government continues in this direction, I do not see any point in discussing the currency board at all. It is true that we will have to get out of it some day. But, as regards the Bulgarian cabinet and the BNB, we have a clear vision as to when and how this should happen. Our policy aims at Bulgarias joining the EU and the European Monetary Union and at adopting the Euro. When this happens we will also automatically go out of the currency board arrangement. We should not be frightened by the events in Argentina; but Argentina has collapsed although its foreign debt, as a percentage of the gross domestic product, is much smaller than that of Bulgaria. Isnt that too disturbing? The size of the debt isnt such a significant indicator at all. Its structure is much more important. Argentinas debt was a short-term one and this year substantial payments should have been made to service it. Bulgaria is in far too different a situation. Our country passed through the period when it had to make its largest annual payments to foreign creditors. From now on these payments will be reducing. Besides, most of our foreign obligations will have to be repaid by 10 to 30 years. And our short-term obligations are not more than 7% of the total debt. Therefore, we do not have Argentinas problem. Should I understand that the foreign debt service is no longer a problem for us? In the next few years the amounts we have to pay to foreign creditors are quite tolerable. The most difficult years, when Bulgaria used to pay over USD 1 billion a year, are over. I think in 2002 these expenses will be about USD 800 million But the projections of the Ministry of Finance indicate about USD 993 million No, the payments will be some USD 800 million, and in the next few years these will be gradually decreasing to USD 600 million. These amounts would be no problem for the government at all, if it would pursue a policy that would ensure the stable development of the economy. Do you think that its right to rush the privatisation of BIOCHIM and the SSB now that over 80% of the assets of the banking system are in the hands of foreign capitals? I cannot say that the privatisation of these two banks is hasty. I even personally insisted that no time limits for their privatisation should be put down in the agreement with the IMF. My view about the SSB is that this bank still needs restructuring and a lot of investment to become a really operating commercial bank. As regards BIOCHIM, if a good investor appears, the bank can be privatised indeed. It is not accidental that the BCC Board of Directors have set requirements directing the sale of this bank to a buyer  Bulgarian or foreign  who will have the capabilities of developing it. It is said that the minimum price of BGN 95 million set for participation in the tender is too high and creates obstacles. But, in my opinion, we have to overcome the general attitude that BIOCHIM is in a bad condition, that it has endless problems and should be sold in order to be rescued. This is not in the least true. The bank is in a very good state. Excluding the SSB, BIOCHIM is the third largest and most capable bank in Bulgaria and I do not see why we should not take good enough a price for it. Is it logical that a portion of the SSB shares should be offered on the stock exchange and be sold against compensatory notes before finding a strategic investor for it? This issue has been discussed with the IMF Mission and at my insistence this proposal has not been included in the agreement with the Fund. Indeed, the views in the BCC Board of Directors differ, but the predominant position is that there is no need for 25% of SSB shares to be sold on the stock exchange in advance. A strategy for its privatisation should be developed instead, and when a strong investor appears, the bank will be sold as a whole not piecemeal. I find it inappropriate for stocks of its shares to be sold against compensatory notes to unknown shareholders simply to assist the development of the stock exchange. Do you have any concerns that the banks, which have been purchased by foreign investors, might purposefully be pursuing a policy of no lending? I cannot affirm that such a policy exists. The large amounts of funds concentrated so far in banks enabled them, without taking great risks, to earn income that covers their costs. Now, however, they will have to reconsider their policy since the interest rates of 1-2% abroad would hardly provide them with the required income. Only that these rates may not stay like this for long and may rise? To my mind, the rates would stay at the current levels this year at least. Even if there would be some rise, the rates would never reach the high levels of early last year. And if they would keep the current assets structure, banks would have problems with making enough earnings to cover their costs. In order to solve this problem, they will have to focus more on the lending in this country, because it brings much more income than the deposits abroad. Yet, lending involves much higher risk and greater danger of suffering losses? Banks are for this  to assess the risk and take a sufficiently measured risk and not rely on the 100-percent safety of the deposits in first-rate credit institutions or of first-rate foreign securities. Banks have been created to give loans. Moreover, our economy is growing. New good companies are being set up; companies with their own history and market positions are getting stabilised. So, there are conditions for lending in this country. Does the BNB have any instruments to encourage banks to lend to the Bulgarian economy? We dont have any particular tools available for this purpose. We can only reduce the amounts that banks are to hold at the BNB as reserve requirements, which are a percentage of the funds attracted by banks. At its last meeting, the Managing Board adopted a decision to exempt the accounts and deposits of over two years maturity from reserve requirements. This would allow banks to attract long-term resources and use them to grant cheaper loans. Why did you decide to close the BNB branches in Rousse, Bourgas and Vratza? We had been discussing this issue in the BNB Managing Board for quite a long time. It has also been discussed worldwide whether central banks should be operating with branches or without them. We decided that for a small country like ours it would be more effective if the BNB would operate with fewer branches. This decision provoked many protests among district governors and politicians. But in taking this decision we have only been guided by economic considerations and mostly by the workload in the individual branches. In some of these it has significantly diminished. So, last year we began closing the most ineffective ones; first, the Haskovo branch. Now its the turn of the branches in Rousse, Vratza and Bourgas. In the next few years we may go on closing branches. Wouldnt this policy cause cash supply problems for commercial banks, for which the branches are used? This activity will be taken over by commercial banks. Even now they supply each other with a portion of the notes they need. This should not necessarily be done through the BNB branches. Is it true that there is a decision of the BNB Managing Board that the collected cash in Bourgas must be transported to Varna? There is no such decision. As for Bourgas, the turnover of our branch in this town is very small. It was claimed that large amounts of foreign currency were purchased there, which is quite strange as foreign currency is mainly purchased by exchange bureaux not by the BNB branches. This has also been proved by the change of the 12 EU countries currencies into Euro. The queues in the BNB head office have been formed by representatives of the exchange bureaux not by citizens. Very small sums pass through the BNB branches and their closure would not impair the delivery of cash or the safety of its storage. But the cash from companies and from commercial bank branches will have to go a much longer way to your branch in Varna which involves more risks. It is not necessary to go all this way. Companies may deposit their cash in the local branches of commercial banks. And the banks will supply one another with the required amounts of notes. Moreover, dont forget that even today the bank cars travel from Sofia to Bourgas to deliver cash. Interviewer: Peter Illiev. PAGE PAGE 3

Title: Welcome to guests and journalists, 12.00, 108 hall, BNB, October 29, 2003.
text: Welcome of Mr. Ivan Iskrov, Governor of the BNB, to guests and journalists, 12.00, 108 hall, BNB, 29 October 2003. Dear Governors: Prof. Dr.Sc.(Econ.) Nikiforov, Prof. Dr.Sc.(Econ.) Valchev, Mr. Kolarov, Mr. Filipov, Mr. Gavriyski, Ladies and gentlemen - members of the Management Board of the BNB, Dear ladies and gentlemen journalists, Dear friends, It is a great honor and a special pleasure to be homekin at today's meeting, attended by five of the governors of the Bulgarian National Bank in different years. BNB has existed for nearly 125 years. From the experience I have as working directly at the Central Bank and as its partner, as a commercial banker and politician, I have convinced that here is given great importance to concepts such as: respect for traditions, respect for work and colleagues, tolerance, continuity and consistency. With the final completion of the Board with a new manager and under a manager, I would like to assure you that the priority for us will be to preserve these virtues, as well as to further develop the positiveattitude towards the institution by its workers and its external partners. I am aware that theBNB is subject to legitimate interest from the public. that we will work together in the coming years to present a true picture of our banking system and the financial and economicsituation in the country. It is hardly necessary now to recall what serious tasks lie before the BNB in the future, which will have a direct impact on the lives of people in Bulgaria  the adoption of THE BNB in the System of European Central Banks, and soon it will be the case for our country in theeuro area. that we will all be at the required heights to meet and deal with trials in a way that will preserve the goodness and good name of the institution, leaving behind a trace that we can be proud of. Dear ladies and gentlemen, BNB existed long before any of us worked in it. I think the unifying thread that connects the colleagues present lies in the traditions of this solid state institution, which have respected and continue to respect everyone who has worked in it and contributed something to the good name of theCentral Bank. It is in this sense that we should regard the centuries-old history of the BNB as a treasure trove not only of material values, but also of knowledge, experience and traditions. The holders of these skills are all of you  esteemed colleagues  managers and members of the Management Board of the BNB, directors and employees. Here it is probably best to inform you that traditionally for nearly 10 years, as an expression of respect for the work and contribution to the Central Bank, at the expiry of a term of office, the members of the Management Board receive a commemorative plaque. I am honored, on behalf of the management of the BNB, to present such a gold plaque to my predecessor, The Governor Mr. Svetoslav Gavriyski. Let this memory always remindhim that we greatly appreciate the efforts, professionalism and ethics of the last six years with which he has maintained and established the authority of the institution in the country and abroad. I particularly enjoy doing this in the presence of the managers who have led the BNB for the last 30 years. Thank you and good luck! Other information BNBmanagers present for the respective periods Veselin Nikiforov, Manager 8 July 1974 - 3 January 1984 Vasil Kolarov, Manager 3 January 1984 - 20 December 1989 Todor Valchev, Manager 9 January 1991 - 24 January 1996 Lyubomir Filipov, Manager 24 January 1996 - 11 June 1997 Svetoslav Gavriyski, Manager 11 June 1997 - 9 October 2003 PAGE PAGE 2

Title: Speech to the National Assembly on the occasion of his election as Governor of the Bulgarian National Bank, 9 October 2003
text: Speech by Mr. Ivan Iskrov to the National Assembly on the occasion of his election as Governor of the Bulgarian National Bank, 9 October 2003 Ladies and Gentlemen MPs, Mr Finance Minister, Mr Gavriiski, First of all I would like to thank for the trust that you have given me by electing me Governor of the Bulgarian National Bank. I wish to state that in my work I will very much rely on the support of all MPs, even those of you who voted against my candidacy.
