The reason is my deep, really deep inner conviction that the financial stability and economic growth in a country are only possible with a sound political consensus on the major issues of the economic, financial and supervisory policies. I do hope that the legislature, represented by you, will consistently continue to bring the Bulgarian legislation in compliance with the EU legislation in accordance with the agreements reached with the European Commission. A lot was said and written in the months before the election of a new Governor of the Bulgarian National Bank. I am not going to analyse all that was said. It was written somewhere By their deeds, you shall know them. Here I would like to thank the previous Governor, Mr Gavriiski, the Managing Board and the staff of the Bulgarian National Bank for their efforts in overcoming the financial and economic crisis of 1996-1997 and for the well-planned and successful campaign for the re-denomination of the Bulgarian Lev. Of course, the stability of the banking system and the economy over the last six years was also achieved thanks to the governments which gave up the short-sighted policy of politically-driven economic decisions. The fundamental structural reforms in the banking and financial sector were carried out and these, together with the tough fiscal policy, ensured the stability of the currency board arrangement. I hope that this sensible and needed policy will continue to be the basis of the financial stability and economic growth in Bulgaria during the accession to the European Union. Mr Speaker, Ladies and Gentlemen MPs, I have presented at length my views in the so-called Strategy for the Management of the Bulgarian National Bank, which even today is on the site in Mediapool. Here I want to stress the three key words that I will try to make indicative of my work as Governor of the BNB: independence, transparency, predictability. The Bulgarian National Bank obtained its operational independence from the central government with the Law on the Bulgarian National Bank of 1991. Despite the legal provisions, there were numerous attempts to exert influence on the central bank and its governors, especially before the financial crisis of 1996-1997. In the last few years a substantial progress was made in this respect and this makes me believe that the political parties and governments would in the future refrain from trying to influence the central banks management. I sincerely hope that during my term of office such attempts would not be undertaken as we all have the common goal to ensure a balanced and sustained economic growth, which would help improve the standard and quality of living in Bulgaria. Transparency is the second requirement that will govern all actions of the Governor and the management of the Bulgarian National Bank. I definitely think that the BNB so far has been in debt to society. Independence should not be used as an excuse for the lack of dialogue and non-substantiation of the decisions taken and the policy pursued. It is unacceptable for an important financial institution of the country to simply present its regular report to the National Assembly twice a year. As Governor of the Bulgarian National Bank I will insist on having a clear democratic mechanism of interaction, accountability and political consensus on the independent BNB with the other government bodies in resolving the important issues of society. Predictability. Dear colleagues, during the mandate of the newly elected Governor of the Bulgarian National Bank, that is myself, two very important historic events should take place: Bulgarias accession to the European Union in the year 2007 and the subsequent joining to the Eurozone in 2009. Apart from the major issues of keeping the Bulgarian Lev stable, the payment system and supervision of commercial banks, these are the two strategic benchmarks to which the BNB activities will be subordinated during my term of office. From a passive observer under a currency board arrangement, the Bulgarian National Bank must turn into a full member of the European System of Central Banks. The BNB should bring back the trust of the public and become a guarantor of price stability and currency circulation in the country, just like the leading central banks members of the ESCB. Only then the BNB would be able to make an efficient and full contribution to the economic prosperity and higher quality of life. Therefore, I will use my knowledge, experience and will for specifying and strictly carrying out the major activities and responsibilities of the Bulgarian National Bank, and those which it shares with other government institutions, for Bulgarias joining the Eurozone and integrating into international financial markets. I sincerely hope for the support and understanding of all government bodies and the National Assembly for the sake of our common goal. I believe that only with a broad public dialogue, transparency and predictability of actions and decisions, and strong public control we could report on a successfully completed mandate. I will take this opportunity, Ladies and Gentlemen, to thank you for your assistance in the heavy task of my two-year chairmanship of the Budget and Finance Commission. I personally thank all the members of the Commission, and especially the people who directly assisted me  my deputies Mr Aliosman Imamov, Mr Georgi Pirinski and Mr Muravei Radev. Thank you once again! I hope that my election as Governor would further enhance the good reputation of the Bulgarian National Bank. Thank you for your attention. PAGE PAGE 2

Title: Presentation before the Fourth Annual Meeting between the Business and the Government, organized by the Capital Weekly and the Confederation of Employers and Industrialists in Bulgaria, Sofia
text: Presentation of Mr. Ivan Iskrov, BNB Governor, before the Fourth Annual Meeting between the Business and the Government, organized by the Capital Weekly and the Confederation of Employers and Industrialists in Bulgaria, Sofia, 3 November 2009 In his presentation at the Annual Meeting between the Business and the Government in Sheraton Hotel, the BNB Governor, Mr. Ivan Iskrov, categorically dismissed the idea launched publicly of currency board modification. "Either there is a currency board or there is not. We witnessed how in a certain country the central bank was trying to implement a modification of the currency board and have money market operations, and we saw where the board ended there", he said. Mr. Iskrov underscored that the BNB had pursued an anticyclical policy in spite of the restrictions of the currency board. At the time of the economic upswing the central bank constrained new bank licensing and implemented measures that allowed for the accumulation of buffers, including through credit ceilings and abrupt increase of the minimum reserve requirements, he indicated. "During the crisis we reversed the measures and by reducing the minimum reserve requirements injected BGN 3 billion in the economy, also easing the loan classification requirements", he emphasized. Governor Iskrov added that as a result of the recommendation made by the BNB Banking Supervision Department not to distribute any profit for 2008, BGN 1.4 billion were left in the economy. The banking systems performance is good and its capital adequacy exceeds 17%, Governor Iskrov noted, adding that as of September the banks earnings were BGN 622 million, and irrespective of their 40-percent drop banks managed to cover bad loan provisions and increased interest on funds attracted by banks. Title: Speech before the Association of Banks in Bulgaria on the occasion of the Bankers Day, Sofia
text: Speech by Mr. Ivan Iskrov, BNB Governor, delivered before the Association of Banks in Bulgaria on the occasion of the Bankers Day, Sofia, 3 December 2009 The crisis in global financial markets has continued even in 2009 but, as it is well known, it has had no direct impact on the Bulgarian banks balance sheets as their major business is lending to the Bulgarian economy, and in their assets there were no exposures to US bonds or to institutions suffering losses from investments in mortgage-backed securities or related instruments or in other toxic assets. Since 2003 the BNB has been pursuing a consistent anti-cyclic policy which in the period of a fast economic growth made possible the accumulation of such buffers that today very few EU countries can claim to have indicators similar to those of the Bulgarian economy. Our banking system and the individual institutions are in good financial shape and with considerable capacity for absorbing negative effects. In 2009 the BNB Governing Council adopted amendments to the BNB Ordinance No.9 on the evaluation and classification of risk exposures of banks and the allocation of provisions to cover credit risk, and also to the BNB Ordinance No.8 on capital adequacy of credit institutions. These measures aimed to ease the conditions of loans to solvent customers having temporary financial difficulties. In essence, all that was a continuation of our anti-cyclic policy, but now during the descending phase of the business cycle. The data on banks' position suggest that the level of capital adequacy as at September is 17.34% and is one of the highest levels in the EU, with the capital cushion above the required minimum being BGN 2.9 billion. Profitability is acceptable as the profits of BGN 657 million, reported for the 10 months of 2009, provide an additional buffer against a further devaluation of portfolios. Despite the decline in lending and the deterioration of loan portfolios, credit institutions manage to keep their interest revenues at levels allowing them to meet the increasing impairments. The outflow of attracted resources, primarily from the corporate segment, is compensated by a steady inflow of funds from individuals and households. The funds from residents remain solid. The liquidity of banks and the system keeps stable, with the liquid assets ratio continuously staying over 20%. The assessments that banks financial fundamentals remain unchanged are confirmed by the regular stress-testing. Their results reveal a capacity for absorbing impairment of assets, an available capital resource, and a good liquidity position. At the same time, however, banks will be facing a few challenges relating to: increasing instability of the environment, with negative effects possibly going deeper; repercussions from the weak lending activities; further contraction of the current possibilities of generating buffers through profitability; deteriorating economic status of some users of bank services. On the other hand, the changes in the legal framework and the supervision architecture being created by the EU will require changes in several directions. As a result of the changes in some key banking directives, discussed at an EU level, and for the purpose of unifying the European supervisory practices, the BNB is going to make concrete amendments to the capital adequacy framework. These amendments will relate to the way of integrating banks current profits as an element of the supervisory capital and to equalising the risk weights of the classes Retail exposures and Exposures secured by mortgages on residential property with the risk weights prescribed in the relevant directive. The easing effect from the above two measures will somewhat be set off by the expected changes in other areas, mostly the accounting standards and the large exposures regime. In response to the crisis, in 2010 a number of changes will be made in IASs and these changes will in all cases be transposed into the Bulgarian accounting rules, and consequently will have an impact on banks balance sheets. A uniform impairment approach is going to be introduced whereby the current incurred loss model will be replaced with the expected loss model. This will affect the amount of supervisory provisions and capital charges. As regards the control of large exposures in banks, the planned changes will mostly involve interbank exposures as the new regime provides a much more conservative treatment of these. I would like to focus on another issue which is of key importance for the future of the European financial system. We are expecting the start of the new European financial supervision system in 2010. Its main task will be to coordinate and facilitate the efforts of national supervisory and regulatory authorities, and in this relation: the European Systemic Risk Council (ESRC) will be established in the European Central Bank and will be responsible for macro-prudential supervision (supervision of financial stability); a European system of financial supervisors will be set up, consisting of three new European Supervisory Authorities: the European Banking Authority (EBA), the European Insurance and Occupational Pensions Authority (EIOPA), and the European Securities Authority (ESA). This set of supervisory institutions will conduct micro-prudential supervision (supervision of individual financial institutions) at the European level. In the future the new supervision structure will play a key role in the development and functioning of the European financial system and will inevitably influence the Bulgarian market given the numerous functions and powers delegated to these pan-European authorities. The BNBs timely actions in supporting the adjustment of the Bulgarian banking system to the new conditions amid the shrinking global financial markets included a reduction in the minimum reserve requirements of banks. Their liquidity management and adaptation to the indirect effects of the financial crisis were buoyed up by the additional amendments, taking effect from the early 2009, to the BNB Ordinance No.21 on the minimum required reserves maintained with the BNB by banks. Therefore, with regard to liquidity the interbank market is meeting with calm the end of 2009. This year a serious challenge for us has been the introduction of the new legal framework for payment services transposing the Payment Services Directive. The new Law on payment services and payment systems was published back in March 2009. Soon afterwards all ordinances and other legal acts for its implementation came into effect, creating normal conditions for banks to prepare for the new requirements. Nevertheless, the streamlining of business processes will continue into next year. The project for the BNB joining TARGET 2 has been going on successfully. We can expect its completion in February 2010. Last but not least, in 2009 we saw the successful launch of the newly expanded credit register. It is expected that its enlarged scope would further facilitate risk management in the system. The Bulgarian National Bank is performing its cash functions by handling the banknotes and coins coming to the BNB; storing Bulgarian banknotes and coins and foreign currency; exchanging damaged Bulgarian banknotes and coins; and destroying unfit Bulgarian currency. The BNB, in its bank hall in Sofia, renders cash services in BGN and in Euro to retail customers; provides services in BGN and in foreign currency to first-level budget spending units; and sells commemorative coins at teller desks. In 2009 we have continued the building of the new modern BNB Cash Centre in Sofia, following the Banks strategy for modernising and technologically renovating its issue and cash activities. The Centre will be complete by the end of this year, and it is expected to start offering services to the Banks customers in the first quarter of 2010. Please let me finish by reminding you that on 6 June 2009 we all together celebrated the 130th anniversary of the foundation of the Central Bank of Bulgaria. Remember that our institution was the 13th national central bank established in the world, and its history is an inseparable part of the history of Bulgarias economy and financial sector and of the Bulgarian people. At the end of the first decade of the 21st century, now within the European Union and the European System of Central Banks, the BNB is fully aware of its institutional importance and its responsibility and will go on working invariably for supporting the Bulgarian banking system and economy and for leading them out of the crisis. Happy Bankers Day, dear colleagues! PAGE PAGE 1

Title: Introductory address opening the international conference "Economic and Political Challenges of Euro Area Accession", Sofia
text: Introductory address of Mr. Ivan Iskrov, BNB Governor, opening the international conference "Economic and Political Challenges of Euro Area Accession", Sofia, 7 December 2009 Ladies and Gentlemen, I would like to thank the organizers for inviting me to this forum. The meeting today will be an opportunity to share experiences and present different points of view: of those who are closest to our Euro area membership decision-making, as well as of representatives of the business community, the financial sector, and independent analysts from Bulgaria and abroad. The presence of the media will provide for an even wider response, beyond the audience specialised in financial matters. Acceding to the Euro area will represent the final phase of our European integration and will reinforce our return as an equal partner in Europe, which is now more than ever mutually dependent and interconnected in a political and economic sense. One day, adopting the Euro will perhaps be considered the most significant event in the economic history of Bulgaria during the 21st century. The immediate reason for the interest in todays meeting comes from the recent talks in Bulgaria about our resumption of efforts to join the ERM II. After I make my statement there are reports and discussions devoted to various details and procedural issues regarding the technology and the macroeconomic context of our Euro area accession. The Bulgarian National Bank will play the leading role in managing this process. What is more, over the past six years my team and I have made it possible to have most of our countrys preparation in legal, technical and operational terms completed. This task remains our key priority as of this moment as well. Please, allow me now to summarize some key aspects, related to our Economic and Monetary Union membership, as well as some challenges expected on the road ahead. Firstly, I would like to take this opportunity and remind you that our Euro area accession will mark the fulfilment of one of the major commitments of the country, stemming from our EU Membership Treaty. Bulgaria, just like the rest of the 2004 and 2007 new EU entrants, does not have the option to choose whether to adopt the Euro as a national legal tender or not. This is our obligation, and not some kind of privilege. However, we are free to decide how to prepare for the effective euroisation of Bulgaria. From this perspective, the time for satisfying the membership criteria is a factor partly under our control. The unfavourable external environment may be a source of shocks to the Bulgarian economy but they can only delay rather than halt our efforts to adjust to the Maastricht criteria. As is well known, these criteria refer to achieving price stability, budget deficit and government debt limits, low long-term interest rates and stability of the national currency. If the five criteria are transposed to the macro data available now (I expect that the forum today will engage several times in this exercise), it will become evident that Bulgaria satisfies most of the criteria even today. The currency board rules automatically help us fulfil the currency criterion. Bulgaria is among the European countries with lowest government debt as a share of GDP, way below the limit required for joining the Euro area. Bulgaria is already internationally recognised for its strong fiscal position, remaining among the few countries complying with the budget criterion of the Stability and Growth Pact and not being in an excessive deficit procedure. No one can say for sure that, by the time of publication of the next Convergence Report by the European Commission and the European Central Bank (just in a couple of months time), Bulgaria will not already be fulfilling all five quantitative Maastricht criteria. However, as our European partners underline as well, a countrys convergence on the Euro area must be sustainable. That means that compliance with the criteria is to be assessed not in one arbitrary moment but over a long time period. Thus, following the Euro area road map rules, Bulgaria should spend at least two years in the ERM II. We will be granted the Euro zone membership only after that, provided that Bulgaria proves to have succeeded in satisfying all criteria. Another important detail is that the Bulgarian National Bank and the Bulgarian authorities are not among those that will calculate and evaluate the compliance with the criteria. It should be clear therefore that adopting the Euro as a legal tender is a process which belongs to our domain and for which we have our own responsibility: but it is not, and it cannot be, Bulgarias unilateral decision. After we satisfy the Maastricht criteria (and much better if even earlier!) we must show the skills to persuade all our foreign colleagues that we are ready and have the capacity to be a part of the Euro area. Capacity implies that we can adequately participate in the decision-making regarding the European monetary and financial policies. Being ready for the Euro area membership means that our economy is both stable and flexible, our policies are credible, our financial sector and its regulation are placed on solid grounds, our commitment to fiscal discipline is not short-term, and certainly - that the Bulgarian economy obtains no competitive edge from a flexible exchange rate. Somewhere along these areas there runs the thin line separating the economic from the political assessment of our readiness. Adopting the Euro is explained as a mostly technical process, related to complying with the criteria for membership in the Economic and Monetary Union, as per the Maastricht Treaty. Experts, politicians, researchers and the public at large are duly focused on the fulfilment of the respective indicators. But in reality it is already obvious that introducing the single currency into a country is a complicated political project as well. It suffices to recall that when on 15 and 16 June 2006 the Brussels summit took the political decision to let Slovenia in the Euro area the two-year period of participation of this country in the ERM II had not even formally expired. Belgium, Greece and Italy met the Euro with government debt in excess of 100% of their GDPs. Bulgaria, however, was advised towards the end of 2007 to refrain from even applying: and not even to the Euro area, but to the ERM II. The high current account deficit at the time was put forward as one of the arguments behind such a stance towards Bulgaria. It can be stated that, while a countrys acceding to the Euro area is based on the political consensus among the incumbent members, the latter applies to an even greater extent to joining the ERM II as the necessary prerequisite for the full Economic and Monetary Union membership. The political factor, rather than the written, concrete and publicly monitored economic criteria, is leading when entering the exchange-rate mechanism. After the big Eastern EU enlargement of May 2004, the inertia to accept new members was carried over to the Euro zone. It took Estonia, Lithuania and Slovenia only a few weeks to join the ERM II. In practice, however, it is possible for the European Central Bank to put a veto even when favourable sentiments exist in the European Commission and the European Council. In the recent years, that scenario was reminded many times to Bulgaria. Over the last 12 months Bulgaria more than halved its current account deficit, and we forecast that its percentage share of GDP will be a single-digit number next year. The last year Bulgaria posted a single-digit current account deficit was 2004. May we already qualify such an external position sustainable? And does that automatically imply that our economy has overcome the most striking imbalances and there is no obstacle to be allowed into the ERM II? Alas, the political considerations for or against the Euro area enlargement are not always predictable: sometimes because of lacking formal and exhaustive criteria, and sometimes because of short-term factors. Formally, in the macroeconomic structure of every European country one may identify phenomena which may be viewed as posing risks to the sustainable development: ceteris paribus, that will provide reasons to punish the country in question. In that respect, one should look at Central and Eastern Europe only. It is enough to point at some of the large European economies and their chronic budget deficits already reaching double-digit numbers. But even if a given economy overcomes some of its most commented imbalances, the mere unilateral desire to adopt the Euro (or even just to join the ERM II) will not be enough. There have been examples that soon after joining the Euro area some countries experienced strong inflationary pressure or loosened their fiscal policy, hence violating Maastricht criteria adhered to thus far. But the current crisis challenged the European economies much more than before, and because of that both Brussels and Frankfurt are much more cautious. That is why it can be said that the unilateral announcement of deadlines for entering the ERM II is not an optimal communication strategy, from todays point of view. For this reason our efforts at this stage should be focused on attaining the much needed consensus among the European countries that Bulgaria possesses a stable economy and predictable policies. For instance, a key and immediate task before Bulgaria now is to present a strong and realistic Convergence Programme. That should take place within the next few weeks. Bulgaria must keep advertising its economic achievements and even its uniqueness. The currency board regime proved resilient both in the years of growth and in the times of crisis. Unlike most EU countries, Bulgaria did not have to capitalise its financial institutions with public funds. In a recent publication the European Central Bank officially acknowledged that only three countries, Bulgaria among them, had faced the initial business cycle downturn with strong enough structural fiscal positions. In 2010 only a few EU countries, Bulgaria among them again, are expected to have a budget balance within the Stability and Growth Pact requirements at all. The signals our country sends should be straightforward and the forum today may facilitate a lot the shaping of new messages. Because we have the difficult task of achieving a double effect: both to prepare ourselves for the Maastricht criteria, and also to encourage readiness among our European partners to accept us. It is not good policy to spend time on changing the existing criteria instead, although it is obvious for example that the inflation criterion is more difficult to satisfy with a Union of 27 than with a Union of 15 members. Only the consistent efforts and hard work of each one of us will every day, little by little, bring us closer to the time when the Euro will be adopted in Bulgaria. Finally, let me assure you that we share a common goal but the Bulgarian National Bank will continue to comply with its share of the duties of Bulgaria, fully aware of the mutual balance of responsibilities within the country and of the requirements of our Euro area partners. Sometimes it is not easy to recognise the most favourable moment to take advantage of a given situation. But for sure we would not benefit much if we plan to go through a door but it turns out to be locked when we knock on it. Then, something very interesting, politically, will happen and I would like to put this as my question, my well-intentioned provocation to the participants in todays forum. Let us imagine that Bulgaria is consistent in its efforts on the road to the Euro, that it strictly fulfils its EU Membership Treaty obligations, and that our economy manifests convergence on the Euro area, covering all Maastricht criteria. Provided that there are no formal criteria to be admitted to the ERM II, what would be the appropriate political response from the Bulgarian side if at the end of the day our European partners have returned to us a negative political response, dressed up or hidden behind technical arguments? For instance if the European Central Bank prefers to wait until the consequences from the current crisis recede and the effects from the large-scale monetary and fiscal operations in support of the European economies are analysed. And if the Euro area faces with a changed macroeconomic structure the new phase of the business cycle, which will correspondingly require the reassessment and adjustment of the Euro area monetary regime, before taking up the challenges of a new enlargement to the East. Thank you for your attention! PAGE PAGE 1

Title: Publication in the quarterly bulletin of the Association of Banks in Bulgaria, issue 21
Subtitle: ON THE CRISIS AND THE PRUDENT BANKING
text: Publication of Mr. Ivan Iskrov, BNB Governor, in the quarterly bulletin of the Association of Banks in Bulgaria, issue 21, January 2010 ON THE CRISIS AND THE PRUDENT BANKING The year 2009 which has just passed was marked entirely by the global financial crisis and the slowing economic activity in Bulgaria. That was reflected in the restructuring of both sides of the balance sheets of banks. Despite the decrease in foreign assets and liabilities, compared to end-2008, the total deposits and the receivables from the non-government sector grew, with the banking system overall balance remaining approximately unchanged. The banks in Bulgaria stood up to the challenges, which is evident from the indicators for their returns, assets quality, the ratio of liquid assets to funds attracted, and the capital adequacy. In 2009 the system continued to generate profits which provided a return on assets of about 1%, while the capital buffers that were kept intact guaranteed an overall capital adequacy ratio significantly above the conservative minimum of 12% legally required in Bulgaria. The liquidity ratio continued to exceed 20% and, unlike many other European Union members, there were no reasons for concerns with respect to any liquidity risk jeopardising the stability of the banking system. The estimated financial soundness of the banks was being confirmed by the stress tests, periodically run by the BNB. These tests revealed the capacity for meeting even the most pessimistic scenarios for the development of the Bulgarian economy. The ascent of commercial banking in Bulgaria over the last few years went hand in hand with the consistent anti-cyclical stance of the BNB. The latter allowed for the accumulation of capital resources and liquidity potential to face the crisis. Under the downturn in the business cycle, the BNB did not step back from its active supervision policies for keeping the stability of the banking system. However, the main focus shifted towards the support of liquidity by alleviating the minimum reserve requirements, as well as the provision of easier lending conditions for temporarily constrained, but solvent, bank clients. In 2010 the first signs of economic recovery are expected, and I hope the banks will themselves contribute to it, by supporting newly-emerging good projects worthy of financing. That is a prudent approach of mutual interests. Still, the continuing high levels of uncertainty in the environment should be considered too, as also the dangers stemming from the decreased room for buffer accumulation from the margins and the worsening economic profile of some of the consumers of banking services. The efficient management of the balance between revenues and expenses, as well as the skilful pricing of risk under the conditions of growing competition, will remain valuable features of the Bulgarian banking system. And the year of crisis 2009 demonstrated that prudent banking always pays off. PAGE PAGE 1

Title: Address to the participants in the Third National Competition Banks in Action of Junior Achievement Bulgaria with the support of Citibank Bulgaria, Sofia
text: Address by Mr. Ivan Iskrov, BNB Governor, to the participants in the Third National Competition Banks in Action of Junior Achievement Bulgaria with the support of Citibank Bulgaria, Sofia, 4 March 2010 Dear Mr. Ivanov of Citibank, Dear Ms Stoycheva of Junior Achievement, First of all, I would like to thank you for your kind invitation which provides the wonderful opportunity to greet personally the participants in the Third National Competition Banks in Action, organized by Junior Achievement Bulgaria with the support of Citibank Bulgaria. I know this competition is part of the financial literacy programme Banks in Action, the raison d'etre of which is to teach participants the principles of the banking industry and to face them with the challenge to try to successfully manage a bank in a competitive environment. I am well aware of the fact this programme is targeted at achieving economic and financial literacy, business and leadership skill, and success strategies. I, on my part, would like to draw your attention to a simple rule of public behaviour of the BNB Governor  this rule requires particular care in selecting the events and public initiatives in which I participate as the Governor of the central bank of Bulgaria. My public appearances are very thoroughly prepared and are, as a rule, very few. Therefore, I answer positively to very few of the numerous invitations received every day at my office. I underscore this fact, as I would like to have my participation here today be understood as a definite proof of the enormous importance of such initiatives as Banks in Action of Junior Achievement jointly with Citibank. The participants in this programme are of the new generation of young Bulgarians, who grow up in an environment totally different from the atmosphere in which their parents and grand parents were brought up. The previous generations were indoctrinated that there is someone else to do the thinking, that there is no need to mobilize their intellectual potential, that someone else will do their job. Today we all know who did what and how this illusion ended. Therefore, I turn to our young generation with the advice  work hard everyday and never give up your dreams. This is my answer to anyone who may ask what the recipe of success is. Compared to our generation, you have the unique opportunities of the Internet, free access to infinite in volume and superior in quality information, and the advantage to travel freely. At your age we did not even dare to think about this, it was beyond our hopes and our dreams. So you start from an incomparably higher starting position, hence we encourage you to reach much higher in your personal achievements, in realizing your potential, than we could achieve ourselves. I am sure, my dear young friends, that your participation in programmes like Banks in Action of Junior Achievement jointly with Citibank helps you directly in accumulating the experience and self-confidence, and the self-assurance that is so indispensable for your future success in the banking industry. You have more opportunities that we had as a generation  I am saying this with a grain of noble envy  you are smarter, braver, and more resourceful than us  but also with a lot of pride. And because of all so far mentioned you deserve to reach far, even beyond your present dreams. Work everyday, do not tire of it, do not give up your dreams and you will make it! I wish health and success to you and to the organizers of todays competition  Junior Achievement and Citibank! Congratulations for the Liberation Day, dear colleagues! PAGE PAGE 1

Title: Publication in the quarterly bulletin of the Association of Banks in Bulgaria, issue 25
Subtitle: ON THE NEW BEGINNING AND THE REALISTIC EXPECTATIONS
text: Publication of Mr. Ivan Iskrov, BNB Governor, in the quarterly bulletin of the Association of Banks in Bulgaria, issue 25, January 2011 ON THE NEW BEGINNING AND THE REALISTIC EXPECTATIONS Despite the first positive signals for turning of the economic cycle and a beginning of the recovery, in 2010 the financial crisis continued to shape the views of the private sector and the households. The combination of their deteriorating economic status and higher cautiousness when deciding about current expenditures and investments exposed the banks to new challenges. The loan portfolios in the banks' balance sheets suffered pressure but the banking system has demonstrated flexibility and efficiency. The banking system overall balance kept increasing and, despite the non-performing loans and the impairments, the system continued making profit. The capital buffers stayed intact; the amount of provisions is also solid. The Bulgarian banking system stands out internationally too, with impressive capital adequacy and overall liquidity ratios. Due to the persistent anti-cyclical supervisory policies, as well as the prudent bank management itself during the recent years, the banking sector has at its disposal enough capital for covering without problems the increased capital requirements under Basel 3 announced last autumn (for which actually a transition period of several years is foreseen). Today the forecasts for a more visible economic recovery this year prevail, and this in turn inspires forecasts for more lending. The correlation between bank lending and economic growth is proven. However, it does not happen automatically and without the efforts by both sides in the process. Here I would like to stress on three aspects, related to the imminent expectations. First, banks cannot escape the laws of demand and supply. They can play a leading role in the recovery of the economy but they alone are unable to cause a twist in the demand. The number of companies with optimistic expectations for the future and good projects for financing should increase over time. Households should start borrowing more when they become less apprehensive about tomorrow. Second, many banks already became active in pursuing a higher market share and taking advantage of the opportunities arising from the crisis itself. Presumably, however, strategies for a more active management of the existing portfolios too could be adopted in some cases, including through the renegotiation of loan positions. Probably, there is also some unused potential in the provision of services to the existing customers. The banks have some room for improvement in working with their clients. The long-term customer relationships are an important strategic goal, since exactly the customers are the most precious asset of each bank. Not least, we can see how the previous credit expansion weighs heavily on many banks and their customers today. Prudent banking does not imply a total restraint from lending. However, the complex and adequate economic assessment of risks should remain the focus on a daily working basis. We hope for, and we are working towards, a new beginning for the banking sector in the country in 2011. Nobody, however, is deluded that the current crisis is going to be the last one. Our judgements should be careful and our expectations should be realistic. PAGE PAGE 1

Title: Opening address at the conference The Banking System in the Global Financial Crisis organized by the VUZF University, Sofia
Subtitle:
THE CRISIS AND FINANCIAL STABILITY
IN THE EYES OF THE BULGARIAN NATIONAL BANK
text: Opening address by Mr. Ivan Iskrov, Governor of the Bulgarian National Bank, at the conference The Banking System in the Global Financial Crisis organized by the VUZF University, Sofia, 27 May 2011 THE CRISIS AND FINANCIAL STABILITY IN THE EYES OF THE BULGARIAN NATIONAL BANK Dear Mr. Rector, Dear conference participants and guests, Ladies and Gentlemen, It is a great pleasure for me to be here today, and together with Professor Vazov to open such an interesting scientific conference. This conference was announced as being both scientific and applied, which implies issues related to banking practices as well as more theoretical analyses and discussions on the stated subject: The Banking System in the Global Financial Crisis. I would like to convey my special thanks to the Rector of the VUZF University, who invited me to open todays event, thus providing the opportunity from the very beginning to present to your attention the point of view of the Bulgarian National Bank. The experience of our Central Bank is unique and very important in the context of the crisis. The BNB is both a key participant in the Bulgarian financial system, a regulator and a supervisor, and in addition to it a factor in the making and pursuing of the national financial stability and economic growth policy. The subject and the timing of this conference are very relevant, as we are at an interesting stage in relation to the economic and financial crisis. On the one hand, policymakers at the national, EU and G-20 levels seem to be still looking for the most appropriate ways out of the crisis for the economy. On the other hand, there is a negative perception in the citizens of a number of leading economies as regards the relationship between the crisis and the behavior of the financial system, particularly strong in the US and other countries where the State had to interfere with multibillion bailout operations. Nevertheless, there is no unanimous position on the measures that have to be pursued to prepare ourselves for any future crises. Crises are a distinctive feature of and an important element in the development of market economy, and we cannot reasonably believe there is any magic recipe for their elimination once and forever. Id rather say that that people empowered to take the political and economic decisions should do their best to minimize the negative effects from the crises. Against this background, analysts and scientists, as are most of you present here, are trying to summarize all the experience from the crisis and offer their theories: about its origin, about the financial sectors future, and about the lessons as regards financial market regulation. Today, I would like to talk to you about two of the BNBs main tasks in the recent 7-8 years, related to financial stability, which perfectly correspond to the subject matter of this conference: namely, the communication and anti-cyclical policies of the Central Bank. Financial stability and the voice of the professionals I would like to congratulate the organizers of this event, since conferences like todays are more than needed, and I believe that the discussions and reports shared in this hall will be well-met and will rouse further interest. With regard to the latest financial crisis, I firmly believe that reasonable, unbiased and professional analysis is rare to find. If we take Bulgaria, in particular - and thus I would like to express some constructive criticism - the voice of our scientific community is either not heard at all, or is weakly heard, while the existing academic potential is not appropriately used. The whole world is actively discussing the new macroprudential tasks of governments and central banks, the regulations and respectively their cyclicality/anti-cyclicality, the pro-cyclical behavior of credit rating agencies, the relationships between macroeconomic policies and financial stability, and so forth. At the same time, the general public in Bulgaria is left with the perception that our academia seems to be busy with its in-house problems! Our several economics universities are unusually quiet when the voice and the opinion of academics on the issues related to the global crisis should be heard. The VUZF University is one of the most recent higher education institutions in the country, and it is greatly to your credit - looking at this events program - that regardless of your young age, you have hit the bulls eye! You, and none of the older universities, first decided to organize such a conference. The voice of professionals influences directly the public opinion and attitudes, and hence the financial stability and economic growth. Fortunately, a new generation of economists with market-oriented thinking, working in non-government analytical centers, has made itself known in Bulgaria. Regretfully, however, they are not always sufficient to put forward all standpoints and analyses corresponding to the significance of the issues at hand. I insist on drawing your attention to this issue, which besides being scientific is also a communication one. Because the niche vacated by you is easily occupied by some self-proclaimed experts and soi-disant media heroes seeking financial or short-term political advantage. I would also put in this group those external commentators whom we often have to read or listen to, and who speak purportedly on behalf of renowned foreign institutions, but are in fact showering us with superficial contentions or outright misrepresentations to gain personal advantage. Although superficial, and often patently comical in their assertions, offered in the vernacular of the mass audience via easily digestible media channels (including the so-called yellow journalism), this type of experts have direct influence on the public behavior in Bulgaria. In this I see an enormous niche for the Bulgarian academia to support the countrys economy. Making assessments in public, particularly ill-judged and misleading talking, can easily turn into a pro-crisis factor and an impediment to development. During the crisis this was a problem we faced, which went beyond the objectively stable position of the banking system and the relatively good macroeconomic indicators (many of which are better to this day than in Western Europe for example). Such conclusions are not anything new, neither are they valid only for Bulgaria. Last week the President of the European Council, Mr Herman Van Rompuy quite pertinently warned European politicians to be particularly careful in their appearances, as money matters and very often public signals become part of the problem, not a part of the solution. At the BNB, we fully agree with the statement of the President of the European Council! All of us in the management team of our Central Bank have put a significant effort during the crisis to respond adequately to the numerous untrue assertions or false negative signals about Bulgaria. Let us remember the long series of apocalyptic scenarios and black predictions: e.g. about a collapse of the currency board (due to a flight of capital or the high current account deficit), about a breakdown of our banking system (due to an avalanche of bad loans) or about a decapitalization of the so called Greek banks (due to some vague contagion effects from the euro area). None of these have materialized. The currency board proved its flexibility and sustainability both during the boom prior to the crisis, and in the period of economic cycle downturn. Our banking system has at its disposal significant buffers and demonstrates remarkable stability, particularly against the background of the developments in some more developed economies. The subsidiary banks of foreign owners in Bulgaria (including the ones with prevailingly Greek shareholders) remain well capitalized and highly liquid. However, our hard efforts to refute all initial myths have been worthwhile, as financial stability is impossible if the credibility of the system is lost. In spite of the hardships of the crisis, the confidence in the currency board arrangement, in the banks, and in Bulgarias economic policies in general, was preserved. And here with you, in this format, is the right place to share that an important BNBs weapon to counter all biased comments about Bulgaria was the analytical and research capacity available at the BNB. Our analytical work is among the less visible functions of the Central Bank. This activity, however, is directly related to BNBs responsibilities, complementing the fulfillment of our statutory goals, namely: to maintain the stability of the national currency, of the countrys payment and banking systems, and to protect bank depositors. Financial stability and the anti-cyclical policy of the Central Bank For the attainment of these goals, before and during the crisis the BNB had to use resolutely the full range of conventional and non-conventional banking supervision regulations and instruments. We were facing phenomena that had never happened before in our modern economic history. The acceleration of credit growth was the Bulgarian response to the upswing of the global economic cycle and was related to the capital inflows, further strengthened by our accession to the European Union. Then Bulgaria was hit by the impact of the global economic crisis (which we already know today is the most severe in decades) and banks balance sheets were subjected to very severe pressures. All this time the BNB was consistently pursuing a policy governed by one guiding principle: the anti-cyclical counteracting behavior to the developments taking place in the banking system. This anti-cyclicality can be clearly seen when reviewing the measures taken over these years. In a functioning market economy the central government and the regulatory authorities cannot and should not replace the individual market entities in the taking of economic decisions. The Central Bank cannot and should not replace the managerial bodies of a commercial bank. That banks executives must have the most detailed picture and they themselves bear full responsibility to the banks customers and shareholders, for which they are paid their remuneration, in order to achieve financial results and manage the various types of risk. Just as the State lays down the Traffic Law but drivers themselves sit behind the wheel and steer their cars, so does the BNB set the framework of principles but the management of each bank must take the daily operational decisions. Along the lines of this logic, during the boom before the crisis the BNB was encouraging banks to accumulate capital and liquidity buffers and to be cautious in lending and assuming risks. We expanded the deposit base for calculating the MRRs, and the banks with excessive credit growth rates became subject to additional higher MRRs. The normative minimum capital adequacy ratio was kept at the level of 12% even after Bulgaria joined the EU (this is 50% above the Basel II threshold). We maintained higher risk weights than those prescribed in the EU Capital Requirements Directive. We restricted the lending in exotic foreign currencies (in the context of the currency board arrangement in Bulgaria this excludes the loans in euro). Mortgage loans could be granted in observing a very conservative threshold for the loan to value ratio, which involved higher down payment on the side of the borrower. However, since the end of 2008 when the global financial crisis began to spread in our country as well, the BNB proposed capital and liquidity reliefs. The MRR rate gradually came down to 7% on average (ranging from 0% to 10% depending on the source of the attracted funds). It became easier for banks to renegotiate loan conditions with solvent customers having temporary difficulties. The range of acceptable collateral was expanded. Risk weights were decreased in accordance with the Capital Requirements Directive (for instance, retail exposures and residential mortgage exposures). Banks were banned from paying dividends. Foreign banks were asked to take the commitment and keep their exposures to the subsidiaries. In this way the banking system in Bulgaria stayed stable, did not need any state aid, and continued to generate enough profits to meet the increased provision costs for non-performing loans. Today the capital adequacy and liquidity ratios largely exceed the averages for the European Union and those in the advanced economies. If we take a broader look, we will see that the focus of the BNB efforts on the banking system is not accidental. It naturally comes from our understanding that the stability of that system is key to the overall economic, political and social stability in this country. Without financial stability there can be no other stability! The sound Bulgarian banks did prove to be the most effective anti-crisis measure. Some researchers into the global crisis today claim that it was the stability of the national financial system that turned out to be the decisive factor distinguishing how the individual countries went through the crisis. From this point of view it is easy to explain why the greater resilience of the banks in Central and Eastern Europe (compared with the Western part of the continent) goes hand in hand with better fiscal and macroeconomic indicators of most countries in our region. Rescuing banks always provokes objections because of the moral hazard it involves: the rest of the market participants become less cautious in the hope that the government would protect them if need be. But politicians are also aware of the opposite: that any hypothetical bank failure might come with a very high economic and social price, and eventually it might also burden the budget and become an impediment to economic growth. The philosophy that financial and overall economic stability should be treated as inseparable was the inspiration behind the creation of the new European supervisory architecture (the European Systemic Risk Board and the related supervisory authorities). And at the national level it is becoming fashionable to talk about the new macroprudential role of central banks. This complements the traditional mandate of central banks to pursue an independent monetary policy. It is believed that synergy would be accomplished if supervisory tools, regulatory powers, and information  both at a macro and at a micro level  were concentrated in one institution. However, while other countries are just beginning, as a result of the crisis, to reform their financial supervision with an emphasis on the overall financial stability, such macroprudentiality has been practiced in Bulgaria for years. We can draw the conclusion that from a supervisory perspective Bulgaria today is advanced and not a catching-up country, given the average level in the European Union. To a large extent this is due to both the lessons learnt from our own banking and financial crisis in the mid-1990s and the disciplinary role of the currency board. With a fixed exchange rate and the impossibility to implement its own monetary policy, Bulgaria had to master almost to perfection various other economic governance tools. *** Ladies and Gentlemen, We do have reasons to be proud of what we have achieved so far in the supervisory policy area and the institutional framework. However, as I mentioned in the beginning, financial stability cannot be taken for granted, nor can it become a constant value. And the challenges we are facing are not over yet, nor will they disappear with the subsiding of the latest crisis. This crisis, however, has enriched our experience. And as with all crises, we need to take a very good look at the past and analyze it thoroughly so as to draw the lessons that would be valuable for the future. If now we could make some more definite conclusion, that conclusion would be that we must be vigilant for the easy solutions: the temptations for more regulations, unnecessary restrictions and unjustified government intervention, even if these are ostensibly dressed up as protection of financial stability or as  fiscal stimulus to the economy. And finally please allow me again to address you, the representatives of the academic community. The people of science can really help the banking community, regulators, and politicians. Apart from the fiscal and financial deficits, this crisis opened up deficits of ideas in the public domain. Many of the old rules, dogmas and practices do not seem to work any longer, but time presses upon us to make radical changes, without always having at our disposal in-depth analyses of the effects, benefits and costs. That is why I am especially grateful for the opportunity to be with you today. Thank you for your attention. I wish you fruitful discussions and success to this conference!

Title: Address on the occasion of the Inauguration of the Euro Exhibition at the Bulgarian National Bank, Sofia
text: Address by Ivan Iskrov, Governor of the Bulgarian National Bank, on the occasion of the Inauguration of the Euro Exhibition at the Bulgarian National Bank, Sofia, 16 September 2011 Your excellencies, Dear Guests, Distinguished Mr Gonzalez-Paramo, Ladies and gentlemen, It is a great honour for me on behalf of the Governing Council of the Bulgarian National Bank and of its employees to bid you welcome at the central bank of the Republic of Bulgaria to this remarkable and symbolic occasion  the opening of the two-month exhibition dedicated to the currency of United Europe. After Barcelona, Tallinn, Rome, Berlin, Bucharest and Paris, today all citizens and guests of our capital city, Sofia, will have the opportunity to visit this exhibition, including on weekend days. The Euro Exhibition is not only an interesting cultural and awareness event. Its display in Bulgaria is a symbol of the historical choice made by our country and the belonging of our nation to the most significant union of democratic nations - and of the thousand years of history and culture  the European Union. The euro is not only legal tender, just one of the tens of currencies on the Globe. It is the pinnacle of integration, an emanation of the desire of the European people for integration, fellowship and doing away with the centuries of disputes, wars and other misfortunes that have rent asunder the history of our continent. We have to realize, however, that the euro also sets a high standard of behavior for the countries that have adopted it as their national currency in the recent 10 years. The single European currency requires fiscal discipline and responsible structural policies. In this relation, Bulgaria can be a model to follow for large part of the euro area member states. Today, in times of obvious difficulties facing the euro area, I would like to note that when we twice expressed our desire to join R 2, being absolutely adjusted  having in place for more than a decade the much more disciplined currency board regime, quite a few member states, as well as some ECB officials, expressed skepticism and mistrust in our readiness. By an irony of fate today some of these countries are in a much worse situation  some due to serious financial troubles, others caught in the inexplicable introvertness and endless domestic policy dialogues, thus disappointing all of us with their inability to make quick and unequivocal political decisions. At the same time, our country inspires stability and calm, although the Bulgarian economy was not immune to the global crisis. The condition of public finances is more than satisfactory, our banking system is very well capitalized and highly liquid. And this is typical for a prevailing part of the new EU member states. It seems that the institutions and the political class in the countries of Eastern Europe turned out to be more prepared for acting in the crisis conditions. I do not say this as if rejoicing over it. Not in the least. It is impossible to be happy when relatives and neighbours are suffering. I am pointing to these facts as now, more than ever, Europe needs solidarity based on sound reason and pragmatism. It is high time to stop diverse talking, particularly in the countries forming the core of the euro area, and to proceed with concrete actions. The plausible solutions are clear and there is no need to invent the wheel again. What is needed is more work and less talking. There is no such thing as Greeks that are the only to blame and Germans that are flawless. The ECB President very appropriately noted last week which were the countries that first loosened the Stability and Growth Pact as early as 2005. We are all in one boat and we should row in one direction. That is why we at the BNB categorically support the ECBs efforts to help the member states facing difficulties, and we are surprised by the calls and critiques voiced for the institutions sterility. We should be absolutely clear that there cannot be any political, social or whatever else stability, including price stability, without the prerequisite of financial stability, and normal operation of the financial markets. The ECB cannot stay away and impassively watch how financial speculators are destroying the European markets  it should definitely continue forward with its efforts. Turning back to this exhibition, and sharing again the BNBs pleasure to host it, I would like to use the presence of so many mass media and through them to invite all the citizens and guests of the capital city to feel welcome to the exhibition, both in business and weekend days. We have made all necessary arrangements to make them feel comfortable with the deserved self respect of citizens of United Europe. Now allow me to give the floor to our distinguished special guest  Mr. Gonzalez Paramo, Member of the Executive Board of the European Central Bank for his welcoming address.

Title: Speech at the Closing Ceremony of the Twinning Project Strengthening the regulatory and supervisory capacity of the financial regulators, Podgorica, Montenegro
text: Speech by Mr Ivan Iskrov, Governor of the Bulgarian National Bank, at the Closing Ceremony of the Twinning Project Strengthening the regulatory and supervisory capacity of the financial regulators, Podgorica, Montenegro, 23 November 2011 Dear Minister Katnic, Your Excellencies, Dear Twinning Partners, Ladies and Gentlemen, Two years ago we gathered here to start the Twinning Project led by the BNB in cooperation with De Nederlandsche Bank and the Bulgarian Financial Supervision Commission. The name of the project is Strengthening the Regulatory and Supervisory Capacity of the Financial Regulators in Montenegro. his project is financed by the European Commission and has to be seen as part of the extensive EU support for the preparation of Montenegro for EU membership. In times of severe pressure on the financial supervisors across the world caused by the global financial crisis, the BNB committed significant resources to this project due to two main reasons: 1. The Republic of Bulgaria has repeatedly expressed its strong support for the integration of all the Balkan countries into the EU and in particular for the accession of the Republic of Montenegro to the European Union. 2. I was also personally convinced to do this project by the great desire and ambition of the then Minister of Finance - now Prime-Minister Igor Luksic and the former central bank Governor Ljubisa Krgovic. And of all the friends around this table. Now two years later, Im glad to say: yes it was worth the efforts. The results are impressive and were highly appreciated by the European Commission in its October Report on the progress of Montenegro where the achievements in the financial sector were highly valued. We made a big step in the harmonization of the Montenegrin financial sector legislation with the EU acquis communautaire. We jointly succeeded in establishing a new legal framework that will better serve the goal of stability and development of the financial services sector as well as the protection of consumers. We have transposed fully or to a large extent the core 15 EU directives preparing 8 draft laws and more than 25 other draft regulations that will guarantee their smooth implementation. We have really strengthened the capacity of the Montenegrin financial supervisory authorities. We were happy to work together with the management and expert teams of our four beneficiary institutions. The acquired training and the lessons learned from our joint work increased the expertise and the knowledge needed to start the negotiation process with the EU in the respective areas of financial services and financial regulation. And let me tell you, in Montenegro you have excellent experts, they are both highly professional and strongly dedicated to the reforms and improvements of that important sector for the benefit of your country. We involved in the project not only Bulgarian and Dutch experts with their experience, but also colleagues from Germany, Italy, Austria and some other Member States. We established excellent working relations and friendship which I believe will continue. The main result of the project is the strengthened cooperation between the financial supervisory authorities. At the national level you have already established financial stability arrangements in line with the best international practices. The high level Financial Stability Council has already functioned efficiently for one year. You have already several MOUs, including the one on anti-money laundering between all supervisory authorities and other institutions involved. One of the most substantial contributions of the project in the banking sector is the preparation of the whole framework for the implementation of Basel II from the beginning of 2012; the implementation of Pillar II requirements of the Basel II Accord; and the introduction of the Internal Capital Adequacy Assessment Process (ICAAP) concept which will sustainably foster the relationship between the risk profile of the bank, its risk management and its capital. In the area of securities, significant progress was made in the overall philosophy of the regulation and supervision of the Montenegrin capital market. One of the most tangible achievements was the development and implementation of a consumer protection and awareness strategy. Another key element of our work was the anti-money laundering policy and legislation. A draft law amending the current anti-money laundering law was prepared in full compliance with the EU directives. It will soon be considered by the Montenegrin Parliament. We all believe that the MoU between the financial supervisory institutions, the Ministry of Finance and the Anti-Money Laundering Authority will strengthen the cooperation and exchange of information between them. There are many other tangible results of the project and I will not list all of them now. Later you will have the opportunity to discuss them with so many Bulgarian and Dutch experts presented here today. Let me now conclude by admitting that this project was not an easy one. It was implemented by 7 authorities - three of them from EU Member States and four from Montenegro. During the two years of implementation we had many changes in the twinning team  our project leader from the beneficiary side, Mr. Katnic became a Minister of Finance, the President of the Insurance Agency, Mr. Kavaric became a Minister of Economy, we have a new Governor of the Central Bank. Nevertheless, all institutions remained strongly committed to the project. I would like to thank the Minister of Finance, Mr. Katnic for his leadership and strong dedication to the project and his ability to strengthen the cooperation between the separate financial sector regulators. I would like to thank my colleague Governor Zugic who joined us one year ago but gave strong momentum to the project and enhanced the project results. I would like also to congratulate and thank the Chairman of the Securities and Exchange Commission Mr. Djikanovic for accomplishing all the tasks of the project. I am also grateful to the President of the Insurance Agency Mr. Vujovic and his team for their contribution to the project. I would also like to thank our partners in the consortium, De Nederlandsche Bank and the Bulgarian FSC. Thank you very much to all of you and I wish you success. I would like to assure you that you can always rely on our support beyond the project term. Why not in other projects? Thank you for your attention!

Title: Speech delivered before the Association of Banks in Bulgaria on the occasion of the Bankers Day, Sofia, December 6, 2011.
text: Speech of Mr. Ivan Iskrov, Governor of the Bulgarian National Bank, delivered before the Association of Banks in Bulgaria on the occasion of the Bankers Day, Sofia, 6 December 2011 Ladies and Gentlemen, Our professional holiday, Saint Nicholas Day, has again gathered us together on 6th December. As enjoined by the tradition of these gatherings, my colleagues from the BNB Governing Council are also attending the meeting, to be able to congratulate ourselves on the Bankers Day and also to share our impressions of the past year and our expectations for the next one. Just a year ago, we discussed here the challenges and the experience gained which helps us pursue the mission entrusted to us by society. Banks are first of all intermediaries for the rest of the economy, and cannot possibly be successful in the long term if they do not support by their activities the economic turnover, and do not facilitate the general economic growth. Banks are also a factor underlying the overall financial stability  which is the most important prerequisite to economic development, and without it all other economic prospects would be jeopardized (as was rather clearly demonstrated by the global crisis). If we assess from this perspective the performance of the banks in Bulgaria, we should have today the self-confidence to note that the banking system continues to act as a significant pillar of and a stabilizing factor for the Bulgarian economy. This stability, however, has never so far been taken for granted, a kind of certainty that we received without any effort on our part, neither is it a constant value, which can be guaranteed in the future without the continuing efforts of each one of us. Several years ago, Bulgaria had the great advantage to face the global crisis with a sound banking sector. This was due to the fact that in the boom years before 2009, our banks, owing to their good management, and also encouraged by the conservative banking supervision, managed to accumulate adequate liquidity and capital buffers. Thus, they were to a great extent prepared for the times of crisis to come. For a third year now, these buffers have been subjected to a strong pressure, but they remain preserved. In the unfavourable economic environment, the quality of part of our bank balance sheet assets continues to deteriorate (as of September the share of bad loans came up to 14.45 percent), but the level of provisioning is high (only by the end of October the sector had allocated BGN 5.8 billion of provisions). What is more, in spite of the increasing provisioning costs, the system manages to generate profit, thus providing an additional capital buffer. How many banking sectors in Europe, or even globally, can boast today our average capital adequacy levels of almost 18% (including Tier I capital adequacy of over 15% ) and overall liquidity ratio of almost 26%? With these indicators, it is no surprise that the banks in Bulgaria remain among the few in the EU which had no need to be bailed out with taxpayers money (unlike those in other countries that otherwise are very fond of patronizing us). At the same time, in the recent years we have evidenced important positive structural trends, such as the reduced reliance on resources attracted from abroad, combined with a sustainable growth of domestic deposits of households, individuals and companies. The substitution of domestic resources for the external ones comes gradually, without the need to increase deposit interest rates (which would have otherwise affected adversely the efficiency of the sector as a whole). The confidence and the sound market logic of the domestic depositors are particularly striking  on an annual basis, until October, the deposits from individuals and companies rose by as much as 13 per cent. I take this opportunity to congratulate the entire banking community, represented by you tonight, on what has been accomplished. I also assure you that the stability and resilience of the Bulgarian banking sector during the crisis do not go unnoticed by external observers. I had the opportunity to be reassured of this again in the last few days when I was listening to the positive assessments of our banking system given by the regular mission of the International Monetary Fund which is presently in Bulgaria. We certainly believe that Bulgaria as a whole, and specifically its banking system, are still unjustifiably underestimated by, for instance, the global rating agencies. But the times are such that each country is busy defending first of all its own interest. And in the current overall situation of uncertainty on the international financial markets and a continuing debt crisis in some parts of the euro area, we must very highly value and keep all that has been achieved. Because new challenges are still ahead and the year 2012 will not be easy for all of us. Here I would like to outline three more significant issues which, one way or the other, are likely to be catching our attention in the months to come. Firstly, we should probably lower our expectations of the speed at which the Bulgarian economy will be recovering. Bulgaria will suffer from the negative effects from the expected slower developments in the external environment and, particularly, in the euro area (our major export market). Since the middle of 2011 the global economic situation has begun showing signs of deterioration, and this might have repercussions on the Bulgarian economy. In the recent months there is a renewed slowdown, and even decline, in the composite business climate indicator for the country, and the results of other business surveys (e.g. about the investment intentions of industrial enterprises and the consumer confidence) also reveal an increased pessimism. With respect to the banks, all this might imply new limits on credit growth. While seeking to strengthen their loan portfolios (i.e. that part of the balance sheet assets which was naturally most heavily affected during the crisis), the credit institutions will have to look for alternative possibilities for generating incomes. Secondly, we often discuss to what extent any possible transformations in the euro area banking sector would affect us, including any consolidations or changes of ownership or changes in the strategies of certain banking groups present in Bulgaria. For us it all comes down to the benefits for the Bulgarian banking system, including the chance for further stabilisation and reinforcement of the capital base. At home or abroad, everybody is interested in actions that would result in even better capitalised credit institutions  whether from own sources, or with external resources, even, if necessary, by attracting new shareholders. In 2011 similar actions were successfully completed in three banks in Bulgaria. Apart from that, in 2012 it is also possible that the market share of domestic banks would go on increasing (a development that has been in progress since the start of the crisis). Anyway, in Bulgaria there is one thing to be sure about  there is no reason whatsoever for changing the conservative nature of the banking supervision. One of the BNBs core tasks is to maintain the stability of the banking system and protect the depositors interests. And as the stable shareholder structure is a key factor to the stability of banks, the banking sector in Bulgaria will remain open to any serious participants having a good reputation and long-term intentions to operate in the domestic market. Thirdly, we should be aware of the possible institutional consequences of the crisis in the euro area and the EU  the major changes in governance and regulations, which are currently a subject of intense discussions. The situation is dynamic. Through our participation in a great number of EU and ECB bodies and working initiatives, the Bulgarian National Bank uses every opportunity to actively express Bulgarias stance. Although most often invisible to the general public (which is why we do not expect to receive any appreciation for it!), this is what has been, particularly recently, an essential part of our efforts to ensure financial stability and more favorable conditions for economic development in our country. To bring one example, which most directly relates to banks operations, that is the idea of the financial transactions tax. We share the position which is also maintained by the Ministry of Finance that this would do harm to the European and to the Bulgarian economy in particular. If introduced in the EU only (more so by individual countries only), such a tax would re-channel a part of the financial operations to other regions and overseas markets. Besides, the added costs to be incurred by such tax would ultimately be passed on to the end-users and would harm them. Especially for a catching-up country as Bulgaria is, a tax on financial transactions would hamper the development of the local financial sector while of immaterial contribution to the state budget. Also, we should not forget that such a penalising taxation on the financial sector would be hard to justify in our country where the banks not only were not the cause of the crisis, but they continue to be among the pillars of stability. Outside the above more significant trends and challenges in store for us, a number of opportunities remain open for improvement and streamlining of the work in every bank operating in Bulgaria. One such example relates to the potential of the Cash Service Company  the more you get involved there, the lower the prices for processing and servicing cash operations along the entire cycle of banknotes and coins. Your personal experience shows that individual decisions are always costlier while the system as a whole can achieve economies of scale. Working with customers remains a field of all-time improvement, as we talked about during our meeting here last year. The banks need each and every customer and it would be understandable if they take the initiative in creating new relationships. Thus, for instance, allocating certain limited resource for support of projects that wouldnt otherwise fit into the most conservative lending criteria should not be disregarded despite the cost. This way, the existing capital buffers acting perfectly as cushions in these difficult times, would also make a crucial trigger for generating a larger economic turnover. A long-term credibility between a bank and a customer is aided by what would seem at first sight the most minor services, such as the replacement of worn out or damaged Bulgarian banknotes and the replacement of Bulgarian coins. I would remind you that the provision of these services is included in the banking operation license. The right of commercial banks to attract deposits from the public presumes the provision of services such as the involvement in ensuring the cash circulation in the country. I believe that as part of the larger efforts towards streamlining of the relations with customers, banks will ever more fully make use of their right to render the above services, without having it as a requirement under a new BNB regulation. In conclusion, please allow me, on behalf of the BNB Governing Council and on my own behalf, to wish you all the very best in your professional and personal lives for the new 2012 year! Happy Bankers Day, dear colleagues!
