Title: Speech on the Occasion of Conclusion of Twinning Project between Bulgarian National Bank, Banque de France and De Nederlandsche Bank, Sofia, 15 September 2004
text: Speech by Mr Ivan Iskrov, Governor of the BNB, on the Occasion of Conclusion of Twinning Project between Bulgarian National Bank, Banque de France and De Nederlandsche Bank, Sofia, 15 September 2004 Your Excellency, Dear Mr. Redouin, Dear Mr. Brockmeijer, Dear Mr. Enk, Ladies and Gentlemen, Dear Colleagues, It is a pleasure for me to bid you welcome at the final meeting under the Twinning Project between the Bulgarian National Bank and Banque de France and De Nederlandsche Bank. When two year ago we launched this joint project, our country was in the middle of the negotiations for EU membership. Today, Bulgaria has already completed membership negotiations and our public institutions are preparing the membership treaty, which is expected to be signed at the beginning of next year. Two years can be a very short, and a very long period of time. In these two years we achieved much more than we initially expected, owing to our institution's will to develop and to the efforts of our colleagues and friends from the French and Dutch central banks. During these two years, the project reached its targets set under its eleven components. Even more, our joint work with the colleagues from Banque de France and De Nederlandsche Bank led to results that cannot be planned in advance, but which an integral part of any well planned and implemented joint project. In the first place, building partnership relations between BNB and Banque de France and De Nederlandsche Bank.The Bulgarian National Bank considers these two Eurozone central banks as strategic partners and intends to continue, in one way or another, its co-operation with them. This intention of ours found its expression in the two bilateral agreements signed early in June with the French and the Dutch central banks. Second comes the establishment of professional and personal contacts between BNB experts and their colleagues from Banque de France and De Nederlandsche Bank. These contacts form the foundations to build on our joint activities within the framework of the bilateral agreements between the BNB and these two central banks, and in the medium term - within the European system of Central Banks and the Eurosystem. The work under the Twinning Project with two Eurosystem central banks allowed the BNB to diagnose better the current status of the institution and its level of preparedness to operate within the European System of Central Banks and the Eurosystem. This experience helped us clearly define the challenges to be faced by the BNB in the accession process. Based on this experience and with the assistance of our colleagues from Banque de France, the BNB Managing Board prepared a Strategy for the Development of the Bulgarian National Bank for 2004  2009. This document describes the changes that have to be made during this period for the future integration of the BNB into the European System of Central Banks and the Eurosystem. The Strategy for the Development of the Bulgarian National Bank will soon be announced to the general public, thereby the whole public would have an insight into the policy of one of the major public institutions, which is responsible for the price and financial stability in the country. The Strategy for the Development of the BNB provided the BNB's management the possibility to plan the institution's medium-term development and to estimate the required investments, which need to be made in human resources, the infrastructure and technologies, and the amendments to the regulatory framework. This Strategy enabled us to draw an in-depth "Roadmap" of the necessary actions and the deadlines for their implementation, so that our Central Bank could successfully integrate into and operate within the ESCB and the Eurosystem. The actions described in the Roadmap and the timing of their implementation are synchronised with the timeframe for the accession of Bulgaria to ERM II and consequently to the Eurozone. The positive outcomes of the Twinning Project are the result of the continuous efforts of its participants from the three central banks. I would like to express my gratitude to all participants in the Project for their efforts and the high professional style of their work. Of course, this Project could not be made possible without the personal involvement of Governors Trichet, Noyer, and Wellink. Special thanks to the Delegation of the European Commission for their all-time support in the course of the Project, for their responsiveness and flexibility. Our colleagues from the Ministry of Finance extended a helping hand in the process of administration of the financial aspect of the Project, which we highly appreciate. Needless to say, we also owe much to the governments of the EU countries and their taxpayers, who funded this Project. I would like to assure them that the funding of this Project by the European Commission is a very worthy investment in the future of Europe. Thanks once again to all for their efforts and support. Thank you for your attention. PAGE PAGE 1

Title: Speech on the Occasion of the 125th Anniversary of the Bulgarian National Bank, 5 June 2004
text: Speech by Mr. Ivan Iskrov, Governor of the BNB, on the Occasion of the 125th Anniversary of the Bulgarian National Bank, 5 June 2004 Dear President Parvanov, Dear Prime Minister Saxe-Coburg, Your Holiness, Dear Members of Parliament, Ladies and Gentlemen Ministers, Your Excellencies, Dear esteemed gentlemen that have had the honour of being BNB Governors in the last 30 years, Distinguished Governors, Ladies and Gentlemen, It is a great honour for me to bid you welcome to the official ceremony and the concert in commemoration of the 125th Anniversary of the BNB. The Bank was founded on 25 January 1879, immediately after Bulgaria was declared an independent state by a decree issued by the Commissioner of the Russian Emperor to Bulgaria - Prince Dondoukov-Korsakov. On 6 June 1879, the country's government deposited the necessary capital for the foundation of the BNB in accordance with the decree. This is the day from which the BNB has started performing in real terms the functions assigned to it. The development of modern societies and their institutional framework and economic development have not always been accompanied by the parallel establishment of a central bank. We are all well aware that many developed economies have established their central banks in the 20th century. As of 1900, there were only eighteen central banks world-wide, the Bulgarian National Bank being one of them. Chronologically, our bank was the 13th to be established in the world. A peculiarity of the BNB compared to great part of commercial banks in the world is that it has been established and developed in parallel with the modern Bulgarian state. It was founded almost at the time of creation of the national currency. Thus, the whole process is not only economic, but rather broader and comprehensive in its nature. It is an integral part of the development of the modern Bulgarian statehood. These 125 years of existence of modern Bulgaria were years of both economic success and economic crisis as the immediate consequence of errors in the political and economic governance of the country. The economic accomplishments and failures of the state were closely interwoven with and exemplified in the history of the Bulgarian National Bank. Today, while we go through its 125-year history, we can see in it the clearly cut outlines of the Bulgarian economy. In addition to its monopoly on currency issuance, a function performed by all central banks, the Bulgarian central bank has for a long period of time played a key role in the development of financial intermediation in this country. The BNB had commitments to provide financial services to the government, to the general public, and to businesses. The Bulgarian National Bank, as one of the pillars of modern market economy, also performs important political functions. In democratic societies the guarantees of private property are a core principle laying the foundations of social prosperity and welfare of the public. This is a principle underlying the Tarnovo Constitution. It is also the mainstay of the new Constitution of 1991. It is beyond any doubt, that there can be no guarantees of private property without stability of the national currency. The value of this same private property is denominated and measured in the national currency. This means that the price stability achieved by the Central Bank is the most forceful guarantee in support of private property. Hence, the BNB as an institution is an integral part of the development of our democratic society. Most of the people in this hall have taken direct part in the historical process of transformation of our society in the recent 15 years. The fundamental change in this society, the transformation of the policy and economy and their alignment along the lines of universal human values was made possible and was accomplished thanks to the efforts of each one of us. For this relatively short period of time, the Bulgarian economy, and BNB in particular, achieved a lot. As a consequence of the broad-based political and public consensus on this country's strategic goals, the Bulgarian society and public institutions have changed more than we could expect and hope for. Today, seven years after the start of the large-scale changes in the Bulgarian policy and economy, our country is a full-fledged NATO member and is in the finalisation phase of the negotiations for EU membership. The BNB as a major public institution of this country has also contributed with its significant input for the accomplishment of these goals. In the coming years, we should go on in the same direction and keep up with the pace with which our society and institutions have been changing and improving. Bulgaria is expected to become an EU member state, and shortly after to joint the EMU. These prospects for integration provide lots of opportunities for our society, but also face it with challenges that we should live up to. From the moment of Bulgaria's accession to the European Union, the BNB will become part of the ESCB, and with joining the EMU - a part of the Eurosystem. Looking back through the 125 years of history of the BNB, I am confident that our Central Bank has the capacities and expertise that would enable it to overcome all possible difficulties. Being well aware of the Bank's institutional capacity, and the knowledge and energy of my colleagues, I am deeply convinced that the BNB will be ready for the process of its integration into the European monetary structures. Ladies and Gentlemen, A fact that further strengthens my confidence and delights me is that, today, on the date we celebrate our 125 anniversary, we have among us our President, and Prime Minister and the Head of the Bulgarian Orthodox Church, the elite of the Bulgarian political judicial and financial system, the Ambassadors accredited to Bulgaria, the persons in charge of the major mass media. We have as our guests the Governors and members of the management bodies of the central banks of more than 35 countries from 4 continents, as well as the representatives of the International Financial Institutions. I would like to thank you for the recognition, and the honour of your presence among us. Thanks to each of you. PAGE PAGE 1

Title: Remarks at the American Chamber of Commerce Meeting, Sofia, 20 January 2004
Subtitle: BULGARIAN NATIONAL BANK POLICY AND ECONOMIC OUTLOOK FOR 2004
text: Remarks by Mr. Ivan Iskrov, Governor of the Bulgarian National Bank, at the American Chamber of Commerce Meeting, Sofia, 20 January 2004 BULGARIAN NATIONAL BANK POLICY AND ECONOMIC OUTLOOK FOR 2004 It is a pleasure for me to take part in this business lunch and to have the opportunity to speak before the members of the American Chamber of Commerce. I would like to express my thanks to Mr. Lefkowitz for the invitation and to the American Chamber of Commerce for this opportunity. As the Governor of the Bulgarian National Bank I have the possibility and the responsibility to directly participate in the designing and pursuing of the countrys economic policy. At the same time, considerable part of my professional experience has been gained in the commercial banking. My private sector experience indicates that it is of paramount importance for the businesses to have a clear, transparent, and consistent policy implemented by the public institutions. Taking this philosophy as a basis, as well as the endeavour of the public institution I head to pursue a transparent and consistent policy, I accepted without hesitation Mr. Lefkowitz's invitation to speak before the AmCham members. What is important for the business is political stability and the prospects for our country's development (NATO and EU membership included), the soundness and efficiency of public institutions and the economic environment in Bulgaria. In this first speech of mine before the American Chamber of Commerce, I will deal briefly with the development of Bulgarian economy in the past year 2003, and the outlook for this year and the effect of these developments on the investment and business environment. The political stability and predictability of the policy implemented by public institutions is one of the most significant conditions for long-term investment decision-making by companies and households. In the recent years, the country achieved considerable progress in terms of public institutions' stability and the predictability and consistency of the policy pursued by them. The Bulgarian National Bank is probably the most indicative example for the change in the second part of the 1990-ies in designing and implementing public institutions' policies in our country. With the introduction of the Currency Board Arrangement in 1997, the central bank's policy has been aimed exclusively at maintaining the price and exchange rate stability, and the stability of the country's financial system. This is the proper time to underline my unconditional commitment that the policy pursued by the central bank will be within the framework of the currency board regime set forth in the BNB Law. Ensuring the price and financial stability in the country is the BNB's contribution to the common policy of all public institutions to create a favourable environment for investments and growth in the economy. At the same time, we are well aware that building of public institutions pursuing effective policies is an on-going process, as the economy and the society are continuously changing. In the current year, our country will become a full-fledged NATO member, and in 2007 also an EU member- country. These processes require continuous improvement of public institutions, the BNB included. At the same time, these convergence processes in our institutions and economy provide a great potential for investments and doing business. I believe that the NATO membership of Bulgaria will undoubtedly improve the investment climate in our country. The medium-term policy in relation to the country's EU and EMU membership will be one of the priorities in the activities of the central bank. At the end of December 2003, the ECB Governing Council confirmed its earlier expressed position that currency boards having the Euro as their reserve currency were ERM II-compatible but they were not its substitutes. This means that until our country's membership in the European Union (EU), the BNB will unconditionally support the fixed exchange rate of the Bulgarian Lev to the Euro at the level set by the BNB Law. After joining EU, all issues concerning the membership in the EMU will be settled in the agreement among Bulgaria, member states and the European Central Bank. In the process of accession of our country to the Economic and Monetary Union and of the central bank into the European System of Central Banks, the BNB clearly recognizes the interests of the Bulgarian society and will unswervingly protect these interests. Allow me to proceed with a synopsis of the macroeconomic development of the country in 2003 and the outlook for 2004. The past year was marked by a high degree of uncertainty as regards the development of global economy. Until mid-year, in US (the world's dominant economy) there was a relatively high risk of a continuing recession and negative inflation rates. As late as in the last quarter of 2003, data unequivocally indicated that the greatest economy in the world has come out of the recession and is not facing the danger of plunging into a deflation spiral. The European Union, our country's major trade partner, recovered at a slower pace, its growth rates approximating zero. In this global environment, the Bulgarian economy realized a GDP growth rate of 4.1% in the first nine months of 2003. We can expect the 2003 GDP growth rate in the range of 4.5 to 4.8 per cent, which outpaces a little the long-term growth rate achieved after 1997. The average annual inflation in 2003 was 2.3 per cent. Traditionally, the high rates of economic growth go together with higher inflation rates. Despite the relatively high growth rates evidenced in 2003, inflation remained at low and stable levels. These developments were determined to a great extent by two strong global anti-inflationary factors: the appreciation of the Euro (respectively the Lev) against the US Dollar and the decreasing global prices resulting from the low growth rates in the leading economies and the strong competition of rapidly developing Asian economies (China, India). The financial sector was among the most dynamically developing ones in the Bulgarian economy in 2003. This development ensured access of more and more companies and households to the credit market. An increasing number of investment projects are funded by the banking system and more households can purchase housing and consume goods through commercial bank lending. For the 11 months of 2003, the average rates of growth of lending to households and to companies were 62 and 45 per cent, respectively. Statistics indicate that considerable part of the rapidly increasing lending to households is spent on import consumer goods, which impacts negatively the trade balance and the current account of the country. Until October 2003, the trade balance and the current account deficits on an annual basis have reached 12.3 and 8.1 per cent of GDP, respectively. These are the highest levels evidenced in our country since the introduction of the currency board. At the same time, the level of the current account deficit is not destabilizing, and I believe in the current year there will be a positive change in the trade balance and current account trend. In 2003, direct foreign investments in the country reached their peak level since the beginning of the economic reforms. They reached up to USD 1.4 billion for the first 10 months of 2003. Such direct investment dynamics comes in to support my position that the current account deficit has no destabilizing effect, and that the Bulgarian economy can attract foreign investments and has the capacity to absorb these investments. Employment and unemployment dynamics in the past 2003 year is indicative for the economic growth sustainability and the potential of our economy to create new jobs. In the first 11 months of 2003, unemployment dropped by 3.6 per cent, while the number of employed increased by 155 thousands. What are the expectations for 2004? Small and open economies, like Bulgaria, are closely dependent on the global economy developments. Therefore, the development of the national economy in the current year will be greatly determined by the dynamics of global economy. What are the expectations for the global economy in 2004? First, further slow recovery of the American and European economies, accompanied by low and stable inflation rates. With the increasing economic growth in the major economies, we can expect an increase in the interest rates by the Federal Reserve and ECB. The pressure on businesses to cut expenses and increase their competitiveness will continue. This trend of cost optimization with a view to maintaining competitiveness will intensify due to strong competition of countries like India and China, that enjoy an oversupply of relatively highly qualified and cheap labour. This is the global economic environment, in which the Bulgarian economy will operate in the current year. I hope that, this expected development of the global economic environment will not be disturbed by the realization of any of the existing risks, like terrorist attacks or security crises in some unstable regions in the world. Exactly due to the existence of such global risks, which inevitably have negative impact on small economies, I emphasized at the beginning of my speech the importance of political stability and the stability and predictability of the institutions, and guaranteeing national security. These are important prerequisites for doing business. I unconditionally believe that in 2004 these prerequisites will be in place in Bulgaria, and will continuously improve. This allows us to expect a good year for the business and for the country's economy. In 2004, we are anticipating up to 5.3% growth of GDP. We expect the growth of investments and final consumption will be preserved at the high rates attained in 2003. This will be the driving force of economic growth in the country in the current year too. The financial sector will remain as one of the main sources of financing investments in the country. The year past was very successful for the Bulgarian banking system. Data concerning the first three quarters prove that the good level of liquidity and capital adequacy (23% capital adequacy) of the banking system and the high quality of commercial banks' portfolios (92% performing loans) has been preserved. In the same period, the profits in the banking system have increased by 34 per cent against the previous year, reaching BGN 293 mill. This development of the banking system allows me to believe that in 2004 it will be one of the most dynamically developing sectors in the country's economy. In 2004, we expect the trend of increasing foreign direct investment will continue. Previous years' experience indicates that the rates of growth of investments are highly correlated to the level of FDI in the country. In other words, maintaining the high equity investment growth rates will be to a great extent conditional upon the dynamics of foreign direct investments. I expect the US direct investments in Bulgaria to increase in 2004, as well as the contribution of US investors towards increasing the amount of foreign investments to our country. Inflation rates will remain at low and stable levels. Both globally and domestically, there are no strong pro-inflationary factors. The appreciation of the Bulgarian Lev to the US Dollar and the stable international prices of basic raw materials will be the main factors determining the low inflation rates in 2004. A temporary price level rise can be expected early in the year accounted for by the increased indirect taxes. his will be a short-lived growth of inflation, and as our early 2002 experience indicates, such one-off inflation increase subside within several months. Dear Ladies and Gentlemen, I can continue with the analysis of the expected developments in the Bulgarian economy in 2004 and the conditions for investments and doing business in our country. Before concluding, however, I would like to thank again the American Chamber of Commerce for the opportunity provided to me to express my views on the development of the Bulgarian economy before such a remarkable audience. Early in my speech, I spoke about the importance of institutions and the unremitting progress of the institution I head - the Bulgarian National Bank - in the recent years. I would like to emphasize that this progress could be achieved to a great extent owing to the assistance provided by a number of international institutions. Thank you for the attention. PAGE PAGE 3

Title: Remarks at the EastEuro Links Conference Growth Toward Synergy: Restructuring Macroeconomics and Finance in Central and South East Europe, Sofia, 30 January 2004
text: Remarks by Mr. Ivan Iskrov, Governor of the BNB, at the EastEuro Links Conference Growth Toward Synergy: Restructuring Macroeconomics and Finance in Central and South East Europe, Sofia, 30 January 2004 STRATEGIES AND PRIORITIES OF THE CENTRAL AND SOUTH EAST EUROPES CENTRAL BANKS It is a pleasure for me to take part in this conference and to open the discussion within which various views on the priorities of Central and Southeast Europe's central banks and the strategies for attaining them can be shared. Money and the various approaches to its management appeared as early as the initial stages of development of civilization. From this long-term perspective, central banks are relatively new institutions. By way of example, I will mention that the first central bank - the Swedish Riksbank - was established as late as 1668. In 1900 there were only 18 central banks worldwide, and one of them was the Bulgarian National Bank, whose 125th anniversary we are to commemorate this year. Today central banks are 174. This relatively short period of existence of central banks, evidenced all through a continuing process of change of priorities in the policies pursued and the strategies for their achievement. The scope and focus of this Conference do not allow for an exhaustive overview of this development. So in this short speech, I will focus on the goals, and the strategies for their attainment, of the Central and Southeast Europe's central banks in the period after 1990, trying also to outline the challenges we presently face. With the start of the transition from a command to a market economy, in the countries in Central and Southeast Europe, governments and central banks were faced with the challenge of formulating the central bank goals and the strategy for their attainment. Of course, this process in the countries of Central and Southeast Europe could not develop in isolation from the global monetary policy and central banking trends. The 1990ies were a period when the developed countries' central banks redefined their ultimate objectives and strategies. The experience from the 1970ies and 1980ies has indicated that higher rates of growth and employment cannot be achieved by allowing higher rates of inflation. Furthermore, historic experience has proven that high and unstable inflation rates result in low and fluctuating rates of economic growth and employment (see Figure 1). Chart 1. Inflation and GDP growth in G-7 economies (annual percentage change) This experience was underlying the change that led to redefining the interrelation between the central bank and the government, the ultimate objectives of its policies, and the strategies for attaining these objectives. The view that central banks should have a high degree of independence, combined with transparency and accountability was generally accepted. They should set maintaining price and financial stability as their main goal, with monetary policy strategies based either on a floating exchange rate and direct inflation targeting, or on pegging the exchange rate and convergence of the inflation rate towards the inflation rate of the country (or area) of its reserve currency. In establishing their central banks and defining their priorities and strategies, the countries of Central and Southeast Europe proceeded from the conventional view of the central bank's role in society, established in the developed countries. To what extent did countries in our region adopt this conventional view and what could they achieve? Central Bank Independence Empirical data and research indicate that today almost all central banks of countries in Central and Southeast Europe enjoy a degree of statutory independence higher, on the average, than the one existing in the early 1990ies in most of the developed countries. Of course, we should note the importance of real compliance with the law, which practically determines the degree of actual central bank independence. It is a well-known fact, that the law is applied in a varying degree in different countries, which determines the degree of actual independence of the respective central bank. Main Objectives As regards the legally set main objectives, the central banks in Central and Southeast Europe have to a very great extent come close to the generally accepted principle that central banks should be responsible for maintaining price and financial stability in their country. In almost all countries in our region, the main objective provided for in the central bank legislation is ensuring price stability, or any other type of stability of the national currency. To what extent do central banks manage to control inflation and ensure price stability? Since the beginning of the transition, inflation in the countries of Central and Southeast Europe dropped from 140 % in 1990 to 4 % in 2003 (see Figure 2). Undoubtedly, considerable part of this significant reduction in the inflation rates is accounted for by the considerable continuous improvement of the practices of monetary policy implementation, the accumulation of expertise and experience, and the institutional strengthening of the central banks in the region. Of course, central banks could not reap alone the ovations for the successful inflation rate reduction. Balancing the fiscal policies of national governments, as well as the continuous process of opening of national economies, market globalization, and the increasing competition also contributed to the reduction of inflation rates. Low inflation rates were made possible because the societies realized the high price of inflation and had the will to take actions ensuring price stability. Chart 2. Inflation in Central and Southeast Europe economies and G-7 economies (annual percentage change) Individual central banks in the region have managed to a different extent to achieve control of inflation rates. At the end of 2002, a prevailing part of the countries from Central and Southeast Europe (with the exception of Romania, Serbia and Montenegro) have one-digit inflation rates of consumer prices. This stabilization of inflation at one-digit levels is a considerable achievement, given the comprehensiveness of the reforms that our countries had to implement for a relatively short period of time. At the same time, we know these countries are characterized by an endogeneous trend of increasing price levels due to the continuing process of convergence of real incomes to the income levels in the developed countries (see Figure 4). Later in my speech, I will provide more detailed observations on the effect of the real convergence process on the inflation rates in the Central and South East Europe countries. Monetary Policy Strategies The monetary policy strategies of the banks in the region developed in time depending on the transition stage their economies had reached. Presently, we can define two main groups of countries - with a floating exchange rate and direct inflation targeting and countries with fixed exchange rate and focusing central bank policy on maintaining a fixed exchange rate. The discussion on the choice of an exchange rate regime and a monetary policy strategy is very enormous and sophisticated to be described in detail in such a short speech. Our countries experience proved that both floating and fixed exchange rates can ensure price and financial stability and a favourable environment for economic growth. I believe that in the countries with less stable or more temperamental political environment, currency boards act as a stabilizing factor. The issue, Central and South East Europes central banks should find an answer to, is to what extent the presently existing monetary policy strategies will allow them to perform their main tasks. The development of the economy and society is accompanied by a high degree of uncertainty. This faces central banks with the incessant need to adapt to the changing economic environment. Which is the major challenge that our central banks will have to face in the medium-term perspective and how will this impact their priorities and strategies? The Challenges It is a fact that 8 countries from the region will join the European Union (U) in May this year. Bulgaria and Romania are looking forward to accession in 2007, and the remaining countries in the region - as a longer-term prospect. The EU accession presupposes joining the Economic and Monetary Union as a next step, as the new EU member-countries cannot exercise an opt-out clause as regards EMU membership. The accession of Central and South East Europe countries to the EMU and of the national central banks to the European System of Central Banks (ESCB) is the major challenge for us in a medium-term perspective. The requirement of achieving real and nominal convergence of the national economies prior to each country's accession to the EMU, assign to the central banks the task to define and implement a monetary policy strategy, which would ensure both price stability and real convergence. The nominal convergence criteria (known as the Maastricht criteria) set five preliminary conditions that each country should comply with before joining the EMU. Achieving an inflation rate, which should not exceed by more than 1.5 percent the average inflation rate in the three Euro area countries with the lowest inflation; Achieving a nominal long-term interest rate, which should not exceed by more than 2 percent the one in the three countries in the Euro area with the lowest inflation; Achieving a budget deficit below 3 percent of the GDP; Achieving a level of the gross sovereign debt to GDP ratio below 60 per cent; Supporting a fixed exchange rate to the euro for a period of at least two years. Inflation Among the nominal convergence criteria, the criterion of achieving an inflation rate equal to the average rate in the three EMU countries featuring the lowest inflation plus 1.5 % is a direct responsibility of the central bank. As already mentioned, the central banks in the region have to a great extent managed to formulate a monetary policy strategy allowing them to ensure price stability. (see Figure 3). To what extent, however, will the existing strategies permit central banks to additionally reduce the inflation rates to a level compliant with the inflation criterion, will depend on some changes in the structure of the respective economies. These changes are beyond the direct control of the central bank, but it should take them into consideration in formulating and pursuing the monetary policy. Long-Term Nominal Interest Rate The convergence of the long-term nominal interest rate is partially a function of the central bank's policy. As we are well aware, central banks can exercise control only on the short-term interest rates. The long-term interest rates are a function of multiple factors, most of which beyond the central bank's control. Since the long-term nominal interest rate incorporates the long-term inflation expectations, managing inflation rates and inflation expectations in the economy is the contribution, which the central bank is able to provide for the compliance with the interest rate convergence criterion. Exchange Rate The countries practicing floating exchange rate and directly targeting inflation will have to adapt their monetary policy strategy in a way allowing them to participate in ERM II. In other words, they will have to fix their exchange rate to the Euro, preserving the possibility to pursue an independent monetary policy to the extent this is compatible with supporting the fixed exchange rate. The countries with a fixed exchange rate of their national currency to the Euro (including the ones practicing a currency board) will not have to make any significant changes in their monetary policy strategy. The ECB's position on the in-principle compatibility of currency board regimes with ERM II, provided that the regime is sustainable in a long-term perspective, does not require from central banks operating under such a regime to change their monetary policy regime in the transition period before their EMU accession. Chart 3. Inflation in Central and Eastern Europe economies and Euro area (annual percentage change) Nominal and Real Convergence As I mentioned earlier, one of the main criteria of nominal convergence is maintaining an inflation rate not exceeding by more than 1.5 % the average rate for the three countries in the Euro area with the lowest inflation rate. I find this as one of the greatest challenges for the national central banks, as to a certain extent this goal comes in contradiction with the goal of achieving real convergence. It is well known that there is a strong correlation between the price level and the incomes in the economy. The incomes increase in the economy goes along with a rise in prices (see Chart 4). The countries joining the EU this year have per capita income that is 47% of the income in the EU and a price level that is 52% of the level in the EU. This contradiction between the requirement for achieving nominal and real convergence before the actual membership in the EMU is one of the most important challenges for national central banks, and they must find an adequate solution by adapting their monetary policy strategies. Chart 4. GDP per head and price level in Acceding and Candidate countries EU15100 (in PPS) As I already said, the uncertainties about the development of the political and economic life in the individual countries faces central banks with many challenges and they must find the best possible solution to these challenges. In this short speech I could not, and I do not intend to, make an extensive review of the evolution of central banks strategies and priorities in Central and Southeast Europe and the challenges before these banks. I rather hope that what I have shared with you today would be a good basis for holding productive and useful discussions during this forum. Thank you very much for your attention. I wish you constructive and useful discussions. ____________ The group of the countries from Central and Southeast Europe includes: Albania, Bosnia & Herzegovina, Bulgaria, Croatia, Czech Rep., Estonia, Hungary, Latvia, Lithuania, Macedonia, Poland, Romania, Serbia & Montenegro, Slovak Rep. and Slovenia. All the data for the year 2004 is forecast data See Cukierman, A., Miller, G., & Neyapti, B., (2002). Central bank reform, liberalization and inflation in transition countries  an international perspective, Journal of Monetary Economics 49, pp.237-264. Except Albania, Serbia and Montenegro, for which we have no data. For an indepth presentation see Objectives of the central bank as set out in legislation, Bank for International Settlements, 2001. See BIS, pp. 13-14. See Rogoff, K., (2003). Globalization and global disinflation, FRB of Kansas City Economic Review, pp.45-78. See EBRD Transition Report 2003, Integration and regional cooperation, pp. 108-212. See European Central Bank Policy position of the Governing Council of the European Central Bank on exchange rate issues relating to the Acceding countries, 18 December 2003. See Eurostat 'Purchasing power parities and related economic indicators for EU, Acceding and Candidate Countries and EFTA' 9 December 2003. PAGE PAGE 6

Title: Statement on the Occasion of Signing of the Treaty of the Accession of Bulgaria and Romania to the European Union, 25 April 2005
text: Statement by Mr. Ivan Iskrov, Governor of the BNB, On the Occasion of Signing of the Treaty of the Accession of Bulgaria and Romania to the European Union, 25 April 2005 Ladies and Gentlemen, I have the great pleasure to congratulate you on the Treaty of Accession of Bulgaria and Romania to the European Union (EU) signed today. This is a remarkable historical event, the final and long-cherished step to Bulgarias full-fledged membership in the European Union. The path to attaining this ardently desired goal started with the Europe Agreement establishing an Association between the European Communities and the Republic of Bulgaria , signed in 1993 and effective from February 1995, continued with the initiation of the accession negotiations in February 2000, and their successful finalization in June 2004. We got here led not only by the great desire of the Bulgarian people and the EU nations for unity, but also through the hard work and commitment of several Bulgarian governments, the state administration, the National Assembly, and the heads of state. The signing of this Treaty is a landmark of our time, that is distinguished by absolute national consensus, an example of coordination and interaction between all state and public institutions for the attainment of a priority goal of national importance. As one of the oldest public institutions in Bulgaria, and one of tremendous importance for the operation of our economy, too, the Bulgarian National Bank significantly contributed to the successful negotiations and the preparation of the Treaty of Accession, and BNB experts participated in 7 working groups: Economic and Monetary Union, Free Movement of Capital, Freedom to Provide Services, Statistics, Consumer and Health Protection, Financial Control, Lisbon Strategy. The BNB worked actively for the fulfillment of the commitments under the Treaty of Accession. Full harmonization of Bulgarian legislation with the EU directives has been achieved in areas such as capital adequacy of banks, cross-border credit transfers, electronic payment instruments and settlement finality in the payment, and securities settlement systems. Much has been done, and is being done in the area of statistical data for the European System of Central Bank (ESCB) and Eurostat. The BNB, as an institution of long-lasting traditions, is continuously working for its advance and improvement, with the goal to more effectively fulfill its mission and the responsibilities delegated to it in the present-day dynamic information environment. After the amendments to the Law on the BNB adopted in 2005, the central bank enjoys unconditional independence allowing for the most effective pursuance of its main goal  maintaining price stability by ensuring a stable exchange rate until the time of accession to the euro area, as well as problem-free and sustainable operation of the financial system. Naturally, independence goes along with the BNBs responsibility to operate in a manner allowing for open communication and transparency and ensuring the most effective distribution of resources. This day marks the beginning of Bulgarias increasing role in the joint decision making process in the EU institutions. Gaining an observer status, from this day on, the BNB will be represented at the sessions of the ECB General Council and Governing Council, at the meetings of the ESCB committees and ECOFIN. From now on, we will have the opportunity to participate in discussions and to call for consultations on issues relating to out interests in the EU institutions. Let us all congratulate ourselves on the magnificent results and the success earned with much effort. What are the prospects before the BNB  more and more effort and broader responsibilities. In the time, a little more than a year and a half, remaining to our full-fledged EU membership, we have on our agenda the integration of the BNB and ECB information systems, initiation of negotiations on the earliest possibilities for participation in the new exchange rate mechanism, ERM II, while preserving the currency board. After the EU membership, the BNBs obligations and responsibilities will expand, as it will become a full-fledged ESCB member with a voting right and obligations to provide information, statements, analyses, and to comply with the ERM II conditions. Subsequently, our euro area membership will bring about our involvement in the formulation of the common monetary policy of the ECB, influencing the uniform statistical activities of ECB and Eurostat, and full integration of the Bulgarian payment system into the euro area one. There are many, and well-known, benefits of the earliest possible accession to the euro area: full elimination of foreign trade barriers; increased opportunities for risk sharing and diversification; access to the developed financial markets that would boost up the development of the domestic financial market; increasing competition, competitiveness, and financial innovation. The unconditional commitment for maintaining price stability before and after the adoption of the euro would minimize the inflation risk premium, which would bring interest rates down, particularly the ones on long-term loans. This would provide a favourable environment for sustainable economic growth and prosperity. Since there are clear, precise, and irreversible phases and commitments in the process of Bulgarias accession to the euro area, and due to the fact that financial markets respond comparatively quickly to any change in the expectations, the benefits will be, to a great extent, available earlier than the date of euro area membership. The integration process unquestionably brings economic benefits to all countries in Europe, but its effect is not limited only to this. By signing the Treaty, we become a full member of a community of kindred states, with which we have common democratic ideals and values, and a shared vision for the future, for attaining prosperity, welfare, and sustainable growth. Thus, we see nations dream come true. Thank you for the attention.

Title: Opening remarks at the Credit Risk Management International Conference, Sofia, 7 April 2004
Subtitle:
CREDIT RISK MANAGEMENT IN THE BANKING
SYSTEM: CURRENT CONDITION AND FUTURE CHALLENGES
text: Opening remarks by Mr. Ivan Iskrov, Governor of the BNB, at the Credit Risk Management International Conference, Sofia, 7 April 2004 CREDIT RISK MANAGEMENT IN THE BANKING SYSTEM: CURRENT CONDITION AND FUTURE CHALLENGES It is a pleasure for me to attend the first conference on credit risk management and to open the discussion, within which various aspects of modern management of credit risk will be highlighted. I am pleased to note that today these issues will be discussed among representatives of the whole range of institutions and sectors of the economy, whose policy is directly or indirectly related to the issues of credit risk evaluation and management. The development of the society and the economy is inevitably accompanied by risks and uncertainties of governance, involving directly or indirectly all its members. Risk management is the foundation for financial and bank intermediation. The management and evaluation of credit risk, as well as of all other risks - market, operational - is the core of banking. The liberalization of capital movement and financial markets, and the ensuing globalization of business, starting in the 80-ies of the past century, necessitated the establishment of a common global standard for credit risk and market risks evaluation and management. This uniform standard was established in 1988 through the adoption by the Basle Committee on Banking Supervision of an overall credit risk management framework, known as the Basle Capital Accord. In 1996, the Accord was supplemented to incorporate market risk in the overall risk evaluation and management framework. The standardized approach to credit and market risks, set by the Basle Capital Accord, became a fundamental global standard, and all countries integrated in the global financial markets base their banking supervision on the principles prescribed by it. The Basle Capital Accord principles underlie the standards of banking supervision of the European Union. The implementation in Bulgaria of the principles of credit risk management laid down in the Basle Capital Accord started in the early '90-ies of the past century. Today, we may say that the Central Bank has accomplished high degree of harmonization of its requirements to credit risk evaluation and management with the ones laid down in the Basle Capital Accord. This was also validated in 2002 by the assessments made by the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank contained in their financial system stability assessment, made in 2001, as well as in the reviews of the Bulgarian financial system conducted by the European Commission. Presently, the assessment of credit risk management in the banking system is regulated by the Law on Banks, BNB Regulation 8 on Banks Capital Adequacy, Regulation 9 on the Evaluation and Classification of Risk Exposures of Banks and Allocation of Loan Loss Provisions, and BNB Regulation 7 on Large Exposures of Banks. The experience gained through the years indicates that in an environment of quick and considerable changes in the economy and in the banking system and of intensified lending, the BNB and commercial banks managed to develop a system of credit risk evaluation and management, which allowed the banking system to make lending decisions based on solid ground. Indicative for this are the portfolio dynamics and quality in the banking system after 1997. In 1997, 58 per cent of the loans in the banking system were performing, and at the end of 2003 the share of performing loans is already 93 per cent. The loan portfolio quality and the capital adequacy ratio in the banking system reveal that the risks assumed are well evaluated and managed by commercial banks' managers. Of course, the dynamic of development of the Bulgarian economy and financial system continually place challenges to bank managers and the Central Bank. The quick growth of commercial banks' loan portfolios raises the question to what extent this growth is commensurate with the rates of growth of the information, technological, and administrative capacity of commercial banks. Not to allow any deterioration in the quality of lending decision-making, in the recent months the BNB took several steps of both regulatory and internal restructuring nature. The most important of these are the amendments made to Regulation 22 on the Central Credit Registry, and BNB Regulation No. 9 on the Evaluation and Classification of Risk Exposures of Banks and Allocation of Loan Loss Provisions. Given the current dynamics of consumer lending, I believe this step will improve to a great extent the information placed at banks' disposal in making lending decisions, and will build up additional reserves against any potential unfavourable changes in credit institutions; portfolios. I would like to clearly underscore, that the activities of the Central Bank in relation to the implementation and compliance control of prudential regulations do not exhaust the measures required to ensure the financial stability in this country. The private sector's role and responsibility for maintaining financial stability can not be assumed by the public sector, and by the Central Bank in particular. The operating management of risks is solely the responsibility of financial institutions' management. Achieving and maintaining financial stability is a process based on commitment and unceasing interaction between the supervision authorities and the financial mediators in the economy. Therefore, the BNB gladly encourages events like today's. In a short-term perspective, the process of Bulgaria's integration in the European Union poses an additional challenge due to the need of full harmonization of the national regulatory framework with the EU acquis communitaire. As I already mentioned, the international principles of credit risk control are fully integrated into the requirements of the Bulgarian banking supervision. Regulations on the evaluation and capital reporting of market risk are to be introduced in the short-term horizon. By the end of the current year, the BNB will make the amendments to Regulation 8 on Capital Adequacy of Banks, thus providing for the capital reporting of market risk. This amendment to the Regulation will become effective in 2005, and with it the BNB will fully integrate the Basle Capital Accord requirements into the national framework of prudential regulation, also achieving the necessary harmonization with the EU prudential principles. It is well-known that financial markets and intermediation are among the fastest developing segments of national and global economies. This requires ongoing adaptation and development of the risk assessment and management models. The on-going integration of national financial markets and systems brought the need to create a new framework for prudential control that would fully encompass the various types of risk taken and managed by commercial banks. In June 1999 the Basle Committee on Banking Supervision initiated a procedure for drawing up a new Basle Accord which will replace the one operative at the moment. This year, the Basle Committee on Banking Supervision will adopt the final version of the new Accord and the countries will begin applying it as early as the end of 2006. During the conference and the debates you will discuss in detail the rationale of the changes in the risk assessment and management, as well as the best practices that the world has in this area. Here, I would like to note that the improved framework of risk control and management in the banking system would be of benefit to both the financial industry itself and the economy and society at large. The incorporation into the new Accord of the supervisory review and the mechanisms for imposing market discipline, by providing more information to society, would enhance the transparency in the financial system and the economic agents awareness allowing them to make better investment decisions. The new regulatory framework would increase the sensitivity of the minimum capital requirements to the risk taken by banking institutions. In this way the banks which take lesser risk would be able to release part of their capital and re-invest it in more productive activities, which will be of use to the economy and society. What are the particular challenges which the new Basle Capital Accord poses to the BNB and commercial banks? First, it should be stressed that the EU member states are determined to fully incorporate the new Basle Accord into the prudential regulatory framework of the Community. As we expect that in 2007 our country will become a full member of the EC, the BNB and the banking system must be prepared to implement the new Basle Accord from the very first year of its effectiveness. For the Central Bank and the banking system this means substantial investments in information technologies, human capital and knowledge, as well as collecting large databases. In addition, the greater freedom that the new Accord gives would require a greater commitment of the commercial banks management when selecting a risk evaluation and management model. Second, the regulatory framework would pose challenges to the rating industry and commercial banks customers as well. As credit ratings are a basic element of the credit risk assessment, this creates incentives for the customers of commercial banks to be rated by a rating agency. At the same time, the existence of credit ratings will ensure better and quicker access of economic entities to bank lending. In this short speech I could not and do not intend to make a complete review of risk management in the banking system and the short-term challenges facing the BNB and commercial banks. I rather believe that what I have shared with you would be a good basis for having constructive and useful discussions during this forum. Thank you very much for your attention, and enjoy the productive and interesting discussions. ____________ Refer to Basle Committee on Banking Supervision International Convergence of Capital Measurement and Capital standards, Basle, July 1988. Refer to Basle Committee on Banking Supervision Amendment to the Capital Accord to Incorporate Market Risks, January 1996. Title: Speech delivered before the Second Annual Conference For The Balkan Countries' Central Banks, Sofia, 17 May 2004
Subtitle: PRODUCTIVITY, INVESTMENT AND GROWTH
text: Speech by Mr. Ivan Iskrov, Governor of the BNB, delivered before the Second Annual Conference For The Balkan Countries' Central Banks, Sofia, 17 May 2004 PRODUCTIVITY, INVESTMENT AND GROWTH As this year we are commemorating 125th anniversary of the Bulgarian National Bank, this Conference is part of a series of events organized by the BNB to celebrate this so important for us anniversary. Probably the people gathered in this hall know that the Bulgarian central bank is one of the oldest in the world. Chronologically, the BNB was the thirteenth central bank established in the world. Due to this particular reason, it is a pleasure for me to open the Second Annual Conference of the Balkan Countries' Central Banks. With this second annual research conference organized by the BNB we are establishing a traditional forum where representatives of the central banks in the region can discuss theoretical and specific banking policy issues and exchange knowledge and experience. The concepts and practices of the macroeconomic policy in the 1990ies changed considerably. A consensus was reached that the key objective of the macroeconomic policy is to provide 'the nominal anchor' for control over inflation and inflation expectations, to act in support of the general stability in the economy and ensure a favourable environment for a sustainable economic growth and for generating wealth in the economy. The monetary policy is part of the economic policy, and as such its ultimate goals should in varying extent coincide with the goals of the overall economic policy. For a relatively long period of time, the central bank was deemed able to influence through its monetary policy the long-term trend of development of employment, income and inflation in the economy. In other words, it was believed that the monetary authorities can control both the nominal and the real variables, thus simultaneously achieving more than one ultimate goal. Both theory and empirical experience have proven that the strategy of aiming at the same time at several monetary policy goals, which are mutually exclusive in most of the cases, would lead to negative results. The better approach, also applied by our country, is to limit the scope of the monetary policy to achieving price stability. Of course, different countries adopt different institutional frameworks and monetary policy strategies, which ensure the accomplishment of this main goal. The change in the perception for the macroeconomic policy, and for the role of the monetary policy in particular, was influenced by the rapid technological developments in 1990ies, which are comparable in their scale with the Industrial Revolution of the 19th century. The rapid development of the information and communications technologies changed both the structure of economies and the way in which central banks analyze the dynamics of the economy and formulate their policies and responses. Productivity, investment, and economic growth turned into key information variables used by central banks in the evaluation of the condition of an economy, and the formulation of the monetary policy. This is exactly why the subject of today's Conference  Productivity, Investment and Growth is particularly topical. Data collection, processing and analysis provided an opportunity to realize what great progress humankind has achieved in the economy and in the standards of living in the past two centuries. By way of an example I will mention that according to an OECD study, for the period from 1820 to 2001, the world's gross domestic product has increased almost 52 times, while the total population has grown 5 times. This means that the income per capita has increased more than 10 times. These aggregated indicators conceal, of course, the difference in the rates of growth and the levels of income between different countries and regions. While GDP per capita in the US and Canada has increased more than 20 times in the period under consideration, in Africa it has grown only 3 times. The basic question, economic theory should provide an answer to, is which are the factors underlying economic growth and why should some countries grow more rapidly than the others. I am convinced this Conference will provide a relevant picture of the development of economic theory and the knowledge of the economic growth determinants, and will be a source of valuable ideas for the policy-makers in this country. My conviction is based on the fact that we have among us Prof. Jorgenson - one of the greatest authorities in the economic growth research. Also present is Prof. Canavese, one of the most prominent researchers of the developing economies and markets, and more particularly of the economic developments in Latin America and Argentina. As I have already mentioned, the 90ies of the past century were marked by a very fast development in the information and communications technologies, which resulted in a permanent change in the structure of all economies. For Bulgaria, this period was also a period of transition from a command to a market economy. In the early 1990ies, Bulgarian economy was characterized by obsolete fixed assets and outdated organization of economic activities. The changes that had to be implemented to transform the economy form a command to a market-oriented model required rapid rates of regeneration of both the human and physical capital. Due to various reasons, however, the restructuring was being postponed all the time, and we paid a high price for this - a long period of stagnation and macroeconomic instability. In the conditions of prevailing state-ownership, high inflation, and quickly changing relative prices, companies refrained from investment and this delayed considerably the process of capital renovation. Only after the introduction of the currency board in mid-1997, our economy started on its upward path. In the period 1999-2003, GDP increased by almost 23% in real terms, and gross fixed capital formation - by 112%. This growth was accomplished while the number of employed was decreasing from 3.15 million in 1998 to 3,09 million in 2003, which means a 25% increase in the average productivity measured as a gross value added per one employed in the period under account. Of course, the change of productivity in different sectors of the economy is not the same. The highest productivity of labour is reported in the services sector, more particularly in transport and communications, and in financial mediation, and the lowest - in the agricultural sector. The high growth of productivity in transport and communications to a great extent reflects the fact that in the recent years almost one fourth of the overall expenses on acquisition of tangible fixed assets in the economy were made in this sector. In the recent 5-6 years, the overhaul of the fixed assets is going on at a rapid rate, and this has increased the growth potential of the Bulgarian economy. The per-capita income remains relatively low - EUR 2255 per annum at current 2003 prices. Taking into due consideration the difference in the purchasing standards, this income amounts to only 28% of the average level in the European Union. At the same time, statistics from the last 6 years indicate that the Bulgarian economy is growing at a higher rate than EU economies. Furthermore, this process was not interrupted in the recent two years when our main trading partners slowed down their growth rate. We can confidently boast that presently our economy is more resistant to external influence (shocks) as a result from the consistent policy of liberalization of the economy, a predictable fiscal policy based on low budget deficits and a monetary policy based on the currency board principles and oriented to maintaining low inflation rates and real interest rates pursued in last seven years. The experience gained in the previous enlargement of the European union indicates that the process of convergence of real income per capital towards the average level in the Union is not achievable for a year or two. At the same time, the comparison between individual countries shows that they converge at a different pace to the average EU income levels, which is a proof that the economic policy pursued determines to a great extent the course of real convergence. We cannot say with certainty what period of time Bulgaria would need to reach the average level of per capita income in EU. We can definitely say, however, that the length of this period depends on our determination and efforts. When seven months ago I accepted the responsibility to head the Bulgarian National Bank, I clearly stated that the central bank would refrain from participation in speculative and premature discussions on Bulgaria's economic development and achieving its strategic goals. Today, in the year when we are commemorating the 125th Anniversary of the BNB, in the year of completion of the EU accession negotiations, and only two years and a half from the accomplishment of this strategic for our nation goal, I would like to clearly declare, that there cannot be a strategy of any economic policy for rapid convergence of per-capita income to the average EU level that would be based on easing up financial discipline and undermining the macroeconomic stability of the country. The macroeconomic stability, the disciplined monetary and fiscal policies are a must for achieving and maintaining a sustainable economic growth. The continuing liberalization of the economy and building up public institutions capable of providing favourable conditions for innovation, investment, and rising productivity is the only economic policy strategy that would ensure rapid and sustainable development of our economy. This Conference is for me an element of the continuing efforts that all of us should make to improve our knowledge and understanding of the economic growth determinants, which would allow us to pursue an economic policy facilitating growth and generating wealth in the economy. Participation in this research conference of representatives of the European Central Bank, the Bank for International Development, and the IMF, and of all central banks in the region, as well as the representation at it of the academic circles, and the private and public sectors of the Bulgarian economy allow me to believe we will have a useful and productive discussion. Thank you for your attention. ____________ Refer to Capie, F., Goodhart, C., Fischer, S., & Schnadt, N. (1994). 'The Future of Central Banking. The Tercentenary Symposium of the Bank of England', Cambridge University Press. Refer to 'The World Economy: Historical Statistics', OECD Development Centre, Paris 2003.
