Title: Speech at the opening of a seminar on the subject of The Economic and Monetary Union and the new member states: one year after accession, Sofia, 3 and 4 October 2005
text: Speech by Mr. Ivan Iskrov, Governor of the BNB, at the opening of a seminar on the subject of The Economic and Monetary Union and the new member states: one year after accession, Sofia, 3 and 4 October 2005 Ladies and Gentlemen, It is a pleasure for me to open this seminar on the experience of the new member states one year after they joined the European Union. The great interest and fruitful discussions during the last years seminar on the challenges facing BNB on its way to the ESCB and the Eurosystem, indicated the importance of this issue not only for the central bank but for the society as a whole. Today, we would discuss the experience of the new EU member states after a year of EU membership, and their strategies for full-fledged EMU membership, as well as the experience of the ECB and some of the old EU member states. This seminar is conducted within the bilateral cooperation agreements of the BNB with Banque de France and de Nederlandsche Bank. I would like to use the opportunity to thank to our colleagues for the extremely fruitful relations and cooperation. To provide a background of my address, I would remind you that in the second half of 2004, the Governing Council of the Bulgarian National Bank adopted the Strategy for the Central Banks Development to 2009, which also outlined our position on joining the euro area. Since for changing over to the single currency, certain economic criteria should be met, which are the function of both the Central Banks policy and the governments economic policy, in 2004, we signed an agreement, outlining the policy and commitments to be pursued in the process of changing over to the Euro in the Republic of Bulgaria in the period until 2010. Quite recently, the new coalition that came into power in our country, confirmed again its commitment to the above strategy and its willingness to pursue a fiscal and economic policy consistent with the goals underlying this strategy. I have no reasons to doubt that the present government would also continue in the policy, implemented by the previous two governments, of transparency, consistency and predictability of the macro-economic policy. The strategy for the EMU membership of Bulgaria outlined in these documents is based on the following principles: Accession to the Exchange Rate Mechanism II (ERM II] in the shortest possible time after Bulgarias official accession to the EU. Preserving the currency board arrangement until we join the euro area while maintaining the fixed exchange rate of the lev to the euro at the current level of 1.95583; Unilateral commitment on the part of the Bulgarian government and the BNB to adhere to the zero deviation of the exchange rate from the fixed level (i.e. continuing in the currently pursued policy); Complying with the minimum term set in the EU legislation for joining ERM II and taking in a timely manner all necessary steps of the procedure for euro area membership. The strategy of Bulgaria will be presented in more detail tomorrow. It is similar to the path to the single currency followed both by old EU member countries (like Austria), and by Estonia and Lithuania  the two countries with a currency board which jointed the EU in 2004. I believe that the afternoon session will be an interesting basis for a discussion on the various approaches applied by the new member states, and the factors determining their choice. The agreement between the BNB and the government on the countrys policy towards EMU membership eliminates to a considerable extent the uncertainty regarding the macro-economic policy, thus creating an atmosphere of predictability and aiding the easier setting of goals by entrepreneurs and households. This is a very ambitious but accomplishable strategy. It is often considered, that the countries practicing a currency board are mechanically importing a monetary policy and credibility from the country or the area of their reserve currency to which their currency is fixed. This is true, of course, but only to a certain extent. The truth is that credibility can be obtained on credit, but only temporarily. In the final run, the credibility should be won through a consistent and responsible policy. And here we come to the importance of the balanced and consistent economic policy of the government, which is a guarantee for the sustainability of the fixed exchange rate. The fiscal policy pursued since 1997, as well as the liberalization and restructuring of our economy, were the main pillars of the confidence of the general public and foreign investors. The fiscal policy consistently pursued since 1997, based on balanced budget or a surplus, helped reduce the sovereign debt to levels much lower than the criteria set by the European Union, and to balance to a great extent the rapid growth of private lending. This diminished considerably the sovereign spread of Bulgaria, reduced the cost of lending and improved the investment opportunities. Pursuing consistently the policy of balanced budget, and where possible of a surplus, will both allow for the fulfilment of the Maastricht criteria for budget deficit, sovereign debt and long-term interest rates, and would provide the needed capability for reaction and macroeconomic policy flexibility. It is a well known fact that in the conditions of a currency board, the fiscal policy remains the only instrument for a relatively prompt reaction to unfavourable developments in the countrys economy. Furthermore, in order to have such a flexibility in a situation of a growing current account deficit and a fast growing private debt in times like the current period, when the economy is growing at rates approximating or exceeding the long-term growth rates, the budget should be able to compensate by a sufficient surplus, that is, to save for rainy days as the saying goes. The strict fiscal policy will also be needed to help the performance of the inflation criterion. It is well known that under a currency board arrangement the Central Bank does not have a direct control on the inflation rates in the country. Actually, that would be the criterion whose performance will be our greatest challenge. Given the existing natural trend of new member-states' price level converging on that of the old member states (as a result of the operation of the so-called Balasa-Samuelson Effect), the fulfillment of that criterion is not only a challenge to the countries with currency boards, but to all countries whose level of prices is below the EU average. The very definition of the inflation criterion, namely, inflation rate not exceeding that of the three EU lowest average inflation rates plus 1,5 per cent, creates a certain degree of uncertainty. All ten new member states, as well as Bulgaria and Romania, are in a situation of shooting at a moving target. At the same time, in the case of 25 member states (27 with Bulgaria and Romania) there is a great probability to have three states, the so-called best performers, with rates of inflation close to zero due to cyclical and other country-specific reasons. This means that the inflation criterion will be very strict and will require reaching inflation rates even lower than the ECB inflation target (lower, yet closer to 2% inflation). Given the highly restrictive inflation criterion and the insecurity related to determining its degree, we expect greater flexibility on part of the ECB and the European Commission in evaluating the performance of this criterion, especially as regards the countries with currency boards. Here I will once again stress the need for a prudent fiscal policy in line with the overall strategy of the country for the successful fulfillment of the Maastricht criteria. To the extent the change in indirect taxes and administratively controlled prices have a direct bearing on the inflation in the country, it is necessary that their catching up adjustment be realised before the years that will be taken as a basis for assessing the performance of the Maastrciht criteria, i.e. before 2008. From this perspective, the intentions announced by the government for moving forward in time the harmonizations of some excise duties is a step that will help significantly the fulfillment of the inflation criterion as it will abolish the inflationary effect from the increased taxes in the years when the assessment will be made. The policy of administratively controlled prices of certain services will also need take into consideration the overall strategy of the country for the adoption of the single currency. As a measure of last resort for the fulfillment of the inflation criterion it is possible that some administrative measures will also be used, such as reducing certain indirect taxes in the year that will be taken as the basis for the fulfillment of that criterion (for example Greece applies a similar approach). Of course, we well understand that the rates of inflation must converge on those of the Euro area and that such convergence must be placed on a sound basis, and not only as at a single point in time when the evaluation of the performance of criteria will be made. Every economy, however, is subject to such a huge amount of internal and external influences, which make it very hard to achieve the highly restrictive inflation criterion, especially in the absence of an independent monetary policy. The Maastrciht criteria can not exhaustively describe the status of an economy and its degree of preparation to become a member of the Monetary Union. The Central Bank and the government that pursue the economic policy should watch for imbalances in the economy that give rise to certain risks for the financial stability and growth. The experience from building up the European Monetary Union shows that countries with lower level of real convergence realised high deficits on the current account of their balance of payments and very high levels of growth of lending to their private sectors in the years immediately preceding and after joining the EMU. To a great extent, these two effects stem from the reduction in interest rates and the increase of the potential rates of growth in these economies. Households are also very quick in reacting to the changes by reducing their savings and increasing their propensity to consume today as a result of anticipation of higher future incomes. These are natural developments, which, however, hide risks that have to be evaluated as well as minimized at the proper time. Even today, one year before our membership in the EU, these effects can be observed in our economy as well. This to a large degree is an indicator of the confidence in the policy pursued. The Central Bank and the government pay a considerable attention to reducing the macroeconomic risks arising from the relatively high rate of growth of credits to the private sector and the current account deficit, and this policy will be continued in the process of joining the single currency. Dear Ladies and Gentlemen, I see today's seminar as part of the continuing efforts that we all need make in order to improve our knowledge and understanding of the way in which our country will most efficiently and smoothly move from its EU membership to the adoption of the single currency. The participation in this seminar of politicians, representatives of the academia, researchers from non-government organizations, and representatives from the ECB, EC and central banks from the member states allows me to believe that we are in for a useful and fruitful discussion. Thank you for your attention.

Title: Speech to the Association of the Commercial Banks, Sofia, 8 December 2004
text: Speech by Mr. Ivan Iskrov, Governor of the BNB, to the Association of the Commercial Banks, Sofia, 8 December 2004 Ladies and Gentlemen MPs, Mr. Finance Minister, Mr. Kostov, Ladies and Gentlemen, I am very pleased to be here with you and together to celebrate the bankers day. I want to thank the ACB for this opportunity, in my capacity as Governor of the BNB, to address the banking community in Bulgaria for a second consecutive year. On days like this we usually look back to evaluate the results achieved and we also look forward trying to predict the future trends of development. In my brief address to you I am not going to break this tradition, and, given the BNBs special role in our banking system, I would like to draw your attention to the central banks policies and to our interaction with commercial banks. First, I would like to say a few words about the results and the excepted trends. In the first ten months of the year the balance sheet of the banking system grew by 29 % against year end-2003, reaching BGN 22.3 billion. As a result of the stable macroeconomic environment, the well-conducted restructuring of the banking system, the efforts and funds that banks invested in improving their credit risk assessment models, the continuous reinforcement of the banking supervision, commercial banks can increase the volume of their portfolios relatively fast and at once control the level of the risk they are taking. We can say that the experience we are gaining now is really unique for our economy and our banking system. Indicators of the better functioning Bulgarian banking system are the very good financial results achieved (rising rates of return on assets and on capital), the steady levels of liquidity and capital adequacy, and the high quality of portfolios, as well as the increasing competition in this sector which eases the access of households and companies to bank funding, improves the services, and promotes the offering of new bank products. In the past ten months of 2004 the profits of the banking sector reached BGN 366 million, against a realised profit of BGN 379 million for the entire 2003. Having in mind the development of the banking sector so far, we can expect that it will end this year with more profits than the previous 2003. Bank managers abilities to keep a high percentage of standard loans (92.97% at September 2004, with 92.72% at end-2003) preserve the quality of portfolios. The increased profits largely result from the high growth rate of the credit to the private sector, which presently is 47.5% annually. This dynamics is very much depleting the capital base of some banks, but the overall capital adequacy of the system remains relatively high - 17.1 percent. This year a trend has been picking up, which the BNB cannot control directly but strongly cherishes and supports  the increasing competition in the banking sector and an emerging consolidation process that hopefully would become a sound trend not just a one-off event. I am convinced that we all in this room believe that the market and competition are the best mechanisms for enhancing the quality of financial services. Very soon, Bulgaria will become part of an enormous financial market  the market of the EU member-states. The increased competition in and consolidation of the national bank market will only help for the faster and smooth integration of our banking sector into the single European financial market. I have already stated that we support each banks pursuit of its own interest and the more intensive competition in the banking sector. At the same time we should not forget that the banking community also has many common interests, which, if neglected (as was the practice in other countries as well), could lead us into a situation where it would also be difficult to accomplish the individual interests of commercial banks. Financial intermediation is a type of trade in trust, and the building and maintenance of a high level of trust in the whole banking system results from the policy of each member of the banking community in this country. Therefore, each one of you should also keep in mind the common interest. Our activities at the BNB are exclusively aimed to protect the common interest, just as the Law on the BNB provides. This year the banking community has been having a lot of discussions about the central banks policy regarding commercial banks lending and the development of the payment system and, particularly, the BNBs giving up its majority stake in BORICA. When you, my colleagues, are defining your policies or trying to assess or interpret the central banks policies, please do not forget the common interest of the banking system, which is different from the individual interest for bonuses, and each one of you should be committed to protecting this common interest. Last year when we met to celebrate the bankers day I talked extensively about the BNBs intentions and policies. Today I will only sum up the policy of the central bank in the past year and in the coming year 2005. In my last years speech to the banking community I stressed how important it was for the public to have a good understanding of the central banks policies and actions, and I took the commitment that the BNB would pursue a consistent and transparent policy. This year the BNB Governing Council took a number of decisions, some of which strongly affected the current operations of the financial sector, and some others were intended to outline the medium-term and strategic prospects of the development of Bulgarias monetary policy and financial system. In terms of the day-to-day liquidity management in the financial system, the removal of the arbitration margin for cashless purchases and sales of euro considerably reduced the volatility of short-term interest rates. In the second half of the year overnight rates in Bulgaria practically did not differ from those in the eurozone. Early this year the BNB adopted measures to further reinforce banks capabilities to manage credit risk and the other types of risk, to strengthen their capital base, and to stabilise the growth rates of the credit to the private sector at a moderate level that could be maintained in the medium term. The expansion of the credit register, through the amendments to Regulation N22, improved the information that banks have to make their credit decisions in the consumer loans segment. From April 2004, through amendments to Regulation N9, the BNB shortened from 120 days to 90 days the period for classifying a risk exposure as loss when there are arrears on the principal and interests. This change made us re-define the groups of risk exposures, shortening the period in which we could receive information on any change in the quality of commercial banks portfolios. From April 2004, through amendments to Regulation N8, commercial banks unaudited current profits were excluded from the capital base. In June and October we changed the regulation on the minimum required reserves and thus in a phase fashion excluded from the recognised reserves the notes in commercial banks vaults and restored the minimum reserves for the deposits of over two years maturity. All these changes aimed to give a signal to the banking community that the more gradual credit expansion to the private sector is in favour of the financial sector and the sustained development of the economy as a whole. I think that everybody in this room would agree that the decisions on these measures have been made in a transparent way (the ACB Chairman attended the discussions of the BNB Governing Council without the right to vote) and were communicated and applied in a way that allowed commercial banks to respond adequately and without being unnecessarily surprised at these changes. Staying on the issue of the communication between the BNB and commercial banks, I would like to express my satisfaction that together we could resume the practice of organising extended meetings of the ACB where we can have in-depth and extensive formal and informal discussions on hot topics. This year the BNB Governing Council discussed and adopted a strategy on the central banks development till 2009. One of the objectives of this document is to give a signal to economic entities and, particularly, to the banking community as to the major tasks and the basic principles of the central banks policies in the period till 2009. The agreement signed between the Government and the Bulgarian National Bank outlines the policy and the commitments to be followed in the process of introducing the euro in the Republic of Bulgaria in the period till 2009/2010 and confirmed the commitments which the BNB Governing Council had taken in their strategy. Here at the BNB we think that determining the central bank's policy over a longer-term horizon and bringing it out to the general public creates an atmosphere of predictability and makes it easier for each member of our society to formulate their goals. In the coming 2005 the BNB will continue to follow a consistent policy that would build on the already achieved results, without any surprises. In the first half of the year the amendments to Regulation N8 on reporting the market risk in banks portfolios will take effect. Our current supervisory activities will be strongly focused on stimulating banks to be more cautious in taking credit risks. We should not at all be expected to lower the standards for credit risk assessment; on the contrary, we should be raising them. We will be good partners to all those banks which put a strong stress on ensuring the high quality of the already large loan portfolios, and not on further enlarging the volumes at any cost. Please, keep to yourselves the explanation we are part of an international bank group... Most important are the balanced interests of society, not of its individual members. Next year the BNB will end the process of reducing its stake in the national card payments operator BORICA. By the end of this year each bank will receive a letter with the parameters of our offer and the criteria for the success of the procedure. In case we fail to achieve the set objectives and criteria, we will move to a new and different procedure. Operating a sound, efficient and low-risk payment system is a matter of common interest and I believe that each one of us will be able to best combine the individual and the common interests. The coming year 2005 should also bear the "sign of consumer protection". The BNB in consortium with the ACB and the ministries with responsibilities in this area will need to prepare a draft law on consumer lending. This law is important not only for fulfilling our commitments in the EU accession process; consumer lending is the most dynamically developing segment of the bank market and has an impact on a great portion of our society. In order to ensure that the process of lending to households stands on a safe and solid foundation, we have to warrant that consumers base their decision making on the right information and are well aware of the risks and commitments they assume. If we examine that segment of the credit market we can see that seven years ago it was practically non-existent. Or to put it differently, this market holds a great potential as well as its own risks since households lack a long experience in the accumulation of arrears and their management. I very much share the opinion of some colleagues in the banking community that lending to households is "the hen that lays gold eggs"; still the key issue to me is what is the best way to guarantee that this hen will continue to lay gold eggs over a longer period of time and in good health at that. I assure you that we will continue the policy of dialogue and discussions with the banking community on all issues of common interest. We will be maximally transparent and consistent in our policies and this will additionally ensure predictability of our actions. We are well aware of the rationale behind the policies of commercial banks, but understanding should be shown by both sides. Dear colleagues, The signing of the contract on Bulgarias membership of the EU in 2005 will ultimately acknowledge the clear prospects of our country and will incite a new wave of optimism in our society, our economy and foreign investors. We have all reasons to expect a prosperous and successful year for the banking sector. Todays development of the world and national economies makes us believe that the coming year will be successful for our economy and, particularly, for the banking sector. Next year we have no reasons to expect changes in the financial results and the stability of the banking system. Given the increase in commercial banks portfolios we could also expect more moderate growth rates of the credit to the private sector, without this affecting the stability of the system. The competition will keep on increasing and will bring more and better services while maintaining a stable level of loan prices. The more intensive competition will inevitably create incentives for consolidation in the banking system as one of the possible response strategies. Finally, I want to express my best wishes to all my colleagues for good health and a lot of success in the new year 2005. Merry Christmas and Happy New Year to you all. Thank you for your attention. Title: Speech Delivered at Workshop on Payment and Settlement Systems Oversight, Sofia, 20 October 2004
text: Speech by Mr. Ivan Iskrov, Governor of the BNB, Delivered at Workshop on Payment and Settlement Systems Oversight, Sofia, 20 October 2004 Dear Ladies and Gentlemen, It is a great pleasure to welcome you and to open the joint workshop on the oversight of payment and securities settlement systems organized by the Bulgarian National Bank and the Committee on Payment and Settlement Systems at the Bank for International Settlement. At the Bulgarian National Bank we attribute a great importance to payment system developments. Therefore, I am delighted with the participation from Central and Eastern Europe Central Banks and the European Central Bank. We appreciate very much the opportunity to discuss issues of common interest and to exchange knowledge and experience in this field. Let me take this opportunity to present to you the challenges we are currently facing and the role of the BNB in the payment system area. Bulgaria faces one of its greatest challenges  that of full EU membership. We expect Bulgaria to become an EU member in 2007 and an EMU member - two years later. At the time the country joins the EU, the BNB will become a member of the European System of Central Banks and through its membership in the European Economic and Monetary Union, it will also be a part of the euro area. An additional challenge that comes as part of the EU integration process is the need for full harmonization with the EU member states legislation. Integral part of the complex euro-integration process is the preparation of the national payment systems for integration with the euro-area payment system. The BNB is responsible for the organization, maintenance and development of the national payments system by contributing to the implementation and the operation of efficient payment mechanisms. The payment system plays an important role in the financial sector, as it is a key channel for liquidity distribution. By the year 2009, the BNB will have to prepare the national payment system for full integration into the euro area one. Maintaining a stable, reliable, secure and efficient payment system will be one of the priority tasks of Central and Eastern European central banks. The decision-makers of the central banks in the new member states should give top priority to the development and support of payment and settlement systems as this is an important precondition for the successful accession to the EMU. The reliable and efficient functioning of the payment infrastructure provides secure and timely completion of financial transactions, thus contributing to the smooth operation of the national economy. It is precisely in this area that the Central Bank plays a key role by assuming several functions: to act as a regulator, operator and payment systems overseer, and as a catalyst facilitating market initiatives. The BNBs primary objective with respect to the national payment system is to reduce the systemic risk and to provide the appropriate conditions for its integration with the euro area payment system. To achieve this goal, the BNB maintains and develops a secure and efficient national payment system and clear legal framework; exercises efficient oversight of the national payment system; ensures full compliance with the Core Principles for Systemically Important Payment Systems and with the Recommendations of the Bank for International Settlement, Basel, and the European Central Bank; works in close co-operation and coordination with national and international institutions involved in the payment process. The BNB performs its operational function as the owner and operator of the Real Time Gross Settlement System - RINGS. The BNB launched RINGS in mid-June 2003 as a state-of-the-art, secure and efficient national payment system, thus reducing significantly systemic risk. The assessment of the national payment system components made by the BNB indicated high degree of compliance of these systems with the international standards and practices. These conclusions were confirmed by the assessment conducted separately by ESCB Member Banks. Another precondition for successful development of national payment systems and their integration into the European payment system is the harmonization of the legislation in this area. The countries represented at this workshop have already carried out this process to one degree or another. Bulgaria is also at the final stage of harmonizing its legal framework in the payments area. The National Assembly will soon pass the Law on the Fund Transfers, Electronic Payment Instruments and Payment Systems. The adoption of this law will complete the harmonization of the legal framework regulating the national payment system operation and the oversight in compliance with the relevant EU directives. This law will also provide the legal basis for the protection of payment services users. To further this, the BNB strengthened its supervision functions over the payment and settlement systems by establishing within its structure a unit responsible for the oversight, security and efficiency of these systems. The payment systems oversight is an independent function ensuring the efficient, reliable and smooth operation of payment and securities settlement systems in the country. That function is conducted through monitoring, analyzing and assessing the compliance of payment and securities settlement systems with existing standards in this area. The BNB has adopted the BIS, Core Principles for Systemically Important Payment Systems and the Recommendation for Securities Settlement Systems as a basis for the development of the payment system oversight. In the future, one of the great challenges for the central banks in their regulatory and oversight functions is the dynamic development of payment systems and globalization. New payment instruments, practices and devices are continuously emerging in the market. They are rapidly spreading as a result of the increasing integration of financial infrastructures. This necessitates an adequate response from central bankers to increase the payment infrastructures efficiency and stability, and also to boost the confidence of the financial agents and the public. We should not forget that the payment infrastructures of a country do not operate separately - they are part of the global payment infrastructure. Therefore, we need to increase the cooperation and exchange of expertise between the national and supranational institutions involved in the management, oversight and regulation of payment systems. I believe that todays meeting is a step ahead in this direction and I am sure that you will have a very constructive and fruitful discussion. I am convinced that this discussion will provide a platform to exchange views on the role of the Central Banks in payment system oversight and in promoting payment system reforms. Finally, I want to extend my special thanks to the Basel Committee on Payment and Settlement Systems and to our speakers. Thank you for your attention. PAGE PAGE 1

Title: Statement on the publication of the "Regular Report of the European Commission on Bulgaria's Progress in Joining the EU", October 7, 2004.
Subtitle: Bulgarian version only.
text: Statement by Mr Ivan Iskrov, Governor of the BNB, on the publication of the "Regular Report of the European Commission on Bulgaria's Progress in Joining the EU", 7 October 2004. Yesterday, 6 October (Wednesday) 2004, the European Commission published the "Regular Report on Bulgaria's Progress in the Accession Process" for 2004. an active participant in the preparation for accession, including through the co-chairing of the Chapter 11 Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) Group, we appreciate that the report needs to be carefully analysed in order to speed up the process. Economic development and financial stability The EC reiterates the stability ofthe monetary council and its contribution to financial stability, low inflation and good macroeconomic indicators. Overall assessment of the banking sector We cannot be unsatisfied with the assessment contained in the report regarding the banking sector. It is noted that the banking sector has significantly increased its role in financial intermediation. Itis believed that despite the growth of loans, the banking sector is stable and that bank indicators such as capital adequacy and quality of the loan portfolio are good. Assessment of progress in banking and related legislation Our efforts to synchronize Bulgarian banking legislation with EU law have been evaluated. I would like to stress that all these recommendations have already been taken into account and included in the amendments to the Law onBNB. On the day the European Commission publishes the Regular Report, the 39th National Assembly voted at first reading the draft of this law. establishing the European Community and the Protocol on the Statute of the ESCB and the ECB, which opens the door wide for the BNB to membership of the European System of Central Banks. In the area of freedom to provide services in relation to the banking sector , significant progress is assessed, indicating not only legal harmonisation, but also successful administrative capacity building. It is noted that "Banking supervision structures are well equipped to supervise commercial banks and financial houses in accordance with supervisory regulations". It is noted that banking supervision has created a good administrative capacity, as evidenced by the results achieved with regard to the low level of NPLs. supervisory challenges is the introduction of the requirements of the new Basel Agreement on Capital and related European Directives. In the field of free movement of capital , a high degree of harmonization of the Bulgarianlegislation with community law is reported. In the field of statistics, where the BNB is actively involved in the harmonisation process, significant progress is being made. As a positive step in the fight against counterfeiting of means of payment, the Regular Report notes the agreement concluded in November 2003 between the BNB and the Interior Ministry and the establishment of a "National Analysis Center" in the BNB. Despite the positive assessments and our satisfaction with them, our efforts are now focusing on those commitments that are yet to be made in order to complete the preparation process: As stated in the Report, community law on capital adequacy is to be transposed. In this regard, the BNB has already prepared a draft new Ordinance No 8 on capital adek vat and we expect it to be adopted by the Management Board of the BNB before the end of this year and thus to fully fulfill the commitment made in due time. It is necessary to synchronize the Bulgarian legislation in the field of electronic money institutions and financial conglomerates. In this area, the BNB will be actively involved in the transposition process. As stated in the Regular Report, significant progress has been made by the BNB in harmonizing Bulgarian banking legislation with the requirements of thecodification bank directive, and it remains to complete the process with the introduction of the principles of a single passport and for supervision by the country of headquarters. We believe that in order to successfully implement the principles of the new Basel Capital Agreement, efforts need to be made to expand the technical capacity for risk assessment. With regard to payment systems, the report states that harmonisation is necessary. In this respect, BNB was an active participant in the preparation of the Law on cash transfers, electronic payment instruments and payment systems, in which all the European Commission's considerations are fully included. Yesterday the Committee on European Integration of the National Assembly unanimously adopted the draft law, tabled by a group of MPs. It is about to be discussed and adopted in parliament, which will fully implement our commitments in this area. In the area of the relations of the BNB and the government, in the part on the prohibition of direct financing of the public sector, as stated in the Redo report, it remains to adopt amendments to the State Budget Act. The Bulgarian National Bank continues to actively work on introducing the requirements of EU law, while building a mechanism and the necessary administrative capacity to successfully join the European System of Central Banks and the euro area.

Title: Speech to the 7th Bulgarian Financial IT Forum
text: Speech by Mr. Bozhidar Kabakchiev, Deputy Governor of the BNB, to the 7th Bulgarian Financial IT Forum "European Challenges for the Financial Sector", Sofia, 13 - 14 April 2005. INTEGRATION OF BULGARIA INTO THE EUROPEAN PAYMENT AREA - MAINPRE-CALLS AND PROJECTS Dear ladies and gentlemen, I thank the organizers for the opportunity given to me to present to you some of the challenges of Bulgaria's financial integration into the euro area. As you know, today is a particularly important day for Bulgaria, as the European Parliament is expected to vote on the signing of the treaty on the country's accession tothe European Union. This is also a step forward in terms of the country's financial integration into the euro area. We have been working for some time to introduce the public to a project that will define in the next few years the development of payment systems  the transmission mechanism for each economy. This project is atthe heart of financial integration  one of the objectives of the EU's 2000 Lisbon Strategy. This is the project for a Single European Payment Area (SEPA or Euroland). Therefore, in my speech, I will present the SEPA project together with its main components: payment systems, payment institutions, legal framework, standardisation and electronic payments, what has been done for the project so far in the euro area and in our country, and also what lies ahead in the long term, medium and long term. What is the SEPA project? Sepa's main objective, as set out in the European Payments Council(SEPA) White Paper, is to ensure the organisation of SEPA payments that each customer can make "as easily and cheaply as they would be where they live". payment within the country. In other words, all payments in the euro area must be local and reach a level of security and efficiency comparable to the best-functioning national payment systems. The European Council Regulation on cross-border payments in euro has lowered the prices of these payments to the level of local payments, but customers still cannot choose one account and one card for the whole euro area. Standards and business practices vary from one euro area country to another. Products and services still differ and are in most cases within national borders. Many national schemes are very effective, but none of them could survive in a more integrated market where, in order to achieve a genuine single European payment area, national standards, business practices, infrastructure and payment instruments need to become pan-European. What is currently the status of the SEPA project? Much has been done so far: aEuropean Payments Council (ERS) has been set up, the Credeuro Credit Transfer Conventions have been agreed, and the first pan-European clearing house is already working. At the same time, much still needs to be done, as there is still no clear plan for the implementation of the project, national banking communities still either do not fully understand or support this project sufficiently. With regard to payment systems, the following questions are important: the extent to which the processes that change payment systems in European countries unify them and whether this similarity will allow their integration and then consolidation. Eu regulatory authorities are not satisfied with the level of integration achieved so far and consolidation is therefore set as an important objective. In the context ofpayment instruments , sepa means that the main payment instruments, such as credit transfers, direct debit (instant collection) and bank cards, must become pan-European. The Cr edeuro standard has been adopted for credit transfers, but so far it is only applicable to cross-border credit transfers worth up to EUR 12 500. National credit transfers continue to comply with national standards and business practices that are highly automated and effective but notcompatible. For this reason, the question is how Credeuro became the main credit transfer service for smaller domestic payments for the whole euro area. Harmonisation of local standards for the client-bank interface is needed by setting a single standard for initiating electronic payments and automated equalisation of balances on accounts. The ultimate objective is to adopt Credeuro as a single standard for full automatedprocessing of credit transfers throughout the single European payment area. Thiswill require Credeuro to be supplemented with a same-day value date payment service (so-called prieuro) to achieve a level of service comparable to that of the best-working national markets. Thus, as of 1 January 2008 at the latest, euro area citizens must have Credeuro and Prieuro at their disposal as a common standard for local/pan-European credit transfers. Currently, direct debit or immediate collection is not available at European level. For this instrument (PEDD Pan-European Direct Debit), the challenge is to achieve its use across Europe by 2010 with the intermediate objective of using a choice of national payments by 1 January 2008 at the latest. Thereis a great deal of improvement in the field of credit and debit cards and international card solutions. The aim is that each cardholder can use their card at any ATM and POS terminal at a reasonable price, without distinguishing which euro area country it is issued in. why the question is whether cardholders will be able to use their cards in the same way in their country and within the single European payment area from 1 January 2007. Mastercard, Visa) provides the right option for action. An important condition to be achieved to ensure integration within the euro area in the area of bank cards is the principle of "every card  at every terminal". As a summary of thethree main payment instruments (credit transfers, instant cash registers and bank cards) it can be said that the euro area is not yet accepted as an area where all payments are local, i.e. they are not pan-European in nature. The next essential issue in this regard is the legal environment. In this area, there is a need for a clear legal framework, defined and applied uniformly for the whole of the European payment area and trusted. It must address the issue of emerging payment instruments, supervision, the fight against crime and, in this regard, the role of self-regulation is particularly important. This is therefore the key point, the EuropeanPayments Council (ERS) is expected to re-impetus the draft Single European Payment Area by reaffirming and clarifying its SEPA objectives as set out in the White Paper and monitoring the implementation of the objectives on the basis of a specific action plan and a clear timetable. The next aspect in this area concerns standardisation. There is no doubt about the need for well-defined and widely applied standards to achieve the joint functioning of different systems. In this regard , the European Payments Council (ERS) is expected to negotiate standards and business practices for each payment instrument so that they are sepa compliant. whereas the setting of standards must be left to the market and to the bodies ofthe b anchovies such as the European Banking Standards Committee and the European Payments Council. In this respect, we have a great example, namely the common IBAN account identifier, but only for cross-border transfers. The main challenge remains: in the introduction of IBAN for all national transfers in SEPA. A good example is the fact that Latvia, Poland, Romania, Slovenia, and as of last week Bulgariahave adopted by regulation IBAN as a national and cross-border payment standard. Currently, national accounting systems are in fact trade barriers that protect different national banking systems from external competition. Of course, just as each country has a common accounting system for its currency, the euro area needs a common accounting structure for the euro. Thus, IBAN is a major driver of change and requires a shift from national to pan-European logic. Pan-European credit transfers (Credeuro) and pan-European direct debits (instant cash) (PEDD) sepa payment instruments, both requiring the use of IBAN. On standardisation, it is clear that efforts are increasingly pan-European. However, many initiatives continue to have local markets as their own and the introduction of the euro is not considered a sufficient incentive. In order to facilitate the full automated processing of payments in the payment chain (end-to-end straight-through processing, STP), it will also be necessary to align standards not only at interbank level. It should be noted, however, that the backlog in sepa implementation is largely due to the fact that standards are not mandatory for commercial banks. This is due to the fact that their implementation is related to substantial investment costs that would only be justified if the standards were applied by all banks. This can only be overcome if certainty iscreated for banks by introducing a clear legal framework. The main issues related to electronic payments are on security and trust. These are issues of an interconnected nature. Trust in electronic payments and the instruments supporting these payments will increase with the protection of electronic payment instruments and, as a major cornerstone of customer confidence, the resolution of this problem must effectively cover all payment instruments, to maintain and improve their level playing field. The generally accepted view is that all actors must be encouraged to operate with standardised security requirements. However, it must be taken into account that a common security framework could, on the one hand, help to achieve a level playing field for serviceproviders but, on the other hand, could erect barriers at the entrance and thus prevent innovative solutions from entering. The question of trust concerns mainly payments made over the internet and mobile networks. For the moment, customers are skeptical about network security (in online mode). This is because the electronic payments market is still at an early stage of development and is rapidly changing. The large number of new entrants and new legislation contribute to the complexity of theelectron payments market. What is the current SEPA Implementation Programme? The Programme currently includes the following: based on the successful introduction of the euro, as a first important step towards SEPA, the next step is to build SEPA for citizens in 2008 and the SEPA for industry in 2010. SEPA for citizens can be achieved since 2008 by presenting citizens and commercial enterprises with the opportunity to use pan-European tools for local business as well. Customers can make all their payments both nationally and cross-border in euro in one format and from one account, which will lead to a significant reduction in costs. Particular attention is paid to the issue of full automated processing (STP), which can become a reality at euro area level. For the corporate client, the most direct effect of SEPA is likely to be the replacement ofnational cards with pan-European cards, which can be seamlessly used in almost any store or ATM throughout the euro area. During the transition period, national services, standards and instruments may exist in parallel with pan-European instrument tools. This scenario will mean phasing out current barriers based on specific national standardsand practices and currently protecting national infrastructures from external competition. Against this background, the nextstep will be to achieve a completed SEPA for the industry in 2010. However, this will still not be enough to achieve a fully effective SEPA, as banks will still have to operate two parallel support infrastructures (national and pan-European). Sepa will therefore require the removal of duplicate national infrastructures or their transformation into pan-European clearing houses, which should be achievable once customers are given the opportunity to usepan-European in-instruments at national level. For citizens and corporations, this means ensuring access to effective pan-European payment instruments for all their payment needs. This will be an important element of integrating financial markets. Currently, the European Commission (EC) is discussing the need to establish regulations in order to overcome the backlog of the project and ensure its implementation. Consultations are under way on this issue and it is expected to clarify at the end of this year whether the EC will take steps to regulate financial integration. innovation and risk-taking and creating legal certainty for banks. In particular, in the next few months, a new strategy for financial integration in the form of a Green Paper is published. This book will be consulted in the summer months and discussed by the EC in November this year. What comes from all this for the national payment system? The SEPA project defines both the scope and timing of the upcoming changes. The first and very important step is the preparation of a national plan for the implementation of the requirements of the project. This plan should be the work of the banking community, but Iwould like to stress that the BNB will not only help to prepare it, but will also contribute as much as possible to its implementation. In this regard, I would like to introduce you to what has been done in our country so far. In the first place, a Law oncash transactions, electronic payment instruments and payment systems was drafted and adopted. At the same time, the National Payment Systems Council has been restructured with a view to implementing the SEPA project and a draft national planhas been drawn up. Also, before oneday, the Management Board of the BNB adopted an ordinance for the application of an international number of bank account IBAN and for bank codes, which determines the normative introduction of the standard in the following year. In the meantime, the BNB uses and will continue to use allpossibilities through forums such as this and through the media to acquaint the banking community with the project and the plan for its implementation. In conclusion, I would like to say that financial integration ismainly accelerated by the introduction of the euro and technological progress. These two exogenous factors should be used as much as possible to improve banking services. Commercial banks need to understand that the time has come and must act now, and the BNB hopes to continue its active role as a catalyst for these processes.

Title: Statement at Ninth International Conference of Clearing Institutions in Central and Eastern Europe
text: Statement by Mr. Bojidar Kabaktchiev, Deputy Governor of the BNB, delivered at Ninth International Conference of Clearing Institutions in Central and Eastern Europe Challenges in Developing Payment System Infrastructure organized by Bankservice, Sofia, 21-22 October 2004 Ladies and Gentlemen, Dear Colleagues, It is a great pleasure to open this Conference and to welcome such a highly professional audience. Payment systems are an extremely dynamic area where new technologies are the driving force for continuous changes in their architecture and regulatory environment. Our country is no exception of this process. Very recently, we celebrated the first anniversary of the new Bulgarian payment system. Therefore, in my speech I will deal briefly with the basics of the Bulgarian payment system, and will also try to outline the challenges facing us in this area. First of all, I would like to expand on how we arrived to the current payment system model. In their essence, payment systems are among the most important and at the same time complex infrastructures not only in the banking sector but also in the economy as a whole. Their operation is related to a continuously increasing flow of payments, both in terms of number and of amount. This is a significant challenge to the payment systems: to be able to transfer the growing number of payments in a secure and efficient manner. This is a challenge not only to the technologies but also to the regulators  the central banks, and to the liquidity management carried out by commercial banks. And here reducing systemic risk comes to the fore. In relation to the effective liquidity management, the so-called netting payment systems started being developed, which considerably reduce participants mutual exposures, and hence allow for considerable reduction of the funds they maintain. On the other hand, this leads to increased systemic risk when a participant fail to meet his obligations and to the possibility for development of a systemic crisis or a chain reaction where other participants fail to meet their obligations as well. Therefore, this resulted in the development of Real Time Gross Settlement Systems. Now, my colleges from the other central banks consider these systems as sine qua non for each developed economy. The RTGS systems, however, do not replace other payment systems  they only provide for the settlement of large systemically important payments. Mr. Tommaso Padoa-Schioppa, determines the best payment system design which permits: (1) more payments to be settled, (2) the earlier the better, (3) with less liquidity consumption, (4) with the lowest risks, and (5) at the lowest costs. Of course, a payment system cannot achieve all these at the same time, and a central bank should decide for itself what is the optimal mix of these 5 characteristics according to national specifics. Against this background, after a careful preparation, our central bank decided to introduce a significant change in the countrys payment system. We decided to implement a state of the art RTGS system, while the then existing payment systems are transformed into netting payment systems. The major requirement was to ensure compliance with the BIS core principles for systemically important systems, and to prepare the country for its future integration into the euro area payment system. The implementation of this large-scale project was made possible only with the active participation of all payment system participants  the Central Bank, commercial banks, and system operators. The development of an adequate legal framework of the payment system was of particular importance. In this regard, the current regulations governing this area were amended. As a result, Bulgarias new payment system was launched into live operation on June 2, 2003. The implementation of the new system required not only serious technological innovations but also reengineering of the business processes, arrangements, rules and procedures. The results of this one-year of operation of the payment system are as follows: The quantitative indicators of the payment systems operation mark a continuous and substantial increase in terms of both number and value. Data on the volume of netted out payments demonstrate the considerable efficiency of the payment system, which has reduced more than six times the banks liquidity needs. Payment systems efficiency is measured through the ratio of turnover to the funds held in accounts within the system. The average value of the efficiency factor of RINGS in the first year of its operation is 1.2, and it has grown by 70% against the average value of the factor for the previous 12 months. Another fact of significance is that over the past period no payment was rejected by the payment system due to insufficient funds. This indicates a good liquidity management by the commercial banks. As under the currency board arrangement the BNB can not provide funding to commercial banks, a Reserve Guarantee Fund was set up to ensure the settlement of the netting systems with and to mitigate systemic risk. Over the past period this Fund was not used, which is yet another proof that the banking sector manages its liquidity well. We should also note a positive effect on the interest rate fluctuations in the financial markets, enhanced efficiency and reduced risk in their operation. Meanwhile, external experts audited the payment system. Their assessment points to a high level of compliance with the Core Principles of Systemically Important Payment Systems. The payment system was qualified as reliable and secure, and creating conditions for considerable improvement of economic efficiency. One year of operation is a relatively short period, but in a highly technological and dynamic area development is a continuous process. Therefore, the BNB continues work on the development of the payment system, and its major challenge will be the preparation of the payment system for its integration into the euro area payment system. The major directions for BNB to follow in a medium-term horizon are to: maintain a safe and efficient national payment system; develop a clear legal framework; carry out efficient oversight of the payment systems; ensure full compliance with the Core Principles of Systemically Important Payment Systems and the recommendations of BIS, Basel and the ECB; maintain close co-ordination and co-operation with the national and international institutions involved in the payment process. Maintaining a safe and efficient national payment system will be ensured by an on-going dialogue with the participants in the payment system and by regular contacts with the ECB and BIS, Basel. Of special significance for the development of the payment system will be the activity of the BNB's Payment System Committee - a co-ordination and discussion body for the development of the payment system. With regard to the security of the payment system, it is necessary that a full back-up of the payment system be created. The BNB will look for solutions not only for the RTGS, which it operates, but also for the whole payment system. Along with the introduction of the new payment system we started working on a new legal framework that would incorporate the existing regulations and meet the requirements relating to the euro-integration process. As a result, we prepared a draft law on fund transfers, electronic payment instruments, and payment systems, which we expect will be approved by the Parliament by the end of this year. The law provides for local and cross-border transfers; the issuance and use of electronic payment instruments; the development and operation of payment systems; the oversight of payment systems and the out-of-court procedure for settling disputes related to accounts, transfers, or the issuance and use of electronic payment instruments. We attach a great importance to this Law because the payment system must be prepared for the introduction of new payment instruments, electronic money, and also to provide the legal environment for their use. The oversight of payment systems is a relatively new activity of central banks, and it is becoming more and more the focus of the developments in this area. The effective oversight of these activities should be carried out by improving the methodology as well as maintaining a data base for continuous monitoring of all systems included in the national payment system. It is vital for all payment systems that they optimally comply with the core principles for systemically important payment systems and the recommendations of BIS Basel and the ECB. At the same time this compliance should be achieved in the most efficient way in terms of cost reduction. Last but not least, I have to mention the efficient protection that should be ensured for the users and participants in the payment system. Dear Guests and Colleagues, One of the key words for payment systems is efficiency and in line with this, in conclusion, I wish you to have effective discussions. Thank you very much for your attention. PAGE PAGE 3

Title: Speech at the Conference on the Financial Sector in the EU Accession Process within the Second International Financial Exhibition Banks, Investments, Money, Plovdiv
text: Speech by Tsvetan Manchev, BNB Deputy Governor, Member of the Governing Council of the Bulgarian Macroeconomic Association and Professor of European Economic and Monetary Integration at the Financial Sector in the EU Accession Process, Conference within the Second International Financial Exhibition Banks, Investments, Money, Plovdiv, February 9-11 2005 Dear Minister Velchev, Your Excellency, Ladies and Gentlemen, First of all, allow me to express my thanks to the organizers of this Conference on the financial sector issues in the EU accession process for the opportunity to share my personal views and the position of the institution I represent on the important and topical issue of the role of financial markets regulation and supervision for the financial stability and our accession to the European Economic and Monetary Union. To be more precise, my colleagues and I as members of the BNB Governing Council have repeatedly expressed the BNB position on the issues of Bulgarias membership in the EMU. This is, maybe, one of the subjects on which the BNB management has always had a most clear and explicit position. It confirms the European orientation of the Bank as an issuing institution and main financial sector regulator in this country, and can be best seen in a synthesized, and yet comprehensive, form in the Strategy for the BNB Development between 2004 and 2009 and in the Agreement between the Council of Ministers of the Republic of Bulgaria and the Bulgarian National Bank on the Adoption of the Euro in the Republic of Bulgaria. Although I am sure most of the audience is aware of the main message, contained in the two documents just mentioned, I will allow myself to reiterate on what is most important in the BNBs position on our countrys accession to the Economic and Monetary Union: The BNB confirms its will to act within the existing currency board arrangement to the time of full-fledged membership in the European System of Central Banks (ESCB) and the euro area; The currency board in Bulgaria is compatible with our countrys membership in ERM II, which is a kind of transitional phase before our full-fledged EMU membership; BNBs position is that Bulgaria should join ERM II immediately after its EU accession, with an unilateral commitment to maintain the currency board arrangement until its euro area membership preserving the exchange rate of BGN 1.95583 to an euro; The BNB will comply with the framework set forth by the European Commission and ECB, which excluded the possibility of unilateral euroization by any acceding country. The BNBs position on joining the euro area enjoys the full support of the government and the National Assembly. In addition to the above-mentioned agreement between the Bank and the government, this is also confirmed by the Law on the amendments to the BNB Law, recently adopted unanimously. This act comes in fulfillment of this countrys commitments on negotiation chapter 11 Economic and Monetary Union in relation to the independence of the Bulgarian National Bank (in all its four aspects  institutional, functional, financial, and personal) and the proscription against direct financing of the government by the central bank. To comply with the provision prohibiting the BNB to provide direct financing to the government, it was agreed that the presently applied scheme for the loans extended by the International Monetary Fund (Art.. 45, paras. 3 and 4), which allows for onlending by the BNB to the government of loans against purchases of SDR from the Fund, will be applicable until Bulgaria joins the European Union. The main goal of the Bank was redefined to fully meet the provisions of the Treaty establishing the European Community and the Statute of the European System of Central Banks and the European Central Bank. After the effectiveness of the amendments to the BNB Law, Art. 2 defines the main goal of the Bulgarian National Bank as maintaining the price stability by ensuring the stability of the national currency and pursuing a monetary policy in accord with the provisions of this law. This new definition of the main goal is not in contradiction with maintaining the currency board regime until Bulgaria joins the euro area. Through the Law on the Amendments to the BNB Law, some amendments were introduced, which though not directly ensuing from the negotiations on Chapter 11 Economic and Monetary Union would contribute to the future integration of the BNB into the European System of Central Banks and the Eurosystem. It is a question of the provisions regulating the powers of the central bank for preventing currency counterfeiting (Art. 27 of the BNB Law). Designating the BNB as the competent authority for verification and expert authentication of Bulgarian and foreign currency causing any suspicions that they may be counterfeit or forged has two significant consequences: Signing, in January 2005, of a Cooperation Agreement between the BNB and the European Central Bank in the area of preventing counterfeiting of euro; Speeding up the process of detailing of the Currency Circulation Strategy for the period 2005  2009 adopted by the BNB. As the above strategy is of particular interest for the representatives of commercial banks attending this event, I will draw a little the curtain and acquaint you with the process of preparation of such documents, by describing briefly the main goals and priorities of the BNB in adopting it, as follows: Achieving high quality of currency circulation and maintaining the credibility of the Lev and the Euro as legal tender; Reliable, efficient, and flexible system for the domestic issuance function, allowing for easy integration into the ECB system and the euro area in 2009  2010; Developing and maintaining an adequate currency circulation regulation and control system. I would like to underline that the fulfilment of the above objectives and priorities is associated with BNB's gradual departure from cash activities, such as distribution, cash collection and processing of banknotes and coins, which are untypical for a modern European issuing institution, and with its establishment as a currency regulator. That would involve more responsibilities on part of the commercial banks related to the cash activities on the territory of the country. Compliance with the ECB requirements for the quality of currency circulation and the quality and security of the overall issue and cash process could only be achieved if they become a common goal of the banking community. I am confident that the bank managers, who are here today, do not regard this important scheme, which is proposed in the strategy, as a superfluous idea of the BNB that would lead to additional costs for their institutions, but as necessary efforts for and investments in the successful integration of the Bulgarian banking system into the European one. I allowed myself to shed light on BNB's future actions in the area of regulating currency circulation because I know that at forums such as this Conference, the representatives of the Governing Council of BNB, as an authority largely responsible for setting the rules of the game in the banking sector of the economy, are expected to suggest as topics of discussion their intentions regarding the future policy. Besides, in this way I make a transition to the next pivotal point in my statement, namely the policy BNB pursues regarding the banking sector. Which are the major elements of the Bank's policy as a regulator of the currently domineering portion of the financial sector? First, the BNB will continue to support enhanced financial mediation while trying to interfere in the processes of deposit multiplication and credit expansion only where it finds a threat to the stability of the financial system. Second, in its policy as a financial regulator, the Bank will make sure that the banking community is informed in advance of the actions applied. A telling example in this respect are the meetings held in January with the management bodies of the largest commercial banks, which account for 70% of the credit portfolios of the banking system in the country. Through these meetings the BNB got an idea about the level of adequacy of the risk management systems of the leaders in bank lending and had a feedback on the possible attitude of the banks to some of the actions applied for reducing credit growth. Third, the BNB gives a positive assessment to the increased competition and the consolidation already commenced in the banking sector, which will lead to more efficient and deeper financial market. It will encourage a "healthy" competition in the sector. In conclusion, I would like to resort to the "trite" reminder of the theoretical formulation, which has been practice-proven many a time, that under a currency board arrangement the stability of the financial sector depends not only on the behaviour of the central bank as a major financial regulator, but even more on the overall macroeconomic policy of the government, of which the fiscal policy weighs highest. The financial stability of the country is a function of the fiscal stability. The BNB is hopeful of a sound fiscal policy that would condition a normal functioning of the currency board and would not trigger increased inflationary expectations. Thank you for your attention! Title: Welcoming Speech at the Sixth Banking Forum Banks on the Path to Europe
Subtitle:
CHALLENGES FACED BY THE BULGARIAN
BANKING SECTOR IN THE PROCESS OF OUR
COUNTRY'S INTEGRATION INTO THE EU AND THE EUROAREA
text: Welcoming Speech by Mr. Tsvetan Manchev, Deputy Governor of the BNB, at the Sixth Banking Forum Banks on the Path to Europe, 21 April 2004 CHALLENGES FACED BY THE BULGARIAN BANKING SECTOR IN THE PROCESS OF OUR COUNTRY'S INTEGRATION INTO THE EU AND THE EUROAREA I have the pleasure to open today's discussion, which continues the series of discussions dedicated on the path the banking sector in Bulgaria needs to go in order to become part of the financial system of the EU and the Euroarea. It is clear to all that in the process of adjusting the Bulgarian banking sector to the conditions of the more competitive European financial market the implementation of state-of-the-art information technologies (IT) plays a key role. The modern information systems, which allow the banks to offer new and higher quality services, as well as to better monitor and manage all their operations and risks, will have to be adapted to the current environment of financial markets globalisation. I will only give a few examples where the role of IT in the next years to come will be of key importance in the accession period. The BNB has included in its regulations the practice of treating banks on equal footing as an important prerequisite for providing level playing field in competition. In keeping with its mission and reputation it will continue to support the process of introducing clear and unified rules (standards) for collecting information on bank transactions from commercial banks in order to limit the effect of the so called "information asymmetry" in various areas. We are heading towards the timely launching of the Credit Registry with information on all loans extended by banks. The BNB Managing Board adopted a Regulation for the amendment of Regulation No. 22 on the Credit Registry of Banks. The new rules for the Credit Registry are envisaged to come into effect as from 1 July 2004. I believe that the creation and keeping of a data base for all borrowers is a good investment for the commercial banks, even at the possible cost of higher one-time expenses in a short-term horizon. Second, the starting wave of take-overs and mergers among banks, insurance companies, investment intermediaries, lease companies, pension and mutual funds also pose a threat to IT in the financial sector during the accession period. A third challenge to IT in the transition period is the uneven development of regions. This creates the danger for part of the population to be left outside the scope of adequate financial services due to the weak incentives for attracting financial intermediaries. The regions of slow growth and lower level of standard are characterised by lower profitability of financial services; however, these regions should not be left without adequate coverage. The examples illustrate the wide possibilities for applying IT in the financial sector in the accession period. However, they also point to the serious need for IT in developing a competitive financial sector in the country. I would like to extend my wishes for a fruitful discussion to the participants in this meeting. I believe that the exchange of information, ideas, and experience at this forum will be a useful step in the process of integration and adaptation of the Bulgarian financial sector to the requirements of the single European financial market.
