Title: The challenges to the bnb and the bulgarian banking sector in the process of european integration
Subtitle:
THE CHALLENGES TO THE BNB AND THE BULGARIAN
BANKING SECTOR IN THE PROCESS OF EUROPEAN INTEGRATION
text: Presentation by Mr. Tsvetan Manchev, Deputy Governor of the BNB, before the Conference on the Role of the Financial Sector in the Development of Bulgarian Economy within the Banks, Investments, Money Second International Financial Exhibition, Plovdiv, 5 February, 2004 THE CHALLENGES TO THE BNB AND THE BULGARIAN BANKING SECTOR IN THE PROCESS OF EUROPEAN INTEGRATION Dear Ladies and Gentlemen, It is first an honour, and also a pleasure for me to speak before such a renowned audience, featuring representatives of the financial interests, public administration, entrepreneurs and academic circles. Introduction My presentation will consist of several interrelated parts. When the issue of the challenges faced by the Central Bank and the banking sector in the process of European integration is brought to the fore, inevitably everyone should outline his own conclusions on at least two questions, namely: Where did we start from about 15 years ago, and where are we now? That is also where I would start myself. Secondly, I will outline the challenges to commercial banks' short-term development, drawing briefly the usual parallel with the trends developing in the banking systems of countries practicing currency board arrangements in the group of countries in the process of accession to the EU. Thirdly, I will talk about the longer-term challenges to commercial banks in the context of the financial sector development trends globally and in the Euro area after the adoption of the EC First Banking Directive and the single currency. And finally, I will focus on the challenges faced by the Bulgarian National Bank as the banking system regulator in the light of the set long-term objectives of EU membership and accession to the Euro area. Where were we fifteen years ago? At the start of the reforms in Bulgaria about fifteen years ago, the Bulgarian banking system had just acquired its post-monobank structure, as it is academically termed. This period was primarily characterized by: general financial and economic instability; domination of state ownership in the banking sector and lack of non-bank intermediation outside the Ponsy schemes; complete isolation of domestic financial markets from international ones; a great number of newly emerging small and undercapitalized banks subject to relatively lax supervisory, shareholders' and management control; absence, by and large, of modern rules and practices governing financial institutions' operations in a market environment. Further fiscal and quasi-fiscal deficits continued amassing in addition to the already non-serviced, at the time, external sovereign debt, all of them financed through currency issues by the Central Bank. This approach to the economy and financial system resulted in the banking crisis of 1996-1997. Where are we now? In the post-crisis period, most of the above-listed features of the financial structure in Bulgaria disappeared owing primarily to: the new and up-to-date legislation and banking sector regulations; the prohibition for the BNB to finance the deficits in the economy by severely restricting, according to the currency board rules, its powers to pursue a monetary policy; the consistent privatization of state-owned banks to the ultimate withdrawal of the state from ownership in the banking sector and the latter's domination by foreign investors of high international repute in the banking business; opting for strong fiscal policy and stringent budget cuts to ensure a stable macroeconomic and financial environment and conditions for economic growth. Seven years after the introduction of the currency board arrangement, we can outline several important outcomes: macroeconomic stability complemented by a sustainable economic growth at a relatively high growth rate and gradual improvement of living standards; low and stable inflation, accompanied by an intensifying convergence of all interest rates to the prevailing Euro area rates, and shrinking of the margin between lending and deposit interest rates; domestic financial markets have overcome their isolation, and long-term interest rates have gradually decreased, following the increased inflow of FDI and the repeated upgrading of the country's credit rating; the continuously growing competition in the banking sector already measured not only through the gradually increasing number of offered products, but also through some positive changes in their quantity and quality, as well as the improving quality of the process of offering. The development of the Bulgarian financial system has already come to the stage of building up of an efficient and competitive private sector for production, distribution and consumption of financial services. The success of Bulgarian banks and financial companies on the single European financial services market is conditional on its successful completion. What are the short-term challenges? In a short-term perspective, there are several risks that the banking system is facing. First, to avoid the so-called 'overshooting effect', in which case the effort to maximize yield could result in an imprudently abrupt increase of high-risk portfolios in the banks' balance sheets, thus undermining individual banks' solvency. For more than six months, the BNB has been consistently cautioning against this risk, in an effort to bring the limits of loan portfolio quality in conformity with the recommended practices, to increase the number of on-site examinations of loan portfolios and to coordinate efforts to encourage client information exchange among banks. To have this risk limited, Banking Supervision should be explicitly supported in their efforts by the owners and managers of individual banks through measures for the implementation of the recommended international practices of corporate governance, analysis, and if necessary - reviewing, of in-house risk management systems. The trends in the loan portfolio dynamics in the recent years in this country are certainly akin to the ones in Estonia and Lithuania small and open economies functioning under a currency board regime, that are currently joining the EU. Immediately after the introduction of the currency board regime, these countries demonstrated a process of stabilization of banking services offered, in parallel with the macroeconomic and financial stability, not combined, however, with growing volume and quality of services. But it was followed by a period of significant growth of credit supply in various forms, while the symptoms of excessive optimism in assessing the absorption capacity of local economies, transpiring in the international financial community and markets, forced central banks to review their risk control systems, and most of them reconsidered their credit exposures. Later on, this turned out to have been a very useful measure, particularly for the early acting ones. Exactly the existence of this self-regulation mechanism in the above countries led to the gradual convergence of credit supply to sustainable levels, which the economy can absorb without generating large losses and arrears undermining bank solvency. This demonstrated that Estonia and Lithuania have learned well their lessons in the period of initial transition to a market economy, and was highly appreciated on merit by the international financial community and the EC. Second, the conditions of competition in the banking sector should be fair. The BNB, as a regulator, has set by its regulations the practice of equal treatment of banks as an important condition for ensuring competition on an equal footing. In their strive for redistribution of clients, banks should comply with the principle of information sharing, particularly of information related to the occurrence of potential risks. And I am glad to share here my satisfaction that quite recently an important step has been made in this direction by the adoption of a Code of Ethics by the Bulgarian Association of Commercial Banks. The BNB will live up to its reputation and will continue, in fulfillment of its mission, to facilitate the process of setting up clear and uniform rules (standards) on the disclosure of information regarding commercial transactions by the commercial banks. This will aid the process of creating a more equitable and transparent environment of competition among banks in the process of attracting clients. It will also restrict the so-called 'information asymmetry' effect. Now BNB should be assisted in this effort by the banking community for the timely starting into operation of the credit register of all bank loans. It is of paramount importance for attaining the long-term sustainability of the domestic credit market to have this project fully implemented in 2004. The willingness and co-operation of the banking community, even at the cost of a larger one-off expenditure in the short-term, would be the winning course of action. This is indicated by the experience of all the countries that have coped with the problem of 'information asymmetry'. Long-term Challenges to the Banking Sector In addition to the enumerated short-term challenges, the banking system and the BNB are also facing the global trends in the banking services markets on the way to the strategic goal of BNB membership in the ESCB and full-fledged European integration of Bulgarian financial markets and institutions. In the recent fifteen years or so, although not fully prepared and integrated, the Bulgarian banking sector luckily did not remain totally away from the global processes in the international financial markets. Deregulation, including banking sector privatization, resulted in the regained credibility of economic entities, and consequently in a manifold increase of bank assets. At the end of 2003, they were by 113% more than at the end of 1997. As various measures like concentration levels and Herfindal indices indicate, the growing competition in this sector in Bulgaria is combined with a gradual, albeit weak, but consistently decreasing asset and liability concentrations. This has provided the solid foundations for further intensification of financial intermediation, and together with economic growth will act for expanding the scope of population exposed to banking services. Disintermediation is over in US, but in Europe the process is still gaining momentum and acts as the main factor of erosion of assets managed by the banking system. On the other hand, more and more companies, even medium-sized ones, have easy access to capital markets. This process is evidenced in Bulgaria, too, and is stimulated by the relatively liberal rules governing debt instrument issuance. Theoretically, this is a very positive and even appealing trend, as it results in cheep allocation of resources. In our case, however, the risk of underrating the creditworthiness requirements, as well as the risk of absence of positive and long-term financial history, are high. The present situation in the Bulgarian financial market generates the danger of unfair competition between direct and indirect financing, which in the longer-term perspective could impact negatively the stability of the banking sector and the economy. Another trend, which is often a subject of strong mass media coverage around the world, is market expansion by means of take-overs and mergers, including in sectors such as insurance, investment mediation, pension and mutual funds management. So far, the Bulgarian banks were in favour of market expansion through privatisation deals within and outside the banking sector. My forecast is that after completion of privatisation of the banking sector, segments of high potential for growth, such as custodial management of assets and pension and insurance funds management will increasingly attract the attention of banks. The fourth global trend, which has been recently observed in our country as well, is the large-scale introduction of IT technologies in the banking sphere. Unlike the situation with the industrial countries, here this is still at an initial stage. Until quite recently, the Bulgarian banks that were able to communicate with each other through a real time transmission system could be counted on the fingers of one's hand. A great number, I believe more than half of the Bulgarian banks, are already mature and have in their strategies the alternative channels for the sale of banking services, although the consumption of such types of services depends on the level of Internet and mobile information networks expansion. The last three of the above trends will again put to the test the ability of the Bulgarian regulatory authorities to react adequately to the global changes in the financial sector and to constructively foster market development. Fifth, typical of many countries, more specifically of a country like Bulgaria in a process of transition and restructuring, is the uneven regional development. This poses the threat for part of the population to be left outside the scope of adequately rendered banking services due to the weak motivation of commercial banks to cover such regions. The regions of slower growth and lower living standard are characterised by lower profitability of financial services; still they should not be left outside the scope of adequate coverage. The practice abroad shows that within a long-term horizon most stable and profitable are the universal banks, which can best strike the balance of their interests. Skilled bankers know how to do it. Medium-term challenges faced by the BNB As I already mentioned, the medium-term challenges to be faced by the BNB as a central bank mainly relate to the preparation for our country's accession to the European System of Central Banks. Firstly, the process of accession requires further stabilisation of and guarantee for the independence of the Central Bank in line with the Maastricht arrangements with the member-countries. The amendments that need to be introduced to the Bulgarian legislation have already been agreed with the EC (European Commission) and their putting into effect by the Bulgarian Government is forthcoming. The empirical data and studies show that today most banks in Central and Southeast Europe, including those from the accession countries, have a degree of legal independence, which is higher in average than that from the beginning of the 90-ies in a large number of the developed economies. Of course, it is worth mentioning here the importance of the actual adhering to the law, which in effect determines the level of the actual independence of a central bank. It is well known that the level of law enforcement differs across countries, which determines the different level of actual autonomy of the respective central bank. Secondly, an immediate responsibility of the central bank in the member-countries - achieving an inflation rate equal to the average rate in the three EMU countries featuring the lowest inflation plus 1.5 % - is one criterion for nominal convergence. The criterion for low and stable inflation was formulated during the 90-ies of the 20th century based on the experience of the industrial countries from the 70-ies and 80-ies. The national central banks in these countries re-defined their ultimate goals and strategies and oriented themselves exclusively towards price stability after their failure to boost up the economic growth and to achieve a high level of employment by means of allowing higher and unstable inflation rates. The central banks from Central and Southeast Europe followed suit. The Law on the Central Bank in almost all countries in the region provides for achieving price stability or stability of the national currency as a major goal. This goal has already been pursued on a consistent basis by the accession countries, as a result of which from the start of the transition the inflation in the Central and Southeast countries has fallen from 140 % in 1990 to 4 % in 2003. This is basically due to the past experience and continuous improvement of the monetary policy practices, the accumulated knowledge and experience, and the institutional stabilisation of the central banks. Of course, the central banks could not and should not reap alone the ovations for the successful reduction of inflation rates. Balancing the fiscal policies by national governments, as well as the continuous process of opening of national economies, market globalisation and increasing competition also contribute to this process. Low inflation rates were made possible because the societies realised the high cost of inflation and had the will to take actions ensuring price stability. To what extent the existing strategies of monetary policy will allow the central banks to further reduce inflation, so that they could fall within the EU inflation requirements, will depend on the changes in the structure of the respective economies. These changes are outside the direct control of the central bank, yet they should be taken into account more and more precisely in formulating and implementing monetary policy. Third, the introduction of the single monetary policy by the BNB, including monetary market operations and unification of minimum reserve requirement, presupposes not only technical preparedness on part of the central bank: this is a process, which requires the co-ordinated efforts of the BNB, the Government, and the financial community in order for it to go in a balanced fashion and promote the consistent development, increased sophistication and trading volumes of financial markets. Our understanding is that, for instance, the gradual and consistent reduction of minimum reserves and the unification of procedures for monetary policy implementation in line with the ECB should be agreed with the interested institutions domestically and realised on a consistent basis, so it does not pose any threat for the financial stability in a longer-term perspective. In this way only, the fulfilment of inflation convergence, as I mentioned earlier, would not be endangered. The ECB position on the in-principle compatibility of currency boards with the ERM II, provided this regime remains stable within a long-term horizon, does not require from the central banks, operating under such an arrangement, to change their monetary standard in the transition period before joining the EMU. Based on their practical experience, the international financial institutions recommend to the countries with unsettled economic and political environment a fixed exchange rate and centering their monetary policy on its maintenance, instead of floating exchange rate and direct inflation targeting. There is a political consensus in our country for continuing the use of the stabilising role of the currency board. However, the existing strong correlation between the level and dynamics of prices and income in every economy adds further to the challenges faced by the BNB in the practical implementation of the monetary policy strategy during the pre-accession period. The countries, joining U this year, have per capita income, which is 47% of that of the EU, and price level, which is 52% of that of the EU; for Bulgaria these differences are even wider  26% and 33%, respectively. This is a challenge for the future monetary policy as this theoretically comes in contradiction with the nominal convergence requirement for inflation rate prior to the actual EMU accession. Therefore, the BNB decided on a pragmatic approach based on preliminary and persistent stage-by-stage preparation and dialogue, which was based on studying and drawing on the experience of other EMU member-countries in the area of managing changes. Fourth, the global presence of Bulgarian banks is a factor for increasing systemic risk. The BNB will carry out supervision, including on a consolidated basis, over larger and even more globally presented institutions. That will call for better co-ordination of the supervisory activities with other organisations both domestically and abroad. Within this context, the BNB has already entered into agreements for exchange of supervisory information with a number of countries, and continues its efforts in this area. Conclusion In conclusion, I would like to assure you that the BNB consistently pursues the targets within the context of our country's eurointegration. The Bank is strongly determined to maintain the progress so far achieved and will continue these sustained efforts, so that at the point of our country's accession to the European Union it would have reached the required preparedness for ERM II membership. As the brief analysis has so far shown, facing the pre-accession period challenges would require the strong will of the Central Bank, the banking and financial community and the Government, as well as co-ordinated efforts to reach the strategic goal for full Euro area membership. The BNB is hopeful and believes that in the face of the financial community and the Government it will continue to have enterprising and upright partners, who respect its independence and sovereignty. This seems to me a proper ending. Thank you for your attention and for the opportunity to speak in front of you on that interesting topic. I wish you success! ____________ BNB Deputy Governor, Member of the Management Board of the Bulgarian Macroeconomic Association, and professor in European economic and currency integration. The theoretical discussion on the choice of a foreign exchange regime and monetary policy strategy is too lengthy and complex to be exhausted in a pragmatic speech. The experience of the countries in Central and Southeast Europe shows that both floating and fixed exchange rates could ensure price and financial stability as well as a favourable environment for economic growth. However, for the small and open economies the advantages of currency boards are denied only by ill-intentioned economists irrespective of their theoretical orientation. Title: Speech at the Congress on Central and Eastern Europe, Frankfurt
Subtitle: BULGARIA AND THE BULGARIAN BANKING TOWARDS THE EMU
text: Speech by Tsvetan Manchev, Ph. D., Deputy Governor of the Bulgarian National Bank, at the Congress on Central and Eastern Europe, Frankfurt, 17 November 2005 BULGARIA AND THE BULGARIAN BANKING TOWARDS THE EMU Ladies and Gentlemen, It is a great honour for me to address today such a renowned audience at the Congress on Central and Eastern Europe. First of all, I would like to thank our hosts for their kind invitation and the opportunity given. In my speech I will focus on two interrelated issues. First, I will briefly present the current economic development, the condition of the banking system, and the business opportunities arising from the macroeconomic and financial stability in Bulgaria during the accession period. Second, I will describe the key points of the national strategy for joining the EMU and the introduction of the Euro. Finally, I will outline the major challenges for Bulgaria on its way to membership in the Eurozone without derogation, as well as, the progress in the adoption of the acquis communitaire in the field of banking so as to ensure the compliance of the Bulgarian financial legislation with European laws. 1. Stable and catching up economy Eight years after the introduction of the currency board arrangement in Bulgaria, we can point out several important outcomes, among them: Macroeconomic and financial stability accompanies by a sustainable economic growth at a relatively high rate - about 6% for 2005, which is considered close to the potential GDP. The growth rate for the last 8 years - 4.5% on average  contributes to the gradual improvement in living standards; A relatively low and stable one-digit inflation for years coupled with an intensifying convergence of all interest rates on the prevailing Euro area rates, and the shrinkage in the margin between lending and deposit interest rates; The tough fiscal stance since the introduction of the currency board arrangement ensured fiscal stability and sustainability through a tight control of non-interest expenditures and the continuing process of budget consolidation. The consolidated fiscal program at the end of 2005 is expected to achieve a surplus of at least 1.5% to GDP. In 2001 the public debt decreased considerably from over 80% to GDP to the acceptable levels of less than 30% to GDP in September 2005, due also to clear debt management strategies and the aggressive exploration of market opportunities. In our pursuing the goal of the EU and the Eurozone accession, the share of the USD-denominated debt gradually declined in favour of the shares in Euro and in Bulgarian Levs; After the successful privatisation of state-owned banks, the banking system is now exclusively owned and controlled by private and foreign investors. From the end of 2003 the share of banking assets owned by foreign banks exceeded 80%. Now more than 98% of commercial banks total assets are privately-owned. The system is dominated by three banks (Bulbank from the Unicredit Group, UBB from the National Bank of Greece Group and DSK Bank from the OTP Group), whose combined shares of total assets reached 35.3% in September 2005. Further restructuring is underway via mergers and acquisitions, which will surely decrease the number of licensed banks (from 34 currently); Although still highly dominated by the banking sector, domestic financial markets have overcome their past isolation from the international financial markets, and long-term interest rates gradually decreased following the increased inflow of FDIs and the repeated upgrading of the country's credit rating. The increasing competition in the financial sector is visible and associated with improvements in several directions - notably a greater customer satisfaction, better corporate governance and risk management, as well as less asymmetry in information; In an environment of almost full capital liberalisation the current account deficit is well backed by FDIs, which further decreases the unemployment and increases the flexibility of the labour market. As regards the economic criteria for accession, the 2005 Monitoring Report of the European Commission comes to the conclusion that Bulgaria is a functioning market economy and the continuation of the current pace of its reforms should enable us to cope with the competitive pressure and market forces within the Union. The long-lasting financial stability and the robust economic growth in Bulgaria have been recognised by international financial institutions and credit rating agencies. Bulgaria received its first investment rating from S&Ps in June 2004, closely followed by Fitch in August. Just a few days ago the third consecutive upgrade by S&P became a fact. 2. The Strategy for the EMU membership and for the Euro adoption The considerable achievements in the reform process over the last 8 years, already mentioned, are a good basis for strengthening further the economic conditions and for setting even more ambitious goals. On April 25, 2005 Bulgaria signed its EU Accession Treaty. The accession to the European Union in a year and half will be a milestone in the modern Bulgarian history, a reward for our efforts during the transition. This is another major challenge, a challenge that the entire Bulgarian society is willing and, I am sure, is ready to face. The Bulgarian economy shows that the country has moved rapidly towards the Maastricht Criteria on nominal convergence. Bulgaria is already steadily within three of them  regarding debt, deficit, and interest rates. In addition, the strong political will to adhere to the currency board rules until Bulgarias full EMU membership without derogation would unconditionally guarantee the compliance with the Maastricht Criterion on exchange rate stability. The main credits for this go to the balanced combination of a strong fiscal policy and a currency board, as well as the increased implementation and enforcement of the European laws. The most important decision that a country joining the EMU with derogation should make is the time horizon within which it wishes (and is able) to join the euro area and to adopt the euro as its currency. This decision must be formulated with regard to the countrys starting position vis--vis the Maastricht criteria and its existing institutional framework for implementing the macroeconomic policy which largely predetermines the social benefits and costs of EMU membership timing. We feel that the existing institutional framework would reduce the social costs to a minimum if Bulgaria chooses to join the euro area immediately after the EMU derogation membership. In line with the above vision, in September 2004 the Governing Council of the Bulgarian National Bank adopted the Strategy for the Central Banks Development until 2009, which presents our position on joining the euro area. Regarding the changeover to the single currency, the full compliance with the Maastricht criteria will be responsibility of both the central bank and the government. Being aware of this, in November 2004 we signed an agreement which defines the policy and the commitments to be pursued during the changeover to the Euro in the Republic of Bulgaria until 2010. Recently, the new coalition that came into power after the parliamentary elections in mid-2005 firmly confirmed its commitment to the above strategy and its willingness to pursue a fiscal and economic policy consistent with the goals underlying this strategy. The strategy for Bulgarias EMU membership, outlined in the above mentioned documents, is based on the following principles: Accession to the Exchange Rate Mechanism II (ERM II) immediately after Bulgarias official accession to the EU. Preserving the currency board arrangement until we join the euro area while maintaining the fixed exchange rate of the lev to the euro at the current level of 1.95583; Unilateral commitment on the part of the Bulgarian government and the BNB to adhere to the zero deviation of the exchange rate from the fixed level (i.e. continuing the current policy); Observing the minimum term set in the EU legislation for joining the ERM II and taking in a timely manner all necessary steps for the procedure for the euro area membership. Bulgaria considers the above path as the only relevant strategy to exit the currency board arrangement. Bulgarias strategy is similar to the path to the single currency followed both by the old EU member-states (like Austria), and recently by Estonia and Lithuania  the two countries with a currency board which jointed the EU in 2004. The agreement between the BNB and the government on the countrys policy towards the EMU membership largely eliminates the uncertainty regarding the macro-economic policy, thus creating an atmosphere of predictability and easing the setting of goals by entrepreneurs and households. We are fully aware of the challenges. It is well known from the theory that under a currency board arrangement the central bank cannot directly target the inflation. Actually, the criterion whose performance will be our greatest challenge is inflation. Given the current pace at which the new member-states price level is converging on that of the old member-states (as a result of the so-called Ballasa-Samuelson effect), this criterion is a challenge not only for the countries having currency boards, but for all countries whose price level is below the EU average. The varying of the inflation criterion due to the definition that the inflation rate must not exceed the three EU lowest average inflation rates plus 1.5% creates uncertainty. In the case of the 25 member-states (perhaps 27 with Bulgaria and Romania), it is very likely that three countries, the so-called "best performers", would have inflation rates close to zero due to cyclical and other country-specific reasons. This means that the inflation criterion will be very strict and will require reaching inflation rates even lower than the ECB inflation target 2%. Given the highly restrictive inflation criterion and the uncertainty about its degree, we expect that the ECB and the European Commission would show greater flexibility in evaluating the performance of this criterion. I would like once again to stress the need of a prudent fiscal policy in line with the countrys overall strategy for successful fulfilment of the Maastricht criteria. As the changes in indirect taxes and administered prices directly affect the inflation in the country, it is necessary that their catching up adjustment should be realised before the years to be taken as a basis for assessing the performance of the Maastricht criteria, i.e. before 2008. From this perspective, the intentions announced by the government for moving forward in time the harmonisation of some excise duties is a step that will considerably assist the fulfilment of the inflation criterion as it will abolish the inflationary effect from the increased taxes in the years when the assessment will be made. The policy of administered prices for some services should also take into consideration the countrys overall strategy for the adoption of the single currency. As a measure of last resort for the fulfilment of the inflation criterion it is possible that some administrative measures may also be used, such as reducing indirect taxation in the year that will be taken as the basis for the fulfilment of that criterion (for example Greece applies a similar approach). Of course, we well understand that the rates of inflation must converge on those of the Euro area and that such convergence must be placed on a sound basis, and not only as at a single point in time when the evaluation of the performance of criteria will be made. However, every economy is under a huge number of internal and external influences, which makes the highly restrictive inflation criterion very hard to achieve, especially in the absence of an independent monetary policy. In meeting the challenge of the inflation criterion, we are going to enhance the banking environment. The recent amendments to the Law on the Bulgarian National Bank brought the Bank's legal framework very much in line with the acquis of the Economic and Monetary Union, while retaining the currency board conditions and principles. Significant progress has been made in transposing the provisions of the EU banking directives into the Bulgarian legislation without any delay whatsoever in the entry in force of these regulations. To date, the following regulations are in place: In the banking supervision area Bulgaria has achieved full (compliance with Council Directive 93/6/EEC on the capital adequacy of investment firms and credit institutions; The newly adopted Law on Funds Transfers, Electronic Payment Instruments and Payment Systems is in accord with the European legislation on domestic and cross-border transfers and on transactions by electronic payment instruments; The legal framework is in place for out-of-court settlement of payment disputes by means of a Conciliation Committee having the competence to settle disputes between an initiating institution and a client in relation to the execution of transfers, as well as between the issuers of electronic payment instruments and their authorised depository as regards the issuance and use of such instruments. Directive 94/19/C on deposit-guarantee schemes is fully transposed in the regulation of the bank deposit insurance. A clear schedule for increasing the guaranteed amount paid to a single depositor for his deposits with one bank, irrespective of their number and amount, has been announced, and this amount is to reach EUR 20 000 by December 31 2006 from the present level of about EUR 12 500. With the amendments to the Law on the Measures Against Money Laundering, the Rules for the Application of the Measures Against Money Laundering Law, and the Rules of the Procedure of the Financial Intelligence Agency, the Bulgarian legislation has been brought in full compliance with the respective EU directives and the Financial Action Task Force requirements on Money Laundering. By the date of the EU membership, Bulgaria will have adopted the remaining laws and regulations in the financial field, namely: A new regime of liquidation and reorganisation of credit institutions compliant with Directive 2001/24/EC on credit institutions reorganisation; Full transposition of Directive 2002/47/EC on financial collateral and Directive 2002/87/EC on financial conglomerates; A Consumer Credit Law; Regulations on credit transfers, cross-boarder transfers, as well as, on preventing and combating crime with credit cards, which will integrate, respectively, the Interbank Convention, the European Banking Standard on Cross-boarder Transfers, the CREDEURO, and the European Banking Standard on Electronic Payment Indicator (e-PI) in the national banking arrangements. Conclusion In conclusion, I would like to assure you that the BNB will consistently pursue the targets within the context of our country's EMU integration. The Bank is strongly determined to maintain the progress so far achieved and will continue these efforts so that at the point of our country's accession to the European Union it would have reached the required preparedness for the ERM II membership. The pre-accession challenges facing us would require the strong will of the central bank, the banking and financial community and the government, and their concerted efforts to reach the strategic goal of full euro area membership.

Title: Speech before the conference "Financial knowledge and protection of the individual consumer of financial services", Sofia
text: Speech by Mr. Tsvetan Manchev, Doctor of Economics, Deputy Governor of the BNB, before the conference "Financial knowledge and protection of the individual consumer of financial services", Sofia, 14 October 2005. Dear ladies and gentlemen, On the one hand, the BNB must adhere to the common policy within the ESCBand this policy must be understood by both the employees inside the bank and the Bulgarian financial markets and the public. extension of its communication. The provision of information and the analysis of its response makes it an even higher priority for the central bank. The successful communication policy will contribute to the effective integration of the BNB into the ESCB and the quality implementation of the bank's new objectives and tasks. Guided by the above understanding of the role of the BNB and the philosophy that one of the main elements for maintaining a stable and competitive financial system is the existence of a well-informed public, we adopted a Development Strategy for BNB 2004-2009. The communication strategy, which the BNB has drawn up and will soon adopt as a development of its general strategy by2009, will be the first act of its kind for the bank. It will use the experience gained from the implementation of the Communication Strategy of the Bulgarian Government in relation to the country's membership in the EU in recent years. The BNB has held seminars for the media on issues related to the introduction of the euro in Bulgaria and they will become a traditional forum in the coming years for the exchange of experience gained in state institutions. which was widely reported by the Bulgarian press. These first steps give us the courage to create and follow a pre-established program of exchange of information and education of society. This kind of dialogue with society is an element of the preparation of Bulgaria's accession to the European Union and, at a later stage, economic and monetary union. The adoption of the principles and means of the ECB's communication policy, as well as the implementation of the BNB's commitments as part of the ESCB, require a number of changes in the communication activity of the Bank. challenges is a key factor in providing public and institutional support for the reforms implemented. The latest amendments to the Law on the Bulgarian National Bank achieved the institutional, functional, financial and personal independence of the BNB in accordance with the requirements of the Statute of the ESCB and the ECB. objectives and tasks. Thus, the transparency of the central bank's activities balances its independence. Effective communication with the public is a top priority for each CB, as transparency contributes to the effectiveness ofthe bank's policy and the achievement of its objectives. The importance of the external communications of the BNB will increase further in preparation for Bulgaria's accession to the Economic and Monetary Union. The BNB will have to introduce a new currency - the euro. In view of these challenges, a working group composed of communications experts will be set up to draw up principles and means of communication policy adequate to the objective of introducing the euro. The bnb's general approach to achieving the objectives of effectivecommunication enshrines the following guiding principles: Communications on bnb policy are made in one voice. That is to say, messages must be clear and unified and must be sent without discriminating against any party or media; The Bank doesnot provide information to the media in exchange for a favourable interpretation of facts, does not allow leakage of information about the content of statements before they are made, nor conducts selective briefings before making policy changes; TheBank shall report to its manager, members of the Management Board and public relations staff in order to promote its policy and ensure transparency; Sensitive information shall be given, as far as possible, simultaneously to all in order toensure equal treatment of stakeholders - markets and media; The Bank takes a longer-term stance in public debate and does not overreact to short-term criticism of its policies and measures; The bank strives to raise the general level of publicawareness and promote its role in the financial system. The main task of the communication activity of the BNB will be through the media for public information and dissemination of information to help the implementation of the objectives and tasks of the BNB, among which is a focus on price stability. To provide understanding and support to the public about central bank policy; To maintain and enhance the reputationof the BNB as a competent, independent, open and reliable institution with a significant role in the economic policy and development of the country; To ensure that economic agents have access to reliable information, analyses and forecasts to supporteconomic decision-making; To contribute to the increase of the financial culture of the population; To ensure the fulfilment of the communication obligations of the BNB in relation to membership of the ESCB and future accession to the Eurosystem; Start the processof adopting the euro. An extremely diverse variety of means will be used to implement the communication policy. In order to achieve the effectiveness of the communication policy instruments, the BNB will use a targeted approach. In a number of cases, communication is aimed at more target groups, in others it is strictly specialised. The most important part of the communication activities that the BNB will carry out are: holding seminars for journalists with a view to achieving correct media coverage; publications of specialized articles and interviews in the social and electronic media; preparationof educational and explanatory television series and radio broadcasts; providing the opportunity for feedback through the BNB website, conducting surveys and participating in discussion forums on various topics; holding conferences and seminars for specialists; conducting seminars for students and educational programs for students; organization of exhibitions of historical and cultural importance; visits to the museum of the bank with lectures for students; meetings with the public and others. One of the new associes in the communicationpolicy of the Bank will be the conduct of sociological surveys, the purpose of which is to establish the degree of effectiveness of the way of communication with the different target groups and to provide for changes in the communication approach in case of neo-bhodity. In this regard, the BNB will conduct the following types of research: studies of the preferences of the different target groups to the information provided by the Bank; studies to assess the effect of the communication activity of the BNB; annual public opinionsurveys and focus groups to assess awareness of bnb's objectives and policies, as well as expectations for the future. We believe that all of the above will make not only consumers of financial services, but also all economic and genti, the wholesociety more educated and, as my colleagues often say, "complex" as clients. Thecentral bank, as the main regulator, will continue to create a balanced environment for the development of both demand and financial services in order to deepen financial markets and further integrate them into the single market for financial services. Thank you for your attention! ____________ Deputy Governor of the BNB, member of the Bulgarian Macroeconomic Association and lecturer on the issues of European economic and currency integration.

Title: Lecture delivered to teachers and students from Sofia University "St. Constantine and Helena"
text: Lecture by Mr. Tsvetan Manchev, Deputy Governor of the BNB, delivered to teachers and students from Sofia University "St. Constantine and Helena". At the invitation of the management of the University, 5 December 2003 I. Emergence and implementation of the idea of establishing a European System of Central Banks The idea of establishing a European Economic and Monetary Union and a system of European central banks was first launched in the Werner Plan in the early 1970s, but its practical implementation beganmuch later d0 in the late 1980s after the entry into force of the Single European Act. role and function constitutes a distant ancestor of the European Central Bank. In practice, however, this is an institution with no real powers. The main reason for the incomplete existence of the Fund is its formal dependence on the Council of Ministers of Economy and Finance (ECOFIN). The Werner Plan provided for the EUSF to be under the control of central bank governors only, but in 1973 it was decided that their powers should be limited by the guidance and directives of the Council of Finance and Economy Ministers (ECOFIN). The EUSF flows into the European Monetary Institute. The establishment of the European Monetary System, taken by the European Council in Bremen in June1978, provides that no later than 2 years after the start of the operation of the system, a European Monetary Fund (EMF) is intended to replace the EUSF in its role as issuer of the European currency unit (ECU) and as the manager of the credit facility system, control over the European exchange rate mechanism. The outcome of the committee's work is a report recommending the introduction of a single monetary policy in the Community to be carried out by a very independent institution by the governments of the Member States and by the Union bodies, the European System of Central Banks (ESCB). the lysma. The Treaty on European Union, signed in Maastricht on 7 February 1992 (which entered into force in November 1993), represents the most decisive step in the construction of emu. the measures and stages envisaged follow the proposed scheme of the Delor Plan. The Treaty provides for the construction of the EMU in three stages.
