Title: Address to the participants in the Conference Financial Services in United Europe
text: Address by Mr. Tsvetan Manchev, Deputy Governor of the BNB, to the participants in the Conference Financial Services in United Europe, 30 May 2005 Dear conference guests and participants, Ladies and gentlemen, Please allow me to congratulate you for the very appropriately chosen conference motto, and for the timeliness of this event. Improving and diversifying financial services is one of the undisputed achievements in the European integration process. The single financial market of the community  open and protected by the continuously developing prudential supervision  is the underlying fundament of financial stability and sustainable development. The Republic of Bulgaria succeeded in implementing within a comparatively short period of time large scale financial sector reforms. Of course, this was made possible by the radical privatization policy pursued in this sector as a result of which significant foreign investments were attracted, and what is more important  which ensured transfer of experience and expertise to the Bulgarian financial market. Banking services remain among the priorities of financial intermediation, which is evident from the fact that about 90% of financial intermediation is effected through the banking sector. Allow me to mark the main successes and challenges posed to the banking services in Bulgaria by the single financial market of the community. Significant success was accomplished in the area of transposing the provisions of the EU banking directives into the Bulgarian legislation without any postponement periods whatsoever for the effectiveness of these regulations. To date, the following regulations are in place: In the area of banking supervision  The Republic of Bulgaria has achieved full harmonization as regards all the requirements of the European Union for access to banking activities, capital and capital adequacy of banks, large exposures of banks, consolidated supervision, measuring banks investments. Domestic and cross-border transfers are provided for in detail in the Fund Transfers, Electronic Payment Instruments and Payment Systems Law (State Gazette, issue 31 of April 8, 2005). Electronic payment instruments (PI) are fully regulated in the above Law, which provides a general and comprehensive definition of the phenomenon electronic payment instruments, which would allow to regulate and control various products. At this stage, only commercial banks are EPI issuers. The transposition of the following acquis into the Bulgarian legislation is forthcoming: Directive 2000/46/C on the activities and supervision of electronic money institutions, and Directive 2000/12/C on taking up and pursuit of the activities of credit institutions - by the end of 2006. The establishment of specialized electronic money institutions is forthcoming, which will allow for the issuance of electronic money by institutions other than banks. The legal framework is in place for out-of-court settlement of payment disputes by means of a Conciliation Committee with competences to settle disputes between an executing institution and a client in relation to the execution of transfers, as well as between the issuers of electronic payment instruments and their authorized depository as regards the issuance and use of such instruments. The Bulgarian legislation has adopted the European payment systems regulations. Special attention is paid to the legislation governing the Real Time Gross Settlement System, and payments supervision. Bank deposit insurance has been fully regulated by the full transposition of Directive 94/19/C. The Directive is transposed by the adoption of the Bank Deposit Guaranty Law. The law is amended on annual basis, and the guaranteed amount reimbursed to a single depositor for deposits held with one bank, irrespective of their number and amount should reach EUR 20,000 until December 31 2006. With the amendments made in March 2005, the amount of the guaranteed deposits of a single person with one bank reached the amount of BGN 25 000. What is to be implemented by the date of EU membership: 1. Single license The issuance of a single license recognized throughout the whole community and the implementation of the prudential banking supervision principle will facilitate free provision of financial services within the whole community. Thus, credit institutions licensed in their home member state will be able, by establishing branches in the territory of the community, to perform any of the activities credit institutions are licensed for. The BNB is preparing some draft legislation in this area, and the draft is expected to be ready by the year end. 2. Supervision by the home member state The supervision by a home member state is effected by means of basic harmonization, the introduction of a single license and mutual recognition of banking supervision systems. The competent authorities of a home member state of a credit institution will control the latters financial stability. The competent authorities of a host member state will exercise control over the liquidity and monetary policy. Market risk will be controlled based on the close cooperation between the competent authorities of the host and home member states. 3. New regime of liquidation and reorganization of credit institutions The introduction of a new regime of reorganization and liquidation of credit institutions is forthcoming. Bulgaria has made the commitment to transpose in the Bulgarian legislation by a regulative act with the status of a law the provisions of Directive 2001/24/C for credit institutions reorganization and winding-up as of the date of its EU accession (1 January, 2007). The principles underlying the new regime  unity, universality, minimum harmonization, and mutual recognition. A working group established under the Ministry of Finance is already working in this area, and the respective draft law will be ready in the coming year. 4. Financial Collateral Directive 2002/47/C on the financial collateral arrangements will be transposed in the Bulgarian legislation by the time of Bulgarias membership in the EU (1 January 2007). The Directive provides for the establishment of minimum general requirements to financial collateral within the EU and the introduction of a uniform legal regime as regards the securities and funds in accounts used as collateral. Thus, a large range of institutions, both banking and non-banking financial institutions, central and multinational banks, clearing houses, settlement agents, and other legal entities acting as parties to financial collateral arrangements are regulated. 5. Financial Conglomerates By the time of Bulgarias membership in the EU (1 January 2007), we will have transposed in the Bulgarian legislation Directive 2002/87/C on prudential regulation of credit institutions, insurance undertakings and investment firms in a financial conglomerate. The aim of the Directive is to guarantee the stability of the European financial markets, to introduce common norms of prudential supervision over financial conglomerates in Europe and to provide conditions for competition and legal security. The Directive provides for the establishment of common standards of prudential supervision over financial conglomerates (comprising credit institutions, insurance companies, investment intermediaries). 6. Measures against using the banking system for money laundering and financing of terrorism With the amendments to the Law on the Measures Against Money Laundering (SG 31/04.04.2003), the amendments to the Rules for the Application of the Measures Against Money Laundering Law, the amendments to the Rules of Procedure of the Financial Intelligence Agency (SG 49/27.05.2003), Bulgarian legislation was brought to full compliance with the provisions of the effective directives and the requirements of the FATF on Money Laundering. 7. Payment Systems Significant amendments are planned in the credit transfers area  the transposition of the Interbank Convention on Payments in the national banking agreements; adoption of the European banking standard and the Credit Transfers Manual; adoption of the European Banking Standard on European Cross-border Credit Transfers; adoption of CREDEURO as a cross-border service for payment of amounts up to EUR 12,500; adoption and implementation of the guidelines under European Banking Standard EBS602 V1  on Electronic Payment Indicator (-)  in the cards area, and the Resolution of 10 December 2003 on preventing and combating card crimes in Europe; migration of bank cards to the V standard and POS and  reconfiguration to the V standard, etc. The adoption of a Consumer Credit Law is pending (and the BNB has already prepared its draft), and of a new Consumer Protection Law, regulating some provisions in relation to the protection of financial services users, etc. In conclusion, I would like to wish you useful and efficient work at the Conference. I believe it is one of a series of small steps facilitating the integration of the Bulgarian financial market into the European one, and that it would also help an increasing number of Bulgarians in their in-depth understanding of the integration processes. Thank you for your attention!

Title: Address to the Sixth Southeast Europe Economic Forum, Panel 1 "Development of the banking systems in Southeast Europe. The role of the international financial groups and the challenges arising from the introduction of Basel II", Sofia
Subtitle:
THE BULGARIAN NATIONAL BANK - A FACTOR FOR
ENHANCING THE STABILITY OF THE BULGARIAN BANKING SECTOR
text: Address by Mr. Tsvetan Manchev, BNB Deputy Governor, to the Sixth Southeast Europe Economic Forum, Panel 1 "Development of the banking systems in Southeast Europe. The role of the international financial groups and the challenges arising from the introduction of Basel II", Sofia, 2 November 2004 THE BULGARIAN NATIONAL BANK - A FACTOR FOR ENHANCING THE STABILITY OF THE BULGARIAN BANKING SECTOR Ladies and Gentlemen, I would like to express my thanks to the organisers, and especially to Mr. Hristos Katsanis, for their kind invitation to me to participate in the Sixth Southeast Europe Economic Forum. I am honoured and delighted to attend this Forum and to take part in the discussion of the challenges faced by the banking systems of the Southeast European countries in the process of their integration into the EC financial system. Clearly, this transition would be unthinkable without the international financial groups, which in effect act as a bridge, as a kind of a "living bond" between the domestic financial markets and the large international financial centres. However, in my brief statement today I will not dwell on the mechanisms of transferring know-how from parent-banks to their local subsidiaries, but I will rather focus on the BNB's role as an issuing institution and regulator of the Bulgarian banking sector in the process of preparation for our country's membership in the European Union and the euro area. I hope that this is exactly what the esteemed audience expects to hear from a representative of the Central Bank. As you might probably already know, the BNB's Governing Council adopted a Strategy for the development of the Bank for the period 2004 - 2009. This document, which is an expression of the management's desire to achieve greater transparency, greatly facilitates my task of presenting the topic chosen by me. In its Strategy, the BNB confirms its will to act within the existing framework of the currency board arrangement until full membership in the European System of Central Banks (ESCB) and the euro area. The currency board in Bulgaria is compatible with our country's membership in ERM II, which is a sort of an interim stage prior to a full membership in the European Economic and Monetary Union. BNB's position is that Bulgaria should join ERM II immediately after it becomes an EU member, while unilaterally committing itself to maintaining the currency board arrangement until its membership in the euro area and to preserving the exchange rate of BGN 1.95583 to 1 Euro. The BNB will adhere to the EC and ECB framework, which precludes the possibility of unilateral euroisation on the part of the acceding country. An important condition for realising the strategy is the implementation of the legislative amendments as agreed upon in the negotiation process in order to ensure: BNB's institutional independence; personal independence of the Governing Council members; impossibility for privileged access of the public sector to funding from the BNB. It is reasonable and realistic for the necessary legal amendments to become effective as soon as possible. As you are aware, the procedure for the adoption of the amendments and supplements to the BNB Law is well underway. The transparency and predictability of BNBs activities are extremely important conditions for the stability of the overall sector. Therefore, the implementation of the Strategy presupposes a continuous dialogue with the public. The BNB accepts the legal amendments enhancing its independence as a responsibility to pursue a transparent and consistent policy, and as an obligation to regularly report its activities to the general public. This is a guarantee that with its increased tasks and growing responsibilities in the process of Bulgarias accession to the European Union, the EMU, and the euro area, the BNB will be a source of stability and predictability. The BNBs main goal is maintaining price stability. Such is also the gist of the new text proposed for the Banks main goal in the draft law on the amendments and supplements of the BNB Law. It is consistent with the ESCB main goal. By the time of this countrys membership in the EMU and the euro area, the BNB will pursue its main goal by maintaining the fixed exchange rate of the Lev to the Euro and the stability of the banking system. These are the Banks immediate goals for pursuing its strategy in the period. After the adoption of the Euro as the official tender in Bulgaria, BNB will pursue its main goal through its participation in the development and implementation of the Eurosystems monetary policy. Maintaining banking stability will remain as a responsibility and an immediate objective of the BNB even after it joins the Eurosystem, given the preserved significance of the banking sector in the process of money supply. Maintaining banking stability by the time of joining the euro area and after it will be ensured by improving the banking regulations and the payment system in compliance with the recommended international standards and practices, exercising effective banking supervision and payment systems oversight. In view of the announced topic of todays meeting, I would like to point out that the Strategy envisages that the Bulgarian banking legislation should be compliant with the future Directive, with which the EU will implement the New Capital Accord of the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (the so-called BASEL II). In this regard, the BNB shall: Continue to train supervision experts in the content of the Accord; Analyze on current basis the effect of the implementation of the new capital standards, including by taking part in quantitative research studies of the Basel Committee, EU, and other organizations; Draft legislative and regulatory texts, which will set forth the regulative conditions for the implementation of the Accord; Adapt accordingly the supervision reporting systems; Require from the commercial banks to work out personal, technical and procedural support programs. The good contacts and constructive relationships established between the BNB and the banking community are a prerequisite for effective supervision, as well as for the proper operation of the payment system, and for the implementation of the monetary policy. The strategy, therefore, envisages these contacts to be developed in the form of regular and ad-hoc committees on technical level, and a top management committee chaired by the BNB Governor. This proposal could be particularly useful both in terms of discussing the specific measures to be taken for the implementation of the above-mentioned New Basel Capital Accord in our banking practices, and of the restructuring of the currency circulation, and in seeking solutions to problems that may from time to time be faced by the Bulgarian banking system. So, I would like to end my address with this constructive proposal for improving the dialogue within the banking community. Thank you for the attention. PAGE PAGE 1

Title: Speech at the ACB spring meeting, Plovdiv, April 23-24, 2004.
Subtitle:
THE PREPARATION AND THE IMPACT OF THE NEW
BASLE CAPITAL ACCORD (BASLE II) ON THE BULGARIAN BANKING SYSTEM
text: Speech by Mrs. Emilia Milanova, BNB Deputy Governor, at the ACB spring meeting, Plovdiv, 23 - 24 April 2004 THE PREPARATION AND THE IMPACT OF THE NEW BASLE CAPITAL ACCORD (BASLE II) ON THE BULGARIAN BANKING SYSTEM Dear ladies and gentlemen, dear colleagues, I am pleased to speak to you today about the New Basle Capital Accord (Basle II) within the framework of the spring meeting of the bankers' association. Before outlining the major features of Basle II and the challenges its implementation will bring to us all, together, allow me to say a few introductory words. Introduction Over the last years the banks in Bulgaria have accelerated their operations and in the last year-and-a-half period they have been maintaining a steady growth of credit aggregates of around 50% on an annual basis. Unlike the end of 1997 when the share of credits in total assets was hardly 22%, now, with the credits exceeding 50% of assets, credit risk has a clearly prevailing importance. The banks offer a wide range of products with different risk levels and in various clients' configurations. Actually, the phenomenon observed in our country is typical of the whole region, and this is easy to explain. Anyway, credit risk management in Central and Eastern European banks has to overcome three obstacles: 1. The ongoing aggressive and nervous creation of credit portfolios and the initial redistribution of markets especially in areas such as consumer lending; 2. The introduction of EU banking directives for capital measurement, which introduce additional requirements. The amendment to the currently effective Capital Accord of 1996 and the implementation of CAD I and CAD II will additionally burden the own funds with market risks; 3. The New Capital Accord which introduces requirements based on new principles as regards credit risk management while also involves capital to support operational risk. This makes today's topic of discussion both current and timely. In the months and years to come it will be a subject of increasing attention by the banking community. Basle II came as a natural response to market developments. Nowadays banking is characterised by unprecedented dynamics stemming from the high level of competition. The pressure coming from the numerous financial market players on the one hand, and the free capital movement and the accelerating global dimensions of competition, on the other, pushes the banks to make the most of every advantage that modern computer technologies, IT systems, and models provide. The tension on loan intermediaries is further heightened by the banking regulatory framework, which relative to the other financial sectors is best developed and most complex. The high level of regulation restricts the risks assumed, while reducing the possibility of banks for manouvering and profits. Therefore, one question stays open to the banking community, namely: How could this regulatory framework best serve its purpose without placing unnecessary restrictions on banks or pressure on their efficiency? The strong competitive pressure from other financial institutions, which started in the last decades of the last century, makes the banks very sensitive to overregulation that reduces their countervailing potential. Clearly, as any other regulation, the banking regulation lags behind and strives to catch up with the object at focus. Over the last three decades the Basle Committee on Banking Supervision gives a lead to the banking regulators. The current Capital Accord When referring to Basle II the most appropriate way of leading into a discussion is to say a few words about the currently effective Capital Accord. The main international consultative body (the Basle Committee) has been making serious efforts over the last 15 years to react in a timely fashion to the banking developments. Undoubtedly, one of its achievements was the International Unification of Capital Measurement and Standards as of July 1988, which defines the most complex indicator for the health of banks - capital adequacy. The level of coverage of the risks in own funds became the basis for the capital regulation of banks in almost every country. Even countries with traditions such as the USA changed their model used by the Federal Reserve System since 1950 and adopted the new rules in 1989. Before 1988, the developed economies introduced at different stages their own capital rules. The evolution of capital regulation led naturally to a stage, where it was inexpedient and wrong to have internationally active credit institutions regulated by a number of different national standards, which led to market distortions and regulatory arbitrage. In this context, the first Basle Accord of 1988 fulfilled its purpose of a world regulator. Allow me to remember that its underlying principle presupposes standardised assessment of credit risks by individual groups of counterparties. Regardless of the fact that for a ten-year period the conceptual framework of the first accord excellently fulfilled its purpose, over the years it became increasingly clear that a better solution had to be sought than the current single measure for all. Asset grouping and the application of uniform risk weights without taking account of specifics distorts the assessment of risk. Currently, this deprives the banks with well developed IT systems and risk measurement and management systems of the possibility to report to their regulators actual risks and to maintain economically justified amount of capital. This and the need to cover other significant risks were the key motives for drafting a new improved accord, which would reflect the current features of banking. Even in the late 90-ies it became obvious to a number of leading banks and supervisors that a new accord was needed. It was imperative to do more than simply revise the minimum capital requirements. Thus, leading internationally active financial institutions and central banks came to the conclusion to have the latest achievements and best practices in risk management and banking recognised and disseminated. This new understanding per se is not aimed at reducing the required capital of banks, but rather to improve the stability of the already globalised financial system - a goal that would be to the benefit of business and consumers even more than to banks. It is essential that banks not only manage their risks well, but also maintain adequate capital levels. In this way the banking sector as a whole would be more flexible and robust, less susceptible to economic downturns, and more reliable as a source of sustained growth. The evidence gathered from our country's experience points that financial and banking stability are indeed such a factor of growth. In addition to stability, transparency is the other significant factor, which strengthens the confidence in the financial sector and adds importance to its role. A free and fair access to a credit of clearly defined terms and price and a stable payment system guarantee consistency and predictability in the funding of business and financial flows. The above two conditions imply active, liquid and reliable markets. Placing the banks at the crossroads between business and consumers in every economy and their specific mediation role means nothing more than denying access to poorly managed and undercapitalised credit institutions. At the same time, from the perspective of the Basle Committee and the supervisory bodies, two other objectives are pursued: first, motivating the banks to develop their own management within the context of corporate governance, and second, reaching a higher level of cooperation and coordination between supervisors world-wide. The belief in the need to update the Capital Accord was initially expressed at the XII World Conference of Banking Supervisors in 1998, where this idea was discussed for the first time. In 1999 the Basle Committee distributed for comments the initial version of the new regulation (consultation paper). In the beginning of 2001 it was elaborated (consultation paper 2). A series of new consultation papers followed related to individual components of the Accord. The initial ambitions were to have the Accord adopted at the end of 2001 and implemented as from 2004. Undoubtedly, the complexity and importance of the Capital Accord required its repeated revision and delay. At the 14th World Conference of Banking Supervisors (September 2002) it was announced that after its repeated delay the finalised version of the New Capital Accord would be approved in the autumn of 2003. Its immediate implementation was left for 2006, although the initial target was 2004. Actually, the latest target, as set at the Basle Committee meeting in Madrid in October 2003, was mid 2004. The Committee issued a 3rd consultation paper, which reflected a huge number of opinions from various countries and institutions, as well as the lessons from the Quantitative Impact Studies (QIS). By the way, 8 Bulgarian banks were also involved in the last study QIS-3. The role of the banking sector in the context of our country's preparation and accession to EU was already mentioned. Concurrently with the final phase of the draft New Capital Accord for credit institutions of the Basle Committee on Banking Supervision, the European Commission prepared a draft new capital directive (Risk Based Capital Directive) in 2003. Its purpose is to introduce the new requirements and to outline a general capital requirement framework for banks and investment companies operating within the territory of the European Community. In this way, the framework will play an important role on the road to achieving a single and stable market of financial services. The Directive will be effective from the beginning of 2007, when Bulgaria is expected to become an EU member. This requires that the BNB and Banking Supervision Department in particular direct their efforts and resources towards harmonising the national regulatory framework with the New Capital Accord. Certainly, a natural prerequisite for the successful implementation of the new accord is the involvement of the banking community in the preparation process. The involvement of credit institutions at the preparatory stage will enable them and the banking supervision to determine the exact parameters of the new framework, which should take into account the differences across institutions, their internal rules and risk profile, as well as the specifics of the national regulatory and market environment. Allow me to remind you in a few words how the architecture of the New Capital Accord and its basic content look like. Basle II is structured in three separate, yet interrelated sections called pillars. The first pillar sets the minimum capital requirements. As is well known, the underlying principle of the New Capital Accord is based on an improved individual credit risk assessment, which allows the banks to increase their efficiency by taking advantage of the capital reserve that could possibly be reversed as a result of more precise risk weighting of assets. The current approach of a single standard risk assessment and capital adequacy calculation, applied by all credit institutions, will be replaced by two more up-to-date ones - a standardised approach and an internal rating based approach. The banks will be able to choose between the two depending on the nature of their activities and risk profile, as well as on their place in the respective peer group. Therefore, the credit institutions' management bodies in our country and their risk assessment experts will not only need to become familiar with the draft New Capital Accord, but to also assess the novelties and advantages related to their implementation. The two new assessment approaches bring different levels of challenges to the internal organisation and resources - such as restructuring of some units, elaborating current and introducing new methodologies, employing and training staff, planning additional financial and other resources. The related costs should be in line with the final effect from the application of the new requirements. The expectations of the Central Bank's experts are that at the initial stage most of the banks in Bulgaria will apply the first approach. Essentially, it is an improved model of the current rules and includes higher risk sensitivity. Under this approach, the risk weighting of assets is based on the credit ratings assigned by external rating agencies. The various ratings carry risk weights from 0% to 150%. This approach assigns to borrowers without a credit class 100% or more risk weight. If we make a brief comparison between the risk weights of the basic types of assets as per Basle I and Basle II, we could mark the main differences in the risk weights applied by major groups of counterparties: Basle I Basle II Governments and central banks 0% 0% - 150% Banking 20% 20% - 150% Corporate 100% 20 - 150% SME 100% varies Retail 100% 75% Mortgage (housing) 50% 35% The standardised approach includes detailed requirements and rules for the assignment of external credit ratings. They refer to the criteria for their recognition, i.e., the recognition of external agencies and their credit ratings, and the manner, in which the banks could use them. In addition to the new methods of credit risk weighting, the new capital framework also includes a wider range of requirements and criteria for the application of various arrangements for credit risk mitigation - collaterals in the form of assets or third party guarantees and sureties. With the second group of arrangements, ratings are applied also to guarantors. In this way, the credit risk of the borrower is transformed into credit risk of the guarantor. The initial drafting and application of external credit ratings will require that the banks create a more comprehensive database, which they will analyse at a later stage as well. Some of the banks would probably decide to move to the second method - the Internal Rating Based Approach (IRBA). It is based on internal risk assessment and calculation of the capital requirements. This approach should more precisely determine the individual risk profile of counterparties, but on the other hand it imposes more stringent requirements such as well-developed risk management and assessment systems. Nevertheless, the more accurate measurement and assessment of the actual risk inherent in each bank will create the possibility to maintain an optimal quality and structure of own funds. In other words, the regulatory capital will move closer to the so-called economic capital of every bank. The core principle in the approach based on internal ratings (classes) includes internal assessment of the probability of default (PD). For the purpose of measurement of the other risk parameters - amount (degree) of loss - loss given default (LGD), part of the exposure at default (EAD) and maturity (M) - every institution employs either standard ratings, incorporated in the draft New Capital Accord, or their own internal ones. In the first case, the banks apply the so-called Foundation IRBA (a basic version of IRBA), while in the second - Advanced IRBA (an improved version of IRBA). An additional factor taken into account in calculating the capital requirements is the term to maturity of the exposure. On the whole, the application of the Internal Rating Based Approach requires that two major prerequisites be in existence: a database with statistical series of 5-year periods and the respective internal risk management procedures. In addition, the new Basle framework allows that newly established companies do not apply the requirement for a 5-year history of data for the purpose of nondiscrimination. Thus, it allows gradual compilation of the required data and sufficient room and flexibility for a step-by-step implementation of the approach in its two variant options - foundation and advanced. When making their choice for credit risk measurement approach, it is necessary that the banks make analysis and assessment of the applicability of methods. They should familiarise themselves with the requirements and the problems related to the appraisal of credit risk factors and the ways of its mitigation. The applicability of the existing database will be of key importance. On the other hand, the banks will need to prepare the relevant set of instruments for both the implementation of the standardised approach and the internal rating-based approach. This would include the type and processing of the database, the choice of statistical models and their in-house adaptation and testing. The banks will have to implant in their internal rules the overall process - from risk management to the choice of method and models (benchmarks) for assessment and reporting. Banking Supervision will monitor their preparation and will give instructions for its improvement. Capital requirements and market risk The New Accord does not change the way of determining the capital charges for market risk. The preparation for its introduction will be preceded by and concomitant with the application of the requirements for market risk measurement in the reporting of capital adequacy under the current Basle Accord. The mandatory introduction of the CAD I and CAD II requirements stems from the accession commitments of Bulgaria to EU, and from the higher diversity and sophistication of banks' portfolios. Those of them that are engaged in active trading in debt and capital securities or their hybrids on the domestic or international markets, and with volume of trading assets steadily reaching and exceeding EUR 15 million, or accounting for 5% or more of assets, will be subject to capital requirements for market risk for regulatory purposes. In accordance with the possibilities that they have, the banks will be able to apply a standard approach or internal models of assessment. Banking supervision expects that in the beginning the banks will start with the standard approach. Regardless of the fact that standard approaches are strictly regulated, the banks will have to make significant efforts to prepare themselves for their appropriate application. Probably, at a later stage of implementation of the standard rating methods after having accumulated sufficient database and having improved their methodological capacity, some Bulgarian banks could apply mathematical models of assessment, based on internally calculated values at risk (VaR). Another major prerequisite will be to run modern risk management procedures and arrangements and to apply them on a consistent basis. In this connection, banking supervision will regularly assess the risk management systems, the sufficiency and reliability of databases, and the results and reliability of internal rules. The respective models will be applied only after supervisory approval. Capital requirements for operational risk Operational risk is another substantial innovation in the New Accord. Its precise weighting is clearly a huge challenge to bankers. I am positive that the disputes and discussions about the scale of operational risk will not end with the adoption of the Accord. On the contrary, specialists are yet to look for an acceptable answer to this problem by using complex models and statistical information. The rules for calculating the capital requirements for operational risk are applicable to a wide range of institutions by means of three methods. The first and simplest method, the Basic Indicator Approach, implies that banks create a capital buffer against operational risk without having to develop sophisticated IT systems and to apply special procedures for managing this risk. The second method is more precise and is called Standardised Approach. It is based on assigning various standardised weights for operational risk applied to the incomes from individual banks' activities. The third and more complex method, the Advanced Approach, applied for the measurement of capital requirements for operational risk presupposes that banks generate their own database for operational risk and apply up-to-date standards for risk management and control. In this respect, it is essential that control systems be in a place which complies with the legal framework and the internal procedures. This approach is suitable for big, internationally active banks with a high level of complexity and sophistication of their operations and procedures. It is necessary that the larger banks in Bulgaria decide whether these prerequisites are in place and to what extent the application of the advanced approach for operational risk assessment is justified. Banking Supervision will approve its application and will monitor the adequacy of the methods applied by individual banks in line with their level of complexity of operations and procedures. Along with these changes, the New Capital Accord retains important elements of the current regulation. As I already mentioned, the calculation of capital premia of market risks remains unchanged. The same applies to the minimum capital adequacy ratio, which is 8%, as well as to the structure and content of the regulatory own capital. Supervisory review (Pillar 2) The supervisory review is a separate element of the draft New Capital Accord. It discusses the relations with the supervisory bodies and the responsibilities of credit institutions regarding internal risk measurement and capital requirements. In keeping with the requirements the banks should ensure their internal methodology for measurement of the capital needed to support the risks in their activities. The banks should define the parameters of their capital based on the concept of the so-called "inherent capital" as proposed in the New Capital Accord. On the other hand, the supervisory bodies should assess at least annually: 1) the risk profile of each institution, 2) the reliability and adequacy of their methodology and the internal ratings of banks, 3) the adequacy of their own funds and inherent capital, and 4) their compliance with the requirements laid down in the capital framework. Market discipline (Pillar 3) Certainly, the third new essential element of capital regulation will be market discipline. Supervisors are increasingly convinced that transparency in the banking business is among the most rational means of its selfregulation and discipline. A widely discussed topic is, however, the extent of disclosure and publicity as the overdisclosure of supervisory information for the public could also lead to a number of adverse consequences. Therefore, transparency of the information published by banks and investment companies as a way of exerting influence through a set of market mechanisms, has an important place in the draft New Capital Accord. The disclosure requirements are that credit institutions should carry out their activities in a prudent and sound manner. Market discipline supports the supervisory efforts for maintaining a high level of reliability of institutions and sound market operation. The key requirements as regards market discipline are for all banks and investment companies to publish expanded internal information such as the methods and assessments applied in their market and risk policy, etc. The supervision should assess the adequacy and quality of the published information depending on the type of activities and the risk profile of the supervised institution. The scope and responsibility for the published information depend on the place of an individual institution in a peer group of banks. In the case of larger subsidiaries or subgroups the parent company should publish additional information regarding their activities and risk profile on an individual and on a consolidated basis at a subgroup level. The banking institutions, which intent to apply the Internal Rating Based Approach and the tools for credit risk mitigation, as well as to issue and trade in asset-backed securities, should also publish a supplementary and more detailed information such as internal rules for risk management, the methods used for its assessment, the ways of avoiding and mitigating risks, etc. Banks and investment companies, who are internationally active, should disclose information on their activities on a more regular basis. In this case, special attention is placed on the own funds, the individual capital requirements and capital adequacy, data on which should be published quarterly. The published information should be user friendly in terms of location and format so that market players could have an easy access and possibility for comparison with other market entities. In accordance with the requirements in the draft New Capital Directive of EU, the data will be collected and archived at a national and European level in an electronic database. It will be accessible to all that might wish to use and download it on their own information media. Is the New Accord too complex? One often asked question is whether the New Capital Accord is really complex? To a certain extent, yes, it is complex. Some will say that external observers find it quite complex when they look at the hundreds of pages of papers supporting the accord (formulae, annexes, footnotes, etc.). It really is complex given the complexity and variety of the instruments employed in the banking practice. Then comes the next question: is it really necessary to have a complex accord? The Basle Committee will agree, and so will supervisors, that it is obviously much easier to create simple rules than complex ones. Banking, however, is no longer simple. The leading banks offer a wide range of sophisticated products and services. They also use sophisticated sets of tools, complex mathematical models, and complex legal papers in order to prevent risks and losses. Moreover, the leading banks demand all the time that they, as well as their products, be differentiated from the remaining competitors. The continuous innovations make the regulatory bodies' task for creating simple and universal rules that are applicable to all banking products and full-spectrum services hard to achieve. In effect, the complex character of the New Accord is partly due to banks, as they want to have the wide range of current risks and practices fully captured. As you could see from the overview, the Accord offers to banks and supervisors various options for capital adequacy assessment, which are aimed to differentiate the levels of complexity. In addition, the banks demanded from their supervisors, from the Basle Committee respectively, to preserve the risk sensitivity in the New Accord even at the cost of a greater complexity. The number of options, which the Accord proposes, allows it to better fit any type of bank profile. At the same time, over the last years the Basle Committee and the different work groups made considerable efforts to simplify some of the elements, where possible. In January and February this year they even went so far as to simplify the treatment of exposures on securitised assets, which are quite complex operations. However, an infinite simplification in this direction would not be possible, as the sensitivity to actual risks faced by banks and the possibility for comparability should be retained. The Basle Committee members believe that the time left until the implementation of the New Capital Accord at end 2006 will allow the countries to adapt their legislation and to prepare banking and supervisory staff for the successful implementation of the principles of the New Accord. The attitudes as to the scope of application went through different phases. The initial idea for the internationally active banks evolved to encompass all credit institutions, while later on the differentiated approach was again discussed as most appropriate. The Basle Committee has announced lately that the national authorities should determine the appropriateness of and the time for the implementation of the Accord in their countries so that they do not feel pressed for time. A great number of the leading countries confess that the new capital standards will be a serious challenge. The main critical arguments normally relate to the complexity, procyclic trends, potential market imbalances and competitive distortions, which it brings with itself. However, EU is determined to have all credit institutions encompassed by the Accord. Moreover, as I already mentioned, a draft Directive has been developed for implementing the rules of the Capital Accord. Thus, all credit institutions in the EU, irrespective of their size, will have to adapt to the new rules. Of course, of greater importance to us are the issues related to the challenges, which accession countries face. Obviously, the EU decision does not give new members the possibility for a choice, so that they too will have to implement the Capital Accord. This implies a serious tension to our country, given that, as was already mentioned, the full implementation of Basle I with regard to market risk (1996) will commence from 2005. Soon after that, the capital regulation will have to be updated in the light of Basle II. Which are the main challenges that we face? A challenge to us is the choice from the list of options, which the banks and the supervision will need to make. Another challenge comes from the serious investments that will need to be made for the innovation of technologies, personnel, and procedures. Although it is believed that countries like ours will use the more simplified standardised models for credit and operational risk because of the great number of subsidiary banks, there is a great likelihood of applying in-house models. Another challenge to the banks and the supervision are the deadlines. The banks should not postpone their preparation for the implementation of the Accord; they should organise their statistical models and databases and work out capital plans, which take into account the effect from the implementation of the Accord. A challenge will also be the need to improve the information environment and to set up and apply feasible ratings to potential borrowers. Market environment should also find a place for the credit rating agencies, which will ensure a more accurate application of the standardised approach to credit risk assessment. Another challenge the banks will face will be the need to operate in a much greater transparency. Challenges arise for the business as well, inasmuch as Basle II introduces specific individual approaches to the different categories of borrowers and counterparties. What are BNB's plans and views for the preparation of the banking sector and for meeting the above challenges? Actually, the preparation for Basle II has already started. On October 1, 2002, the Basle Committee sent to the national supervisory authorities a package of questionnaires and methodological guidelines for the purpose of testing the draft New Basle Capital Accord. The purpose of this test (Quantitative Impact Study 3 - QIS 3) is to establish how the new methods of calculating the risk weighted assets and the methods of calculating operational risk will impact the capital adequacy of banks in various countries. The outcomes were used to improve the draft. Bulgaria, as is known, was represented by 8 banks from group 1, which as at 30.06.2002 held 64% of the assets in the banking system. For assessment and weighting of the credit risk in assets the standard approach was applied. The results showed: Moderate increase in capital expenses for sovereign risk (governments and national banks). This effect is due to the banks' exposures in foreign currency to the Bulgarian Government and Sofia Municipality, including USD and EUR denominated Brady bonds, bonds for the conversion of the external government debt and the municipality credit, which is assigned 100% risk weight under the external rating of the country as at the time of the study. As a result of the application of external ratings BBB/BBB- or BB/- to foreign and local banks, as well as to local banks without external credit rating, the risk weighted assets under this group of counterparties also marked an increase relative to the currently applied standards. The Banks in our country use in effect option 2 as regards short-term claims on local institutions to a limited extent, as most of the subsidiaries have strict limits set by their parent banks and the weight of positions under that option is immaterial. The methods of operational risk measurement proposed in the study showed that additional portion of the capital base would be spent for it, too. Reduction in the risk-weighted assets will be observed with the exposures to individuals and households (bank loans and other retail services). This is due to the drop in the risk weight from 100% under the currently effective Accord to 75% in the draft New Accord, as well as to the decrease in the risk in credit exposures backed-up by real estate mortgage, from 50% to 35%, respectively. Of course, banks with small weights of their retail credit portfolios in total assets will not benefit much from this reduction. The exposures to other groups of counterparties did not show any peculiar changes in the study as a result of applying the standard approach from the New Capital Accord. The general conclusion was that following the Basle II introduction and if the present levels of own funds remain unchanged most of the Bulgarian banks will be able to comply with the capital adequacy requirements. The significance and complexity of the requirements laid down in the new international capital accord, the need for harmonisation of the standards and practice in the operation of the credit institutions and the supervision in our country with those in Europe requires a higher level of cooperation and unity of purpose between banking supervision and commercial banks in the course of preparation. In addition to the quantitative study of the impact and the discussions of the New Accord, the BNB has directed its efforts to the preparation of a plan for the implementation of CAD I and CAD II, as well as for the introduction of the New Capital Accord. What does this plan include in most general outlines? This year banking supervision will: Have the New Capital Accord and the new European Directive translated and published on the BNB's web-site with a view to facilitate the working groups in both the commercial banks and the supervision; Develop and publish a glossary of terms for the sake of uniformity of the translated concepts and their understanding; Develop and coordinate with the commercial banks a report with proposals for a national choice of the capital requirements for credit risk and requirements to the treatment of collaterals; In conjunction with experts from leading commercial banks will prepare and publish a report on the applicability of internal credit ratings and the outlook for their application in Bulgaria. It is supposed to bring to light the issues of internal rating application and the applicability of the existing databases, and the possibility for some of the local subsidiaries to apply the basic variant option; In conjunction with experts from leading banks will prepare and publish a report on the feasibility of an advanced approach to operational risk assessment. It should include analysis of the issues related to the segregation and reporting of types of incomes in the credit institutions, and of the adequacy of databases. For the next year we plan to publish supplementary material for the internal models of credit risk assessment with a view to facilitate the commercial banks in preparing their in-house methodologies for credit risk reporting and assessment, for facilitating the supervision in assessing the models used by the banks, as well as regarding the methods of operating risk assessment, appendices for reporting of banks' incomes by type of activity. In 2005 banking supervision will also prepare a draft new regulation on capital adequacy for coordination among banks based on the new European Directive with a view to the unification of the capital requirements in our country with those applied in the EU. For 2006 we have envisaged the following actions: We will offer the commercial banks new reporting forms and guidelines for supervisory reporting of risk assets and capital adequacy (including credit risk, market risk, and operational risk); In joint efforts with the banks we will hold a test for reporting the risks in capital in keeping with the new requirements and the results compared to the reports under the current standards. The purpose will be to establish the level of impact in applying the new methodologies, and to introduce possible corrections to the reporting forms of the banks; The supervision manuals will be supplemented and the questionnaires and the bank examination procedures will be updated; A supervisory methodology for the testing of internal banking models will be prepared; The commercial banks will have to prepare internal methodologies, rules and procedures for the application of the New Capital Accord requirements. They should decide for themselves the parameters of their capital based on their business plans and risk profile, and in line with the requirements of the Supervisory Review Pillar II of the New Capital Accord. We will supplement the Supervision Examinations Manual in accordance with the requirements for supervisory review and actions included in Pillar 2 of the Accord; We will prepare supervisory requirements for information disclosure with a view to strengthen market discipline as a tool for selfregulation of banks by means of improving the transparency of their activities and the risks incurred by them. The banks, on their part, will have to develop their own action plans in this direction. It is necessary that they start to prepare from now (some of them have already commenced preparations) and include the individual components of the Accord in their annual operation plans. Dear ladies and gentlemen, dear colleagues, While not pretending to be exhaustive, I have tried to introduce the views of the Central Bank on the challenges faced by the banking sector in the light of the new international and European banking regulations. There is no doubt that we will have to make a lot of joint efforts and resolve great many complex problems. I believe that the traditions of successful cooperation between the Central Bank and the commercial banks will be the stepping stone for overcoming the above challenges. ____________ The immediate reason for the establishment of the Basle Committee on Banking Supervision is the banking failures in 1974. The dramatic collapse of major banks in two countries at that time shook up the banking world. In June 1974, the authorities in West Germany closed down Herstatt Bankhaus as a result of the bank's losses from foreign currency operations, without taking into account or assuming responsibility for the subsequent substantial losses of a great number of banks in other countries. In October the same year Franklin National Bank in the USA was closed due to poor deposit base management, overspeculations on the international foreign currency markets and overambitious expansion. This negative experience brought together in end 1974 the G-10 countries, which set up under the umbrella of the Bank for International Settlement a Committee on Banking Regulations and Supervisory Practices, which is known today as the Basle Committee on Banking Supervision. Hereinafter this expression will be referred to as the Capital Accord, which for convenience sake is accepted to be referred to in the Accord. PAGE PAGE 10

Title: Speech ahead of the annual meeting of the Association of Commercial Banks, Plovdiv, April 22, 2005.
text: Speech by Mrs. Emilia Milanova, Deputy Governor of the BNB, ahead of the annual meeting of the Association of Commercial Banks, Plovdiv, April 22, 2005. TOPICAL QUESTIONS ABOUT THE DEVELOPMENT OF THE REGULATORY ENVIRONMENT FOR FINANCIAL INTERMEDIATION Dear colleagues, In connection with the signing of the Treaty of Accession of Bulgaria to the European Union next week andthe membership of the European Union forthcoming on 1 January 2007, I consider it necessary to draw your attention to the forthcoming work on the legal framework for the activities of banks and, in particular, to regulate them. From the date of Bulgaria's membership in the European Union, the banking sectorwill be able to participate fully in the single market for financial services, having adopted and implemented a number of acts of European law in this field. The Bulgarian banking sector is already preparing for the challenges of membership related to the implementation of a line ofnew regulations that will help to maintain customer confidence in the banking system and strengthen competitiveness within the single market. I will emphasise the requirements, the introduction of which in the Bulgarian legislation regulatingbank activity is imminent. In the field of banking supervision in Bulgaria, almost full harmonisation has already been achieved on all current requirements of the European Union in terms of access to banking, capital and capital adequacy, large expositions, supervision on a consolidated basis, regulation of the amount of banks' investments. The provisions on mutual recognition of licences issued, supervision by theMember State of credit institution, additional supervision of financial conglomerates and new Capital Requirements of the European Union stemming from Basel II are to be introduced in our legislation. I will focus your attention on several main projects affecting the activities of the banks in Bulgaria. First of all, it is necessary to draw up an entirely new draft of the Law on Banks, for which we have set ambitious deadlines. The aim of this bill is to cover all the provisions of thecodified Directive 2000/12 on the activities of credit institutions, including the single licence provisions (mutual recognition of licences) issued by the supervisory authorities of the Member States, responsibilities with regard to consolidated supervision, additional definitions, as well as the new Basel II provisions to supplement this Directive. Some sections of the current law will be implanted in the new one without substantial changes, while other sections will be fully updated. Our second significant commitment is the development of a draft new cap ital adequacy ordinance, which will have effectfrom 1 January 2007 and which will implement the new capital requirements of the European Union deriving from Basel II. risk. All new will be the sections on own funds requirements for credit risk, including requirements under the three approaches, credit risk mitigation sections, securitisation, capital requirements for operational risk. The Ordinance will also integrate all annexes of the revised and supplemented EU directives 2000/12 and 93/6. To carry out this task in October last year, we set up a working group and subgroups on individual topics and issues. At this stage, the group has prepared a table of discretions that will find a place in the ordinance. This table will soon be sent to you to express your comments on our proposals. that we have taken a more conservative approach. We are also preparing preliminary guidance for banks on operational risk and IRB models. We believe that the capital requirements for operational risk, as well as the very assessment and management of this risk, are something new for Bulgarian banks and therefore they need to make some adjustment before the new regulation becomes a fact. The development of the draft ordinance shall be carried out in modules according to the risk, which shall be treated in the relevant sections, taking into account the changes in the draft Directive. Our intention is to have a readyinitial draft of the ordinance to be sent to the ATB for discussion as soon as possible after the final adoption of the amendments to the Directive by the European Parliament. As we have already spoken about Basel II at last year's banking meeting, I would also like to inform you about the incidents that took place afterwards. In June last year, as you already know, the final basel committee document - International Unification of Capital Measurement and CapitalStandards (revised framework) was published. (is) the following month, in July, a draft amendment to Directive 2000/12 on the activities of credit institutions and 93/6 on capital adequacy was submitted to the European Parliament. The first has been mainly revised in the context of Basel II, whereas the PR and the second changes relate mainly to the provisions of the International Financial Reporting Standards in force in the Community this year for public companies, including banks. In parallel to this process, a process of preparation for the implementation of the Directives has also begun. The Committee of European Banking Supervisors (CEBS), established in 2004, has been tasked with this work. I would also like to inform you about the application of Ordinance No 8 on the capital adequacy of banks, which was adopted in December last year. We have already prepared a package of new reporting forms and detailed instructions to them, which will be sent to you by the end of the monthvia VPN (virtual private network) so that the necessary tests can be done before the regulation takes effect. so that we can correct or supplement them in a timely manner, if necessary we will make the necessary amendments to the ordinance. Our third commitment is related to financial conglomerates. By the date of membership of the Republic of Bulgaria in the EU (01.01.2007) directive 2002/87/EC on additional supervision of credit institutions, insurance companies and investment firms in a financial conglomerate will be introduced into Bulgarian legislation. The purpose of the Directive is to ensure the stability of European financial markets, to introduce common rules for the reasonable supervision of financial conglomerates in Europe. The Directive setscommon standards for the reasonable supervision of structures that include regulated institutions (banks/insurance companies/investment firms). Under that Directive, the competent authorities assess on aconsolidated basis the financial performance of the conglomerate as regards solvency, risk concentration and intra-group transactions. Supplementary supervision on a consolidated basis of financial conglomerates shall be carried out by a coordinator designated between the competent supervisory authorities of the Member States concerned. A working group of experts from the BNB and the Commission for Financial Supervision has already beenset up, which is tasked with drafting a bill that will implement the requirements of this directive in Bulgarian legislation. In the area of consumer protection, regulatory regulation of consumer credit agreements will be forthcoming, which will have implications not only in the banking sphere, but also in a number of other areas, such as trade and services. In the framework of Working Party 23 on Consumer Protection and Their Health, the Bulgarian side is committed to introducing into Bulgarian legislation the requirements of EU law in this field, namely Directive 87/102/EEC on the approximation of the laws, regulations and administrative provisions of the Member States relating to consumer credit and amending Directives 90/88/EEC and 97/8/EC . The matter is specific, therefore it cannot be included in the general Consumer Protection Act, but will be subject to an act of law. The transposition of the Directives will lead to a clear regulation of the conditions for granting and paying off consumer loans, balancing the interests of both parties  banks and customers. Increasing competition needs unambiguous rules on the calculation of the annual percentage rate of consumer credit costs, advertising and obligations of lenders. Following the trend at European level to strengthen the protection of a better countryin financial services contracts, the law will provide for obligations for lenders, including banks, in order to better inform and guarantee consumer rights. Providing consumers with sufficient and comprehensible informationis a fundamental principle in ensuring a high level of consumer protection, as this avoids the advantage of lenders in information asymmetry. The requirement for disclosure of the "annual percentage rate of consumer credit" (APRPC)  a new concept in the Bulgarian legislation is the total cost of the loan to the consumer, expressed as an annual percentage. Following the requirements of this Directive, the Formulafor calculating the APRC will be introduced in the Bulgarian legislation. Compliance controls on consumer credit agreements will be exercised by the Committee on Trade and ConsumerProtection, which is the specialised public authority in the field of consumer protection and which has the necessary experience and tools to ensure the effective implementation of the future law.
