Title: Congratulatory Remarks on the Occasion of Completion the Banking Supervision Development Project of USAID, Sofia, May 28, 2004.
text: Congratulatory Remarks by Mrs. Emilia Milanova, - Deputy Governor of the BNB, on the Occasion of Completion the Banking Supervision Development Project of USAID, Sofia, 28 May 2004 Ladies and Gentlemen, I am honoured to speak at the ceremony for the completion of the banking supervision development project of USAID. The USAID project for the development of banking supervision can be assessed as extremely successful, hence I will outline several main tasks BNB has fulfilled in the area of banking supervision for the performance of one of its key functions - to regulate and oversee the activities of domestic commercial banks in view of supporting the stability of the banking system and protecting depositors' interests. The preparation and implementation of the new supervision framework for banking in compliance with the new Law on Banks, the Basle Core Principles of prudential banking supervision, and the EU directives; Reorganization along the lines of the best international practices and institutional strengthening of BSD; Effecting complex supervision and instilling discipline in the banking sector for the stabilization and strengthening of credit institutions. Directing banks to a new type of market behaviour and gradually restoring their credibility; Enhanced monitoring and oversight of the restructuring and privatization developments in the banking sector; Expanding the supervisory capacities to counteract adequately money laundering and financial fraud perpetrated via banks; Training BNB and commercial bank experts for and introduction of the IAS as the only reporting basis for commercial banks. Introduction of new call reports giving better account of banks' risk profiles; Increasing the transparency of the equity interests in commercial banks. Establishing and strengthening international relations with other supervisory institutions and active participation in the regional and international supervision organizations; The six years of united efforts of the management and the staff of the BSD and our advisors from BearingPoint resulted in a modern dynamic and efficient banking supervision and to a more stable banking system. Please allow me to mention some of the most significant attainments of BSD and the BearingPoint team during the project: On-site supervision BSD developed a robust and effective program for on-site supervision, which is capable of determining the level of risk and the capacities of the bank's management to efficiently control and manage risk. The BearingPoint consultants, both working on long-term and short-term basis - all of them with many years of experience in US supervision agencies - provided advisory support to BASD in more than 60 on-site inspections and directions as to the overall assessment of the management of banks, of market risks, capital adequacy, asset quality, earnings and liquidity. The preparation of the Banking Supervision manual was a very significant project directed by our BearingPoint advisors. The Manual focuses on risk-based supervision and describes the concepts and procedures of efficient banking supervision and on-site supervision. It details the system for assessment of risk in individual banks (CAMELS) and formalizes the processes for applying enforcement measures and the supervision of problem banks. Naturally, the Manual was developed with the significant input from the Inspections Directorate, so that they should own it and trust it. The BearingPoint consultants assisted BSD in the development of several supervision tools for on-site supervision. These include a standard inspection report, a standard asset quality control examination, a questionnaire on a bank's practices for securing loans, and a supervision profile report from. Significant consultancy support was provided in the supervision of problem banks. Off-site supervision BSD developed and implemented an effective risk-based approach to the off-site supervision and analysis. The risk-based supervision requires from the inspectors to incessantly monitor the types and developments of risks faced by banks, and to judge how the existing and occurring events may influence individual banks and the sector as a whole. The approach of the BearingPoint consultants in providing their assistance to BSD in accumulating such experience was focused on providing the necessary training, guidelines and analytical tools to the Off-site Supervision Directorate. The BearingPoint consultants assisted BSD in developing a detailed financial reporting framework to use as a basis for the Early Warning System of BSD. The CAEL rating system, the Uniform Bank Performance Report, and the periodical financial analyses of individual banks by the Off-site Supervision and Analyses Directorate. A model Analysis of Overseas Parent-companies was also developed. Considerable element of the Project was focused on the Risk-based supervision approach The BearingPoint consultants assisted BSD in tracking from a suppression approach based on compliance with the regulative framework to a risk-based supervision approach . Underlying the risk-based supervision approach was the introduction of a risk-assessment supervision system following the one applied by the US banking regulators. The integration of the activities of the off-site and on-site supervision in a single supervision program facilitated the on-going and preventive supervision of banks. The result of the joint efforts of the Bearing Point team is a Banking Supervision Process manual, which details the rights and obligations of each of the five directorates in BSD and the interaction between them. Part of the USAID Project was related to the training of BSD experts Approach/regular training courses/ on-the-job training/ based on the US experience Another area of technical assistance - special supervision activities Inspection procedures under the Law on the Measures against Money Laundering A model program for compliance by banks with the measures against money laundering Inspections on the measures against money laundering - on-the-job training by a consultant. Today, I can note with satisfaction that in terms of its supervision activities BNB has earned its high ratings by both the international financial institutions (IMF and the World Bank) involved in the financial sector reform, and by the specialized supervision authorities of the EU. The contribution of the USAID Project to these ratings is great. So allow me to express my great thanks to Mrs. McFarland - the Director of the USAID Mission to Bulgaria for the financing provided by the USAID, thus providing us the opportunity to work together and avail of the experience of such renowned experts like James Reeves and Paul Sachtleben. You will always be our friends and will have your deserved place in the almanac of Bulgarian banking supervision. Thanks to Alan Hawkins and Chris Thompson. On behalf of Mr. Stoyan Manolov - Off-site Supervision and Analyses Director - and the team of the Directorate, I would like to thank to: Donna Rose, Raihan Zamil, Glen Tasky, and Martin Guilfoil, who worked on the off-site supervision project. On behalf of Tatiana Petrova - Inspections Director - and the team of the Directorate - thanks to Larry Hawly, Ken Walker and Michael Carlton, who advised the project in its on-site supervision element. And once again - thanks to USAID.

Title: Lecture before the Greek economic and financial elite, Central Bank of Greece, Athens, 14 July 2006
Subtitle: BULGARIAN ECONOMY ON THE ROAD TO EU AND EMU MEMBERSHIP
text: Lecture by Mr. Ivan Iskrov, Governor of the BNB, before the Greek economic and financial elite, Central Bank of Greece, Athens, 14 July 2006 BULGARIAN ECONOMY ON THE ROAD TO EU AND EMU MEMBERSHIP I would like first to express my sincere thanks to Governor Garganas for the invitation extended, and the opportunity provided to me to talk on the development of the Bulgarian economy before such an esteemed audience. On the verge of Bulgarias membership in the European Union, I have chosen as the subject of my presentation the path that our society and economy went from the beginning of the transition from a centrally planned to a market economy, and about our plans for full-fledged membership in the Economic and Monetary Union (EMU). To be able to outline for you a clearly-cut picture of the road we went so far and to come to an evaluation of the results achieved, I should first describe in short the initial conditions the Bulgarian transition started from. I. Initial conditions after the collapse of the communism and prerequisites for successful transition Probably most of you know that before the market reforms launched in 1991, the Bulgarian economy, like the other economies of Eastern and Central Europe, was based on the principles of central government planning. There were no commodity, labour and financial markets. These economies were highly integrated among themselves within the Council for Mutual Economic Assistance (CMEA) according to an administratively regulated specialization in specific industries. The existence of guaranteed markets within the CMEA isolated these economies from any competitive pressure and brought the incentives for seeking competitive advantages to a minimum. In the early 1990s a unique transition process from a centrally-planned to a market economy started in the post-communist countries. It was unique because we could not draw on the historical experience of other countries, nor could we rely on the research in the academic literature, because literature on these issues did not exist. We all had to learn ad-hock. Each post-communist country could to a different extend implement reforms that would, quickly and with low social costs, improve the welfare of its society. Regretfully, the Bulgarian society could not achieve, as quickly as the other Central European countries, a consensus and set its priorities, thus allowing for the implementation of quick and efficient pro-market reforms. In the early 1990s, the Bulgarian economy had at its disposal an obsolete physical capital and an outmoded organization of business activities. The changes that had to be implemented for the transformation of the economy from a command into a market-oriented one, required the quick renovation of physical and human capital. Due to various reasons (primarily lack of political will and consensus), however, the restructuring was continuously postponed, hence we paid the high price of a long period of stagnation and economic instability. In the conditions of a prevailing state-ownership, high inflation and quickly changing relative prices, the companies refrained from investments, and this slowed down considerably the pace of replacement of capital assets. In the mid-1990s our country inevitably lapsed into a deep political, economic, and financial crisis. Crises, however, can serve as a catalyst for comprehensive economic reforms. II. Current macroeconomic and financial framework at place in Bulgaria Underlying the economic reform of mid-1997 was the achievement and maintenance of macroeconomic stability, the States maximum withdrawal from the business, the full liberalisation of domestic and foreign trade, and the introduction of free movement of capitals. The implementation of the Currency Board Arrangement in mid-1997 by fixing the national currency to the German Mark (and since 1 January 1999  to the Euro) and prohibiting any lending by the BNB to the government and the commercial banks in whatever form was a milestone of the economic reform, along with the large-scale privatisation of state-owned assets. At the time of introduction of the currency board, the US Dollar was the major foreign currency dominating the countrys foreign trade and was used by the population as a means of saving. The selection of the German Mark (respectively the Euro) as the reserve currency reflected rather the consensus in the society and the political class, that Bulgarias accession to the EU is the political project around which our energy and efforts should unite. Countries with a currency board are viewed as mechanically importing the monetary policy as well as the credibility of the country or area to whose currency they peg their own currency. This is true, of course, but only to a limited extent. The truth is that you can obtain credibility on credit only temporarily. In the final run, credibility should be won through a consistent and responsible policy. That is exactly why repudiating the implementation of an independent monetary policy requires to orient ones fiscal policy towards supporting the fixed exchange rate regime and to pursue structural reforms that would enhance the economys flexibility and competitiveness. The fiscal policy implemented since 1997, as well as the liberalization and restructuring of the economy were the main pillars, on which the confidence of the population and of foreign investors were built. The fiscal policy, consistently pursued since 1997, based on a balanced budget or a budget surplus helped the government to bring this parameter to levels far below the criterion adopted by the EU. This resulted in a significant improvement of the countrys credit rating, decreasing the sovereign spread, reducing the cost of the credit and improving the investment opportunities. The stringent macroeconomic policy framework adopted, and the structural policy aimed at privatization of state-owned enterprises and market liberalization inevitably brought to significant changes in the real economy. Since 1997, our economy has been on the rise at relatively high growth rates, which have been accelerating as a result of the microeconomic reforms already in place, and due to the countrys forthcoming accession to EU. The main factors underlying this economic growth are the growing investments and household consumption, and to a lesser extent - exports. The macroeconomic stability, the privatisation and liberalisation of the economy, as well as the high degree of predictability of the pursued policy, significantly improved the incentives for investing into the Bulgarian economy. From 1999 to 2005, the amount of foreign direct investment is sustained at 8.5 % of GDP as an annual average, and only one third of these investments are generated by privatization deals, the remainder being green-field investments. This process of massive capital inflow accelerated considerably in the recent three years due to the favourable international situation and the approaching full-fledged EU membership of our country. As a result of this, the growth rate of investments increased, as well as their share in the GDP  up to 28% in 2005  thus reaching the highest level since the beginning of economic reforms in the country. The high investment levels inevitably brought about an increase in the productivity of labour with a moderate increase in the salaries and wages and the unit price of labour, which allowed our exports to sustain their competitiveness and our country to continue attracting direct investment. At the same time, the growing economic activity was accompanied by a stable growth of employment and the consequent reduction of unemployment. The growth of disposable income of households resulting from the increased employment and salaries was the initial stimulus, which set the beginning of the stable growth rate of consumption in the economy. Subsequently, this effect was considerably reinforced by the development of the domestic banking sector and the enhanced access of households to the credit market. The eased up access to the credit market combined with the decreasing interest rates due to the countrys higher credit rating and the global excess liquidity in the recent three years resulted in a reduction of households savings and growth of consumption. The reduced savings of households and companies accounted for by the growth of consumption and investments, inevitably resulted in the accumulation of a current account deficit. The budget surpluses maintained by the government in the recent years managed to some extent to set off the reduced savings in the private sector. Given the latters significant share in the domestic economy, however, (70% of GDP is generated by the private sector), this policy can have only a limited effect on the countrys external position. III. Economic and monetary developments and challenges for the policymakers As a result of the above discussed processes, the current account deficit increased, reaching levels above 5% of GDP in 2003 and 2004, and additionally grew to 11.9% at end-2005. Significant role in the development of our countrys current account deficit in 2005 was played by two groups of factors. First, the already mentioned investment growth was accompanied by an increase of imports of investment goods. In 2005, the imports of this group of goods grew by 31.2%, and their share in the overall composition of imports reached up to 28%. This trend was combined with the downward trend in the growth of non-energy raw materials and consumer goods. In the last year, a number of one-off factors had considerable effect, comprising the abrupt increase in the prices and volume of crude oil and the massive floods in the country which hindered exports in the third quarter of the year. It is a well-known fact that the current account deficits are highly inert, which presupposes that reducing the countrys external disbalance will be a gradual process. In addition, the Bulgarian economy is at the initial phase of its convergence, which means a longer period with high growth rate of investments and capital inflows. As I have already mentioned, in the recent several years large volumes of capital were channelled into the country, and the banking system acted as the natural intermediator for the efficient distribution of these resources. This is not at all surprising, given the process of privatization and restructuring of the Bulgarian banking sector. Presently, 99.7% of the banking sector is private, and over 80% of the banks in Bulgaria are owned by foreign investors prevailingly from euro area member states. As a consequence of the strong competition and the good investment opportunities, the growth rates of credit to the private sector have increased to the level of 48.6% at end-2004. In several years only, the ratio of bank credit to GDP has grown from 12.1% in 1999 to 45.0 % as of end-2005. Of course, these dynamics reflected to a great extent the process of our economys convergence, and in particular  the intensification of financial intermediation to the levels evidenced in EU member states (112% of GDP). This process was propelled not only by corporate behaviour. Households were also very quick to react to changes by reducing their savings and increasing their propensity to consume now, as a result of their expectations of higher future incomes. These are natural developments though entailing risks that had to be evaluated and measures had to be taken for their minimization. The BNB had to determine the point in time, after which convergence develops into a self-propelling process of struggling for a market share. Such a transition entails considerable risks, as it leads to no sustainable rates of growth both in terms of financial intermediation, and economic activity and employment. Therefore, from the beginning of 2004 the BNB started a process of phasing in of measures (mainly supervisory and administrative) aimed at slowing down the pace of growth of banking credit to a sustainable level, which would not pose significant risks to the stability of the economy. The data indicate that the central banks policy changed the behaviour of commercial banks. Credit growth rates fell to 32.4% at end-2005, which also stopped the process of depleting the banking systems capital adequacy. This year, by keeping the current measures in place, we expect that the banking credit would grow at a rate lower than, but close to, 20%. A very large part of this audience consists of representatives of commercial banks which operate in Bulgaria or plan to come to our financial market, so I should say that the BNB already began to gradually loosen the current administrative restrictions on the growth rates of banking lending (the so-called credit ceilings). This policy is needed because during our countrys integration into the EU, the commercial banks regulated by the BNB and those regulated by the supervisory authorities of the other EU countries will be placed on an equal footing. However, the gradual removal of the administrative restrictions on banking lending should not be viewed as a BNB policy aiming to relax the current stringent regulatory framework which limits the risks in the banking system. The strict supervisory framework introduced and applied by the BNB will remain unchanged. IV. EU and EMU perspectives By signing the Treaty of Accession to the EU, Bulgaria made the commitment to join the Euro zone and introduce the single currency. The current European legislation does not allow the new EU member-states to use an opt-out clause for their membership in the EMU. This means that after becoming a member of the EU, Bulgaria will have to decide not if it would join the EMU and introduce the single currency, but when and how this should be done. The European legislation does not provide any explicit date for the Euro introduction or a period for complying with the convergence criteria. Moreover, the European Central Bank (ECB) and the European Commission (EC) decided that they could not accept the currency board arrangement as a substitute for the participation in the Exchange Rate Mechanism II (ERM II), but that the ERM II did not rule out the unilateral operation of a currency board arrangement in the countries where this arrangement already exists. Having in mind what was said above and the principles of the macroeconomic policy pursued in our country, with a currency board arrangement based on the Euro, in 2004 the Government and the central bank signed an agreement whose purpose is the only logical decision  the introduction of the Euro in the shortest possible time horizon. This document describes Bulgarias strategy for membership in the EMU and this strategy is based on the following principles: Joining the Exchange Rate Mechanism II (ERM II) as soon as possible after the date of Bulgarias official membership in the EU (probably in the first quarter of 2007). Keeping the currency board in place until we join the Euro zone, with the current fixed exchange rate of the Bulgarian Lev to the Euro - 1.95583 BGN for 1 Euro; The unilateral commitment of the Bulgarian Government and the BNB to maintain a zero fluctuation of the exchange rate from the fixed level (i.e. carrying on the present policy of maintaining the currency board arrangement); Meeting the minimum period set in the EU legislation for participation in the ERM II and taking in time all the necessary steps of the procedure for membership in the Euro zone. This strategy is very similar to the way of introducing the single currency adopted by some of the old member-states (e.g. Austria) and by Estonia and Lithuania  the two countries having currency boards, which joined the EU in 2004. The agreement between the BNB and the Government on Bulgarias policy for our membership in the EMU largely decreases the uncertainties about the macroeconomic policy and provides predictability, facilitating entrepreneurs and households in formulating their objectives. This strategy is ambitious but attainable. Following the current policy of balanced budget, with a surplus if possible, will enable us to meet the Maastricht criteria in terms of budget deficit, government debt and long-term interest rates, and will also make the macroeconomic policy more responsive and flexible. It is well known that under a currency board arrangement, the fiscal policy is the only tool available for a relatively quick response to adverse developments in the economy of the country. Furthermore, in order for us to have this flexibility with the growing current account deficit and rapidly increasing private debt, in periods like this where the economy is growing at rates close to or a little above the long-term growth rates, the budget needs to compensate by generating a sufficient surplus. The tough fiscal policy is needed also because it will help us comply with the inflation criterion. Operating under a currency board arrangement, the central bank has no direct control of inflation rates in the country. Practically, this particular criterion will be the biggest challenge for us. Given the current trend of price levels in the new member-states converging to the levels in the old member-states (a result of the well-known Balassa-Samuelson effect), this criterion is a challenge not just for the countries with a currency board in place, but also for all countries with price levels lower than the average in the EU. The very definition of the inflation criterion, i.e. inflation not higher than the average of the three lowest rates of inflation in the EU plus 1.5 percent, creates some uncertainty. The ten new member-states, as well as Bulgaria and Romania, find themselves in a shooting at a moving target situation. At the same time, with the 25 member-states (27 with Bulgaria and Romania) it is very likely that we would have three countries, the so-called best performers, with rates of inflation close to zero because of cyclic or other specific for those countries reasons. This means that the inflation criterion would be very strict and would require reaching inflation rates close to or even lower than the ECB inflation target (lower, but almost 2% inflation). Considering this strongly restrictive inflation criterion and the uncertainties about determining its level, we expected that the ECB and the European Commission would show greater flexibility in assessing the compliance with this criterion. Unfortunately, Lithuanias assessment published in the Convergence Report in May this year suggested that the expected flexibility would not be demonstrated. A very bureaucratic approach has been used, neglecting the fact that each economy is affected by a large number of internal and external influences and this very much hinders the fulfilment of the heavily restrictive inflation criterion, especially with the absence of an autonomous monetary policy. In the particular case of Bulgaria where a fixed exchange rate regime is in place together with a very conservative fiscal policy, reserves should be looked for in promoting the competition and improving the business environment so that the economy would have greater flexibility to respond to changes in the external environment (including raw materials prices), and the supply could react faster to the increased demand (internal and external). Last year inflation reached 6.5%, and the increase in energy prices was a strong inflationary factor (its direct contribution is 1.0% of the overall price rise). In addition, the heavy floods led to an unexpected rise in foodstuffs prices (a contribution of 2.6% of the overall price rise). This year we expect that inflation would fall to 6.0% in spite of its faster growth rates over the first two months of the year. The slow process of decreasing the inflation rate is largely determined by the harmonisation of indirect taxes, undertaken early this year, with the EU minimum levels. As the changes in indirect taxes and administered prices directly affect the inflation in the country, their catching up adjustment has to take place before the years that will be the basis for assessing the compliance with the Maastricht criteria  before 2008. From this perspective, the ahead-of-time harmonisation of some excise duties is a step that would very much help for the compliance of the inflation criterion because it would eliminate the inflationary influence caused by the increase in these taxes over the years that will be used for the assessment. V. Conclusions Before I finish, I would like to point out the regional factor for the successful development of the Bulgarian economy and the role of Greece. I have already mentioned that in the early 1990s Bulgaria began the transition from a centrally-planned to a market economy, and in the mid-1990s we went through a profound political, financial and economic crisis. Throughout this period the Greek business and political elite supported the efforts of the Bulgarian society to handle these challenges. After the economic stabilization in 1997 the Greek businesses were among the first to provide credit of confidence to the Bulgarian economy, investing in the banking sector of the country and in a number of other important sectors of the economy. At the end of 2005 the commercial banks with Greek share participation held 19% of the capital of the Bulgarian banking system, 18% of its total assets and deposits, and 22% of the lending to the private sector. Through the capitals that they are investing and the transfer of knowledge and expertise, these institutions have a major contribution to the economic growth in our country. Apart from that, the Greek business is the second largest direct investor in Bulgaria by 12.4% of the foreign direct investments made in Bulgaria from 1999 until now. Greece leaves far behind much larger in size economies, such as Germany, France and Italy. The intense investment activities of the Greek businesses in Bulgaria definitely affect the direction of our foreign trade flows. Greece is the third most important trading partner of our country, holding 12.9% of our foreign trade in 2005. The accession of Bulgaria and Romania to the EU and the prospects for membership of the other countries in this region, give the Balkan countries a chance for full integration into the world economy. We can say without hesitation that the countries in this region have never before had a chance like this in their history. By developing the regional cooperation and promoting the political and economic ties between our countries, the Balkan region can become competitive not only within the EU but also in the global economy. Finally I would like to express my highest appreciation of and gratitude for the steady and consistent support given by Greece and the Greek elite for the reforms in Bulgaria and especially for our accession to the EU. This support is very well known in the Bulgarian society. We do hope that this friendship and assistance will continue during Bulgarias accession to the Euro zone and afterwards. PAGE PAGE 2

Title: Speech delivered to the conference 60 days before EU membership: what should we expect, what should we do?, organized by Capital newspaper and Handelsblatt, Sofia, 18 October 2006
Subtitle: MACROECONOMIC STABILITY AND ECONOMIC GROWTH
text: Speech by Mr. Ivan Iskrov, Governor of the BNB, delivered to the conference 60 days before EU membership: what should we expect, what should we do?, organized by Capital newspaper and Handelsblatt, Sofia, 18 October 2006 MACROECONOMIC STABILITY AND ECONOMIC GROWTH Dear Minister Oresharski, Ladies and Gentlemen, The process of negotiations and preparations for Bulgarias membership in the European Union (U) required not only the enormous efforts of the Bulgarian government institutions, but also an intense mobilization of efforts of the whole society. We had to pursue multiple reforms and to adjust our work and our lives to these changes. And this opinion is not just ours, it is also shared by our EU counterparts. I would allow myself to quote some of the conclusions made in the Report of the European Commission of 26 September this year, stating that: Bulgaria and Romania have made considerable efforts to complete their preparations for EU membership since the Commission issued its last report in May. Bulgaria and Romania are sufficiently prepared to meet the political, economic and acquis criteria by 1 January 2007. As a result of the progress made, Bulgaria and Romania will be in a position to take on the rights and obligations of EU membership on 1 January 2007. The successful completion of this process is an achievement for all Bulgarians and for all governments since 1997. At the same time, the significant endeavour made by the Bulgarian society prevailingly focuses our attention on the period up to the EU membership of Bulgaria. My message to the participants in this Conference today is that joining the EU from 1 January 2007 is not the crowning end of the integration process. It should be considered as the end of the preliminary phase of preparation and as the beginning of the next phase, which is to achieve integration of commodity and capital markets, free movement of people and a single labour market, as well as the introduction of the single currency. Todays forum gives us the opportunity to look up from the pre-membership period and further ahead to the time when we will be part of the European Union. Maybe the requirement for every EU Member State (except the UK and Denmark) to mandatory join the euro area is the integration aspect which most clearly indicates that EU membership is not an end in itself but the beginning of the integration process. It is worth noting that our countrys accession into the European Union automatically brings us into the Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) with a derogation (Art.5 of the Accession Treaty), whereas Bulgaria makes a commitment to satisfy the Maastricht criteria and become a full-fledged member of the Union. The period within which a country can meet the criteria and join the euro area is conditional on the preparedness of the fiscal sector for this, and on the degree of convergence of inflation rates. On this point we often face the erroneous view that real and nominal convergence are two incompatible processes which cannot be achieved simultaneously. We believe the competent combination of fiscal, structural and regulatory policies that would encourage competition on a micro economic level can bring about a quicker process of real convergence while achieving also the nominal criteria. The very accession to the euro area and the changeover to the single currency will be an additional strong impetus to converge to the level of productivity and incomes existent in the EU countries. Irrespective of my introductory words, accentuating on the focus of orientation of all  politicians, mass media, and public interest  in the recent years on achieving goals related to our countrys EU membership, with regard to adopting the single currency, the country, and the BNB in particular, have always pursued a consistent and long-term oriented policy. This position has been to a great extent determined by the existing currency board regime and by the awareness of all responsible political parties of its significance for the economic stability and growth. I will make a short review. In 2000, in Bulgarias position on Chapter 11 Economic and Monetary Union, the government expressed its intention to join Exchange Rate Mechanism II (ERM II) in the shortest possible time after EU accession, while maintaining the existing currency board and exchange rate parity. This position was confirmed by the previous government with the three pre-accession economic programmes it submitted to the European Commission. The current government also confirmed in its 2005-2008 pre-accession economic programme the countrys consistent strategy since 2000 of joining ERM II and the euro area. The consistency and continuity in the policy pursued by three consecutive governments, elected by constituent elements of the electorate with different political orientation, provide an extremely good basis for the operation of the remaining public institutions, including the BNB. The predictability of public institutions policies underlies the decisions made by households and companies, as well as by foreign investors. Based on the consistent stance of all Bulgarian governments, in 2004 the Bulgarian National Bank adopted its strategy for the development until 2009, which outlines the necessary institutional policy that would facilitate the preparations and the successful accession to the euro area. In addition to it, in the same year the government and the central bank signed an agreement aimed only at the introduction of the euro in Bulgaria in the shortest possible horizon. And I would again reiterate the publicly announced principles outlined in the countrys strategy for achieving EMU membership: Joining the Exchange Rate Mechanism II (ERM II) in the shortest possible timeframes after the date of Bulgarias official EU membership. Maintaining the currency board regime to the time of joining the euro area at the existing level of fixed parity of the exchange rate of the Bulgarian lev to the euro of 1.95583; Unilateral commitment by the Bulgarian government and the BNB to maintain a zero deviation of the exchange rate from the fixed level (i.e. keeping up to the current policy of preserving the currency board); Comply with the minimum term set forth in the acquis for participation in ERM II and proceed in a timely manner with all the necessary steps of the procedure for joining the euro area. The Agreement between the BNB and the government on the policy pursued for EMU membership significantly reduced the uncertainty with regard to the macroeconomic policy, thus creating an atmosphere of predictability and facilitating the entrepreneurs and households planning process. Incidentally, in their effort to initiate a discussion on the rationality of the countrys euro area accession strategy, some economists (both in the country and in the EU Member States) made reference to the newly acceded Member States, which have different strategies. The information about other countries strategies is very interesting and useful, but our plans should take into consideration what is useful for Bulgaria in particular and should be based on the specifics and potential of our economy. With regard to euro area membership, Bulgarian economy has a number of advantages compared to most of the new Member States, which advantages underlie the policy pursued. I will outline in short the main specifics of Bulgarian economy, which determine the appropriateness of our strategy: The presently pursued economic policy, based on the synthesis of macroeconomic stability and relatively rapid process of real convergence enjoys high credibility. The confidence is to a great extent based on the intention voiced by the government and the central bank to maintain the currency board arrangement until the country joins the euro area, and to keep to the timeframes set and the measures implemented. We have paid a high price for this credibility since 1997, and not only should it not be squandered, it should be strengthened in stead. For almost a whole decade, the country's economic policy is consistent with the Stability and Growth Pact (in terms of fiscal policy and government debt) and to a great extent to the Lisbon Strategy (in terms of structural policies, the policies of encouraging participation in the labour market and employment). These are founding economic policy principles for the Union, with which no compromise is permissible. Since the introduction of the currency board in Bulgaria and the establishment of the euro area the ECB monetary policy has largely determined the monetary conditions in our country, and with the acceleration of the integration processes following our accession to the EU this influence will grow. As a result, our membership in ERM II, followed by euro area membership, will not lead to any essential change in the conditions in which our economy operates. Bulgaria's economy is in an ascending phase of development. This momentum and dynamism should be used to expand the structural reforms and implement a prudent fiscal policy. We cannot disclaim that this is a very difficult policy, as in times of quick economic growth and high budget revenues a wishful and populist policy could take the upper hand of common sense. Yet, here exactly the role of economic policy makers in the country comes into play. I hope they will not let us down. The last but not the least advantage is that we currently comply with all the Maastricht criteria but one - the inflation rate. Dear Ladies and Gentlemen, My next message is that the macroeconomic policy and rates of economic growth achieved over the last years do not automatically lead to a future real convergence in the fiscal policy area and the reduction of inflation rates to levels that meet the Maastricht criterion. The success of the policy pursued depends on identifying the weak areas in the Bulgarian economy and conducting a purposeful policy to rectify them. Every country's economy is a complex system influenced by a number of internal and external factors. Bulgaria is a small and open economy and a large part of these factors are outside the direct control of the people and institutions conducting the economic policy. Still, does this mean that we should get discouraged and allow ourselves to be carried along by the tide? Of course not! I'd rather avoid the experience of the "best performers" from the so-called Vishegrad Four, which after May 2004 did not only stop reforms, but stepped back in their performance in many respects. The bitter fruits of such policy are being reaped by the entire population of these countries. What we are required to do is identify and address the issues that we directly or indirectly control in such a way so as to warrant the creation of an economic environment that leads to stability and higher economic income. Without trying to be exhaustive, I will mention some of the key areas where improvement can and should be sought: The level of productivity in the economy. The current level is around 30 % of that in the EU. The regulatory and educational policy in the country, as well as the policy related to the investment environment, should be oriented towards improving the incentives for investment in physical and human capital and enhancing productivity in the economy. The only factor that will guarantee to the public higher incomes in the medium term, while preserving price stability, is the increase of productivity. Competitiveness of the Bulgarian economy. In the last years, our analysis was entirely focused on the competition of the sectors of the economy, which produce tradable goods and the possibility of these sectors to compete on the international markets. This is a very important segment of the Bulgarian economy; however, the experience shows that the competition in sectors producing non-tradable goods and services is also of great significance. On the one hand, the lack of competition leads to higher prices of the goods and services in these sectors, which directly affects the inflation rates in the country, the purchasing power of the public and its perception of social development (a typical example is the production and distribution of electricity and heat). On the other hand, the firms producing tradable goods often use as intermediate products goods and services from the non-tradable sector, which often affects their competitiveness on the international markets. Ensuring a high level of competition in all sectors of the economy is an essential precondition to uphold our competitiveness, fulfil the inflation criteria and improve the well being of the whole society. Participation of Bulgarians on the labour market. It is more than clear to each and every one of us that unless we are economically active and highly productive, we could not expect that our incomes would approximate those of the EU member-states. Unfortunately, the labour market data in the country suggest a very low level of economic activity in society. Many factors could be decisive here  the qualification of the labour force and the incentives for training and re-training; a social policy encouraging economic activities and not just the passive receipt of benefits from the state; a tax policy stimulating the official employment of staff instead of hiding labour costs because of the high labour taxes. The behaviour of households and companies is determined by the incentives offered by both the internal environment, including the regulatory framework, and the external environment. Therefore, any economic policy which distorts the incentives for economic activities is doomed to fail. Before summarizing, I would like to point out a very important aspect of the implementation of an economic policy. In todays world the small and open economies are affected by numerous factors, and only some of these are under the governments direct control. This fact, however, does not imply that we should immediately take a passive position and refrain from acting, saying as an excuse that we only control very few of these factors. On the contrary, we should follow the opposite thinking. Knowing that a very small number of factors is under our control, we should do all we could to manage what is under our control in the best possible way. This is the only way to keep the confidence that has already been built in the Bulgarian economy. These should be the fundamental principles of our policy towards the coming integration into the EU economy and the euro area. We should do an impeccable job of all that depends on us. And one more thing. When speaking about the comparable advantages of the Bulgarian economy, we forget to mention one very important advantage of our country, i.e. over the past ten years we have learnt to carry out reforms and to get adapted to the fast changing external environment. Just for comparison, many EU countries cannot find a solution how to restore the dynamism and impetus for changes in their society. They lack the social and political will for changes, and the Euro is blamed for all the difficulties. Luckily, the desire for changes and resurgence has deep roots in our society and we should keep this momentum and channel it towards improving the welfare of the entire society. You understand very well that the continuity that I described in the policy of three consecutive governments and of the BNB in terms of Bulgarias accession to the euro area being the macroeconomic policys top priority is not accidental. It is a well-known fact that the macroeconomic policy oriented towards price and fiscal stability after 1997 is and will be the basis of economic growth and the increased public welfare. Bulgarias accession to the euro area would give additional impetus to our economy, eliminating some of the potential macroeconomic risks (domestic and foreign debt in foreign currency, the BoP current account deficit), which would increase the scope of freedom of those implementing the macroeconomic policy. Furthermore, our participation in the euro area would speed up the process of real convergence that is the basis for increasing our societys welfare. I have already mentioned that all of us here should not only devise the strategies that are of benefit to our economy. We should also put these strategies into practice and thus the improvements in peoples lives will become a reality. Once we have come to the conclusion that Bulgarias accession to the euro area is a priority of the macroeconomic policy, then the governments policies outlined in the strategic documents that it presented to the European Commission  the Convergence Programme, the National Programme for Reforms, the National Reference Framework  should support the major objectives of successfully joining the ERM II and later the euro area. We cannot afford to waste our limited resources in pursuing many, and sometimes contradicting, objectives. This is my third and last message to this conference. Thank you for your attention. Title: Speech in front of a seminar for journalists "Integrity and development of the financial system: communication challenges", organized jointly by the BNB, the FSC and the FSVB with the support of USAID/FSIP, Bankya, November 24-25, 2006.
text: Speech by Mr. Ivan Iskrov, Manager of the BNB, in front of a seminar for journalists "Integrity and development of the financial system: communication challenges", organized jointly by the BNB, the FSC and the FSVB with the support of USAID/FSIP, Bankya, 24-25 November 2006. COMMUNICATIONBETWEEN THE BNB AND SOCIETY  WHY WE NEED TO ADAPT AND LEARN Dear ladies and gentlemen, Today's seminar is held as part of the U.S. Development Agency's (USAID) Project "Financial Sector Integrity". Within the framework of the project, technical assistance is provided to the regulatory authorities of the financial sector  the Bulgarian National Bank (BNB), the Bank Deposit Guarantee Fund (NGVB) and the Financial Supervision Commission (FSC). supervisory authorities to thank USAID for their support. The issue of communication between supervisory authorities, financial intermediaries and the general public has become very important since the early 1990s. With the liberalisation of financial intermediation, the information link between supervisors, financial intermediaries and the public is also possible. If we look back in time (e.g. in the 1970s and 1980s) we will see that when it comes to communication, the key word is "secrecy". Today, when talking about communication between financial regulators , and central banks in particular, keywords are 'transparency' and 'accountability'. The change in the way central banks communicate is determined by a number of factors, but two of them are crucial. Firstly, this is the fact that central banks around the world have been given a much greater degree of independence in the conduct of their policy (mainly monetary and financial stability policy). whendecision-makers are not directly chosen by the people, but their decisions affect the life of the individual, they need to give more information about their work, the way in which decisions are made and the arguments that underpin these decisions. european and global practices. This of course requires an adequate level of transparency and communicationwith society. Secondly, the main factor in changing the way of communication is purely economic. With significant liberalisation of financial markets, the best way to ensure their effective operation is for regulators and, privately, central banks to provide the maximum amount of information to market participants. This is the standard argument from economic theory that, when they have sufficient information, market participants make rational decisions. (a) defining importance for the communication policy of the Bulgarian financial regulators, given the strong openness of the Bulgarian economy, the large influx of capital and the dominant role of foreign investors in the capital of our banking system. I would now like to address the extent to which these global factors affect the BNB and how we respond to these developments. First of all, I would like to point out that I, as governor of the BNB, have always placed a very high emphasis on transparent decision-making and the timely and complete communication of these decisions with the financial community and society as a whole. To base this statement, I will quote two passages from my first speech as Governor of the BNB to the Association of Commercial Banks in December 2003. "It is very important for society to understandthe central bank's olytics and actions not only in terms of having legitimacy given the high degree of independence of the institution, but also in terms of the effectiveness of this policy. The more society-friendlythe principles on which central bank policy is based, the more effective this policy is. It is no coincidence that since the early 1990s there has been an increasing talk of central banking as a policy of managing expectations of economic agents and financial markets. principles and expected effects ofthis policy. The central bank's communication policy will be further developed so as to be understandable to the maximum part of society. Special attention will be paid to communication between the BNB and the banking community as a whole. TheCentral Bank will follow a uniform policy with regard to commercial banks, without having a discriminatory approach in terms of size and ownership of capital. As is well known, effective communication requires efforts from all parties involved in this process. In order for the central bank to take adequate account of the interests of commercial banks, the ATB must be able to generate and present to the BNB a single and consistent position expressing the preferences of the banking community." It is often said that it is not how many good ideas you have had, but how good ideas you have realized. For this reason, I would like to present two statistics which unambiguously show the radical change in the communication policy ofthe BNB in 2003. (see Graph 1 and 2.). The data are indicative that for the period 2004 - October 2006 the BNB issued 2.3 times more press releases and the manager and sub-managers made 2.8 times more public speeches and speeches than were the six-year p eryod from 1998 to 2003. At the heart of the policy change regarding the issuing of press releases is the changed approach to informing the general public and banking institutions about changes in the bank's policy and of regulations affecting the b anchovies industry and the individual consumer of financial services. and no one receives an information advantage. In terms of officialpublications, the bank's policy has also changed. One of the main publications, Commercial Banks in Bulgaria, has been expanded, with an analytical part added to the pure statistics, which gives the bank an assessment of the state of the banking system in the specific quarter. policy of the bank, as well as the opportunity for each of you to form your own position on the state of the banking industry. In the same direction of development was the establishment since the beginning of 2004 of the new quarterly publication of the BNB  "Economic Review". The purpose of this publication is to inform the public about the view and analysis of the BNB with regard to the development of the national economy and the international environment, as well as to outline the expectations of the Bank for the development of the Bulgarian economy in the short and medium term. Another novelty in the BNB's communication policy, which I consider essential, is the change in the way economic statistics are provided by the bank to users of this information. Until 2004, the bank had a practice of offering a paid subscription for electronic transmission of statistics, with subscribers receiving the data before they were available on the BNB website. The current statistical disclosure regime treats all users equally. Speaking to this audience, I am very aware that your natural reaction is that the central bank can communicate even more intensively with the media. However, I am deeply convinced that, with regard to print and electronic media, the BNB is considerablymore open and willing to explain the policy that we have followed. Moreover, the process of integration of the country into the EU has inevitably increased the interest of the international media in the work of the BNB. My personal experience from this year has shown that that media of international importance (Reuters, Bloomberg, Wall Street Journal, NIKKEI, Forbes) sought interviews with the governor and the bank's sub-managers. This is a new and essential part of the bank's communication policy. As we join the EU, there will be much more interest from our partners (other central banks) in our work, as well as in the European public. As an example, I can point to the invitation in the middle of this year from my colleague from the Greek central bank to give a public speech on the state and prospects for the Bulgarian economy. Our understanding is that we at the central bank must constantly accumulate new knowledge, but also to present thisknowledge to journalists reflecting our work, and through them to the whole society. The journalistswere also accredited for the press conference of the President of the ECB  Mr Trichet, who has been to Bulgaria twice this year and you had the opportunity from him to get directly information on a number of issues of interest to you. This autumn, the BNB also organized a meeting of journalistsat the European Investment Bank, one of the key international institutions for the further external financing of projects in the country. Expanding citizens' knowledge of the rapidlychanging financial services sector is primarily the task of those providing these services, but the BNB, as a public institution, is also taking initiatives in this area. payment services. This brochure we have issued to help promote the Conciliation Commission for Payment Disputes  this is one body involving the Consumer Protection Commission, the Association of Commercial Banks and is chaired by a judge appointed by the BNB. The purpose of the Conciliation Committee is to resolve out-of-court disputes between banks and their customers in connection with the provision of payment services. To expand communication activities, next year we provide communication seminars for journalists with the participation of lecturers from the European Central Bank, the European Commission and other institutions. Today's seminar for me is part of the BNB'sunceasing efforts to improve, on the one hand, the understanding of the role and policy of the central bank and, on the other hand, of us policy-making, how print and electronic media interpret our actions. that we will have a useful and fruitful discussion.
