Title: Speech before the Bulgarian Association of Commercial Banks, Sofia, 4 December 2006
text: Speech of Mr. Ivan Iskrov, Governor of the BNB, before the Bulgarian Association of Commercial Banks, Sofia, 4 December 2006 Ladies and Gentlemen, I am extremely pleased to be with you today to celebrate together the Bankers Day. As the Governor of the Bulgarian National Bank, I will celebrate with you the Bankers day for a fourth year in a row. But today's holiday has an atmosphere of its own, quite different from all previous ones. We are on the verge of a new era in our countrys history  the accession of the Republic of Bulgaria into united Europe. What Prince Boris Michail did with the adoption, and in some cases the enforcement, of Christianity and the Slav alphabet is happening again after a period of more than 1100 years. From 1 January 2007, Bulgaria will not just be a member of the European Union (EU). On 1 January Bulgaria will take its due place as part of the European civilization, to which we have always spiritually and culturally belonged in spite of the vicissitudes of history. We all have the great chance to have been born, and to be living and working in a historic time of our countrys development. Of course, this reunion with Europe did not happen on its own. The Bulgarian institutions and our whole society made significant efforts to make this accession happen. I am proud that Bulgarian bankers were and are in the front line of change. There is no other part of Bulgarian economy that is more prepared and more integrated into the European economy than the banking system. This evening I will follow the tradition and outline what has been achieved in this year and what are the challenges we will face in the coming one. The current year was very successful for the national economy, and in particular for the banking sector. The information to date indicates that in 2006 we will achieve the highest rate of economic growth since the beginning of economic reform in the country, and our expectations are that this high growth rate will probably be outpaced in 2007. The speeded-up growth in the current year was generated by the approaching full-fledged EU membership of Bulgaria and the accompanying mass inflow of foreign investment into the country. Unemployment ebbed below 10% and was kept at a sustainable one-digit level  a development not seen for more than 10 years. Employment and households income continued to grow which, combined with the intensifying investment activity in the economy, provided a very good environment for the development of the banking sector. As a natural outcome of the high investment activity and the strong capital inflow, the countrys external position stabilized around the level reached in the year past. The relatively high level of the current account deficit requires on-going efforts at increasing the competitiveness of our economy, but the very nature of the deficit, and the manner of its financing (more than 100% foreign direct investment) indicate that it has no destabilizing impact on the countrys economy. The favourable external and domestic economic environment provides a good basis for banking sector growth while preserving its stability Compared to the previous year, in 2006 we expect the balance of the banking sector to grow by 22% up to BGN 40 bill. Profit will probably reach BGN 700 mill., thus marking a 20% growth against 2005. In spite of the increasing competition in the credit market, the preserved levels of interest rates on loans and the increased cost of attracted funds, the return on assets (ROA) in the banking system is kept at the 2005 level (2.05%). The return on equity (ROE) has also stabilized at the levels reached in 2005 (22.1%). For the sake of comparison, in the EU-25 these indicators are 1.2% return on assets and 16% return on equity, respectively. After the categorical interference of the BNB, from the second half of 2005, the rates at which commercial banks attracted resources from abroad decreased, thus the banks net foreign assets became positive. This trend was also preserved in 2006, primarily due to the effect of the extended administrative regulation of credit growth, which forced commercial banks to curb credit growth, and some of them to sell part of their credit portfolios. In 2006, commercial banks managed to preserve the quality of their portfolios, and even the share of performing loans increased slightly from 92.3% at end-2005 to 92.5% as of September 2006. The continued measures aimed at curbing the growth rate of credit to the private sector, and the increase in some banks capital throughout the year allowed for preserving the capital adequacy of the system at a level near to the 2005 one. At the end of October 2006, the capital adequacy of the banking system was 15.21%, against 15.17% at end-2005. Maintaining good financial results and stability were accompanied by the successful introduction of many new products and services. BNBs Policy towards the operation of the banking industry was consistent, predictable, and co-operative In the passing 2006, BNB continued pursuing a transparent and consistent policy towards the banking industry. All central banks decisions were carefully discussed with and properly communicated to the Association of Commercial Banks (ATB). I believe that our consistent efforts to create an atmosphere of predictability of BNBs activities are gaining further success. In practice, the signals of the central bank were properly understood, and the tendency of previous years of misconstruing BNBs intentions was a rare exception in 2006. In this year, the main efforts were aimed at pursuing the already established policy of maintaining the stability of the banking system, including through maintaining certain restrictions curbing banking credit. The BNB has already adopted the changes through which the administrative restrictions on banking credit growth will be removed from the beginning of the next year. As we repeatedly underscored, the elimination of this measure should not be viewed as a change in the central banks position regarding the need of keeping to moderate rates of credit growth. In case of an abrupt upward trend of banking credit growth in 2007, the BNB would, without any hesitation, use the tools at its disposal to curb any such development. In 2006 we managed, together with the other public institutions and the ATB to prepare and adopt in a timely manner some key regulatory acts governing the operation of the banking industry  the Credit Institutions Law, the Law on the Supplementary Supervision of Financial Conglomerates, the Consumer Credit Law. In practice, we are ready with all the ordinances and regulations ensuing from the changes in the legal framework. From the beginning of 2007, the banking community will be able with no difficulties to tune its work to the new regulatory environment. This year, thanks to the good interaction between the banking community and the BNB, we successfully introduced the international format of bank accounts (IBAN). The successful implementation of a project of this magnitude, involving a significant number of participants, indicated that there is a good synchronization/synergy in the operation of the central bank, other public institutions, and the financial sector. In 2006, in the area of currency circulation, the BNB started actively implementing the strategy it adopted to guarantee the required level of currency purity, and the security, and efficiency of issue and cash operations within the country. With the adoption of Ordinance No. 18 on the Control of the Quality of the Currency in Circulation, the BNB set the general framework for the organization of the currency circulation, which is fully compliant with the ECB standards. We would not lack challenges in the coming year too The new year 2007, with the exception that it is very special for us, will not differ from previous years in the need of hard work for overcoming multiple challenges that we are going to face. The Bulgarian financial market becomes part of the single European financial services market. As I already mentioned, I believe we are well prepared and we have the experience in integration, and good competitive positions. Inevitably, however, the participation in the single European market will bring about certain changes in the manner of operation of the Bulgarian financial sector. The accession process imposed some significant changes in the regulatory framework of the banking sector. Two new laws will become effective from the beginning of 2007  The Credit Institutions Law, and the Law on the Supplementary Supervision of Financial Conglomerates. At this stage of development of the countrys financial sector, the latter will have limited effect. The Credit Institutions Law, however, introduces a number of amendments, which will result in some changes in the operation of the banking sector and the BNB. It is sufficient to mention the rule of the single banking passport, the extended framework of supervisory corrective and rehabilitation measures, and the implementation of the new capital requirements, known as Basel II. The principle of single banking passport introduces a free access for EU credit institutions into the Bulgarian banking market, which will have its impact on the central banks licensing policy. We have to admit that with its extremely conservative policy in terms of licensing new banks in the recent years the BNB strongly assisted the commercial banks in the process of attracting strategic partners. It is another issue, to what extent they could avail of this policy. The most important change will come with the new Capital Adequacy Ordinance No. 8. Its provisions entail very important elements  both for the commercial banks financial capacity, and for their technological, procedural, and staffing capabilities. The successful implementation of the new capital adequacy ordinance faces the central bank, too, with a serious challenge. In addition to the amendments to the regulatory framework, we have also forthcoming an overall redesigning of the supervision reporting. In the coming year, banks will have to submit reporting forms from the FINREP package (for financial reporting), and COREP one (for capital requirement reporting) to the Committee of European Banking Supervisors. This change is part of the EU long-term plan of convergence of regulatory and supervision regimes in the Member States. The actual accession of the domestic credit institutions to the common EU financial services market cannot be treated as a one-off act, which would be effected in the night of 31 December 2006 to 1 January 2007. The integration of the domestic banking sector has started and has been successfully developing in the recent 10 years. We are all aware, that we should not expect any abrupt changes in the operation of the banking sector. Nevertheless, banks operating in the Bulgarian market should be ready to face the competition of EU institutions, which will continue forcing them towards more versatile services offered at lower prices. Further to this, the capital potential of each bank will be more important than ever, not only because of the new capital requirements, but also due to its key role in the long-term positioning, development, and coping with the challenges of competition. In the recent two years, we made considerable efforts to find, in cooperation with the commercial banks, an effective solution for the organization of currency circulation, that would work for the banking community and for the society as a whole. Since the implementation of this task is an important priority for the BNB, we cannot allow ourselves too long a period of consultations, and not particularly effective negotiations. We have achieved some progress to date, but we need the final impetus to bring this project into fruition. Commercial banks should express clearly, and shortly too, their commitment to the joint project, otherwise the BNB will launch the implementation of an alternative project, which excludes any participation of the banking industry. The BNB Governing Council has already made a decision, and has started the construction of a new cash center. After year 2008, the cash center will be the only place where the BNB will offer the free cash services regulated by the ECB. All other services will be offered on market-oriented basis. Pursuing a policy of saving ones skin on solo basis not only would be unwise, it would be rather too expensive for all commercial banks and for their customers. Before concluding, I would like to pay special attention to the issue of the relations between commercial banks and banking services consumers. The BNBs active participation in the process of designing the Consumer Credit Law, and our support for the institutional strengthening of the Conciliation Board are indicative of the attention paid by the central bank to this issue. Better awareness of banking services consumers with regard to the credit price and the risks coming as consequence of debt accumulation is a guarantee for both achieving equality in the contracting process between the two parties, and for preserving the stability of the banking system. The sales of banking services and products should not, and cannot be treated in the same way as selling household appliances. This is not a good banking practice, and may develop a wrong attitude to their personal liability in the process of obtaining and servicing a bank loan. As I have often mentioned, it is in the interest of both consumers and the banking industry to establish between the two sides of the process long-term relations based on transparency of financial services pricing, and on the strict observance of obligations by both parties. And at the end of my speech, allow me, on behalf of the BNB Governing Council and on by own behalf, to wish you health and lots of success  in your family life and in the banks you manage  in the coming year 2007, as well as very merry Christmas and New Year festivities. Thank you for the attention. PAGE PAGE 3

Title: Speech delivered during the official visit at the Deutsche Bundesbank, 20 December 2006
Subtitle:
BULGARIAN ECONOMY ON THE ROAD TO
EUROPEAN UNION AND ECONOMIC AND MONETARY UNION
text: Speech of Mr. Ivan Iskrov, Governor of the BNB, delivered during the official visit at the Deutsche Bundesbank, 20 December 2006 BULGARIAN ECONOMY ON THE ROAD TO EUROPEAN UNION AND ECONOMIC AND MONETARY UNION Dear Mr. President of Deutsche Bundesbank, Ladies and Gentlemen, First of all, please let me express my most sincere thanks to President Weber for this invitation and for the opportunity to speak today, a few days before Bulgaria joins the family of the European Union. Today I would like to talk about the condition of the Bulgarian economy, the development of the financial sector, and Bulgarias economic prospects. I know very well that my audience today is very special. Bundesbank is the central bank that has been and will be fundamental to the philosophy of price and macroeconomic stability consistently followed both in Germany and in United Europe. The strong historical connection between Germany and Bulgaria Todays meeting is extremely important to me also because of the fact that between Germany and Bulgaria, and between our banks, there have always been very strong ties based on mutual respect and good cooperation. The relations of Bulgaria and the Bulgarian National Bank with Germany and the German banking system were established as early as 1879, immediately after the liberation of Bulgaria and the foundation of the BNB. In the period from 1879 to 1944 the BNB and the Bulgarian banking system went on strengthening their relations with Germany. The BNB signed the first two agreements on the extension of foreign loans with Deutsche Bank and Dresdner Bank in 1889 and 1893. In the early 20th century the first subsidiaries and branches of German banks were set up in Bulgaria, and they continued their operations until 1949. In the late 19th century and the early 20th century the BNB and Reichsbank had a very close cooperation. The end of the Second World War, the establishment of a pro-Soviet socialist regime in Bulgaria, and the existence of the Iron Curtain in Europe considerably constrained the economic ties between Bulgaria and Germany. The dramatic political changes in Europe after 1989, the removal of the Berlin Wall, and the subsequent EU enlargement were favourable conditions and made possible the strengthening of the good economic relations between Germany and Bulgaria. The productive interaction between the economies of Germany and Bulgaria was continued and was given new incentives by the start of the economic reforms in the early 1990s. From the very beginning of the transition Germany became the biggest trading partner of our country, reaching, in 2005, a 12.1% share of Bulgarias foreign trade. Over the last few years, German investments have been increasing and we expect that this process would carry on and even speed up after Bulgaria becomes a full-fledged member of the EU. Current macroeconomic policy framework In order to understand the way that the Bulgarian economy has developed since 1989 one should know the starting conditions of the Bulgarian transition. I will not go into details on the characteristics of the transition from a centrally-planned to a market economy. However, I would like to point out an important fact which largely distinguishes Bulgaria from the other Central European countries. This is the fact that the Bulgarian society could not, as quickly as the other Central European countries, reach a consensus and set its priorities. Therefore, we did not carry out prompt and effective market reforms. For various reasons (mostly the lack of political will and consensus) the restructuring was delayed and we paid a high price for this  a long period of stagnation and macroeconomic instability. In the mid 1990s our country fell into a profound political, economic and financial crisis which eroded the savings of the population and undermined the confidence in public institutions. But crises, as we know from both the Bulgarian and the German economic history, bring a new impetus which triggers large-scale economic reforms. The most important thing about Bulgarias economic policy after 1997 is the drastic change in the philosophy that underlies the macroeconomic governance of the country. The new culture of stability, predictability and lasting sustainability is the foundation of the economic reforms in Bulgaria. This has been the driving force behind the high economic growth, foreign investors confidence, and the increasing prosperity in our society. In order to overcome deep economic and political crisis, in mid 1997, Bulgaria adopted a monetary policy based on currency board arrangements. The Bulgarian Lev was pegged to the Deutsche Mark (and from 1 January 1999 to the Euro) and the BNB was banned to lend to the government and commercial banks in whatever form. There was a period of painful adjustment of economic agents  a process that is well-known to and even ongoing in some of the Euro area countries. Today, 10 years later, the currency board symbolizes stability, predictability and sustainability of Bulgarias economic policy. At the time when the currency board was introduced the US Dollar was the foreign currency that dominated our foreign trade. The population and the companies definitely preferred the dollar for their savings. The choice of the Deutsche Mark (the Euro respectively) as the reserve currency stemmed from the political consensus for EU accession. A country with a currency board in place is viewed as mechanically importing the monetary policy and confidence of the country, or area, to whose currency it has pegged its national monetary unit. This, of course, is true but only to some extent. Confidence can be credited, but only for a while. Ultimately, confidence must be built by a consistent and prudent policy. Therefore, giving up an autonomous monetary policy would require a fiscal policy oriented towards supporting the fixed-exchange-rate regime and carrying out structural reforms that would enhance the flexibility and competitiveness of the economy. The fiscal policy systematically conducted since1997, based on a balanced budget or a budget surplus reduced the government debt to levels much lower than the criterion of the European Union. This significantly improved Bulgarias credit rating, decreased the sovereign spread and the cost of credit, and provided better investment opportunities. The sound macroeconomic policy and the structural policies aimed at privatization of state-owned enterprises and liberalization of markets inevitably brought about significant changes in the real economy. Since 1997 our economy has been growing at relatively high rates  5% on average. The growth sped up in the last two years due to the microeconomic reforms and the forthcoming accession of the county to the European Union. The macroeconomic stability, privatization, and liberalization of the economy, and the high degree of predictability of the policy pursued, provided far better incentives for investing in Bulgaria. Between 1999 and 2005 the amount of FDIs on an average annual basis was 8.5 % of GDP. Only about one third of these investments came from privatization deals. These massive inflows of capital largely accelerated over the last 3 years as a result of the favourable international situation and Bulgarias approaching membership in the EU. As an outcome, investments began to increase faster and their share in the GDP structure went up to 33% over the first three quarters of 2006  the highest level since the start of the economic reforms. The high levels of investments certainly increased labour productivity and, along with a moderate increase in wages and unit labour costs, helped our exports to remain competitive and the country to keep on attracting direct investments. At the same time the more intense economic activities were accompanied by stable growth rates of employment and a parallel decrease in unemployment. The higher disposable household income generated by the increased employment and wages was the initial spur to a stable growth rate of consumption in the economy. Subsequently, this effect was reinforced by the rapid development of the banking sector and the improved access of households to lending. The easier access to the credit market, coupled with decreasing interest rates due to Bulgarias better credit rating and the global excess liquidity over the last 3 years, led to reduced household savings and increased consumption. The lower levels of savings by households and companies resulting from the increased consumption and investment inevitably gave rise to a deficit on the BoP current account. Challenges facing the policy-makers As a result the current account deficit increased, reaching levels of more than 5% from the GDP in 2003 and 2004, and increased even further to 11.3% at the end of 2005. It is expected to reach 13.9% of the GDP in 2006. Current account deficits have a high level of inertia, which presupposes that the shrinking of the external imbalance of the country will be a gradual process. In addition, the economy of Bulgaria is in its initial stage of convergence, suggesting an accelerated investment growth and inflow of capital for a longer period of time. As I have already mentioned, during the last few years the country received a substantial inflow of capital and the banking system was the natural intermediary in its effective distribution. This does not come as a surprise, having in mind the successful privatization and restructuring of the banking sector in Bulgaria. At present, 99.7% of the banking sector is private, and nearly 85% of the banks in the country are owned by foreign investors  most of them from Euro area member states. Due to the strong competition and good investment opportunities the growth of the private sector lending reached levels as high as 48.6% at the end of 2004. Only for a few years the ratio between the banking credit to the GDP increased from 12.1% in 1999 to 46.0% at the end of September 2006. To minimize inherent risks from the beginning of 2004, the BNB started a process of gradual implementation of measures (mainly supervisory and administrative) which aimed at diminishing the growth rates of banking credits, down to stable levels, which do not jeopardise the stability of the economy. The data indicate a slower growth of banking credit - 23.4% as of September 2006. We do not envisage a considerable and fast credit growth in 2007. The debt burden accumulated during the last few years, as well as the monetary policy tightening in the Euro area will curb credit to a great extent. The Prospects of the Bulgarian Economy By signing the Accession Treaty with the EU, Bulgaria has committed itself to join the Euro area and to adopt the single currency. The current EU legislation does not give member states the right of an opt-out clause for their membership in the EMU. This means that the decision which our country will need to make is not whether to join the EMU and to introduce the single currency, but how it is going to be done and in what time period. Regarding the introduction of the single currency, Bulgaria and in particular the BNB, have always had a consistent, long-term policy. This policy is determined by the existing currency board arrangements and their broad national and political support. Having in mind the governing principles of the state policy and the requirements of the acquis communautaire in 2004 the government and the BNB signed an agreement, aiming at the only logical decision - to introduce the Euro in Bulgaria in the shortest possible time horizon, conditional on fulfilment of the Maastricht criteria. The document outlines the following basic principles of EMU membership: Joining the Exchange Rate Mechanism II (ERM II) as soon as possible after Bulgarias official accession to the EU. Keeping the currency board until Bulgaria joins the Euro area, with the current exchange rate of the Bulgarian Lev to the Euro - 1.95583 for Euro. A unilateral commitment of the Bulgarian government and the BNB to maintain a zero fluctuation of the exchange rate from the fixed level. Meeting the minimum period set in the EU legislation for participation in the ERM II and taking in time all the necessary steps of the procedure for membership in the Euro zone. The time horizon for meeting the Maastricht criteria is determined by the state of fiscal preparedness and inflation convergence. Very often nominal and real convergence processes are wrongly perceived as two mutually exclusive goals. We believe that the competent combination of fiscal, structural and regulatory policies that would encourage competition on a microeconomic level can bring about a quicker real convergence while simultaneously achieving the nominal criteria. The aspiration for Euro area membership has dimensions that go far beyond the domestic economic and political aspects. From an economic perspective the adoption of the single currency is in itself the ultimate stage of the European economic integration. All national governments in their pursuit of multiple political and economic goals are often faced with contradictory objectives. Sometimes populist and short-term goals seem to supersede the main long-term ones. Therefore, the states that manage to follow a sound macroeconomic policy favouring Euro adoption set a positive example to those member states whose policy deviates from stability and long-term sustainability objectives. The political will in itself is not sufficient, but extremely necessary precondition for Euro adoption. I highly appreciate the fact that Germany has laid down in its programme for EU presidency next year that it will support the member states in their aspiration for Euro area membership. Moreover, each country will obtain a prompt and detailed assessment regarding ERM II membership and Euro adoption. I believe that this is the only prudent approach that guarantees equal treatment to all member states. All member states  both present and prospective  are responsible for the sustainability of the EMU. This sustainability favours their own interests. Bulgaria is now ready to contribute to this global aim. In the past 5 years we have fulfilled all Maastricht criteria, except for the one on inflation. We envisage to maintain this consistency in the years to come. Our efforts will be directed at curbing inflation to the compliant level. Today Bulgaria already meets 4 out of 5 Maastricht criteria and we believe that our strategy for ERM II participation as soon as possible we be fully supported by the German presidency. Our state of preparedness could be assessed by the fact that even though no preconditions for ERM II entry are required, Bulgaria has committed to proving its capacity by sustainably meeting 4 out of 5 Maastricht criteria. This provides us with the confidence that we will be a full- fledged member of the EMU at the beginning of next decade. Following the current policy of balanced budget, with a surplus if possible, will enable us to continue meeting the Maastricht criteria in terms of budget deficit, government debt and long-term interest rates, and will also make the macroeconomic policy more responsive and flexible. It is well known that under a currency board arrangements, the fiscal policy is the only tool available for a relatively quick response to adverse developments in the economy of the country. Furthermore, in order for us to have this flexibility with the growing current account deficit and rapidly increasing private debt, in periods like this when the economy is growing at rates close to or a little above the long-term growth rates, the budget needs to compensate by generating a sufficient surplus. The tough fiscal policy is needed also because it will help us comply with the inflation criterion. Operating under a currency board arrangements, the central bank has no direct control of inflation rates in the country. Given the current trend of price levels in the new member-states converging to the levels in the old member-states (a result of the well-known Balassa-Samuelson effect), this criterion is a challenge not just for the countries with a currency board in place, but also for all countries with price levels lower than the average in the EU. In the particular case of Bulgaria where a fixed exchange rate regime is in place together with a very conservative fiscal policy, reserves should be looked for in promoting the competition and improving the business environment so that the economy would have greater flexibility to respond to both external and internal challenges. In 2006, we expect an average inflation rate of 7.2 %. The main factors driving inflation at the present moment are the increase of excise duties on alcoholic beverages and tobacco. In 2007, we foresee the declining trend from the second half of 2006 to continue and our forecast is that inflation will be approximately 3.7%. Finally, I would like to express my highest appreciation of and gratitude for the steady and consistent support given by Germany and the people of Germany for the reforms in Bulgaria and especially for our accession to the EU. This support is very well known in the Bulgarian society. We do hope that this friendship and assistance will continue during Bulgarias accession to the Euro zone and afterwards. Thank you for your attention. PAGE PAGE 2

Title: Lecture delivered by the Governor of the BNB
Subtitle:
THE IMPLICATIONS OF EU MEMBERSHIP FOR BULGARIA  RECENT
ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENTS AND CHALLENGES FOR THE FUTURE
text: Lecture of Mr. Ivan Iskrov, Governor of the BNB, delivered during his official visit to the Austrian National Bank, Vienna, 27 April 2007 THE IMPLICATIONS OF EU MEMBERSHIP FOR BULGARIA  RECENT ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENTS AND CHALLENGES FOR THE FUTURE Dear Governor Liebscher, Ladies and Gentlemen, I would like first to express my sincere thanks to Governor Liebscher for the invitation extended, and the opportunity provided to me to talk on the development of the Bulgarian economy before such an esteemed audience. A few months after Bulgarias membership in the European Union, I will talk about the implications of the membership for the Bulgarian economy and medium- term prospects and challenges. In particular I will focus on our monetary regime and our strategy towards EMU. I know very well that my audience today is very well informed about the mechanism and specifics of the fixed exchange rates. In the course of EU and subsequently EMU membership the Austrian government and central bank had followed an exchange rate regime and monetary policy strategy similar to the Bulgarian one now. At that time this policy strategy was known as hard currency policy. It was successfully followed by Austria for 18 years until the countrys eventual membership in the EMU. Basically this policy strategy is now followed by countries that operate currency board regimes, namely Bulgaria, Estonia and Lithuania. Now I would like briefly to go back 10 years ago and then to the main topic of my speech today  recent economic development and future policy challenges. In mid 1997 there was a deep economic and political crisis in our country. In order to overcome it Bulgaria adopted a monetary policy based on currency board arrangements. The Bulgarian Lev was pegged to the Deutsche Mark (and since 1 January 1999 to the Euro) and the BNB was banned to lend to the government and commercial banks in whatever form. The choice of the Deutsche Mark (the Euro respectively) as the reserve currency stemmed from the political consensus for EU accession. A country with a currency board in place is viewed as mechanically importing the monetary policy and credibility of the country, or area, to whose currency it has fixed its national currency. This, of course, is true but only to some extent. As all of us know credibility can be borrowed, but only temporarily. Ultimately, credibility must be built up by following a consistent and prudent policy. Therefore, giving up an autonomous monetary policy would require a fiscal policy oriented towards supporting the fixed-exchange-rate regime and carrying out structural reforms that would enhance the flexibility and competitiveness of the economy. Thus the currency board is a very strong tool to push all policymakers to make reforms. The Bulgarian fiscal policy systematically conducted since1997, based on a balanced budget or a budget surplus reduced the government debt even to levels much lower than the criterion of the European Union. This significantly improved Bulgarias credit rating, decreased the sovereign spread and the cost of credit, and provided better investment opportunities. The sound macroeconomic policy and the structural policies aimed at privatization of state-owned enterprises and liberalization of markets inevitably brought about significant changes in the real economy. Since 1997 our economy has been growing at relatively high rates  5% on average. The growth accelerated in the last three years due to implementation of microeconomic reforms and the prospective accession of the county to the European Union. The macroeconomic stability, privatization, and liberalization of the economy, and the high degree of predictability of the policy pursued, provided far better incentives for investing in Bulgaria. Between 1999 and 2006 the amount of FDIs on an average annual basis was 10.2% of GDP. Only about one third of these investments came from privatization deals. These massive inflows of capital have accelerated significantly over the last 3 years as a result of the favourable international economic environment and Bulgarias approaching membership in the EU. As an outcome, investments began to increase faster and their share in the structure of the GDP went up to 32% in 2006  the highest level since the start of the economic reforms. The high levels of investments increased labour productivity and, along with a moderate increase in wages and unit labour costs, helped our exports to remain competitive and the country to keep on attracting direct investments. At the same time the more robust economic growth was accompanied by stable growth rates of employment and a gradual decrease in unemployment. The higher disposable household income generated by the increased employment and wages was the initial spur to a stable growth rate of consumption in the economy. Subsequently, this effect was reinforced by the rapid development of the banking sector and the improved access of households to credit. The easier access to the credit market, coupled with decreasing interest rates due to Bulgarias better credit rating and the global excess liquidity over the last several years, led to increased household consumption. The low levels of savings by households and companies accompanied by increased consumption and investment inevitably gave rise to a deficit on the balance of payment current account. As a result the current account deficit increased, reaching levels of more than 5% of GDP in 2003, and increased even further to 15.8% at the end of 2006. In 2007 the current account deficit is expected to remain at the levels reached last year. Current account deficits have a high level of inertia, which presupposes that the adjustment of the external imbalance of the country will be a gradual process. In addition, the economy of Bulgaria is in its initial stage of convergence, suggesting an accelerated investment growth and inflow of capital for a longer period of time. As I have already mentioned, during the last few years the country received a substantial inflow of capital and the banking system was the natural intermediary in its effective distribution. This does not come as a surprise, having in mind the successful privatization and restructuring of the banking sector in Bulgaria. At present, 99.7% of the banking sector is private, and nearly 85% of the banks in the country are owned by foreign investors  most of them from Euro area member states. Due to the strong competition and good investment opportunities the growth of the private sector lending reached levels as high as 48.6% at the end of 2004. Only for a few years the ratio of the bank credit to the GDP increased from 12.1% in 1999 to 47.4% at the end of 2006. To minimize inherent risks from the beginning of 2004, the BNB started a process of gradual implementation of measures (mainly supervisory and administrative) which aimed at diminishing the growth rates of banking credits, down to stable levels, which do not put at risk the stability of the financial sector and the whole economy. The data indicate deceleration of the growth rate of banking credit in 2005 and 2006 to 32.4 and 24.6 percent respectively. Notwithstanding the positive outlooks due to EU accession, we do not envisage a considerable acceleration of the credit growth in 2007. The debt burden accumulated during the last few years, as well as the monetary policy tightening in the Euro area, which has direct influence on our economy, will curb credit growth to a great extent. Economic and monetary integration By signing the Accession Treaty with the EU, Bulgaria has committed itself to join the Euro area and to adopt the single currency. The current EU legislation does not give new member states the right of an opt-out clause for their membership in the EMU. This means that our decision was not whether to join the EMU and to introduce the single currency, but how it was to be done and in what time horizon. Regarding the introduction of the single currency, Bulgaria and in particular the BNB, have always had a consistent, long-term oriented policy. This policy is determined by the existing currency board regime and its broad public and political support. Having in mind the governing principles of the state policy and the requirements of the acquis in 2004 the government and the BNB signed an agreement, aiming at the only logical decision - to introduce the Euro in Bulgaria in the shortest possible time horizon, conditional on fulfilment of the Maastricht criteria. The document outlines the following basic principles of EMU membership: 1. Joining the Exchange Rate Mechanism II (ERM II) as soon as possible. 2. Keeping the currency board until Bulgaria joins the Euro area, with the current exchange rate of the Bulgarian Lev to the Euro - 1.95583 for Euro. 3. A unilateral commitment of the Bulgarian government and the BNB to maintain a zero fluctuation of the exchange rate from the fixed level. 4. Meeting the minimum period set in the EU legislation for participation in the ERM II and taking in time all the necessary steps of the procedure for membership in the Euro zone. The time horizon for meeting the Maastricht criteria is determined by the state of fiscal preparedness and inflation convergence. Very often nominal and real convergence processes are wrongly perceived as two mutually exclusive goals. We believe that the right combination of fiscal, structural and regulatory policies that would encourage competition on a microeconomic level can bring about a quicker real convergence while simultaneously achieving the nominal criteria. The preparation for Euro area membership has dimensions that go far beyond the domestic economic and political aspects. From an economic perspective the adoption of the single currency is in itself the ultimate stage of the European economic integration. All national governments in their pursuit of multiple political and economic goals are often faced with contradictory objectives. Sometimes populist and short-term goals seem to supersede the main long-term ones. Therefore, the states that manage to follow a sound macroeconomic policy favouring Euro adoption set a positive example to those member states whose policy deviates from stability and long-term sustainability objectives. The political will in itself is not sufficient, but extremely necessary precondition not only for Euro adoption, but also for the success of the entire union. Bulgaria is now ready to contribute to this global aim. In the past 5 years we have fulfilled all Maastricht criteria, but one  the inflation criterion. We envisage to maintain this consistency in the years to come. Our efforts will be directed at curbing inflation to the compliant levels. Today Bulgaria already meets 4 out of 5 Maastricht criteria and we believe that our strategy for ERM II participation as soon as possible will be assessed without prejudice and fully supported by the other member states. Our state of preparedness could be assessed by the fact that even though no preconditions for ERM II entry are required, Bulgaria has committed to proving its capacity by sustainably meeting 4 out of 5 Maastricht criteria. This provides us with the confidence that we will be a full- fledged member of the EMU at the beginning of next decade. Following the current policy of balanced budget, with a surplus if possible, will enable us to continue meeting the Maastricht criteria in terms of budget deficit, government debt and long-term interest rates, and will also make the macroeconomic policy more responsive and flexible. It is well known that under currency board arrangements, the fiscal policy is the only tool available for a relatively quick response to adverse developments in the economy of the country. Furthermore, in order for us to have this flexibility with the growing current account deficit and increasing private debt, the budget needs to compensate by generating a sufficient surplus. The tight fiscal policy is needed also because it will help us comply with the inflation criterion. Given the current trend of price levels in the new member-states converging to the levels in the old member-states (a result of the well-known Balassa-Samuelson effect), this criterion is a challenge not just for the countries with a currency board in place, but also for all countries with price levels lower than the average in the EU. In the particular case of Bulgaria, where a fixed exchange rate regime is in place, reserves should be looked for in promoting the competition and improving the business environment as well as conducting a conservative fiscal policy. In this way the economy would have greater flexibility to respond to both external and internal challenges. In 2006 the average inflation rate was 7.4 %. The main factors that were driving inflation in the last three years are the increase of excise duties on alcoholic beverages and tobacco, adjustment of the administered prices and global increase of energy prices. In 2007, we expect the declining trend from the second half of 2006 to continue. Our forecast is that end of period inflation and average inflation will be approximately 3.7% and 4.5% respectively. Austria is a very good example for us. As I already mentioned in the beginning of my speech, Austria had followed hard currency policy for 18 years and it turned out to be a very successful monetary strategy towards euro adoption. From theoretical and policy point of view the main disadvantage of this strategy is the lack of independent monetary policy. But this is more theoretical rather than policy issue. In the environment of free movement of goods, services, capital and labour it is extremely difficult, if not impossible, for a small open economy with strong presence of foreign banks to control domestic interest rates and at the same time to contain appreciation pressure on exchange rate. In other words the central bank of a small and open economy cannot have full control over domestic monetary conditions (interest and exchange rate levels). In this case domestic market interest rates are disconnected from the central bank policy rates. Therefore it is more the appreciation of the nominal exchange rate that contains inflation rather than the interest rate policy of the respective central bank. Practically, inflation is controlled through exchange rate and import prices rather than other channels of the transmission mechanism. But this policy is not sustainable in the long-run, especially for a country which will eventually join monetary union (in European context - the euro area). When we have ERMII participation, based on maintaining currency board arrangements, inflation dynamics is determined by euro area monetary policy. This policy is imported through the mechanism of currency board. Other country specific factors as administrative prices and indirect taxes, as well as Balassa-Samuelson effect, also could play an important role for the determination of inflation. This environment is identical to the situation of the EMU membership where monetary conditions for small economies are determined exogenously and adjustment of the economy has to be done through other policies like fiscal policy, restructuring and economic reforms. Our judgement is that experience from the operation of the EMU so far clearly shows that countries, which had maintained a firm fix for a long period of time prior to their membership into the monetary union show better performance than other economies. This is a natural outcome since these economies have adapted to operate under conditions of exogenously set monetary conditions. Logically currency board regimes are better policy framework for the preparation for monetary union membership. The historical experience of Austria and the Netherlands, which had followed hard currency policy for a long period of time before their EMU membership, is clear evidence that supports our view. Before I finish, I would like to point out the regional factor for the successful development of the Bulgarian economy and the role of Austria. Austrian authorities and business community have played a very positive role in the process of transition from command to market economy in all central and eastern European countries. This is determined by geographical proximity, as well as historical factors. It is well known for this audience that in the early 1990s Bulgaria began the transition from a centrally-planned to a market economy - a unique process without historical parallel from which we could learn. Throughout this period the Austrian business and political elite supported the efforts of the Bulgarian society to handle these challenges. Austrian businesses provided credit of confidence to the Bulgarian economy, investing in the banking sector of the country and in a number of other important sectors of the economy. At the end of 2006 the commercial banks with Austrian share participation held 27.9% of the capital of the Bulgarian banking system, 28.4% of its total assets, 27.8% of deposits, and 25.6% of the lending to the private sector. Through the capitals that they have been investing and the transfer of knowledge and expertise, these institutions have a significant contribution to the economic growth in our country. Today the Austrian business is the biggest direct investor in Bulgaria by 22.0% of the foreign direct investments made in Bulgaria from 1999 until now. Austria leaves far behind much larger in size economies, such as Germany, France and Italy. Finally I would like to express my highest appreciation of and gratitude for the steady and consistent support given by Austria and the Austrian policymakers for the reforms in Bulgaria and especially for our accession to the EU. This support is well known and appreciated in Bulgaria. We do hope that this friendship and collaborations will continue during Bulgarias accession to the Euro area and afterwards. Thank you for the attention. PAGE PAGE 2

Title: Speech at the opening of the seminar Bulgaria  from Transition to Convergence: New Challenges jointly organized by the BNB and the IMF, Sofia, 2 May 2007
text: Speech by Mr. Ivan Iskrov, Governor of the BNB, at the opening of the seminar Bulgaria  from Transition to Convergence: New Challenges jointly organized by the BNB and the IMF, Sofia, 2 May 2007 Excellencies, Ladies and Gentlemen, It is a great pleasure for me to open todays seminar which has been jointly organized by the BNB and the IMF. During this seminar and with the participation of so many prominent economists we intend to sum up the lessons from the transformation process in the Bulgarian economy over the last 15-16 years and to outline the major objectives and challenges ahead. The participation of our colleagues from the IMF suggests that, without underestimating the role of policy-makers in Bulgaria, we should not neglect the external incentives for transformation as such an incentive has been our countrys relations with international financial institutions. Now that we have become a full-fledged member of the EU and have ended our last agreement with the Fund, all those involved in the decision-making process and the implementation of the decisions taken should have a clear answer to the question: Now can we go on unaided, without the IMFs advice? We, at the BNB, believe that if we are able to clearly see the successes and unsuccesses, and especially the reasons behind them, if we are able to show that we can learn from our experience and set and stand up for our priorities, then we can be successful in implementing an economic policy even without the IMFs direct guardianship, without the traditional IMF missions visiting our country every few months. My fellow colleagues, all of us here today are well familiar with the starting conditions of, and the external economic environment during, the transition of the Bulgarian economy, a transition that began in the early 1990s. The Bulgarian economy, like the other Central and Eastern European countries, was based on the principles of state central planning. There was no commodity, labour, financial or capital market. The so-called socialist economies were largely integrated into the Council for Mutual Economic Assistance (CMEA), with administratively determined specialization in some sectors. The existence of guaranteed markets within the CMEA very much cut off these economies from competitive pressures and minimised the incentives for seeking competitive advantages. In the early 1990s the post-communist countries began a unique transition process from a centrally-planned to market economy. It was unique indeed because we could not draw on the historical experience of other countries or on any academic literature as such literature simply did not exist. Even the IMF had no expertise in carrying out a transition from a command to market economy. We all had to learn ad-hoc. For various reasons, objective ones and also for the lack of political will and consensus, the restructuring of the Bulgarian economy was delayed and we all know that in the mid-1990s Bulgaria logically fell into a deep political and financial crisis. The good news was that that crisis triggered profound and extensive economic reforms. The foundation of the reforms which started in mid-1997, encouraged and supported by the IMF, was the achievement and maintenance of macroeconomic stability based on a strict fiscal policy and a currency board arrangement, the States maximum withdrawal from the business, full liberalization of domestic and foreign trade, and free movement of capitals. The fiscal policy pursued from 1997, and the liberalization and restructuring of the economy were the main pillars on which the public and investors built their confidence. These starting conditions in the Bulgarian economy coincided in time with a process of re-defining the principles of the economic policy in the developed market economies as well. The vision and practice of economic policies changed drastically in the 1990s. A consensus was reached that the main objective of a macroeconomic policy was to provide a nominal anchor for controlling inflation and inflationary expectations, to help the overall economic stability and build a favourable environment for a sustainable long-term economic growth. Macroeconomic stability and liberalization of markets became fundamental to any successful economic policy, even to the principles of the EU and EMU development. Throughout this transformation period our society was discussing two issues: 1. What is the role and merit of Bulgarian politicians and economists for the formulation and implementation of economic reforms, and what is the IMFs role?; and 2. Can we possibly follow any other economic policy philosophy that does not put so much stress on macroeconomic stability and liberalization of the economy? Over the years of transition the Bulgarian society seems to have formed the perception that all economic reforms have been carried out under some external pressure, primarily the IMFs pressure, against the will of our politicians. In the last few years the European Commission was added to the IMF. These institutions certainly did play an important and catalytic role. But those of us who have been involved in the formulation and implementation of the countrys economic policy over the last 15 years know that this perception is totally wrong. There is not and there cannot be a successful economic policy without the required domestic political support. It is not accidental that one of the main criteria used by the IMF in structuring its programs is the degree to which the proposed reforms are supported by the national authorities. Or, to put it another way, to what extent governments recognize the need for reforms and are ready to carry them out. Not infrequently over the years of transition, particularly after 1997, it was talked that there could be an alternative model of economic policy that did not give so much importance to macroeconomic stability, liberalization, and economic reforms. Experience, however, shows that a policy aimed at short-term populist effects is doomed to fail and, eventually, costs too much to society. Hungary, once a best performer among the countries in transition, which after May 2004 not only stopped the reforms but in many aspects even went backwards, is a good example of the importance of a prudent economic policy as the basis of a sustained economic growth and prosperity. The EU membership is very important in itself, but not sufficient. All I have said so far gives the answer to the questions  what economic policy should we follow to speed up the convergence process, and who should be the key driver of this policy  Sofia or Brussels. The very EU membership entails commitments to follow an economic policy that enhances flexibility and competitiveness, while maintaining macro-stability. The Stability and Growth Pact and the commitment to prepare and use convergence programs practically keep in place the general economic policy framework which our country has been following since 1997. Real convergence or the Bulgarian citizens improved living standard should be and can be achieved only by maintaining macroeconomic stability and attaining nominal convergence. In the years of transformation Bulgaria carried out unprecedented economic and social reforms which began to produce results in the last years. Bulgarias EU membership is primarily due to our readiness and will for reforms. In this period we managed to gain a relatively important competitive advantage over the old member-states and some new member-states of the EU  we learned to carry out reforms and to quickly get adapted to the rapidly changing global economy. We must keep this advantage because our countrys integration into the European economy has not come to an end but is still ahead of us, after joining the EU. Bulgarias economic results over the last 10 years indicate that we are able to pursue a successful economic policy and can be competitive even at a European level. Without exhaustively listing all possible challenges that will be discussed today, I would like to mention one of our commitments in the EU  our commitment to join the eurozone. I am not going to dwell on the advantages for the Bulgarian economy created by Bulgarias membership in the eurozone as I have spoken about this many times. I will only remind you that the current macroeconomic policy framework in Bulgaria, based on a fixed exchange rate, presupposes big benefits from the eurozone membership, without any significant costs to society. This is why three successive governments, although coming from different parts of the political space, have been following a strategy and a policy aimed at Bulgarias quick accession to the eurozone. It is well known that the Maastricht Treaty defines very strict criteria for membership which must be met on a continuous basis. This virtually means that Bulgarias commitment to eurozone membership would have a disciplinary effect on its economic policy. In other words, the EU general economic policy framework and our commitment to eurozone membership are the economic policys external anchors which will play the role that the IMF used to play in the last 15 years. And finally, on behalf of the BNB I would like to express our gratitude to all executives and members of staff of the IMF who worked with the Bulgarian authorities over the years. I want to thank them for the political, financial, and technical support for the economic reforms in the country. I also thank you for the moments of disagreements and heated debates. Ultimately, all these also proved to be extremely useful. I do hope that this conference will be very interesting and I wish you productive discussions. Thank you for your attention! PAGE PAGE 3

Title: Speech at the spring meeting of the Bankers Association in Bulgaria, Sofia, 16 May 2007
text: Speech by Mr. Ivan Iskrov, Governor of the BNB, at the spring meeting of the Bankers Association in Bulgaria, Sofia, 16 May 2007 Ladies and Gentlemen, It is a great pleasure for me that today we are once again together and have the chance to discuss professionally the condition, the prospects and challenges to the domestic banking sector. Some six months ago I said to this audience that we were on the threshold of a new era in the history of our country  the accession of the Republic of Bulgaria to united Europe. It is equally true that we have to tread a path which our country has not walked before. From 1 January 2007 our integration into the European economy does not finish, but begins. As I have pointed out on quite a few occasions, there is no more prepared and better integrated part of the Bulgarian economy than the banking system. At the same time, however, it is exactly this high level of integration that adds to the challenges to the national banking system. 2006 Results The favourable external and internal economic environment in 2006 was a good basis for banking sector growth and for keeping its stability. The banking systems assets grew by 28.3% on the previous year up to BGN 42.2 billion. Profit reached BGN 786 million which is a 37.2% increase on 2005. Despite the increasing credit market competition, the retained interest rate levels on loans and the higher cost of attracted funds, the return on assets ratio (ROA) of the banking system went up to 2.15% against 2.01% in the previous year. The trend from the last five years of growing return on equity (ROE) continued. In 2006 it reached 23.7% against 21.6% in 2005, and 20% in average for the last five years. For comparison, in EU-25 the return on assets and equity is respectively around 1.2% return on assets and approximately 16% return on equity. Following the BNBs decisive interference, from 2005 second half the rate of growth of credits for the private sector slowed downed reaching 24.6% in 2006. This trend continued throughout 2006 mainly as a result of the extended action of the administrative regulation on credit growth, which made the commercial banks contain their lending, and still many of them to even sell part of their loan portfolios. In 2006 the commercial banks managed to keep the quality of their loan portfolios with the ratio of standard loans growing from 92.3% at the end of 2005 to 93.9% in late 2006. The prolonged action of the measures aimed to restrain credit growth for the private sector and the increase of capital in some of the banks during the year conditioned unchanged capital adequacy level of the system close to that of the preceding 2005. As at 2006 year end the capital adequacy of the banking system was 14.5% against 15.3% for 2005 year end. In 2006 the country reached a relatively high BoP current account deficit  15.8% of GDP. A trend of slight increase of the deficit has been observed since the beginning of 2007. As we well know, this deficit is not destabilizing but is rather a reflection of the high rate of investment growth in the country as a result of the strong capital inflow and the process of our economys convergence to the EU countries. Further to these factors the switch to a new way of compiling statistical data on foreign trade based on the so-called Intrastat creates certain difficulties and leads to omissions in the reporting of foreign trade flows. Amid these uncertainties, it would be good for the country to build up reserves to allow for greater flexibility against potential adverse developments in the international markets. Such reserves could be accumulated by realising in 2007 a higher fiscal surplus than our governments commitment to the European Commission (2% surplus of GDP). 2007 Challenges The broadening and deepening of financial co-operation in the country brought about the more and more frequent use of market indices: LEONIA, SOFIBID and SOFIBOR. As a result, the Bulgarian Bankers Association and the Bulgarian Dealers Association are planning to extend the term of SOFIBID and SOFIBOR from 3 months to 12 months, which will bring Bulgarian indices closer to EURIBOR. In the process of Bulgarias accession to the pan-European payment infrastructures, the banking community in the country is facing two major projects  SEPA and TARGET2. For the purposes of organizing and coordinating the process of the countys integration to the payment systems area, a National Payment Systems Council (NPSC) was established in 2005. In January 2007, the NPSC decided to set up consulting groups, to deal with the main aspects of harmonization with European practices  payment instruments, infrastructures, card systems and TARGET2. The participation of the BNB and Bulgarian banking community in TARGET2 provides an opportunity for the revision and optimization of payment processes with a view to participation in TARGET2. The SEPA project is a priority project for the countries which had introduced the euro as their national currency. Nevertheless, from the very beginning, all countries outside the euro area were allowed to use SEPA when executing payments in euro, and to implement the SEPA standards for their payment instruments. By mid-2007, the NPSC will have an estimate as to the possibilities implement a project on a single entry point for Bulgaria, and will set a starting date for the project. The single entry point project will be executed jointly with the commercial banks. Over the past two years, we have attempted together with the commercial banks to find an effective solution, to satisfy both the banking community and the public, on cash circulation arrangements. From the beginning of 2007, together with Unicredit Bulbank, DSK Bank and United Bulgarian Bank, the BNB had negotiated and launched the procedure for establishing a joint venture for coin and banknote processing. Until the end of the current year, the BNB and the founding banks will work towards achieving as quickly as possible tangible results - launching the new joint venture - which will be a big step towards the creation of new secure and effective cash circulation arrangements. The BNB began the construction of a new cash centre. I would like to remind you again that after 2008, the cash centre will be the only place to provide free-of-charge cash-desk services, as regulated by the ECB. All other services will be offered at market-based cost. The combined efforts of the BNB and commercial banks lead to the successful development of the Central Credit Register system. Starting from mid 2007, the scope of credits in the register will be expanded to include subsidiary non-banking financial institutions among the participants. The access to this data will facilitate participants in the decision-making process in lending. At the same time, the quality of information had improved due to the regulated access of borrowers to the information concerning them, and the existing means for timely adjustment of such information. The introduction of the new capital requirements is running smoothly, as expected. Most of the banks have planned their capital parameters adequately. Very few banks have allowed temporary deviations from the minimum capital requirements, in most cases due to technical causes, and on rare occasions  due to insufficient capital planning. Another challenge to the banking industry from the start of the year was to adapt to the requirements of financial and supervision reporting. All banks implemented the new reporting standards successfully. The introduction from the beginning of this year of Basel II will have an impact on the BNBs policy with regard to the publication of non-aggregated data about individual commercial banks. Each quarter since 1999, the BNB has been publishing the balance sheets and income statements of individual commercial banks. These data enjoy the particular interest of the specialized media, and the banking community. From the first quarter of 2007, the BNB will also start publishing part of the additional reference information collected by the banking supervision function. This will assist both commercial banks in analyzing market trends, and individual banking service users in their choice of a servicing bank. With regard to the BNBs licensing policy, the principle adopted on EU level of freedom of establishment and provision of financial services by banks licensed for business in another member state is of paramount importance. On this basis the BNB receives notifications by European credit institutions expressing serious intentions to enter the Bulgarian banking and financial services market through the so-called direct banking. As of end-April, 42 such notifications were received. As regards licensing of new domestic banks, the BNB will continue to pursue its cautious licensing policy, which requires from applicants to provide proof that with its presence the new financial institutions will contribute to the enhancement of banking intermediation and will add value to the market by offering innovative products and services. In addition to the intensifying competition among banks, the banking sector should also anticipate the increasing competition of the non-bank financial intermediaries. This is a global trend, which has gained in strength in Bulgaria in the recent years. The administrative restrictions enforced by the BNB on bank credit growth definitely had their positive effect on the development of the non-banking financial market. From the beginning of 2007, the BNB revoked the additional minimum reserve requirements in effect in the country from the second quarter of 2005 . After the revocation, credit growth has again shown signs of acceleration, reaching in March 36.1 percent. Of course, these data contain information about multiple factors having their impact on the banks lending policy - some of them of temporary nature. Firstly, these data reflect the return to some banks balance sheets of loans that were sold in the period of effect of credit restrictions. In addition, the accelerating rate of credit growth also reflects the replacement by some corporate clients of foreign financing with domestic financing. Practically, these two trends have not changed the amount of lending within the economy. They only transfer credit risk into the balance sheet of the Bulgarian banking system. Although we have no reasons for serious critique as to the way commercial banks manage their risks, we find that the competition for customers and a market share, which seems to be evidenced again as a consequence of the optimism in relation to our EU membership, should be based on prudence and caution. The need of greater caution in accumulating credit risk is determined by two factors. Firstly, with regard to the level of indebtedness accumulated in the economy. At the end of 2003 and the beginning of 2004, when the BNB took the first measures for restricting the pace of bank credit growth, the level of indebtedness of the private sector was much lower than in the newly acceded EU member states. The credit to the private sector was about 27 percent of GDP, while private external debt was about 23 percent of GDP. This relatively low level of indebtedness, combined with the historically low interest rate levels worldwide, allowed us to believe that the high credit growth rates are of limited nature and are determined by the growth in the economy and deepening of financial intermediation. Today, the level of debt in the Bulgarian economy is above the average in the newly acceded EU member states, while the level of our per capita GDP is lower that the average for these economies. Commercial banks should take account of the fact that the degree of indebtedness reached by companies and households makes them more vulnerable to changes in the interest rate levels. Neither should we overlook the interest rate cycle in the euro area, which is transmitted domestically through the mechanism of the currency board. Since end-2005, the European Central Bank has started to increase interest rates, reaching presently an increase of 1.75 percent. The good development of the economies of euro area member states gives us no grounds to believe that the upward cycle of interest rate growth has peaked. In this period of rising interest rates in the euro area, the cost of credit decreased domestically, stabilizing relatively in the recent months. The decrease in the interest rate came as a result of strong competition among commercial banks for a market share, and the large capital inflow to the country, and the reduction of country risk premium as a result of Bulgarias higher sovereign rating. However, the shrinking of the net interest margin has its limits, and with the continuing increase in the euro area interest rates banks will have to increase the cost of credit at a certain point in time. This generates certain risk, as in the recent several years companies and households have got used to operating in an environment of decreasing interest rates. The BNB is of the position that any acceleration in the rate of growth of lending to the private sector may put to risk the quality of commercial banks credit portfolios. The central bank is monitoring with enhanced attention the increased credit growth rate evidenced from the beginning of 2007, and if we find that this is a sustainable growth entailing risks to the stability of the banking system, we will take steps to restrict credit growth. Thank you for the attention. PAGE PAGE 4

Title: Speech delivered during his official visit to the Bank of Albania, Tirana, 18 May 2007
Subtitle: THE ROAD TO THE EU: THE ROLE OF THE CENTRAL BANK
text: Speech by Mr. Ivan Iskrov, Governor of the BNB, delivered during his official visit to the Bank of Albania, Tirana, 18 May 2007 THE ROAD TO THE EU: THE ROLE OF THE CENTRAL BANK (A Point of View of A New Member State Central Bank) Governor Fulanis invitation came in the most appropriate time, since Bulgaria has already been in the EU for five months after a long accession process. I came here not to give recommendations or recipes. I am here today to share with our friends the challenges we faced, the mistakes we made, and the lessons that we have learned. I believe our experience could be beneficial for Albania and the BoA due to geographical proximity and historical background of our countries and the fact that we are small and open catching-up economies that are converging institutionally and economically to the more advanced countries. In addition we have recent experience in the negotiation and accession process that is very relevant for the countries that set off on this road now. On behalf of the Governing Council of the BNB I would like to congratulate you for signing on 12 June, 2006 the Stabilisation and Association Agreement with the EU which is an important step towards your EU membership. Another reason for my visit is our new role as an EU member state. We just switched from a status of a country subject to assessment to a country that is part of the assessing side. The ECOFIN Council and its committees, of which top Bulgarian officials are members, discuss and assess the Economic and fiscal programme (EFP) submitted by your country. Our participation in this dialogue requires knowledge and expertise on the Albanian economy. Hence, as a new member state we have to build up capacity to be an active participant in the EU enlargement process. And last but not least, the enlargement process that integrates the countries from the Western Balkans into the Union, irrespective of its timing, is a crucial factor for the stability and future prosperity of our region. Bulgaria highly appreciates the benefits of enlargement for the whole region and supports it. As you know during his January visit in your country the Bulgarian Prime minister publicly stated our full support for the Albanian accession into the EU after the necessary preparation and fulfilment of the admission criteria. Today I am going to share with you a short historical review of Bulgarias accession and the role of the central bank in this process and then I will talk about the challenges that Albanian policy-makers may face from the central bank perspective. First of all, I would advise you to be patient and not to waste time. It took us 14 years to prepare ourselves for EU membership. I hope you will make it faster. In 1993 Bulgaria signed the European Association Agreement that entered into force in 1995. In December 1995 Bulgaria submitted its application for EU membership and in November 1998 the Commission presented its first Regular Report on Bulgaria's progress towards accession. Accession negotiations between Bulgaria and the EU started on 15 February 2000 and we finalized them on 15 June 2004. The European Parliament gave its support to Bulgaria's EU membership on 13 April 2005. The vote was 522 in favour and 70 against, with 69 abstentions. The Accession Treaty was signed in Luxembourg on 25 April 2005 and Bulgaria entered the EU on 1 January this year. But integration does not finish from the date of accession. It continues and intensifies. Even now we still have to harmonize some issues and to catch-up in many areas. The general principle is that the government is the leading and most responsible institution for the accession, but the role of the central bank in the process is also very important. By maintaining price stability through ensuring the stability of the national currency the BNB contributed to the financial and economic stability of the country, which was a crucial precondition for the successful negotiations, preparations and eventual membership. Being a truly independent central bank since Bulgarias political and financial crisis in 1997 we have extended our co-operation to the last three consecutive governments on the solid grounds of the political consensus to preserve the currency board arrangements, to pursue strict fiscal policy and to implement structural reforms. Therefore, both building a political consensus on the national priorities and sustaining it are the major prerequisites for the EU accession. I would focus on the main aspects of the EU integration where the BNB actively participated in the course of accession. In the area of harmonization of the financial sector legislation we have applied a strategy for as soon as possible compliance with the acquis communautiare. I am confident that the economic and financial stability of the country has been reinforced by this fast harmonization of our financial legislation and regulations. There were three main areas of legal harmonization where the central bank played a very active role: Independence of the central bank and prohibition of government financing and privileged access; Banking sector legal and institutional framework; Financial services consumers protection. The acquis in the area of the Economic and Monetary Union contains specific rules requiring the independence of the central bank in the Member States, prohibition of direct financing of the public sector by the central bank and prohibition of privileged access of the public sector to financial institutions. Member States are expected to co-ordinate their economic policies and are subject to the Stability and Growth Pact with regard to fiscal surveillance. New Member States are also committed to comply with the criteria laid down in the EC Treaty in order to be able to adopt the euro in due course after accession. Until then, they participate in the Economic and Monetary Union as a Member State with derogation from the use of the euro and they treat their exchange rates as a matter of common concern. Every Member State shall ensure that its national legislation, including the statute of its central bank, is compatible with the EC Treaty and the Statute of the European System of Central Banks and of the European Central Bank.
