The participation in EMU presupposes the adoption by the candidate country of the Single market acquis, more particularly of the acquis on free movement of capital, as was the case for the present member states. The opt-out status being disregarded for the candidate countries, no transitional periods or special arrangements are therefore permitted, nor have they been requested by any of the countries with which negotiations have been carried out until now. Independence of the central bank and prohibition of government financing and privileged access Independence of the central bank is one of the main pillars of financial stability and fiscal soundness. Independence in all respects  functional, financial, institutional, and personal  must be guaranteed by Law, but also to be well understood, accepted and strictly respected by the Governments and the other public authorities. I should mention that the amendments of the Organic Law on the Bulgarian National Bank in respect of strengthening central bank independence were supported by the Government and adopted by the National Assembly with full consensus between the governing majority and the opposition parties. The principle of functional independence requires maintaining price stability to be set as a main goal of the central bank. The central bank should be independent in order to fulfil this task, regardless of political demand for achievement of other goals, for example higher economic growth. The institutional independence is formulated in art. 108 of the Treaty establishing the EU and art. 7 of the Protocol on the Statute of the ESCB and of the ECB. It stipulates that neither the ECB, nor National central banks (NCBs), nor any member of their decision-making bodies shall seek or take instructions from Community institutions or bodies, from any government of a Member State or from any other body. The Community institutions and bodies and the governments of the Member States undertake to respect this principle and not to seek to influence the members of the decision-making bodies of the ECB or of the national central banks in the performance of their tasks. That means, that third parties cannot provide instructions to the NCBs; cannot adopt, stop, repeal or postpone the implementation of decisions of the NCBs; cannot censor decisions of NCBs; cannot participate with a voting right in the NCBs decision-making bodies and cannot be consulted in advance with regard to decisions to be made by NCBs. Personal independence is guaranteed in the basic EU legislation through the requirement for a minimum 5 years mandate for the governors and the members of the NCBs decision-making bodies. It is prohibited to dismiss governors and members of the decision-making bodies of the NCBs prior to the expiration of their term of office. Yet in the case of dismissal of the governor, the dismissed governor or the Governing Council of the ECB has the right to refer to the Court of Justice in Luxembourg to appeal. Financial independence of the central bank requires that the central bank should have at its disposal all the financial resources needed to fulfil its duties. This provision includes the requirement that the central banks annual budget be independent from any political interference. Prohibition of financing to the government and privileged access establishes the following principles: Overdraft facilities or any other type of credit facility with the ESCB or NCBs in favour of Community institutions or bodies, central governments, regional, local or public authorities, other bodies governed by public law, or public undertakings of member states are prohibited; Direct purchases of debt instruments from the above institutions or bodies by the ECB or the NCBs are prohibited. Banking sector legal and institutional framework Another important requirement of the EU in the field of the financial sector relates to the banking sector legal and institutional framework. The main objective of the Codified Directive on the credit institutions, regulating the banking activity and supervision, is to introduce the principle of the single passport. What does the single passport mean? It is the principle that ensures freedom of establishment and freedom to provide services in the banking sphere all around the EU. The directive lays down the principle of home country control - the prudential supervision of a credit institution shall be the responsibility of the competent authorities of the Member State where it is licensed. The harmonized rules on credit institutions (banks and electronic-money institutions) give them the right to carry out the explicitly enumerated activities either by the establishment of a branch or by way of the direct provision of services in all Member States once these institutions are licensed and supervised in a Member State. There is harmonization of the requirements for the following: granting and withdrawal of a bank license; own funds of credit institutions; capital adequacy; large exposures; exchange of information between the competent authorities while ensuring the observance of the professional secrecy principles; imposing certain sanctions by the competent authorities; etc. Furthermore, in the field of supervision, the EU requires supplementary supervision to be exercised when credit institutions, investment firms and insurance undertakings form a cross-border group, called a financial conglomerate. In addition to drafting the necessary legal framework, it is particularly important to have in place well-organized institutions capable of supervising efficiently the financial sector and thus guaranteeing the correct application of the legislation. Financial services consumers protection One of the main areas of the EU regulation concerns consumer protection and more specifically the consumers of financial services. This is an important aspect of the regulation which must be regulated in the countries where there is no tradition for consumer protection but in the same time the market is growing fast. Establishing rules for consumer credit and mortgage loans is an important factor for stability and the quality of the portfolios of credit institutions and consumer credit providers as well as for the consumers of financial services. Creation of out-of-court mechanisms to resolve disputes between credit institutions and their clients is an important step further. The Bulgarian National Bank has already gained some experience in this area and I would like to emphasize the importance of this legislation and its effective implementation. Let me now share with you my understanding on the role of the central bank in the EU integration process. We took a proactive position during the preparation for EU membership unlike some other public institutions that completed their preparation just before the day of accession, even in the last minute. What does that mean? We choose to be part of the process, to provide our expertise, knowledge and institutional capacity for the successful completion of the accession objectives. The BNB was proactive, we did not wait for anyone to give us an incentive to work. The BNB took part in the negotiation process actively participating in 7 out of all the 30 negotiation chapters. They covered EMU, free movement of capital, free provision of services, consumer protection, economic and financial affairs, statistics, and financial control. Our experience indicates that the active role of the central bank in the accession process (certainly in the areas of our competence) is beneficial for the process itself but also for the financial sector and for the central bank. We have opted for a strong involvement of the banking sector in the whole accession process. This approach helped to prepare Bulgarian banks for the challenges of the large EU financial market. Moreover, we did not propose any single piece of legislation concerning the financial sector without an open discussion and consensus reached with the bank association. This was not always a smooth process, but we have learned to make compromises and to reach agreements. Last but not least, in the course of accession we learned that the success of the process is impossible without investing in training of our human capital. Continuous training of our staff made it possible for us to keep the same number of employees although our functions and tasks increased substantially due to the accession. Unlike some other parts of the public sector, we have carried out our internal reforms and capacity-building at the earliest possible stage and in parallel with the legal alignment. This strategy proved to be the right one. The main lesson from the accession process is that the benefits will come as early as the institutional and structural reforms and legal harmonisation with the acquis are implemented. External anchors versus domestic political will We learned that the dialogue with the EC and the ECB offers the best opportunity to create a sound policy mix and to make the economy functioning stable and predictable. From that standpoint we find as an excellent opportunity for Albania the invitation extended by commissioner Almunia to the aspiring countries to submit to the European Commission the so-called Economic and Fiscal Programme (EFP). This is an excellent starting point to map the economic and fiscal framework that will further bring about growth and stability. This initiative is an important step in supporting countries in their economic development and integration with the EU. It is also deepening and focusing the political dialogue between the authorities of the aspiring countries and the Commission on economic and fiscal issues. And again our experience in the preparation of the Pre-accession economic programs and the first Convergence programme shows that the role of the Central bank is crucial in the process of drafting and discussing these documents. Albania submitted in December 2006, for the first time, its Economic and Fiscal Programme. The implementation of the programme will help Albania to meet the Copenhagen economic criteria for EU accession, i.e. to establish a functioning market economy and to raise competitiveness to a level which would allow the country to meet the competitive pressure within the European Union. This process and the programme represent an immediate goal that requires prudent economic policy and broad consensus between the central bank and the Government. From another point of view this represents an external anchor for the policy, which is complementary to the other one  the IMF programmes. External anchors are extremely helpful because they bring knowledge, external assessment and pressure. But make no mistake that only external pressure could drive your economic policy and reforms. At the end of the day, the national policy-makers are the ones who have to define, support and implement domestic economic policy. There is no external substitute for the national political consensus on the main principles of the domestic economic policy. Sometimes national governments in their pursuit of multiple political and economic goals or just re-election are often faced with contradictory objectives. Then populism may supersede the main long-term goals. In this case the external anchors, provided by the EU and the IMF surveillance or stand-by agreements play a very important role for the correction of the economic policy in line with the long term stability and predictability. But again, let me emphasize that the political consensus on the main goals of the economic policy and the political will to adopt and implement suitable reforms are crucial for the sustainable success. It is true for the central banks, too! The monetary policy framework has to guarantee low inflation and the central bank has to be predictable and accountable in its monetary and prudential policy. However, irrespective of the monetary policy framework, whether based on currency board as is the case in Bulgaria or implicit inflation targeting, as is the case in Albania, the fiscal and structural reforms are decisive for the success of the overall economic policy. We all know that in a transition economy it is very difficult to restructure the public sector and to optimize and balance the public accounts. However short term sacrifices, which are necessary to achieve a fiscal balance, inevitably will bring substantial medium and long term benefits for the economy. My personal opinion is that under the current favourable economic environment all around the world, and in Albania, a fiscal policy oriented towards a balanced budget or surplus will generate significant economic benefits and will increase the flexibility of the macroeconomic policy. Finally, once again I would like to assure you that we are ready to share with you our modest experience and to give you our support to fulfil the accession criteria so that you eventually become a member of the EU. Today the Greek long experience in the Union, the accession of Bulgaria and Romania to the EU and the prospects for membership of the other countries in our region, give the Balkan countries a chance for stability and full integration into the European economy. We can say without hesitation that the countries in this region have never before had a chance like this in their history. We have to do our best to utilize this historical opportunity. Thank you for the attention. PAGE PAGE 2

Title: Speech at the opening of the Conference 10 Years of Currency Board and the Challenges of the Euro Adoption, Sofia
text: Speech of Mr. Ivan Iskrov, Governor of the BNB, delivered at the opening of the Conference 10 Years of Currency Board and the Challenges of the Euro Adoption , Sofia, 18 September 2007 Ladies and Gentlemen, It is a pleasure for me to open this conference that marks the tenth anniversary of the introduction of the currency board, as in practice it is the system of rules governing the operation of the BNB in the monetary policy area. As all of you [present here] are well aware the management of short-term interest rates is a fundamental occupation of the governors of central banks pursuing a discretionary monetary policy, and the currency boards seem to be underrated as second best central banks. But a monetary policy cannot be successful and facilitating the development of the economy and society, nor can it control the inflation rates, if stable foundations are lacking: such as an operating real economy, a well supervised and stable financial system, an effective judiciary, good and efficient institutions, and the political will to pursue reform. Hence, in stead of feeling underrated, I as the BNB Governor and we all should share with a justified pride our 10-year practical experience. We should declare that the currency board arrangement is not as simple as a fixed exchange rate and giving up pursuing an independent monetary policy. It is much more! The currency board imposed a fundamentally different philosophy and behaviour of the economic and political entities in this country. The currency board is a symbol of the countrys economic policy reorientation towards liberalization, greater economic freedom, stability and consistency, as well as to a prudent behaviour of the political class. This change exactly underlies our countrys greatest political success  Bulgarias full-fledged EU membership. Therefore, I will examine the currency board from the point of view of what it has given to us as a monetary policy regime, and in what way it can contribute, given our countrys membership in the EU and the commitments and challenges ensuing from this membership. The choice of a monetary policy regime in an economy has never been and can never be done only following the models described in academic literature. Theoretical models may be a good framework for speculation and analysis, but they always tend to be based on specific assumptions and simplification, which we cannot afford to have in our everyday decision-making process. There is no way to view a society as a tabula rasa on which we can build and implement a brilliant theoretical model. Societies have their own history, political situation, public attitudes and preferences and external limitations, determined by their geographic location and their interaction with other counties. Further along this line, some countries are on a lower level of economic and political development, and have their short-term and long-term aspirations to join economic and political unions, to converge with their more developed member states. To this end, they should formulate a convergence strategy taking into account both the initial conditions and the membership requirements. These and many other factors should be considered in the selection of a monetary policy regime of a country. Bulgarias experience of 1997 with the introduction of the currency board and the results of its operation are indicative of the complexity of the choice of a monetary policy regime. The prevailing approach of analysis in the selection of a monetary policy regime was based on the comparison of the advantages and disadvantages of a flexible and inflexible monetary policy regime. As we are all aware, the flexible regime of monetary policy is identified with inflation targeting and floating exchange rate, and the inflexible regime  with a fixed exchange rate and giving up direct control of monetary conditions in the country. The standard view, often reiterated in the first years after the introduction of the currency board in Bulgaria, was that abandoning the implementation of a discretionary monetary policy reduces the independence of the countrys economic policy and limits the degree of freedom and room for manoeuvre to internal and external shocks. Let us, however, look deeper into the facts and the developments in the global and national economy, and try to answer the question to what extent we were able to pursue an independent monetary policy, and what degree of freedom we have relinquished. Initial Conditions In 1996 and early 1997, the Bulgarian economy suffered a deep financial and economic, as well as a political crisis. There was strong mistrust in the public institutions, the financial system and the national currency, as well as great uncertainty which additionally reinforced the distrust, and intensified the crisis. The inflation rates came up to hyperinflation levels. In this uncertain environment, there was mass run on the banks, and substation of foreign currency for the national one. In such a situation pursuing an independent monetary policy had practically no value, as nobody wanted to hold lev-denominated financial assets, regardless of the interest rate levels. Furthermore, the high interest rate levels in levs additionally deteriorated commercial banks portfolios and decreased the credibility of the national currency. In other words, the control of the short-term interest rate by the central bank gave it no possibility to influence the decision-making of households, companies, and the financial sector, and through it to impact via the transmission mechanism the inflation rates. A key precondition for implementing a successful monetary policy is the existing confidence in the central bank and its policy. The lost confidence in the BNB monetary policy in 1996 and early 1997 necessitated a change in the regime in a way that would restore the credibility of the central bank and the national currency. Of course, this goal could not have been attained without a change in the general economic policy of the country. The structural changes, privatization and liberalisation in the economy, and orienting the fiscal policy towards reducing the tax burden and achieving a balanced budget or a budget surplus were and still are the foundations for the successful operation of the currency board in Bulgaria. Global Trends and External Environment The period in which Bulgaria had to redirect its economic policy towards stability and growth, following nearly a decade in search of a unique model of transition from a command to market economy, coincided with a massive turn in global economy. That was a period in which the world experienced an unparalleled liberalization of the global financial markets, an IT and telecommunication technologies revolution, the integration of millions of people from Southeast Asia and Central and Eastern Europe into the global labour market, the creation of the Single European Market, the EU enlargement and the formation of the Economic and Monetary Union in Europe. Furthermore, the world economy also went through numerous disruptions, such as the financial crises in Russia and Asia, the collapse of the currency board in Argentina, the crisis in Kosovo, and the subsequent slowdown of global economic growth, the terrorist attacks in the USA in 2001, the fall in the hi-tech companies equity prices, the war in Iraq and the unprecedented increase in energy prices and the global imbalances over the recent years, as well as the ongoing crisis on the international credit markets triggered by the problems with USA subprime mortgages. The overall impact of all these changes was reflected in increased financial flows worldwide (in the form of portfolio and direct investments), and the interdependence between individual economies. In this environment the control over monetary conditions in a particular economy is decreasingly determined by the monetary policy of its national central bank and is ever more influenced by the policies of the major international central banks (the ECB, Federal Reserve System, Bank of Japan), and the investment decisions of global companies and households worldwide. This practical conclusion is particularly valid for small and open economies with a strong presence of foreign financial intermediaries in their financial markets. The data indicate that in these economies the interest rates that affect investment and saving decisions of households and companies could for quite a long period depart from the national central bank rate, especially in cases of substantial capital inflow and a high risk appetite on the part of economic agents who are inclined to accumulate foreign currency denominated debt. Moreover, the attempts to maintain an independent monetary policy in an environment of a strong capital inflow lead to a strong appreciation of the local currency, with the interest rates of the national central bank having very little impact on the economic decisions of financial intermediaries, companies and households. In this context, an independent monetary policy is a myth rather than an objective reality. A similar situation is observed in almost all new EU member-states. Long-term outlook The choice of a monetary policy regime in 1997 was influenced by both the long-term outlook and Bulgarias strategic objective to join the EU with the subsequent obligation to adopt the single currency. This long-term prospect also determined the choice of the German Mark (the Euro from 1999) as the reserve currency, although at that time the US Dollar was the currency in which most of our foreign trade was carried out and most of the savings of companies and households were held. The currency board arrangement is practically the most transparent and consistent strategy for jointing the euro area. It is compatible with participating in the Exchange Rate Mechanism II (ERM II)  which participation is a precondition for joining the Economic and Monetary Union. At the same time, the currency board arrangement rules out any change in the exchange rate regime through which many of the new member-states must go when joining ERM II (this is especially important for the countries having an inflation targeting regime with a floating rate). The currency board reduces the uncertainties in the economy and makes the macroeconomic policy more predictable for households, companies and foreign investors. I am not going to dwell on the operation of the Bulgarian currency board arrangement over the last ten years. I see in the programme the participation of colleagues who are serious researchers and analysts and they probably would speak on this topic. I would rather present the position of the Bulgarian government and the BNB since the year 2000 as to why the currency board arrangement is the optimal regime for us to achieve our objective  euro area membership. Euro Area Preparations and Challenges Our experience of the past ten years shows that the currency board is the most appropriate monetary policy regime that a country may follow in its accession to the single currency. The currency board arrangement to the highest possible extent reproduces the conditions in which a euro area member-state economy operates. On the one hand it limits the central banks instruments to pursue a discretionary monetary policy, as is the situation in the euro area member-states where the common monetary policy takes account of the economic conditions not in the particular country but in the entire EMU (i.e. the dominating 3-4 economies in the Union). On the other hand, the currency board arrangement, to a much lager extent than the other monetary policy regimes, demands and calls for governments to implement prudent and reliable fiscal and structural reforms policies compatible with the Stability and Growth Pact and the Lisbon Strategy. The pegged exchange rate ensures the unique possibility for the Bulgarian economy to simultaneously reach nominal and real convergence, while keeping high and sustained economic growth rates. In a world where the individual economies and financial systems are strongly interlinked, the coordination of national monetary policies is done by markets through the free movement of capitals. Particularly in the case of small open economies, the monetary policy of the major central banks strongly influences the monetary conditions in these economies (the so called carry trade is a clear example). The formation of monetary unions is a natural reaction to this interdependency. It is not accidental that at the end of the 19th century, when there was a very high level of globalization, the gold standard played the role of a coordination mechanism for the monetary policies of the different countries. In that period the Latin and the Scandinavian Monetary Unions were set up, and the European Monetary Union began to be talked about for the first time. Today this trend is incorporated into the EU institutional structure. By signing the Treaty of Accession, Bulgaria made the commitment to join the euro area and adopt the single currency. I will remind you once again that the current European legislation does not allow the new EU member-states to use an opt-out clause for their membership in the EMU. With regard to the adoption of the single currency, Bulgaria, and particularly the BNB, have always had a consistent and long-term oriented policy. This position is largely determined by the operating currency board arrangement and all responsible political parties awareness of its importance for the economic stability and growth. The period in which a country can meet the criteria and join the euro area is determined by the preparedness of the fiscal sector and the extent of inflation rate convergence. And here a view, in my opinion a wrong one, is often expressed that the nominal and real convergence are mutually exclusive and that they cannot be accomplished at once. We believe that the skilful combination of fiscal, structural and regulatory policies which encourages competition on micro-level can lead to a faster real convergence process, while also meeting the nominal criteria. Over the last five years Bulgaria has sustainably met all Maastricht criteria with the exception of one  the level of inflation. The policy followed over the last ten years of a balanced budget, or a budget surplus if possible, will both allow continued fulfilment of the Maastricht criteria with regard to the budget deficit, the government debt and the long-term interest rates, and will ensure the necessary room for manoeuvring and flexibility of macroeconomic policy. The stringent fiscal policy is also needed to help us meet the inflation criterion. Under a currency board arrangement the Central Bank has no direct control over the inflation rates in the country. With the existing natural trend of the levels of prices in the new member-states to converge to those in the old member-states, the fulfilment of this criteria is not a challenge only to the countries operating currency boards, but also to all countries with levels of their prices lower than the average EU price level regardless of their monetary policy regimes. In the case of Bulgaria with a regime of fixed exchange rate and strongly conservative fiscal policy, reserves should be sought in promoting competition and improving the business environment so that the economy could have greater flexibility to respond to external changes and supply could faster meet growing demand. For me, todays conference is part of the continuous efforts that we all must share to improve our knowledge and understanding of the way in which our country could most efficiently integrate into the global economy and the EU, to increase the welfare of the Bulgarian people and to complete our integration into the EU by adopting the single currency. The presence of politicians, researchers from NGOs, representatives of the academia, the EC and central banks from the member-states allows me to believe that we will enjoy a useful and fruitful discussion. Thank you for your attention! PAGE PAGE 4

Title: Speech at the International Conference on Theory and Practice of Financial Crime, dedicated to the 55th anniversary of the founding of the Faculty of Finance and Accounting at the University of National and World Economy, Sofia
text: Speech of Mr. Ivan Iskrov, BNB Governor, delivered at the International Conference on Theory and Practice of Financial Crime, dedicated to the 55th anniversary of the founding of the Faculty of Finance and Accounting at the University of National and World Economy, Sofia, 29 November 2007 First, allow me to say that it is a great honour and pleasure for me to be a co-patron, together with the Minister of Finance  Mr. Oresharski, of the Jubilee International Conference, dedicated to the 55th anniversary of the founding of the Faculty of Finance and Accounting at the University of National and World Economy, as this university is a leading economic education institution in the country, and the Faculty of Finance and Accounting was, and I am sure still is, the core of the UNWE. The topic of todays conference is of particular importance to every country and economy, Bulgarias included, irrespective of the fact that these issues are put aside as not so interesting to be discussed. In our everyday work we focus on the bright side of the economic and financial globalization and Bulgarias EU integration. However those processes have a darker side, which has its impact on the development of every society. These two days you will have the opportunity to discuss thoroughly the theoretical and practical aspects of financial crimes. I will briefly outline here their impact on the general development of economy. Globalization, the creation of a common market, the free movement of goods and capital generates great potential for business and economic growth. On the other hand, they provide greater opportunities for financial offences. These practices may have a large scope of activity and include every fraud related offence: Misuse of inside information; Bad market behaviour; Damage of third party interests; Corruption; Money laundering, etc. One could hardly determine the complete range of financial crimes and their immediate financial and economic effect. Exact data on the number of financial offences could not be collected and summarized. The data we have only show the part we have managed to uncover, or prevent, but does not give the full picture of the damages sustained. Irrespective of the lack of full information on the volume of financial offences, we are in the position to identify the negative economic and social effects they have on economies and societies. I will only name a few of the negative effects they have on the economies of every particular country: Negative impact on the business environment, which reduces the competitiveness of companies observing strictly the law. The competition advantages of the sort impede immensely the work of those observing the law and result in a decrease in the volume of investments and capital inflows into the country. Bad financial practices create a risk for the reputation of financial institutions as well as potential destabilization. Economic incentives are distorted, leading to ineffective distribution of resources, which makes the economic policy of the country less effective. Most cases of financial offences are by rule accompanied by a substantial loss of tax revenue. Due to the great importance of the issue, the fight against these practices and their prevention should not only be considered a national problem, but they should be prioritized on an international level as well. The fight against financial crimes within the EU is a joint responsibility of all European institutions and member states. The European legislation in place aims at protecting the financial system and all other sectors and activities, which are susceptible to the actions of criminal formations. On EU level, several strategies have been adopted for coordinated activities in the areas of: Financial services; Supervision; Commercial legislation and corporate management; Accounting policy. Aiming at ensuring transparency, information exchange and reducing the risk in commercial and financial relations not only within the EU but also with countries outside the Union. Specific steps have been developed ensuring an effective legal framework for protection against financial crime. The directions of action, on which the European Commission and the ECB focus their attention with regard to combating financial crime are primarily related with: curbing corruption, including misuse of financial resources, harmonization of criminal law, prevention and combating organized crime, money laundering, preventing unlawful acquisition of public property, strict application of accounting and audit standards, protecting financial market participants and the general public from fraud, manipulations and malpractices in relation to financial and commercial instruments. A number of steps have been made in the area of harmful unlawful use of the worldwide web, copying and personal protection of data, forgeries counterfeits of legal tender. I would like to give you two short examples of successful fight against theft of personal data, and misuse of financial information. The introduction of modern chip technology for debit and credit cards is one of them. In our country, the exchange cards with a magnetic band for chip-based ones was speeded up in 2007 following the trend in the developed countries. Some Bulgarian banks intend to complete in full their replacement of already issued debit and credit cards by the end of 2008. Another example of successful counteraction of internet credit card fraud is enhancing the level of protection of commercial banks and traders websites. The introduction of electronic signature has significantly facilitated the growth of internet payments in Bulgaria. To keep the trend sustainable, the central banks requirements as to improving security are growing in pace with the development of IT and communications technologies. To have better results, the cooperation between banks is of key importance. The Bulgarian National Bank has a statutory obligation to play an active role in preventing any possibilities to use the banking sector for the purposes of financial fraud. This policy of prevention starts as early as the stage of licensing  in the procedure of granting a license to a credit institution and a payment system operator, and invariably goes along the whole business process in each institution. Therefore, the BNB pursues a highly conservative policy both in licensing of credit institutions and payment system operators, and in the process of oversight of prudent business operation and compliance with the laws and best banking practices. The BNB acts, within the scope of its competences, according to the commitments made to apply the most up-to-date international criteria for identification of financial fraud in banks. The central bank is putting much effort for curbing the possibilities for using regulated institutions for the purposes of financial fraud, and in the direction of preserving the credibility of the banking system, protecting depositors, increasing their awareness. And last but not least, enhancing consumer culture of the general public is also a way to combat financial fraud. Well informed consumers are more difficult to get involved in a financial fraud. So, special attention should be paid to acquainting and educating the general public about bad financial practices and crime, and their adverse effect on the economy and society. This conference is an important step in this direction. I thank you for your attention, and wish you an interesting and fruitful discussion. PAGE PAGE 3

Title: Speech at a meeting of the Association of Banks in Bulgaria
text: Speech of Mr. Ivan Iskrov, BNB Governor, at a meeting of the Association of Banks in Bulgaria, 5 December 2007 Ladies and Gentlemen, I am extremely pleased to be with you today to celebrate together the bankers day. A year ago, I told you that the atmosphere is different because we were on the verge of the EU membership of Bulgaria. Today, a year later, we can make a recapitulation to what extent our expectations of the initial impact of EU membership to our country have materialized, and what the first lessons from an economy operating within the single market are. Tonight, by a tradition I will dwell on the achievements of the passing year and the challenges facing us in 2008. Today, at the end of the first year of membership, we can say that to a certain extent we underestimated in our projections the positive effect of Bulgarias membership in the European Union. The data so far indicate that in 2007 we will realize the highest economic growth rate since the start of economic reform in this country. A fundamental change compared to previous years can be seen also in terms of the structure of economic growth. This year, the factor most contributing to GDP growth is the growth of investment. This high growth rate of the economy will most probably persist in 2008 in spite of the mid-year uncertainties in the international financial markets. The upward development was achieved in an environment characterized by two opposite trends. On the one hand  the strong optimism in relation to the countrys EU membership continued to generate a strong capital inflow and high consumer and investor activity. On the other hand, our economy was exposed to the effect of adverse changes in the global environment. The crisis starting at the beginning of the year in the American mortgage market intensified and spilled over to other parts of the world, which resulted in a global tight liquidity situation, reduced propensity to assume risk and increased risk premium, particularly of the countries known as the emerging markets. In addition, the dynamic growth of global economy and the bad weather conditions brought about a continuous increase in the international energy and food prices. The combination of a conservative fiscal policy and the BNBs consistent policy for preserving financial stability determined the developments in the Bulgarian economy in the first year of its EU membership, and did not allow the above outlined trends to pose any risks to the sustainable economic development of the country. As a natural consequence of high investment activity and the strong capital inflow the current account deficit increased year-on-year up to about 20% of GDP. This high deficit reflects the successful development of the Bulgarian economy and the favourable business conditions in this country. Due exactly to this, Bulgaria continues to attract record-high foreign direct investment even in a period when the international financial markets go though very difficult times. The high level of deficit, however, requires continuous efforts for increasing competitiveness of the economy through continuous enhancement of the investment environment, the quality of human capital, and the operation of the public institutions and balancing the shortage of savings in the economy by pursuing a prudent and disciplined fiscal policy. The first year of EU membership proved that the Bulgarian economy is built on sound foundations and can successfully integrate and compete in the single European market. Bulgaria, together with the Baltic states practicing a currency board, is one of the few countries in the EU which is successfully competing with the Asian economies and increased its exports to the single market and its share in the common imports of the Union. We should be satisfied with the achievements, while not underrating the challenges accompanying our success, and the commitments assumed when we joined the EU. With the Accession Treaty, Bulgaria committed to introducing the single currency. In spite of the fact that superfluous talking is more detrimental to than facilitating the process, I insist noting that the accession to the euro area and the introduction of the euro as a national currency remains a major goal of the macroeconomic policy. The countrys strategy for attaining that goal by preserving the currency board and the existing parity of the exchange rate of the lev to the euro remains unchanged. What we should concentrate on is pursuing a policy of sustainably meeting the membership criteria. For the successful model of development of the Bulgarian economy of the last decade to be maintained and to have our country as a stable and predictable partner in the EU, it is necessary to further focus the economic policy on fiscal stability, streamlining the public sector and pursuing structural reforms, particularly in the education and healthcare sectors. The main economic policy directions, on which we are happy to have no differences with the current government, should be aimed at maintaining an adequate level of budget surplus and reducing the government debt; optimization of government spendings, and reorientation to investments in infrastructure and human capital; increasing the incentives for participation in the labour market, and reallocation of resources from social assistance to retraining and acquiring new knowledge and skills; pursuing a remuneration policy in the public sector, that is directly related to labour productivity in the overall economy, rather than generating inflationary pressures; simplifying regulations and licensing regimes and encouraging competition in various economic sectors; continuing with the policy of maintaining a conservative banking supervision framework and an adequate level of capital covering the credit risk accumulated in the system. The favourable domestic economic environment provided, in spite of the turmoil at the global markets, good conditions for growth in the banking sector and preserving its stability For 2007 the balance sheet of the banking sector is expected to increase by about 30% against the preceding year, reaching BGN 55 bill. The profit will probably reach up to BGN 1 bill., thus marking a growth of about 27% compared to 2006. As a result of the increasing interest rates in the euro area and the increased risk premium after mid-2007, and the growing minimum required reserves from the beginning of September, the cost of credit resources of commercial banks increased slightly (from an average of 2.6% for the first nine months of 2006 to 2.8% up to September 2007). In spite of these developments, the profit of the banking system continues to rise due to the considerable growth of credit, the increased profitability of the other interest-earning assets, and to a lesser extent to the very slight growth of interest rates on loans. This allowed for a growth of the return on assets (ROA) by September up to 2.51% (against 2.01% for the same period of the previous year), as well as of the return on equity (ROE)  up to 23.3% (against 21.7% for the nine months of 2006). In 2007, commercial banks managed to preserve the quality of their portfolios, even increasing the percentage of performing loans from 92.5% as of end-2006 to 94.9% as of September 2007  the best indicator in the recent two years. It should be noted, however, that the increased percentage of performing loans is to a great extent accounted for by the quick growth in the total amount of new loans, which are by rule performing. For the nine months of 2007, the absolute amount of classified loans grew by 24.8%, which indicates that the significant improvement of portfolio quality comes as a consequence of the rapid credit growth. The developments in the absolute amount of classified loans should be closely monitored by commercial banks, as it is a clear early signal of the changed capabilities of clients to take up and service new debt. The rapid growth of loan portfolios throughout the year was partially compensated by the increased bank capital, which resulted in a good capital adequacy for the system  13.9% as of September 2007. The domestic banking system remains stable, with an increasing number of households and companies having access to a growing number of banking services. BNB policies related to the Banking Industry Activities Over the year, the BNB continued with its transparent and consistent policy with regard to the banking industry. All central bank decisions were thoroughly discussed and properly communicated with the Bulgarian Bankers Association. As from the beginning of the year the credit growth rates in the private sector marked a stable increase, reaching almost 60% in October 2007 (63.2% of the GDP). Unlike the last two years, most of the newly granted loans were channelled to the corporate sector. This strong growth was based on the very optimistic outlook for the development of the Bulgarian economy following the countrys EU membership, which lead to a rapid investment growth. Although loan portfolios quality indicators have improved (mostly due to the rapid credit growth), the rapid growth of bank loans lead to accumulation of higher credit risk in the system. On the one hand, the level of risk in the banking system was increasing, on the other  the strong competition and market share race lead to loosening of loan standards and decrease of loan interest rates. The reduction of interest rates happened in a period of global increase of loan interest rates and tightening of credit standards. The real interest rates on households and corporate loans were and still are with values near zero or below. This creates unrealistic expectations with the borrowers, hence they underestimate the risk they are taking. It is only logical to expect the higher interest rates globally would, sooner or later, have an impact on the loan interest domestically. The credit market turmoil in the US and UK showed how important it is that the businesses and the general public have realistic expectations that loan interest rates not only decrease but may also increase. Thus, they will have a realistic idea of the amount of loan they could take up and service. The increase of the minimum required reserves at the beginning of September was a sign to the banking community that the Central Bank did not approve of such developments in credit activity. The strong momentum of lending in this country does not yet allow the effect of the raised minimum required reserves to show. The interest rate growth on the inter-bank market indicates that the improvement process has started and it will soon impact the credit activities of commercial banks in the manner aimed by the BNB. The Law on Credit Institutions introduced a number of amendments, which lead to significant changes in the regulation of the banking sector. An example of this is the rule of uniform banking passport, a broaden framework of supervisory, corrective, and strengthening measures, as well as the implementation of the new capital requirements, known as Basel II. The principle of uniform banking passport gave free admission to EU credit institutions on the Bulgarian banking market. Over the past few years, the extremely conservative policy of the BNB regarding the licensing of new banks was a strong support to commercial banks in attracting of promising partners. In order to provide further clarification for potential candidates for banking licenses, the Governing Council of the BNB adopted General Principles of the BNB Licensing Policy, where the Central Bank endorses yet again the principles of its licensing policy complied with over the recent years. Like I said a year ago, sudden changes in the operation of the banking sector are not to be expected after Bulgaria joins the EU. The high level of banking system integration achieved in Bulgaria accounted for the lack of mass entry of credit institutions from the member states into the Bulgarian market. Nevertheless, banks operating on the Bulgarian market should be prepared for competition pressure on the part of EU credit institution (either direct  by entering the Bulgarian market, or indirect  by attempts to acquire Bulgarian banks), which will force them to provide greater variety of services at lower prices. Moreover, the capital potential of every bank will be more important than ever, due not only to the new capital requirements, but also to its key importance for the long-term positioning, development and coping with the challenges of competition. In 2008, no significant changes in credit institutions regulatory framework are envisaged, except for the amendments to the Law on Credit Institutions, which introduce a new European directive on cross-border mergers and acquisitions of credit institutions. After the significant amendments made at the beginning of 2007, the overall framework will remain stable and generally unchanged over the next two years. The co-operation between the supervisory bodies of member states will increase, accentuating on the introduction of the lead supervisor principle. BNB will continue to closely monitor the banking credit growth rate. As I have already highlighted, the current growth rates of 60% may not be considered sustainable and posing no risk to the stability of the system. The lending standards are tightening on the international financial markets and this will inevitably affect the Bulgarian credit market. Currently the BNB follows very closely the adjustment of the local banking system to the changes at the international markets. At the same time, if this adjustment is not adequate, we are ready to implement additional measures to decrease the growth rates of banking credit down to more sustainable levels, which are significantly safer for the financial stability. In 2007 the BNB continued to fulfill its long-term Strategy for restructuring of cash circulation and adjusting it to market economy principles and the requirements of the ESCB. Over the year, a few very important stages of this strategy were completed. The BNB completed the preparation for the project and is commencing the construction of its own Cash Centre, where the cash operations of the entire system will be carried out away from the busy city centre of Sofia. Alongside with this, a new project begins with the joint participation of the largest commercial banks for the introduction of market principles governing the processing and recirculation of cash, which materialized through the incorporation of the Cash Services Company. All commercial banks participating in the project deserve to be complimented for their constructive participation and co-operation in the implementation of this extremely important for the future of the cash circulation project. A few key stages in the preparation of the companys operation were carried out, and it will gradually start providing services in five Bulgarian towns, namely, Sofia, Plovdiv, Varna, Burgas, and Pleven, in the first half of 2008. Alongside with the amendments in the regulatory framework, which have been carried out in 2006, the entering of private market participants, such as the company, in this market niche, provided a solid foundation for the development of a normally-functioning market of services related to cash circulation. The appropriate regulatory framework, the well-trained staff, and permanent constructive information exchange within the banking community in 2007, were important factors contributing to the improvements in the organization of cash circulation and the quality and frequency of currency used by the public. The payment services are among the significant activities to undergo further development. One of the important tasks for next year will be to transpose the 2007 Payment Service Directive. In order to keep the deadlines, we ought to prepare the draft amendments to be made to the regulatory framework  a new law on payments and the relative ordinances, starting from next year. The development of the Single Euro Payment Area project (SEPA) remains one of the greatest challenges. The successful integration of the Bulgarian banking system into this project is an important condition for the competitiveness of banks on the single European market of payment services. The membership of BBA in the European Payment Council is a significant step in the right direction. The BNB will continue guiding and supporting the development of payment services, both within the National Payment Systems Council, and in line with its own responsibilities and powers as a payments regulator. Dear colleagues, Before I finish, I would like to pay particular attention to the issue of the relations between banks and consumers of bank services. It has always been and will continue to be an issue of great importance to the BNB. If consumers of bank services are better informed about the credit costs and the risks resulting from accumulation of debt, this will guarantee that the two parties are placed on an equal footing in the negotiation process, and will preserve banking system stability. The crisis in the US mortgage market showed how creating in consumers unrealistic expectations as to the cost and conditions of credit can cause huge problems for banks and the economy as a whole. As I have stated times and again, it is beneficial for both consumers and the banking industry to maintain long-term relations based on transparency of financial services pricing, and strict performance of obligations by both parties, both as regards lending and the payment products and services. I do think that banks have to pay more attention to the feedback from clients (client complaints etc.), because the trust between the two sides, is the basis of success for the banking system. On behalf of the BNB Governing Council and myself, I would like to wish good health and lots of success to you personally and to the banks you are running in the on-coming 2008, as well as family well-being and happy holidays! Thank you for your attention. PAGE PAGE 5

Title: Speech at the spring meeting of the Bankers Association in Bulgaria, Sandanski
Subtitle:
TURBULENCES ON THE AMERICAN CREDIT MARKET
AND ITS INFLUENCE ON ECONOMIES ACROSS EUROPE
text: Speech by Mr. Ivan Iskrov, Governor of the BNB, at the spring meeting of the Bankers Association in Bulgaria, Sandanski, 16 May 2008 TURBULENCES ON THE AMERICAN CREDIT MARKET AND ITS INFLUENCE ON ECONOMIES ACROSS EUROPE Charachteristics of the Turbulances on the Global Markets (1) The tension on the international financial markets, unlike the turbulences and the crises in 1990s (Mexico 1994-95; Asia 1997-98, Russia 1998, Brazil 1999), started namely in a developed economy (USA) and not in a developing one. The problems in the USA are a result from low credit standards, distorted incentives for banks and borrowers due to the massive credit securitization, historically low interest rates in the USA, due to the Central banks policy and the high level of savings in Asia economies, and the rich-in-resources countries, which created a strong demand for such instruments. Last but not least important  weaknesses of the supervisory policy in the USA (above all weaknesses in the supervision of the so-called originators ) The disturbances in the USA were partially carried over to Europe and the rest of the world via the exposures of some banks (mainly investment banks) to American securities backed by sub-prime mortgages and revaluation of risk premiums for all countries and instruments. Due to the lack of information about commercial banks exposures there is a growing tendency in retaining liquidity and increasing the three-months interest rates. This lead to widening of the spread between the overnight and the three-months interest rates as well as an intensive short term liquidity lending by the main central banks (FED, ECB, Bank of England, Bank of Canada), including the introduction of new instruments for liquidity lending. Interest Rates in the Euro Area Short Term Interest in Great Britain Short Term Interest in the USA Sovereign Risk Premiums J.P.Morgan Emerging Market Bond Index Charachteristics of the Turbulances on the Global Markets (2) The initial expectations and speculations were, that turbulences in the USA will affect very quickly the developing markets, especially those with relatively high deficits on the Balance of Payments current account. This view was based on the general assumption that these economies need a strong inflow of capital, in order to cover the deficit on the current account, and in times of crisis the access to capital would be difficult. The above does not take into account the fact that these economies (Bulgaria included) have marked a strong inflow of direct investment, which created the deficit on the current account themselves, i.e. the relation is contrary to the general view. In addition, as by rule, these economies had a stable fiscal position, low public debt, favourable tax and business environment, growing productivity and relatively inexpensive labour. In effect the crisis did not stop the capital inflow to the fast-developing economies. Charachteristics of the Turbulances on the Global Markets (3)  The developing economies with stable macroeconomic policy continued to have access to global financial markets, as the crisis influence manifested itself mainly by increasing the risk premiums and the price of financing based on the market assumption that the risk for those economies have grown.  The risk premia for the new EU member states, measured by the spreads of their global bonds (JPMorgan Emerging Market Bond Index), have increased, again under the influence of the deeply rooted assumption, that countries with high deficit on the current account are a bigger risk, irrespective of the fact that their public debt is smaller, i.e. the risk of default is less probable for those economies. This is an irregularity caused by the automatic application of standard models by the participants on the market, without taking into consideration the driving factors of large deficits on the Balance of payments of those economies. Similar volatility showed the credit default swaps, driven by similar factors and line of though and analysis. The premiums on them grew quicker, but those instruments are less liquid and very often the data include only quotations, and not the actual transactions. Global Growth (IMF forecast for 2008 and 2009) Charachteristics of the Turbulances on the Global Markets (4) The second channel which could be considered a possible conduit for the USA pressure influence onto the developing economies, including the New Member States, is the international trade influence. The assumption, that the slowdown of the economic growth in the USA (or the recession) due to the very tightened access to credit, could lead to a slowdown in economic growth in the euro area and in Asia (mainly China). Historical data show strong dependence between the growth rates in the USA and in Europe. These correlations are also factual grounds of the IMF forecasts for a slowdown in the euro area growth rates. It is believed that, since the new EU member states, Bulgaria included, trade mainly within the euro area, then a potential slowdown in the growth could reduce the demand for goods from these countries and to influence negatively their export. In addition, there exist as well the assumption, that a great part of the foreign investment (including the direct and portfolio investments) in the countries are coming from the euro area economies, therefore the deterioration of access to credit in the euro area countries will probably influence the capital inflows in the new member states. Economic Growth of Bulgaria Fiscal Position of Bulgaria Inflation Rate in Bulgaria Bulgarian Balance of Payments Is Bulgarian Economy Influenced by Turbulences? (1) 2007 was the first year of Bulgarias membership in the EU. Citizens, companies and international investors were very optimistic about the development of the economy. By mid-2007 the external environment was quite favourable, and this together with the optimism of households and companies speeded up investing, employment, wages and the economic growth, as well as the falling rates of inflation due to the subsiding effect of the increased indirect taxes in early 2006. This beneficial environment considerably accelerated the private sector lending and the continuing increase in the current account deficit as a result of the massive inflows of capital. From July 2007 the inflation trend changed because of the higher prices of foodstuffs (determined by global and local factors), energy resources and the fast rise in wages which kept consumers demand at high levels despite the increased consumer prices. At the end of July 2007 the BNB Governing Council decided to raise, from the beginning of September, the minimum required reserves which commercial banks hold with the BNB  from 8 to 12 percent. As a result, commercial banks reserves with the BNB went up by BGN 1.8 billion. The purpose of this measure was to withdraw liquidity from the banking system and thus influence the cost of credit and the growth rate of credit, as well as store liquidity at the BNB. Sovereign Risk Premiums JPMorgan Emerging Market Bond Index Premiums on Credit Default SWAPS Short-term Interest Rates in Bulgaria and the Euro Area Quarterly Interest Rates in Bulgaria and the Euro Area Short-term Interest Rates in Bulgaria Is Bulgarian Economy Influenced by Turbulences? (2) Bulgarias fiscal position was stable, and the wage growth rate in the private sector was outpacing that in the public sector. In these conditions, at the beginning of August 2007 we saw the first disruptions in international financial markets. The spread on the Bulgarian global bonds, as a measure of the country risk market assessment, rose from 18 b.p. in mid-2007 to 150 b.p. at the beginning of 2008, and fell under 90 b.p. in the last few weeks (by the JPMorgan Emerging market Bond Index). The premiums on Bulgarias credit default swap also rose from about 20 b.p. in mid-2007 to nearly 150 b.p. at the end of the year. This trend carried on into the first three months of 2008 as the CDS premium for Bulgaria reached 200 b.p., and thereafter it fell to 140 b.p. in early May 2008. The turbulences in international markets directly affected short-term interest rates in the country. The average spread between the overnight rate in Bulgaria and that in the euro area from January to August 2007 was 1 b.p. (5 b.p. only for August). From September to December 2007 the spread increased to 48 b.p., and from early 2008 until now to 84 b.p. This spread increase was determined by several factors: Is Bulgarian Economy Influenced by Turbulences? (3) To a small extent (up to about 20 b.p.) as a result of the increased minimum reserve requirements, although the MRR in Bulgaria were higher than those in the euro area even before September 2007, but there was no premium in the Bulgarian short-term interest rates. Risk premiums increased because of the international financial turbulences and the greater uncertainty and speculations about its possible effect on the developing economies. Some commercial banks refrained from opening long positions in BGN and covered their purchases in Euro for BGN with spot repurchases. This groundless fear caused, as we already saw, by the speculative statements about the vulnerability of the countries having high current account deficits, led to a decrease in the BGN supply and an increase in the BGN interest rates. The ECB was massively providing liquidity and this brought the European market interest rates down even below the reference rate which contributed to widening the spread with the BGN interest rates. Interbank Market Volumes Net Currency Purchases by the BNB Is Bulgarian Economy Influenced by Turbulences? (4) On the whole, Bulgarian banks kept their trust of each other and the volumes in the interbank market even rose in early 2008, after a slight decline in the last quarter of 2007  due to some uncertainties as well as excess liquidity at the end of 2007 caused by end year government spending. The BNB is still buying the reserve currency (the euro) from commercial banks, and in 2007 these purchases reached a record level of Euro 2.5 billion (8.6% of GDP). This trend continued in the first four months of the year 2008. The banks operating in the country still have access to international financial markets. From August 2007 to March 2008 they increased their loans from abroad by Euro 2.2 billion. The expectations were that the new financing would be at a much higher cost. The data on the foreign loans (including the subordinated term debt) registered by commercial banks at the BNB do not show a large increase in the cost of funding from international markets. The data is very volatile but what we see as a trend is a very small rise in the cost of external financing. Access of Commercial Banks to International Markets Price of Foreign Financing of the Banking System (Based on data of the Balance of payments) Is Bulgarian Economy Influenced by Turbulences? (5) The increased uncertainty concerning the access to and the price of foreign financing, forced banks to enter into more severe competition regarding the local deposits, which have been growing in a steady rate. This lead to an increase in the price of local deposits (denominated both in BGN and in EUR) to a degree much higher that the price increase of foreign markets financing. The higher price of the commercial banks resource naturally reflected in the price of household and business loans  this trend is very explicit in the area of euro-denominated consumer loans and in the lev-denominated mortgage loans. Household Deposit Interest Rates Is Bulgarian Economy Influenced by Turbulences? (6) The higher price of loans, combined with the relatively high level of loan to GDP reached so far, creates conditions for the slow down of private sector credit growth rate. This development, was recommended by the BNB, and results both from the developments in the international financial markets and the BNB policy decision to increase the level of minimum required reserves. There was a slight slow down in the credit growth rate in the beginning of 2008 (the growth of household loans is also influenced to a small degree by portfolio sale, but adjusted for this effect there is a tendency of growth rate to slow down), and by the end of the year it is expected to be around 40%. The growth of loan interest rates does not lead to deteriorating of the quality of loan portfolios. The wage increase has a steady growth rate (around 17.6% in 2007). The profit in the corporate sector allows a higher interest expense to be made. Annual Percentage of Expenses on the Newly Granted Household Loans Credit Growth Rate Status of the Banking System (1) Despite the tension on the international markets, the favourable internal economic environment provided a good basis for the growth of the banking sector and preserving of its stability. As a consequence of the euro area interest rates increase and the reassessment of the risk premium over the second half of the year, as well as of the increase of minimum required reserves from the beginning of September the price of the commercial banks resource has gone up slightly (from the average of 2.6% in 2006 to 2.9% in 2007, and 3.4% in the first quarter of 2008). The banking system profit continue growing as a result of the increased volume of loans, the growth of yield on the rest of interest bearing assets, and to a very small extent due to the slight increase of loan interest rates. In 2007 the return on assets (ROA) grew to 2.37% (2.15% in 2006), and the return on equity (ROE) remained at a level close to the one it had over the past year  23.9% in 2007,( 23.7% in 2006). The quality of portfolios remain unchanged, and the percentage of the standard loans even grew from 93.9% at the end of 2006 to 95.4% as at 2007. Status of the Banking System (2) The fast loan portfolio growth over the year was compensated partially by the increase of bank capital, which lead to maintaining a good capital adequacy of the system - 13.9% as at 2007, from 14.5% at the end of 2006. These trends continued into the first quarter of 2008. The Bulgarian banking system is dominated by European banks, which had no direct exposures and suffered no losses from the turmoil in the USA mortgage market. Therefore they continued providing liquidity to their Bulgarian subsidiaries and branches. Bulgarian banks have no direct exposures of securities backed by sub-prime mortgage loans. Furthermore, the lending practices in the country are substantially different than the ones common for the USA over the past few years, and which are in the heart of current American problems. Bulgarian banks follow the classical model of banking, maintaining high credit standards, irrespective of the strong competition. Banks operating in Bulgaria, with domestic and foreign shareholders, are healthy, and have an adequate level of liquidity, capital adequacy and profits. Status of the Banking System 2006 2007 Q1/2008 Banking system assets, million BGN 42201 59094 59491 Banking system assets growth, % 28.3 40.0 33.6 Banking system profit, million BGN 786 1151 359 Banking system profit growth, % 37.2 46.4 50.2 Classified loans, % 6.08 4.56 4.81 Non-serviced loans, % 2.19 2.14 2.13 Capital adequacy, % 14.5 13.9 14.5 Return on assets (ROA), % 2.15 2.37 2.47 Return on equity (ROE), % 23.7 23.9 24.3 Liquidity, % 33.5 28.0 24.0 Economic Growth Expectations about the Development of the Bulgarian Economy (1) Current developments do not justify any presumptions that the instability in the global financial markets will have a tangible negative effect on the Bulgarian economy. Data for the first four months of 2008 show no signs of any negative developments in the countrys economy. As already mentioned, a process of risk reassessment is underway with a consequent upward trend in interest rates. This is a process of very gradual adaptation as part of the overall mechanism of operation of the currency board. This is the tenth month from the start of the turbulences in the international markets. This has been a sufficiently long period during which the Bulgarian economy demonstrated it was built on sound fundaments and there should be no doubts as to the adequacy of the countrys macroeconomic framework and policy. Naturally, there will always be institutions voicing negative or more conservative forecasts  the IMF among them. We believe some of these projections are unjustifiably pessimistic  a view already expressed by Mr. Bernanke and Mr. Trichet. Expectations about the Development of the Bulgarian Economy (2) The BNB has positive expectations for the economic developments in the current and the next year. We can already see some developments that confirm our view: The countrys fiscal position is stable and the tax revenues in the first quarter of the year are steady, as evidence that economic activity keeps growing at sustainable rates. Data to March show indications of stabilization and slight improvement of the BoP current account. The countrys exports have been growing at high rates, with decelerating growth rates of imports. Capital inflows, including FDIs remain strong. Inflation rate monthly data already show signs of abating inflationary impulses, which allows us to expect that inflation will decline to the range of six  seven percent by the year end. Conclusions (1) We evidence the first signs of remission of the financial market turmoil in the US, but it is still early to make any definitive conclusions. The Bulgarian economy demonstrated its resilience to the externalities of financial market developments and the commodity and food market dynamics. The macroeconomic framework  based on the fixed exchange rate of the lev to the euro within the currency board arrangement, prudent fiscal policy and the structural reforms  proved its sustainability and ability to ensure macroeconomic stability and growth. The currency board and the fixed exchange rate of the lev to the euro at the existing parity (BGN 1.95583 to EUR 1) will underlie the macroeconomic policy to be pursued by the time Bulgaria joins the euro area. Conclusions (2) The regular convergence reports of EC and ECB of May 2008 assessing the compliance with the convergence criteria and the consistency of national legal frameworks with regard to the monetary and economic union contain, in their part on Bulgaria, positive assessments of both our progress and of the degree of meeting convergence criteria. Inflation remains our fundamental challenge. The reports rightly underscore that the persistent strict fiscal discipline, the labour market reforms aimed at enhancing economic activity, the restructuring of the health and education systems, and the increased efficiency of public administration (including taking care salary growth not to outpace the rate of productivity growth) underlie the increase in productivity and efficiency in the economy and will help us meet the inflation criterion. In terms of convergence of the legal framework, although noting some specific imperfections, both reports stress that the Bulgarian legislation is compliant with the requirements for joining the EMU. The banking system is in a good condition, but we should not feel complacent. Instead, we should keep up the high level of credit standards. Banks belonging to international groups should not try to balance their weaker results in other parts of the world by pursuing a very aggressive credit policy in Bulgaria and trying to slacken their credit standards as the price for a bigger market share.
