Title: Speech delivered to the OTP Investor's Day Forum, Sofia
text: Speech by Mr. Ivan Iskrov, BNB Governor, delivered to the OTP Investor's Day Forum, Sofia, 18 September 2008 Dear Minister, Ladies and Gentlemen, It is a great honour for me to be here today and I would like to thank the organizers OTP and DSK Bank for the opportunity to present the BNB position on the development of Bulgarian economy to this investment forum. DSK Bank is among the pillars of the Bulgarian financial system, a bank with long-standing traditions in providing financial services in our country. As all of us know it definitely deserves the high confidence of the general public and businesses. It is a pleasure for me to take part in this forum, because the trust of international investors in individual financial institutions in Bulgaria means trust in the Bulgarian economy as a whole, as well as credibility of the economic policy. Principles of Bulgarias Macroeconomic Policy Nowadays investors pursue global strategies and invest in various countries and regions. We could say that globalization and economic integration result in convergence of business practices, economic policies and paradigms. At the same time, however, countries preserve their significant features in terms of institutional framework and macroeconomic policy. In many cases exactly these divergences are of determining importance. Investors should know well the framework in which the macroeconomic policy of Bulgaria is formulated and implemented. They should also understand the mechanisms of its operation in order to be able to adequately assess the investment opportunities and the risks entailed in them. Disregarding national specifics sometimes results in reports published by reputed institutions and renowned analysts who seem to draw ridiculous conclusions based on superficial comparisons of things that cannot be compared. The principles underlying the framework of the Bulgarian macroeconomic policy since 1997 are as follows: Fixed exchange rate of the Bulgarian lev pegged to the Euro under currency board arrangements. That means that the BNB international reserves always cover at least 100% of the reserve money and the deposit of the government with the central bank. The BNB buyes and sells the reserve currency unconditionally and at the pegged exchange rate upon any request by commercial banks and the general public. Independence of the central bank and full ban on financing the government or any other public entities. The central bank may act as a creditor of last resort only in the event of a systemic risk to the banking system. Prudent fiscal policy directed towards a balanced government budget or a budget surplus, reduced tax burden, government expenditure cuts down to 40% of GDP and increasing the share of investment spending. Implementation of structural reforms through privatization and liberalization of the economy. Reducing regulatory regimes and improving the business environment. Improving labour market flexibility and increasing incentives for participation in the labour market. Continuity and consistency. Three consecutive governments since 1997, each appointed by a different parliamentary majority, have kept to these macroeconomic principles. These governments cover the whole political spectrum  from Christian democrats through liberals to socialists. In other words, there is a consensus in society on the principles of our macroeconomic policy, oriented to maintaining macroeconomic stability and sustainable economic growth. Predictability. All main political forces, and the central bank, have clearly declared that the currency board and the fixed exchange rate will underlie the macroeconomic policy until Bulgaria joins the Euro area. Thus the predictability stems from the above  mentioned consensus and our positive experience of the last 11 years. Since 1997 the framework of the macroeconomic policy makes the economy very robust and allows our country to quite easily adapt to any changes in the domestic and international environment. To those not well familiar with the currency board regimes or those who still doubt their resilience to pressures and external crises, I would like to remind that since the mid  90s the world has been faced with unprecedented challenges and even crises which we survived. I will not enumerate them because you know them. I will just mention some of the main ones. Those are: the liberalization of financial markets and revolution in the information and telecommunications technologies the integration of millions of people from Southeast Asia and Central and Eastern Europe into the global labour market the formation of the single European market, the enlargement of the European Union and establishment of the Economic and Monetary Union in Europe the slowdown of the global economic growth, the September 11 terrorist attacks and the burst of the dot.com bubble the war in Iraq, and the unprecedented rise in energy prices and global disbalances of the recent years the credit crunch underway in the international credit markets as a result of the US subprime mortgage crisis. Therefore, it is crucial for investors to know that irrespective of any turmoil globally, the Bulgarian economy will continue to adapt as it has done so far, under the conditions of the existing currency board arrangements. This is because economic integration between individual countries, and in particular the financial markets integration, significantly reduces the possibilities of central banks of small and highly open economies to pursue a successful discretionary policy. Their behaviour may not significantly diverge from the one of the major central banks (ECB and the Federal Reserve). This is particularly obvious in the case of small and open EU-member economies. In their case there is a very high degree of economic and financial integration and considerable capital inflows, which result in the countries with floating rate in a long-term appreciation of the nominal exchange rate. The nominal exchange rate appreciation in these economies has an anti-inflationary role. It comes, however, not as a consequence of the national monetary policy, but as a result of the inflow of foreign direct investments determined by structural factors (such as return on equity). These arguments make us highly skeptical as to the potential of the independent monetary policy in a small and highly integrated economy. The Bulgarian approach to attaining macroeconomic equilibrium is aimed at achieving maximum flexibility of all markets, however, keeping the exchange rate unchanged. This is our permanent anchor. Since 2007, the developments in the economy have been determined by two important factors  Bulgarias membership in the European Union and the global financial markets crisis starting in August 2007. Bulgaria is a small and open economy highly integrated in the global economy. Hence, the EU accession and the turmoil in the global financial markets inevitably affect the dynamics of the Bulgarian economy. Our countrys EU membership was accompanied by an increase of optimism among households and companies, accelerated capital inflows, higher investments in the economy (internal and external), higher employment rate, growth of wages, as well as accelerated rate of credit growth for the private sector. At the same time, the global financial market disturbances triggered by the US credit crunch and its subsequent spillover across Europe and other parts of the world led to increased risk aversion and the subsequent increase of risk premiums. The initial expectations and speculations were that the turbulences in the USA would hit very quickly the emerging markets, especially those with relatively high deficits on their balance of payments current account. This view was based on the theory that these economies need strong capital inflows to finance their current account deficits, and in times of crises the access to capital would be hampered. However, it did not take into account the fact that the fast developing economies from the so-called emerging markets have received strong direct investment inflows that was itself the cause of the current account deficit, i.e. the relationship is contrary to the standard view. Bulgaria is a typical example in this respect. Moreover, the Bulgarian economy is characterized by a stable fiscal position, low public debt, favourable tax and business environment and growing productivity together with relatively cheap labour cost. Due to those factors, in practice the crisis did not stop the capital inflow to the fast developing Bulgarian economy. The effect of the crisis resulted mainly in higher risk premiums and cost of funding due to the increased risk aversion. Main macroeconomic challenges Approaching the end of the second year of Bulgarias EU membership we can say that in our projections we somewhat underestimated the positive effect of our EU membership. It appears that it has been affected to a much lesser degree by the global financial market turbulences. The major challenge turned out to be prevailingly the mobilization of our internal capacity to administrate the European programmes  difficulties that are typical for any new EU member. But this is a subject of another discussion. Economic growth and investments continue to increase steadily regardless of the problems faced by international financial markets and the signs of moderation of the economic growth in the Euro area. Quite often, however, the main comments on the development of the Bulgarian economy focus largely on the imbalances formed in the process of quickly growing investment activity, employment and economic growth. The imbalances most often cited are the deficit on the balance of payments current account, the inflation rate and the growth of lending to the private sector. Attention to these imbalances is largely justified as both investors and we, the people in charge of the economic policy in the country, would like the favourable developments of the economy to be on a stable footing. At the same time, however, not giving due consideration to the policies that address and mitigate these imbalances (fiscal consolidation and discipline, structural policies, policy promoting the economic activity and labour market flexibility, conservative and stringent supervision of the banking sector, etc.) leads to overestimating risk factors. In order to understand the potential risks of the current account deficit we should study the nature of it, e.g. : Bulgarias exports have been growing every year since 2000 (at an annual average rate of 10% in real terms). Bulgaria is among the few countries with a steadily growing market share of its exports in the EU imports. The trade deficit, which is the main factor driving the current account deficit is neither the result of low competitiveness of the countrys export sectors, nor of an unsustainable boom of household consumption. The current account deficit is the result of the relatively low yet stable level of savings in the economy, which generates a certain shortage of capital and leads to a very high return on capital. The predictability and stability of the macroeconomic policy, and the EU membership created conditions for foreign capital to fill in the savings gap in the Bulgarian economy and gain a relatively high return at a continuously decreasing risk in our economy over the last 11 years. (For example, the average return on the DSK Bank capital in the last three years is 36.4%, compared to an average of 16.9% for the EU banking system. Furthermore, DSK Bank can boast an excellent CAMELS rating according to the strictest supervisory standards). Investments in Bulgaria increased from 9.9 % of GDP in 1997 to 36.8% in 2007, while preserving savings at the stable level of around 15% of GDP. Of course, in addition to this main structural factor the continuously growing prices of commodities over the last five years have also had an impact on the widening current account deficit. The current year developments do not differ substantially from the above described long-term trend. As a natural consequence from the continuing high investment activity and the strong capital inflows, as well as the sharp increase in energy prices in the second quarter of 2008, the year-on-year current account deficit until July reached around 23% of GDP. At the same time, however, Bulgaria continues to attract record high FDI even at a time when the international financial markets are going through a very hard period. For the first seven months of 2008 the FDI account for EUR 2.85 billion and are expected to reach EUR 6.5 billion by the end of the year (that is 20 % of GDP). The high level of deficit calls for continuous efforts for enhancing the competitiveness of the economy by means of continuous improvement of the investment environment, the quality of the human capital and the operation of public institutions, and balancing the shortage of savings in the economy by pursuing a prudent and well-considered fiscal policy. Another often discussed macroeconomic issue is the relatively high rate of growth of consumer prices over the last year. The inflation dynamics in developing economies such as Bulgaria is conditioned by two main factors: the long-term trend of convergence of price levels to those in the advanced economies, and short-term cyclical factors triggered by the developments of the international prices and monetary policies of the major central banks. The dynamic growth of wages and domestic demand coupled with the global increase in energy and food prices and the severe drought, which affected badly the harvest in Bulgaria, exerted a strong pressure on the overall level of prices in 2007, with the end-of-year inflation reaching 11.6%. The increase in food prices contributed to 60% of the inflation in 2007, while 10% were due to the increase of the prices of energy commodities. Since the beginning of 2008 we have seen a slower monthly growth in prices as a result of the exhausted effect of past surges in food prices in the preceding year. However, trend of slowdown in inflation rates is somewhat neutralized by the surge in energy prices. For the first eight months of 2008 the accumulated inflation is 7.1%. It comes from the higher prices of foodstuffs (0.6 %), the higher prices in the catering sector (1.2%) and the higher prices of fuels and transportation (2.1%). Although wages are still rising steadily (by 24% on annual basis for the first six months of 2008) and energy prices stay at relatively high levels, we expect that at the end of 2008 inflation would drop to about 8%. Just like inflation, the banking credit dynamics in developing economies, such as Bulgaria, is determined by two basic factors: the long-term upward trend of financial intermediation and its convergence to the levels in the advanced economies (especially in very open financial systems); short-term and cyclical factors caused by the major central banks monetary policies and investors risk appetite. The favourable domestic economic environment in the last two years, despite the disturbances in international markets, was a good basis for growth and stability in the banking sector. The beneficial macroeconomic environment in 2007 significantly speeded up the lending to the private sector, and at the end of the year the growth rate reached 62.5 %. In July 2007 the BNB Governing Council made the decision to raise the minimum reserve requirements from 8 % to 12 %. As a result of this measure commercial banks reserves at the BNB increased by 50% from the beginning of September 2007. Because of the higher interest rates in the Euro area, the higher risk premiums required after mid-2007, as well as the increased minimum reserves requirements, commercial banks cost of funds went up from 2.6% on average for 2006 to 2.9% for 2007 and 3.4% for the first six months of 2008. The greater uncertainty about the access to foreign financing and its cost resulted in higher competition among banks for domestic deposits which are growing at a stable pace. This drove up the cost of domestic deposits (both in BGN and in Euro) much above the increase of the cost of funding from the international markets. Commercial banks higher cost of funding was clearly translated into the cost of credit for households and companies. Since the beginning of 2008 we have seen a slow down in credit growth rates, and by the end of this year they are expected to reach nearly 40%. Due to the above-mentioned reasons, the BNB decided to discontinue the policy of increasing minimum reserve requirements. It should be noted that the rise of interest rates has not yet worsened the performance of loans. This is because wages are still going up steadily and profits in the corporate sector are at levels allowing the absorption of the higher interest expenses. Performance of the banking system The Bulgarian banking system is dominated by reputed European banks (81% of the total assets) which did not suffer from the turbulences in the US mortgage markets. Therefore, they have continued to provide liquidity to their subsidiaries and branches in Bulgaria. Bulgarian banks have no direct exposures to subprime mortgage-backed securities. Moreover, the lending practices in Bulgaria drastically differ from those in the USA. The originate  to - distribute model is not typical for Bulgaria Our banks follow the classical banking model, maintaining stringent credit rules, irrespective of the strong competition. The profits in the banking system are still on the increase due to the considerable rise in the volume of loans, the higher yields on the other interest-bearing assets, as well as the higher interest rates on loans. Return on equity (ROE) by mid-2008 went up to 24.3% (against 23.9% for 2007), and return on assets (ROA) remained at levels close to that of the preceding year - 2.4% until June 2008 (against 2.37% for 2007). The quality of credit portfolios remains the same, and the percentage of standard loans is steadily 95.5%. The fast growth rate of credit portfolios over the last two years has been partially offset by the increased bank capital, which helped for maintaining good capital adequacy of the system  13.9% at end-2007. The interbank market, both secured and unsecured, is operating smoothly at a good level of liquidity in the banking system. Ladies and Gentlemen, In conclusion I would like to draw your attention to an important issue for all investors in Bulgaria  the adoption of the Euro. With the Accession Treaty Bulgaria committed itself to adopting the single currency. We do not have an opt-out clause, and for us the adoption of the Euro is not a possible option or privilege. It is a duty. That is why the accession to the Euro area and the adoption of the Euro as legal tender in Bulgaria is the primary goal of our macroeconomic policy. Since 2004 Bulgaria has been pursuing a strategy for accomplishing this task. This strategy is based on keeping the currency board arrangements and the current parity of the Bulgarian Lev to the Euro until the adoption of the single currency. This is a transparent, predictable and legitimate in terms of EU legislation strategy. We have never and in no way doubted the implementation of the above legitimate strategy. Discussing other options indicates either lack of knowledge of the national policy, or poor interpretation, or just speculation. What we focus on is pursuing a macroeconomic policy that would allow us in the shortest possible period to meet the Maastricht criteria on a sustainable basis. As you can see from the development of the Bulgarian economy since 1997, Bulgaria has been consistently in compliance with four of the five criteria for Euro area membership. For the time being the inflation criterion remains the biggest challenge. The experience gained from the enlargement of the Euro area (mostly that of Slovenia and Slovakia) shows that overcoming inflation with our strategy would maybe be more difficult then expected. Nevertheless, in terms of sustainably meeting this criterion and adapting our economy to the next stage, the currency board arrangements come closest to the environment in which a small Euro area member-state operates. Thank you for your attention. PAGE PAGE 2

Title: Speech before the Third Annual Meeting of the Business and the Government The Financial Crisis: Bulgaria in the Global Economy, Sofia
Subtitle: THE FINANCIAL CRISIS AND BULGARIA
text: Speech of Mr. Ivan Iskrov, Governor of the Bulgarian National Bank, before the Third Annual Meeting of the Business and the Government The Financial Crisis: Bulgaria in the Global Economy, Sofia, 28 October 2008 THE FINANCIAL CRISIS AND BULGARIA Global Financial Crisis Impacts The global financial crisis still has a limited impact on Bulgarias economic indicators. However, after the failure of Lehman Brothers and the developments in the US and some euro area countries, there are signs of increasing indirect effects of the global crisis on the Bulgarian economy. And this is not a consequence of any serious problems in specific sectors of the Bulgarian economy that have surfaced now. This comes as the result of the developments after September 15, which brought about a complete loss of confidence between the financial institutions in the US and Europe, and the lack of clear prospects for solution of the problems faced by these economies. It was the lack of clear prospects for the resolution of the crisis in the United States and Europe that led to foreign investors growing conservatism. This lack underlying the potential slowdown in the capital inflows  as should be clearly understood is not any fault of the Bulgarian economy but of the economies of foreign investors home countries  increased investors conservatism and risk premiums. The first bout of the crisis involved the stock exchanges worldwide. From the beginning of 2008, the stock exchanges worldwide fell  in the range from 10% in Slovakia to 80% in Ukraine. Due to the global uncertainty and decreasing liquidity, domestically the indices and daily turnover started a downward trend from October 2007. In the period from mid-October 2007 to mid-October 2008, the SOFIX index lost almost 70% of its value. The increasing risk perceptions and the lower liquidity globally affected commercial banks' behaviour. Since the last quarter of 2007, the interbank market interest rate spreads against the euro area interest rates started growing. In mid-October 2008, the spread between the LEONIA and EONIA indices reached up to about 250 basis points compared to the levels below 20 basis points in mid-2007. As a result of the amendments made by the BNB last week to the Ordinance on Minimum Required Reserves, the demand for short-term liquidity decreased and the spread shrank to 176 basis points. Similar dynamics are seen in the lending and deposit interest rates, which have also been growing in the recent months. On 21 October the BNB Governing Council approved amendments to the Ordinance on the Minimum Required Reserves, and its publication in Darzhaven Vestnik is pending. However, the signals that the interbank market interest rates have exceeded our expectations came on 16 and 17 October. Publicizing the pending changes had an immediate impact on the money market and the average interest rate started decreasing (LEONIA dropped from 6.37 % on 17 October to 5.29 % yesterday - 27 October). Foreign direct investments in Bulgaria were also affected by the crisis. A comparison of the initially published estimates in relation to Bulgaria indicates a 10% growth of FDI in the first half of 2008 against the same period in 2007. At the same time, the growth of FDI in the first half of 2007 against the same period of 2006 was 67.6%. In July and August 2008, there is a decrease in the FDI compared to the same months of 2007, and since the beginning of the yer the direct investment inflows to the real estate sector have been diminishing. The impact of some one-off factors should be taken into consideration in this regard  such as the privatization of the Rousse Thermal Power Station, the purchase of DZI, and other transactions which boosted the FDI last summer. The global crisis had a positive impact on fuel and food prices in international trade. The decrease in a number of international prices in the recent months influenced the inflation in Bulgaria, and in August and September pushed down the inflation of fuel prices. Probably such an impact will be evidenced in the prices of transport services and food in the coming months. The crisis in the global financial markets does not impact directly the balance sheets of Bulgarian banks, as their credit activities are targeted towards the Bulgarian economy and they have no exposures in US securities. The main channels of influence of the crisis on the Bulgarian economy are as follows: The Bulgarian economy will be directly impacted by the expected decrease of external demand as a result of the slowdown in the US and euro area growth rates, which will probably limit the growth rate of Bulgarian exports. The decrease in the foreign capital inflows, both in the form of direct investments and of loan funding, will be reflected in a weaker investment activity and deceleration of credit growth in the economy. The diminished capital inflow, combined with the higher interest rates, will result on their part in a limited access to lending and possible deceleration of domestic demand (mainly through the lower growth rates of investment and to a smaller extent of consumption) If global liquidity conditions deteriorate further, there is the risk of continuous upward trend in domestic interest rates. At this stage, however, just the opposite signs are evidenced. In the middle of the month, the governments of US, EU, and other countries affected by the crisis voiced their obvious political will to fully support their systemically important banks, while the five largest central banks made commitments to provide unlimited liquidity at a lower price. In practice, this brought the end of the so-called financial crisis and we started talking of a decrease in growth and employment, i.e. of potential recession in the developed economies and slowdown in the growth rates of developing economies, including Bulgaria. The fourth channel of influence on our economy is the decrease in international prices as a consequence of the crisis. It will be reflected in lower prices of Bulgarian exports and imports. The effect of these processes on the conditions of trade will probably be neutral or even slightly positive, and as a spill-over effect it will be transmitted over to domestic prices and will facilitate the decrease in inflation rates in the country. Risks to the Bulgarian economy as a result of the crisis The main risk to the Bulgarian economy is lower GDP growth as a result of the effects described above  decrease in the foreign capital inflows or exodus of capital from the country, which will cause a significant deceleration of investment and credit activity. This would probably lead to a relatively rapid reduction of the BOP trade account deficit and current account deficit, accompanied by shrinking employment in certain sectors of the economy. If the developments described in the above risk scenario continue in a longer-term horizon, further effects can be expected along the line of price and labour market dynamics. Under such circumstances, we will probably have minimum inflation or even periodically deflation, as well as lower employment, increased unemployment and holding back wage growth. The policy pursued by the government and the central bank for mitigating the effects of the crisis As evidenced by the experience in the developed and developing economies, the main channels for response to the crisis are under the control of the government and the private sector. Minister Oresharsky discussed in detail the possibilities open to the fiscal policy to respond to the negative developments in the global economy. I will only add that both in the recent decade and in the current uncertain environment, fiscal policy will have a leading role. The difference is that today it will not be as simple as to continue maintaining a budget surplus and to support sound public finances. In 2009, Bulgaria will have to restructure its budget spending so as to avoid funding projects involving significant outflows of international reserves. Costly public investments in sectors which do not boost productivity in the economy should be postponed. If the scenario of decelerated economic growth becomes a fact in 2009, we should not expect it to dramatically influence the stability of the domestic financial system. As we have often emphasized, the Bulgarian banking system is well regulated and capitalized and enjoys a high level of liquidity. The September data indicate that: The profit of the banking system continues to grow, coming up to BGN 1100 million. Compared to the same period of 2007, profit has increased by 29%. By the year end it is expected to increase to BGN 1500 million. The return on equity (RO) and the return on assets (RO) remain at a very good level, 24.5% and 2.32%, respectively. The portfolio quality is preserved, with a percentage of standard loans as high as at the end of 2007 - 95.04 percent. The capital adequacy of the banking system remains high  14.35%. The liquidity in the banking system remains high  22.3%. September 2008 data indicate that the unfavourable conditions worldwide have had no impact so far on the portfolio quality and the level of profitability of the Bulgarian banking system. Furthermore, the positive development so far has created considerable buffers (both in terms of capital and liquidity), which can be used in 2009, so that any potential deceleration of domestic economic growth would not result in a serious pressure on the financial stability in the country. It is very important that the business, households and foreign investors know that, no matter what changes and shocks may occur globally, the Bulgarian economy will continue to adapt under the conditions of the existing currency board arrangement (CBA). The monetary and supervisory policies of the BNB under the CBA, as is the practice of the recent eleven years, can and will have only a supporting role in the process of adjustment of the Bulgarian economy to the effect of negative external factors. The main contribution of the BNB to counteracting the crisis is its effort for supporting and ensuring the stable operation of the currency board regime in the country. The currency board is an important policy tool, which eliminates such an important source of uncertainty in the economy as the exchange rate, thus facilitating the decision-making of economic entities. With the instruments available to the BNB, we have always acted anticyclically in the recent years. In a period of rapid economic growth and strong optimism of companies, households and foreign investments, the BNB tightened prudential regulations to ensure a more sound capital base and buffers in the Bulgarian banking system, and to curb credit growth. In the coming period when we may possibly face an economic growth deceleration and slowdown of capital inflows into the country, the BNB can be expected to take actions not to allow quick deceleration of the rates of growth of lending to the private sector, and to calm down interest rate growth. The recent eleven years, in which the Bulgarian economy managed to achieve macroeconomic stability and high rates of economic growth evidenced lots of shocks in the global economy. Bulgaria managed to go through all the turmoil. What is different today is that the crisis started from the most developed economy in the world and it is of a magnitude much exceeding initial expectations. All of us, private sector, government, mass media, should realize clearly our responsibility, so that Bulgaria preserves its stability and economic growth. Thank you for your attention. PAGE PAGE 2

Title: Speech before the Association of Banks in Bulgaria on the occasion of the Bankers day, Sofia
text: Speech of the BNB Governor Mr. Ivan Iskrov before the Association of Banks in Bulgaria on the occasion of the Bankers day, Sofia, 4 December 2008 The recent seventeen months were extremely stressful and difficult for the financial industry worldwide. Governments, central banks, regulators, analysts and the academia will yet try to determine the factors that caused this situation, and to define the necessary changes in the global and national financial systems, with the aim to limit the possibility of turbulences of such magnitude happening in the future. I will try to summarize from a more pragmatic perspective the conclusions from the developments since August 2007, and to answer the question about the consequences thereof for the Bulgarian financial system and economy. As we are all very well aware, the crisis in the international financial markets had no direct effect on the balance sheets of Bulgarian banks, as their credit activities were targeted at the Bulgarian economy and they have no exposures in US securities or to US institutions, which suffered losses as a result of their investments in such instruments. After the bankruptcy of Lehman Brothers in mid-September 2008 and the later developments in the US and in some euro area countries, however, we evidenced a notable indirect effect of the global financial crisis on the Bulgarian banking system and economy. This impact is in the form of limited access to new financing and considerable increase in the price of external financing. As a result of the downturn of economic activity of our main trade partners, the inflow of FDI to the country decelerated and a decrease is observed in the external demand for Bulgarian goods. These developments, however, should by no means be perceived as dramatic. They should be viewed as a painful but normal cycle of adjustment of the Bulgarian economy to the adverse developments in the international financial markets and the global economy. For a period of eleven years Bulgaria has pursued a policy of reforms, fiscal consolidation and accumulation of reserves, strengthening of the capital base and banking sector regulation. Now is the time when these reserves should be used prudently. As can be seen from the recent year, the developing economies, including Bulgaria, are at a quite better starting position with regard to coping with the current crisis, compared to most of the developed economies. This is so because our countries managed to learn their lessons from the crises of the second half of 1990-ies. Now I will discuss the conceptual conclusions we can make from the developments in the world financial markets in the recent seventeen months: Firstly, the assessment and perception of market participants of the level of risk turned to be highly procyclical  in good times we are prone to underrate the risk, and in difficult ones  to overrate it. There is a propensity to turn from one extreme to the other. In the transition years I used to warn you that it is not prudent to move at a very high speed if you want to reach from point A to point B, because of the risk to run off the track. Now I want to draw your attention to the fact that putting on the brake is not a bit less dangerous. The innovative instruments and products have a great profit potential, and this exactly is the incentive for innovation in the market economies. The new instruments and products, however, have a potential for incurring losses, as their features are not well known and tested both in an environment of growth, and of market downturn. This is true not only for financial innovations  remember the burst of the tech bubble in 2001. Therefore, regulators should pay greater attention to sophisticated financial instruments, and where necessary to require more available capital for covering risks entailed in these products. Mutual control among market participants is an important mechanism underlying the market economy, but it cannot be a substitute of the regulators role  particularly when market participants expose to risk the funds of the entire society. Obviously, the global process of financial deregulation, such as we have known it in the recent 20-25 years, is over. Stringent capital requirements and the sound banking system capital base ensuing from them are the most important preconditions for the existence of a sound financial system. Such a policy not only builds up capital buffers against adverse developments in the financial markets that are hard to predict, it also limits excessive risk assumption by the banks. Last but not least, I would like to emphasize that not only the monetary but also the regulatory policy of central banks should be of anticyclical nature. This is a principle well known to all market participants, but in good times they see only the arguments against implementing it. Remember, for example, how many opinions, even of people from the banking industry, have been voiced against the BNBs policy of tightening liquidity and prudential regulations since 2003. Today we hear only the arguments in favour of slackening of regulations, and of doing it immediately and at any cost. Has anyone asked himself the question  what if these regulations were not tightened in the period of rapid growth, what potential for slackening would there be today, in a period of economic slump? Exactly this was the rationale behind the policy pursued by the BNB since 2003  to act anti-cyclically accentuating on maintaining high the level of liquidity and capital adequacy in the banking system. We gradually tightened the provisioning rules, the capital requirements, and increased the minimum reserve requirements. In a period of rapid economic growth and buoyant optimism of companies, citizens, and foreign investors, the BNB kept tightening regulations to restrict credit growth rates and ensure a more sound capital base, and a capita cushion for the Bulgarian banking system. Today very few countries can pride themselves on the indicators featured by the Bulgarian banking system. Despite the weaker development in the current fourth quarter, we expect a 15% growth of the 2008 balance sheet of the banking sector against the previous year, thus reaching BGN 68 billion. Profit will probably reach BGN 1.5 billion, thus registering almost a 30% growth on 2007. As a result of the increasing risk premium of the country and the increased cost of domestic deposits, the average cost of resources for the commercial banks increased from 2.92% on the average for 2007 to 3.65% in October 2008, which resulted in a very slight contraction of the net interest margin of the banking system (4.94% in October 2008). In spite of this development, the profit in the banking system continues to grow due to the significant increase in the amount of loans in the recent five years and the increasing interest rates on loans in the last twelve months. This allowed for preserving the return on assets (ROA, 2.3%) and return on equity (ROE, 24%) at their last years levels. In 2008, commercial banks managed to maintain the high quality of their portfolios, preserving the percentage of nonperforming loans at a level near to the one of the end-2007 (2.03% in September 2008). Loan portfolio growth throughout the year was partially compensated by the increased bank equity, which raised the capital adequacy of the system to 14.4% in September 2008, against 13.9% at the end of 2007. The liquidity in the banking system remains at a good level, and is expected to stay in the range of 18-20% by the end of 2008. In the coming 2009, the BNB will continue pursuing the anticyclical policy in the area of minimum reserves of banks, and capital adequacy regulation and provisioning norms implemented so far. Now that we see there will be some deceleration of foreign capital inflow and domestic economic growth, the BNB is taking measures to take the edge off the commercial banks. In October and November, the BNB made amendments to the Ordinance on Minimum Required Reserves, thus giving commercial banks some leeway for flexibility in the access to their liquid assets. Additional alleviations will be effective from January 2009, as already announced. In practice from the beginning of 2009 the average effective amount of the minimum required reserves for the whole banking system will be reduced to about 7.2%. This however should by no means be interpreted as a signal to banks to keep their liquidity at lower levels. The reduced minimum required reserves on funds from abroad will encourage attracting additional external resources to our banking system. We intend to make amendments to the provisioning ordinance in the direction of bringing the provisioning requirements near to those prior to the strong acceleration of the credit growth rate. By this change commercial banks will be allowed greater flexibility in managing their portfolios and in their relations with their customers, which will ease the process of renegotiation of maturity terms in the conditions of a complicated economic environment. We intend to make amendments to the capital adequacy ordinance in the direction of increasing the share of primary capital to reach the minimum level of 10%. In addition, the BNBs policy will be aimed at creating incentives - and if needed requirements - to the banks for the capitalization of the 2008 profit. Implementing such a policy of relaxed regulations, the BNB will expect from the commercial banks to keep their liquidity and capital adequacy at sufficient levels, with an emphasis on primary capital adequacy, while advising them not to be misled by the attitude of changing over from excessive optimism to utmost pessimism evidenced in the society. The actions planned by the BNB will add to the commercial banks flexibility thus enabling them to relatively more easily absorb potential losses from deterioration of their credit portfolios as a result of the lower rates of economic growth in 2009. Here I would explicitly stress that the BNB monetary and supervision policy under a currency board, both over the last eleven years and henceforth, can and will play only a supportive role in the process of adjustment and development of the Bulgarian economy. It could be expected that the BNB will maintain, just as it so far has, the stability of the lev by means of the currency board arrangement and the stability of the banking system through its supervision policy. For the Bulgarian economy to pass less painfully through the current economic crisis, not only the BNB, but the Government and every firm and household as well, must take relevant individual steps to optimize and attune their activities to the temporary less favourable external and internal economic environment. We do not need to be pessimistic, yet a bit more realism would not be too much. Of key importance in 2009 will be the view of international market participants on the risks and the development in our region, Bulgaria in particular. I certainly believe that the international banks represented in Bulgaria should take a more definitive stand regarding the outlook for the Bulgarian economy. It is hardly possible that anywhere, either locally or abroad, more data and knowledge exist about the state of the Bulgarian economy than the information available at the commercial banks. These are the institutions, which are familiar with the balance sheets of firms and households and which, based on in-depth analysis, finance our economy. We cannot take seriously analysts, sitting in London and dedicating 30 minutes per month to look at the data on the Bulgarian economy, to determine the view on risks in the Bulgarian economy and the outlook for its development. This has a negative impact not only on foreign investors, but also on the assessment of the risk level in the Bulgarian economy, which parent banks use in drawing up their plans and the cost of funding. Risk managers in the banks in Bulgaria should be more active in the process of the countrys risk assessment. I would also dare recommend to the Bulgarian media to use more critical judgment when recreating the opinions of well-known or not so well-known smart-alecky analysts and often outright speculators. Do not let others form your opinion on the Bulgarian economy, or use you as a mailbox only because they happen to live in London or Vienna and write for the global media. Have self-confidence and be critical. There is no way that they can be better informed about the Bulgarian economy, anyway. In 2008 we completed an important phase of the reforms towards implementing market principles in the cash-cycle area. In April the Cash Cervices Company (CSC) that was set up the previous year effectively started offering services to the commercial banks. By mid June its five units started operation. Almost two-thirds of the banks operating in Bulgaria have already signed agreements with the CSC and use its services to one extent or another. The competitive environment created conditions not only for enhancing the quality of services and gradually adjusting their prices, but the quality of the cash cycle improved significantly as well, so that now it already conforms to a much greater extent to the BNB requirements as introduced with Ordinance No 18. The Central Bank will continue to be involved in the project for creating a cash-cycle services market. In 2009 other commercial banks will also be invited to join as shareholders in the CSC. The dynamic development of credit activities determines the need for gathering more extensive and better quality information in the Central Register system. This required redesigning of the Register. With the current amendments to the Law on Credit Institutions the Central Credit Register will cover all institutions engaged in credit activities as a line of business and registered with the Central Bank. Expanding the Registers scope allows for a better assessment of the credit risk and the behaviour of credit applicants. Renovating the CCR information system will enable a better assessment of the creditworthiness of loan applicants and will improve the control over the credit risk. In February 2008 the amendments to the BNB Law on Funds Transfers, Electronic Payment Instruments and Payment Systems and Ordinance No 3 provided for the necessary legal and technical details related to licensing and activities of cash transfer companies. In October 2008 the Governing Council of the Bulgarian National Bank issued licenses for cash transfer activities on the territory of the Republic of Bulgaria to six companies. The payment services market will undergo considerable changes in 2009 with the forthcoming adoption of a new Law on Payment Services and Payment Systems. The new legal framework will expand the competition on this market by allowing non-bank institutions to render payment services as well. The new law will introduce clear information requirements, as well as rights and obligations for providers and their clients in rendering payment services, which are largely aimed at user protection. An important step in the development and improvement of the payment mechanisms in the country is the BNB decision on launching a project for joining the TARGET2 payment system before adopting the euro as a national currency. Joining TARGET2, which we expect to occur in 2009, will bring about optimization of the countrys payment process, thus improving liquidity management and achieving higher speed and security of euro funds transfers. The new 2009 promises to be a year of ample challenges for our whole society, the banking sector and the BNB in particular. The positive in each crisis is that besides a beginning it also has an ending. Over its thousand years of history our country has gone through all sorts of trials and has always managed to survive. Over our recent 130-year history numerous persons and institutions have come and gone; weve passed through a number of difficult periods, wars including. All those years, one institution has invariably stood at its post as a fundamental pillar of the Bulgarian society and system of state  the Bulgarian National Bank. On 6 June 2009 all of us together will celebrate the 130-year anniversary of the establishment of our Central Bank. Congratulations for the Bankers day, dear colleagues! PAGE PAGE 2

Title: Speech before the economic forum Bulgarias Development in the Conditions of the Global Financial and Economic Crisis organized by the government, Sofia
text: Speech of Mr. Ivan Iskrov, BNB Governor, before the economic forum Bulgarias Development in the Conditions of the Global Financial and Economic Crisis organized by the government, Sofia, 18 February 2009 Dear Prime Minister, Ladies and Gentlemen, I would like to draw your attention to something we find quite important - that we should not expect or encourage excessive expectations about the potential of the state, the central bank included, to cope with the effect of the current global economic crisis. If there was such a potential, the US would have reported a two-digit economic growth by now. For example, when discussing the policy pursued by the BNB, we should very clearly recognize the BNBs main tasks, namely: supporting the stability of the lev and its fixed exchange rate and ensuring the stability of the banking system, hence of household and corporate savings. The BNBs task is not to encourage lending  as we have been urged recently primarily by various banking industry organizations. When discussing an anti-crisis programme on national level, we should be well aware of the globally changed realities and the limitations of the Bulgarian economy. Firstly, the world economy and global financial markets, such as we have known them in the recent 10-15 years, are irreversibly changed. The access to practically unlimited credit resources at a very low price (interest) has already ended. Secondly, Bulgaria is not a country issuing a global reserve currency and so having an unlimited access to financing. This means that we cannot afford to copy the stabilization packages implemented in the US, UK, France or Germany. Thirdly, as a consequence of the first two, at this stage we cannot allow ourselves to go into any budget deficit. Simply because we cannot finance it at the international markets, or we can at a prohibitive cost of financing that will translate into a very stringent limitation of our budget capabilities in the coming years, and into a further increase in the cost of lending to the private sector. I would like to clearly emphasize that for years our economy has been developing based on foreign, rather than Bulgarian, savings. In the last 12 years our economy was growing owing to the macroeconomic stability and structural reforms consistently pursued. This policy fostered our credibility among foreign investors. In the recent 5 years, the Bulgarian economy has been attracting FDI of about 20% of our GDP on the average, which is at the root of the economic growth in Bulgaria. Therefore, our principal goal should be to preserve this credibility by consistently going on with the policy so far pursued of macroeconomic and financial stability secured by the currency board, banking system stability, and prudent fiscal policy, and by carrying on with the implementation of reforms and the improvement of business environment (in its comprehensiveness from the rule of law and public order to the conditions of doing business, and the development of human capital). The attempts at advocating the precedence of the rights of debtors over those of creditors evidenced in the recent weeks are impermissible. Such slogans or legal amendments will take us back where we started more than 10 years ago. The Bulgarian economy is highly dependable on the developments in the global, and particularly in the European, economy. We can already see signs of a slowdown in the growth rates, prevailingly in the industries highly dependant on external markets, luckily at slower rates compared to what we see in other EU member states. The factors for this slowdown are the ones we knew and expected would have the strongest and immediate effect  the decline of foreign trade and the deceleration of the inflow of capital to the country. Finally, whatever measures we may take, we should realize that our economy will accelerate its growth only when our main partners (Germany, Italy, Greece, France) restore their growth again. The crisis was imported to the country, so will be its resolution. We should position ourselves so as to be ready, and capable of taking advantage when the world economy starts recovering. As I have been pointing out since the end of the last year, we should stay calm and composed and make no blunders. We should not mechanically quote plans and approaches devised in Washington or London and appropriate for economies of a different scale and traditions. That is not what we need. Our economy will adapt itself to the new conditions, as far as we maintain financial stability and discipline. Some sectors that evidenced unwarranted optimism, we may even say excessive greed for profit, rather than balanced growth, will adapt in a more painful way than others. However, no matter what adaptation our economy may undergo, it will be under the existing monetary regime of a currency board arrangement and at the same exchange rate level. Let us stop listening to any fortune-tellers, with or without academic ranks and degrees. There have been enough bad examples in the recent months (from Iceland to Hungary and Romania) of the damages a floating exchange rate may cause  particularly at a time of global crisis. This is the top priority of the BNB. So you should rest assured. _______ PAGE PAGE 2

Title: Speech before the Bulgaria Business and Investment Summit, Invest in Bulgaria 2009, Sofia
text: Speech of Mr. Ivan Iskrov, BNB Governor, before the Bulgaria Business and Investment Summit, Invest in Bulgaria 2009, Sofia, 5 March 2009 Dear Ladies and Gentlemen, First of all, please let me thank the organizers of The Bulgaria Business and Investment Summit for the kind invitation and the opportunity to attend this forum. It is a pleasure and honour for me to be together with you. If you are interested and have questions I am prepared to give you particular information concerning Bulgarian economy and banking system, but since we have a certain time limit please let me draw your attention to some more conceptual issues. 1. Firstly I would like to express my surprise at the increasing aggressiveness towards emerging European economies, demonstrated by some Western analysts and institutions, especially Anglo-Saxonian. During the last several weeks the attention of the media and analysts was heavily concentrated towards Central and Eastern Europe and in particular South-East Europe. Somehow almost everyone has started to make comments, forecasts and recommendations for our economies. By reading such ridiculous materials one could start to believe that our economies have caused the current global financial and economic crisis. Some investment bankers, independent analysts and even simple speculators are rushing to explain how bad the economic situation in our part of the world is, which makes no sense when one checks the figures. It is important all the observers never to forget what caused the crisis and where it started. The current financial crisis is a result of inadequate regulations and supervision of the financial markets in the most-developed economies and extreme greediness of some market participants. These were developments that were not caused by our citizens, companies, governments or central banks. It is also ridiculous that the institutions which criticize us most, are themselves the ones, which needed government support to cope with the gaps in their balance sheets. But they still continue to give advice to the investors in emerging market countries. 2. Secondly, the practice to draw conclusions for the state of the whole region, that comprises a variety of countries with different economic features, seems like comparing tomatoes and cucumbers. Both are vegetables, but there are big differences between them. It is very important when someone talks about the adjustment processes of the Central and East Europe economies, to try to differentiate and to understand weaknesses and advantages of each country. In the past 5-6 years when everything was growing and there was the perception that everything is possible in the globalized world, financial markets and investors did not make efforts to differentiate. It was simply not necessary. Nowadays, however, policy-makers and market participants must be aware of the particular features of each country and economy. There are a lot of similarities, but there are also significant differences of crucial importance  stable or unstable governments, good or bad fiscal policies, consistency of macroeconomic policy, financial sector conditions and regulations, labour market situation, etc. Moreover, we need to differentiate between the new member states and the other emerging markets in Europe, as well as among the new member states. 3. And last but not least, if we take medium-term view on our economies and their long-term perspectives for economic growth and further catch-up and integration to the EU, we will notice one interesting thing. It is that risks in our region are not greater than risks in the older member states. On the contrary! The fall of the Iron curtain created enormous opportunities not only for former communist countries, but also for Western Europe. If old member states like Austria and Greece had not invested in our region and taken advantage from our integration into European economy, then where would their investment opportunities have been today? Probably the City of London or Wall Street would bring them higher yields at lower risk? I doubt it! To my mind in the future the only region in Europe destined to have stronger economic growth is Central and East Europe. And this is despite the current short-term difficulties that were imported from developed financial markets. 4. Finally, I would like to make some specific comments on the Bulgarian economy. As I already mentioned Central and East Europe as a term is a very general concept. In order to make proper assessment and take adequate decisions we have to take into account countries record in terms of governance, fiscal stance, structural reforms and consistency of their macroeconomic policies. If you take Bulgaria as an example, you will see that for more than 12 years three consecutive governments have followed very consistent and stability oriented fiscal and structural policies. Since 1998 we have either a balanced budget or significant budget surpluses. Government debt was reduced from close to 100 % of GDP in 1998 to 16% of GDP in 2008. Even now, when we expect economic growth to slowdown, the Bulgarian government have prepared a budget with surplus. There are significant buffers built in the budget in order to assure that we can preserve the stability of the fiscal policy even in the case of a greater slowdown. This stability of the fiscal policy is of crucial importance. The main goal of this policy is to rule out the possibility to end up in the situation to depend on financing from the financial markets. This is because today the international markets are frozen or they demand too high prices. Nowadays, when the national governments are running massive fiscal deficits in order to stimulate domestic demand, financial markets will put more and more emphasis on the sustainability of those policies and sources of their financing. 5. In the context of recent developments in Central and East Europe I would like to underline that the Bulgarian economy has one very big advantage  a monetary regime based on the principles of the currency board arrangements and fixed exchange rate. The lack of exchange rate volatility is an enormous advantage for us, especially in the current situation. It is now clear, that the floating exchange rate can not bring long-lasting competitive advantages, but only problems and to feed speculators. Central and East European banking systems are dominated by foreign banks (mainly from the Euro area) and significant share of credit to households and corporate sector in our economies is denominated in foreign currencies (mainly euro, but in some countries also Swiss frank and Japanese yen). The fluctuation of the exchange rate in these economies creates balance sheet effects and transforms exchange rate risk into credit risk. I would like to stress that the advantage of the Bulgarian banking system is that foreign currency credit is predominantly in euro and there is no fluctuation of the euro/leva exchange rate. It is crucial for investors to know that, no matter what adjustment the Bulgarian economy may undergo, it will be under the existing monetary regime of currency board arrangements and at the existing level of the exchange rate. That was the case over the last twelve years. Bulgaria will not make any experiments and gamble with its monetary regime and macroeconomic and financial stability. This is a common commitment of the Bulgarian political class, citizens and business community. Tank you for the attention! _______ PAGE PAGE 1

Title: Speech before the 40th National Assembly of the Republic of Bulgaria on the occasion of his election for a second term of office
text: Speech of the Governor of the Bulgarian National Bank, Mr. Ivan Iskrov, before the 40th National Assembly of the Republic of Bulgaria on the occasion of his election for a second term of office, 28 May 2009 Mr. Speaker, Ladies and Gentlemen MPs, I would like to thank you for the enormous trust of 165 votes for', which is more than two thirds of the number of deputies and practically means a constitutional majority. Thank you very much for the vast support that you have given to the BNB and its Governor, Ivan Iskrov, at this moment. I take this exceptional confidence as a serious commitment for me and my team to go on maintaining financial stability in the Republic of Bulgaria over the next six years. Just as responsibly I took the decision of the Parliament back in 2003 when I was first elected as Governor of the Bulgarian National Bank. At that time I expressed my deep conviction that financial stability and economic growth in a country could only be achieved if there was a sustained political consensus on the major issues of the economic, financial and supervisory policies. I am very proud of this parliamentary consensus and I would like to loudly voice my gratitude for it. Throughout my first term I was privileged to be one of the few governors of central banks inside and outside the European Union whose policy was supported by three successive parliamentary majorities  from Christian democrats through liberals to todays parliament dominated by socialists and social democrats. In all my statements, in the debates at international forums, and at bilateral meetings with European and world leaders I have pointed out this impressive political consensus, and I have always felt the admiration for my country because when it comes to the financial fundamentals in a country there are very few countries that could be proud of such a consensus. This is only possible as a result of an agreement. Ladies and Gentlemen, six years ago here at the National Assembly I pronounced three key words that hopefully would be remembered as characterising my work as Governor of the BNB: independence, transparency and predictability. Today I stand before you and with clear conscience I can say that all through my term of office I followed these principles. These are principles not only of my work but are principles of operation of all central banks in the world. I want to share some personal feelings  I was ready to leave the institution on 10 October with a sense of having fulfilled my duty, a sense of satisfaction with the job that I have done. But today I receive this support by a constitutional majority, for which I sincerely thank you once again. I would like to re-state that my second term of office will be governed by the same principles, by the same golden rule that I have just mentioned - independence, transparency and predictability. As there would probably be new configurations in the next National Assembly, I would like to stress that I have not allowed any political interferences in the Banks operation. And ignoring some attempts (over the last few days Ive been carefully following all statements in the media, even in the pre-election campaigns), I declare that I am not going to allow such interferences in the work of the BNB over my next term either. So far I have worked with all Bulgarian institutions and all legitimate political parties and their representatives no matter whether they belong to the right, the extreme right, the left, or the centre, and they will always be welcome to the Central Bank to discuss any issues as long as this is in the interests of the stability in Bulgaria and, in particular, the banking system. Ladies and Gentlemen, finally and in the context of everything said by me and by the speakers before me during this debate, I believe that now the most important thing is predictability; predictability because the world is full of aggressive speculative players, and the BNB's role is to secure both financial stability in the country and the robustness of our strictly regulated banking system. Now it is extremely important that we ensure predictability not only by choosing a Governor, but also by clearly demonstrating our commitment to the fundamental regime, i.e. the monetary regime in Bulgaria. This is the currency board arrangement, the pegged rate, and it should be clear that there will be no hesitations and no changes and that this regime may not be questioned either in investment banks in London or New York, or here in our homeland. Therefore, Ladies and Gentlemen, after consulting with the Central Banks Legal Directorate that has never once in the last six years misled me, nor has it misled my predecessor, and that has interpreted the law in the light of the Statute of the European Central Bank and the European System of Central Banks, which Statute is an integral part of the Maastricht Treaty of 1992, I express my deep conviction that there are no legal obstacles for me to immediately choose a Deputy Governor for the sake of the institutions predictability and stability. In a few minutes I am going to submit in the Office of the Speaker of the National Assembly a candidacy for a Deputy Governor in charge of the Issue Department as this Deputy Governors term of office expires together with mine. Ladies and Gentlemen, thank you very much for your confidence in me. In the next six years I will do my best not to make any one of you who have voted for me feel uneasy or ashamed of having done so. Thank you for your attention. _______

Title: Speech on the Occasion of the 130th Anniversary of the Bulgarian National Bank, Sofia
text: Speech by Mr. Ivan Iskrov, BNB Governor, on the Occasion of the 130th Anniversary of the Bulgarian National Bank, Sofia, 12 June 2009 Mr. President of the Republic of Bulgaria, Mr. President of the European Central Bank, Your Grace, Your Excellencies, Members of Parliament and Ministers, Distinguished Guests, Ladies and gentlemen, It is a high honour and privilege for me to welcome you with the warm Bulgarian Dobre doshli at the culmination of the series of events by which the Bulgarian National Bank celebrates its remarkable 130th Anniversary. The first date of this chronology, quite long for the Bulgarian modern history, is 25 January 1879, the date of foundation of the central bank of a liberated Bulgaria just starting to rebuild its statehood. On 6 June the same year, the government invested the capital needed for the operation of the bank and it effected its first transaction. Thus, the Bulgarian National Bank set the beginning of its activities and became forever part of the destiny of our nation. Statisticians may note that chronologically the BNB is the thirteenth national central bank founded in the world. From a national perspective, however, the BNB is not just the first Bulgarian public institution in the ecstatic atmosphere of our newly liberated Fatherland. In the century to come the National Bank was to become an integral part of the highly dramatic fate of the Bulgarian people. No matter what heavy blows our country had to withstand after its liberation, the BNB always took its part in the national anguish and responsibility, and shared with dignity in the woes of the people. With each resurrection of our Motherland from the ashes for a new national revival, the National Bank, in a dignified, but unostentatious manner, took its institutional responsibility, and was instrumental in laying the foundations of economic recovery. In all our post-liberation history, through all these 130 years to this very day, the BNB has always been part of the continuous aspiration of the Bulgarians for freedom and independence. Furthermore, the BNBs guaranteed independence, going hand-in-hand with the responsibility for national financial stability, has become a symbol of sovereign dignity and institutional prestige. This is true today, so I feel honoured and gratified to share with the whole Bulgarian people that in a period of a global financial crisis and lack of confidence, a period of unprecedented economic turmoil worldwide, not a single bank in Bulgaria had to be forcibly capitalized by the state, as is the case in many of the most developed market economies. Although we are a small country, and some world media turn their attention to us mainly with negative expectations, the truth is that presently the Bulgarian financial system is a synonym of stability, predictability and order. This stability, that some find astonishing, is deeply rooted in the solid currency board arrangements and the policy of rigorous regulation and stringent banking supervision pursued by the Bulgarian National Bank. In the eve of the general elections for the 41st National Assembly, and amid often senseless political confrontation, I am bound to underscore that the domestic financial stability and predictability should be greatly credited to the solid political consensus achieved among the main political parties. The accord and consistent policy of three successive parliamentary majorities in the recent 12 years have been of paramount importance for the financial system stability. Many of our international partners have been pleasantly surprised to learn that in three parliaments in a row, successively dominated by Christian Democrats, Liberals, and Socialists, there has been a clear and categorical consensus in support of an independent and properly operating central bank, of the currency board arrangenments, and of the fixed exchange rate of the Bulgarian national currency. I believe that we will see again such a commitment and consistency after 5 July in the newly elected National Assembly and the government formed by it. Bulgaria, Ladies and Gentlemen, is one for all of us, and public interest should not be governed by narrow party interests and political chicanery. Today I would like before you once again to repeat the words that I said before the constitutional majority in the Parliament who reelected me just a few weeks ago. Id like to make it quite clear that during my next term of office I will do my best to ensure the independence of the BNB and its responsible efforts to preserve the stability and predictability in the future. As the Governor of the BNB, bearing a huge responsibility, though sometimes unnoticeable for the general public, I am absolutely convinced that there should be no experiments with the central bank of the Republic of Bulgaria and its principal functions and tasks neither on national nor on international level. All we have been discussing at the central bank over the years has been confirmed  the BNB experts projections have proved accurate and we managed, to a very high degree to contribute to the preparation of our country for the global economic crisis. Today our banking system has robust shock absorbers against crises and future loses  protections that have been carefully, purposefully and consistently built over the recent years. Bulgaria is a small country and as such it is often under-rated, and yet today it is a well-known fact that we have institutions whose professional capacity deserves to be rated very highly. In less than 20 years, only within one generation, the Bulgarian society made a colossal change that we, the contemporaries, can hardly assess impartially and thoroughly at this close distance in time. From the very beginning of this historical process of re-integration into the economy and culture of United Europe, to which we belong by right, by volition, and by dedication, the BNB has worked hard and with dedication to its maximum expert capacity. As the Governor of this institution and before so many guests, I am very proud to say that from the year 2003, when we took on our responsibilities in the Eurointegration process, to date there has been no single note of criticism on the work of the BNB. I would be very happy if any one of the Bulgarian political and business leaders could work in such a way that our country would receive no justified criticism in the areas they are responsible for. Ladies and Gentlemen, Finally I would like to express my sincere thanks to all those without who I would be like a general without an army. The tremendous responsibilities assigned to the central bank and the Bulgarian societys very high expectations of the BNB cannot be met without the inconspicuous but hard and highly responsible work done by the hundreds of BNB employees, experts and managers. Thank you very much, dear colleagues! Contributing to the preparations for Bulgarias successful membership in the European Union, in 2007 the central bank of Bulgaria joined the European System of Central Banks, and with hard work and commitment it became an important integral part of the working process of the Union. Ladies and Gentlemen, please allow me to express my personal gratitude to our colleagues from the other central banks of the Community for their help and cooperation. I cannot help mentioning the warm and friendly attitude of the ECB President and the great person Jean-Claude Trichet and I would like to thank him for the steady support. I shall not forget the friendly hand that we can always rely on. Id like to thank all the friends and partners of the Bulgarian National Bank! Ladies and Gentlemen, thank you for your attention! _______ 171 Members of Parliament participated in the session; "For" - 165, "Against"  6. PAGE PAGE 2
