Title: Speech before the Fourth International Financial Exhibition
text: Speech by Mr. Dimitar Kostov, Deputy Governor of the BNB, before the Fourth International Financial Exhibition, Plovdiv, 15-17 February 2006. DEVELOPMENT OF THE PAYMENT SYSTEM Dear ladies and gentlemen, I would like to briefly present to your attention the central bank's approach when working on the issue of the development of the payment system. First of all, I must point out that the development of the payment system is a continuous process. This is determined by the dynamics of demand for one or other payment services and by the development of the capabilities of payment service providers, payment system operators and, more generally, of infrastructure. In addition, the very process of defining, directing and implementing the development of payment systems becomes an independent and important issue, not only research but also regulatory attention. For example, the work of the Payment and Settlement Systems Committee of the Bank for International Settlements can be cited. Before I move on to the issue of development, I would address what the national payment system is. This is the system by which cashless payments are made, i.e. payments in which the debt between the two partiesis settled by transferring claims from cash institutions d0 commercial banks and the central bank. These claims are not money, but money can be obtained quickly and easily. as follows: payment instruments used to transfer funds between the payer's and the payee's accounts with financial institutions; payment infrastructures processing payment instruments, clearing, exchanging information and transferring funds between paying and receiving institutions, i.e. banks, including the central bank; institutions involved in the payment process, which are financial institutions providing current accounts, payment instruments and payment services to their customers, as well as payment system operators; market mechanisms, i.e. arrangements between payment service market participants; regulatory environment, which includes laws and regulations regulatingthe relationship between participants in the payment process. All these elements act as a single system. Banks and operators institutions use payment instruments within market mechanisms and regulatory rules to provide payment services to consumers. What does the payment system look like in Bulgaria? With regard to payment instruments, we have all the main varieties: credit transfer, direct debit , budget payment instruments, payment cards, etc. Cheques have not been development, but there is potential for greater diversity in electronic payment instruments. The payment infrastructure includes the necessary set of payment systems that complement each other: large payment system d0 RINGS; retail payment system d0 BISERA, card system d0 BORICA, systems that provide trading and settlement with securities. 34 financial institutions and three operators are involved in the payment process. The central bank participates as both the main financial institutionand as the operator of the main system d0 RINGS. Market mechanisms consist of a wide network of arrangements with regard to procedural rules, pricing and otherups and downs, ensuring the necessary coordination between participants in the payment process. The regulatory environment has been substantially developed in recent years with the Money Transfers Act, electronic payment instruments and payment systems, as wellas with accompanying regulations. The complexity and complexity of the payment system shows that it cannot be static. The changes are the result of a number of factors: developments in the financial and non-financial sectors identify both the needs and opportunities to use more efficient payment instruments and services; better understanding of risks and growing concerns about financial stability also require development in individual elements; orientation towards compliance with international standards, as well as joiningthe European Union, are also important factors for change. These factors determine the need for development, but this cannot happen only as a result of the action on the market. Changes in payment systems occur not only in the competition process, but on the contrary - in order to happen in a sufficientlyorderly manner, a high degree of cooperation and coordination between market participants is also needed. In determining the policy and actions for the development of the payment system, BNB is led by several basic principles: the central bank must play a leading role, as the functioning of the national payment system is an important element of the quality and reliability of the national currency. At the same time, banks and other financial institutions providing payment services must not only compete but also cooperate in the development of the payment system; When planning the development of a payment system, account must betaken of the complexity of the system, the specificity of the individual elements and the main factors determining the development. the institutional framework for the development of the payment system must ensure stakeholder involvement, supervisory cooperation, a reliable legal framework, and the promotion of market mechanisms towards the expansion of self-regulation; with regard to infrastructure, the guiding principles are to expand the provision of payment services for retail payment; coordination of the settlement of large payment systems, retail payments, including card payments, and securities settlement. Summarizing in this way the principles from which the BNB is being led in shaping its policy on the development of payment systems, I must stress that they have been successfully implemented overthe last 5-6 years and will continue to be at the heart of the process in the future. Of course, work on their detailed development and refinement will continue. is also benefiting from the recently published 'Guidelines for the Development of National Payment Systems', which were approved by the Payment and Settlement Systems Committee of the Bank for International Settlements. In its work, this committee aggregates the experience of many countries in the development of payment systems, although it stresses that universal recipes do not. In Bulgaria, a number of decisive steps have been taken in recent years in the development of the payment system. First of all, I would point to the introduction in20003 of the 2003 gross settlement system in real time NINGS, which has decisively improved the reliability and efficiency of the national payment system. Since the beginning of this year, some improvements have also been put into operation, strengthening the technological capacity of the system and expanding some functionalities. An equally important step was the establishment of the legal basis with the adopted Law on Money Transfers, Electronic Payment Instruments and Payment Systems and the relevant regulations. An important step was theestablishment of the National Payment Systems Council, which established the direct involvement of institutions involved in the payment process in the formulation and implementation of the payment system development policy. In order to expand the coordination of participants inthe payment services market was also the sale of a majority package of the shares of the card operator of the banks. Over the past year, serious progress has also been made in the development of securities settlement systems, especially in government securities. At the moment, all participants in the payment system are actively working on the so-called "IBAN" project. It includes not only the introduction of an international bank account number, but also the preparation for the use of new payment documents. A significant change will also be made to the retail payment system d0 BISERA. The format of the messages will be based on theso.SWIFT so-called standard, which will make it easier for banks to maintain and develop their systems. The introduction of the international number of bank accounts, as well as the new payment system, are also the first steps towards the next stage of the development of the national payment system. What we are about to do is to join the construction of the single European payment area. This task is large-scale and will affect all the payments system, although for some of them what has been done so far is in line with the development of the processes in the European Union. to note that the interest in joining the single European payment area is determined by the fact that this will be a very important condition for the real utilisation of our accession to the European Union and, subsequently, to the euro area. The economic benefits for each company and every household of our participation in the European single market will be greater, the more integrated this market is, including with regard to payment systems. In conclusion, I would like to stress that the Bulgarian National Bank will continue its participation in the development of the payment system not only in its role as a supervisory authority, as wellas as a basic operator and user, but especially as a catalyst and initiator of processes. Title: Speech at the 9th Bulgarian IT Financial Forum
text: Speech of Mr. Dimitar Kostov, Deputy Governor of the BNB at the 9th Bulgarian IT Financial Forum, Sofia, 18  19 April 2007 Ladies and Gentlemen, It was with great pleasure that I accepted the organisers invitation to represent the Bulgarian National Bank at the opening of the 9th Bulgarian IT Financial Forum. The review of the topics included in this forum reconfirms the importance of IT technologies for the financial sector development. The operation of business processes, the risk management, the supervision and observation of regulations  are all dependable on the existence of reliable and effective information and communication technologies. Since the ability of banks to effect payments between economic agents, is one of the pillars of financial mediation, I will briefly discuss the development of the payment system. The efforts so far have resulted in the implementation of a payment system, which generally corresponds to the European Union standards: the relevant legislation is in place, the settlement systems  RINGS and BISERA comply with the requirements of the common general principles of large and small payments, the card payment system BORIKA has been successfully brought into compliance with IMV standards, the IBAN standard for bank account numbers was successfully introduced for all types of accounts. No matter how much was achieved, the future development will require greater efforts, as we are now involved in the overall process of payment systems integration in the EU and development of payment services single market. I would like to first point out that along with the adoption of the payment systems directive, a new legislation will be introduced. The deadline for this is the end of May. The basic elements of the new legislation are related to the standardization of the rights and obligations of the payment services users and providers: introduction of clear and harmonized information requirements with a view to improving market transparency; increase of competition and opening of the market, including for non-bank payment services providers. The payment services directive is to be incorporated into the national legislations no later than November 2008, and the expected results are: increased competition, quicker and more secure payment transactions, unified high level of customer protection, smaller price margins of payment services at lower average levels. Another leading project in the development of the European market of payment services is TARGET 2. The development of a system for large payments in euro will contribute to a further integration of the financial markets in the euro area on the basis of higher efficiency and broader range of provided services, allowing for a more flexible and effective liquidity management. The migration to TARGET 2 of the first group of central banks, together with the relevant banking communities, will commence in November this year. The TARGET 2 Securities project will have a similar scope regarding the integration of securities settlement systems. The project of greatest importance is the development of the Single European Payment Area  SEPA. The implementation of this project will have direct impact not only on banks and financial intermediaries, but also on all commercial entities, regardless of their size; it will impact individuals and households, as well as government bodies. Two different presentations on the topic will be made on this forum. Therefore I would only add that the development of the separate elements of this large-scale project will start in the beginning of next year, and continue through to 2010. All these projects and changes determine the Bulgarian environment in which the payment system will be developed. The directive on payment services will have a more direct impact on the latter, as it will be implemented in all member states, irrespective of their euro area inclusion. The creation of a single European payment services market with unified standards, requirements and high degree of liberalisation will set its mark not only on competition, but also on the quantity, quality and prices of the provided services. The TARGET 2 and SEPA projects may seem at first glance to deal with payments in euro rather than in levs. Their importance for the country, however, is significant. Firstly, the euro will keep its leading role due to the objectively undisputable and needed existence of the currency board arrangement founded on the unconditional and unrestricted exchange of 1,95583 levs against 1 euro. Secondly, the importance of the euro will grow as a result of its role in the settlement of accounts between the Bulgarian companies and individuals and those of the other EU member states in the conditions of increasing integration and convergence. Undoubtedly, economic entities in Bulgaria can use all new instruments and payment schemes, as these will be first implemented with regard to cross-border payments, and euro-denominated payments will be cross-border ones until the time of our accession to the euro area. At the same time, the effectiveness and efficiency of this opportunity will depend on the way Bulgarian banks implement their part of the overall payment process. For example, the different prices for direct and indirect access to a Paneuropean clearing house would result in a different price per a credit transfer. As early as at this stage, the Bulgarian National Bank starts broad consultations for the initiation of negotiations on good projects that would allow for making earlier and better use of opportunities opened under European projects in the area of payment systems development. A number of consultative groups were established under the National Payment Systems Council, on which the banking community, payment systems operators, and, of course, the BNB and the Ministry of Finance, are well represented. In the next presentation you will get more information. For the time being, I will only note that the BNB will seek to combine its role of a payment market regulator with that of a catalyst of the development processes. The expectations and wishes not only of the financial sector, but of the businesses and the real sector, consumers and the public sector will also underlie initiatives under preparation. The projects to be generated will also be part of the preparations of the Bulgarian payment system for joining the euro area. So far, accession to the euro area was pursued while following the existing national practices, standards, mechanisms and payment instruments. As of 2010, the adoption of the euro will entail the requirement of adopting the respective uniform conditions for cashless payments in this currency. This will not be just the accession to a single currency, but rather to a single payment services market, which is a greater challenge to market participants. As already noted earlier, the Bulgarian payment system is in a good position to cope with the above-outlined challenges. Success, however, will depend on the full awareness of responsibilities, and on the proper definition and implementation of the roles of all participants in the change processes. The business assessment of change also merits serious attention. There will be changes in the existing cash inflows, but multiple additional opportunities will open also, such as the automation of the processes underlying higher standardization, adding additional services to the payment ones (e.g. an -invoice), etc. In conclusion, I would like to assure you that the development of the payment systems will continue to have its due place in the next editions of the Bulgarian Financial Forum (not driving out, of course, the other subjects of discussion), and also to wish you fruitful work in all the sessions of this Forum. Thank you for the attention. PAGE PAGE 2

Title: Speech delivered to IIF Spring Membership Meeting
Subtitle: ECONOMIC AND FINANCIAL IMPLICATIONS OF EU ENLARGEMENT
text: Speech by Mr. Dimitar Kostov, Deputy Governor of the BNB, delivered to IIF Spring Membership Meeting, Athens, 31 May  1 June 2007 ECONOMIC AND FINANCIAL IMPLICATIONS OF EU ENLARGEMENT Ladies and Gentlemen, It is an honour for me to speak to such a distinguished audience. I will address the issue Economic and Financial Implications of EU Enlargement by drawing your attention to the Bulgarian case in terms of economic performance, policy responses, and prospects. Due to the sound macroeconomic policy and sustained structural reforms Bulgaria has achieved a good pace of economic growth. The average real GDP growth for the last three years has been 6.3%. The main driver for this performance is the investments reaching 32% to GDP for the last year from levels of around 20% five years ago. Of course this level of investments compared with domestic savings at the level of 16.2% to GDP creates a gap reflected in the current account deficit at the level of 15.8% to GDP at the end of last year. Despite the strong growth in exports reaching over 26% last year, the trade balance was in deficit of 5.4 bln. Euro. Besides the oil prices, the high imports level is determined by the import of investment goods, as well as the import of raw materials driven by the export growth and investment activities. The current account deficit is fully financed by Foreign Direct Investments. The FDI inflow for the last year reached 4.1 bln. Euro, or 16.1 % to GDP. This ratio is among the highest in the EU and the highest in per capita terms. These were predominantly green field investments, and only 10% came from privatization deals. Since 1997, when Bulgaria embarked on the path of sustained reform process, around a quarter of the FDI inflows was in the manufacturing, close to 20% in trade, 15% in the financial sector (banking), 7% and 8% correspondingly in the communications and energy sectors. Investments in real estate, rental and business services reached the significant share of 15% based on the activity over the last few years. Importantly, around 85% of FDIs originate from countries within the EU. Apart from the favourable global conditions, other factors driving FDIs in Bulgaria are the low wage cost and skilled labour force; the favourable profit tax treatment, with the profit tax reaching 10% from the beginning of this year; the reasonable and predictable business environment. Although the domestic market is relatively small, the growth prospect is good, and this attracts not only big players, but also a number of mid-size companies looking for growth opportunities outside the congested developed markets. Cost and growth considerations are the driving factors in allocation decisions as well as the positioning for third market expansion. When a country is attracting foreign savings of this magnitude due consideration is given to the development on the debt side. The private external debt is on the rise, reaching 60.4% to GDP. A large part of this debt  nearly 37% is actually intra-company debt, i.e. mother companies debt financing subsidiaries and branches. The improved excess to foreign financial markets has led to an increase in cross-border lending, with a 36% share of the external private debt. About 22% of the external debt is channelled towards the economy through bank intermediation, and a substantial part of it is also intra-group financing. These developments are largely offset by the sharp decline in the public debt and the accumulation of foreign assets so that the net debt remains at the levels of 21-22% to GDP. To complete the overall picture of the economic performance I would add a few words on inflation and unemployment. With an employment growth of 4.3% for the last year, the average unemployment rate has reduced to 9%. There is a need and room for further increase in employment. There are indications of shortages only in some specific segments of the labour market, such as IT professionals. The average inflation rate over the last two years has been in the range of 6-7%, reaching 7.4% last year. Around 1/3 of this is due to the front-loaded alignment of indirect taxes (excises) to the minimum EU levels and adjustments in the administered prices. In summary, our experience shows that by opening its economy, a country can better pursue growth and improvement in living standards. However, this also means that there is a strong need for adequate policy responses to the market developments in order to ensure stability, continuity and further improvement in performance. Now I will turn briefly to the policy responses. The cornerstone of Bulgarias macroeconomic policy is the maintenance of the currency board-based monetary regime. Though it might be looked at as a constraint, it greatly helped to put emphasis on the right components of economic policymaking, i.e. fiscal policy and structural reforms. The pursued sound fiscal policy can be illustrated by the fact that after maintaining a nearly balanced budget until 2003, since then the country has been running surpluses, reaching 3.6% last year. Meanwhile the external public debt went down to 15.9 % to GDP at the end of the first quarter this year, and fiscal reserves were built amounting to 10% of GDP. It is important to note that this fiscal stance was achieved by keeping the expenditure levels below 40% to GDP, and even reaching 37% last year. The savings of the government partly compensated for the savings investment gap in the economy, and greatly supported the macroeconomic stability. The targets for the next years are set at a 2.3% fiscal surplus. This is not a meaningful easing, having in mind that the contribution to the EU budget is 1.2% of GDP. At the same time the institutional settings provide a strong control on the expenditure side and save a potential over-performance on the revenue side in case of a higher economic growth. Within this framework key emphasis is put on the supply side policies, or structural reforms. After the largely completed privatization, high on the agenda are labour market flexibility, including responsible wage setting rules; efficiency and smoothness of market entry and exit; education reforms; healthcare and pension system sustainability. On the monetary side the currency board serves the country well and we consider it a valuable asset. Its viability is determined by the ample foreign exchange reserves. Being at the level of 8.9 bln. Euro, the reserves cover almost twice the amount of money in circulation. Compared to the reserve money, the excess is more than 70%. Special attention is paid to the functioning of banking intermediation. The banking system is nearly 100% private. Foreign ownership controls around 85% of banking assets. The banks being part of big Eurozone banking and financial groups hold a 75% market share. The main emphasis is put on the stability and soundness of the banking system. The prudential regulations are completely in line with the EU legislation, including the Capital Adequacy Directive based on BASEL II standards. Moreover the national minimum standards are based on 12% capital adequacy ratios and high requirements are in place for loan classification and provisioning. The banking supervision is strong and the necessary cooperation has been established with all the relevant home country banking supervisors. The performance of the banking system can by briefly described by the capital adequacy ratio of 14.5% at the end of last year, as well as the RoE of 24.4% and the RoA of 2.2%. The credit growth is closely monitored. After approaching 50% on an annual basis two years ago, measures were taken to tighten the prudential requirements and even some temporary administrative measures were introduced. The effect of the latter exhausted, and from the beginning of this year they were removed. The credit growth slowed down to around 24% at the end of last year, still we closely monitor the further developments in the light of the prudential considerations and the macroeconomic developments. The third set of issues to which I would like to draw your attention is about the prospects and challenges ahead. Obviously as a member of the EU we see our future in the integration into and convergence towards the European economy. This inevitably means concentration on competitiveness, with the important clarification  competitiveness based on productivity and efficiency. So far the performance in terms of export growth and market share, as well as unit labour cost and productivity, is reasonably good. Yet, the structural reforms agenda cannot be seen as finished. In todays increasingly globalised and fast moving world there is no substitute for microeconomic foundations and economic structure which allows and presses the entrepreneurship initiative to adjust and move quickly. I cannot skip another challenging issue - the adoption of the Euro. The creation of the Euro as a single currency is definitely one of the wisest and most forward looking decisions in the European Union. As a new member we have the obligation to join the Eurozone, but apart from that there is a clear understanding and awareness in Bulgaria of the benefits and the efforts related to such an achievement. At present we fulfil 4 out of the five Maastricht criteria on a sustainable basis. We are aware of the difficulties related to the inflation criterion. Yet it is an achievable task. The Ballasa-Samuelson effect requires an adequate policy response encouraging productivity, and the same is relevant to the issue of the external sustainability of the economy. We believe that a policy mix with an emphasis on structural reforms and macro stability based on the currency board and fiscal soundness is the right approach for us to achieve a sustainable, mutually benefiting, and reinforcing nominal and real convergence. It could take more than two years of being in ERM II. Still the important fact is that even if we stick to our national priority project to follow an economic development based on the currency board, the efficient and effective policies are the same. In addition, the level of the actual transmission of the eurozone monetary policies will be the same. In the end I would like to add that the present economic policy approach can be seen also as institutionalized because it has been followed by three consecutive governments coming from different parts of the political spectrum. This consensus has also been reflected in an agreement between the Government of Bulgaria and the Bulgarian National Bank. At this point I would like to thank you for your attention and I remain open to the questions you may have. PAGE PAGE 2

Title: Speech before the Third Annual International Financial Conference for Central and South-Eastern Europe dedicated to financial and banking modernization in Central and Southeastern Europe, Sofia
text: Speech by Mr. Tsvetan Manchev, PhD, Deputy Governor of the BNB, before the Third Annual International Financial Conference for Central and South-Eastern Europe dedicated to financial and banking modernization in Central and Southeastern Europe, Sofia, 30 January 2006. BULGARIAN BANKING SECTOR ON THE WAY TO THE EU Ladies and gentlemen, It is a great honour to address today the much-respected audience of the Third Annual International Financial Conference for Central and South-Eastern Europe, dedicated to the financial and ban kova modernization in Central and South-Eastern Europe. Above all, I would like to thank our hosts for the politeinvitation and the opportunity given. In the presentation, I will draw your attention to three interconnected issues. Firstly, I willbriefly address the stable economic development of Bulgaria as a key factor in the expansion, good condition and stability of the Bulgarian banking system . full membership of the euro area. 1. Currenteconomic development Eight years after the introduction of the Monetary Council in Bulgaria, we can point to several important results, including: Macroeconomic and financial stability, accompanied by strong economic growth at a relatively high rate d0 around 6% for 2005, which is considered close to potential GDP. Relatively low and stable single-digit inflation in recent years; Increasing convergence of all interest rates to those prevailing in the euro area and a contraction in the ratios between interest rates on deposits and loans; Gradually decreasing level of baswork; Solid fiscalpolicy d0 according to non-final data, the state budget ended 2005 with a surplus of 2.3% of GDP, and the government debt is expected to decrease to a level of about 30% of GDP. As you may have already guessed, most of these achievements relate to a long-term eye strategyfollowed by the government and the BNB on the way to meeting the Maastricht criteria for full membership of the Economic and Monetary Union. signed in November 2004 and in the Central Bank Development Strategy until 2009. The review of the current compliance of the criteria shows that Bulgarihas already consistently met all the criteria except for inflation. 2. Reform of the banking sector Most of the important reforms in the Bulgarian banking sector were implemented after the introduction of the monetary council and their success reflects the good economic condition of the country. After the successful privatisation of state-owned banks, the banking system is now owned and controlledby foreign investors. Now more than 98% of the total bank assets are in private hands. The system is dominated by three banks (Bulbank of the Group of UniCredit, UBB from the Group of the National Bank of Greece and DSK Bank of the GROUP of the TSC), which as of the end of September 2005controlled 35.5% of the total bank assets. which will certainly reduce the number of licensed banks (from 34 ongoing) and demonstrate the irreversible nature of the reform process. Restructuringwill further increase competition in the sector and facilitate economic growth. Although still heavily dominated by the banking sector, local financial markets have overcome their once isolation from international financial markets and long-term interest rates have gradually decreased due to the increased flow of foreign direct investment and successive increases in the country's credit rating. The role of other financial intermediaries is gradually increasing. Increasing competition in the financial sector is evident and is associated with improvements in several guidelines, namely: greater customer satisfaction, better corporate governance, and less asymmetry in information. Although its assets are growing rapidly, the banking system remains re-capitalized and liquid. The quality of assets has not deteriorated. So far, despite credit expansion and strict banking regulations, banks are financiallystable and their efficiency is increasing. Over the past five years, the Bulgarian banking system has strengthened its role as a major financial intermediary in the economy. The rate of credit growth has jumped to 50% per year, but is now returning to its normal low-risk level. The other key factors for the current state of the credit card are: Banks are raising resources for lending predominantly from abroad; The demand for loans by the business is investment driven; Long-term loans to business are growing faster than short-term loans; The business has access to external lending; Home loans to households are growing very quickly. 3. Challenges What are the challenges that the Bulgarian banking system still faces on the eve of theEU's membership? The smooth implementation of EU financial directives requires a strong commitment to their implementation by banks; The practical implementation of Basel II is crucial for maintaining the financial stability of the system and managing the different types of risks accompanying banking; Achieving an adequate level of risk in the system is also linked to banks' desire to maintain a stable level of credit growth and strengthen corporate governance; Convergence ofinterest rates requires banks to further improve their performance; Mergers and acquisitions have already started in Bulgaria with the increasing presence of financial groups combining traditional banking services withinsurance and investment services; Transparency. We believe that transparency is good for competition and the exchange of information between banks serves well to preserve the stability of the system. Thus, bnb constantly supports the banking community in its quest for greater transparency andsymmetry of information. The challenges facing the BNB as an institution of monetary power and as the main financial regulator in the country are even greater. In the very short term, we need to tackle the fine-tuning of the bank creation process and help implementthe new legislation related to EU membership. As regards the introduction and application of acquis communautaire, recent changes to the Law on the Bulgarian National Bank have brought the legal framework of the bank almost in full compliance with EU law in the field of Economic and Monetary Union, while maintaining the conditions and principles of the Monetary Council. legislation without any delay in the entry into force of those legal acts. The following EU financial directives are currently in place: In the field of banking supervision, Bulgaria has achieved full compliance with council directive 93/6/EEC on the capital adequacy of investment firms and credit institutions; The newly adopted Law on Remittances, Electronic Payment Instruments and Payment Systems is in line with European legislation on internal and cross-border transfersand on transactions through electronic payment instruments; The legal framework for the out-of-court settlement of payment disputes has been introduced through a conciliation committee with the competence to settle disputes between the originating institution and the client in connection with the execution of transfers, as well as between issuers of electronic payment instruments and their authorised depositers as regards the issuance and use of such instruments; Directive 94/19/EU on deposit guarantee schemes has been fully transposed into deposit guarantee legislation. A clear scheme has been announced to increase the guaranteed amount for the payment of a depositor for his deposits with a bank out oftheir number and amount and this amount will reach EUR 20 000 by 31 December 2006 compared to its current level of EUR 12 500; With the amendments to the Anti-Money Laundering Measures Act, the Rules for the Implementation of Anti-Money Laundering Measures and the Rules of Procedure of the Financial Intelligence Agency, the Bulgarian legislation has been brought into full compliance with the relevant EU directives and with the requirements of the Working Party on Financial Action on Money Laundering. By the date of EU membership , Bulgaria will have adopted the remaining laws and regulations in the financial field. The Law on Credit Institutions transposing the following directives into Bulgarian legislation: Consolidated Banking Directive 2000/12/EC on the activities ofcredit institutions; Directive 2001/24/EC on the reorganisation of credit institutions; Directive 2000/46/EC on the establishment, operation and supervision of institutions operating electronic money. Consumer Credit Act; Full transposition of Financial Collateral Directive 2002/47/EC and Directive 2002/87/EC on financial conglomerates. The medium-term challenges facing the BNB relate to full membership of the European Economic and Monetary Union. Bulgaria's strategy for full membership of the ISS, as mentioned above,is based on the following principles: Adoption in Exchange Rate Mechanism II (EM II) immediately after bulgaria's formal admission to the EU; Maintaining the monetary board regime until our adoption in the euro area while maintaining the fixed exchange rate of BGN to the euro at the current level of BGN 1.95583 per EUR 1; Unilateral commitment by the Bulgarian government and BNB to apply zero deviation from the central exchange rate of BGN within the framework of THE II World Bank (i.e. maintaining the current policy); Compliance with the minimum time limit set inEU law for accession to THE II and taking all necessary steps of the euro area membership procedure in a timely manner. Conclusion In conclusion, I want to assure you that the BNB will consistently pursue the objectives in the context of the integration of our network into the ISS. The Bank is determined to maintain what has been achieved so far and will continue these efforts so that at the time of ourcountry's admission to the European Union it has achieved the necessary readiness to participate in THE II. The challenges we face in the pre-accession period require strong will from the central bank, the banking and financial community, as well as the government, and their joint efforts to achieve the strategic objective of full membership of the euro area. Title: Speech in front of the Faculty of Philosophy of St. Constantine and Helena. Kliment Ohridski" academic expert debate on the overall EC Monitoring Report of May on the degree of readiness for Bulgaria's membership in the European Union, Sofia

Kliment Ohridski" academic expert debate on the overall EC Monitoring Report of May 2006 on the degree of readiness for Bulgaria's membership in the European Union, Sofia, 12 June 2006. I believe that the general conclusions of the report that Bulgaria is a functioning market economy and the continuation of the reforms implemented will make us able to withstand the competitive pressures of market forces in the Union in the short term are objective from both a purely theoretical and practical point of view. This gives me reason not only to fully share the conclusions of the report, but also to believe that it is in Bulgaria's interest not to resume at all the purely theoretical philosophicaldiscussion about the basics of modern economic policy - monetary and monetary regime, fiscal policy and industrial policy. because every novice economist knows that fundamental changes in economic policy are accompanied by at least a few years of painful period of adjustment of the economy. Both our closer and further history is full of examples. Instead, we should work to reinforce the public consensus on the most important reforms that the EU offers us in order to secure competitive advantages at the very beginning of our membership of the Union. also supports, with analysis and concrete arguments, the necessity andinevitability of certain reforms, as also talked about by the Monitoring Report of May 2006. To complete the privatisation of monopolies without replacing the state monopoly with a private monopoly; Ensure the implementation of the legislation already adopted to regulate the business environment so as to make it possible to enter andexit a particular business at minimal cost to entrepreneurs and society. The effect on public spending is very significant, but often underestimated, because it is more difficult to measure and see. In practice, however, the more opportunities there are for non-judicial resolution of problems related to the start-up and withdrawal of a business, the less pressure there will be on the justice system. and the budget will be given more flexibility d0 to reduce the tax burden or to channel some of the allocated resources towards financing other reforms. The legislation on the entry and exit of each business must continue to be improved towards the imposition of the principle of maximum efficiency by the functioning of markets. (l) reducing inevitable additional costs. Otherwise, the short-term negative effects on economic growth in early 2007 will not come as a surprise. Increasing the efficiency of the justice system. This will also help to limit the growth rates of maintenance of the system, and therefore to increase disposable income of households and businesses. However, the whole process inevitably implies accountabilityand transparency to the public at every level of this independent system. The labour market must become flexible enough to ensure lasting and irreversible macroeconomic stability, and in particular the stability of the monetary council. In this regard, it is of particular importance that the recommendations of the European Commission and the International Monetary Fund on changes in labour law, which are in practice the same, are immediately and unconditionally implemented. All literate economists d0 theorists and practitioners d0 know that the proposed changes will increase labour market flexibility and overcome practices inherited from the transition economy, incentives to offer labour. In my view, reforms at different levels of education should be seen as an integral part of labour market reforms. It is also very important that business and the non-governmental sector are attracted as drivers in this part of the reforms, as it is not the state, but in the market economy that divides the desired characteristics of the workforce and its demand. Successful reforms everywhere in education, as well as successful educational establishments are associated first and foremost with one d0 their graduates are sought from the market and flexibly integrated into it. Iknow that I am seriously provoking the academic audience by saying that education management at all levels should be entrusted to professional managers. Since these negotiating chapters are related to the processes of liberalisation in the world economy, we should have a clear idea of how important progress is in these areas not only for our country's membership of the EU, but also for creating additional advantages for the growth of the Bulgarian economy by attracting foreign capital. Most of the analyses of the report to date focus, above all, on the ec's criticisms. Objectivity requires us to stress that Bulgaria respects thecommitments made in the negotiation process to align Bulgarian legislation with acqis communautaire in the economic, financial and free movement of capital. negotiation process is one of the most important conditions for ensuring the future inflow of capital in the country and hence for higher economic growth. It is also pleased that, according to the report, the competitiveness policy has joined the areas where the most progress has been made in bringing Bulgarian legislation into line with EU law. This is a good signal for both Bulgarian society and business and international markets and investors. However, some of the areas identified as problematic d0 for example, money laundering and the fight against corruption d0 are destabilising to the credibility of the country as a whole and the investment process in bulgaria, especially against the background of increased global competition to attract foreign investment. only from a purely economic point of view. The responsibility for curbing corruption and money laundering and creating public intolerance is bilateral between the state (represented by the administration at different levels) and citizens. Finally, I would like to express my conviction that our country is able to meet the challenge of meeting the European Commission's recommendations from the Monitoring Report in all problem areas and becoming a full member of the EU from 1 January 2007. but it definitely requires us to discuss what additional measures besides the EC's recommendations can and need to be implemented, to reach consensus on their priority and to quickly make them part of the current economic policy. Title: Speech at the Conference The Future Competitiveness of the EU and Eastern Neighbours, Turku, Finland
Subtitle: THE ROLE OF EUROPEAN PERSPECTIVE IN BULGARIAN ECONOMIC REFORMS
text: Speech by Mr. Tsvetan Manchev, Ph. D., Deputy Governor of the Bulgarian National Bank, at the Conference The Future Competitiveness of the EU and Eastern Neighbours, Pan-European Institute, Turku, Finland, 1-2 September 2006 THE ROLE OF EUROPEAN PERSPECTIVE IN BULGARIAN ECONOMIC REFORMS First of all, I would like to express my gratitude to the Pan-European Institute for the opportunity to talk before such a renowned audience and to present my point of view as an economist and a central banker on the role of economic policies for strengthening competitiveness of the EU and its eastern neighbors. I will speak about the experience of my country in achieving high and sustainable economic growth and competitiveness by means of an economic policy based on political stability and consensus among major political parties and within the society on the main economic priorities and aimed at winning investors confidence. To be honest, this broad consensus on economic policy priorities did not come out of the blue. It was archived after a long period of inconsistent, indecisive, and unproductive market reforms, which started at the beginning of the political and economic transformations in the country and ended with the profound political, financial and economic crisis of the end of 1996 and the beginning of 1997. The crisis changed dramatically public opinion on the need to speedily build up a market-oriented economy, and catalyzed the process of accumulation of political will to start real reforms based on proven values like democracy, liberalization, restructuring of the economy and maximum withdrawal of the state from business. Since 1997, all three consecutive governments, irrespectively of their political orientation, have broadly followed one and the same economic policy, which contains the following main elements (as mentioned in one of the first Pre-accession Economic Programs of the country): retention of the currency board and irrevocable peg of the national currency; prudent and flexible fiscal policies based on balanced budget or a budget surplus; reinforcement and completion of the privatisation process of all state-owned assets earmarked for privatisation; deregulation of state (natural) monopolies in compliance with the best international practices and cost-reflective (investments included) price adjustment of the services rendered by them on the basis of a wide social consensus; business-friendly improvement of the legal, regulatory and institutional framework based on the agreements reached in the negotiation process with the EU and consensus within the framework of the three-partite partnership between the government, trade unions and employers; equal treatment by the state of local and foreign investors and entrepreneurs in the legal process, regulatory and institutional framework; institutional capacity reinforcement of public administration and the judiciary by implementing appropriate structural reforms and improving training efficiency; decentralisation of the decision-making process by redistribution of resources, delegation of powers and responsibilities to the different levels of public administration based on the analysis of the currently applied mechanisms of operation of the administration; a swift shift from predominantly passive to active labour policies oriented towards achievement of labor market flexibility fully in line with EU Directives; completion of the reforms in social and health insurance, education and local government taking into account the arrangements agreed upon in the course of the ongoing broad social dialogue. These relatively simple logically linked guidelines contain in fact the philosophy of liberal economic reforms, and in the same time they are a universal framework limiting the field of action of a government of a small open economy. We do not pretend that they are our invention. In fact they are, to some extent, inspired by factors outside the country (IMF, EU), but they do work. After eight years of implementation of this policy the following outcomes have been achieved: Macroeconomic and financial stability accompanied by a sustainable economic growth at a relatively high rate and gradually declining unemployment. The growth rate for the last 8 years - 4.5% on average  contributes to the gradual improvement in living standards; Relatively low and stable one-digit inflation for years coupled with an intensifying convergence of all interest rates on the prevailing Euro area rates, and a shrinking margin between lending and deposit interest rates; Sound public finances, evidenced by three consecutive years of budget surplus and decreasing public debt. Since 1998, the public debt has been decreasing steadily from over 80% of GDP to the acceptable levels of less than 25% of GDP in 2006; Financial integration is evidenced by gradually declining long-term interest rates following an increased inflow of FDIs and the repeated upgrading of the country's credit rating; Domestic financial markets, still highly dominated by the banking sector, but increasing their depth and overcoming their past isolation from the international financial markets. The banking system, exclusively owned and controlled by highly reputable European banks, is competitive and already well integrated into the single market; A relatively high level of foreign direct investments. In an environment of almost full capital liberalisation the current account deficit is well backed by FDIs. The list of achievements could be even longer, but this is not the main point in my message to you. I just want to stress once more the importance of the continuity in the governments economic policy and the broad political and social consensus on the priorities of this policy for increasing and preserving investors confidence. In my view, this confidence is the key to the improvement of the competitiveness of our small open economy. We should be aware of this when tackling the challenges we are still facing in the economic field. It would be rather exaggerated and unrealistic if we considered all our experience in the economic policy implementation after 1997 as a success story. In fact we are still far away from excellence in macroeconomic management. What are, in my opinion, the main challenges we are faced with. First of all, society on average is still very short-sighted. What I mean by saying that. Many of the politicians and highly placed civil servants are accustomed to a manner of working in which they put emphasis on imminent problems mostly, without paying enough attention to long-term effects. This manner could be appropriate for crisis and post-crisis periods but not for the present moment of long-term macroeconomic stability. The stability of the Bulgarian economy provides an opportunity for policymakers to broaden the time horizon and it is up to them to use this opportunity of taking long term strategic decisions. The lack of active long-sighted statesmen is, to some extent, related to still existing social disparities in Bulgarian society, which give rise to political parties with populist platforms. The poverty is the basis of populism, but it could not be overcome by the means proposed by populists. The phenomenon of populism and its social roots could be overcome by means of medium-to-long-term policies oriented towards persistently increasing the quality of life and the competitiveness of the economy. Clear values like these of the Economic and Monetary Union are preconditions and catalyzing factors for long-term looking policies. I would say that the potential for a better economic policy in Bulgaria is related to the opportunity before politicians to take long-term decisions based on economic stability, further liberalization and restructuring of socially important and sensitive at the same time areas like public utilities system, health care and education. The overcoming of the challenges we are facing largely depends on the realization of this potential. I will try to clarify my position.We all believe that Bulgaria is about to become a member of the EU in a few months. This is one of the greatest achievements of our country, showing that our persistence in applying the above mentioned rules of economic policy has been rewarded. But if, blinded by the euphoria of the moment, we consider that it is enough with the reforms and we should not hurry to make the next step towards becoming an EMU member without derogation, the Bulgarian economy could lose momentum. In fact, the membership in the eurozone fully complies with the present economic policy principles whose core is the currency board arrangement, and it is a consistent and logical step towards taking all possible benefits of the integration process. The Bulgarian National Bank is perhaps the greatest proponent of the EMU in the country. It sounds strange for a central bank, which, by becoming a member of the Eurosystem, will lose its possibility of implementing the monetary policy in the country. But in fact we lost this possibility with the introduction of the currency board arrangement and that was for good. Normally, the national bank is a national institution which stays away from everyday political struggles, but is the most forward-looking. Taking into account that Bulgarias full fledged membership in the EMU is a question of a great public interest and importance, we adopted and published a Strategy for the Bulgarian National Bank Development between 2004 and 2009 with the main purpose to draw up a clear timetable of our medium-term objectives and tasks related to the introduction of the euro. Moreover, the Bulgarian National Bank initiated talks with the government which led to the signing of an agreement between two institutions on the introduction of the euro in Bulgaria. This agreement is a guarantee against ungrounded and unexpected changes in the priorities of the economic policy. When thinking of our experience with economic reforms, I always ask myself how to multiply the positive effects. The internal inclination I have is that the answer to the above question lays in the further enlargement of the EU. In that way the community undoubtedly realizes the economy of scale and promotes the real values, such as democracy, liberalization and economic reforms, in the countries, for which currently the prospect of becoming a member of the EU is not so clear end imminent. Everyone might remember at the moment the proverb One mans meat is another mans poison. Nevertheless, in my opinion it is incontestable that objectives and policies, behind which a large part of society stands, are more likely to succeed. The integration into the EU helped us introduce reforms which seemed impossible ten years ago. The clear European perspective could help other South-East European countries boost economic reforms. Moreover, the European integration is a process, which brings together political and economic transformations, the establishment of the parliamentary democracy and the promulgation of the right of private initiative. This symbiosis is an additional guaranty for success, giving impetus to economic reforms, acting as a catalyst of the transformation of the society and last but not least attracting foreign investors. Correct me if I am wrong, but all these considerations and suggestions seem incomplete if the role of the institutions of the EU is not mentioned. A clear signal from these institutions in support of integration strives of South-East European countries could help. It seems that Old Europe is tired of the enlargement. The current situation of the labour market of some old member states of the EU could not be an argument against the enlargement. The history of the integration in Europe has indicated clearly that in the long run the newcomers have always contributed to the wealth and competitiveness of the Union and its members. At the end, I would like to reiterate the main conclusion from the Bulgarian experience with economic reforms: the success of these reforms was a function of the ability of politicians to formulate and implement a sustainable economic policy, whose principles are largely accepted by the society. The existence of a clear long-term strategic objective of EU integration, shared by the society, can give impetus to reforms and assure the continuity between the priorities of different governments. Thank you for the attention. ____________ The views expressed in the speech are those of the speaker, and do not necessarily reflect the policy of the Bulgarian National Bank. PAGE PAGE 2

Title: Bulgarian banking system towards the emu
Subtitle: BULGARIAN BANKING SYSTEM TOWARDS THE EMU
text: Presentation by Mr. Tsvetan Manchev, Deputy Governor of the BNB, to the High Level Evening Panel Discussion Welcoming Bulgaria and Romania in the EU: Maintaining the Momentum for Economic Reform, Brussels, 17 January 2007 BULGARIAN BANKING SYSTEM TOWARDS THE EMU Your Excellencies, Ladies and Gentlemen, Dear Colleagues, It is a pleasure and a privilege for me to take part in this high level discussion and I would like to thank the organizers - the Brussels Representative Office of the Oesterreichische Nationalbank  for the opportunity given. Please allow me also to congratulate our northern neighbour Romania on its successful completion of the accession process and its membership in the European Union. For both countries, this is possibly the greatest achievement in recent history. In my presentation, I would like to focus on the policy of Bulgarias further integration in the EU and on the role of the banking system in the process of adopting the euro. Bulgaria has recently joined the European Union with the irrevocable commitment to become part of the euro area and to introduce the single currency. As part of the fifth wave of enlargement, both Bulgaria and Romania are not given an opt-out clause with regard to their EMU membership. Bulgaria is aware of the consensus among the Commission, the ECB, and the Member States on strict implementation of the Maastricht criteria against any threat for the stability of the Union. We would not be questioning at all the commitment. It was a long time ago when the Republic of Bulgaria declared its intention to design and implement a policy developed in compliance with the criteria for euro adoption within a short period of time. Perhaps, one might regard this goal as overambitious for the new-entrants and driven by the recent euphoria. I would like to draw your attention to the fact that the above stated political commitment was expressed officially for the first time in the position on Chapter 11 Economic and Monetary Union submitted to the European Commission in November 2000. I am really proud to highlight the continuity of the broad political consensus on the goal of euro adoption within a short period of time. The political will for adopting the single currency as early as possible was reconfirmed in many other official documents among which: the five consecutive pre-accession economic programs of the country, the programs of two consecutive governments, the Strategy for the Development of the Bulgarian National Bank 2004  2009. Over the years, it has gained such an increasing public support that on the day of accession some Bulgarians were astonished that the BNB still offered Bulgarian levs at its tills. The key principles of the national strategy for the adoption of the euro are formulated in a precise and concise way in the Agreement between the Council of Ministers and the Bulgarian National Bank on the Introduction of the Euro in the Republic of Bulgaria signed at the end of 2004 and reconfirmed by the current government in office. They include: Joining the Exchange Rate Mechanism II at the earliest possible date after the date of the official accession of Bulgaria to the EU; Maintaining the currency board arrangement until joining the euro area at the existing level of the fixed exchange rate of the Bulgarian lev; A unilateral commitment on behalf of the Bulgarian government and the BNB to maintain a zero deviation of the exchange rate from the fixed level (i.e. maintaining currently existing parity); Adherence to the minimum period defined in the EU legislation for participation in Exchange Rate Mechanism II and proceeding in a timely manner with all the necessary actions concerning the euro area membership application procedure. The fact that the above mentioned principles became an integral part of the first Convergence Program of Bulgaria, submitted recently to the European Commission, gives another clear political signal. The Convergence Program confirms that Bulgaria fulfills in a sustainable way all the Maastricht criteria for full-fledged membership in the third stage of the Economic and Monetary Union except for the inflation criterion. As could be seen in the Convergence program, our strong intention is to comply with this criterion within the current policy framework including a currency board arrangement, tough fiscal policy, and further extension of structural reforms. Although Bulgaria still does not meet the inflation criterion in a sustainable way, the inflationary path shows that since the introduction of the currency board arrangement, the rate of inflation has been declining towards levels close to the ECB target during the accomplishment of every single stage of the reform process. Thus, the volatility of inflation is declining and the natural rate of inflation in Bulgaria is not far from the euro area one. We consider the goal of euro adoption within a short period of time consistent with the broad Community perspective, the requirements of the Growth and Stability Pact and the Lisbon Agenda. In that respect, the continuous efforts of the Republic of Bulgaria to promote further the stability and sustainability of government finance, to design and implement strong anti-inflationary policies and to increase competitiveness through implementation of structural reforms should be welcomed and should receive vast support by the guardians of the European idea. Our conviction in the feasibility of the strategic project of introducing the euro in Bulgaria after the fulfillment of the Maastricht criteria is to a large extent based on the development of the financial sector, and of the banking system in particular. As mentioned in the Bulgarian Convergence Program, in the absence of active monetary policy and control over interest rates in the country, the currency peg to the euro and the full liberalization of the financial account substantially facilitate further financial integration with the euro area. Our studies have shown that the decisions of the ECB concerning the euro interest rates are transmitted to the interest levels in Bulgaria. The relatively quick transmission of the interest rates is a function of almost full capital mobility, of the increased competition in the banking system, of the large share of floating-rate loans, and of the property structure of the commercial banks in the country. As of the end of 2006, about 75% of the banking system assets were governed by financial institutions based in EU Members States, and about 60% of the assets were governed by Euroland investors. We know that maintaining the stability of the banking system, while preserving the currency board arrangement, is an important precondition and a pillar for achieving the inflation goal, as well as for keeping up public confidence in the euro adoption project. That is why the measures to maintain a sound and stable banking system are among the cornerstones of the Strategy for the Development of the Bulgarian National Bank until 2009. They include timely implementation of the acquis communautaire in banking and the best international sound banking practices. In line with the above, from the beginning of 2007 Bulgaria launched the Basle II principles. The central bank closely monitors the banking sector dynamics, applies stringent supervision requirements, and is ready to use all available instruments at its disposal to achieve and maintain the price stability objective. I started my rather short presentation by saying that we are all still under the spell of the realization of the EU membership project  that is perhaps the greatest achievement in our countrys recent history. I would like to finish it by saying that we are determined not to lose momentum and even to speed up our pace in the integration process by making in a timely manner the next step towards becoming an EMU member without derogation. ____________ Welcoming Bulgaria and Romania in the EU: Maintaining the Momentum for Economic Reform is the topic of the High Level Evening Panel Discussion organized by the European Commission, Economic and Financial Affairs DG and the Austrian National Bank (Oesterreichische Nationalbank) on 17th January 2007 in Brussels. The speakers are Mr. Josef Christl, Executive Director of the Oesterreichische Nationalbank, H.E. Ambassador Gregor Woschnagg, Permanent Representative of Austria to the EU, Mr. Marco Buti, Deputy Director General of the DG Ecfin of the European Commission, Mr. Tsvetan Manchev, Deputy Governor of the Bulgarian National Bank and Mr. Cristian Popa, Deputy Governor of the National Bank of Romania. Title: Presentation made at the seminar Bulgaria - from Transition to Convergence: New Challenges jointly organized by the BNB and the IMF, Sofia
Subtitle: LESSONS DRAWN FROM THE IMF-SUPPORTED PROGRAMMES
text: Presentation of Mr. Tsvetan Manchev, BNB Deputy Governor, made at the seminar Bulgaria - from Transition to Convergence: New Challenges jointly organized by the BNB and the IMF, Sofia, 2 May 2007 LESSONS DRAWN FROM THE IMF-SUPPORTED PROGRAMMES Ladies and Gentlemen, It is a pleasure for me to take part in this seminar which looks into the results of the cooperation between Bulgaria and the International Monetary Fund (IMF). I would like to thank the IMF Mission in Bulgaria for the kind invitation and for the opportunity to present here my personal opinion on the lessons from the fulfillment of the IMF programs in Bulgaria. I am going to present very briefly the relations between the Republic of Bulgaria and the IMF and then draw your attention to two issues: Classification of Bulgarias programs with the IMF according to the extent to which their goals have been accomplished; Lessons for Bulgarias economic policy from the 17-year cooperation with the IMF. In my speech I am not going to talk about the discussion on the adequacy of the Funds program objectives and the IMFs international role. This should be done by economic historians and researchers into the IMFs activities in the global economy. This discussion goes far beyond the short time horizon and scope of the relations between Bulgaria and the IMF that are todays topic. At the beginning I will remind you that Bulgaria became a member of the IMF in September 1990. For a period of nearly 17 years our country signed 13 short-term agreements with the Fund, and under these it received altogether 2.2 billion Special Drawing Rights (SDRs). Ten of the agreements are of the Stand-by Arrangement type; two are Contingent Compensatory Financing Facility (CCFF); and one is a Systemic Transformation Facility (STF). These agreements differ in the conditionalities for using the tranches (purchases) under them, the requirements for signing them, and their repayment terms. Stand-by Arrangements are the main credit instrument of the Fund. They establish the use of the so-called upper tranches - loans exceeding 25% of the respective countrys quota. Their use depends on the fulfillment of conditions described in the Adjustment Programs, or better-known in Bulgaria as Stabilization Programs. After gaining access to global capital markets, many IMF member-countries prefer to treat their stand-by arrangements as precautionary and draw funds only if needed. The last 13th arrangement between Bulgaria and the IMF was of this nature  a precautionary arrangement  and no SDRs purchases were made under it. Contingent Compensatory Financing Facilities are signed to overcome difficulties with the respective countrys balance of payments, caused by adverse foreign trade developments as a result of events beyond that countrys control. Their tranches are smaller in size in terms of the quota; they have relatively less conditions in order to be used; and shorter repayments terms. Systemic Transformation Facilities are special credit instruments created to support the transition from a centrally-planned to market economy and are no longer actively used by the Fund. It should be noted that Bulgaria has always been a perfect payer on all its agreements with the IMF. Of all agreements with the IMF, only the fourth one, signed in 1996, was terminated early because the Bulgarian side had not carried out the agreed reforms. For the same reason, in the early 1990s the last tranches under a number of agreements were not allowed. Therefore, we can classify the agreements of the Republic of Bulgaria with the IMF in accordance with the extent to which the agreed objectives have been achieved into three periods: First period (1991  1997): Promised but not delivered; Second period (1997  2001): Promised and delivered; Third period (2001  2007): Promises are not simply delivered but the reforms are consistent and long-term oriented  towards the full membership in the Economic and Monetary Union in Europe. The first period of the relations between Bulgaria and the IMF, whose logical ending was the termination of the fourth agreement and the economic crisis at end-1996, is characterized by short-term inconsistent objectives and an intransparent economic policy. The BNB monetary policy had a legally established twofold purpose  to maintain the internal and external stability of the national monetary unit. The attempt to maintain at once price stability and exchange rate stability under a floating rate regime with the same instrument  money supply  proved to be both theoretically and practically unsuccessful under an inconsistent, ill-aimed and unpredictable fiscal policy in an economy dominated by the State and burdened by huge matured government debts and a moratorium on them. At the end of the first period Bulgarias obligations to the IMF were reduced not because the economy did not need any funding but for the lack of political will for reforms in the state economy. In the second period Bulgaria reached the highest level of its obligations to the IMF. Given its isolation from international financial markets, the country received IMF financing against the fulfillment of economic reforms commitments made to the Fund. This period is characterized by clarity and publicity of the monetary and fiscal policies goals and enhanced coordination between them for carrying out the agreed reforms. The monetary policy followed a simple rule  the money supply is legally pegged to the foreign exchange assets by the currency board arrangement and the fixed exchange rate of the Bulgarian Lev to the Deutsche Mark (the Euro). The fiscal policy was cautious and predictable aimed to avoid further accumulation of government debts by means of a large-scale privatization of state-owned enterprises. The stringent fiscal policy was supported by structural reforms designed to liberalize markets and improve the investment climate in the country. In 2000 Bulgarias outstanding debt obligations to IMF amounted to more than SDR 1 billion; however, in the next year they began to decrease. That exactly was the beginning of the third stage of relations between Bulgaria and the Fund. The restored confidence in the domestic markets owing to the policy conducted during the second stage reduced the need for financing through IMF-supported programs. This last stage preserved most of the characteristics of the macroeconomic framework of the previous stage. The new in the second stage was the political will and the public support of reforms aimed at a sustainable economic growth. This will was expressed in several directions. First, official announcement and pursuit of the Strategy of the BNB and the government for euro adoption upon compliance of the Maastricht criteria for a full EU membership in the third stage of the European Economic and Monetary Union while maintaining the current fixed exchange rate at 1.95583 lev per euro. Second, the fiscal policy was already aimed at repaying the government debts inherited in the 1980s and 1990s and restraining the accumulation of new debts. Third, strengthening the coordination of long-term economic policies within the limits set by EC by means of Pre-accession economic programs (2001-2005), the first Convergence Program (2007-2009), the National Reform Program and the National Strategic Reference Framework for Community support (2007-2013). Thus we come to March 2007, when the term of the last Stand-by Arrangement expired and to 27 April 2007 when Bulgaria paid in full its obligations to the IMF. IMF withdrew both as a partner in formulating and conducting the macroeconomic policy, as well as a creditor. This is a sign that Bulgaria is already recognized as a full member on the international financial markets and in the world economy. Such expression of confidence in the Bulgarian macroeconomic policy is without parallel, at least in the last two decades. Here, logically comes the question of what we have learnt from the fulfillment of the thirteen arrangements with IMF. I believe the main lessons form the programs with the Fund for those involved in the implementation of the macroeconomic policy are as follows: First, the IMF-supported programs do not automatically guarantee by themselves a sustainable long-term economic growth and development. The IMF programs are short-term looking and their success depends on the consensus between the Fund and the national authorities on an adequate choice of measures and actions, or in other words about the specific policy mix. Second, IMFs expertise is strong and effective in managing strong economic fluctuations, shocks and crises. After closing the programs with Bulgaria the IMF and its partners will still have the challenge of translating the results achieved into successive long-term models and strategies for sustainable development. Third, IMFs role in formulating the macroeconomic policy of countries implementing programs is and should remain short-term oriented. It is the responsibility of the national authorities and of the public to formulate and build a public consensus on a consistent set of structural and microeconomic reforms necessary to attain the national goals for sustainable growth. Fourth, involving all national stakeholders in the discussions of IMF programs (political parties, entrepreneurs, investors, and syndicates) is key to successfully accomplish them. For that purpose, the partners in the social dialogue need have about the same institutional capacity in order to efficiently achieve and realize consensus on reforms within a program. They should be able to understand the IMF language, as well as to have sufficient political will to seek, achieve and realize a consensus. To me, the major conclusion is that the political will and the public consensus on reforms aimed at achieving specific long-term (or Community) objectives can not be replaced by the above arrangements with IMF. Of course, the lessons could go even further, especially if we explore one by one all economic policy areas - why not also look into the social, health, education or any other policy of the government? Over the last 15-16 years the whole society was, willingly or not, integrally linked with IMF. Politicians at first, then the businesses and the media, and finally the users  i.e. the general public  became used to the clamour that went with the negotiations over the arrangements with IMF. All these agents began to take seriously in their economic and political actions what those arrangements said and to adapt themselves to the results of the negotiations, irrespective of whether they emotionally agreed or disagreed with them. This involvement of the public is also a lesson from the implementation of the programs. I would like to finish my statement with the question: Which way now? What course the process of formulation and implementation of the macroeconomic policy should take without the disciplining effect of the arrangements with IMF? I hope this question will provoke the esteemed audience to discussion. Without pretense to exhaustiveness, I will only say that the decision should inevitably take into account both the limitations of a small and open economy within the context of the global economy and our EU membership, and the long-term objectives on which a public consensus was reached in the third stage of our relations with IMF. Having already the significant institutional capacity and experience from the dialogue with IMF, I hope together we will find the most proper answer to the above question. Naturally, the relations of the Republic of Bulgaria with the IMF do not cease upon repayment of the last debt obligation accumulated in the 1990s. I believe that we should continue using in the form of technical assistance the vast knowledge of the Fund on the world economy and finance and the recommendable international practice for resolving strategic macroeconomic problems and shocks. The continuous dialogue with IMF as well as with the other international financial institutions and the European institutions will also be indispensable for creating in our partners understanding of and confidence in the Bulgarian economy, and for accumulating and drawing on their knowledge of global economy. Thank you for your attention! ____________ Initially these were planned as precautionary arrangement, i.e. purchases should be made only in case of financial difficulties for the countries that have signed them. Later they began to be used as a source of external financing. PAGE PAGE 2

Title: Speech to the European Bankers Symposium, Vienna
Subtitle: FINANCIAL STABILITY FRAMEWORK IN BULGARIA
text: Speech by Mr. Tsvetan Manchev, Deputy Governor of the BNB, to the European Bankers Symposium, Vienna, 3 May 2007 FINANCIAL STABILITY FRAMEWORK IN BULGARIA Ladies and Gentlemen, It is a great pleasure for me to participate in the European BANKERS Symposium and to speak in front of such a distinguished audience of professionals. I would like to thank the organisers  Finance Trainer International - and Dr. Hannes Enthofer personally for the kind invitation.
