As the topic of our panel is the Contribution of the Central and Eastern European Countries to global financial market stability, I decided to put the emphasis of my short speech on the institutional framework which guarantees the financial stability in Bulgaria. You probably know that the monetary regime in Bulgaria is a currency board arrangement, which presupposes the importance of sound public finances, on the one hand, and the stability of financial institutions, on the other hand, for the preservation of the overall financial stability in the country. I think that we all can agree that Bulgaria contributes to global financial market stability by maintaining the confidence in the currency board arrangement through the countrys conservative fiscal policy and the rigorous regulatory framework of its financial system. Public finances have been put in order with the consolidated budget on surplus for the last 4 years and the government debt declined to the level of 20% to GDP. Although the market economy in Bulgaria was restored not so long ago, the country has made great progress in market-oriented reforms in all economic spheres and particularly in the financial sector. The development of financial markets in the early 1990s made Bulgarian politicians fully realise the need of concerted efforts of the various public institutions for maintaining economic and financial stability, and now most of the important legislation in this area has already been adopted. Purportedly the bulk of legislative decisions in this field have been taken after the introduction the CBA. The institutional framework for maintaining financial stability in Bulgaria is tripartite. The Bulgarian National Bank (BNB) is responsible for establishing the institutional capacity in the banking supervision field. The supervision of other financial markets is exercised by the Financial Supervision Commission (FSC). The Ministry of Finance is responsible for the general regulatory framework of the financial sector and financial control. There is a legally established coordination mechanism for the three parties - the Financial Stability Advisory Council, consisting of the Minister of Finance, the BNB Governor, and the Chairperson of the FSC. The first task of this coordination mechanism, after its introduction in 2003 with the Financial Supervision Commission Act, is to contribute to the increase in the information shared between the above-mentioned institutions. It took us some time to clarify and define the information frameworks for which each one of these institutions is responsible. This having been done, the Financial Stability Advisory Council started functioning as the main forum for coordinating the efforts of its members in supervising financial markets. After the accession of the Republic of Bulgaria to the European Union the importance of the Council increased as it became the forum where the Minister of Finance, the Bulgarian National Bank and the Financial Supervision Commission effectuate the coordination of their positions on the new European legislation and initiatives on financial markets. The Bulgarian financial markets deepen fast as foreign investors with different and rich corporate cultures are coming in, and this has triggered a process of coordination between the Bulgarian authorities and their counterparts in the investors countries. The Bulgarian National Bank has signed supervisory cooperation agreements with 11 foreign banking supervisory authorities, 8 of which are with supervisors from EU member states. As you might expect these agreements involve the supervisory authorities of almost all foreign banks which have branches or subsidiaries in Bulgaria, the same being true for the supervisors of branches and subsidiaries of Bulgarian banks abroad. Since most investors come from the EU, this process is backed up and facilitated by the harmonization of the financial sector legislation in the EU as well as by the Community coordination mechanisms. The BNB relies on the cooperation with international financial institutions represented in Bulgaria as well as with foreign investors in the Bulgarian banking sector. The Central Bank seeks to maintain the dialogue with these institutions and investors, trying to support their initiatives for increasing the exchange of information. Moreover we consider that the competition between banks should not exclude the principles of sound banking practices but, on the contrary, these principles should be embedded in the banking business. How do we do this in practice? The Bulgarian National Bank creates a foreseeable environment for commercial banks by putting in place strict regulations. The BNB has been among the first regulatory institutions in the EU which implemented the capital requirements directives. Directive 2006/48/EC is fully transposed into the Law on Credit Institutions in force since the effective date of the Treaty of the Republic of Bulgarias Accession to the European Union (01.01.2007). Directive 2006/49/EC was fully implemented in the BNB Ordinance No. 8 on Capital Adequacy of Credit Institutions from the beginning of this year. The BNB has taken a more conservative approach than the one recommended in the latter Directive. For instance, the capital adequacy ratio for Bulgarian banks is set at 12%. The BNB measures for containing credit growth in the country is another good example in this sense. We introduced these measures after taking into consideration the opinion of the commercial banks holding 70% of the loan portfolios that they would prefer measures enforced on all banks but with in-built elements taking account of the banks individual risk characteristics. The essence of the measures  the additional minimum required reserves, which the banks called credit ceilings, affected mostly the business of credit institutions which take relatively more risk due to their aggressive lending policy. Moreover, we announced that these measures would be temporary and would be in place until the private sector lending reached more moderate and stable growth rates, and we did keep our promise. Since June 2006 the BNB has started to gradually remove the credit ceilings. Having achieved the desired stability effect in the banking sector as of 1 January 2007, the BNB abolished the restrictions. In conclusion, let me say that there is still a lot of work to be done by the Bulgarian authorities responsible for maintaining financial stability so that they can increase their capacity for coordinated action. The main challenge for them remains the timely reaction to the rapidly changing markets. We, in the Bulgarian National Bank, believe that investing in market knowledge, a dialogue with financial institutions, and the cooperation within the EU for maintaining financial stability at the European level, is the key to success. I hope that soon we will be able to demonstrate again this conviction in the initiative to publish on a regular basis a Financial Stability Report, whose main purpose will be to promote the awareness of the Bulgarian financial institutions and the public at large of issues that are relevant for safeguarding the stability of the countrys financial system. Thank you for your attention. PAGE PAGE 2

Title: Speech delivered at the opening of the The Challenges of Euro Area Membership panel as part of the Conference 10 Years of Currency Board and the Challenges of the Euro Adoption, Sofia
Subtitle: WITH A CURRENCY BOARD TO THE EURO AREA
text: Speech of Mr. Tsvetan Manchev, BNB Deputy Governor, delivered at the opening of the The Challenges of Euro Area Membership panel as part of the Conference 10 Years of Currency Board and the Challenges of the Euro Adoption, Sofia, 18 September 2007 WITH A CURRENCY BOARD TO THE EURO AREA Ladies and Gentlemen, Dear colleagues, This mornings discussion suitably summarized Bulgarias experience of living under a currency board with the advantages and requirements of this monetary regime to the other economic policy elements. I call them requirements and by no means disadvantages because the currency board is a regime practiced according to rules. This presupposes, both theoretically and practically, that the results are highly dependent on the understanding and accommodation of all economic agents, and the social and economic policy to the currency board rules. Ten years are a right period to make a recapitulation, so I would also want to support the conclusion already made this morning that the result is unequivocally positive. As Mr. Ganev convincingly proved, the recent ten years are the most successful in Bulgarias modern economic history in terms of growth and improved living standards. This is owing, on the one hand, to the last three governments which pursued a consistent economic policy, and on the other  to the patience and public support for reforms. It is not less important, however, to note the support provided by the international financial and political community for the reforms in this country, irrespective of the numerous shocks that the Bulgarian economy suffered, as mentioned this morning. Bulgaria is already an EU member. The high score naturally generates high expectations. As the saying goes, not only in Bulgaria, appetite comes with eating. So this is exactly the aim of our afternoon session  to discuss the framework within which our expectations can be rational, balanced, and supportive of the economys sustainable growth and increasing the nations welfare. The experience and results in the recent ten years are a good basis for discussion. In his presentation this morning Governor Iskrov clearly proved the idea that Bulgarias next aim should be the introduction of the euro and preserving the currency board at the present parity of the fixed exchange rate of the lev to the euro. Until then the natural monetary regime is the currency board as it ensures the least cost of accommodation. He added another important argument in support of his thesis, namely that the modern global financial market inevitably drives small and open economies to use the umbrella of economic and monetary unions to best develop the competitive advantages of their economies. The good thing is that the above view is a long-supported decision of the last three Bulgarian governments. It is an integral part of a number of important state documents: The positions on Chapter 11 Economic and Monetary Union in the course of negotiations for EU accession, 2000; The Agreement between the Council of Ministers and the BNB on the adoption of the Euro in the Republic of Bulgaria, 2004. A Pre-Accession Economic Program of the Republic of Bulgaria 2006-2009; The First Convergence Program of the Republic of Bulgaria 2007-2009. The above shows that the adoption of the Euro is a strategy strongly embraced both socially and politically in Bulgaria. It is also supported by the Bulgarias Treaty of Accession to the EU, which clearly and explicitly restates the text on the mandatory adoption of the single currency by the Member States as laid down in the Treaty establishing the European Community. Of course, the road to achieving the important goal  the adoption of the euro  holds a number of challenges. First and foremost, Bulgaria will have to firmly continue its consistent policy of structural reforms. Which are the most sensitive reforms became already clear from this mornings discussion, so I will not dwell on this. I presume Mr. P. Chobanov will bring out and systematize them again in his capacity of a Managing Director of the Agency for Economic Analysis and Forecasting. This is the institution which is in charge of the coordination of developing the Convergence programs in our country. Sticking steadfast to the course of reforms is needed leastways to root out (do away with) the inflationary expectations that recently recurred after a long pause as a result of the development of the international environment and the increased domestic demand. To speed up implementing structural reforms in the fields of education, labour market, healthcare, social insurance, and institutions is the only theoretically and practically known and proven recommendation in such situations in small and open economies running currency boards. I would like to remind you that the inflation criterion is the only Maastricht criterion that Bulgaria does not meet sustainably at present. At this point I would like to open up a bracket to highlight the importance of planning and development of institutions as an important challenge towards the adoption of the Euro. I would use the BNB as example, being one of the institutions whose mission is to support the economic policy in controlling and restraining the disbalances, on the one hand. , and on the other, the European institutions expect the BNB to vouch that Bulgaria fulfills the technical criteria for Euro adoption. In order to close the bracket quickly I will discuss only two things. First, the last ten years of experience gave strong proof of the positive effect of the BNBs pro-active policy orientated towards ensuring the stability of the banking system and the sound functioning of financial markets, observing at all times the strict rules of the currency board. Secondly, the BNB already conducts large scale reforms aiming at improving the quality of the cash circulation and the creation of a cash market in Bulgaria, which are also part of the technical requirements for the euro adoption. I am closing the bracket here and would like to thank our partners in those processes, namely the Bulgarian Government and Parliament, the international financial institutions, the European institutions, the commercial banks and the Bulgarian public. I hope that this spirit of mutual trust and support will continue to exist along the way to the euro adoption, as these are important conditions to achieving our goals. Yet another and not less important challenge on the way to the Euro adoption is international support, and I would presume that the rest of the participants from the panel of National Central Banks of EU Member States and the EC will also address this topic. I would like to point out that the BNB is well aware that we could seek and receive external support into adopting the Euro only if we strictly observe the Treaty establishing the European Community. In this relation I can assure our partners present here, that we do our homework regularly and I hope they are convinced we do so. Thank you for your attention! PAGE PAGE 2

Title: Speech delivered at the Annual Meeting of the Business and the Bulgarian Government Second Decade of Growth: Risks and Opportunities, Sofia
Subtitle:
THE INTEGRATION OF BULGARIA
INTO THE EUROPEAN FINANCIAL SYSTEM
text: Speech of Mr. Tsvetan Manchev, BNB Deputy Governor, delivered at the Annual Meeting of the Business and the Bulgarian Government Second Decade of Growth: Risks and Opportunities, Sofia, 3rd October 2007 THE INTEGRATION OF BULGARIA INTO THE EUROPEAN FINANCIAL SYSTEM Ladies and Gentlemen, I am particularly pleased to take part in this meeting of representatives of the business and the government that has already become a tradition. First, I would like to thank the organizers of Kapital Handelsblatt for the opportunity provided to me to speak to such a demanding audience. The trends in and prospects to the Bulgarian economy only at first sight make my task easier as there are still challenges in the global economy, and shocks become more and more difficult to foresee and with an yet greater amplitude. This forces small and open economies to preserve their solid foundations and consistently and unswervingly pursue structural reforms. I will focus my presentation on two areas only: Macroeconomic development and prospects; Major challenges facing the economy and the banking system and the policy response. The Bulgarian economy has already reached a sustainable state in the phase of its initial integration into the European economy after the first and second generations of reforms pursued. It registers growth for a tenth year in a row after the introduction of the currency board. In the recent four years, real GDP growth has sustainably establish itself around and a little above 6%. It is considerably higher than the average EU level and approximates the average growth of the 12 new Member States. Economic growth in Bulgaria is supported by the positive trends in the labour market where the level of unemployment has repeatedly fallen  down to 7%, a level near to the average EU one. The strong foundations of the economy come as the result primarily of the condition of government finances. They have consecutively stabilized and improved owing to the established anchors  public expenditures sustainably stabilized at around 40% of GDP, consistent consolidation of budget cash flows allowing for improved efficiency of utilization of public funds. This has permitted a phased reduction of tax incidence in the recent 5-6 years and sharp reduction of public debt  down to below 20% of GDP. Bulgaria is in full compliance with the Stability and Growth Pact and is deservedly rated high both by the rating agencies and by the international financial institutions, investors, the Commission and our EU partners. In terms of development of major macroeconomic processes, however, the country is facing a number of important challenges  first of all the external imbalances and the relatively high and volatile inflation. The increased volatility of international financial markets and global economy has recently come into the picture, too. The latter have no visible unfavourable impact, at least for the time being, on the Bulgarian economy owing to the principles of the currency board and the strong relatedness of the Bulgarian currency with the euro, and due to the deep integration of our economy, and particularly of the prevailing part of our banking markets, with the European ones, especially with the euro area member states. Besides, the structure of investors in the domestic banking sector is well diversified, and can acts as an important buffer against the spread of shocks like the one seen in the recent months in the financial markets. There is no broad use in Bulgaria of the financial instruments causing the shock  securitized debt bonds, which additionally guarantees our economys robustness. All challenges enumerated so far require adequate response and adaptation, particularly by such a small and open economy as the Bulgarian. I believe an economic policy to cope with the challenges and risks entailed in them should be based on several important principles tested in our practice in the last decade:  To preserve the currency board and the existing exchange parity of the lev to the euro until the time of joining the euro area;  To continue with the stringent and flexible fiscal policy, implemented so far, as the only efficient instrument to cope with the above challenges;  To speed up structural reforms in the economy for improving its competitiveness; to continue with the liberalization of all markets and areas of economic activity;  To further strengthen the stability of the financial system through a regulatory policy consistently and unswervingly implementing good international practices and standards. The above-mentioned principles would guarantee the preservation of the economys solid foundations that have made possible the high and sustainable growth in the recent years. There is no country in the world that has achieved permanent improvement of welfare and living standards without continuous, consistent and well planned and communicated reforms for strengthening its economic foundations. In order to countervail external imbalances, it is particularly important to retain the current high rate of investments in the economy. Currently, foreign investments not only cover the current account deficit, but are also a basis for the technological restructuring of the economy. The investment inflow can be sustained not through magic but by means of creating competitive advantages for investors. The tools for this are clear: they only need to be efficiently directed. Labour market liberalization needs to be given further impetus in order to enhance the control over the wage growth in the public sector and the size of administration, as well as to continue the consolidation of public finances. BNBs measures aimed to contain the high liquidity accumulated due to various factors, which was also reflected in an abrupt increase of the credit growth in the last 4-5 months, can only temporary reduce the imbalances. This is the time to apply a targeted package of measures to boost up savings and ease the pressure on the balance of payments by reducing domestic demand. The accelerated rate of inflation over the last months is an important signal and it has to be properly read. I do not agree with the opinion expressed by some Bulgarian economists that there is no need to curb the growth of incomes in the public sector in order to meet the inflation convergence criterion for euro area membership on the argument that economic growth should not be limited. Effectively, such arguments denounce the policy followed so far, which led to a long-term growth, and take us ten years back. I do not know a country whose modern economic theory has led to a significant improvement of its living standard and quality of life without rooting out the inflationary expectations from peoples behaviour. Only a consistent policy of liberalization and disinflation is the well-known and proven remedy in global economy. The rest is economic utopia and leads to conjuncture effects which only add to the cost of adaptation at a later stage. Led precisely by these principles and knowledge of economy, the BNB will continue to follow a policy of speeding up the processes of liberalization and integration in banking and financial services after Bulgaria accession to the EU. The implementation at the beginning of 2007 of the EU directives on the capital adequacy of banks, respectively the New Capital Accord, known as Basel II, through the new Ordinance No. 8 on the capital adequacy of credit institutions, adopted by the BNB Governing Council, is already an indisputable success. The new rules substantially improve the risk management in banking and reduce Bulgarian banks exposure to shocks. The challenge facing Bulgaria in the next few years in the payment systems area will be to create pre-conditions and adopt the requirements of the Single Euro Payments Area (SEPA). For the European Economic Area (EEA) countries it will start to operate from the beginning of 2008. This project is the next big step towards the creation of a single integrated financial services market in Europe, giving all market participants equal access to it. The purpose is to introduce new standardized generally-accepted instruments for direct debit and credit transfers at a Pan-European level. It gives payment services users new possibilities of making payments in a unified way at home and abroad. The above would bring down payment costs within the European Union. In order for Bulgaria to successfully get integrated into the Single Euro Payments Area, it is very important that it should be looked at not as a single act but rather as a constantly developing project which would strengthen European integration and improve all aspects of the retail payments market in the euro area. The further development of this project would also support the accomplishment of the Lisbon Strategy objectives and promote the competitiveness of the local economy  something that we need more and more given the challenge of external misbalances. The massive change in the payments business would affect all participants in the payment process  commercial banks and their customers, the state administration (especially the National Revenue Agency, the National Social Security Institute, the Customs, etc.), and the central bank. Each one of these participants has a specific role. One of SEPAs major features is the removal of the differences in terms of ease, time and costs of making euro payments no matter whether national borders are crossed or not. Only one account is needed and it would provide access to the entire euro area. Corporations, traders and consumers alike would benefit from the successful implementation of this project. Decreased charges and the uniform payment mechanisms would largely reduce the payment costs of companies. It would be possible to use electronic invoicing and reconciliation, eventually facilitating trade in the euro area. Now analyses are being made of the new processes effects on the payment mechanisms in Bulgaria. After that a National Migration Plan will be developed and it will extensively describe the schedule and the obligations of the various participants. Over the next few years during the so-called migration period, a full harmonization will be achieved, and as a result, there be no difference between domestic and cross-boarder payments within the EU. The specific environment in each country determine the difference in approaches for the implementation of the SEPA project. The national bankers associations of the euro area member states are responsible for transposing of SEPA targets in the national migration plans, allowing every bank and every system operator in the payments infrastructure to adapt their strategy and system for a smooth transition towards the Single Euro Payment Area. The national bankers associations should elaborate ordinances, conventions and agreements, which should provide for the fulfilment of the decisions of the European Payments Council and their implementation on national level. The BNB will facilitate the fulfilment of the goals and the establishment of SEPA in Bulgaria as the process accelerator and coordinator. I will finish by presenting to the attention of the business community another project, which is directly related to the European integration and is an example of good co-operation between the BNB and commercial banks, namely the project for establishing a Cash Services Company (CSC). This project aims at the providing the technical prerequisites for the smooth changeover to the euro, and the main aim of the project is above all the liberalization of the cash services related to the cash circulation within the country, and the gradual development, with the BNBs support, of a market for such services. The Cash Services Company has already been incorporated, and as of the beginning of 2008 will start effectively providing cash services to commercial banks and their clients. The project also contributes to a more effective and secured fulfilment of one of the BNBs main tasks  to provide the security and maintain the quality of the cash circulation in the country. As a regulator, the BNB will continue with its equal treatment policy regarding all banks participating in the cash payment process. On the territory of Sofia, the BNB will provide, free of charge, sealed parcels, pursuant to the ECB regulations. Thank you for your attention. PAGE PAGE 4

Title: Speech at the Adam Smith Seminar 2007 and Beyond: World Economic Prospects (III), Paris, France
Subtitle:
THE PRESENT CONDITIONS, THE MONETARY POLICY
AND THE OUTLOOK FOR THE ECONOMY AND INVESTMENTS IN BULGARIA
text: Speech of Mr. Tsvetan Manchev, Deputy Governor of the Bulgarian National Bank at the Adam Smith Seminar 2007 and Beyond: World Economic Prospects (III), Paris, France, November 13-14, 2007 THE PRESENT CONDITIONS, THE MONETARY POLICY AND THE OUTLOOK FOR THE ECONOMY AND INVESTMENTS IN BULGARIA Ladies and Gentlemen, It is a great pleasure for me to be here again at this seminar and speak in front of such a distinguished audience of highly placed professionals in the field of central and investment banking and government finance. I would like to thank Professor Campos for the invitation and for the opportunity to once again take advantage of this really unique forum for exchange of ideas and experiences and to present my views on the current economic development, policy options and prospects in Bulgaria. Just as a joke, I would suppose that today you would expect me to make a long and perhaps boring speech about the stability of the currency board arrangement (CBA), which together with the fiscal discipline and structural reforms, forms the solid foundation of the last decades economic recovery in Bulgaria. Firstly, if you did have such expectations, this would be a good thing because since the introduction of the CBA, the Bulgarian governments economic policy has been so consistent and predictable, irrespective of the political parties and coalitions in power, that no one would expect anything different from the fixed exchange rate, conservative fiscal policy and ongoing structural reforms. There is no doubt that the success of this policy lies in the wide support and confidence of large parts of the Bulgarian society. Secondly, having achieved a very important and long-awaited goal, such as Bulgarias membership in the EU, it is getting more difficult for the Bulgarian policy makers to convince the public of the need of continuing this policy, which is still related to some socially unpopular measures. In Bulgaria and in most new member states there are over expectations about the margins of the income policy in the public sector after the accession to the European Union. These over expectations are used by some populist political groups and this threatens to undermine one of the main pillars of the present economic policy  the sound fiscal policy. Thirdly, with the CBA in place Bulgaria and the other new member states have successfully passed through many shocks  the Asian crises, followed by the Russian crisis, the stock market crash and the historically low global interest rates  without any sizable theoretical or political dispute on the viability and sustainability of this arrangement. Moreover, both the Council and the ECB have recognised the compatibility of the CBA with the ERM II framework, although this regime is not considered a perfect substitute for the mechanism. Unexpectedly, after Lithuanias attempt to joint the euro area last year and after the recent turbulence in financial markets, the member states with a CBA have increasingly become the focus of European researchers, investors and politicians. The increased interest in and the attempts to analyse the modern CBA in the global economy against the standard macroeconomic and monetary models of the 1960s and 1970s led to some wrong conclusions, and hence to a number of contradicting signals to investors, the people and politicians. These conclusions shoot at the heart of the CBA, neglecting the fact that the confidence of the people and investors in this regime is more important for the political stability than for the growth stability and convergence in compliance with the Maastricht Treaty. My presentation is structured as follows. I will start with a short description of the recent economic development in Bulgaria, trying to outline the main tendencies and the major challenges in the field of economic policy. Than, I will present the possible policy responses to these challenges. Finally, I will unveil Bulgarias official policy to address these challenges. The Bulgarian economy has been on the growth path since the introduction of the currency board ten years ago and already reached a sustainable state in the phase of its initial integration into the European economy after the first and second generations of reforms pursued. Since 1997 the average GDP growth has been 5% annually, while in the last three years it accelerated to about 6%. It is considerably higher than the average EU level and approximates the average growth of the 12 new member states. The real growth rate of the GDP expected for 2007 is 6.3%. The economic growth in Bulgaria is supported by the positive trends in the labour market where the level of unemployment has repeatedly fallen  down to 7%, a level nearing the average EU rate. The strong foundations of an economy with a CBA come primarily as a result of the condition of government finances. A high level of public finance consolidation was achieved in Bulgaria, expressed in increased levels of budget surpluses in recent years. In October this year the public debt decreased to about 15% of GDP and public expenditures were continuously restricted to 40% of GDP. Bulgaria is in full compliance with the Stability and Growth Pact. It has deservedly been given an investment grade with stable or positive outlooks by international rating agencies and has been rated high by international financial institutions, investors, the Commission and many of our EU partners. The consistent macroeconomic policy and the significant improvement in the business environment led to an increase in foreign investors confidence accompanied by a sizable capital inflow to Bulgaria. Over the last decade foreign direct investments were about 10% of GDP annually; right before Bulgarias accession to the EU they rose to 16.4% of GDP and are still on the increase despite the changes in international markets and interest rates. In terms of the development of major macroeconomic processes, however, the country is facing a number of important challenges: Increasing external imbalances; Inflation - higher than that in the euro area and persistently volatile; Relatively high and volatile credit growth; Very low, even negative real interest rates; Doubtful flexibility of the labour market with low levels of unemployment and relatively low levels of labour force participation. The relatively high current account deficit (expected to be about 18-20% of GDP for 2007) follows the sizable FDIs inflow, but not vice versa. It is important to stress this because it is essential for the choice of a theoretical model for analysing the economy. Inflationary pressures are partly reflecting one-off effects from the recent droughts and floods and from the EU accession, and also from economic agents increased costs due to the higher global energy, metal and food prices. On the other hand, the rapidly growing labour demand in some labour market segments creates conditions for upward pressure on wages. This particularly affects the public sector given the nature of the services it renders and the related difficulties in measuring their efficiency. The rapid and volatile bank credit growth leads to risk accumulation. It is driven mainly by the European banks struggle for a market share in Bulgaria, which leads to decreasing interest rates on loans. In an environment of high capital mobility and profit margins, real interest rates on household and corporate loans are close to or below zero. At first, the sharp reduction in interest rates automatically followed the period of historically low global interest rate levels, but it continued even after the major central banks started tightening the monetary policy. The long period of decreasing interest rates creates unrealistic expectations in borrowers and results in underestimating the risks they take. In response, the Bulgarian National Bank repeatedly resorted to a set of modern prudential instruments; in early 2007 the BNB introduced Basle II as a better risk management system and demands that banks keep a much higher minimum capital adequacy as compared to European practices. Responding to the increased liquidity in domestic markets, from September 2007 the BNB raised the level of commercial banks minimum required reserves from 8 to 12 percent. The Bulgarian government, like these of the other new member states, is already well aware of the importance of the labour market flexibility for the CBA and macroeconomic stability in the early years of the accession process. It has steadily implemented active labour market policies with visible results. It is prepared to provide an additional buffer for the labour market through restructuring administration and introducing modern emigration policies, as can be seen from the measures of next years state budget. As a general conclusion, we may say that Bulgarias recent development is similar to that in all the other newly acceded countries with a CBA. The recently increased volatility of international financial markets and the global economy has already come into the picture, too. The latter has had no visible unfavourable impact, at least for the time being, on the Bulgarian economy thanks to the CBA principles and the strong relatedness of the Bulgarian currency to the euro, and also due to the deep integration of our economy, and the predominant part of our banking markets, into the European ones, especially in the euro area. Besides, the structure of investors in the domestic banking sector is well diversified and can act as an important buffer against the spread of shocks like those seen in financial markets in recent months. Ultimately, in Bulgaria there is no broad use of the financial instruments causing the latest shocks  securitized debt bonds, which additionally guarantees our economys robustness. Thus, we arrive to the unexpectedly increasing attention to the CBA on the part of analysts, politicians and speculators. In a currency board regime, the central bank is committed to unlimited interventions to keep the exchange rate at the pre-announced target level, and the amount of available foreign exchange reserves has to be equal to (or exceed) the outstanding monetary base. Bulgaria strictly keeps its FX reserves far above the minimum levels of monetary base coverage. As long as the currency board regime is maintained, it would be impossible for the central bank to run out of FX reserves without, in the case of Bulgaria, causing full euroisation and practical use of the euro as the local currency. Even if it should come to a complete loss of confidence in the domestic currency, the reduction in the central banks FX reserves would lead to a massive contraction of the basic money supply, and local rates would skyrocket in response. There is no theoretical upper limit to the levels that could be reached by the local currency rates; they would rise sufficiently until capital inflows return and balance the external pressure on the currency. The flip side of this arrangement is obviously that central banks have a very limited control over the domestic money market, and interest rates can fluctuate wildly in line with capital flows. Also, shocks cause adjustments to the domestic price level, implying inflationary pressure when capital inflows are strong, and deflationary pressure when capital is flowing out. The discussed theoretical model shows that a country operating a currency board technically cannot run out of reserves and change its monetary and exchange rate regime under market pressures. These aspects of the currency board regime and the unavoidable fluctuations may not be well understood by politicians, which could make them abandon this framework for political reasons, even if in purely technical terms this arrangement would be sustainable. So, what are the policy options or policy frameworks for coping with the above challenges, which are most discussed in the Bulgarian media and by politicians, academics and professionals in the country. I will start with the policy framework supported mostly by populist groups, stemming from the above mentioned over expectations for higher incomes after the EU membership. This position in itself is rather a problem than a solution. According to this view, the low incomes in some new member states, like Bulgaria, are the major challenge for the economy and our society. Such groups proposed solution is to use money from the governments fiscal reserve to drastically increase incomes in the public sector. According to the propagators of this view, this step would also boost incomes in the private sector and would finally result in the acceleration of economic growth and the convergence with the EU old member states. Of course, inflation is inevitable but, without being discussed as an element of a specific model, these apologists assume that it would be moderate and would not hamper the confidence in the CBA. Inflation is a synonym of price convergence, even without taking into account the role of productivity. According to this populist view, Bulgaria may preserve the currency board arrangement but not hurry to join the euro area. The second option for policy reaction to external imbalances and higher inflation has been put forward by some analysts working for investment banks and by some high-level representatives of the ECB. They propose that the member states with a CBA in place should allow more exchange rate flexibility and focus the monetary policy on the domestic inflation as a variable target. The logic is that higher short-term interest rates could be accompanied by an appreciation of the currency prompted by stronger capital inflows or vice versa. They underrate the fact that it is up to the market to establish the necessary exchange rate adjustments. Even if the member state could recover some degree of its monetary policy independence, it would hardly be able to use it and rebuild the lost confidence in the monetary and exchange rate regime. I call this opinion friendly fire not only because it comes from people working for respectable institutions and is supposed to be based on serious theoretical grounds, but also because it could, if it were accepted by our government, unexpectedly cause even more serious damages to the Bulgarian economy and the people than the populist policy option. The reason for my thinking in this way is simple: the friendly fire strikes directly at one of the basic elements of the current macroeconomic policy framework  the confidence in the currency board. The ultimate result of the lack of public confidence in the currency board would be a financial crisis and, again, a unilateral euroisation. I suppose the latter should not at all be considered an option given the official position of the European institutions and the ECB. The third policy option for CBA-operating member states in response to the latest shocks in financial markets and the macroeconomic development trends is mainly associated with the analyses done by the European Commission and the IMF. Their models do take account of the role and importance of the currency board as a monetary and exchange rate regime. The main idea of these models is that we should reconfigure the available policy instruments in order to face the new challenges coming from the internal and external background, without resorting to the exchange rate as an economic policy instrument. This, in fact, is also the firm position of the Bulgarian government, the Bulgarian National Bank and the political majority in the Bulgarian Parliament. The main points here are: Fiscal and income policies should continue to avoid adding pro-cyclical pressures that could widen internal and external imbalances. The spending and tax levers of the budget could be used so as to accelerate real convergence and productivity growth, including through the absorption of EU funds; Financial sector policies should contribute to safeguarding financial stability through continued close monitoring of the risk management of banks and financial intermediaries and their capacity to absorb adverse shocks; Structural reforms are essential for accelerating real convergence in the sense that the scope for sustainably catching up the living standards in the EU should be looked for in raising the efficiency of the available labour and capital resources and providing incentives for adding to these resources. In the Bulgarian National Bank we have always thought that the introduction of the euro in Bulgaria should go hand in hand with the sustainable fulfilment of the Maastricht criteria. This is a logical step which derives from the policy framework followed after the introduction of the CBA. This step corresponds to the interests of the country, and its opportune completion would bring more stability, sustainability and competitiveness. We will keep on working for its realisation. Consequently, we highly rate the adjustments to the governments policy reflected in the budget framework for 2008. I started my todays presentation by talking about expectations. When I was getting prepared for the seminar I found out that at the same seminar two years ago I expressed the opinion that the public expectations management was the key challenge for the new member states to successfully implement the policy framework whose core element was the CBA. Today I would like to finish my presentation by saying that the consistent implementation of this policy framework has brought the Bulgarian society a sustained economic growth for ten years in a row. The best way to manage public expectations of the Bulgarian economys future is not to deviate from the successful model and politicians to be persistent in the implementation of all measures which derive from this model. Thank you for your attention. PAGE PAGE 2

Title: Welcome to a Discussion Forum on "Professional Financial Consulting: Condition and Prospects", organized by the Higher School of Insurance and Finance, together with the Institute of Graduate Financial Consultants
text: Welcome of Mr. Tsvetan Manchev, Deputy Governor of the BNB, to a Discussion Forum on "Professional Financial Consulting: Condition and Prospects", organized by the Higher School of Insurance and Finance, together with the Institute of Graduate FinancialConsultants, 19 November 2007. Dear ladies and gentlemen, Dear Associate Professor Vazov, Dear Associate Professor Nikolov, I thank the organizers  the Higher School of Insurance and Finance  the Institute of Graduate Financial Consultants" - for inviting the discussion toopen it. financial markets. The important thing is that the initiative goes down to a micro level  it focuses on how to help the average person manage his personal finances in the described new global integration process of the country. Twice as long as the discussion on professional personal financial advice develops at a time of macroeconomic stability and the upsurge of the Bulgarian economy, when ordinary people and institutions are supposed to be able to look significantly longer. From a generally economic point of view, the benefits of the discussion can be sought in at least two ways. Firstly, as a new MEMBER of the EU, Bulgaria is only now gaining a practical insight into the scope and depth of the integration process in which it participates. to achieve its objective of membership of the Union. Now, as a member of the EU, Bulgaria is a full participant in the process of drawing up these rules. Bulgarian experts and institutions are involved in the process of preparing common European legislation and re-grationing at different levels. I will only remind the participants in the discussion that the EU is a union aimed at ensuring the rights and freedom of people in the Union, as well as increasing their standard of living . The second benefit I see from the discussion in general economic terms is related to the moment of development of the global economy. After the turbulence of international financial markets 1-2 months ago, investors are rediscovering the importance of diversification. begin to reassess the risks. This does not always happen smoothly and expectedly. There is a growing volatility in the markets. At the same time in Bulgaria we do not have many years of experience in the market economy. People have no habits of working with complex financial instruments, and competition in the banking sector prompts them to offer more and more complex products. In this environment, specific knowledge of the respective niche of the market and the correlations between the price dynamics and income of specific financial products, rather than the macro-economy, becomes of paramount importance. The modern economy has changed and even the big central banks cannot succeed without supporting those with the specific knowledge. It is important to find ways to get people to hear and capture the signals of regulators. However, central banks cannot be heard and understood at the same time by everyone. It is obvious that they need intermediaries to spread knowledge and translate where necessary, as the central banks and other regulators say. that the specific need is well understood by the organisers of the discussion. Before I wish to do a successful job on the forum, I would like to stress one more important thing that needs to be considered from the outset. The presence of Toryregulation, the increase in people with knowledge, the development of financial markets and regulations and skills in portfolio constructing and risk management does not override everyone's personal responsibility for managing personal finances. We should all be aware from the outset that the responsibilities for risk-taking and management are personal. Thanks for the attention. I wish the forum a fruitful job! PAGE PAGE 2

Title: Speech delivered to the round table under the heading Bulgarias Progress on the Implementation of the Lisbon Strategy: a Discussion on the EC Assessment", Sofia
text: Speech by Mr. Tsvetan Manchev, BNB Deputy Governor, delivered to the round table under the heading Bulgarias Progress on the Implementation of the Lisbon Strategy: a Discussion on the EC Assessment", organized by the Delegation of the European Commission to Bulgaria, Sofia, 17 January 2008 Ladies and Gentlemen, Allow me first to express my thanks to the organizers from the Delegation of the European Commission to the Republic of Bulgaria for the opportunity provided to me to present the position of the Bulgarian National Bank on our countrys progress in the implementation of the Lisbon Growth and Jobs Strategy in the context of the Commissions Strategic Report of 11 December 2007 on the implementation of the Strategy. For me this round table is yet another evidence of the already functioning constructive dialogue and the relations of partnership between the Commission and the Bulgarian public institutions as regards the on-going process of preparation, implementation, and reporting of the progress on the National Reform Program (NRP), as well as for the transparency characteristic for these relations. This may be the right place to share with you my institutions and my personal attitude of support for the ambitious goals of the Lisbon Strategy. Even in their initial form, although realizing they are very far off in time, and that there are no sufficient mechanisms in place in the Union for their attainment, these goals have been an important cornerstone for the long-term economic policy of Member States in their effort to bring substance to the democratic and humane principles of this Union. Therefore, I was following with interest the work of the high-level group headed by Wim Kok, which was to identify the obstacles to the implementation of the Lisbon Strategy, and whose report in the final run was the basis for the development of the European Council decisions of March 2005 on the new beginning, slating economic growth and employment in Europe as priorities. The BNB believes the assessment made by the Commission of the National Reform Programme of Bulgaria, and the progress report issued in 2007 are objective and provide a good basis for a discussion on the challenges and opportunities for speeding up the Programs implementation. We fully agree that maintaining macroeconomic stability in the context of the Currency Board Arrangement by pursuing a strict fiscal policy, preserving the long-term stability of public finances and further structural reform are properly slated as the major challenges for the implementation of the NRP. I would like, however, to underscore that for the BNB the NRP is a very important official document of Bulgaria, which yet again clearly confirms that the country will not modify its monetary regime until the time of its euro area membership. We believe that the successful implementation of the macroeconomic guidelines as part of the Integrated Guidelines for Economic Growth and Employment means for Bulgaria to continue along the lines of the macroeconomic policy pursued so far, which is based on the currency board and the strict fiscal policy. I insist noting that on this issue we have always been in full accord with the Bulgarian government. We fully support the recommendation that strict fiscal policy, improving the quality of public spending and keeping the salary growth within the levels of productivity growth are the most important instruments for coping with the growing BOP current account deficit and the inflationary pressures on the Bulgarian economy. In this relation, however, I cant help mentioning the unequivocal fact that at least in the recent 5-6 years all Bulgarian governments have unswervingly pursued a balanced state budget, or even a budget surplus as a means of evading a pro-cyclical fiscal policy, which, together with the decreasing government debt, is an important evidence of the political will and the courage to respond adequately to the external environment of shocks and fluctuations by pursuing a consistent fiscal policy. We should also clarify once again for our EU and ECB partners that our EU membership has changed the model of operation typical for small and open economies like Bulgaria, hence they should change their model of analysis. The bigger FDI boom, exceeding even the optimistic expectations, turned into a major factor for the dynamics of trade deficit, and the latter increased sharply. This, together with a number of technical modifications ensuing from our EU membership, and adapting the statistic methodology and practices of collecting foreign trade statistics brought about a structural change in the existing macroeconomic time series, as well as greater uncertainty of the initially published foreign trade statistics. At the same time, the countrys economic policy is and should be aimed primarily at preserving the long-term stability, and should not be used for hasty neutralization of often technical fluctuations in undoubtedly important macroeconomic indicators such as trade deficit. Given the areas of central bank competences, it is of particular importance to pursue an adequate and coordinated policy in response to the growing inflationary pressures. There is no doubt that many of the inflation fluctuations evidenced in the first year of EU membership of Bulgaria come as a consequence of external factors (international prices of energy, commodities and foods). This is also indicated by the symmetry of magnitude of the shock on the overall price level in Bulgaria compared to the euro area member states. Bulgarias entry into the EU common market triggered market mechanisms of convergence of domestic price levels to the European ones. Given that, the economic policy may and should be focused primarily on the inflationary factors arising from the dynamics of domestic demand and increased liquidity. In this context, we believe it is very important that the domestic economic policy is compliant with the recommendations of the European Commission to bind the growth rates of public sector salaries and social payments with the pace of growth of productivity in the economy. As to the speed of the structural reforms in the economy, we believe that their success is largely dependent on the speed of implementation of the next long-term objective  the full membership in the European Economic and Monetary Union. We share the EC position that the speeding up of structural reforms aimed to relieve the pressure of the labour market, improve qualifications and boost up the competitiveness of goods and services markets are essential for curbing the imbalances in the economy and the inflationary pressure. This however also requires timely, clear and explicit signals from our partners regarding the prospects of full membership in the European Economic and Monetary Union. With no clarity on this issue, the public support and the political will for reforms would be hard to keep up or guarantee in the long term. In this connection, the BNB highly appreciates the Governments will to budget for 2008 a set of measures aimed to boost employment and the degree of labour force involvement by creating higher incentives for labour market participation. We think that a decrease in the number of unemployed receiving social benefits, along with a possibility created for their inclusion under various programs and employment measures, training and retraining courses, is an important step to enhancing the flexibility of the labour market. Optimizing employment in the public sector is another important measure for enhancing the efficiency of the labour market. In a longer perspective, a positive contribution to this effect will provide the new social contract on education reforms, related to the establishment of minimum education standards and decentralization of the education system administration, which involves certain distribution of decision-making authority between the government and the local authorities, as well as the school management, observing the principle of subsidiarity. This significantly more flexible approach reduces the government responsibilities to establishing general standards of education quality, and relieves it from the full responsibility for administration of the education system, providing at the same time more powers to local authorities, school boards of trustees and principals, corresponds entirely to the European Commission recommendation for conducting of a education better meeting the needs of the labour market. I agree with the European Commission that the Bulgarian National Reform Programme focuses on the right challenges. It allows us to take even further the constructive dialogue covering the specific areas and measures of Bulgarias economic policy, as part of the policy of common interest. The Growth and Stability Pact and the Lisbon Strategy will remain important anchors for the countrys economic policy. We believe that their guardians, namely the European Commission and the other EU institutions will treat the member states equally and will provide clear, unambiguous and definitive incentives for steady progress towards the achievement of EMU goals. Thank you for your attention! PAGE PAGE 3

Title: Opening Address to the Conference Forecasting Models and Procedures of EU Central Banks, Sofia
text: Opening Address by Mr. Tsvetan Manchev, BNB Depury Governor, to the Conference Forecasting Models and Procedures of EU Central Banks, Sofia, 23 April 2008 Ladies and Gentlemen, Allow me on behalf of the Governing Council and the Governor of the Bulgarian National Bank to welcome you to the workshop Forecasting Models and Procedures of EU Central Banks, organized by the Bulgarian National Bank. The workshop is organized as a part of the twinning project Adjustment of the Bulgarian National Bank to operate as a full-fledged member of the European System of Central Banks and the Eurosystem. We are highly indebted to our partners banks in this project - Banque de France, De Nederlandsche Bank, Banca dItalia. We at the BNB appreciate the importance of economic modeling for both enhancing our understanding of the driving forces of economic development and improving the quality of short and medium term projections. In this context, the aim of the workshop is to bring together experts from the central banks of the EU who will openly share their experience with the practices, challenges and achievements in model building and forecasting in their institutions. On a more general level, our hope is that the exchange of knowledge and experience at this workshop will be helpful for all participants in their efforts to further improve their modeling and forecasting practices. We also hope that the workshop will promote the communication and cooperation between central-bank economists and will facilitate the development and future advancement of modeling and forecasting practices in the central banks of the EU. Let me now offer a few remarks on the role of forecasting in the policymaking process at the Bulgarian National Bank and its relation to the present workshop. Under the existing currency board arrangement the choice of policy instruments at the disposal of the BNB is more limited as compared to a traditional central bank. Apart from the use of minimum reserve requirements, most of the options in our case come on the prudential regulations side. This implies that the value of information becomes even higher than usual and, in particular, the availability of a consistent set of projections is indispensable for constructing an appropriate policy response. The consistency requirement on the forecast has much deeper implications than the obvious need to observe standard accounting conventions. Given that we are often interested in the medium term, a set of projections has to be generated by a theoretically coherent construct that includes those economic mechanisms that are deemed important by the BNB management. Moreover, it has to be flexible enough to allow us to seamlessly incorporate expert knowledge and intuition in the projections. In that sense, the forecasting tools and process aim at much more than producing numbers that are likely to be close to reported statistical data; they become story-telling devices and provide a powerful two-way channel of communication between policymakers and forecasters. These observations should hardly be news to any of you as your experiences in forecasting probably confirm them first-hand. Therefore, I am sure you will appreciate the need for a well-structured and organized forecast preparation procedure. This institutional side of forecasting is often overshadowed by the technicalities of model development and forecast performance, yet a properly timed and smoothly functioning forecasting procedure is the backbone of a forecasting exercise that ultimately allows both modeling tools and experts to develop their full potential. In this respect each of you can make an important contribution to the workshop by sharing your forecasting practices and experience, thus helping enhance the overall efficiency of the forecasters work. Once again I welcome you to the workshop of the Bulgarian National Bank and wish you an enjoyable meeting and fruitful discussions. Thank you! PAGE PAGE 2

Title: Macroeconomic policy framework in bulgaria: In view of recent financial turmoil
Subtitle:
MACROECONOMIC POLICY FRAMEWORK IN BULGARIA
IN VIEW OF RECENT FINANCIAL TURMOIL
text: Speech by Mr. Tsvetan Manchev, BNB Deputy Governor, delivered to the Meeting of the Competition and Development Policy Commettee of the European Association of Public Banks, hosted by Bulgarian Development Bank, Sofia, 26 September 2008 MACROECONOMIC POLICY FRAMEWORK IN BULGARIA IN VIEW OF RECENT FINANCIAL TURMOIL Ladies and Gentlemen, First of all, I would like to thank the organizers from the Bulgarian Development Bank and personally Mr. Dimitrov and Mr. Chakalski for the invitation to speak in front of such a distinguished audience. The current global financial crisis, although not unique in respect to the origin and the major driving factors, poses tremendous pressure on bankers and policy-makers. It requires a clear, consistent and predictable response from all interested parties, which could re-establish the confidence among market participants and recover the smooth functioning of markets and the global economy. I believe that todays Meeting of the Competition and Development Policy Committee of the European Association of Public Banks will also bring value in this regard. In my speech I will add value to the meeting by focusing on the policy framework in which Bulgaria responds to the challenges arising from the external shocks, recent developments in the economy and the stance of the markets. As many of you may be aware, for more than a decade the key component of the Bulgarian macroeconomic and monetary policy has been the Currency Board Arrangement (CBA) with legislatively irrevocable exchange rate of the lev  the national currency  to the euro at the rate of 1 euro equal to 1.95583 leva. The Currency Board Arrangement represents a simple rule according to which all monetary liabilities of the Bulgarian National Bank, including the monetary base and the deposits of the government, are covered by the foreign reserves. Of course the logic of this monetary regime presupposes independence of the central bank from the government. As it is evident from the 2008 Convergence reports of both the European Commission and the European Central Bank, as well as, from the ECOFIN report to the European Council in Nice at November 2000 and the Position of the Governing Council of the ECB at December 2003, this type of monetary and exchange rate regimes are fully compliant with the participation in the Exchange Rate Mechanism Two (ERM II) and the following euro adoption process. The Convergence reports also stressed on the broad compliance of the BNB Law with the Treaty and specified only a limited number of inconsistencies which had to be regarded by the Bulgarian authorities. The steadily growing foreign reserve assets of the Bulgarian National Bank backing the high coverage rate of the reserve money and money supply demonstrate that the currency board continue to function well and all the time it has enjoyed a high degree of public confidence (graph 1). From the early days of the introduction of the CBA the Bulgarian policymakers are well aware that as an automated monetary regime it implies simply following the monetary policy of the central bank, issuing the reserve currency. In our case the Bulgarian National Bank passively follows the monetary policy of the European Central Bank. It may act as a lender of last resort but only in the event of a systemic risk to the banking system, upon the provision of highly liquid collateral and solely up to the amount of the excess of the lev equivalent of the gross foreign reserves over its total monetary liabilities. This automated regime could not serve as a buffer to external economic shocks; it could even be a source of external shock if the monetary policy of the ECB did not correspond to the economic trends in Bulgaria. In order to assure the above condition the focus of the authorities has been on the transmission channels of the ECB monetary signals to the Bulgarian economy. The introduction of the CBA has been part of the package of political, legislative, fiscal, budgetary and structural reforms, which impose hard budget constraints economy-wide. The 3 consecutive governments in office, although dominated by 3 different political poles  conservatives, liberals and social democrats  have pursued tough fiscal policy oriented toward budget surpluses and dismantling the public debts. (graphs 2 and 3). The government drastically privatised the banking sector so most of the banks are now subsidiaries or branches of highly-rated European banks (graph 4), which rely on vast depository base and are less dependant on temporal market liquidity conditions and constrains. The BNB has contributed with high-quality prudential banking regulations consistent with modern banking practices as well as with a stringent control over the ability of the corporate governance of banks to observe these regulations and to manage the banking business-related risks. Moreover, the liberalisation and integration of domestic financial markets to those in EU and the free movement of capital further facilitate the smooth transmission of the signals. As a result, the Bulgarian economy has registered eleven consecutive years of growth and decreasing unemployment (graphs 5 and 6). At present the Bulgarian banking system is well capitalised and profitable. The capital adequacy ratio is 14.6% at the end of the first semester of 2008 and is well above the minimum standards. Despite the high credit growth the capital adequacy of the banking system has even increased compared to the end of the previous year due to faster increase of the bank capital. Return on equity (ROE) at the end of June 2008 stood at 24.3% and return on assets (ROA) was 2.4% (graph 7). There are no signs of deterioration of the quality of credit portfolios  the classified loans currently are almost at the same level as that at the end of the previous year (graph 8). The exposure to the exchange rate risk is limited (graph 9) and the interest rate margins between respective lev and euro-denominated instruments remain stable (graph 10). The predictability and stability of the macroeconomic policy, the relatively high return at a continuously declining risk in our economy over the last 11 years, as well as the EU and NATO membership created conditions for foreign capital to flow in (graph. 11) and fill in the savings gap in the Bulgarian economy. The increase of the current account deficit has been a reciprocal effect following the massive inflow of foreign direct investments. The nature of these inflows, namely the direct investment in the real economy, mitigates to a large extent the risk of sudden reversal of their sign. It is also worth noting that in the case of Bulgaria the high current account deficit does not erode the competitiveness of the countrys export sectors. Since 2000 exports have been growing every year (at an annual average rate of 10% in real terms). Bulgaria is among the few countries with a steadily growing market share of its exports in the EU imports (graph 12). The recent Bulgarian development is accompanied by a relatively high inflation (graph 13). Similarly to the other new EU member-states it is determined by two main factors: the long-term trend of convergence of price levels to those in the EU and short-term cyclical factors triggered by the developments of the international prices, as well as by the monetary policies of the major central banks and natural disasters. For instance, the sharp bound in 2007 inflation (11.6% at the end of the year) is due mainly to the severe drought, which affected badly the harvest in Bulgaria and caused approximately 40% real decline in the agriculture sector in the third quarter. The coincidental move of the global factors such as the increase in energy and food prices, as well as the dynamic growth of wages and domestic demand also exerted pressure on the overall price level. The increase in food prices contributed to 60% of the inflation in 2007, while 10% were due to the increase of the prices of energy commodities. Summing up, the Bulgarian economic development over the last 11 years is an indisputable success, which should be attributed to the consistent macroeconomic policy framework applied and the political will to implement it. The broad consensus and firm support among the key political stakeholders and politicians in the country to keep unchanged the existing framework until the introduction of the euro has been well received by both agents and markets. It provides equal treatment and equal incentives to all market participants. It is simple and fair enough for the development of both small enterprises and well established corporations. Of course, the risk of high inflation calls primarily for a consistent counter-cyclical fiscal and budgetary policy aimed at maintaining a sound budgetary position with high general government surpluses, as well as a new generation of structural reforms to promote the competitiveness and sustainability of economic growth. Thank you for your attention! ____________ Dr. Tsvetan Manchev is Deputy Governor and Member of the Governing Council of the Bulgarian National Bank. PAGE PAGE 2

Title: Bulgarian macroeconomic policy: Response to the global financial crisis
Subtitle:
BULGARIAN MACROECONOMIC POLICY
RESPONSE TO THE GLOBAL FINANCIAL CRISIS
text: Speech by Mr. Tsvetan Manchev, BNB Deputy Governor, delivered to the Bulgarian Day Forum within the German Equity Forum, Frankfurt am Main, 10 November 2008 BULGARIAN MACROECONOMIC POLICY RESPONSE TO THE GLOBAL FINANCIAL CRISIS Yours Excellencies, Ladies and Gentlemen, It is a pleasure and an honour for me to be among you at the Bulgarias day on the German Equity Forum. First of all, let me thank the organizers from die Deutsche Borse and the Bulgarian Stock Exchange for inviting me today to share with you my views on the current economic development in Bulgaria and the possible macroeconomic policy responses to the impact of the global financial crisis. As I suppose the audience is mainly interested in the investment opportunities in Bulgaria, my task today will be to convince you that the macroeconomic environment and policy framework in Bulgaria are, and will remain in the medium-term, attractive to foreign and domestic investors. In line with the above task, I will focus on the policy framework in which Bulgaria responds to the challenges of external shocks, the recent developments in the economy and the stance of the markets, as well as on the latest central bank measures aimed at protecting the Bulgarian financial market against the risks of the global financial crisis. As almost all of you may be aware, for more than a decade the Currency Board Arrangement (CBA) has been the key component of the Bulgarian macroeconomic and monetary policy, with statutory irrevocable exchange rate of the lev  the national currency  to the euro at a parity of 1.95583 leva to 1 euro. The Currency Board Arrangement represents a simple rule according to which all monetary liabilities of the Bulgarian National Bank including the monetary base and the deposits of the government are covered by the foreign reserves. Of course the rationale behind this monetary regime is conditional on the independence of the central bank from the government. As it is evident from the 2008 Convergence Reports of both the European Commission and the European Central Bank, as well as from the ECOFIN report to the Nice European Council of November 2000, and the ECB Governing Council Position of December 2003, this type of monetary and the exchange rate regimes are fully compliant with the participation in the Exchange Rate Mechanism Two (ERM II) and the adoption of the euro that follows as a next stage. The reports also stressed on the broad compliance of the BNB Law with the Treaty and recommended only a limited number of inconsistencies which are already jointly addressed by the Bulgarian authorities and the ECB. The amendments will be adopted, I believe, at the current session of the Parliament. The foreign reserve assets of the Bulgarian National Bank - steadily growing even these days  that ensure the high coverage rate of the reserve money and money supply, demonstrate that the currency board continues to function well and enjoys, as always, a high degree of public confidence (graph 1). I would emphasize that todays stability and high degree of resilience of the Bulgarian economy to the recent shock is the result of long time of consistent reform policies. From the early days of the introduction of the CBA Bulgarian policymakers are well aware that as an automated monetary regime it implies just following the monetary policy of the central bank, issuing the reserve currency. In our case the Bulgarian National Bank inactively follows the monetary policy of the European Central Bank. This automated regime cannot possibly serve as a buffer to the external economic shocks; it could even be a source of external shock if the monetary policy of the ECB did not correspond to the economic trends in Bulgaria. In order to assure the above condition, necessary for smooth functioning of the CBA, the focus of the authorities has been on the transmission channels for the ECB monetary signals to the Bulgarian economy. The introduction of the CBA has been part of the package of political, legislative, fiscal, budgetary and structural reforms, which impose economy-wide hard budget constraints. The 3 consecutive governments in office, although dominated by 3 different political forces  conservatives, liberals and social-democrats  have pursueed a tough fiscal policy oriented toward budget surpluses and reducing of public debt. (graphs 2 and 3). The government promptly privatised the banking sector. Although most of the banks are now subsidiaries or branches of highly-rated European banks (graph 4), we enjoy vast diversification of countries whose banks have market presence in Bulgaria. Bulgarian banks also rely on a vast depositor base and few of them depend on the temporary market liquidity conditions and constrains. The BNB adds to this with its high quality prudential regulations consistent with modern banking practice, and with the stringent control on the corporate governance capacities of banks to observe these regulations and to manage the risks related to the banking business. Moreover the liberalisation and integration of domestic financial markets into the EU ones, and the free movement of capital further facilitate the smooth transmission of the signals. My conclusion is that the continuity and predictability of the Bulgarian macroeconomic policy is and will remain a major asset an investor can buy in Bulgaria. All political stakeholders, no matter if they are presently in the Parliament or are leading the forthcoming election polls, have been deeply committed to keep the currency board and the level of the peg until the euro adoption, as well as, to implement consistent policies to preserve the stability and sustainability of the regime pursued. As a result, the Bulgarian economy has evidenced eleven consecutive years of growth and declining unemployment (graphs 5 and 6). At present the Bulgarian banking system is well capitalised and profitable. The capital adequacy ratio is 14.6% as of end of the September 2008 that is well above the minimum standards, and serves as a buffer during the current rally of the turmoil. Despite the relatively high credit growth, the capital adequacy of the banking system even increased compared to the end of the previous year as a result of the faster increase of bank capital. The end-September 2008 return on equity (ROE) is 24.5%, and the return on assets (ROA) is 2.3% (graph 7). There are no signs of deterioration of the quality of credit portfolios even under the much tougher provisioning requirements applied. Classified loans currently are almost at the same level as at the end of the previous year (graph 8). The exchange rate risk exposure is limited (graph 9) and the interest rate margins between respective leva and euro denominated instruments remain stable (graph 10). The predictability and stability of the macroeconomic policy, the relatively high return with a continuously declining risk in our economy over the last 11 years, and our EU and NATO membership, created conditions for foreign capital to flow in (graph. 11) and to fill in the savings gap in the Bulgarian economy (graph 12). Our view, consecutively reconfirmed by the economic trends, is that the sharp increase in the current account deficit in the recent couple of years comes as a reciprocal effect of the massive inflow of foreign direct investment. The nature of the inflows, namely the direct investment in the real economy, mitigates to a large extent the risk of sudden reversal of their sign. It is also worth mentioning, that in the case of Bulgaria the high current account deficit does not erode the competitiveness of the countrys export sectors.
