Since 2000, exports have been growing every year (at an average annual rate of 10% in real terms). Bulgaria is among the few countries with a steadily growing market share of its exports in the EU imports (graph 13). The recent Bulgarian economic development has been accompanied by a relatively high inflation (graph 14). Similarly, it is determined by two main factors in the other new EU Member States. On the one hand, there are short-term cyclical factors triggered by the international price developments, the monetary policies of the major central banks and also by natural disasters. On the other hand, this is the long-term trend of convergence of price levels to those in the EU. For instance, the sharp bounce in 2007 inflation (11.6% at the end of the year) was due mainly to the severe drought, which affected badly the harvest in Bulgaria and caused approximately 40% real decline in the agriculture sector in the third quarter. The coincidental developments in the global factors, such as the increase in energy and food prices, as well as the wage growth dynamics and domestic demand also pushed upward the overall price level. The increase in food prices contributed to 60% of the inflation in 2007, while 10% were due to the increase of the prices of energy commodities. The relevance of our analyses is confirmed by the recent declining trend in Bulgarian HICP inflation. Until September 2008, the impact of global financial turmoil on Bulgaria has been limited due to the absence of toxic assets in the portfolios of Bulgarian banks and institutional investors. It was mainly felt at the stock exchange, where the prices dropped by more than 60% from the beginning of the year, with no second-round effects on the other sectors because of the relatively low importance of this channel of financing for the economy. Since then, the international financial environment has changed tremendously and the financial crisis expanded to the European economy. The subsequent effects on us are mainly related to the already seen signs of a declining trend in the total FDI inflows, including those to Bulgarian banks from their headquarters. As a small open European economy, highly dependant on the European FDI, and taking into account all said above about the monetary regime and banking structure, Bulgaria logically supports and works for a European-wide approach to tackling the effects from the financial crisis. One can hardly say that the measures pursued so far at EU level have only positive effect on the financial markets in Bulgaria. This implies that during the next rounds of discussions the EU Council should look a good deal more into the effects on the non-euro area economies, and the need for parent banks to accept group level responsibility in supporting subsidiaries based in these countries in case of liquidity strains. The ECB should also consider supporting with appropriate measures the liquidity of the banking systems in non-euro area Member States. For the measures at national level, I can discuss only the BNB measures. Nevertheless I assure you we are in permanent contact with the government, and the central banks initiatives and interventions are well integrated in the overall framework of the macroeconomic policy response to the shock. The BNB recently amended the Ordinance on the minimum required reserves to increase commercial banks access to their required reserves held with the BNB. This has not impacted the aggregate level of the reserve requirement ratio, which stays at 12%, and the market rates charged on banks utilising this extra liquidity. The immediate result of this measure was a sharp decrease in the interbank lending rates by more than one percentage point (graph. 15) even before the official effectiveness of the amendment. If needed, we are also ready to respond in a timely manner to any deliberate and permanent shrinking of funding provided to domestic banks by their headquarters. As a concluding remark, I would like to remind you that the current macroeconomic policy framework in Bulgaria, with the currency board arrangement as its core, was introduced more than 11 years ago after a deep financial crisis, which came as the result of the previous inconsistent government policies. Since then, the Bulgarian economy has been hit by several external shocks, but the currency board as well as economic growth survived without any problems, proving its long-term resilience. Furthermore, its simple but rigid rules have a disciplining effect for itself and on other macroeconomic policies and especially on policymakers and politicians. May be this disciplining effect of the CBA has been one of the major factors for preserving continuity, consistency and transparency of the macroeconomic policy in Bulgaria, despite the political orientation of the parties in power. We are very well acquainted with the critics of our approach and the sustainability concerns shared by some researchers. However, please, correct me if I am wrong, but we consider that the transparency, consistency and continuity make the macroeconomic policy predictable therefore investor-friendly. This is what actually should matter when determining the countrys sovereign spreads and credit default swaps. So, it is crucial for investors to know that irrespective of any turmoil globally, the Bulgarian economy will continue to adapt as it has done so far, under the conditions of the existing currency board arrangements and strong fiscal stance aiming at the fulfilment of the Maastricht criteria and the adoption of the euro. Thank you for your attention! ____________ Dr. Tsvetan Manchev is Deputy Governor and Member of the Governing Council of Bulgarian National Bank. He is also a member of the International Relations Committee of the ECB and an Alternate to the Governor in the General Council of the ECB. PAGE PAGE 2

Title: The financial crisis and the initial eu response
Subtitle: THE FINANCIAL CRISIS AND THE INITIAL EU RESPONSE
text: Opening presentation of Mr. Tsvetan Manchev, BNB Deputy Governor, at the seminar Changes in the European Financial Services Legislation: Impact on the Bulgarian Financial Market, Sofia, 25 November 2008 THE FINANCIAL CRISIS AND THE INITIAL EU RESPONSE The conclusion the man in the street would make today is that the international financial markets, the global economy, and the life of the people as economic agents have significantly changed in the recent two months. For financial analysts and the academia this is a very short period of time and probably from now on they will come up with in-depth analyses of what is happening, although the institutions have already offered many improvisations and suggestions of proper behaviour. Not only have the people who are professionally and administratively responsible for the development and implementation of the macroeconomic policy in individual countries and unions experienced a change, they are faced with a professional and personal challenge. None of the above-mentioned groups had ever imagined that the bankruptcy of the fourth largest US investment bank Lehman Brothers declared in the second Monday of September 2008 will cause such large-scale detonation impacting not only the financial world and the global economy, but the lives of us all. If this response could have been predicted, now we would not have been talking about the world financial history before and after the bankruptcy of Lehman Brothers, or about a global financial crisis. Among the multiple important questions that surge after the above-said, I will deal with only three: How have the world economy, financial markets, and peoples lives changed? What was Bulgarias response?, and What was EUs response? How have the world economy, financial markets, and peoples lives changed? Before proceeding to the first question, however, I would like to make the provision that to my mind any final assessment of or final conclusion regarding what is happening would be rather premature. Hence, I would allow myself to leave my presentation without the customary conclusion in such cases. We still do not have sufficient reliable information both about the damages suffered by the financial system and the global economy and about any possible results from the measures already taken and the time needed for the sustainable recovery of growth worldwide. This is so as confidence is an indicator difficult to define and measure unambiguously, not only in macroeconomic but also in purely emotional and personal terms. Exactly this loss of confidence between the entities concluding transactions, initially only in the financial markets and only in the US, rapidly spread contagiously after the Lehman case. It unexpectedly quickly went beyond the US financial markets and took over the whole US economy. Gradually the lack of confidence contaminated the international financial markets, as the preliminary economic estimates that came out after mid-October already indicate that the mistrust has plagued the whole world. This lack of confidence between economic agents is the simplest and at the same time the most accurate description of what is happening. I intentionally would not show diagrams as illustration, as in the recent weeks the whole Bulgarian and foreign press was flooded with information. Any piece of information in the above-mentioned situation has its strictly individual value with regard to the degree to which the confidence in a particular person, market, or national economy has dwindled. The only possibly unharmed by this process are the few economic agents which do not participate in the international division of labour, world trade and finances. For me the question to what extent each economy, including the Bulgarian economy and banking system, is affected by the spreading loss of confidence between economic agents is not subject to measurement, hence irrelevant. Any estimates, projections, including downright speculations, are possible on it. Regretfully the latter are not only unpleasant exceptions. What was Bulgarias response? The appropriate approach to the situation evidenced worldwide, is for everyone to describe briefly and clearly his behaviour and to leave the others to judge purely subjectively what confidence they would have in him or whether they would have dealings with him. Taken to the macroeconomic level, this would mean that each country should describe its economic and financial policy and leave the domestic and foreign economic agents, other governments and international financial institutions judge what transactions they will have with it. The market, together with many other factors beyond the control of national authorities, is the one to provide an answer to the question about our future share in the international division of labour, and in the world and European trade and investments. Along the line of what I have already said, according to the BNB it was mandatory to reconfirm as valid in the changed external conditions the most important elements of the macroeconomic and financial policy pursued so far: Compliance with the statutory principles of the currency board under the existing exchange rate parity of the lev to the euro; Further strengthening of the independence of the central bank in line with the Treaty establishing the European Community (TEC); Compliance with the ban on central bank financing of governments and public institutions at home and within the EU imposed by TEC ; Not allowing any consolidated government budget deficits; Continue the liberalization of all domestic markets in all areas in line with the commitments made to the EU; Participation in and full compliance with the joint EU framework in response to the crisis. What was listed so far as the Bulgarian response fully meets, in BNBs opinion, the concerted EU approach. On 6 October the French presidency of the EU published a declaration voicing the readiness of EU leaders to take all necessary measures to maintain the stability of the financial system, including through providing central bank liquidity by actions targeted to particular banks or by improving the deposit protection schemes, emphasizing the need of close coordination and cooperation in implementing these measures. Although there are no data and significant external impacts on the banking system and the economy, by joining the declaration the Republic of Bulgaria commits itself to the need of discussing and agreeing on European level coordinated activities to ensure the best possible solutions for limiting mistrust among economic agents in Europe. Only a day later, the EU adopted a framework for action of the member states in response to the financial crisis, which has been consistently supplemented and fine-tuned. In October 2008, key agreements were reached among the EU member states, articulated in the Conclusions of ECOFIN of 07 October 2008 and of the Council of 15-16 October 2008, including in the Declaration on a concerted action plan of the euro area countries and in the subsequent sessions of the ECOFIN Council and the summit of the heads of state and government on 7 November. At each of the above fora, high level Bulgarian officials took part in the formation of the consensus. Given the extreme importance for each member state of the decision made, I would like to briefly acquaint you with them as a reply to the third of the questions I mentioned earlier. The EU response It should be emphasized from the very beginning that the main goal of the EU framework in response to the financial crisis is the sustainable recovery of confidence. Three aspects can be clearly outlined in it  short-term strategy, continuity of the response until the recovery of financial stability and confidence on European scale, and participation in the international dialogue about the future of the global financial architecture and restoring confidence worldwide. The EU short-term strategy is fully consistent with the Roadmap of immediate responses to the financial turmoil in the US adopted by ECOFIN in October 2007 which, if I may remind you, covered: Agreement on providing support to systemically important financial institutions, and taking all necessary measures to increase the sustainability and stability of the banking system and to protect the deposits of individual depositors; Support for the actions taken by the European Central Bank and the national central banks from the beginning of the crisis; Appeal to the financial institutions in Europe for achieving full transparency of their activities, while the Council monitors the progress achieved in this regard; Agreement on close coordination in the actions for recognizing potential cross-border effects of decisions made on national level, and also that public intervention decisions should be made on national level but should be part of a coordinated framework; Recapitalization of vulnerable systemically-important financial institutions. The main principles of the EU short-term strategy are: Interventions should be timely and the support should be in principle of temporary nature; The protection of taxpayers interests should be monitored particularly closely; Shareholders should suffer the consequences of the interventions; The government should be in a position to impose a change in the management of the recapitalized institutions; The management teams of decapitalized institutions should not retain unwarranted benefits  governments may, inter alia, have the powers to intervene on the issue of compensations; Legitimate interests of competitors should be protected, more specifically through the EU state aid rules; The spillover of unfavourable effects of government intervention on other market participants should be avoided. An important decision for the EU is the development of an informal mechanism for warning, exchange of information and evaluation (financial crisis response centre) with a view to quickly and efficiently react to a crisis situation. The mechanism will be triggered at any given moment by a member state hit by the crisis and will allow for monitoring the good coordination of taken or pending actions. The Republic of Bulgaria already participates in it. Another important aspect of the framework is that it further strengthens the leading principle of equal treatment. Emphasis was put on the need to avoid any difference in the treatment of American and European banks due to accounting rules differences. EU supervisors and auditors were asked to immediately implement the new guidelines of the International Accounting Standards Board which apply marked-to-market valuation in the framework of the International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS). In principle consistency should be provided on issues relating to reclassification of assets by the IAS Board and the IFRS Board before the completion of the 2008 financial reports. And last but not least, with a view to encouraging convergence of practices, an agreement was reached that for a preliminary period of at least one year all member states will provide deposit insurance protection to private persons of at least EUR 50,000, recognizing also that a number of member states are determined to increase this minimum to EUR 100,000. The implementation of the framework includes a number of specific measures on European level as an immediate response to the financial crisis: For the purpose of quickly implementing the decisions on granting state aid within the framework of the single market regime and the state aid regime, on 25 October 2008 the European Commission (EC) approved a Communication on the application of the state aid rules to measures taken in relation to financial institutions in the context of the current global financial crisis. This facilitated the prompt evaluation of the compatibility of state aid for recapitalization and the insurance schemes in the cases such schemes are applied. On 16 October the European Commission submitted a draft amendment of Directive 94/19/ on the deposit insurance schemes to encourage the convergence of deposit insurance schemes. The Commissions proposals for amendments to the Directive relate to the insured amount of deposits and the term for disbursement. According to the proposals made by EC, the 3-day period for decision-making by the respective authorities remains in effect. With regard to the insurance amount, the proposal includes a guaranteed amount of EUR 50,000 effective to the end of 2010, and after 2010 a minimum threshold of EUR 100,000 for the deposit insurance, and from 2012 this amount will become a maximum threshold. By its representatives in the working groups under the Council and EC, Bulgaria actively participates in the debate on the draft amendments to Directive 94/19/. The European Commission submitted Regulation (EC) No. 1004/2008 on the amendment of Regulation (C) No. 1725/2003 adopting certain accounting standards in accordance with Regulation (EC) No. 1606/2002 of the European Parliament and the Council concerning International Accounting Standard (IAS) 39 and International Financial Reporting Standard (IFRS) 7. As the regulation is directly applicable in the member states, the Bulgarian National Bank on its part notified commercial banks on 28 October 2008 that they may make reclassifications of the financial assets held by them, subject to compliance of the requirements of IAS 39. In addition, the Bulgarian National Bank will not require from the banks and foreign bank branches to restate financial and supervision reports. The second aspect of the EU framework is the continuity of the response to the time of restoring financial stability and confidence across Europe. On 30 October, the European Commission published a Communication From Financial Crisis to Recovery: a European framework for action. The document sets a triple approach to be further developed into a joint action plan or a common framework for EU recovery: New financial market architecture at EU level Dealing with the impact on the real economy A global response to the financial crisis As part of the process of building up the new architecture of the EU financial markets, support was already voiced by all member states for the EC proposals for amendments to the Capital Requirements Directive. They cover such areas as risk management, possible prudential supervision framework for cross-border groups, crisis management and enhanced requirements to securitization for the purpose of further strengthening of the existing supervision framework and the risk management framework in the financial sector, in relation to the originate-and-distribute model. With regard to the convergence of supervisory practices in the EU, an agreement was made on a broad scope of issues, the ones of particular importance for the Bulgarian National Bank being as follows: By 2012 to put into effect uniform reporting formats across the whole EU in relation to the uniform requirements to the reporting data and terms. This is essential for ensuring effective and concerted supervision and for reducing the administrative burden of the groups; By mid-2009 at the latest, the mandates of the national supervision authorities should allow them to take the European dimension into consideration in performing their duties. Establishing a more efficient system for European prudential supervision of cross-border groups. With regard to the inclusion of this European dimension in the supervision authorities mandate by mid-2009 at the latest, the Bulgarian National Bank, has already taken jointly with the Ministry of Finance actions for the amendment of the Law on Credit Institutions. Specific wording reflecting the ECOFIN requirements was formulated, namely that in performing its prudential supervision functions the BNB shall recognize the possible impact of the actions pursued by it on the financial stability of other member states. The draft law on the amendments to the Law on Credit Institutions was submitted for approval to the Council of Ministers. Similar actions were taken along the same lines by the Financial Supervision Commission. Thus, Bulgaria is among the few countries that have already taken steps in accordance with the decisions of ECOFIN. On 26 November 2008, the Commission will propose a more detailed EU framework for restoring the confidence as part of the Lisbon Strategy for Growth and Employment. It will clearly indicate how the short-term strategy aiming to help overcome the negative effects of the crisis on the economy as a whole will be adapted to the medium- and long-term measures of the Lisbon Strategy. As in the current situation it is essential to monitor and adjust potential procyclical effects of the EU short-term strategy on the financial system and the economy, a European working group was established to make such analyses. The third aspect of EU activities is the participation in the international dialogue on the future of the global financial architecture and the recovery of confidence worldwide. At its session of 4 November ECOFIN came to an agreement on a document concerning the pending debate on the future of the international financial architecture. The document suggests the ideas which were the EU input at the summit of the heads of state and government held on 15 November in the US. The following principles were suggested: To guarantee that financial frameworks are not overly short-term oriented, which necessitates a change in the culture of management of the financial industry aimed at discouraging of excessive risk assumption. To increase the responsibility of all financial sector participants, particularly along the lending chain, specifying the role of banks in the debt securitization process; To work for pursuing and enhancing transparency in all financial market sections  financial institutions, financial products and evaluations , or jurisdictions; To ensure enhanced coordination among standard-setting bodies and between regulatory and prudential supervision frameworks with the common aim of facilitating financial stability, and in this relation it is of particular importance to eliminate regulatory arbitrage; It is better to project risks and more appropriate to manage risk based on the enhanced cooperation between institutions and bodies maintaining financial information; To give to the International Monetary Fund a key role in a new financial architecture. ____________ Mr. Tsvetan Manchev is a member of the BNB Governing Council and Deputy Governor in Charge of the Issue Department of the BNB. Title: Rule-based versus discretionary policy: Responses to the recent financial crisis
Subtitle:
RULE-BASED VERSUS DISCRETIONARY POLICY
RESPONSES TO THE RECENT FINANCIAL CRISIS
text: Speech by Mr. Tsvetan Manchev, BNB Deputy Governor, at the International Discussion Forum Resolving the Financial Markets Crisis, Brussels, 8 December 2008 RULE-BASED VERSUS DISCRETIONARY POLICY RESPONSES TO THE RECENT FINANCIAL CRISIS Ladies and Gentlemen, It is a pleasure and privilege for me to take part in this discussion forum devoted to the need of global response to the financial markets crisis. First of all I would like to thank the organizers from the European Finance Convention for the invitation and for the opportunity to share with such a renowned audience my personal views on the possible policy approaches to tackle the global financial crisis. The most characteristic feature of the international financial markets and the world economy after the failure of Lehman Brothers is the lack of confidence among market participants. We are not far from a world economic crisis. The mutual mistrust results in significant decrease of the number of deals and transactions not only in the financial sector but in the real economy. There is no doubt that in todays global world an internationally concerted policy response is needed to restore the confidence in the markets. Unfortunately, most of the policy measures up to now have been taken on national level and the rounds of various international fora have not been effective enough in restoring confidence as initially expected. The initial responses primarily addressed the financial sector issues and hence happen to be rather discretionary than rule-based. In the common case, the national governments and central banks are committed to inject more and more money in the markets but this is done without transparent and widely publicly accepted rules, and with even less clear and understandable for the general public analysis of their medium and long-term effects. As a result the markets remain insecure, because people feel insecure and exposed to a greater uncertainty. My personal conviction based on my, although very short, experience and knowledge of resolving crises of confidence, is that the rule-based approach is much more effective than the discretionary approach. Let me first clarify what I call the rules-based approach. This is an approach consisting of only a few simple principles, which can be easily understood by all economic agents and people concerned. All discretionary measures and changes in legislations and regulations should be taken after setting up of the principle rules for reaction and should not breach them. It is important to stress that in the implementation phase of the principles policymakers should avoid any misunderstanding on the part of the general public and the economic agents. Let me briefly tell you as an example our experience in resolving the wide-spread financial and economic crisis in Bulgaria at the end 1996 and the beginning of 1997. In the first half of 1990s, we had initial discretionary approach of the government and central bank to coping with the transition crisis from a centrally planed to a market economy. Even though the attempt was supported, guided and partially financed from the very beginning by the international institutions, people really did not understand the principles behind it, and how these principles affected their everyday life. This steadily exhausted the government and central bank resources, as well as peoples patience. In 1996 the crisis in Bulgaria started as an exchange rate crisis. The real reasons for the market depreciation of the lev were not only speculative attacks but the structural deficiencies in the financial and real sector together with wide-spread mistrust among economic agents. When the crisis developed into a loss of confidence in the financial system, the authorities continued with discretionary measures deciding to give financial support to some banks and to close some other banks without disclosure of any information of the grounds of their decision which appeared more or less arbitrary to the general public and the market participants. The confidence was not restored even after the decision of the government to cover with a state guarantee all deposits of the households and half of all deposits of corporations. The widespread lack of confidence in the reforms on the part of the general public and the markets in the very short run turned the steep economic slump into a deep social and economic crisis. I briefly refer to the Bulgarian case from mid-1990s because of several similarities with the recent developments in many economies both mature and emerging. There have been abrupt adjustments in the exchange rates, followed by severe banking problems or buyouts of failed institutions by governments, and finally a sharp decline in growth toward recession. Economic decline is accompanied by increasing uncertainty and lack of confidence in the authorities, which in some of the cases already asked for assistance from the international institutions. What proved to be a successful policy in Bulgaria was the implementation of very basic principles easy to understand by the general public. The Bulgarian political class was committed to: adopt the currency board  bring 1 euro, receive 1.95 leva and vice versa; refuse any financing from the central bank; reduce substantially the size of the government sector in the economy; balance the consolidated budget; and refuse the accumulation of new debts; liberalize immediately both the current and capital account transactions; and adopt European legislation. The continuity and consistency in implementing the above principles has been the most important factor for the recovery of public confidence, which not only increased the foreign investors interest, but also facilitated the implementation of socially painful structural reforms, privatisation, and finally returned the economy on the path of sustainable growth. Three consecutive governments since 1997, each appointed by a different parliamentary majority, have kept to these principles despite the external shocks. These governments cover the whole political spectrum  from Christian democrats through liberals to socialists. In other words, there is a consensus in society on the principles. During the current global financial crisis the above consensus is upheld also by the widely accepted and publicly supported goal following the accession in the EU to preserve the principles until the euro adoption. This makes the current macroeconomic policy of Bulgaria predictable and easily understandable for all interested stakeholders during the recent crisis. We will rely on them while adding one more principle - participation in and full compliance with the joint EU framework in response to the global financial crisis. I think that from this example one could derive an appropriate approach to the confidence crisis evidenced worldwide: to describe briefly and clearly for the general public the behavior at every level and to leave the general public and the market participants to judge purely subjectively what confidence it deserves. There is no doubt, the efforts of the G-20 leaders and those of the French presidency of the EU, of the Council and the European Commission for coordinated EU-wide response to the global financial crisis are a manifestation of the same rules-based approach to restore the confidence of the markets. In my view their success depends on the wide acceptance of the proposed rules and policy by the national authorities of the member-states, as well as by the general public and market participants from the EU. That is why we have to simplify the language and to stick to a few very clear messages easy to be understood by all citizens worldwide. At the international level, world leaders should principally explain clearly to the public their attitude to the process of future financial and capital liberalization. Second, they should set clear inter-temporal limits for the government deficits and debts. Third, the market participants selling hedging services should be prevented from selling fear at the same time. In this respect, I have in mind some banks, dealing with hedging of market risks and at the same time publishing forecasting or advice to global investors that could increase market participants perceptions for these risks. Rating agencies, selling ratings and consultations at the same time, are another example of conflict of interests in this respect. The leaders should principally explain in a manner understandable for the general public the way international institutions assess different monetary regimes and their sustainability in the long run, because recent vast debates on this issues brought further instability to the markets. We have several issues to make principally clear for the general public across the whole EU to restore the confidence. The most important among them, I believe, is the leaders attitude to the Stability and Growth Pact. We need a very clear message to the public that recent liquidity and rescue operations will be kept strictly within the current requirements of the SGP and the Commission would control their application in a timely and transparent manner with zero tolerance to the boarder line cases. Even a prospective discussion on the flexibility of the current SGP rules will seriously damage the fragile confidence among the economic agents. Another important topic is the future role and usage of the euro. The role of the ECB and the Commission in providing liquidity and restoring confidence in non-euro area countries should be much better communicated to the general public in these countries. Here domestic governments face a rather complicated situation. On the one hand, the sustainability aspect of the criteria for euro adoption is not clearly defined in the Treaty and the respective EU official documentation. The eligibility to have the euro as a national currency is far from being clear for the general public, but also for market participants in the EU. On the other hand, practical examples of the euro area participation provide further contradicting signals and additionally throw into confusion the general public and market participants. And thirdly, the banking and financial systems in non-euro area countries are dominated by euro-area banks. At the same time, in the last 2-3 months the enlargement has been far from the EU leaders focus, which is visible from the documentation. All these further erode the confidence in the authorities because in the eve of the crisis, the monetary and exchange rate regimes and the exchange rate dynamics are in the centre of public interest, as it is also seen from the Bulgarian case described earlier. As a result, we need the leaders clear and timely principal message on that. In conclusion, I would like to say that dealing with financial crises and setting rules for resolving them is quite a challenging and risky task. We all know that mistakes are possible and what is most important  their impact on the financial system could be disastrous. The story of resolving the financial crisis in Bulgaria, I told you about, in fact could not be described only as a success story, as the Bulgarian GDP dropped by more than 15% for two years. The appropriate rules-based policy response was determined after the devastating effect of the financial crisis to the Bulgarian economy. Today our task is to prevent such a development from happening on national and international level. One of the best ways to avoid mistakes in tackling with financial crises is not only to discus proposed measures, but without delay to opt for and stick to principles that are clear for the general public and to immediately communicate and implement them in plans, policies and regulations. I believe the forums like the present one, gathering together academics, politicians and professionals will also contribute to that. Thank you for your attention! ____________ Dr. Tsvetan Manchev is Deputy Governor and Member of the Governing Council of Bulgarian National Bank. He is an alternate of the BNB Governor in the General Council of the European Central Bank (ECB) and a member of the International Relations Committee (IRC) of the ECB. He is also a member of the Economic and Financial Committee (EFC) of the Council of the European Union. PAGE PAGE 4

Title: Speech at the Spring Meeting of the Association of Commercial Banks Plovdiv, May 5-6, 2006.
text: Speech of Mrs. Emilia Milanova, BNB Deputy Governor in charge of the Banking Supervision Department at the Spring Meeting of the Association of Commercial Banks Plovdiv, 5-6 May 2006 Ladies and Gentlemen, Dear Colleagues, The final conclusions from the past year 2005 for our country, the national economy and, particularly, the banking sector are positive. The final data show that in 2005 we managed to keep a high rate of economic growth in spite of the temporary decline in the third quarter caused somewhat by the political cycle, the sharp rise in fuel prices and the heavy floods aftermath. Now we have enough reasons to expect that this high growth rate would most probably continue into 2006. Employment and household incomes are on the rise, which, coupled with the increasing investment activities in the economy, creates a very good environment for the development of the banking sector, but it also hides some risks of overoptimisim and rapid accumulation of unduly high credit risk. The condition of the banking system can be considered very good In 2005 the balance sheet total of the banking sector rose by 32.2% against the previous year and reached BGN 32.9 billion. The reported profits amount to BGN 573 million, by 36.1% up on the year 2004. Despite the intense credit market competition and the reduced interest rates on loans, the return on assets (ROA) of the banking system remained almost unchanged as compared with the previous year  2%. The return on equity (ROE) improved, reaching 21.6% in 2005, with 20% a year back. For comparison, in the EU these indicators for 2004 are respectively 0.5% (ROA) and 12.2% (ROE). In 2005 bank managers did keep, as a whole, the quality of portfolios, and the share of standard loans slightly fell  from 92.9% at end-2004 to 92.3% at end-2005. Of course, when comparing the years 2004 and 2005, we should remember the changes in Regulation No.9 on the evaluation and classification of risk exposures and the allocation of provisions to cover impairment loss. The growth in classified household loans was one of the main reasons why the BNB increased the minimum provisions required for these loans. At the end of 2005 the capital adequacy of the banking system was 15.3%, against 16.6% at end-2004  a level which the central bank finds very comfortable in terms of financial stability. The BNB policy regarding the banking industry was predictable and discussed with the banking community Early last year the BNB took measures which aimed to further strengthen banks capabilities of managing credit and other major risks, to reinforce their capital base and stabilize the growth rates of the lending to the private sector at a moderate level that could be maintained in the medium term. In early November the BNB Governing Council made amendments to Regulation No.21 on the minimum required reserves which banks hold at the BNB and thus decided to keep the measures in place till the end of 2006; the improvement in the Regulation was intended to ensure the achievement of the benchmarks for the private sector credit growth rates for the years 2005 and 2006 set earlier in that year. Every one of us who is well familiar with the nature of banking and the role of prudential and administrative regulations knows that market participants will always try to observe the regulations in a way that will allow them to achieve the maximum market share and income. So, in early 2006 the BNB had to make more changes in Regulation No.21, extending the restrictions so as to cover certain types of bonds and reducing, from 70% to 50% of the housing value, the amount of mortgage loans that can be risk-weighted at 50% under BNB Regulation No.8 on banks capital adequacy. The final assessment of the effect of the BNB measures indicates that they brought the outcome expected for 2005  a considerable slow-down in the accumulated credit risk and in the risk to the stability of the banking system. Besides the slower growth rates of the lending to the private sector, banks reported a steady increase in their capital and in loans, i.e. the credit risk accumulation was supported by a parallel proportionate increase in the own funds unlike the previous year 2004 when loans were increasing 10 times as fast as the capital. The measures eased the aggressive competitive environment resultant from the fight for a market share which did not always include all risk factors in the loan price and was producing lower and lower credit standards. The extended effect of the additional required reserves till end-2006, together with the continuous tightening of this Regulation and the overall supervisory policy, and the large demand for credit resources for investment and consumption purposes, made banks actively seek ways of lending outside their balance sheets. For the last two months we have seen that considerable loan portfolios are being taken out of banks balance sheets. Although such a development was expected and could be considered acceptable if it would lead to an efficient credit risk transfer and reduction, the central bank is not going to encourage it on a massive basis. Initially, the restrictive measures on credit growth rates were intended to reduce the risk to the banking system arising from the very fast pace of credit risk accumulation in banks balance sheets. Many economists intuitively looked for and are still looking for a direct cause-and-effect link between the credit growth rate and the BoP current account dynamics. They follow the logic that the increasing bank intermediation would increase the opportunities for consumption and investment which, together with free trade and the slowly responding domestic supply, would generate external imbalances. This way of thinking sounds quite sensible but it should not lead, and the BNB policy clearly states this, to the definition of the simple rule that the BoP dynamics can be directly controlled by controlling credit growth rates. In the environment we work in  a small and very open economy with a fully liberalized BoP capital account where the presence of foreign banks is significant and there are considerable capital inflows - the high credit growth rates are a reflection of these inflows of capital. I already mentioned that commercial banks are trying to provide lending outside their balance sheets, and this, together with Bulgarias forthcoming accession to the EU and the adoption of the single passport policy, raises to the BNB the question as to what extent the current measures would be efficient and would help for reducing the risk in the banking system. As I said, it is very difficult, if not impossible, in the environment of the Bulgarian economy to draw a direct and indisputable connection between the dynamics of banking lending and the countrys external position and the overall dynamics of economic activities, nevertheless the decision on the future of the current restrictive measures would also more or less reflect the development of the countrys external position, the fiscal policy and the indebtedness of households and enterprises, and the relevant risks to the financial stability in Bulgaria. In a very open economy, like the Bulgarian economy, the discussion on the possible future policy should definitely take account of the development of the international economy and interest rates (mainly in the eurozone because of the strong link between the Bulgarian interest rates and those in the eurozone). Those who keep an eye on the development of the eurozone economy know that after a long period of very low interest rates (there have not been such low rates in Germany since Bismarcks time) the ECB began increasing them, and the pace of this increase would depend on the condition of the European economy. Due to the strong relation between the interest rates in BGN and in Euro resultant from the currency board arrangement and to the large share of the Euro in the structure of loans, this interest rate increase in Europe would inevitably affect the credit price in Bulgaria. This process is already there for the floating rate loans (though it can hardly be seen in the interest rate statistics as the data reflect the rates on new loans). The increase in interest rates would show to what extent the balance sheets of borrowers (households and companies) are sensitive to this increase. Market developments would also strongly influence the BNBs decision about the measures constraining credit growth rates. Unfortunately, at this moment I could not give, on behalf of the BNB, a definite answer to the question about the future of the credit restrictions. The results of these measures, what we see happening in banks balance sheets and outside their balance sheets, our assessment of the development of the national economy and the governments fiscal policy, and the developments in external markets  all these things will be the basis of our decision on whether we would keep the measures in place increasing their intensity or we would start gradually removing them. Our preliminary analyses show that at this stage it is a bit more likely that we would decide to gradually remove the measures, but no compromise will be made with the financial and macroeconomic stability in the country. Banks should pay special attention to their preparations for the new capital requirements known as Basel II. We had the impression that banks ignored the first signal that the central bank sent to them to draw their attention and suggest that we would most likely introduce the new capital framework in a more stringent and more conservative version, and this would not initially bring the expected advantages for retail exposures (this approach would fully agree with the BNBs current policy and should not be a surprise to the banking community). Consequently, all banks should accurately evaluate what their capital adequacy will be after 1 January 2007 and, eventually, the required capital support. The efforts in this direction require that even now the credit growth should move within the existing capital capacity and reserves. Banks should also be ready for a substantial change in the rules and forms for financial and capital reporting that will be made from the beginning of next year. Over the second half of the year the BNB is going to put a lot of effort in this direction, engaging the commercial banks as well. The competition will be getting more and more intense and will increase the number and quality of the services offered. This competition that will become more severe with the approaching Bulgarias membership in the EU and the introduction of the single passport will inevitably deepen the consolidation process in the banking system. There is no doubt that the BNBs very conservative policy of licensing new banks strongly supported the process of commercial banks attracting strategic partners. It is another matter altogether who and to what extent managed to take advantage of this policy. What is coming up before 2007 By the end of this year the BNB and the Government will have to carry out the technical preparations, so that after Bulgarias accession to the EU we could very quickly join the Exchange Rate Mechanism II as well, keeping the currency board in place. This would allow us to move on to joining the eurozone by 2010. An essential framework for the banking sector will be the new law on credit institutions. The draft law has been approved by the Council of Ministers and will be presented for discussions and adoption to the National Assembly. One of the new points in this law is the introduction of the so-called single passport and the term credit institution which will include not only banks but also E-money companies. The draft of the new regulation on capital adequacy is well under way. During the second quarter of 2006 we are going to send this draft to banks for discussions and it will be adopted immediately after the adoption of the new banking law. This regulation will define the requirements and the procedure for determining capital adequacy in accordance with the New Capital Accord (Basel II). By 5 June 2006 we are going to finish the project for the introduction of the international bank account format (IBAN) in the national banking system, which format corresponds to the format used by the EU countries. The introduction of the IBAN standard is a huge project involving the BNB, the Association of Commercial Banks, all commercial banks, the system operators, the National Social Security Institute, and the Ministry of Finance. The successful and timely implementation of this project depends on the mobilization of financial and human resources by all commercial banks, system operators, and the BNB. This year, in the cash circulation area, the BNB has started to implement the adopted strategy for ensuring the required level of purity, safety and efficiency of the issue and cash operations on the territory of the country. The new BNB Regulation No.18 on the control over the quality of banknotes and coins in circulation describes the general framework for the cash circulation organization which fully complies with the ECB standards. Now commercial banks and the BNB need to find a solution to the cash circulation organization that would be efficient for the banking community and the entire society alike. Commercial banks will have to express, as soon as possible, their firm commitment to this joint project with the BNB. Apart from the joint efforts that we all are making together, the BNB Governing Council made a decision on the establishment of a modern cash centre. After 2008 this cash centre will be the only place where the BNB will be offering the free cash services regulated by the ECB. All other services will be offered on a market principle. Ladies and Gentlemen, thank you for your attention. PAGE PAGE 4

Title: Financial progress and prospects
Subtitle: Speech by Mr Ivan Iskrov, Governor of the Bulgarian National Bank, at the Sixth Business Roundtable with the Government of Bulgaria, Sofia, 21 March 2006.
text: Ivan Iskrov: Financial progress and prospects Speech by Mr Ivan Iskrov, Governor of the Bulgarian National Bank, at the Sixth Business Roundtable with the Government of Bulgaria, Sofia, 21 March 2006. * * * Dear Minister Oresharski, Ladies and gentlemen, It is a pleasure for me to participate together with the Minister of Finance in this panel event dedicated to the financial development and prospects of this countrys economy. Based on the statutory division of labour between the Central Bank Governor and the Finance Minister on the one hand, and between the Central Bank and the Government on the other, in my speech I will deal mainly with the issues relating to the countrys external position, the development of bank lending and inflation, and the impact these variables have on the BNBs policy. I would like to immediately underscore that these issues cannot be discussed, outside the context of economic growth prospects, the accession of our country to the EU, and the trends of development in world economy. For better understanding of Bulgarian economy in the recent years, several global trends influencing significantly the development of our economy should be highlighted. Firstly, the dominance of the principle of free trade and the liberalization of capital movement, combined with the investors increasing propensity to hold assets issued by third country residents, brought about the on-going growth of international trade and exchange of capital. In such an environment, where domestic demand is no longer restricted within the amount of the current national income, the current account deficits are not always an indicator of fundamental imbalances. As has been emphasized by an increasing number of scientists, central bankers, and finance ministers, the imbalanced external accounts of individual countries have become rather the rule than an exception (A. Greenspan, M. King). In addition, empirical research, as well as the European institutions (European Central Bank, European Commission) point out that the process of convergence is inevitably accompanied by current account deficits. Secondly, the decrease in the long-term interest rates in the developed economies, and the accompanying reduction in the risk premiums in the developing economies, resulted in investors pursuit of higher yield in the developing markets. There are multiple factors determining these developments, on which I would not focus today. What should be underscored is that these global trends channel significant in amount capital flows to the developing economies. Irrespective of the monetary policy regime (fixed or floating exchange rate), the absorption of larger capital inflows inevitably puts the monetary authorities to trial. To illustrate the large scale of this process, I will give Bulgaria as an example, where the capital inflow (in the form of direct investment and debt) was 1.5% of GDP in 1998, and in the recent two years it approximates 15% of GDP. Thirdly, the significant and long-lasting growth since 2003 in the prices of oil and other energy resources considerably contributed to the international imbalances, and more particularly to Bulgarias current account deficit. This process accounted for the considerable growth of the expenditures for imports of energy resources incurred by the importer countries, and for the enormous cash flows channeled to the exporting countries. For Bulgaria, these developments in energy resource prices resulted in an increase in the costs of import of such products from EUR 1.7 billion in 2002 (the year after which the process of sustainable oil price increase started) to almost EUR 3.0 billion in 2005. This trend was very strongly manifested in the past year, when the countrys expenditures for energy resource imports grew by 52% against 2004. These three global trends, in combination with the approaching full-fledged EU membership of our country, produce a unique environment that the Bulgarian economy has never before faced. This makes the analysis of the processes and economic policy decisionmaking very complex and difficult. As I have already noted, in the recent several years, enormous volumes of capital were channeled into the country, the banking system acting as the natural intermediary for the effective distribution of these resources. This is not surprising at all, given the successfully implemented privatization of the banking sector in Bulgaria. At present, over 80% of the Bulgarian banking sector is owned by foreign investors, the majority of which are from euro area countries. As a consequence of strong competition and the 22/2006 1 good investment prospects, the growth rate of lending to the private sector accelerated to levels of 48.6% at year end- 2004. The ratio of banking credit to GDP increased from 12.1% in 1999 to 45.0% at the end of 2005. Of course, this dynamics reflected to a great extent the process of convergence of the countrys economy, and in particular the degree of financial intermediation, to the levels evidenced in EU Member States (112% of GDP). At the same time, the central bank cannot help asking the question to what extent the quick growth of bank credit may result in potential risks for the financial and macroeconomic stability in the country. The BNB was to determine the moment, after which the convergence grows into a self-propelled process of struggling for a market share. Such a transition entails considerable risks, as it does not lead to sustainable growth rates of both financial intermediation and economic activity and employment. Therefore, since the beginning of 2004, the BNB started a process of phasing in measures (primarily prudential and administrative) aimed at slowing down bank credit growth to a sustainable level, which would not put to risk the stability of the economy. Data indicate the central banks policy resulted in a change in commercial banks behaviour and reduced the growth of bank lending to 32.4% at the end of 2005. In the current year, while sustaining the effect of already implemented measures, we expect banking credit to grow with a rate below or near 20%. As I mentioned earlier, the dynamics of banking intermediation in the country cannot be contemplated in isolation from the process of free movement of capital and the accompanying dynamics of the balance of payments current account. Intuitively, many economists tend to seek direct cause and effect relation between bank credit growth and the current account dynamics. They rely on the logic that the growth of banking intermediation increases the possibilities for consumption and investment, which combined with the existence of free trade and the slower response of domestic supply leads to the accumulation of external imbalances. Such reasoning is to a great extent rational, but it should not lead, as is clearly manifested in the BNBs policy, to defining the simple rule that the balance of payments dynamics can be directly controlled through controlling the banking credit rates of growth. This clarification allows me to turn to the next issue I would like to discuss, namely the dynamics of the countrys external position. The stable macroeconomic environment in Bulgaria, plus the sustainably high rates of economic growth and the prospects for its membership in the EU brought in an increasing amount of investments. Their share in the GDP in the first three quarters of 2005 increased to 26.6%, which marks the highest level reached since the beginning of economic reforms in the country. The growth of investments and the concomitant improvement of employment, increase both the current incomes of households, and their expected future incomes, which is associated with increased consumption and decrease in the savings in the economy. As a consequence of these processes, the gap of the balance of payments current account widened to levels over 5% of GDP in 2003 and 2004, and further expanded to 11.9% as of end-2005. From the perspective of current account immediate dynamics, each economy faces the question if the current level of deficit or surplus is determined by structural factors, i.e. it is close to a balanced level, which can be maintained within a medium-term, or it is the consequence of unsustainable trends and one-off factors. Both groups of factors played an important role in the development of the current account deficit in 2005. First of all, the above-mentioned growth of investments was accompanied by considerable imports of investment goods. In 2005, the imports of this group of goods grew by 31.2%, while their share in the total structure of imports reached up to 28%. This trend was associated with a slow-down in the growth of imports of non-energy raw materials and consumer goods. In the current year, we expect the rate of import of investment goods to remain high, given the rapid pace of technological innovation of the economy, which is mainly accounted for by the forthcoming EU membership of our country. Multiple one-off factors had significant effect in the past year, which include the abrupt increase in the prices and volumes of oil imports, and the sweeping floods, which troubled our exports in the third quarter of the year. This year, the current account deficit is expected to drop below 11 % of GDP, mainly due to the slowed down growth of imports, and the recovery of exports growth, which has been evidenced since the last quarter of the previous year and the beginning of 2006. In January, the exports of goods increased by 27.5% on annual basis, and exports, excluding energy goods, increased by 17%. The continuing implementation of the reforms in the labour market and education, and the improvement of the business environment, including a significant improvement in the operation of the judiciary, are of key importance for maintaining competitive advantages and ensuring sustainability of the countrys external position, as well as preserving the interrelation between salary growth and productivity of labour. As we are well aware, the revenues from tourist services influence considerably the countrys balance of payments (15% of the countrys exports of goods and services in 2 22/2006 2005), which necessitates the very fast elimination of all existing obstacles to the development of this industry. Before I conclude my presentation, I would like to focus on inflation dynamics. At first sight, this variable does not seem to be such a great challenge for us, compared to the issues discussed above. Looking at the prospects and having in mind the countrys strategy for expeditious accession to the euro area, however, this is a macroeconomic variable which faces the country with the greatest challenges. The inflation criterion, as defined in the Maastricht Treaty (this is not the place to deal with the issue how good this definition is), is very strict and requires a purposeful policy going beyond the monetary and fiscal policies. In Bulgarias case, under the currency regime of fixed exchange rate and extremely conservative fiscal policy, untapped prospects should be sought in encouraging competition and improving the business climate, thus ensuring to the economy the flexibility to respond to exogenous changes (including with regard to the prices of raw materials) and enabling supply to react more promptly to increases in demand (both domestic and external). In the past year, inflation reached 6.5 % under the strong proinflationary impact of the increase in the prices of energy resources (direct contribution of 1.0 % in the overall price increase).In addition, the largescale floods resulted in an unexpected increase in foodstuff prices (contribution of 2.6 % in the overall price increase). This year, inflation is expected to decline to 6.0%. The slow process of decreasing inflation is mainly determined by the harmonization of indirect taxes with the minimum levels in the EU, pursued early in the year. As the change in indirect taxes and administered prices has a direct effect on domestic inflation, their catching-up adjustment should be effected before the years during which they will be used as basis for evaluation of compliance with the Maastricht criteria  i.e. before 2008. From this perspective, earlier timing of harmonization of some excise taxes is a step to facilitate significantly the performance on the inflation criterion, as it would eliminate the proinflationary impact of an increase in these taxes in the years in which such evaluation will be made. In conclusion, I would like to sum up that, in the light of the rapid change in the structure of our economy, the stable macroeconomic policy pursued by the Government and the BNB, and the prospects for EU membership, the concerns, expressed in the leaflet for this Conference, of possible overheating of the economy and the risks this entails for its stability, seem rather exaggerated. The countrys external imbalance financed by capital inflows is more of a signal of stability, credibility and potential for development of our economy. Of course, the economic policy makers are not and may not be complaisant. The challenges Bulgarian economy is facing are well recognized, and there is the will to take all the necessary measures to preserve the stability and growth in the economy. Ladies and gentlemen, thank you for your attention. 22/2006 3

Title: Bulgaria and the Francophonian movement
Subtitle: Speech by Mr Ivan Iskrov, Governor of the Bulgarian National Bank, at the opening of the 13th Annual Meeting of the Governors of the Central Banks from the Francophonian countries, Sofia, 12 May 2006.
text: Ivan Iskrov: Bulgaria and the Francophonian movement Speech by Mr Ivan Iskrov, Governor of the Bulgarian National Bank, at the opening of the 13th Annual Meeting of the Governors of the Central Banks from the Francophonian countries, Sofia, 12 May 2006. * * * Dear Governors, Dear Ladies and Gentlemen, Welcome to Bulgaria, one of the oldest countries in Europe! It is a pleasure and honour for me to open the 13th Meeting of the Governors of the Central Banks from the Francophonian countries. I am also very much flattered by the fact that this meeting is for the first time held in a country from Central and Eastern Europe and it is precisely the Bulgarian National Bank's privilege to host such an event. This is also the year of the centennial anniversary of the birth of Leopold Cedar Senghor - the founder of the Intergovernmental Francophone Agency and the conceptual father of the Francophone Movement (La Francophonie). Tomorrow, the conceptual father of our gatherings and ECB honourable President, Jean-Claude Trichet, will join us. The fact that the BNB hosts this meeting is not only the result of the formal acceptance of Bulgaria to the Francophonian community in the early 90-ies of the past century. The French language and culture made their way into the country already in the first half of the XIX century when we were still part of the Ottoman empire. The channels of this penetration were similar to those observable today  through Bulgarians studying in Belgium, France and Switzerland, and through trading in goods. These initial contacts had a very strong impact on the subsequent formation of the modern Bulgarian State and its institutions. The Bulgarian National Bank, being the first public institution established after the restoration of the independent Bulgarian State, was strongly influenced by the economic and cultural relations with the Francophonian world already established. On the day of founding of the BNB on January 25, 1879, its capital was subscribed in French Francs. The subsequent reforms of the Central Bank, the Ministry of Finance and the financial system in the country drew on the experience of Belgium and Switzerland, as well as on the knowledge and expertise of a great number of French advisors. The Francophonian movement in the period after the restoration of the Bulgarian State until the beginning of the World War II was further strengthened and expanded by the great number of Bulgarians who studied in Belgium, France and Switzerland. Especially telling of the scale of this process is the number of the senior managing officers in the area of finance and banking who graduated in countries from the Francophonian world. Of the sixteen Governors of the Bulgarian National Bank who managed it during the period from its foundation to the Second World War, eight received their higher education in economics, political science and law in Belgium, France and Switzerland, or specialised there. In the same period, thirty-two people held at different times the position of Minister of Finance, of whom nineteen graduated or specialised in these countries. Today, many Bulgarians continue studying the French language and culture in our schools or receive their education in Francophonian countries. They are part of the 175-million French-speaking community and in addition to the common language they are part of a common culture, which extends to all spheres of our life. I am proud that part of these people work in the Bulgarian National Bank and contribute a lot to the success of our institution. The increased economic and financial interrelatedness and interdependence of the countries call for ever-greater co-ordination of the economic and financial policies of the individual governments. The establishment in the 90-ies of the past century of the principles of free movement of goods and capital increased the interdependence of the financial systems across countries, so that financial stability is no longer a national but a global issue. The significant participation of foreign capital in the banking system of a country and the massive movement of capital, largely contributing to the formation of serious imbalances, changes significantly the understanding of systemic risk and the approaches to its assessment. The above process of interrelatedness of the banking systems of individual countries necessitated the adoption of new principles of surveillance over the banking sector, as well as analysis and control of the risks arising from the ever-increasing interrelatedness between the banking sector and the other segments of the financial market. The implementation of Basel II will pose a challenge to the entire 42/2006 1 financial community, while for the newly emerging economies this process will be a serious test since their banking systems are very much open. The discussion of the common supervisory framework also brings forward the question as to what extent the high rates of growth of credit for the private sector, globally, and in many of the dynamically developing countries, in particular, poses a risk to financial stability and how much supervisory policy could be used as a tool for solving this problem. The process of financial sector globalisation, which I already mentioned, raised for many countries the issue of choosing between either following a national monetary policy or joining a monetary union and carrying monetary policy to a supranational level. The experience of a successful realisation of the Economic and Monetary Union in Europe, as well as the experience of the countries from the area of the Frank are a good practical example for all of us about the potential advantages and challenges associated with a country's participation in a monetary union. Taking monetary policy to a supranational level is inevitably related to providing greater independence for the national central banks and delegating certain powers at a supranational level. In the democratic world, the independence of conducting policy on the part of central banks is inseparably linked to the higher degree of their transparency and reporting. Of course, striking the right balance between these three principles is a process related to the economic and political traditions of individual countries. The issues I touched upon are important for the operation of any modern central bank. Today, I am particularly happy with the fact that these issues will be discussed within the club of the Francophonian central banks, where we have a very broad set of traditions, experience and knowledge. I believe that we are going to have a useful and fruitful discussion. Thank you for your attention! 2 42/2006

Title: Bulgarian National Bank - independence, predictability and transparency
Subtitle: Speech by Mr Ivan Iskrov, Governor of the Bulgarian National Bank, before the 41st National Assembly of the Republic of Bulgaria on the occasion of his election for a second term of office, Sofia, 26 August 2009.
text: Ivan Iskrov: Bulgarian National Bank  independence, predictability and transparency Speech by Mr Ivan Iskrov, Governor of the Bulgarian National Bank, before the 41st National Assembly of the Republic of Bulgaria on the occasion of his election for a second term of office, Sofia, 26 August 2009. * * * Ms. Speaker, Ladies and Gentlemen MPs, Allow me first and foremost to thank you for the enormous trust and the strong support you just now gave to the Central Bank and its Governor, Ivan Iskrov. I dont know of any head of any public institution that has so far enjoyed such a vast parliamentary vote of confidence with the support of 195 MPs. This result exceeds the 165 votes in support of my nomination in the previous 40th National Assembly. When a week ago I shared with the person closest to me that I had decided to use the parliamentary case of Mr. Nenovsky to submit myself to a confidence vote by the 41st National Assembly, I heard the following: Isn't this step rather too risky, besides the Prime Minister publicly announced that he did not approve of the procedure but he respects the BNB as an institution, and highly values you as a governor and wishes you to continue on the post?" I replied that no one could predict the possible deliberations and how the 240 MPs would vote, but that I was nonetheless obliged to ask for their confidence. Or else on 9th October this year I leave! Because, Ladies and Gentlemen, as I have repeatedly shared with my colleagues at the Bank, when requiring the tasks to be performed with 100% precision, rather than in a slapdash manner, we in the central bank have an asset even more valuable than its international reserves. This key asset is the reputation of the BNB and of each of its employees. I promised to your colleagues of the 39th National Assembly that I would never take part in fruitless discussions, neither would I refute any possible silly allegations of dishonourable people or of unqualified know-it-all experts. The people around me, however, know how painful it was for me to bear any stupidity or slander, not for my own credibility but for the confidence the Bulgarian society should have in our National Bank. The BNB is de jure and de facto the most independent public institution; it owes its independence to you  the elected representatives of the people, and reports only and solely to you, to the Bulgarian National Assembly. Therefore I felt I needed to have again assurance of your confidence after such a long and fierce pre-election competition. Dear Ladies and Gentlemen MPs, Only two months ago in this hall I reiterated, and I would like now to reconfirm, the three key principles I have abided by since 2003, for which I will try hard to be remembered as characterizing my work at the central bank  independence, predictability and transparency. Throughout my whole first term of office I followed these principles, and today I would like again to state that my second term of office will be governed by the same principles. I have permitted no political interference in the activities of the Bank, which is a fundamental principle underlying the Law on the BNB and the Treaty on the accession of Bulgaria to the EU. I will not allow any political meddling in the work of the BNB in my next term of office. I highly appreciate the first words of the newly elected Speaker of the 41st National Assembly at our first meeting: Mr. Iskrov, we are well aware of the Law on the BNB, of BNBs key role for the financial stability in the country, and in spite of our disagreement with the early timing of your reelection, no one questions the independence of the central bank. This is a question of principle, on which there is no argument. These were Ms. Tsachevas first words, and I am really grateful to her for them. 104/2009 1 Independence should certainly not be an excuse for idleness or work not done. I would emphasise once again, just as I have so far worked with two Bulgarian Governments and all legitimate political parties and their representatives regardless of the political spectrum they belong to, so they too can count on BNBs expert advice and support in the future. Every one of you is welcome to the Central Bank to discuss any issues as long as this is in the interest of the stability of our country, and the banking system in particular. Dear Ladies and Gentlemen, finally and in the context of everything said by me and by the speakers before me during this debate, I believe that now the most important thing as regards the country macroeconomic and financial policy is preserving stability and ensuring predictability; predictability, because the global financial and economic crisis has shown that countries, which follow stability-oriented and consistent macroeconomic policies are going less painfully through this difficult for all countries period. The BNBs role is to secure the countrys price and financial stability and the soundness of our strictly regulated banking system. Over the next six years the focus of my work will be on preserving and maintaining the macroeconomic stability in the country by keeping the fixed exchange rate and the currency board arrangement. The currency board will continue as the foundations underlying the stability and economic growth in Bulgaria. Second comes preserving and maintaining the stability of the banking system. Over the last two years, we have been witnessing globally the catastrophic consequences of poorly regulated and supervised banking and financial institutions. Bulgaria too was affected, but unlike some other countries it stayed outside the centre of the storm due to the consistently implemented conservative model of licensing policy, supervision and regulation of the banking sector. Over the next years, supervision and regulation within EU will change and improve significantly with the ECB and NCBs playing an important role. Being part of ESCB, BNB is going to take an active part in the process. Third, the next six years will be crucial to accomplishing one of the countrys major commitments stemming from the EU accession Treaty, namely the adoption of the euro as a national currency. The preparation for this has been a priority for the BNB over the past six years with a significant part of the work in legal, technical and operational terms having already been completed. This task will continue as a major priority in the next six years. Adopting the singe currency by an EU member state is not and cannot be a unilateral decision. In addition to fulfilling the Maastricht criteria, we should also be able to convince all our EU partners of our readiness and capacity to be part of the euro area. This is why the BNB and its Governor need the utmost confidence; this is why I resigned to make it easiest for the Parliament to take a decision. In conclusion, demonstrating effectively compliance with the principle of predictability, I am going to submit to the Office of the Speaker of the National Assembly a nomination for the election of a Deputy Governor in charge of the Issue Department as this Deputy Governors term of office expires on October 22. I appeal for this decision to be made this week, if possible, for the sake of assuaging all concerns regarding BNB's governance. Ladies and Gentlemen, thank you very much for the confidence Ive been given. Thank you for your attention. 2 104/2009

Title: Strengthening the regulatory and supervisory capacity of the financial regulators
Subtitle: Opening remarks by Mr Ivan Iskrov, Governor of the Bulgarian National Bank, at the off. opening ceremony of the Twinning Project "Strengthening the Regulatory & Supervisory Capacity of the Financial Regulators", Podgorica, Montenegro, 15 December 2009.
